_childDocuments_.review: I wish there were an in-between option for leaving reviews on Steam.To start, I was thrilled to see a sequel. Aside from some jank platforming, I was happy with Blasphemous 1 and was keen to see where this one would go. I'll start with the positives.The artwork is phenomenal. Whoever designed the art for the different areas is fantastic. I prefer the art of this game to the first one. The controls also seem more stable, as I had no problem with the platforming outside of human error. The music is also perfect, just as good as the first game. It was also fun seeing some familiar enemies tied into the various new enemies in the game. There's also a lot of fun exploration and abilities to unlock. We have the choice of three new weapons that are fun to use. On top of that, I like the addition of the alter-pieces. That said, that's really where my praise ends.Like the first game, the first enemy we encounter is a boss fight. The boss is really cool and sets up what kind of game this will be. However, the boss feels disconnected from the story, as it doesn't connect with the story. The bosses also have a really bad problem with them either being easy, albeit tricky at times, or insufferably difficult. Odon is a prime example of this. With several attacks, a large arena, minion summoning, and the fact that you can't dash through water, of all things, it just really put a damper on my mood with this game overall. The final boss, Eviterno, has a similar problem, but it would be fine if you could skip the dialogue. EVERY other boss in the game skips the dialogue and goes right into the fight, but for whatever reason, the devs decided not to make this the case here. The bosses are all right, but one does stand out to me. Afilaor was genuinely creepy, and I loved the overall vibe.Despite the game being a lot more full of life, character interactions are rather bland. They just say who they are and offer one service for another. The sculptor effs off to die, I guess; the merchant just disappears, and the forgotten tribute people just vanish as well. This last one, in particular, sucks because I would have loved to see more lore surrounding them. Two NPCs die, lol, but they had some fun dialogue. On top of this, the execution animations are all the same, whereas, in the first game, each enemy had unique animations. This would take a while to create, but it feels like it could be more varied. There's also a weird glitch with the prayers and chants; despite having all of them, there are several empty slots. It might mean DLC is coming, but I need clarification.The story also feels rather barebones, almost copying the events of the first one. Ultimately, I like this game, which is why I recommend it. I wish there was more to it at the end of the day.

_childDocuments_.review: It's... ok. It's still a decent metroidvania, but not as good as the first I feel overall. Combat's a bit less ballanced, it's a LOT buggier, and the story, world, exploration, etc... are all a bit... simpler and less enjoyable. The new art for cinematics and stuff I'm not as much of a fan of as the old stuff, and overall, it just came off as a bit more... meh... Doesn't have the strong impresion the first had.First thing of note, it's easier. Noticeably easier overall, both the jumping/platforming puzzles, and the enemies and the boss fights. It's, shorter feeling, less hidden, simpler story, etc... again. Still some plenty confusing parts to the story, but even delving into it with more time and stuff, it's not as interesting as the first, both because the first was the introduction to a new story/setting so naturally it was more unique then, but also just in complexity and interesting points on their own.For the most part, the core combat is fairly good. Though... use the big mace, veste something, as your main weapon, or the big sword. Mace is best imo, but the daggers/dual blades... the lack of vertical reach/arcing on those attacks is really annoying especially against certain enemy types. For puzles you swap weapon and use them on different things, it's ok, but again never too complex. And the fighting itself is mostly ok feeling. If again, a bit easy.Most bosses I beat first or second try, only a few went beyond three tries. Unforunately the one truly... good, challenging fight, the second to last boss... is the most frusterating moment in the game, as they have a pair of bolted on unskippable slow cutscenes that make it feel just horrible to start that fight, or switch to phase 2. So being the only fight that you'll actually die on and have to learn some complex attack patterns on an enemy that can actually kill/hurt you fairly badly with majorly varied movesets between phases... ya, you'll keep dying second phase as that's the hard one, but then everytime you come back... slow annoying cutscene, guy talks... slowly... then it just hangs and waits for awhile, nothing happening, before finally letting you get control of your character. The phase 2, you stand back and let him talk, get better armed, and he says a line... long wait... a second line... long wait... then phase enviornment transition... it's ok the first time, but when you experiencce it ten or twenty or more times...  while learning his phase 2 rules of teleporting around and cutting you up in two or three hits, finding the few safe times to heal or attack... oh ya, it makes this fight go from a possibly good and fun one, arguably the best mechanicly, to the worst feeling as the player experience of going through that evertime you start it is just horrible!Final boss at least lets you skip through his text after the first time, as did some others keeping it shorter. Final boss, ok fight... but think it only took three tries to win? Second attempt for alternate ending was identical fight, beat it first time then. So ya... only one really memorable feeling boss fight, but it was the worst part of the game because of simple issues on user experience as its like the game is trying to waste my time and frustrate me.I will say, in the end... it didn't leave a particularly strong impression on me overall, so not the best of signs for a metroidvania or game in general. So if you like them, and you liked the first game, then sure try this if on sale, or you just don't have any other to play now... but there's plenty of other ones out there that I'd put above trying this one out first, as while again, it's ok... it's just not great or the most memorable in any real way. The exploration/discovery felt lacking, the art wasn't quite as good for story or other things, story was... a bit more meh... gameplay wasn't as challenging or interesting, if still somewhat fun in general. So ya, it's just ok feeling for now.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: Blasphemous 2 is a decent metroidvania, that suffers only when directly compared to its supremely excellent predecessor. writing this review is painful for me. Blasphemous 1 (B1) is one of my all time favorite games, but having finished number 2, I cannot recommend the sequel with the same level of enthusiasm. Its still a decently solid metroidvania, but it lacks the thorns that made the first game so special. I am grateful for the hard work the team put into this project, but truly wish more resources could have been devoted to the development of the story, the characters, and art direction.Listing positives first: Blasphemous 2 features some fun mobility puzzles that utilize its game mechanics well. The game remains somewhat difficult throughout, never allowing the player to let their guard down completely. There are several boss fights that force the player to slow down and react rather than win through ruthless aggression, and it was rewarding learning their patterns.  The map is populated with enough obstacles to keep you revisiting previously completed sections, but the game gives you enough fast travel options to keep it from becoming tedious. the music is quality, and the pixel art and most animations are beautiful at any resolution. The negatives: the game is still fairly glitchy- I required several hard resets after being stuck in  looping animations, some achievements are currently broken, I glitched into a room in a way that ruined a quest outcome, and somehow became invincible during a boss fight. some deaths just feel unfair due to a lack of invincibility frames and knock back. the punishment is never rage quit worthy but it can kill the fun for a bit.The wildly subjective:now onto the difficult part. I've attempted to avoid spoilers but will be discussing my thoughts on the entire game and its mechanics. This is all said with love and through the lens of someone who is a fan of the franchise, and is grateful to have a Blasphemous 2, but feels like opportunities were missed.The World of Blasphemous 1 was clearly twisted and tragic. Even with limited explicit exposition we are informed of everything we needed to know about the results of the miracle. we witness the evolving horror of every character as we progress their story lines, often becoming sympathetic to the suffering we are causing them. we engage with reoccurring adversaries on their own pilgrimages. By the end of the game we feel closure. we cant possibly comprehend everything we've seen, but we are given enough to feel like we probably helped save the world and made a friend along the way.Blasphemous 2 lacks or dilutes many of these elements. The plot is less defined. The who and why left too vague to relate to. we enter into a world that we are told needs our help, but little is done to show it. the main town seems to be prospering, there is an abundance of grand architecture, and while people seem downtrodden and meandering, its a far cry from the abject destitution of the first game. no one seems particularity bothered by the looming heart in the sky.Despite having a more cohesive aesthetic and apparent relation to each other, your adversaries in this game are given no personality. save for one meaningless encounter, you never cross their paths before killing them, you are never reminded of their existence, and there is no buildup to their confrontations, . There is clearly meant to be some implied relationship between you and these characters, but very little if anything is done in game to flesh this out or explain why they are there. We never see the dynamic between themselves. The frustrating aspect is, if they were not made to clearly have some implied relationship with the penitent one, then it would be less of a factor. The monstrous bosses of B1 didn't need additional information because they were of the Miracle's world, not your own.  the NPCs are aslo given uneven attention with some story lines having no clear resolution. often this could be solved with additional dialogue. realizing a quest is over only because an achievement tells you as much, is not strong story telling. quests also just somehow felt less engaging than in B1. Artistically, Blasphemous 1 (pre DLC) felt like one person's cohesive vision. The art was consistent across characters, environments, bosses, and cut-scenes. At times some animations appeared uncanny or choppy, but that nuance lends itself to the general unease of the experience and adds character.The choice to continue with the hand drawn cut scenes of a style inconsistent to the rest of the project greatly mars the visual experience of the sequel. Suddenly transitioning from dark, detailed, bloody pixel art to a short clip of smooth, pleasant, higher frame-rate animation is astoundingly jarring. If these videos were long, featured quick movements, or were more complicated, perhaps an argument could me made for the choice over the pixel cut-scenes of the original, but given the lack of overall movement in these cut-scenes, its difficult to appreciate them to the same level as the pixel ones, or even the animation featured in B1's DLC which while different, still felt a bit more raw and inline with the game. Several examples of  bosses, enemies, and executions in this game also stand out as being visually inconsistent with the rest of the games art direction, notably the  appears to be from a completely different game, and the  feels very diluted and cartoony compared to the previous entries. overall there is a smaller quantity of the gore, and disturbing imagery that gave the original its unique identity.I appreciate the attempt to set this game apart from B1 by giving the player 3 weapons to cycle through, but I spent the whole game hoping that in a moment of abject defeat and desperation a facsimile of the Mea Culpa would erupt from the penitent one's thorny arm. Even if  for the end game, it would have been so gratifying. sadly, splitting the Mea Culpa's abilities across 3 weapons was never as satisfying as having one Iconic blade.  I found that i rarely used the activation on two of the weapons, and primarily relied on the one that gave me a dash attack - until i was forced to change them up for puzzling and boss encounters. The origin of the Mea Culpa was so visceral and cool. it was difficult to relate to the new weapons in that way.Having said all this, I think i'm still glad i experienced the game. I'm hopeful we will get some killer dlc that will flesh out the story a bit more. Sequels are always tricky, esp when the first entry is so so good. I wish B2 took more risks to really push the envelope, raise the stakes,  and elevate the story, instead it feels more like a diluted reboot with a lot of the stuff i was looking forward too removed.

_childDocuments_.review: This acclaimed sequel to one of my favourite Metroidvanias of all time was one of my most anticipated games ever since it was announced. Now that I've played through it and sunk 18hrs into it all I can say is that this sequel is all style but much less substance than its predecessor. While I would like to recommend this game I can hardly do so with how much better the first one was. Blasphemous 2 suffers from a multitude of problems that the first one did not in my opinion and at a much higher price point. Maybe if the game receives updates and DLCs like the first one did my review might change but as it stands I simply cannot recommend it over the sequel or any of the other big metroidvanias on Steam.Pros: The art style and music are still very much a sight to behold. The tracks are atmospheric and epic as they were in the first and the art style is still just as visually stunning so props to the composers and artists that worked on this game.Cons: This is where I might catch some flak for my takes but here they are. The level designs are poorly thought out and kind of bland which culminates in a lackluster experience that does not make me want to chase secrets, achievements or subsequent playthroughs like the first one did.The zones themselves don't feel unique enough and are not as visually interesting as the zones in the first game. A lot of textures and backgrounds seem to repeat and the enemy placements don't always make sense in regards to what zone they are in. Traversing the areas does not offer a challenge in terms of the enemies encountered and the secrets to be found are rather obvious this time around which means that you won't really need to go too far out of your way to acquire what you need or discover interesting upgrades that will enhance the experience overall.The enemies are rather boring and uninspired in this sequel. Most of them are recolors or re-used assets from the first game. This wouldn't be such a big deal if the second game introduced more enemies but to me it feels like the game has much less variety in its enemies populating the world and the sheer amount of enemies that are simple a red/green/blue palette swap (i.e the hammer knights, the bed-men, etc) just further dilute the already lacking variety the game has.The combat has seen some "improvements?" personally I much preferred the parry sword combat from the first game compared to the variety weapons we got in the second. Most weapons feel rather useless when traversing the world because of their short range, low damage and laughable hit stun. I found myself mainly playing through the game with the mace because of its multi-hit jumping attack, higher damage and higher hit stun which made moving around the world extremely easy. There were a few instances where the other weapons could shine but they were few and far between for me personally. I didn't really feel like I wanted to block/parry as much as the first game because I had other safer options in the form of the aforementioned range and hit stun of the mace.Executions seem to have taken a back seat this time around, there are very few unique executions compared to the first game, most of them are simply the Penitent One wrapping the enemy in roots and squeezing them. It feels kind of lazy and uninspired considering that the first game had some pretty gnarly executions.The boss fights albeit very cool looking we're not all too challenging but this point is entirely subjective. I didn't really get a sense of scale or experienced epic moments like the battle between the Penitent One and Crisanta from the first game instead it just felt like I was hitting a sponge with a few attack patterns until they were dead. As far as I know I don't believe that there are any secret bosses to fight in the second game which would've been a really neat thing to tie up some of the questlines like in the first game. Finally, later in the game I also discovered a rather funny exploit with the mace and stop time chant but I won't delve too deep on the latter.No alternate outfits/unlockables in the second game. Bit of a shame because finding secrets and unlocking outfits in Blasphemous 1 was a neat and replayable aspect to the game which I enjoyed.The animated cutscenes although nice looking don't mesh very well with the overall look and aesthetic of the game. They feel a bit out of place and for me cause this weird dissonance between a game that's supposed to be grim, dark and brutally oppressive and the more tame, pretty line work and vibrant colors of the animated scenes.I also ran into some annoying bugs? or oversights like picking up items prevents the menu/map from being opened, playing the game fullscreen with a controller still had the mouse cursor visible on the screen, the ending credits not taking up the entire screen and instead had 2 small gaps letting me see my background, the map centering on a different area from the one I was in to name a few off the top of my head. From what I remember the first game felt much more polished on launch.Overall maybe with time Blasphemous 2 will live up to the masterclass of game design that the first one was but as of writing this review I can't in any way recommend it over its prequel. The prequel is cheaper, has more content, is more replayable and there are multiple other metroidvania games on Steam that far surpass Blasphemous 2 especially at its current price tag of 40$. I'm genuinely curious as to if the same people worked on the sequel as the prequel because it feels like the game was made by a completely different team of people trying to emulate the first game rather than attempting to push the bar even higher to surpass it. I really wanted to enjoy this game and was so very excited for it but after completing the game, 100%ing the collectables and achieving both endings I can safely say that I left feeling unbelievable disappointment and expected a lot more after the triumph of the first game. I hope that over time more content will be added to further expand the game/lore/variety but I am in no way playing through the game again currently in the foreseeable future. Blasphemous 1 is in my top 3 of favorite metroidvanias of all time but sadly I cannot say that for its sequel. If you've run out of Metroidvanias and need to scratch that itch then consider picking this one up on sale or waiting a bit for more updates to hopefully roll out.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, while the art design and lore are really great, actually playing the game can be a real slog. There are just too many artificial difficulty spikes and long, tedious combat arenas to make it worth finishing. Your weapons are absurdly underpowered - I can't believe I haven't seen any other reviewers point out that heavy enemies regularly take *twenty or thirty* hits to go down. Meanwhile, those same enemies can take half your health bar in one swipe, so the best option for every fight is to turtle up and slowly, slowly, slooooowly whittle your enemies down without exposing yourself to any risk. It's not hard, really. It's just dull. And what's worse is that many enemies (and a lot of platforming sections too) are clearly designed to reward this sort of play by having devastating attacks or traps specifically designed to catch you getting lazy. As if it's somehow *my* fault that I wanted to skip a few rounds of the same attack-dodge-jump cycle I've been doing for five minutes straight! Ultimately, Blasphemous 2 ends up being my least favorite type of game: One that, after failing to provide you with enough to keep you invested, turns around and punishes you for getting bored. It's a shame too, because I would have loved to see the rest of the world and the lore. But as an actual game, it burned me out fast, and I wouldn't recommend it to anyone who has a low tolerance for the braindead "get gud" attitude so many developers are leaning into nowadays.

_childDocuments_.review: Its too bad this game is turning out the way it is.  There is some sort of delay in the controls that make the split second reaction times that you need to kill enemies proficiently rather hard and really frustrating.  Its almost like you need to see into the future to react properly.  There is also another issue where I end up facing the wrong direction when attacking but I'm pushing in the other direction and dude doesn't turn around.  You have to let go of the d-pad or analog stick to, I guess, reset his direction, and in the process of doing that, you take critical damage or die.  I dealt with these issues for most of the game, but now I'm on one of the final bosses and the 2nd phase is stupid hard.  The first phase was simple, 2nd phase damn near impossible, especially with the control problems mentioned above.  There needs to be an attack break when you hit the dodge button.  I cant tell you how many times I've died because of these controller issues and frankly, I'm FU#^ING done with it.  Its not that I don't think I can beat that boss, but the level of frustration with the controls is game killer.Also, I never felt the need to use any other weapons other than the big mallet during fighting, the other weapons seem like they were only good for solving some puzzles and access to different sections of the level.  The 2 swords and the single sword were just way too under powered.  The block only works on standard enemies not bosses in my experience. The prayers should stop an enemy or boss from attacking.  Seeing how you only have a split second to initiate the prayer and if your a split second to late, your taking damage or getting dead while casting the prayer.  Other than that, the story is ok, pretty hard to follow and doesn't really make much sense to me.  Because of the control problems and the kinda lame story, I wouldn't recommend this unless you really enjoy getting frustrated.Fix those control issues and maybe I'll come back to finish the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Man I really liked this game up to a point, the three core weapons are fun, good exploration and secrets, and the vibe is unique and enjoyable. But my enjoyment was ruined by some poor design decisions for a certain boss near the end and it totally killed my desire to finish the game. This is a case where, IMO, the game designers need to learn the difference between hard in a fun way and hard in an un-fun way. This late-game boss has a completely, comically insane jump in difficulty unlike anything else in the game up to that point (or from what I'm reading online, anything after). This alone would be okay if it wasn't stuck after a trivially easy first part and an annoying unskippable dialog/cutscene you have to get through Every. Time. So every attempt is 3-5 minutes slogging through the boring first part and dialogue, and then get murked in 10 seconds by the second part. If they just broke that second fight into its own part so you can jump right into it and start working out how to win, that would be hard in a fun way. But here the unskippable slog is not worth it — probably going to give up on the game here even though I want to see the rest.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah yes, Catholicvania!You play as a traffic cone with a sword. ‘Nough said.If you're gay and grew up Catholic, this is the game for you.It's like Hollow Knight, but Christian and people say big words you don't understand. Spain sure is scary!I was raised Catholic, so this is pretty normal stuff for me though.Blasphemous 2 is a phenomenal game and does nothing to color the original in a negative way, but as a sequel it somewhat drops the ball in atmosphere, characterization, and storytelling. It's also far less violent. This is hurt further by the inconsistency in tone due to the outsourced cutscenes which, while great in a vacuum, are a far departure from the gritty, uncanny cutscenes in Blasphemous 1 that were dripping with flavor. Blasphemous 1 worked hard to earn its horrific, grotesque reputation. In contrast, I'm surprised Blasphemous 2 even has an M rating.I think the biggest problem with this game, is the reason why it was made. Blasphemous was a unique game, and while it was rough around the edges at first (which they mostly fixed with the free DLCs) it was clearly a labour of love, made with tons care and passion. They had a clear idea what they wanted to make, hence why that game felt that great to play.Blapshemous 2 on the other hand was made because it's prequel got popular, and made money. That's why I think it was a major letdown for the people who loved Blasphemous for being Blasphemous, and not because it was yet another metroidvania. The game feels less in general, more of a generic metroidvania so it can appeal to larger audiences, the story is told in an extremely blatant and boring way, so everyone can understand it, and the game overall holds you hand waaaaay more than it did in B1 originally.I think Blasphemous 2 is a wonderful game in the context of Blasphemous 1. However, outside of that context, it feels as though it is hollow, because it lacks the core of B1: repentance. In B1, there were no great warriors or horrific beasts—not narratively, at least (except for Sierpes). What made B1 so beautiful was that every monster and every NPC was a being shaped by true and tormentous guilt. In B2, bosses like Lesmes and Orospina are simply powerful beings. Characters like the Sculptor and the Rosary Weaver are simply talented artists. There is no beautiful struggle they impress upon me. Not like the Kissers of Wounds or Altasgracias, at least. Where Deogracias was bound to witness and never act, Anunciada is literally above the torment of the earth. I miss the definition that suffering gave B1. But I do appreciate that they tried something new here.There are naturally some really great improvements like the fluidity of the platforming and expanded combat, there are more abilities and ways to explore the map. There's also lots of segments where you revisit and flip levers and stuff without it ever being tedious or puzzly, I really enjoyed navigating its areas, and for the most part I liked how it tackled being more of an MV. As I progressed through, I started to appreciate the game more as you unlock more abilities and some of the puzzles and secrets were really engaging. I liked the envelope side quest and the added altarpieces. There are also many QoL improvements that make the game far less frustrating to play. The new prayers also add more layers to the combat as well. After defeating the first 3 guardians, the game really clicked with me and I was really hooked as the new weapons provided new ways of exploration. With some of the new traversal abilities, the game felt so fresh and fluid to play. I got so engrossed that I almost hit 100 percent by the end and think that it is a great game. Nevertheless, I prefer B1 much more due to its dark atmosphere and unique atmosphere. B2 just doesn’t capture the same disturbing intrigue that B1 does. Rather, B2’s relative strengths lie in its expanded MV mechanics (actual movement upgrades) and increased character customization options (a cool synergy engine called the Altarpiece). The best way I can describe it is this: B1 feels like more than the sum of its parts; it transcends its characteristics on paper. Conversely, B2 is merely the sum of its parts, not more, not less, but the parts are good, so the game is good. I ultimately think B1 is the more memorable experience (it’s a top-5 all time game for me), but they’re both very good and worthwhile games.I don't dislike or hate the game at all (minus Eviterno phase 2, that can f*ck right off), I just simply expected more. I really hope we get as amazing DLCs to it as we did for B1, so it might improve in the future, just like how that game did. To conclude, I think that B2 improves much from a gameplay perspective but lacks some of the cool designs of the first game. Still, giving this game anything lower than an 8 is outright Blasphemous! And, it’d be blasphemous of you not to buy this sequel and try it out!8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Another excellent metroidvania, but there are definitely changes that have been made compared to the original that people might be miffed about.If you enjoyed the slower, deliberate pace of the original, the double jumps, air dashes, level ups, weapon swapping, fast travel, and generally more arcadey style of gameplay might not be to your liking.Additionally, the original's abundance of monstrous bosses are mostly gone, replaced with human sized opponents.Lastly, the payout for going for the "best" ending is just some more dialog and a cutscene. There is no additional boss phase or difficulty, which, following a zone which is almost all platforming with really poor loot, does feel undercooked.

_childDocuments_.review: I will start off by saying that this game is an upgrade from the previous one  for most cases(both in terms of gameplay mechanics and ability balance). The fact that you get to have 3 weapons is a major upgrade since it will gives you the option to choose the style that suits you the most (the abilities and alterpieces are also a huge upgrade from the previous one). The map design is also really well done and you can orient yourself better than the first game. The difficulty balance is actually worse than the first one. The first bosses are actually pretty hard (due to your limited move set), then the bosses at the middle are easy as hell and barely offer any resistance, while the final boss is the biggest pain in the ass that you can play against due to the way his move sets are animated and projected (it's annoying and you can't skip the dialogue scene which just adds to the frustration). The side quests were fine and the story is more easy to understand and piece together  (which for me partially removes the charm which the first one had). The design of the enemies in my opinion was pretty basic and I liked the looked of the first one. Music was pretty great but there weren't any cool pieces that made me want to listen to when walking down the street.My major issue with the game is the fact that there is sometimes a delay when pressing the attack button (veredicto is mostly the case) which can cause you to die since it was badly programmed.The second is that the story is incredibly mid and not really worth the time to completely grind for it in order to beat the final (awfully made in design) boss.The third and final is that there is something incredibly off with the overall design of this game. The first one had this incredible spanish catholic design that was put everywhere (from the town to all the levels) which made the game really cool looking and beautiful and gave you that old school religious vibe. I am not sure if they changed the lead artist or whatever but everything looks a bit off which removes (partially) the charm of the franchise.I can only suggest you buy this when it's on a discount and once they have done major updates to the combat mechanic(potentially future DLCs also).

_childDocuments_.review: Blasphemous 2 is a great game, and frankly this franchise is the reason alone I even got into metroidvanias. But there are certainly flaws. Despite having fantastically tight gameplay and world design, I think it's sense of aesthetics is far less interesting. Whereas Blasphemous 1 was a morbidly bleak game, palettes of dark greens and umbers, Blasphemous 2 is far more vibrant, and it's cutscenes switching to fully animated instead of the utterly brilliant pixel art versions is a major step down imo, as well as every time I saw them it took me right out of the games synchronicity with the stylistic whiplash. Outside of that, very good to outright great bosses. All in all, a worthy successor that innovates in some very good ways, has it's own unique potholes, but is a very tight and strong experience nonetheless. I look forward to the day more DLC gets added to this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Post Boss Buff Review (Spoiler Free)I have thought about Blasphemous 1 like it was a lost love. I thought about it at work, while eating and even during workouts. Its twisted world,sombre soundtracks and demented NPCs made it one of my favourite games of all time. So, when I saw the announcement of Blasphemous 2, the only thing that kept me from wetting myself was the vow of bladder control I chose as my penance. On release, it seemed to have a few bugs and boss difficulty issues.None of the bugs were game breaking but some bosses in late game were apparently too easy. I only found out about this after watching a walk through where I saw a boss I was struggling on, look like a middle school kid in a varsity football game.After the update though, I can safely say that the bosses are definitely not easy but at the same time feel less punishing than my time during the first penance. The game still poses a fair challenge and requires practise.  1)The boss designs and the art builds on the first game and had me smiling the whole time. I cannot even begin to fathom the talent of this team.The atmosphere and the music are truly phenomenal, they complement each other like bread and butter or slide and sword strike. 2)The map flows effortlessly from one area to another and is designed masterfully.Each Prie Dieu is placed perfectly and never fails to fill me respite. Every time I kneel at a new Prie Dieu, I know I made progress and I know I am safe. The upgrades to these however, require you to play hide and seek with nuns. Depending on how you feel about them, this can feel like a tedious side quest forcing you to swipe at walls when you hear even the slightest of whispers. I much prefer the upgrade system of Blasphemous 1.There are many tricky areas in the map that are expertly tucked away and require some keen eyesight or even spidey senses to dig out. You will side-eye many walls because it just doesn't "look right". When you do end up finding a secret room, it makes feel like a true XxGamerGod69420xX(let's not talk about the times you embarrassingly swung your weapon on a regular wall)4)Exploration is rewarded HEAVILY. The emphasis on exploration puts the games ultra-polished movement in the spotlight( Compared to the previous game where it felt 'floaty' and had me screaming "I DEFINITELY HIT THAT BUTTON" or " YOU'RE LOOKING THE WRONG WAY, YOU MORON"), the movement here is tight and consistent. The penitent one no longer slides a few extra inches forward or bumps into ledges he clearly made it to. 5)The NPCs are generally vendors for different items but seemed not to have too much lore to them compared to the previous game. I somehow found them less interesting.6)The combat this time seems to emphasise movement more. You now have 3 weapon choices:less damage more speed, more damage less speed and a balanced third. This choice however is a bit redundant since you can get all three by exploration. One of these weapons cannot parry which makes it so that all attacks need to be avoidable for players who only have access to this weapon. Parrying in this game just does not meet the risk-reward it did before. Since the movement is so great, you have a million ways to reliably evade an attack.The executions are good but can be very repetitive. Once you've seen the ones that you already saw in the first game, there are not many that are new. It mostly consists of crushing the enemy with briars. This is understandable however since there are quite a few enemy types even if you don't consider the re-skinned enemies that just do a different type of elemental damage and are a different colour corresponding to the colour of the element.I absolutely adored all the lore added to this game and i'm hoping for some DLC with cool skins and content(hopefully with Crisanta)On the off chance that the devs read this I want quickly want to talk about some issues I faced while playing this game. Minor annoyances that I hope will be fixed so future players don't have to face it:1)In the elevated temples, there was an area where I died to spikes and it kept reviving me at the portal that takes me back to the spikes. This effectively locked me into dying by plunging into the spikes repeatedly without having any control over it.2)During an interaction with the statues in the Severed Tower, I was hit by an enemy attack and knocked back, this locked me to only be able to move and not attack, the player sprite was also not changing with direction inputs or going into run animation. I'm guessing the player state transition did not happen correctly and it forced me to interact with the statue again a couple of times.3)The ghost enemies in Streets of Wakes will often fly into areas where they cannot be hit but will still target you. This is especially frustrating in the house of grief gauntlet challenges.4) During my boss fight with Svsona, I was trapped in the left corner under her and was stuck there by what seemed to me like an invisible wall. The run animation would play but the player could not move back to the main arena. I just accepted my death here and it did not happen again.5) I had random areas where the music would just suddenly stop playing. I'm sure this is not intended but, I quite liked this bug since it gave me some time to really reflect on the journey and feel the environmental details.Finally,My fellow brothers in penance, I highly recommend that you awake from your thousand year rest and look upon the land where Cvstodia once stood. Resume your penance O silent one, for the miracle is giving birth anew. You must vanquish it with the very hands that once did wield the Mea Culpa. My favour is with you. For the penitents who read reviews upon completion of their penance,Requiem Aeternam

_childDocuments_.review: When it comes to games getting a sequel, I never really saw  ever getting one, but it seems I was wrong because of the first game's true ending. It pretty much said that the devs were working on a sequel so with all of that said,  has come out. Despite me having a number of issues with the first game, I enjoyed it quite a lot and was actually some what looking forward to playing the sequel. Although with all of that said, I do think the devs of , took a step forward but a few steps back.The story for  is a bit interesting because there is actually a story that makes sense here.  is resurrected and is tasked with retrieving these three regrets, he must go and defeat someone by the name of . Who is trying to get the  new child born so the  can be prevented from returning.I am conflicted about the story of this game, but it is nice to have a story that makes sense. It does take away something that I think the first  got right and that’s the mystery that the story had with it. This game does have mystery to it but not as much as the first game had and I think it’s missing from this game.An interesting thing to note for  gameplay is that you have three to choose from instead of having one weapon with you. Although you can only select one from the start, you can eventually find the other two. This also gives you access to what secrets and hidden items you can get from the game.The weapons I went with first were the , as they were a sword and dagger combo, as they are usually my preferred weapon of choice in hack and slashes because they can do high amounts of damage with their combos. Although I’ll get back to this whole combo thing later down the line in the review. Overall though the gameplay is very funThe three weapons that you have access to, each have a unique ability for platforming.  give you the ability to teleport from certain mirrors, you can access other platforms, you can also chain to other mirrors and you will need to attack that mirror in quick succession to get to other mirrors. is the slowest of the three weapons but it does the most damage out of them all. It has the ability to attack these bells that will give you access to these platforms that will disappear after a few seconds. This is my favorite weapon to use when it comes to the platforming as I do think the devs took advantage out of it, unlike the other two. Also if you time it just right,  can actually damage enemies twice in one attack. I have no idea if this is a glitch or not but it’s something I did like. is the last weapon and is pretty much my favorite out of the three, I’ll get onto why soon though. This weapon is the most balanced out of the three but it’s the least useful for platforming, as it only gives you the ability to destroy these walls. However, now I can go onto why this weapon is my favorite and I will also be talking about one of the biggest issues I have with the weapons in . , can combo, the other two weapons can’t, you only get a basic attack for those two.This is very odd, as this is a platformer/metroidvenia, so you would expect all three of these weapons to combo, even when you put upgrades into these two weapons. As a matter of fact, in the later parts of the game,  just out-classes these two weapons, it’s sad because I like the ideas they had for the gameplay.Although speaking of platforms, that’s one thing the game has improved on, so there is that, no more broken ladders in this game. The upgrades you can get have also gotten a major overhaul and are actually useful. There are upgrades for your weapons, weapon memories for new abilities and more. The abilities you can get also have changed in some ways, instead of them being for combat, they are instead used for platforming, which is something I did like.There are also some side quests for you to do and they can offer some very nice rewards, like some upgrades or abilities. There are a ton of collectibles for you to go out and find and the game does encourage you to go out and explore its world.Although that’s really it I have to say on some of the other positive stuff because I have a few more negatives that the game has. One of the issues is that the enemies are just sometimes reused. The only difference that these new enemies have is that they have a different elemental attack that they can use and are reskinned. They end up being a bit boring to fight, just like the bosses. However, the boss fights are another issue here and in my opinion, are the worst aspect for this game. They aren’t fun to fight and are just giant sponges, the only two bosses I actually liked were  and this may be a hot take but  were my favorite bosses.Although that was it, sadly the rest are pretty bad, with  is the worst boss. It has an easy first phase, a massive difficulty spike in phase two that makes you do things the game has never thrown at you and you can’t afford to make a mistake due to you not having many opportunities to heal. All of this combined makes this boss not very fun but the worst part is his unskipable dialog that he does every time.The overworld is also at times not very interesting to explore, even with the new abilities and collectibles I can get. There isn’t really a reason to go and revisit the areas of the game due to them all being interesting.The pixel art style is something I would like to praise the game for, even the animation during the cutscenes were also nice, even if a little odd for this game. I tested the game on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50, and 16 GB of RAM, I experienced no issues while I was playing and the game ran very well, should be able to work on any computer.I am at odds with , while I had a ton of issues with the first game, I still enjoyed it but in here. I had more good to say but the cons outweigh the pros, I am kind of sad because deep down, this game is good. If you do want to pick this game up, I recommend you wait for a sale but if you are someone who really liked the first game, you may be a little disappointed here.

_childDocuments_.review: I am writing this review after getting every single achievement like I did on blasphemous 1, I wish steam had a neutral option for reviews because compared to blasphemous 1 this game lacks a lot in, yes the new movement is awesome and a great addition. The good:The first half of the game is magical and really gets you hooked, the environments are beautiful and the music is better than in the first game. The addition of new weapons allow for a slight difference in playstyle that can offer a bit more variety. They removed relics which I think was a good idea since you don't have to go into the menus to swap everytime which is good. To finish, the map is much more interactive and fun to explore and well connected together with more portals for faster travelsTHE BAD:lot of reused enemies and attacks which can be understandable from a lore perspective but from a game perspective it gets repetitive, the new weapons have lacking movesets and don't really become interesting until you pump some upgrades in. The second have of the game felt more tedious than anything and the bosses have been mediocre and even felt like early game bosses. This game also lacks what blasphemous 1 had like NG+ which is a huge part of games like these, they also removed skins and backgrounds in the menu which is really weird because they already know how to code it from the first game. With all this and the game costing $40 I think people should wait for it to be around $20 for it to feel worth it, it's still a really good game but I don't know if I can recommend it for this price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most frustrating and dissapointing games i've ever played. Blasphemous 2 tried to address some minor complaints people had about the first game, but for the most part they didn't do anything or even managed to make it WORSE:- Contact damage is worse than ever, never i've seen this mechanic be implemented in such a horrible way in any game i've played. Bumping into any enemy will take large amounts of your HP. Every enemy has a gigantic hitbox and a lot of them CANNOT be dashed through, so you have large meat columns blocking your path and restricting your movement, setting you up to either a boring walk back and forth until they die or you just dying.Worse yet, Blocking and Parrying CONSISTENTLY will result in you taking very high amounts of contact damage after executing a successful block or parry. - The new weapon system is bad. Unlike the first game where you had a weapon with a large array of strings and combos with your weapon, they gave you three weapons that don't have any strings and scattered some regular Mea Culpa moves (Lunge, Charge, etc) between the three. In the end you still have less unique moves than Mea Culpa. Basically we lost the move depth for a very meager variety of weapons. - Blocking and Parrying are now tied to specific weapons (Rapier and Scimitar), weakening the base kit of the Penitent One. The Heavy weapon (Veredicto) doesn't even have a defensive move tied to it.- Rebinding is limited and just really bad for keyboard. Prayers require Down + Quick-verses key to proc, causing Prayers to be extremely unprecise and unresponsive.Overall the main aspect of the game - The Combat - is boring and slow, not only being worse than the previous game, but also being far below all other Metroidvanias i've tried in the last year. If you want something that plays similar to the original, just buy The Last Faith instead, it has more similar combat to the prequel, much better OST and pixel art.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like the sequel to Blasphemous, as I am a big fan, however based on the writing done for the sequel I cannot recommend the 2nd based on that alone.TL;DR: Gameplay fun, Story BadSo here is where my issue is with the writing:The writing at the end really does come off like they wanted to make a sequel, had planned out levels and enemies to fight with new weapons, but didn't have a story to give them an excuse to make a sequel. So they basically just threw a bunch of crap together so they could make a second game. No. No it doesn't. I'm so glad that I looked into the endings before fighting the final boss, because I wanted to get the true ending, and if I had played through that entire game a second time just to watch , I would've been so freaking pissed.

_childDocuments_.review: While I do recommend the game I would say that Blasphemous 2 is a slight downgrade from the original. If the original one was rated 10/10 I would rate this one 7.5/10.B2 felt like a bunch of leftover ideas from B1 stitched together.  The story elements felt very disconnected from one another without much thematic ties to each other which made the game feel a bit incoherent. The dialogue felt like it was trying too hard to sound old englishy and it came off confusing and pretentious. The executions also didn't feel that imaginative as the first. While the game still have the gruesome and dark theme it doesn't feel as meaningful as the first one. B1 had a lot of symbolism and vivid imagery that left deep impression in me, the intro with a mountain of corpse, filling the helmet with blood, Lady of the perpetual agony, mountain of ashe, the bent pilgrim, all of which I still remember off the top of my head. For B2 outside a few notable characters it just doesn't feel as deep. I am coming off pretty harsh in my critiques but I enjoyed the game and really hope my thoughts aren't going to taint your enjoyment of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Blasphemous II is a huge improvement from the first one, and I loved the first game for what it was: a punishing metroidvania with great art, music and storytelling.The second one is somehow easier than the first one, thanks to the fact that you don't die when falling into pits or spikes (You still die if you fall into them with low HP!).The gameplay is where the game shines the most from the first one, the three weapons are great to use and the fact that they're also useful for platforming is a great cherry on top.Musically I first felt that the tone was darker and with less melody, but the later areas are bangers on bangers. You'll probably hear some similarities with the first game, and you'll be right, keep exploring and you'll find out why!I don't mind the anime cutscenes. Yeah they're a little too clean, I wouldn't mind darker cutscenes, but that's no deal breaker to me, I enjoyed them nonetheless.For a sequel, it totally works and I'm happy to have played it through its entire length (almost 20h). Now, hoping to see a NG+ and the same amount of additional content as the first game.TLDR: Great sequel, if you loved the first one, the second one will be a great addition to your library. If you're new to the genre, you can still play it but I would advise going for Blasphemous first as Blasphemous II is a "direct" sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, REALLY liked the first game. The art style, the gameplay, how subjective and vague the lore was. But this game just feels so lackluster in a few of those components, like small unnecessary changes. I liked the difficulty scaling of the first game, it was difficult in some areas but it forced you to get better at certain mechanics like parrying or dodging. But there are so many enemies that have attacks that you cannot parry, and makes it feel like you have to cheese some fights by abusing a game mechanic or just spamming a single attack hopefully before your life hits zero.The next issue I had personally was the exploration and wondering what to do next in the sequence of the game. The first game didn't give much guidance, but the way the areas were set up make it easier to understand where to go next. Like you could just look and see you have an unexplored part of a region, or go a certain direction based on where you have already explored. Unfortunately, the second game I feel like drags on coming back to areas you've already explored to do a specific puzzle. It's fine coming back to one region to obtain a specific item, but doing it for the story just adds unnecessary time to gameplay. Every region has a good fraction of it you wont be able to access until way later, and it feels like every region was put together with the intention of coming back to it once you get something way later. I just wish it could be a little more direct on where to go next, or have the areas grow in difficulty in that regard once you have more items in your arsenal.These are very minor things that just proved to be consistently inconvenient for me personally. This is in no way is a bad game, I just found things to be inconvenient as it felt like some enemies or regions were specifically meant to slow the progress by an unreasonable amount. Wah wah skill issue. The changes to the gameplay were necessary like the weapon variation combined with the puzzles associated with a specific weapon. Was a fun change of thinking compared to the previous game with various enemies and platforming puzzles. The boss fights themselves were great, I personally loved how some had a second phase and changed their moveset slightly, it made the fights require a lot more attention to what was happening. The new change of scenery with slight reference to the previous game and figuring out the various mysteries in game proved to be more challenging than before which I am thankful for.I don't LOVE this game as much as I liked the first, but that being said Blasphemous 2 is still a good game. In my personal experience playing the game I found enough parts to be overly inconvenient and unnecessary. My personal views lean towards the thought that there could be a couple tweaks and fixes that updates could change in the future. Womp womp skill issue, its a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is the embodiment of vast improvements from the first game with some exceptions: mainly being the plot direction (ending still wraps up nicely at least with ending A), potential for stun-locking, and the incentive to use the three new weapon types. I was most pleased with the graphical improvement, and its obvious creativity with environments as well as boss dynamics (deformity). Plot: Game Kitchen made it a lot easier for players to know where they need to go. The story as a result is much more linear; no longer possessing any real mystery beyond learning minimal plot from the 2-3 collectathons providing wooden figures for stat improvements. As opposed to the 3 endings in the first game, which granted weren't complicated to achieve yet was motivation to get the true ending acting as the beginning plot for this second game (I played after the entire story was completed through the Wounds of Eventide dlc), there are only 2 in the second game. These two endings are only dictated by either you chugging along in the game doing what you're told, or doing enough of the collectathons to figure out something really subtle for what I think wasn't all that justifiable (had to look it up after getting ending B).Stun-locking: Contact damage being in the same area as enemies wasn't anything new but sometimes it causes stagger if the damage is repeated. Stun-lock is not a real issue until the second to final boss when you're knocked into the air after back-to-back slashes.Weapon incentive: I went through 90% of the game using Alba (the most similar weapon to Mea Culpa from game #1), and sparingly used Veredicto (the flail). I respect, as well as understand the different Mea Culpa abilities being split into 3 weapons with perks/improvements but it simply didn't convince me to utilize all three in a manner beyond the platforming requirement. I resorted to using the flail in situations that encouraged reach, but punished the performance of frequent counters. Summary: This game was definitely meant as the resolution for the first game in which we all cherished. It couldn't be recommended as a game to play stand-alone. Playing this without prior knowledge of the true ending from the first game is simply asinine. It's why game #1 is blasted for 75% all the time, and its worth it. The improvements they made stand as testament for whatever projects they pursue in the realm of metroid-vanias, especially through the art style. It's a miracle in itself bearing witness to a studio that improves upon well-justified belief from a fan-base.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: A quality search-action (Metroidvania) game that doesn’t scratch the same itch as the original, but is a lot of fun nonetheless.I played these two games back-to-back in 2024. I was absolutely taken with the original, and immediately wanted to know how Blasphemous II stacked up. As it turns out, this is a pretty different experience from its predecessor, and while I definitely enjoyed it, it felt less inspired and unique.Taking place some thousand years after the events of the first game, the story starts with the Penitent One rising once again from his place of rest. Following the events of the “canonical” ending added to the first game in free DLC, the Miracle has materialized a massive heart in the sky, in which gestates a looming, gargantuan figure. It’s up to you to ascend to the heavens and face down this likely threat. Like the original, the story here takes a back seat; it provides direction but little explanation, and that’s perfect for a game that relies so heavily on its vibe.Where the game stumbles is in the new art direction. Blasphemous was set in what looked and felt like an unmistakably grimdark universe, every setting dripping with the symbolism of its smothering, suffering-based religion. This game has a notably lighter color palette and overall tone, providing an adventure that takes the player through a thriving city, shadowy woods, and other locations that don’t serve the central theme. The animation feels smoother, but the multitude of unique execution animations have been axed in favor of generic “tree arm” kills that I still don’t understand. The music is great again, but overall this outing feels significantly less dire.In my first review, I praised Blasphemous for its tight combat and limited moveset, and said that it specifically lacked double-jumping and air dashes. Both of those moves feature here, and the result is that the game feels more frenetic, but also more generic. Mea Culpa has been replaced with an arsenal of three weapons you switch between on-the-fly. Their different strengths and weaknesses mean that you’ll likely find a favorite, but again the overall experience has been watered down. Parrying has especially suffered, as dodging is now almost always the correct solution in boss fights. There are plenty of great bosses, some of whom are probably the hardest in the series, but the action feels  different this time out.Rereading this review, it sounds like I’m being harsh, but I’d like to emphasize that these complaints are only relevant when comparing this game to its parent. Taken out of context, I would be very happy with Blasphemous II; it’s a solid game, and while it didn’t wow me like the first, I had a great time playing it. For my personal tastes, I just wish it had continued to draw from its soulslike influences instead of going all-in on search-action, and I feel that they made a crucial mistake in dulling the thorns of the original’s gruesome tone. There is real horror in zealotry, and this game shies away from that in favor of providing a more broadly-appealing experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is framed around someone having played through Blasphemous 1 having also recommend that game.In comparison to the first game this one is more polished, streamlined and more emphasis on tight, smooth gameplay/combat than the first one. The first game had a slightly clunky charm to it, both in art direction, mechanics, story and gameplay. The first game had more impactful decisions and elements to the story that you could avoid/miss if you took a different path than the one specific to that characters destiny within the game. There were many characters and threads woven into the game like this. Meaning you had to play through the game multiple times to experience most of them. This was a good thing to most people, it added mystery and complexity but it could also be seen as a negative. This game has stream lined it, there are interesting characters you come across but you cant really miss out on there dialogue or interactions and if you do there are failsafes built in so that you can still obtain their items not requiring multiple play throughs, this is the same with the story ending. This can be seen as a good or bad thing but ultimately imo loses some of the games original charm.The art direction is fantastic, just like the first game but again the ingame cutscenes are much smoother and cleaner than the first, while this is a technical improvement it also removes some of the dark hand made grit of the first and overall gives a slightly different feel, some of the more graphic gothic imagery is also slightly watered down from the original although not much.The ingame systems overall feel far more polished. There is now purpose to executing enemies other than it just being a cool thing to do. Although most of the enemies now share an execution animation which is slightly disappointing. The rosary beads have been simplified leading to less collectables and micromanaging  with many of the abilities from the first game obtained via these now built into another system that permanently upgrades your character to have them. This again, could be seen as good or bad. There is also a new system of figurines which is a fun and interesting mechanic that lets you buff your character in different ways. This however leads to you being able to buff already strong miracles or weapons in the game to overpowered levels that let you triviliase the games boss encounters.The game has less boss encounters than the first and they have mostly done away with much of the gimmick fights from the first although none of them are frustratingly difficult this time round, given the availability of overpowered weapons and spells. There are almost no cheap deaths in this one and everything is less lethal, it results in an easier game experience although still challenging in places. This game is far more forgiving than the first.Mea Culpa the first games iconic weapon is no more and is replaced with 3 separate weapons that infer exploration abilities and combat sets that you can quickly chop and change between, the weapons abilities are needed to fully explore the game and are a fun mechanic and the switching between them for different enemy types is also a great addition. However i suspect this new style of upgrade will put people off that preferred the original games 1 weapon upgrade system.  There is also not enough opportunity during boss encounters to switch weapons, its basically never needed because you can usually brute force most of them.There are less collectables than the first game. Again a good or bad thing.Despite this lengthy and overall critical look at the game, this is still a superb game and i would say on par with the first and a worthy sequel, its great but not in the same way as the first. Ultimately it is a much smoother and streamlined game with less jankiness and quirks than the first. However, to many people the quirkiness, clunk and charm of the first game is why they loved it and i would say those will not be content with this game and will find it a watered down, more casual game. I can appreciate this for what it is and i thoroughly enjoyed the game even if ultimately i do prefer the first game. Although it is also a somewhat unfair comparison given the first games DLC which greatly expanded on the content of the first and also vastly improved its combat. This is also a much longer base game than the first but currently little replay-ability. You won't find anything in this game as difficult as the dlc bosses in the first one.

_childDocuments_.review: Blasphemous 2: The Selected Works ReviewSteam Curator page: If you liked the first Blasphemous, Blasphemous 2 improves upon it mechanically in pretty much every way. The Game Kitchen loosened up the joints in the combat, the almost Castlevania-style stiffness from Blasphemous 1 is gone; and the Penitent One now has three weapons to choose from (you get one at the beginning but find the others out in the world), and they're all fun to use; I chose the Tonitrus-like thurible-flail, Veredicto, and used it almost exclusively throughout my playthrough; not sure if the devs intended this or not, but the combat/enemy/boss design does not necessitate switching up your weapon at all, so if you were hoping for that to play a part here you might be a little disappointed; personally I was happy to have a favorite and be able to stick with it.Where the three weapon mechanic does play a part, however, is in navigation. Each weapon is keyed to a different type of obstacle in the world, which only it can surmount. It's an interesting and not unpleasant concept, but didn't amaze me either; you're expected to switch between the three weapons for these sort of navigation gauntlets, and that's cool, but the precision required in these sections doesn't jibe with the weapon swap system; basically, there's always one of the three weapons that takes two button presses to access, and, while it's not a huge deal, this slight bit of friction makes these sections more shambolic than I'd like. It's an idea that's like 80% of the way there, it needed just a bit more refinement to really cohere into something special.The overall navigation, and the way the PO controls, has been refined too. He's a much nimbler protag this time around, and, once you get your four additional movement abilities, he can really zip through areas, which makes the backtracking a much more pleasant experience. Speaking of, the overhaul to the metroidvania structure is pretty much a total success. There aren't any meaningless, Kickstarter backer trinkets to collect this time around, and any time you delve into some hidden cranny or other, you're going to end up finding something decent, if not game altering, at the end. If we're going to keep being inundated with metroidvanias, I'd like them all to be shorter, like in the 3-5 hour zone; Blasphemous 2 took me 15 hours to (nearly, see below) finish, but I will say it justified its length by never being less than engrossing, both in terms of main quest stuff as well as self-directed exploration.I also really enjoyed the bosses. Blasphemous 1 had some stinkers in that department and the average boss quality has been much improved. I stopped playing on the penultimate boss, not because he was too hard, but just because I didn't find him interesting enough to keep learning his patterns and, while I absolutely love the Blasphemous 1/2 atmosphere and aesthetic, the story itself doesn't interest me, so I wasn't really compelled to finish for narrative closure either. I think most people who get as far as I did will see it through, though.My biggest gripe with the game is my general fatigue with the looming specter of Dark Souls. Blasphemous 2 obviously comes from a team very much enamored with, and very much inspired by, the whole FromSoft gestalt; it does much better than most souls-inspired stuff in terms of standing on its own artistic feet, thanks mainly to the huge talent of its pixel artists and the umbrageous, ecclesiastical, Goya-esque grue of its world, but I am so, so, so very tired of Souls tropes: parrying, duel-like fights against big armored guys, oblique NPC quest lines...it's all here, just as it's been in every indie action-adventure for like a decade. What has been extracted from the Souls games as tropes are not the things that make them actually special; the true FromSoft achievement is in the creation of convincing, artistically distinct and powerful worlds. Again, Blasphemous 2 has a much stronger individual identity than, say, Salt and Sanctuary; but I think Game Kitchen has diluted its own achievement by clinging to so many of the same things we've been seeing Souls fan-devs do for years. Case in point:   I long for the day when I don't have to have every other game winking and nodding and going "Hey man, have you played Dark Souls??" in lieu of exploring new artistic zones of their own.A few other minor complaints:Quite a few enemies are reused from the first game, which is boring.There are less bespoke execution animations.The level themes are kind of scattershot, they don't cohere; it's almost like these were half-developed or DLC ideas for the first game and just reused here without considering how they fit into the world.The spell abilities are cool but some of them, ones that I found early one, were so powerful I never switched to the others.The "go find your ghost to recover X" thing sucks and should just go away.But I want to end on a positive note, because Blasphemous 2 is a very well-crafted, very fun, very beautiful game for the most part. I found it totally engrossing all the way through, devouring it over the course of two days. The NPC visual design is really phenomenal; the Game Kitchen has a real line in gigantic, sorrowful humanoids laboring under malefic curses and I don't think anybody who meets Cesareo, or witnesses the Lady of the Chalice's degradation throughout the game, will ever forget either one. If the Game Kitchen can just break away from the Souls-obeisance, and sand down a few incongruities in their overall design priorities, their next game will be a knockout. Even as it stands, Blasphemous 2 stands out in a teeming genre, and I would be happy to hear they're working on another one. Good stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. If I had to put it on a scale, I think I had more fun with this one than with Blasphemous 1.I liked:- The choice of starting weapon changes your path through the early-game stages and (arguably) also the early-game difficulty.- A lot of the minor annoyances of Blasphemous 1 have been fixed. Ledges and ladders work more reliably now and the spikes of inevitable doom are less inevitable and less numerous.- The wording of dialogues and items isn't quite as obtuse as with Blasphemous 1. You at least get the gist of the storyline without digging through inventory lore or wiki articles.- The  fight is nicely challenging without being unfair.-  is back.- Artwork and soundtrack are still great.- Some minor details show how much love went into the game. For example, once later stages become available, some earlier stages reflect this in their background art.- Biomes (notably, candle tower and crimson rain) are more creative this time around.I didn't like:- The second half of the game is rather linear: Later stages need to be completed in order, with rooms that, for the most part, have to be finished one after another.- The predecessor had a weird difficulty curve where item hunting made the end-game much easier than the early- to mid-game. They fixed this --- by making the early-game easier instead of the late-game harder. In other words, Blasphemous 2 is still balanced for sloppy exploration, which doesn't seem like the best idea for a metroidvania.- Most of the bosses are now push-overs that you can just head-on tank through. With this in mind, it is obvious why some players are suprised by the difficulty peak on the  fight.- Blasphemous 2 isn't quite as grotesque and much less gory than its predecessor. It also is somewhat missing the religious undertones. From artwork to characters to storyline, everything feels less gloomy or bleak --- more toned to appeal to the masses, maybe.- In-game music sometimes (mostly when changing biomes) glitches out and stops.- When hitting flying enemies (heads, coffins), they can glitch out of the current screen bounds and can't return. If this happens in a locked battle arena, you can't finish the arena and need to reload.- Some parts of the game feel unfinished. For example, the Labyrinth of Tides stage is just a few empty and unremarkable rooms without music or ambient sound effects.- The brutal but funny enemy-specific execution moves of the predecessor have mostly been replaced by a bland, generic and quite un-bloody animation. Boo.- The good ending still requires some obtuse steps that aren't even hinted at during normal gameplay. Likewise, the Yerma questline fails under rather unpredictable conditions.
