_childDocuments_.review: From what I've played, it's pretty good. The original is my favorite game and this should be an easy recommend, but wow this PC port is bad. Unreal Engine 5 continues to prove itself as the worst optimized modern graphics engine. There are frequent traversal stutters, but they become increasingly, and significantly more annoyingly, common in Silent Hill itself (particularly around Neely's Bar for some reason). The traversal stutters are up there with Star Wars Jedi: Survivor as some of the worst I've seen in a PC release. It is incessantly common to experience multiple stutters within a few seconds of one another. There are occasional white banding artifacts from heavy occlusion-culling that can break immersion. There is also very noticeable ghosting that made me wonder if the QA testers even had eyes. Floating leaves, shoes, entire characters, whatever moves can and WILL cause ghosting artifacts on the ground and puddles that use Lumen reflections. It's very easy to see this when looking at the falling leaves to the right of the car in the opening cinematic. The fog looks great, pooling toward the ground in thick patches, but the ghosting is especially bad there. Whenever a character moves when the fog is in the background, they leave a very noticeable trail that is a very common issue with temporal anti-aliasing, but it also happens with DLSS. This fog ghosting also happens whenever you move the camera, making it impossible for me to get immersed. This visual bug is also present on the PS5 release. I guess some people are blind to it and think it's intentional, but it's a common enough issue with UE5 that it's disappointing to see. It's a real shame because I love Silent Hill and was really looking forward to this one, but I simply can't recommend this game in its current state.REVISION: I'm running on a 4090 and a i7-13700k. I didn't mention that because framerates are about what you'd expect from a UE5 game (running in DirectX 11 through "-dx11" in the launch options helps greatly). Traversal stutter occurs when an influx of assets are loaded onto the GPU at once, typically measurable through a sudden increase in VRAM usage. If traversal stutter exists (in this case it does), then it will ALWAYS happen at the same locations in-game on EVERY PC regardless of your PC configuration; you can't brute force through it with more powerful hardware. Unreal Engine has had this issue for decades; I remember it being an issue with the original Gears of War. Anyone saying, "it runs fine on my PC" is either used to poor PC versions of UE5 games or are blind to inconsistent frame pacing and stutters. Not calling anyone out, I wish I could also enjoy games regardless of technical issues. As an update after completing the game, the game is great but performance really sours it for me. Would definitely recommend once the PC version is in better shape.

_childDocuments_.review: Silent HIll 2 is a great survival horror game whose main faults are its authenticity to the original.  The visuals and sound design are fantastic, presenting a truly grotesque experience.  The puzzles are fun and I like the return of independent combat and puzzle difficulty.  The combat is fairly basic.  It works, but it has nothing on the combat of modern Resident Evil or Dead Space.  The boss fights are annoying at best and luckily few in number.  The second half of the game is spent almost entirely in complete darkness.  Not being able to see more than a few feet in front of you with your light on gets boring.  The criteria for the different endings seem to be arbitrary too.  Much of this is a fault of the original that should’ve been updated here.  Still a great game, just wish it felt a little less like a PS2 game at times.
_childDocuments_.name: SILENT HILL 2

_childDocuments_.review: The original Silent Hill 2 was one of my favorite games growing up. I rented it for PS2 from one of the early rent-by-mail companies (I forget the name exactly, it had "angel" in the name, pre-Gamefly) because of how cool it looked in GamePro previews. I ended up playing it from start to finish and was blown away. I ended up buying it again on Xbox along with SH3 and the first SH, but I never got into them like I did this game. It was just so odd and so engaging.When I heard that Silent Hill 2 was being remade I was intrigued. Konami had been a shell of itself for years ever since the release of Metal Gear Solid 5, largely being just a pachinko company instead of resembling the video game company I grew up playing dozens of games from. More intriguing was that Konami was partnering with Western gaming studios to help them make new video games. I hadn't played any of Bloober Team's games before, but I knew their reputation for making "walking simulator" games, and so I wondered how they would approach this remake.I ended up being pleasantly surprised by this remake. The art direction and sound direction are phenomenal. My first playthrough took almost 22 hours because I wanted to go anywhere I was allowed to on the map, inspecting every nook and cranny, just because of how damn cool everything looked. The remixed/remastered soundtrack by Akira Yamaoka is also excellent, with excellent themes during cutscenes and key moments, along with awesome ambient audio throughout the game that evokes various emotions of dread, mystery, fear, and sadness. The combat is very simple on paper, with a melee button and dodge button, along with a few ranged weapons later on. I never grew tired of combat, though, as it straddled the line exceptionally well between overpowered and annoying. With the dodge button you could theoretically dodge every attack in the game, but the mix-ups in enemy attack patterns along with the general atmosphere of encounters being calm to especially nerve-wracking made combat a welcome sight throughout to break up any potential monotony. I played on Hard combat and I never felt any encounter was too difficult to progress through, and instead getting through each combative section felt like I accomplished a feat thanks to being cautious and picking up the timing needed. I don't believe combat difficulty affects health pickups, either, and so by the end of the game as I had mostly mastered the combat I had something like 23 health drinks and 14 syringes saved up after not ignoring any enemies save for a couple frantic sections in the game where it throws a lot of enemies at you at once.The elephant in the room is the performance of this port: if you don't have the patience to tweak your settings to find your sweet spot then you'll get a frustrating experience. This is very much a "next-gen" game, but it is also not optimized well, and so if you want a smooth framerate then you'll need to tinker with settings as your performance in other recently-released games doesn't mean settings from those games will translate 1:1 to the same performance in this game. On launch there was very, very obvious traversal stutter, no frame generation, DLSS issues, and a puzzling 30 FPS cap on in-game cutscenes. Thankfully, a patch (and follow-up patch to that) was released that didn't fix , but made the game perform better than at launch and easier to tweak to hit high framerates without sacrificing too much fidelity. Traversal stutter still exists, but it either lessens further into the game or the patch mitigated it a bit compared to the 1.00 performance.Another interesting thing about this game is that it switches up various things in the original to keep things fresh, but also not to erase from the original (for the most part). I loved how they expanded the city of Silent Hill and the various "levels" throughout the game. I never got the feeling that I was playing through "padding", and instead it felt like the natural evolution of the original game with today's technology to expand environments. Also, the  boss sequence is probably the most horrifying and disturbing sequence I've ever played through in a game. While the original game had a lot of ambiguity (especially for a kid playing the game like I was lol), this game is less subtle in ways without insulting your intelligence in the process, and it makes for a very memorable and disturbing section in the game.One of the charms of the original SH2 was the weird, stilted dialogue that almost felt alien at times. I appreciated Bloober Team going a different route with this remake, instead taking advantage of modern tech to utilize emotion in faces to accentuate the excellent voice over performances. Everyone in the cast did an excellent job delivering their lines, and the motion capture is great. Differences in puzzles, items, and story beats were also handled well with the "memory fragments" or "echoes" throughout the game where you could find a location or item from the original SH2 that no longer is utilized in this remake to give a wink and nod to those that played the original. I also thought the puzzles & riddles were excellently done. They were challenging and made me think, but never made me frustrated where I felt I needed to check a guide. The nice thing is that solutions change based on the difficulty you choose, which can freshen the experience up in multiple playthroughs.Speaking of which, it was cool to see that all of the original endings from SH2 return in this game, with some slight differences in each, along with two additional endings. There's also some new collectibles like the strange photographs along with new and remixed notes/memos from the original that also are fun to seek out. Besides the uneven technical performance in the game, there were some changes that I didn't think were great, but also didn't ultimately sour my experience in the game. I miss the videos during the credits that the original had based on what ending you got, as in this remake you always get the same text-only credits sequence with only the music differing based on what ending you got. There was also a poignant moment towards the end of the game where in the original SH2  while in this game  which just comes off as silly and unnecessary. I also didn't like how we aren't given  and you don't get to use . At least the new game+  is there, and it's needed for one of the new endings, so it's not all bad.Overall, I am very happy with this release. I hope its success leads to Konami green-lighting "Born From a Wish" DLC for this game, and I would love to see how Bloober Team could expand upon that original mini scenario since it was so short in the original game's Xbox and PS2 Greatest Hits release. I would also love to see a remake of the first Silent Hill to see how either Bloober Team or another team could tackle that challenge. Konami seems to be very enthusiastic on expanding the Silent Hill IP, so while I didn't care for Ascension, I'm interested to see what comes of the upcoming Silent Hill f and Silent Hill: Townfall. But please, Konami, after how great this game was, give us more remakes in addition to new Silent Hill games.Highly recommended for anyone that is a fan of the Silent Hill series, horror games, and adventure games.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought after some progression and exploration I'd give a brief but clear review. I'm a fan of the OG games, and I have respect when someone wants to make changes while still paying homage to the feel, atmosphere of the core essence of what came before. The game does a great job of retaining the isolated feeling of Restless Dreams, the score by Akira Yamaoka is still very much haunting, beautiful and melancholic and amplifies the gameplay and overall feeling by miles. While I obviously haven't finished the game cause I want to slowly engange in the foggy nightmare of suffering, fear and sadness, I with what I've experienced so far, would recommend this to newcomers, oldschool fans of the OG. Also a short round up of the GOOD and the BAD:- THE GOOD: - Gameplay mechanics, newly implemented like breaking car windows to get items.- The world is more free to explore, more buildings and places than before.- Excellent score by Akira Yamaoka, absolutely breathtaking and relaxing.- Stunning visuals and various options in the main menu to somewhat change the look of the game.- JAMES IS VERY CUTE :3- The overall atmosphere in indoor areas is especially chilling.- Even small details like puddles, the reflections and leafes flying around in front of James are so pretty to look at.- Mrs.Legs is so funny standing motionless in a corner :D Ah...THE BAD:- Honestly for me not so major but the performance could be better in certain situations like entering new areas or when coming face to face with a monster...there are issues with stuttering (microstutters) when you're about to hit a Lying figure for instance, and opening some doors, or when breaking windows to gather items. The performance isn't so bad  that it always drops low but it's frequent and awkward when in combat with multiple enemies (it's nothing horrendous like other games) but it still needs to be adressed in a future patch. With that being said, it's currently definitely very playable but I just wanted to mention it since it's the only "bad" thing I consider. I still think very highly of the game and will continue to enjoy it for a long time.Cheers ^^

_childDocuments_.review: One of the main biggest fears I had about Silent Hill 2 being remade was the botched remixes of the original music, which unfortunately indeed did happen.. some songs from the original Silent Hill 2 soundtrack made appearances without any changes but other songs like Heavens Night & Magdalene had a complete overhaul rearrangement, it made me a bit disappointed truthfully, because I think the classic soundtrack didn't need anymore tweaks whatsoever, it is as perfect as it is. Besides that small little speck, the acting overall is great, the gameplay is phenomenal, including the improved combat system. the game did in fact get a lot more lengthier due to puzzles being in random spots and a bit more puzzle fillers that weren't in the original game in general. So if you had any intentions of speed running this game like classic Silent Hill 2, you'll be caught off guard on your first playthrough Bloober Team has proven to us they can get the job done, so I hope Konami has a agreement with them on remaking the rest of the Tokyo developments, especially Silent Hill 4: THE ROOM. No matter what though, nothing can ever recapture the true essence and aesthetic of the original Silent Hill 2. I still prefer playing it over this one, but for new Silent Hill fans who are trying to get their feet wet, or just someone simply craving another modern Silent Hill experience after playing Silent Hill: Downpour, than this is RIGHT up your alley.

_childDocuments_.review: Silent Hill 2 Remake is a masterful blend of modern graphics and classic horror elements, creating an experience that both honors its origins and leverages contemporary technology. The remake beautifully captures the advanced graphical capabilities of today's generation, with stunningly detailed environments, lifelike character models, and atmospheric lighting that enhances the eerie ambiance.However, what truly sets this remake apart is its ability to evoke the same sense of dread and unease that defined the original game. The developers have meticulously preserved the unsettling sound design, haunting music, and psychological horror elements that made Silent Hill 2 a cult classic. The remake doesn't just rely on visual fidelity but also ensures that the core essence of horror and creepiness remains intact.In conclusion, Silent Hill 2 Remake is a testament to how modern advancements can be harmoniously integrated with classic game design. It provides a visually striking experience while maintaining the spine-chilling atmosphere that fans of the original have cherished for years. This balance makes it a standout title in the realm of horror games.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, it's pretty good.I have a few things to address :As per usual, some people lie about performance.Sure there are a few stutters but barely.Performance is okay otherwise.With settings on mid, the game runs well, i noticed (because of an fps counter) a drop to 58fps for a second or two. That is not 10-25fps lost very often as some pretend.All my specs are on my profile. Some of this folks, of course, have a far better rig than i do and supposedly get faaaaaaaaar bigger issues, far more often than me.To be polite, i'll call... nonsense on that. Konami having killed one of (if not the biggest) stealth franchise is no excuse to lie.--------------------Story remains faithful enough to the 2001 classic.However, we are getting a new ending. Maria is a bit more slutty and Angela is far more believable.Portrayal of characters changed a bit in a good way. They feel more alive.Gameplay has been massively modernized (ik, it sounds scary). What i mean is that it is closer to the Resident Evil 2&4 remakes (not like the utter disgrace Resident Evil 3 is). You don't have an added upgrade system, you are not getting boring fetch-quests... Nothing of the sort. The new dodge and melee is snappy and accompanied by a very satisfying feedback in both the visual and audio department. Difficulty is satisfying thankfully.Graphics aren't mindblowing but they do the job quite well. The dynamic fog is not bad but less thick than in the OG. I think it should have been thicker... on the other hand, it looks more realistic. As i wrote in the story section, characters are mostly improved, partly with new facial animation mostly on point. Maria and Angie still have their distasteful haircuts though.However, it is not a perfect remake :Performance is okay but a few bugs remain.UE5 may not have been the go-to but bloober team still did decent work.The game is quite demanding, a bit more than i expected...Framerate is stable once you find the right settings.One final note, this game might not be what it seems.Play the 2001 PS2 version before this. It will help you formulate your own questions bout the nature of this entry.Story : 10/10Gameplay : 9.5/10Graphics : 8.5/10Performance : 6/10Total : 8.5/10While a good remake, i will not consider it for awards.First off because of Konami's actions and this being a remake.Be thankful for the money and f*** off.Keep up the good work Bloober Team.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's my review: A rotund and utter success at capturing the visual essence of the original game while translating it into modern graphics. The scenery looks absolutely stunning from start to finish, the characters look insanely detailed and the monsters perfectly capture and recontextualize their bizarre grotesqueness in great detail. Another straight win for the game, the sound effects and ambience are absolute ear candy. Furthermore, a huge number of sound effects have been repurposed from the original game, so keen ears or those who have played the original recently might pick up on them. Nothing bleeds Silent Hill like Akira Yamaoka's music does. Having him back on the team was the absolute best choice they could make regarding the soundtrack. His reimagination of the original tracks are wonderfully tasteful, although I wish a couple of them made it into the remake, like A World Of Madness or Alone In The Town. Pretty much all of the sequences and pathing have been completely reimagined in a way that doesn't conflict with the map layouts of the original game. This not only offers a whole new experience for people who have already played the original, but also offers a more concise sense of flow and progression through the levels. The fact that they also kept several references to things that were changed from the original, like old puzzles or segments, is a nice detail for keen eyes. The gameplay itself is pretty good. Exploration is smooth and quick to the point, not having to interact with the doors to check if they are locked is great and the "parkour" points allow for more dynamic and intricate level designs. As for the combat, it feels impactful and violent, but also fluid thanks to the dodge, as a whole the combat isn't complicated enough to be overbearing. I was surprised to see the dialogue was largely kept the same except for some needed changes. Along with the great voice acting, the conversations between characters no longer feel as awkward as in the original, granted there are some moments that still feel a bit weird, but not out of place. The game runs quite acceptably on my laptop, in some very specific moments it dropped to about 20 fps for some seconds then went back to unlimited, I assume to load something in the background. I also had a couple of moments where the game lightly stuttered, but at no point it became prominent, overall the performance was good. The thing that definitely impressed me the most about the performance is that there are absolutely no loading screens other than the one you see when loading a save, other than that, the game is completely seamless. That would be the full extent of my review, overall it has been a superb experience and I'm really hoping Konami and Blubber work together again to remake Silent Hill 3, as I think it would make for an astonishing game the same way this remake has been.I hope this review has been of help.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually write game reviews, but this one truly deserves recognition. As a lifelong fan of Silent Hill, the series holds a special place in my heart. While I never got the chance to finish any of the original games as a kid, as I would often get stuck when I played them. I have a lot of fond memories of those experiences.When this remake was announced, I was both thrilled and skeptical. I had heard mixed opinions about Bloober Team, with some claiming they were known for producing "mid-tier" games. However, I did not expect a remake of this quality.Exploration and Level DesignThe exploration in this game is phenomenal. The level design, meshes, environmental effects, textures, and lighting are simply unmatched. Every corner, room, hallway, and any part of the map, really, is ridiculously well done. There isn’t a single moment that takes you out of the immersive world. It’s been a long time since I’ve seen such attention to detail and quality in a game.Audio and Visual ExcellenceThe voice acting is superb, with every line delivered with authenticity. The sound design complements the atmosphere perfectly, and the soundtrack is a masterpiece on its own. While I do have a preference for some of the original tracks, the new ones still hold their own. The facial animations, both in gameplay and cutscenes, are top-notch, I was very surprised.Combat and AnimationIf I had to point out a minor flaw, it would be in the animations, particularly during combat. Some of the transitions between actions feel a bit off, and certain animations lack the weight they should have. However, these issues are forgivable in the grand scheme of things and don’t significantly detract from the overall experience.Story and CharactersThe story is dark, deep, and emotionally resonant. Watching the development and eventual fate of each character is captivating and heartbreaking. The narrative is incredibly well done,  keeping you engaged throughout.Final ThoughtsOverall, I give this game a solid 10/10. It’s a REALLY long, rich experience—I spent about 19 hours playing through it, and that doesn’t even include the multiple endings you can unlock. Bloober Team has truly outdone themselves, creating an unforgettable experience that has earned a spot among my favorite games.I am not happy with the ending I got, so i'll most probably try to unlock all of them anyway.Bravo, Bloober Team!
_childDocuments_.name: SILENT HILL 2

_childDocuments_.review: Fans of the original Silent Hill 2 should have a glorious time with the remake, and newcomers will find a highly competent third-person survival horror game with tremendous narrative intrigue. The remake preserves the original’s story practically verbatim, and it is probably the game’s biggest strength. New and decent adventure tasks help to make the game substantially longer, and combat alterations bring it closer to that popular series from Capcom. Unfortunately the action is a little plain given the lack of weapons and limited enemy types. And the performance stutters are a shame given the high quality visuals and captivating atmosphere. We have seen a few strong remakes already, each taking their own route, so it will be interesting to see what comes out of the fog next.

_childDocuments_.review: Am a long time fan of Silent Hill. I received this game as a gift on my birthday which also happens to be the same day it released on Oct. 7th. WITHOUT A DOUBT the scariest game I've EVER played and I've played a LOT of games including Silent Hill 1-3 and The Room. If you're a Silent Hill fan or like a good horror you will NOT be disapointed! The game, for me has also been more or less 100% stable. No crashes, no glitches, no visual errors or sound problems. More or less a FLAWLESS game and I have been playing since release! DEAR KONAMI AND BLOOPER TEAM: Please please please, do a Silent Hill 1 and 3 remake, starting with SH1. You guys are doing GOD'S WORK for the series and fans alike. Please remaster the entire TRILOGY!
_childDocuments_.name: SILENT HILL 2

_childDocuments_.review: Despite not recommending the game I actually think it's pretty good. The atmosphere is top notch and can be quite unnerving at times. Objectively speaking, I'd say the game is quite good for the right player.For me, though, I just can't get over the obtuse and tedious puzzles. Especially the poem puzzles. I've seen them in other games and I just absolutely hate everything about them. I spent way too much time backtracking trying to figure out if I missed something before finally looking up a guide and realize I needed to complete the puzzle that I thought I didn't have all the items for. Or I would get to a puzzle and find flaws in it that because of my interpretation made it completely impossible to complete.There's one section with a bunch of coins where you have to solve a riddle and place the coins in the correct order to complete the puzzle. The first part suggests the direction that the woman coin is facing is important but then the second part tells you the woman should be running away from the man but you have to place her facing backwards like she's running away backwards. That makes no sense at all.Honestly, if it wasn't for those puzzles I'd probably have really enjoyed the game.
_childDocuments_.name: SILENT HILL 2

_childDocuments_.review:
Having received a letter from his deceased wife, James heads to where they shared so many memories, in the hope of seeing her one more time: Silent Hill. There, by the lake, he finds a woman eerily similar to her...

"My name...is Maria," the woman smiles. Her face, her voice... She's just like her.

Experience a master-class in psychological survival horror - lauded as the best in the series - on the latest hardware with chilling visuals and visceral sounds.

name: Loop8: Summer of Gods
detailed_description: Loop8: Summer of Gods Digital Deluxe Edition Loop8: Summer of Gods 'Digital Deluxe Edition' Contents: Loop8: Summer of Gods game Digital soundtrack with 23 songs Digital artbook "Ashihara Town Guide" (English) About the Game Your choices shape the world in this coming-of-age RPG set in 1980s rural Japan. Step into the life of Nini, a newly earthbound teen who arrives in the quaint Japanese town of Ashihara in August 1983. Explore the town, befriend its people, and face off against the Kegai in turn-based battles where the outcomes depend on the relationships you’ve built and the decisions you’ve made. Use Nini’s special connection to the gods to reset the world, with each loop allowing Nini and his allies to relive the 8th month over and over until they get it right...or the Kegai overcome them entirely. With one month until the world ends, how will you spend each day? Live an Ordinary Life, Fight Extraordinary Enemies Build bonds with Ashihara's residents while protecting the town from the ever-present threat of the Kegai, repeating the cycle to uncover how your everyday actions impact your battles in the Underworld, and vice versa. A Picturesque View of Rural Japan Your adventure takes place in a nostalgic and beautifully recreated snapshot of a rural Japanese townscape. Head downtown to recharge at a local restaurant, or hang out at the shops to strengthen your bonds with other characters. Relive the Past to Alter the Future Though the deadline for humanity's extinction draws ever closer, Ashihara's fate remains in your hands. Repeatedly return to the start of August, alter your actions, and see how they turn the tides of destiny across multiple endings. Choices That Can Change the World Loop8’s emotion-driven AI system responds to every action you take and decision you make. Characters’ emotions and stories will vary greatly based on your choices, making each playthrough wholly unique.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop8: Summer of Gods animated intro actually starts off promising. This is also the first introduction of the Kegai. They are monsters that resemble natural disasters and threaten to destroy mankind. The Space Station, where our protagonist Nini grew up, even served as a place to retreat to in the intervening years. Now that the station has fallen apart, the part-time astronaut is forced to return to Earth, or more precisely, to the tranquil village of Ashihara.There, you'll meet villagers, who, due to the complete lack of other NPCs, seem to be the only ones going about their lives here. They stand out mainly because of their strange backstories. For example, there's the protagonist's grandmother, who not only completely ignores her relatives, but also looks and talks like a woman in her mid-20s. Or the teacher, who tries to replace his dead sister with a homemade robot who looks like a middle-schooler and also attends Nini's class.There are also various references to the mysteries surrounding Kegai and Nini's family, as well as the character's claim to be a godfighter or god himself. Unfortunately, none of this is ever explained in the context of the narrative. The plot, which lasts for roughly 17 hours, doesn't change this at all. As a result, the superficial conflict between good and evil persists, drawing Nini in as an apparent outsider and driving him to fight for humanity's survival. The locals of Ashihara don't talk much, but you can invite the characters to different places, like a café, for example.The majority of the time, you'll hear pointless phrases before being forced to pick between a number of options like "get to know them better" or even the brave "tease them," which results in a courteous word of gratitude and increased friendship, affection, or hate. As a result, the game more closely resembles a dull status simulator than a visual novel because the interactions with the various people are purely about improving your relationship values rather than engaging in meaningful conversations.So you must choose one of the three aforementioned social values with which to carry out your attack in battle. However, the differences are too small to talk about tactics here. So the actually interesting concept can't push the combat system beyond monotonous button-pressing. In addition, you do not have any control over your party members in a fight. They will just do what they want, and this can quickly lead to game over. The few battles Loop8 has to offer also take far too long—an odd contrast given the lack of complexity and depth. Also, be prepared to have the same enemy in normal battles throughout the whole game without any variation.On the other side, you can enhance combat-specific qualities like strength, agility, or intelligence when you aren't clicking through uninteresting cliché structures to raise your social stats. You do this by interacting with selected locations throughout Ashihara. The rest of the town, however, is nothing more than beautiful scenery. On the main street, you can find a restaurant and a café where you can regenerate your energy and stamina. Otherwise, there is not a single spark of a living game world in the entire village.A bigger issue with Loop8: Summer of Gods than the characters meaningless dialogue, the lack of variation, and the repetitive action is the game's fundamental idea. You are forced to repeatedly experience the month of August because you are caught in a time loop. Once game over and you go back to August 1st, where you encounter Ashihara's residents again.When a loop is completed, not only is your progress reset, but your relationships, emotional states, and character values will be reset as well. The only exception are the so-called blessings, which can be found at certain locations in Ashihara and permanently increase your stats, so it's worth visiting these places again and again just to read the same text phrases over and over again. On the other hand, regular conversations with other characters or interaction with such a location, while a character is on your team, will grant character-specific blessings that will then strengthen your team members.At least the presentation of Loop8: Summer of Gods doesn't have to hide behind the wooden animations of the characters in battle and everyday life. The backgrounds are picturesque and capture the atmosphere of a small Japanese village in the hot midsummer splendidly. A few flower petals sailing through the air also brighten up the static images. A soft soundtrack also accompanies your walks through Ashihara. All that's missing for the perfect summer feeling are the chirping birds and the pleasant sound of the waves. Additional flair is provided by the dubbing, which is available in Japanese as well as English and is performed by talented voice actors. It's a double pity that only some of the texts were dubbed.Loop8: Summer of Gods was something I was actually looking forward to. On paper, the digital short vacation in Ashihara read like an entertaining title for in-between times, with its gameplay mix of turn-based battles and dialog-heavy cast of characters reminiscent of Persona. However, an extremely boring gameplay loop is hidden behind the picturesque facade: A Kegai sneaks into Ashihara, you have five days to prepare by boringly increasing your stats and deepening your relationships with the townspeople with meaningless dialog, and finally you have to slog through a dark parallel world and a turn-based slideshow before the threat starts all over again. The context of the time loop only adds to the monotony. The 17 hours it took me to complete the game were one of the toughest experiences I've had in a long time. The well-done summer atmosphere of the village, the visually impressive art style, and your decisions about the number of available characters are unfortunately not enough to pull you out of the vortex of monotony.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not fun. Don't buy it. Don't play it. It is EXTREMELY slow. Loading screens happen every 5 seconds. 85% of the gameplay is waiting for the game to let you press the A button to advance a dialogue. It takes 15 seconds -- literally, fifteen seconds -- to complete ONE of the mood-boosting dialogues. You have to do this hundreds of times. There is no gameplay except waiting to press the A button.Oh, I almost forgot: Your dialogues are RNG. They have a substantial chance of failure. In that case you just wasted 15 seconds of your life, and then an additional 15 seconds required to do a successful dialogue to push their stats back to where they were before the failure. With Loop8 you are sucking your life away for no gain.Your character moves extremely slowly. In regular gameplay you have fast travel to alleviate this. But once you get to the dungeons, you have no choice but to walk on foot, and your slowness makes itself known. The combat system is very simple, there is almost no brainpower required to succeed. If you fail it's because your stat numbers were too low, not because you could have strategized better.If you lose, the game world resets and prestiges.  The problem is you still have to suffer through every character's mandatory dialogue, which takes literally 15+ minutes per character, because each dialogue takes 15 seconds and they have dozens of lines and need dozens of prep talks.When other reviews talked about grinding, I assumed it would be like doing a lot of battles. That's not it. I don't know who thought this was fun. It's awful. And it's overpriced.Don't buy it. Don't play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Loop8 is an awe-inspiring anomaly when it comes to game design and execution. You have a neat idea: come live in a cozy town for the summer whilst navigating relationships and saving the world. If you thought "isn't that just Persona 4 but only one month?" then you'd technically be right in your assumption, but Loop8 is at an astronomically lower depth than simply "Persona at home". No, it commits the one fatal sin of any media: being mind-numbingly boring.The main character, Novus Nemo... or, Nini for short, is blander than un-toasted toast. He's a shell of what an AI imagines a real human behaves like, with non-dialogue and an expression that screams "I'm trying to imitate life, is it working?" He came to Ashihara to live with his cousin (once-removed, very important) after his parents... uh, died? I guess? I don't actually think it's mentioned why he's even there in the first place. The fact of the matter is, the only actual plot occurs in the first few minutes and it all goes downhill from there. What strikes me the most is that the opening cutscene music video is probably the best part of the game. The visuals look good and it almost feels like it's going to be interesting. They even show locations that you never see in the game itself! But, soon enough... you realize, that it's all smoke and mirrors, and the actual content of the game is shallower than a puppy's piss puddle. So Nini arrives in Ashihara and meets his cousin, Konoha, and she gets him acquainted with the town. Standard stuff, and the music and backgrounds are very pleasant. After day one of Konoha giving you the tour, your second day is spent giving you a bit of freedom to check out the town's various activities. Unfortunately, here's where the trouble begins, because this game runs on a time system, not unlike Persona, but instead of time only passing when you do an activity, it also ticks by every second you're in the overworld at all, and this can lead to some complications. What, you thought they'd pause the timer during your second day to get acquainted with where everything is? HAH! NO! On day 2, you're dumped in front of the schoolyard and told to attend supplementary lessons, but the game doesn't tell you AT ALL where that is inside the building. So you run across the schoolyard and... oh no, is that really Nini's top speed? A comfortable jog? It takes about 6 agonizing seconds for him to walk from the school entrance to the building. And no, despite him blazing around on foot in the intro, he never does that here. Not even in the combat zones! A ♥♥♥♥♥♥, comfortable jog like he just dumped ass for the entire. Game. The lessons are on the second floor in class 1-A, the first of only two enterable classrooms. I actually took too long to get there and the game gave up and warped me to the room. Absolutely amazing. You get some more cutscenes and it all seems fine. The tutorial that comes next is to play around on the iron bars in the schoolyard, and thankfully that one's easy to follow! Mostly because there's nothing else in the schoolyard. It's just a big, empty space that you cross on foot every time you enter the school. Awesome. After the tutorial to receive a blessing at the shrine, you rendezvous with Konoha to learn about the relationship mechanic. Your only option for her is "Get to know better", with Nini thinking to himself "I just know this'll work", so you select it, and Konoha just says "Thank you!". And that's it. Then a screen pops up that shows the relationship between the two characters. Afterwards, the game tells you to try eating at the restaurant. But again, they don't show you where it is, it doesn't stand out, and time continues to tick on by. You are left to flounder around while being forced to run at the slowest speed imaginable. It's AGONIZING. That night, Nini sees a vision of a Kegai (the mythical monsters), breaking through the barrier and entering Ashihara. When you wake up the next day, the game deadass says "An entrance to Yomotsu Hirasaka (the shadow version of Ashihara) has appeared in the shrine. Nini can somehow sense this." Even the game has NO EXPLANATION as to how Nini is even a protagonist. You go there and meet up with Beni and Ichika, two girls from your class who have experience fighting the Kegai. And this is just a big tease because the game makes it out to be like they're going to be easily accessible to fight with, but no, not at all. Then, you get a battle tutorial, and if you thought that the framerate wasn't distracting before, then it kicks into overdrive here, especially with Beni. While the devs call it "artistic choice", I'm inclined to call it "we don't know how to fix this and we're all out of ideas, so just call it artistic." If you're photosensitive enough, it'll give you a headache.Anyway, the tutorial battle makes it seem like the game has depth. But no, there is no depth, it's all useless. Battles in this game all boil down to numbers. If your numbers are high enough, you win. Though I should mention that the only REAL "depth" of the combat is that attacking with friendship is neutral damage, affection is weaker but lowers the enemy's attack, and hate is the strongest but builds up to make your enemies stronger. So most of the time, you'll be using friendship, MAYBE affection if the boss you happen to be fighting goes higher than threat level 1. Also, you can't control your party members, and outside of this tutorial, if anyone dies in battle, they CANNOT be revived and you will be locked out of the true ending. So... you know... better to just run the game solo. Bringing others along will just slow you down. So much for the power of friendship!The tutorial fight ends with a boss you can't defeat, so you wipe and get a soft game over, or a loop. You might think, "oh, so the loop will tie into the narrative now and get the ball rolling?" Hahaha, no. No, silly child. The only thing looping is good for is to go back to the beginning of the month. And to also get to read all the dialogue you read before, see all the scenes you saw before, and relive all that ♥♥♥♥ you just went through. NO ONE remembers the loops. Not the other characters, not Nini, no one. Mercifully, your stats DO carry over, so really the only point of looping is to get strong enough to defeat a boss if you couldn't before. Your relationship with the characters doesn't either, but it DOES get put on steroids so it will get to its former value in half the time. It's a juiced up NG+. But uh... that's it. That's the flow of the game. It's broken into 5-day cycles. On the second or third day of the 5-day cycle, a non-combatant character will be kidnapped by the Kegai, and it's up to you to boost Nini's stats and go rescue them. (There's 5 of these, and then the final boss.) I just hope you accurately predicted who is getting kidnapped first, because without enough friendship with them, Nini simply kills them and they die, so you'll be forced to loop. So really, the beginning of the game is where you'll loop the most, trial-and-erroring until you get high enough friendship with the first victim to avoid killing them. Also, if you need to bring a companion in to pass a friendship/affection trial to reach the boss, you should probably avoid bringing someone who has a poor relationship with the kidnapped, because that strengthens the boss and your companion will likely die. That is THE ONLY level of strategy that really exists going into boss fights. Your main focus is just buffing your stats, boosting your relationship with the upcoming victim, and mingling with the characters that fight on the side. Actually, I just saved after each successful boss and then slept for 2-3 days in a row to see the future of who would be kidnapped and then reload and focus on them, lol.All the girls are thirsty for Nini too, despite being his cousin and even his Grandmother. Yep. I hit the character limit. The game sucks. Do not waste your money.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: The game is a time management sim where you take your best friends into the underworld to beat up the people you didn't make friends with. In-game, every week presents an underworld encounter with one boss. In the 8 hours I've got logged as of writing, I've actually entered combat fewer than 5 times.Very little by way of unique dialogue, animations are nonexistent for character interactions (even during cutscene events!)They went with a "true" groundhog day scenario type deal.By "true," I'm referring to the fact that you, the player, experience everything again. Every intro cutscene [there are 6 on your first day], every exposition dump [there are 50+ dialogue boxes associated with repeated information that you'll be skipping over with every loop], and every character interaction.Despite dumping hours of lore to the player, they decided to leave the combat system ambiguous. As previously stated, most of the game is boosting relationship and stat points, so while this issue isn't high impact, I'd like to know why it is I'm mashing "A" to "get to know" somebody.Stat increases and character interactions are the focus of the game. As for why they neglected even a minimal amount of polish for these activities is beyond me. They did an OK job with the aesthetics of the combat. The music for the overworld is determined by the "mood," which is largely determined by time of day, activities available, and the characters present (and their relationships with one another). The music is NOT synced to anything that's actually happening in game, so there are some jarring tonal shifts where the peppy "normal mood" music kicks in after the protag shoots a 1 minute monologue about how he got one of his friends killed.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This is absolutely not a finished product, it's a concept pitch for a game that has a price tag.The idea of the game is simply this: You move into a Japanese town and you have the power to see yokai and people's inner thoughts. Time loops during the month of August and a yokai occassionally breaches the town and possesses someone who is stressed and sad about something. Some of the civilians can fight and some are aware of the time loops. You have to talk to people to increase friendship affection and hate parameters which each have different affinities in battle and increase your own stats to fight in the underworld when someone gets possessed.Almost none of the story elements in the game has a scenario that plays out. You are from a space colony that orbits Earth and 80% of the population is secluded to small areas that are protected by barriers from the yokai that destroyed the world. All that is not relevant, you just ride a train to town and all the civilians comment occasionally that you're from space and that everyone is trapped. You increase parameters by picking dialogue options with people that show favorable odds of success and all of them (Greet, Flirt, whatever) that don't raise hate just have them thank you unless it's an event where you take them somewhere. When you go to save someone, it's just a bunch of stat checks and few encounters walking through an inverted version of town to gain access to the boss and when you defeat them, depending on if you have the right friendship levels with the person you battled, if you get the option to not kill them. During all of that there's small scenes where they talk about their feelings and everyone mostly doesn't acknowledge what happened, nobody panics when someone disappears and aren't very sad if someone dies. There are very little cutscenes in the game.I completed a playthrough by just spamming favorable dialogue with the party members I wanted, kept going across town each day to all the hidden blessing locations that permanently increase stats for the save file, and focused on 2 choices of the potential 5 party members that would make the battles easiest and beat the last boss in 2 or 3 loops.I see what the game is supposed to be but it's just skipping through generic dialogue responses for 80% of the playthrough and I'm disappointed that I didn't get to have sex with the teacher.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fascinating in that it presents interesting ideas for how the "social life" part of RPGs that is kind of typical to the contemporary setting JRPG but unfortunately the execution is so baffling that I can't imagine some of this stuff is even working right let alone working to how it was envisioned on paper.like you talk to a girl for 10 minutes and she decides you are now dating and then you get a blessing every time you talk to her for the next 20 minutes of clicking through dialogue after which she has become God's Strongest Warrior. It's hilarious, but also *completely* baffling.if it kept up that kind of baffling energy all the time it'd be at least funny but the moments where the social system produces really bizarre interactions are spread over hours of just clicking on the same menus over and over again to make numbers go up in probably the most insipid way possible. You can occasionally see a spark of an interesting idea sometimes but it always manages to tragically end up being the most boring version of itself possible. this review is kind of a mess but the short version is that Loop8 is bad, but like, Fascinating Bad and a bit Boring Bad rather than like Evil Bad. An attempt was made and sometimes it's hard to even see what was being attempted, but at any rate, it really doesn't work at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Hard to recommend. Definitely wait till it's on sale for around $30 or less. Now I haven't beaten the game yet, but if anything changes from the 7 hours I've played if it so far in the future I'll change the review accordingly.The game has a lot of interesting ideas, soundtrack is good, environment is gorgeous, voice acting is great, and the characters are memorable for the most part. However, while it has a good concept going for it with the relationship and stats systems it fails to really do much with it other than stat boosts. So the game quickly becomes a stat grinder.The characters, while they will comment on your progress with other characters; the town feels pretty dead since these are the only characters that exist there, no background characters or even silhouettes indicating there are other people living there and they don't interact very often in big ways. No group activities, get togethers, or festivals. It all feels self contained between you and that character.While playing I did find myself really wanting a sprint button of some kind since the casual jog was a bit too slow for me.I'm not sure if it was a stylistic choice or not but the low framerate animations on the models bugged me. It didn't bother me too much in the "overworld" but the animations look really bad in battle. Largely just makes the animations look like the game is lagging during the fights.All in all, what I'd say is I'd like to see more relationship content and more reactive content with the characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: The map/battle animations are kind of choppy in a netflix anime kind of way, and there's some obvious jank that could leave a bad first impression. But I'm having a pretty good time just grinding stats in a comfy anime town, feels nice.Edit: A few more notes on what to expect, the JRPG combat isn't much of a focus outside of specifically boss fights and is pretty much just a stat/relationship check. Improving relationships and stats unlocks more powerful skills and increases max HP/MP.Party members act on their own, but their battle AI works well.Since the bosses (at least the ones i've seen so far) are all possessed characters, a big part of preparing for them is social manipulation tactics and making sure you have party members that are:1. strong enough to survive the fight,2. Good enough friends/rivals that they will use support skills on each other and,3.  don't hate the possessed character too much. Hatred can give a power boost to the boss and can get out of hand pretty fast.Because of this, the game mostly revolves around stalking friends with your magic eyes to take advantage of their moods for mad stat/relationship gains, hunting down blessings for stat buffs that carry across loops (fixed interaction points on maps alone or with a friend, bonuses from viewing special character interactions, and as rewards for earning a talisman (keys to the boss room.)The tension from having to keep pushing back doomsday as more characters are possessed, and playing around the moods and schedules of the AI keep things hectic and engaging, and between  that, seeing numbers go up, and pretty enjoyable character interactions, its a pretty enjoyable experience for the main meat of the game.There are a lot of rough points and a lack of some quality of life features. The protagonist doesn't really keep memories between loops, and you'll have to sit through a lot of repeated dialogue and the default window size cropped out the key prompts showing that there actually has been a fast forward toggle the whole time. The keyboard controls for the menus are strange and take some getting used to, And the way events work in order to accommodate the AI world/character simulation the game revolves around can make for some strange interactions.On the other hand you get double stat gains as a catch up bonus on new loops until you reach your personal best, and the permanent blessings mean you can maintain a pretty good baseline for any character you invest time in.All and all I would say this is a very unique and interesting game that can reward someone willing to explore it and play a bit past the tutorial, and the bad first impression they'll probably have.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Loop8 might be the funniest game I've ever played. Is it good? No. Is it fun? Sometimes, but never for the right reasons. But I can't deny that while playing it, the strange mixture of how the game handles how it tells you it's story, along with the baffling combat system didn't make me laugh. You should play it, but not to enjoy it traditionally. After all, hay is for horses.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I thought that this game would be a good contender against the Persona franchise. And boy how wrong I was for thinking this. The game is not horrible, but gameplay is mediocre. The relationship system is just another by number system, the story is non existing and visuals are nothing to write about. The time loop system only existe to waist your time and create a false sense of depth.  This game would be a 6/10 even if it was at a lower price, but as it is I would say that is a 4/10. I don’t recommend this game until it drops down to $15-$20 dollars.

_childDocuments_.review: Not the greatest JRPG, but still a nice game. It's very relaxing increasing relationships stats, trying to improve from your previous "loop", and a battle system where your relationship stats are key. If you fail, you can do it all again in another "loop." Not worth the $50 price tag, but if it goes on sale for around $30 I'd definitely recommend getting. Pros: Great relationship system that consists of friendship, affection, and hate. You might feel friendly towards someone and the other doesn't like you at all and will treat you as such. Excellent voice acting in both the Japanese and English dubs.Good soundtrack that I enjoy listening to.Cons: Can be repetitive having to relive the same month.Battle system a tad boring with the other two in your party acting on their own.In the English dub, the mouth still moves considerably after the line had finished. Very noticeable and slightly jarring. Overall I'll give it a 7/10 for now. I'm enjoying it so far and am looking forward to playing it more. Definitely not for everyone though.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of SteinsGate and Tokyo Revengers, Loop 8: Summer of Gods manages to hit the time loop trope perfectly; even when you think you have all the answers, there is potentially another factor that you might have missed that throws a wrench into your plans. The game does not hold back the punches by having the player find out the game's mechanics on their own rather than having their handheld. The game's combat system and friendship system can take a while to get used to and the game's AI can be a headache. On one hand, it is nice not having to control everything in battle, but on the other, some of the choices that are made can be infuriating.When it comes to each character in the game, they all have their own unique personalities and emotions. Each character has their own likes and dislikes that impact their relationship with you and other characters. Losing a character due to death in the underworld can be heartbreaking, but makes you want to do a new loop in order to save them. Each character has so many reactions based on their bond with the player creating a variety of responses. This makes it so that you will want to replay the game in order to learn more about a character.Our biggest complaint comes down to the inability to adjust the game's settings outside of visuals. Honestly, it would have been nice to turn off certain character voice lines or make it so every character has fully voiced lines. The voice acting within the game was enjoyable, but after you heard it once, it is fine to skip it on the next go around.Loop 8: Summer of Gods is an enjoyable game but it is not for everyone. If you are a fan of strong narratives, then I recommend picking it up. If you are a fan of traditional JRPGs then it might be better to watch some gameplay first. Full Review:

_childDocuments_.review:
Eight months after hope for humanity was destroyed...

Nini, the protagonist who lost his home and family to the ancient calamity known as the "Kegai," arrives at the peaceful countryside town of Ashiharanakatsu to stay with his mother's relatives.

In this town where everyday life and the extraordinary intertwine, Nini's radiant and stressful summer begins.

LOOP8 is a juvenile RPG in which you live your "everyday life" and fight "the extraordinary." Live a summer all your own while forging relationships with the people around you, while fighting calamities known as "Kegai."

The game's unique emotional artificial intelligence, the "Maturity System," controls all aspects of the game's progress, and the character's emotions and stories are constantly shifting. Each "choice" you make influences the game's world, offering a different experience every time you play.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a blast! Whether I'm dying or clearing a run, I'm constantly drawn back for another round. The urge to discover new builds and unlock items through the quest system keeps the game play fresh and exciting. With ample content and clever item synergies, this game promises a long-lasting and varied experience.The game mixes fast-paced action with turn-based strategy, offering moments that require thoughtful planning alongside sequences that mimic the intensity of an action game. A standout feature is the innovative link between weapon direction and movement, demanding strategic foresight for effective play. The chip system further enriches the gameplay, where you not only have to manage your movements to make the best use of each chip but also survive challenging encounters. The ability to reroll chip patterns allows for tactical optimization, adding depth to each session. While activating chips perfectly can be tough due to the game's complexity, achieving it is immensely rewarding. The unpredictability of some enemies initially adds to the challenge, although it contributes to a steep learning curve that enhances the game's overall engagement.The demo felt comprehensive, but the full game expands further, offering a vast arsenal of weapons and ensuring that familiar items are rare. The upgrade system and weapon duplication are well-implemented. Each boss demands a new strategy, reflecting their unique strengths and weaknesses. Additionally, post-game challenges in harder modes add longevity, promising at least 40-50 hours of engaging gameplay.While not groundbreaking, the visuals have a distinctive style that enhances the game world's vibrancy. However, some animations appear rough, and certain movements feel too abrupt. Thankfully, visual effects and solid gameplay compensate for these shortcomings.The background music is excellent, perfectly complementing the gameplay, but sound effects are inconsistent. Some attacks lack auditory feedback, and volume levels fluctuate. Despite these issues, the sound design is generally well-executed, with room for polishing.While I typically play games more for fun than for story, the narrative here is serviceable. It unfolds through cutscenes and dialogues, offering enough character insight to keep me engaged without demanding my full attention.Don't judge this game by mere spectating; playing it is a whole different experience. It's incredibly addictive, especially for those who enjoy mastering randomized elements to craft powerful builds. I highly recommend giving it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Needs a bit of balancing but otherwise not a bad rouge-lite game.The shields are too OP as they block 1 instance of any damage. Getting stacks per kill and doubling overkill gets you maybe like 10-20 shields per round. You get to the final boss and I was almost at 100 stacks of that. Tanked all the damage and just kept attacking. Too easy.One con so far, also just as negatively OP is enemy stun. When you get stunned, you skip a turn. HOWEVER if they apply 2 STACKS or there is 2 enemies applying one stack each. You are perma stunned FOREVER. Doesn't matter that i had full HP with 70 shield and can 1 or 2 shot them. Run over. Worst in boss rooms because they have a bigger AOE. If you get hit. Run is OVER.As of 5/18/24, LITERALLY the day after posting this. They patched both issues I brought up. _childDocuments_.review: It is like combination of Hades + Into The Breach: rogue-lite adventure, but the combat is turn-based tactics. The best thing is that they made it feel very fast, while still requiring you to think. You move and attack with a single button press, and enemies move together with you, so you never wait (unless you want to). This allows you to make a turn in less than a second on easy levels and take all the time you need on hard ones. Tons of weapons and quite a significant number of mechanics to play with - loving it so far. Perfect for Steam Deck. English translation is a bit rough though.

_childDocuments_.review: Really neat idea for a game and I see some of the reviews referencing other games that I have not played before. This is my first exposure to a game like this. I generally enjoy turn-based RPGs, so I felt this was up my alley. I only put 30 minutes in and ended up putting it down because I just wasn't enjoying the style of the gameplay rhythm very much. The bottom line is I just didn't enjoy assigning my equipment and items to movement keys and using this positional dance to choreograph the fight. Instead of feeling dynamic and free flowing it felt clunky and restrictive. This gimmick is necessary, because without it the game would truly be a bland affair, however this gimmick is not interesting enough to me to carry the game.The relic system is the same thing you've seen in almost any other game that has relics. Neither good or bad - not breaking new ground here. Very safe.The AI was a bit too self-destructive for my liking, in my half hour I saw multiple enemies wander back and forth in environmental effects and kill themselves. The enemy units run very predictable and reliable attack and movements patterns and don't deviate at all. From my perspective, the overall concept was simple, which is not all bad, but too clunky for me to get lost in and enjoy.All the pieces are here for a good game if you like the concept, but I can't recommend it because I wasn't having fun.

_childDocuments_.review: The devs understood what roguelikes are all about. The progression increases in complexity unlike other games that exclusively increase enemy hp and damage. The theming and music are adequately developed and the game has a way of presenting its characters and the general conflict/story. The background seems a little repetitive per section but the gameplay is so engaging you might never notice. There is an archive that you can access for reference. Runs have a way of feeling a bit too long for about 15 - 20 minutes per area. It may seem like a run is staling out, but it allows you to explore your build and pivot at any point. The interesting weapon system linked to the movement does provide asymmetry combos, something I've never seen. The game is also 'turn based' and they can go as long as you need or as short as you want. Very interesting indeed. Worth checking out? Definitely. Not sure the balancing is exactly where we want it to be, but for a recently released game, this is excellently polished.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit of a stranger to the turn-based strategy genre, and I got this game after trying the demo thanks to the selling point of "rooted in Welsh mythology". And it mostly delivers on that front, though it feels more inspired by Celtic myth in general, since I'm pretty sure one of those guys was Cornish. The sprinkling of Welsh words here or there kept tripping me up, and I imagine this is what it's like for folks knowing French, German, Japanese etc to see stuff they can read just popping up amongst the English language...The story was generally alright. I could keep up with what was going on, though I'll admit I'm amused to know what the final split ended up being for folks needing to take a side, going by achievements - it seems the player-character's assistant didn't just grate on me! It lost my vote once it brought out the old "Welsh names are hard ¯\(°_o)/¯" line. Some super-computer! 🙄I like the approach to unlocking new gear being tied to doing stuff in the game. Initially the play seems to be pick up weapons and try to beef them up, but as the pool gets more cluttered and duplicates dry up, it leans more into the use of relics to throw damage numbers through the roof. I imagine if I'd ended up getting the -DMG/+CritDMG item on my last run, that poor final boss would've been the first recipient of a OHKO! The chip abilities seemed interesting enough, though I managed to do just fine with the starting set of Heal/Fireball/Enrage. The variety on offer will keep some folks entertained as they go for 100%The rogue-lite stuff mainly comes from "soul" currencies - collect a bunch on a run, and increase your starting cash, relic slots, starting freebies etc. It works well enough, though the end-game costs were pretty comical. But then at the same time, there's means of getting more "soul" currency in a run with the relics, so it's just a matter of playing smart.Music was alright. Not the most stand-out stuff but it gets the job done.There were a couple of negatives for this, though. Primarily bugs and glitches, which only really turned up near the end of the game. One time I got hit by a few guys at once and lost full control of my guy, including the loss of the Esc key, and was forced to close the game. Another time I died when some enemies were charging their attacks, and those charging noises never got halted, which whilst not game-breaking, was particularly annoying to deal with. There's also one last bit at the end where the game unlocked an extra stage for me to play, but didn't signify that this was an extra, so I went through the whole last level thinking something had broken as I got to fight the character I'd actually sided with. Feels like that could be signposted a bit better.But all in all, not a bad game! I'm glad I gave it a chance when it popped up on the queue.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm honestly surprised at how good and enjoyable The Land Beneath Us turned out to be.It has solid gameplay with a tight game loop and tasteful pixel art to boot. I've found myself on more than one occasion starting it up just to kill a few minutes while waiting for food in the oven or between meetings and subsequently losing track of time because I got so engrossed in playing in just a few minutes.If you're interested in story, TLBU has one, but it's much more compact compared to similar games that would be more described as RPGs.My only gripes with it are very minor, and on the whole I'd say it's worth picking up if you like turn-based, tactical games with a loop you can just pick up and play.Said gripes (stressing that they are very minor):* Some of the challenges are just grinds. The ones for gaining shields come to mind, as there are far fewer items and opportunities to gain shields to complete the challenge compared to others like triggering overkill or teleporting, for instance. This was especially painful in the last few challenges that required gathering 1000 shields to complete, to the point that I would start runs looking for a specific legendary item that  so I could exploit certain enemy AI to allow me gain hundreds of shields in a single room to complete the challenge. Having those challenge requirements tuned down a bit would be a good move IMO* Items from chests are placed at random, and oftentimes means having to move around to the opposite side from where I opened it. Just kind of annoying to do, especially in rooms that contain chests that are side-by-side and don't just place items next to each other when being opened* If items drop behind tall objects (the pre-boss healer room, namely), you often won't be able to see them because of the angle of the camera* The computer sidekick character greets you with smarmy dialogue when you die. Its part of the character, so I get it, but I wish I could slap the thing sometimes* Certain enemy layouts can feel a bit unfair without the right items on-hand. They're usually navigable if you're upgraded enough, but can otherwise feel almost too punishing compared to others in the same level

_childDocuments_.review: 10 minutes pass. Okay, what did I miss?20 minutes pass. Wow, that was nice. Maybe I'm moving a bit too fast?30 minutes pass. Wow, the boss is really hard. I know how to handle it.50 minutes pass. Seriously!? Let me try again.60 minutes pass. Yeah, I finally arrived at the first world Boss. . .61 minutes pass. Oops, my hand slipped too fast; let me try again.80 minutes pass. Let's try defeating the first-world boss again.82 minutes pass. Darn, I knocked myself back and died again!?90 minutes pass. The white/black flash screen is so disturbing. . .100 minutes passed. And hell yeah, I finally eliminated the world boss.Wow, the 2nd upgrade progression. Holy moly, It's helldiver! This is amazing!Holy! 3rd upgrade progression!And I take a break at the 2nd World Boss to review this game first.////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////- The pixelated top-down graphics and sound are charming yet intriguing.- The illustration art is somehow unrelated to its style, but that's not the point!- The music is really great. I can even listen to it during work days!- This is a new turn-based roguelite game set in action combat, and it's really outstanding so far.- The combat mechanics are really intriguing, especially the weapon slot and relic. And what's really fun is the magic casting (Chip Mode), which reminded me of Helldiver. But it's super fun here.There are numerous choices for you to try out your combo and style. It could take up to 20-30 hours, even 100 hours, to try it out.- Sadly, I have to pause it; otherwise, my work will be totally ruined!- The control and input should be replaced with only one hand that can play. The game is good enough with only one-hand control. I just don't understand why Dev doesn't place everything close to WASD. (Well, this is not much to disturb on gameplay)- This game has the potential to be ported to Mobile. It's really easy to control and understand everything clearly.STORY: (N/A)- Well, I don't care much about the story and usually skipped for this type of game. So. . . I will give the review on this later.- With this price, it's really worth owning the game. The price should be more for this creative and fun game!This is a really fun game with charming, unique gameplay that everyone should try out. Be warned that, don't move too fast while engaging with overwhelming enemies. XD

_childDocuments_.review: While I haven't put in a lot of hours into this game because I have so many other games building up that I am going through. But I really liked the premise of ; think of it as one of those frustrating (but entertaining) turn-based musical games. Necrodancer, or Hi-Fi Rush. Sure, those games are wonderful, but sometimes you simply don't want to be forced into a certain mindset, you know? Constantly moving to gain the best score / damage output, making it very tense and relying on movement timing skills rather than strategy it scratches that itch. You drop down into the stages and have the option of selecting different portals for currency, elites, fights, and weaponry. You have four distinct weapon styles on each movement key! You can even use the same styles if you want (Range, 2 Tiles, Melee) which is extremely cool because it drastically changes the strategy game while also incorporating specific movement combos to help you out in a pinch. It may take some time to adjust to the boss dynamics and how to properly defeat them (shields, etc) with whichever set of weapons you choose at the start and leveled up throughout your run, but it is a worthwhile experience to try.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm on the fence about it. I got it on sale so I'm not really bothered. I'll admit there is difficulty but I don't believe if I'd label it as "challenging". _childDocuments_.review: This game really scratches that itch iv'e have for a while. It's so fun with so many ways to fight. I've played a lot of similar games but none of them have felt quite as satisfying to play. You can dance around enemies and really engage with them in whatever build you are going for. When I die it's usually something I could have prevented if I had just played better, which makes you just want to play again. Try the demo and get used to the mechanics. But note it doesn't really get good and interesting until you get more options like chips, more relics, and teleport
