_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the overall series, and someone who enjoyed Cold Steel while still acknowledging its rather major flaws, this game feels like a return to form for Falcom in many - but not all - aspects. The combat system has been completely revamped, the MC is refreshingly mature, the cast size has been reduced back to about Sky/Crossbell size, and world building within the legendary nation of Calvard is as enjoyable as ever. Characters die, actions have consequences, and Van isn't being followed around by a harem. Clearly, Falcom is listening to fans, but there are still a few issues I think need some improving:The Soundtrack: I think the main problem with the OST isn't the songs themselves, but their usage within the game. Any track bearing Jindo or Koguchi's name is practically guaranteed to be excellent (notably, Jindo composed both the final dungeon AND final boss themes, while Koguchi composed the main battle theme and many of the more soulful town and field themes), and Sonoda was certainly no slouch either. While I do tend to take issue with Singa's instrumentation, laying the blame solely on him is hardly appropriate either, and overall the soundtrack is, at the least, comparable to previous heights. The real issue is that it felt like said tracks were being used almost willy nilly, without giving thought to the  of those tracks. A great example is "What is Ahead of You." This song first played in Elaine's daydream in Reverie, and the first time we hear it in Daybreak is when Elaine makes her first appearance. "Cool, Elaine gets her own theme." But as the game progresses, it starts getting used more and more in scenes that are not only not related to Elaine, but with entirely different tones and themes. The song eventually loses all meaning due to this seemingly random usage, and there are many more examples of the game just not understanding how to imbue songs with meaning and make a soundtrack flow smoothly. Field themes randomly became event themes, "The Realm of Death and Play" was used once in a segment shorter than the song itself, and  The other big problem is bloat. Chapter 3 could have just not existed and nothing meaningful would change (just introduce Risette somewhere else), and Chapter 5 and the Finale really feel like they should have been combined into one chapter rather than split into two separate chapters that end up treading a lot of the same ground. That Cold Steel feeling of every character needing to say their little line after every proclamation unfortunately still exists, just with less characters.Overall, I'm glad to have played this game, and the cast and narrative has a lot of potential moving forward in the Calvard arc. Stakes were rather high for a "first in arc" game which I appreciated, and there were many great callbacks/reveals to enjoy. I can only imagine what kind of insanity awaits in Daybreak 2 and Kai no Kiseki.  I just hope Falcom will hire another composer (or bring back Unisuga), hire a sound director, and start leaning away from bloated 100 hour games and back towards tight 60-80 hour games.

_childDocuments_.review: It is overall fine. I wasn't a fan of how modern Calvard looks. Most of the locales are boring. There are only two highways you can walk on. Doesn't feel like a realized fantasy world like Trails in the Sky or Trails of Cold Steel.The combat was serviceable. Game was too easy even on nightmare difficulty. Except for the true final boss' second phase, I never really had to buckle down and try to optimize my builds. The new boost gauge incentivizes weird gameplay of stacking your characters closely together and hoping that as many of them get hit by enemy AoE attacks as possible so you can fill the gauge and boost/buff up your characters more often. The main cast was pleasant but not captivating like the Sky and old Class VII characters. Everyone except Bergard felt derivative of older characters. The secondary characters were a lot more interesting.The game suffers from severe pacing problems. It is 110 hours long (the longest first game yet) but nothing exciting happens until chapter 5, which was 70 hours into the game. Everything before chapter 5 felt like filler where I wasn't making any progress towards defeating the bad guys. There are also too many NPCs and their dialogue updates too often, which makes talking to everyone a chore. Chapters 2 and 3 and the final chapter really dragged on. Chapter 5 was pretty enjoyable, though. The writing is sloppier than previous Trails games but overall still enjoyable enough.Music was okay but not as memorable as prior Trails OSTs.Visual presentation is nicer than prior games.PC port: overall great, except that I got stutters during some S-craft animations (namely Van's, Feri's, and Aarons, and maybe a few other's I'm forgetting) when v-sync was turned on, even with graphical settings set to default. I have a Nvidia 3070 Ti. With v-sync turned off I get no stutters but I did get screentearing. I do not have a Nvidia g-sync compatible monitor so no idea if that could have fixed the problem. Kuro got a patch yesterday so this might still get fixed. Given how fast the the S-craft animations are, the stutters are a little disappointing, but it's not a dealbreaker.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm still a bit mixed about Daybreak. It's not a bad game at all, and I had fun exploring Calvard and getting to know Van and his crew. Agnes's character development was a highlight, as she grew from an insecure student to a confident young woman.However, the game falls short in terms of plot progression. While it does a great job building the world and introducing new organizations, it doesn't provide many answers to the overarching mysteries. Van's character, despite being interesting, feels somewhat underdeveloped and similar to Rean.The biggest disappointment for me was the lack of meaningful character interactions. The banter between party members often felt repetitive and uninteresting. While there are a few good moments, the majority of the game lacks the depth and development that a 100-hour RPG should have.Overall, Daybreak is a solid entry in the Trails series, but it plays it safe and leaves much to be desired.

_childDocuments_.review: Trails is my favourite series. I've played every one (excluding non-localized ones) including Nayuta, and this is by far the best in the series. What stood out the most in Daybreak is how it addressed the few complaints I had about the series as well. Everyone from major characters to a random NPC you've never seen before having plot armour (LOOKING AT YOU DE-RAILED TRAIL FROM AZURE)... You actually see people die instead of everyone miraculously surviving every tragedy/terrorist attack that happens. S-crafts eating all your Craft Points on use? They now only cost 100 with the caveat of needing to be at full S-Boost (and it's not too hard to build up your S-Gauge). But I do still miss the elemental values of your quartz determining your arts. You do get some passive skills instead though, which is nice. It was also refreshing to have villains that were straight up just evil. The dub was great as well. Especially Van's and Dantes' VAs. If you're looking to get into the series with this one though, I wouldn't recommend it since it does reference A LOT of stuff that happens in previous games and expects the player to already have the context. _childDocuments_.review: Easily the strongest opener for an arc since Zero. Just about everything in it feels wonderful, from the new combat system and cast, to the various regions of Calvard itself. Speaking of Calvard, it is as much a character as Erebonia and Crossbell were in their respective storylines, and its blend of French, Chinese, and Middle-Eastern influences makes it a joy to explore alongside Van and his various employees.The writing in general is a considerable step up in quality compared to previous arcs, with much improved pacing and real stakes in a way that is quite refreshing. Interactions among the main cast are extremely well done, and made me enjoy my time with them enormously. The villains are sadly a little under-cooked when it comes to character development, but not to a degree that it detracts from the fantastic overall quality of the experience.While the general trails disclaimer of "If you start here you're going to feel really lost for a bit" definitely applies, the game does its best to accommodate new players and help them catch up to speed on Zemurian lore organically.Don the Nightmare and TAKE THE GRENDEL; you'll have a blast doing it.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing new entry to the best RPG series of all time. Daybreak is a smart dialing back of how crazy the Cold Steel arc got, and as much as I like those games this is far more smart about its usage of the standard tropes you see across Trails. Despite a lower overall stakes compared to previous games, the stakes SEEM higher because this is the first game in the series that is willing to have actual violent consequences from all of the fighting that takes place. I don't have a fresh count, but I'm pretty confident more people die on screen in this game than the entire rest of the series combined, and that gives it a certain edge the other games don't have. Calvard is the best realized country so far. Like others, its full of the crafted dialog from NPCs that constantly changes as you progress through the game, and its impossible not to have some of their little arcs worm your way into your brain as you play. Since it's a melting pot of a country, racial tensions is a common theme throughout the game...and I am pleasantly surprised they didn't fumble handling such a sensitive subject. It's more than just "racism bad" its more like, showing what it does to people and how people deal with it....as well as the fact that just because a government tries its best to create a free country and put in anti-discrimination laws, it doesn't erase the prejudices still held by people that have very real effects on the population. I wouldn't be surprised if there's some holes someone more analytical than me could poke into this aspect of the game, but I am kind of grading on a curve for RPGs here.I would say the combat is very fun and the best its ever been. It's not quite expansive enough to maintain variety across at 90+ hour game, I personally found my builds and stuck with them at around hour 60, but it was fun enough to never skip any fight. Don't be mislead by some of the real time aspects, this is definitely a turn-based game, the real time combat is simply basic attack button mashing, dodging, and special attacks to get the enemy stun bar up so you can start your actual turn base battle with an advantage. This always feel good though, hitting the "start turn based battle" button when the enemy is stunned does a really cool attack and delay's their turn a lot, so its always worth going for it.The more nuanced changes to the combat both make it harder to abuse in some ways and easier in others. There's a real lack of turn advance specials (the only one in the game is from a guest character that rarely shows up), and delay seems heavily nerfed to the point where I could barely tell if it was doing anything a lot of the time. The main interesting addition is that AT bonuses are no longer based on the action order...for example in the older games if a Crit bonus was coming up in the action order you could do an S-craft to steal it from whatever enemy/allie was going to go on that turn. This is no longer possible, AT bonuses are tied to a character/enemy, you have to stun the enemy to steal it. Once you get more than 4 characters you can still switch to a character for free and take the turn with them, if you have an arts user that needs the zero arts bonus or something. A lot of the more BS bonuses have been removed, so you don't have to deal with Deathblow or Vanish AT bonuses ruining your battle or anything.The main aspects you can abuse to become unstoppable are boosts and shard skills. Shard skills are the new element that gets changed by your quartz layout, which no longer affect arts. Mixing quartzs of different elements gives characters shard skill access, which by default is a 25% chance of procing at whatever condition. Boosting a character 1 level or 2 levels increases this chance to 75% or 100% respectively. Some of these shard skills and boost bonuses are insanely strong and boost meter is easy to come by, so it honestly contributes to a game that just can't really keep up with your power level at the default difficulty if you put even a modest amount of effort building characters. I played about 30 hours of the game on hard difficulty and once it became clear I was way outmatching the game I put it on nightmare for the rest of it. Even still, while some later boss fights were kind of tough the game remained pretty easy going...just a few times I had to pay attention when I put it on nightmare. Its so easy to recover a fight though, Agnes has a full heal+ revive + ailment cleanse s-craft from the very start of the game, so dying isn't really a concern as long as you keep her alive. An easy game isn't really a knock against it when the combat remains fun, and I can't wait to see how the next entries refines this system because I think it has the most potential out of any Trails combat so far.So that's rambly review of the game, I just love Trails games, inject this stuff into my bloodstream and give me the next game so I can go back to Calvard.

_childDocuments_.review: As a massive fan of the series, I am exceptionally happy that we are finally getting the level of localization that this series has deserved.tl;dr This game is great and you should 100% pick it up if you are a JRPG fan, or a RPG fan in general. I've thoroughly enjoyed my time thus far, and I expect you will too.With every entry, Falcom appears to be improving and innovating in ways that are refreshing. This game introduces a "field combat" system that I seem to be enjoying immensely. I love the ability to swap back and forth between the field combat and turn-based combat. Engaging and stunning an enemy before moving to turned based combat gives you the typical "Advantage" that previous titles would for attacking an enemy in the field. The transitions are smooth - no loading screens and a satisfying animation - especially when you engage a stunned enemy.I'd like to go over the combat system for a bit, as there are some substantial changes here.Combat is slightly simplified, removing the Orders and Battle Point system from Cold Steel. This is generally replaced by the Boost system, which works similarly to the Assault Gauge system. You can "Boost" your character for a couple turns, which powers up their abilities. There are two states - Boosted and Full Boost. Moving from Boosted to Full Boost extends the timer. Each state also takes one Boost Gauge, and thus, moving from a non-boosted state to Full Boost would require two Boost gauge.The largest departure is related to the S-crafts. The main differences are that S-crafts can no longer be used outside of Full Boost, and that they only ever take 100 CP. This means that a single character if at 200CP can use their S-craft twice in a row as long as they are in Full Boost. If you have available Boost Gauge (Or if the character is already in Full boost), you can activate the S-craft just like in previous titles. The game will even tell you how many Boost Gauges you require to active a character's S-craft. This will immediately move the character into Full Boost and then activate the S-craft.The result is that S-crafts cannot be freely spammed in a row from every party member at once (Which was my favored tactic from Cold Steel 1 through Reverie), as each party member would need two Boost Gauge each. Seeing as you start with 3 Boost Gauge, the best you can realistically pull off is two S-crafts.However... using an S-craft increases your maximum Boost Gauge. This has turned the previous combat system on its head, where instead of hoarding your S-craft for countering the enemy's S-crafts, you are now encouraged to spread out your S-crafts over the course of the battle. The end goal is to build up for that all-satisfying finish.They've also instituted a chain attack system, where every hit you inflict upon the enemy (Each ability inflicts a number of hits) causes your damage to be multiplied. This counter stacks up between all hits you inflict in a row, incentivising you to stack your attacks together as much as possible.With that out of the way, let's move onto the story and characters.The story has been great thus far - as per the standard from Falcom. It's entirely possible to predict where you may be going next, and in general what may be happening next. However, they also throw in plenty of curveballs that are going to keep you guessing. I'm not going to go into much more detail, as you should really experience the story yourself.The characters have been great, and Van - the MC - is an extremely relatable and likable guy. The dynamic between Van and Agnès has been absolutely top tier. There's plenty of callbacks and references to previous games, characters, and situations, so I would not put this game as a place where you should be jumping into Trails for the first time.The game uses very similar graphics as instituted in Cold Steel 3 - not much is changing there in any regard.The music is on point as per usual. The zone themes are fantastic thus far. The boss music is an absolute banger. Every time it comes up, I end up running around in the turn based mode for a few minutes just to listen to it.In my VERY humble opinion, yet another GOTY (2024)!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic entry in the Trails series, and honestly might be the best "first game" in any of the arcs.  The most obvious improvement over any of the previous games is a completely new game engine that is graphically more advanced that any of the previous games, but there are a lot of other improvements, too; the story gets started almost immediately and keeps moving at a good pace through the entire game, and the combat system discards or streamlines a lot of the cruft that had accumulated through all of the previous games in order to provide much smoother gameplay.  If you're a fan of any of the previous Trails games, or if you just like story-heavy JRPGs, you should definitely play Trails through Daybreak.If you're not a Trails fan, the biggest question you probably have is "Can I start with this game?"  Good news, the answer to that is actually "yes".  All of the Trails games are set in the same world and take place in the order they were released, and many of them expect you to have played and remember the games that come before them; but Daybreak is set in a new location with a (mostly) new cast of characters, and it has a self-contained story that doesn't require any knowledge of the previous games.  If you have played the previous games, you'll spot a lot of cameos and references to the older ones, but you can definitely jump right into Daybreak if you just want to see whether this series is for you or not.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid addition to the Trails world. It has all the usual hallmarks of a good Trails game: good writing, good characters, great music, and excellent art.  That said if you are new to the Trails series of games I would recommend starting with a different game either Trails of Cold Steel (which is where I started) or Trials from Zero (which is probably the most well rounded intro game of the series). This game simply assumes you know too much background unlike those two games which is why I recommend this. Still a worthy introduction to Calvard.To continue with the good, I liked that they dropped the fishing minigame and all the other minigames. They were frankly a distraction, not much fun, and didn't really add to the story much. The only minigame I wish they had done would have been a racing minigame which would have made sense with the plot.Fie grew up and she grew up hot. I did not like her in Cold Steel but man she has matured nicely. Gone is her abrasive attitude and now you have a very cute deadpan snarker.  It really works for her and it was great that she is now highly useful in combat.It was also great to see the development of Renne. At this point she probably has the longest running and most dramatic character progression of any character in the series.  She is fantastic and it was great to get more of her.It was great to see Zin in a new light. I never liked him very much in Trials to the Sky but he's much better in this game. I liked his relationship with Van and his leadership of the Bracers.Van himself is a worthy protagonist, though not my personal favorite (who is Rean for me). He has a good character design, and solid combat style. The antihero is an overplayed trope at this point but he fits in a nice niche with all the other protagonists in Trails and I'm interested to see how he eventually interacts with Estelle, Lloyd, and Rean.Now for my complaints:1. There are a few misses with the music. This is unusual for Trails games which normally have amazing soundtracks. This one certain has a great one but there are a few of times where the music just does not match the settings.2. The dancing sucks. They needed to get better choreography and motion capture for those. They have done dancing amazingly before (see Trials from Zero), and for a story that depends on it you have to get it right else it just looks goofy which it did this time.3. No Olivert in this one. This makes the second game in all of Trials where Olivert does not appear in some form. He is alluded too and shows up in a picture in the end credits but that doesn't count for me. He has a worthy stand in with another character, but Olivert should have been worked in some how to keep the streak alive.4. There needed to be more backstory and context. One of the things that ditched in this game that was in previous games was a library where you could read up on the context of the game. Trials is massive as a world and to get a grasp of it you need that backstory. This is especially true with the discussion of things like the DG Cult, and the Erebonian War. Even for long time fans of the series, refreshers are appreciated. This game also abandoned all the random novels you would find lying around, which is another way to grow the mythos of the world. 5. The new combat system needs work. I thought the combat system had gotten to a good place in Trails to Reverie. The overhauled combat system though ditches all of those hard learned lessons and features. While I don't mind the shard system, and actually appreciate the way S-boosting helps encourage using S-breaks, the free combat system (the system outside of turn based combat) felt lame. Really it was a balance issue. They should have made it that enemies that you aren't going to gain much XP from are enemies you can just beat on the field with out deploying shards in a hit or two.  Often I was going to turn based combat with enemies that gave me no or very little XP.  Normally I am all for turn based combat as its fun to strategize and have time to think and because you can get into a good groove. This system though made it hard to get into that groove of plowing through enemies. I think some more work needs to be done on balance, especially with respect to enemy difficulty and XP reward. Also the last boss fight was unbalanced for what it was supposed to be and given where your character were.6. The new orbments are a step back. I really liked the way orbments were handled in the Trials of Cold Steel and Reverie arcs. The new orbment system makes it hard to customize the loadout of a character and really tune them the way you want. Instead it feels like we've regressed to where we were in Trials of the Sky. It made it hard to get a really good magic user going.7. 8. Story pacing needed a bit work. It could have been tighter and especially at the end it felt like it was wandering and dragging on. The story is quite good, but needed a bit more focus.9. Elaine should have been a principle companion. She was frankly the best new character and it felt like she should have been a member of the team or at least part of the final battle. She was too important to leave on the sidelines.For all those complaints though this is definitely a good game and if you are a fan of Trails definitely pick it up.  Even if you aren't a fan of Trails this may be the one to pull you in (though I would recommend Cold Steel as the place to start). It's a solid game that has some really awesome moments and a satisfying conclusion.

_childDocuments_.review: I always heard good things about this series i see people calling it "the best video game franchise" or "the best jrpg series of all time" i was excited to dive into this hoping this game will get me into the series but after giving it almost 5 hours i have to say, This might one of the worst paced games i have ever played.Here is how it went:-You start a game with a long cutscene which is normal and expected.-You can walk around the shop but dont dare stray to far your character will automatically turn his back and force you to run back to the area you are allowed to explore (ok i can be a bit forgiving in that regard)-Another long cutscene with new character being introduced with too much dialogue that adds nothing.-You go to a town but nope you are not allowed to explore either despite the game telling you to find an npc there is a point where you are not even allowed to climb up stairs.-Another cutscene.-Dungeon with tutorial after tutorial and more gameplay mechanics being shown and guess what? MORE CUTSCENES WITH POINTLESS DIALOGUE after each tutorial, the dungeon design felt like some greybox ♥♥♥♥ its so basic and lazy dungeon design.-Rinse and repeat until i finished the prologue and can finally start exploring towns it felt liberating, ah ♥♥♥♥! now the game wants to explain side quests and you can only do 1 at a time and you are forced to do them and yeah side quests are explained via long ass cutscenes i pretty much gave up knowing the game will throw more tutorials and cutscenes at me.This is not the first time i played a wordy/cutscene heavy game i played games like Disco Elysium, planescape torment and many more but the problem with this game is that Pacing as a concept does not exist like...AT ALL, i dont mind the story focus nature of the game and i understand how hard it is to nail the initial hours, but this game takes players patience for granted with 0 respect to the players time and for a game that is beginner friendly there were so many moments where i was confused and alienated for not knowing certain concepts or factions and even characters, what makes it worse is that 70% of the dialogues are filler and adds nothing to the characters or story, a dialogue that could end in a sentence is stretched out to an entire paragraph, as for the much hyped worldbuilding its all text with nothing in the "show dont tell" department everything is spelled out for you, as i mentioned before the dungeon design is quite terrible and as basic as it gets.I may revisit this game and my opinion my change, but first impressions are important and im not impressed so far, if the pacing is like this through out the game and even series then i dont recommend this AT ALL even if there are some promised pay offs.

_childDocuments_.review: Before reviewing:No, you cannot start with Kuro no Kiseki/Trails Through Daybreak. It WILL spoil all previous arcs and that is just a straight up fact. Especially the Erebonia arc. So please for the love of all things trails do not start here. Also for the remainder of this review I will be referring to the game as Kuro or Kuro no Kiseki, since that's the name I've been used to calling it. Review:Kuro no Kiseki has become my absolute favorite game in all of the trails series. The story pacing is great, the characters are lovable, the whole premise of the Calvard arc is really different and takes a different turn from the rest of all of the trails arcs. It is genuinely an amazing game, and even the gimmicks they added to this arc are really fun to play with. These gimmicks mainly focusing around an alignment system of Chaos, Grey, and Law. In addition to this, combat is now free roaming instead of using a turn to move, with the option of doing some action RPG combat for some of the trash mobs. However, like my previous reviews I'll break everything down into general sections.Story:The story for Kuro no Kiseki is possibly one of my favorites of the whole entire series as a whole. There is a significant change in themes/mood compared to the previous arcs. If I could put it into words, I think the best way to describe it would be more dark and mature themes compared to the rest of the series as a general thing (of course very specific things that happen in very specific games in the series are excluded  . This mood/theme change in and of itself brings a really interesting aspect to the whole story and gets you invested in a slightly different way than previous entries. However, it doesn't forget any of its story roots and continues to thrive off the trails formula for story. They have additionally added an interesting gimmick to the story where if you complete certain quests or pick certain options, they can impact your alignment. These alignments can give you different items in addition to having an impact later on in the story. So I recommend trying to evenly level all alignments so you are not locked out of certain things. There are a lot of moments in this game where you'll be smiling, laughing, genuinely hating certain characters, and as with most trails games, you will be crying. There are lots of emotions packed into this game as a whole and it never fails to hit hard, even in side quests from NPC. Overall, there was genuinely no downsides or downpoints in the whole entire ~92.5 hour game that I could see. Gameplay:The Calvard arc/kuro changes up A LOT of the usual combat system that we've grown used to over the previous 10 games. One of the major changes is that to movement within the combat environment. Instead of being limited to using up your turn to move your characters as in the previous games in the series, you can not move around freely within a certain designated range that your characters can reach. This allows for a lot more precise positioning of characters and not having to worry about wasting turns that could be used to dealt damage or heal, moving. This also plays well into the new combat system gimmick they have added to the game. That being the SCLM system, where you can get follow up attacks or boosts to a certain character's attacks by being within range of a ring around the character. This is also accompanied by a combo system which allows for more damage to be dealt depending on how high of a combo you can create. This can majorly help with defeating tougher enemies and also changes the way you would come up with strategies in previous entries in the trails franchise. It took a little bit to get used to, especially trying to heal characters, but it was a really fun system that I enjoyed. The game also adds the ability to boost your character's power/strength by using certain things in the game that generate via attacking or getting attack by enemies. Another different note was being able to do Action RPG style gameplay for some of the trash mobs in the game. This Action RPG style really helps with getting rid of annoying low level enemies when trying to go towards a boss, however the main focus is of course still turn based, so in a sense it is still the same system we all know from before. Overall, I genuinely think the combat in Kuro is a lot of fun and really easy to get used to. Graphics/Art Style:The graphics and art style for Kuro are GREAT. Just like how Cold Steel 3 was the turning point of really good looking 3D models for trails games, Kuro just takes that even further and makes BEAUTIFUL models. All the characters, even the NPCs look great in the game, especially when thrown up to higher resolutions like 4K. There were a lot of times when I would just look out onto the landscape of the game in awe because of how pretty everything could be. They really put a lot of work into both the character models and the whole entire world design of the game. The cities feel crowded and lively, the smaller areas also have a lively feel to them as well, there is just so much to love about the graphics of this game. The art style change as well is really lovely too. The character drawings, the other drawn scenes like flashbacks, and anything that has been drawn in 2D look spectacular in almost every way. Honestly, trails never fails to make really lovely looking characters whether it be from back in the Sky/Liberl arc or in the Kuro/Calvard arc. I can't recommend this enough, especially if you like playing games at higher resolutions. Music:The music SLAPS, every song is a banger no matter what it is. The main opening song for the game is so good and is probably one of my favorite opening themes for a trails game thus far. In addition to this, the night theme is something amazing. The calming jazz music for the night theme perfectly fits the theme of Calvard and more specifically the cities that you visit within the game. Each area has their own songs and I can't get enough of all them. I really hope that in Kuro 2 there will be a lot more lovely songs just like the ones this game has given us. The trails series never disappoints with its banger soundtracks game after game after game, I need to get a hold of the OST for this game ASAP. Especially if it means that I can listen to that banger night theme even more. Conclusion:I think Kuro no Kiseki is an amazing entry in the trails franchise and an even better start to a new arc in the whole entire series. The new combat gimmicks are a lot of fun, and really easy to get used to. The story is really interesting and the theme changes only add more to the amount of amazing plot that this game has. The graphics and art style are some of the best in the series and looks amazing in both the character models/designs and the surrounding environments that you play in. The music is top tier and the night theme is an absolute banger, as you would expect with any trails game. You can even watch Orbal movies too, which is a lot of fun in and of itself. Overall, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is working their way through the series.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been pondering whether I should recommend this game because Kuro no Kiseki has been quite the mixed bag for me after reaching the end credits. I ended up leaning on "Not Recommended" for my review. Part of the reason why this game didn't click for me is because I might've gone through the Trails fatigue. The game doesn't really innovate all that much from the Cold Steel series to keep it interesting. It has become Call of Duty all over again, albeit in a different genre. Yeah you get Ys-like action combat but this feature is not the focus of the game and the action combat sequences are kind of janky, and you'd also get to position your characters before performing an action in turn-based mode but this feature really feels like a QOL feature rather than an entirely new mechanic.Don't get me wrong; I do think that the game is still fun to play. To be honest, I don't think recurring mechanics in the Trails series is a bad thing. I mean, the more Trails games the better, right? After all, I've played through the entire Cold Steel saga and still enjoyed it a lot. So the issue had to be something else other than the gameplay itself.I think the biggest issue I had was with the world-building of Kuro. I was told that Falcom used an entirely new engine for Kuro. I don't know whether they made that decision out of creative vision or something else, but the world and environments in Kuro looked bland and generic, worse than Cold Steel 3 & 4. I still think that the graphics in the Ys VIII/TOCS 2 era are the best. Perhaps they wanted to make the world look a lot more gritty to match its mature story theme, but in doing so they ended up botched the environments to look less appealing to the eye. I get it, gloomy environments can be memorable if, and only if, it was done right; like in the Souls or the Xenoblade series.For the story, I think that Kuro's storyline is a lot more mature and catered towards adult audiences unlike their previous games, which I think is a good thing. But the problem with this is that the childish and quirky trope that the Trails series is known for really didn't fit this genre, because at one point you'll see some cartoonish "goofy-ahh" moment then a few moments later a person got their throat sliced off. I do think this adds hilarity to the game but it feels like Falcom is having an identity crisis here.Alright, let me just tell you that I adore the characters in Kuro. All the casts are amazing and it made me care for them, though I do think that Falcom has their favourites, which is why I felt like my favourite character (Risette) gets less attention than the more important characters like Agnes. Not a big issue for me, since Trails games are known to ignore less famous characters anyway. What I have an issue with is that the characters' voiceovers (in Japanese) are often interrupted by a sudden silence, maybe due to the fact that Falcom ran out of budget for voice acting and had to settle by cutting their voices off in between dialogues. It felt really out of place and can make some longer sequences in the game feel boring to go through.Myriads of issues, yet I won't stop anyone from trying out the game. If you're new to the game and a JRPG player, Kuro might be a good place to start since you'd still lack the Trails fatigue I mentioned earlier, and if you're a Trails fan who is looking forward to the game, definitely try it. If you're a regular JRPG player who had played the previous Trails games and wanted to try this one as well; I'd say wait until the game goes on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: To start off, , but to truly appreciate it, one should at the very least start with the earlier Trails games. This is because in many ways, this game is revolutionary by Trails standards, offering a lot of improvements and new features that were absent in the previous games (mostly Coldtrails and Crosstrails), while at the same time containing heavy spoilers for the previous games. Better start with at least Coldtrails 1 (The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel on Steam). Otherwise, at minimum you might find the earlier games boring and less fun to play through, and it will become a drag if you actually want to get into the lore of the game, which most likely you will want to do because Trails is horrible when it comes to localization and newer games take years to translate. This review was written before the official localization of Trails through Daybreak was released. Note that I am a supporter of NISA, so this by no means an attack on their efforts. I take issues with their liberal translations, but it's very good that they do voiceovers for the game and localize it in general, and yet, because the games notoriously take long (when the game was actually released in Japan, I was the same age as the protagonist of the game) to translate, you'll most likely want to play earlier games while waiting for the newer ones.The game scores, by Trails and JRPG standards a 11/10 for me. The added extra point is for the surprise effect. Excellent. I began the game on hard difficulty, and played the entire game, doing all quests I could find and partaking in all events, and talking to all available people. The overall quality of the writing, which began to rise already starting with Coldtrails 5 (On Steam: The Legend of Heroes: Trails into Reverie) has risen further. The writers have clearly put in more effort to both make the story make sense and also make a more serious, adult plot. A stark contrast to the asinine and childish stories of Skytrails 1-3. Noticeable effort went into creating different characters and making them actually different rather than making huge stacks of characters that are largely blank and offer exactly the same opinions with no disagreements whatsoever. A big plus is periodic separation of characters, allowing for more personalized, choice-based experience rather than having a crowd follow you around and needlessly extend dialogs because everyone has to say something. The game is very long, having done all I did, it took me 178.2 hours to finish, which equals 37.125 standard anime seasons (12 episodes, 24 minutes per episode format). The most important change is addition of choices, both in the main storyline and in sidequests which also influence the main story line. Without spoilers, it's really better if you do side quests, so don't miss any. Choices begin to have consequences and are often very noticeable, overall Trails seems to go into a much better direction than before, the more choices and more consequences, the better. Side quests are no longer a boring drag that you do just for points, considerable effort went into making them actually interesting and different, it's no longer running around looking for a cat (it happens only once from what I remember) or doing some dumb stuff. Also, children worship is gone. The main protagonist is a fixer, he is made out to be a cold-hearted, nihilistic person who dabbles in the "underworld", a bad guy, so to speak, almost a criminal but not really. In reality, he's just a very simple guy who keeps to himself and tries to earn a living by solving people's problems, very painstakingly making sure to not cross the law. The "grey" area that people talk about in the game sums up to "not legally penalized, but people don't like it". The extent to which he is a "bad guy" is that he interacts with criminals and terrorists and takes requests from them. If you have reservations about playing as a morally questionable character in this game, don't, Van is doubtlessly one of the most moral and righteous people in the entire Trails series. The protagonist for me felt very relatable and sympathetic. By both anime and JRPG standards, this is even a beautiful story where you actually care for what happens to people when dramatic things happen, as opposed to the game just dumping crocodile tears on you with sad music, expecting you to care while nothing of significance happens. The game has a right balance of humor, drama, action, romance and slice of life, giving you a pretty much complete anime experience without making it feel like too much.This is not to say the writing is flawless, but in comparison to the earlier games, its flaws are rather minor in comparison. Heavy spoiler: Excellent. The entire game feels very cinematic. It has essentially become an interactive anime at this point. No complaints, just good.Never feels like a drag, never feels repetitive. Often times it's fitting for the scenes it's played in. Very good. A lot like Coldtrails 5.Very different from the previous games. It takes some using to, but not much. You quickly get used to it, it's not difficult. For those who worried that addition of two combat systems (turn-based and action-based) will make the turn-based combat worse, don't worry, it didn't. Battles  feel very fresh, very actiony. I started the game on hard difficulty, and already a few days later regretted not having started on nightmare. The game is probably not too easy, it's just that I am too good at it. Fighting never feels stale, and is very enjoyable even if you grind, which I almost didn't do in this game. That said, I did clear out entire areas in full because fighting alone was very fulfilling. Contrary to what the store page says, I didn't find the topic system to actually be of any advantage in battle whatsoever. The topic system largely just lets you bring up things without changing normal dialog with NPCs

_childDocuments_.review: A good game that continues the Trails Saga well. Still a bit too much sappy friendship speeches for my liking but otherwise a good story with good gameplay. Happy to see also that Falcom and PH are no longer afraid of blood and death. In Trails of Cold Steel 1, my first Trails game, there was tension as terrorists were attacking the military and casualties were unavoidable on both sides. The stakes were indeed real. Afterwards though, the other games, Cold Steel 3 and 4 and Reverie were very guilty of big attacks and explosions but everyone was safe or fine or got sleepy and fell down. Only dramatic slow dialogue deaths for main characters. Made the stakes feel underwhelming when you knew everyone was going to be fine.   So why then am I not recommending this game? Two things. First, while it may not bother me too much, I recognize censorship is an issue still. Hardly a moral or cultural problem since we have plenty of examples of Western made games getting away with simular content. The bigger problem of the two is the translation. A common problem you might say for most translations for Japanese games for a long time and yes you are correct. But the bigger problem of it is the localization portion of it. The political localization. While not affecting the main story overall, several bits of background and character dialogue has been changed to fit with certain political views being pushed by NIS America, even if it means changed the context entirely of the original text. Basically, just buy the  original Japanese games and uh finds ways to fully enjoy the content without censorship and translation 'liberties'.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan of the Trails games for years now, since the Skies trilogy was first released back on PSP over a decade ago, and that was also my first foray into the Trails franchise. Every single Trails franchise (Skies, Crossbell, Cold Steel) reeled me from the start to the end.However with this game, something feels a little off. The beginning of the game was great. Van as a character is very different from Estelle, Lloyd and even Rean - with those three being more on the side of 'justice', so to speak, being a bracer, a cop, and while I'm not sure what to tag Rean with, he isn't the one to err on the side of the gray either. But Van does. He does things that are borderline illegal, and as a character, I find him a big fresh of air as compared to the previous protagonists. And this is also the first game in the Trails series I saw that really tackles the topic of deaths and how certain characters in the game doesn't fear to kill. (At least so far, the characters that died actually STAYED dead)Daybreaks starts two years after the end of the events of Reverie, and Calvard had taken the spot as most powerful nation in the world thanks to the reparations that Erebonia has to pay due to the instigation of the war during Cold Steel IV. Daybreak embarks on a new adventure revolving around Van and his assistance given to Agnes who wanted to track down a family heirloom so to speak that lands them in adventures and meeting a mysterious group that seems oddly familiar with Ouroboros, though there were also hints pertaining to a certain organisation that two certain individuals used to belong to in Reverie. And while the characters that joined Van were quirky and funny, by Chapter 4, I already found myself getting bored. It is more the world I guess, and even where the storyline is going by that point.I played this on both PC and Steam Deck, and it runs pretty smoothly on both.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a good game, and I'm excited for the sequel. It's a big step up in writing and dialogue quality from the Cold Steel games, which I felt were just kinda lazy in that regard. Also has a really innovative battle system, and generally good pacing, + good visuals for the budget. The only really weak point I can think of is the music, which isn't offensive or anything. It's just really really forgettable.

_childDocuments_.review: New battle system and I believe new engine for the series. This combination improves what I though was already a great turn based combat system. I am happy to say that the story is surprisingly solid with the addition of more adult themes this time around which I think is fitting for the characters and narrative. Gone are the mech battles (thank God), gone are the cliche bait and switch bad guys that are actually good guys, and gone are the kid friendly resolutions where everyone actually lives and turns good again because of friendship. People die in real life Nihon, its okay to use that in game too.Cast of characters is also solid, while some cliches of past games are present, it is toned down a bit in this entry, though to be honest I enjoyed the my harems in previous games (we are playing an anime game after all guys) so take this with a grain of salt from me. Criticisms? Its feels like lesser % of the dialogue is actually voiced this time. Why? The voice actors are fantastic, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ have them record more lines! Also I wish that the bonds that you form with other characters actually had more of an effect on the overall story, but I think this can be said about all past games as well. One can hopeFantastic continuation of the series. Excited for the next entry

_childDocuments_.review: This is the beginning of a new saga. We enter the Calvard saga and I am so excited! ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'s been so long since I wrote a review that I might be out of touch. But I’m here to spill some tea and give my insight (Big Spoiler Warning)This is the eleventh instalment of the Legend of Heroes, and I recommend that those who want to enter this game follow the story in order: This is a new region and saga but you will miss too much context and pivotal story points if you don’t……Trail in the Sky FC,Trail in the Sky SC,Trail in the Sky the 3rd,Trails from Zero,Trails to Azure,Trails of Cold Steel 1,Trails of Cold Steel 2,Trails of Cold Steel 3,Trails of Cold Steel 4,Trails into Reverie.There is one optional thing to know going into Trail through Daybreak. There is an old book called Gambler Jack. It’s a story about two gamblers who will appear in this game.Read it here or not. It’s not that important honestly. This story introduces a new main character and takes place a year and half after reverie. Van Arkride is what you call a spriggan, he accepts work from any client. This includes work even the police or bracer guild can handle as they can not be discussed in public. You walk a fine line between law, gray and chaos throughout the journey. A freshman at Aramis named Agnes Claudel, heads to Van’s office to enquire about an artefact that belonged to her great-grandfather. As you gather a team of different circumstances and stories to find these 8 Genesis artefacts and uncover the story of our characters. Along the way, you will meet a fairy holo core named Mare who will pretty much be another pivotal point throughout the story. You also have a  mafia group called Almata who are your bad guys in this game and have the genesis to bring chaos. There are a lot of factions in this game and you are given a lot of difficult choices in this game that can have an impact during your playtime. It’s extremely interesting than previous games because this game plays more heavily into a dark fantasy/grunge theme than previous sagas. There are also some serious returning characters, some you expect, some you haven’t seen since the Librel saga and some you just don’t expect at all. They bummed up the camera angles, cinematics and cutscene even better this time again. Their experimental phase during trails into reverie showed in this game and it’s refreshing and beautiful to watch. I wished they played more into the animated cutscenes because there wasn’t much and they were always a treat. But I have to do with the direction they are going forward with these games and it’s looking nice.The character roster is like the beginning of Trail of Cold Steel 1. You are introduced to a set of lovable characters that will be with you for the rest of the saga and more to come. However, these characters grew much faster on me than Trail of Cold Steel. Maybe it’s because they came from different settings and you can tell through their environment and story that just makes each of them interesting. The combat system has drastically changed. We are introduced to two combat systems called field battle and command battle. Field battle is your stand-alone full-action hack and slash where you can go out on the field and start hacking at the enemy health bar. (Kinda barebone Xanadu ex game). You can kill them or you can stun them for a benefit in command battle which is your normal turn-based combat. It is entirely original than previous games but I can’t help but wonder how lacklustre the command battle was. SCLM is pretty much linked and the same with burst being ways to utilise S craft and buff yourself. It’s a small pet peeve with SCLM having to be close to each other and how there is a lack of position mapping in the game which is a huge bummer. I hope to see more in the next game. We were also introduced to the Xipha system which is honestly a better quartz system than Trail of Cold Steel by far. You can manually set arts as its own section (arts driver) and add in different quartz to diversify the build even more(Holo Core). You also play into the classic line system from older games with the introduction of shard skills. The amount of diversity in creating a build using shard skills(passive skills) along with what you want your character style to be is crazy gameplay building. If they actually lean into more mechanics in Trails through Daybreak 2 and improve more on command battles and field battles. You got a contender for best gameplay of the series. (Bring back field orders lowkey and team attack pls)This game got rid of the abyss mode from the last game and we have a nightmare difficulty as usual. Honestly, it wasn’t that hard because there is some cheap stuff you can abuse. The issue is that fights are drawn out for so long that it is pretty much necessary to speed up fights. Unless you are a masochist and love to suffer through hours of farming and battles.The music is alright as usual. I actually do like some of the music in some areas and even throughout the city. I wish the battle music was better though, I miss the music from Crossbell Saga and I don’t think we're ever gonna get that feeling of music ever again. Unless the goat comes back, they have done some decent music in trails into reverie so I have to hope harder again.Sidequest in this game is actually insanely interesting. When you finish a sidequest your choices will cause Van’s three alignments of LAW, GRAY and Chaos to fluctuate. They not only affect your combat stats but also plot points and abilities in later chapters. Along with that, you have probably the most interesting sidequest lineup of all time. You really get to do quests from police, bracers, mafia, ouroboros and other faction members throughout the game. Along with that, you have some pretty fun side character affection stories and bonding events that really had me invested throughout the game. If you combined all that with how the game rewards you for doing them actually made sidequesting one of my personal favourites.The gifting system is still in the game which is fine and all…… BUT THEY GOT RID OF FISHING!!! (It’s in the next game). ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, how the heck am I gonna fill my craving for fishing now that I have to wait until 2025 for the next game. Not only that, it lacked any minigames whatsoever besides a battle simulation and team cinema session. I riot at the fact they made a game solely to not add many fun elements into doing side content. It was just doing sidequests, talking to everyone, buying stuff and finishing the day. Sometimes I just want to chill and play card games or fish on the side you know? On a serious note: I was actually surprised by a lack of them, I heard it will bring it all back in the next game but I have to see.Before I recommend the game. There is a big spoiler con, and that spoiler con is the misuse and building up of Van’s character arc. I feel like it gave way to so many hidden secrets and future setups that we will overcome, and face. But it felt like a shot in the face when it abruptly ended with the power of friendship to fix everything. I hope there is more building to Van as a character because it made me feel like there is not much for the character Van in the next game. But I have two other games to worry about till I have a final say on that. I do recommend this game because it is a new saga in the mix that plays heavily into dark settings. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love that and I actually do love the overall cast of the game. Their new combat system is great along with the xipha system. I look forward to seeing how they expand on it even more. I still hope we get to see a danger that will persist as the overall true saga villain but we have to see. I am looking forward to the next game. I will see you all over in the next upcoming Legend of Heroes game:THE LEGEND OF HEROES: TRAILS THROUGH DAYBREAK 2!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

_childDocuments_.review: I loved every minute from this game. I love Cold Steel and Rean as a protag, but Van and the new crew are certainly a breath of fresh air. You'll recognize some faces from CS but for the most part, all of the new characters are very memorable and enjoyable! _childDocuments_.review: Trails is my favorite JRPG series of all time. I discovered trails during the pandemic and started with Sky (which should be the most recommended entry point), struggled at the early chapters but oh my god it really picked up the pace halfway, and the slow burn was worth it. I fell in love with Liberl and the world-building of Zemuria. I fell in love with the characters (even the npcs), how the they evolve as the story progresses and also how the world changes as the characters slowly learn of the plots happening. And here I am after that game, caught up with the latest english translated game of Trails which is Daybreak.I would say that Daybreak feels more of a modern approach of Sky. It has everything I loved about sky, the slow introduction of the characters with their arcs, the slow bustling travels of them to different cities and how cozy it is to be a part of Arkride Solutions. I loved every moment of it and seeing recurring characters from past games which has a big impact on the storyline and how they interact with the new cast. I especially love that Renne is here again, who is my favorite character of trails. Van as the protagonist was refreshing. Aaron was my favorite in Daybreak since he has so much chemistry with everyone and made the interactions more fun. I guess I'm just biased since he reminds me of Olivier. Though I wasn't that impressed with the antagonists of the story this time, It still was an enjoyable game because we learn more of the lore and how everything was connected from the past games to now. The new game combat system is cool but I miss the orbment system from the past games. It was so satisfying when I get new orbments and customizing the build for each character. I wished that would be back in later installments because I feel that orbment in Daybreak didn't have a big impact for each character build. The graphics also improved a lot compared with cold steel.AND ALSO I CANT WAIT FOR THE SKY REMAKE!!! For future players, please start there and not in Daybreak because there would be a lot spoilers for you unless you're the type who isn't bothered playing games out of order.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid entry in the Trails series and a strong start to the Calvard arc. It is easily the best starting place for the series after the Sky trilogy. However, there are so many references, characters, and backstories tied to past games that someone without knowledge about them would miss a large chunk of the experience and emotional beats of this game.The new MC serves as an incredible liaison between the good, the gray, and the bad parts of the world unlike previous games where your affiliation naturally tied you down in one way or another. The banter between some of the new cast was also quite entertaining.This game is the first Trails game that introduces a mix of action combat in field battles with turn-based combat. While it has some room for improvement, I thought it was a great addition. The combat and art systems have been reworked once again. I hope there is some rebalancing in future games because the amount of new systems and abilities made things a bit too easy imo, but the new systems were still fun to use.All in all, I'm looking forward to seeing where the arc is headed to next!

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best entry points into this absolutely monolithic JRPG series. The game is the 11th in a long series that is excessively well connected and often demands that previous games in the series be played to have a decent understand of the overarching plot and past events as they feature prominently as the main drive to the world that is Zemuria.Daybreak is absolutely no different in this regard. However it stays relatively light on the details and references in a way that even a newcomer to the series can enjoy and understand. However as is usually the case, future games in this series will definitely take the gloves off in this regard.The Music and battle system are both enjoyable to listen too and fun to partake in, even if there isn't as many great bangers or that the combat is really easy even on its hardest difficulty, the action combat is also kinda ass as well - but I've heard it gets improved in future games in the series. In the end I find Daybreak to be one of the best trails games, especially for a newcomer. Asking someone to play 10 previous games is a daunting task and usually causes quite a lot of people to just bounce right off. Daybreak is different, it holds your hands and introduces you to the world and shows you that Zemuria is a lovely place. (kek)If you enjoy Daybreak I implore you to check out previous games in the series from the beginning, you will definitely find characters you enjoy and said characters will almost with certainty, show up again in future games. Understanding their motives and realizing how these characters grow into their roles is what makes Falcom games so good, and its something that will outright ruin your enjoyment of other JRPG games.But Man do I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LOVE it. Its my favourite JRPG series bar none, and I don't think any game will ever surpass it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: Another fine entry to the Trails series. There are a lot of refinements to the combat system with a sort of interesting hybrid between their old systems which adds some new depth to it. The mixed command/ field battle was interesting and I am sure that system will grow as currently its quite basic, I am glad the majority is still focused on the turn based battles though.Falcom are really improving on their environment design, the locations you visit look better than ever and Calvard has quite a unique identity. The characters and story were good, it builds quite a lot on events from previous games so you are well rewarded for your knowledge of the series. The biggest drawback is probably pacing issues, which is quite common in trails. Usually the start is slow and the end goes crazy but its almost the inverse here, Daybreak has a very strong start but the end starts to drag a little with a very long final chapter which doesn't add too much.Overall though a great entry to the series and I am looking forward to seeing how this arc progresses.

_childDocuments_.review: Was scared while playing this game because while I was playing the first couple of chapters it felt like a slog to go through. _childDocuments_.review: A good start for a new arc.  Good new protagonist.  Good new graphics engine.If you are coming from earlier Trails games and are vested in the lore, this may feel a little bland for the first couple chapters.  I think that's due to introducing the new region, characters, and cities that you'll know little to nothing about at first.  Fighting has changed enough that you may feel lost for a while, but it's solid once you figure it out.  At least for me, the trick to turn-based was to jump straight into buffing the team first, especially with food, then start hammering on the enemy.  Holo recommendations during battle are junk.  You can often just press the Attack button and deliver far more damage than, "Use an art to attack their weakness!" which is what the Holo will tell you to do.Several systems have been simplified.  No fishing.  Cooking is just press a button to cook and wait for the pre-assigned character to cook it.  Exploration feels kinda pointless, which seems odd since this is a whole new region.  I guess people really hate missables.  Music is subjective, but for me seems unusually bland except for a few exceptions that are jarring in how good and appropriate they are compared to the other 80%.Not as much fan service as some earlier titles.  This game is more adult in a gritty way, not in a revealing way.  That said the protagonist is older than usual for a Trails game, and hangs out with 16 and 13 yrs old girls most of the time, so... JRPG, what can you say?Well worth your time just to experience Calvard and a new protagonist if you are a prior Trails fan.  If you are new to the series, maybe try Sky FC or Cold Steel III instead.  So far, about a 3rd of the way into this game, I don't think it would make me want to try other Trails games.

_childDocuments_.review: Only 3 hours in, but this feels like it's winding up to be another solid entry into an already venerable series, and the first on the new engine. Game looks and plays great, seems set to elevate both the storytelling and the gameplay from the prior arc. Wasn't 100% sold on the real-time field combat, but after experiencing it I can say it makes fighting non-boss enemies in areas much less of a slog. It's still a bit simple (I hear they've added more options in the next entry), but maybe that's it's strength - it gets out of it's way and lets you enjoy the game. Sad to hear this series is just about over, but hopefully Falcom can put these game mechanics to use in their new IP.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first game bought on Steam as I played the rest elsewhere, but this game was an absolute blast to play through as a fan of the Trails series. I found it to be the perfect introductory point to a brand new arc with a lot of twists and turns to keep me on my heels, witty dialogue from all the NPCs to keep me engaged, and characters that made me feel like I was frolicking around Crossbell City again. The soundtrack seems divisive among the fandom but I highly enjoyed it as well. The gameplay can get a bit easy over time after you figure out the mechanics, but it's still a fun time for me nonetheless. Even if someone never tried the Trails series before, I'd still recommend this game if they have a passing interest and can tolerate the long run-time, as I feel it has a lot of what makes this long-running JRPG series appealing to many hardcore fans wrapped up in this neat little package.

_childDocuments_.review: And a new arc begins. The classic structure of main- and sidequests and talking to NPCs in a fairly linear but slightly open world remains. New lead and crew, new combat system that feels very fluid and fast. Some familiar faces return, as usual, but that's not where the focus is this time as Van builds up his crew. There's a sense of road trip adventure as we finally get our first personal look at Calvard. At this point in the timeline, this world is now effectively modern-day with cars, the internet and mobile phones, implemented with shards and sepith instead of silicon and gas.The larger plot is fine, but clearly still ramping back up after the last mega-arc. Series veterans will not be shocked to learn that the game has the usual sense of repetition in structure, but the main critique would be a particularly uninspired final dungeon. Visually not bad, but effectively a linear hall with some one-room "sidepaths" so pointless that it made me wonder why they even bothered.Is it a good entry point? It does not require you to know much about previous games and stands well on its own I think, but it will spoil you on some of the character arcs and plot points that came before, of course, as all of these games in the end are tightly woven together into a single, continuous story.As usual, the western Steam port is simply excellent. Visually there were some upgrades to previous games. Falcom is fairly locked into "their" look at this point, so some of it is subtle, and some a bit more obvious (like the new water system). The camera work has improved a bit and some of the most dramatic scenes get a bit more cinematic oomph now. The music continues to be mostly beautiful and very loopable.TLDR: changes to combat and new setting and crew mix things up, but it sure is Trails through and through. If you love it you love it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: Another phenomenal iteration to the best JRPG world. The group, while not my personal favorite is varied enough that everyone should find one or two peeps they enjoy. For myself, Van has become one of my favorite protagonists, and characters, of the series. The mystery behind his past and his street smarts are a joy to explore as he strolls through the odd jobs helping people who don't want to or can't get the authorities involved. His three loves in life — sweets, cars and baths — are a fantastic addition to make an already intriguing character so much more "alive". A simple idea, but one that many games and stories could learn from. The main story itself — in the typical trails fashion — is one of escalating stakes, improbable odds, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fights, and with more twists than a mountain pass. A trail's story through and true; what's not to love.The world building, as always, is rich with fantastic "NPCs" (perhaps the best set in the series), references to previous games and bits of lore about event we have been introduced to years ago.The game-play sees some innovation and change from the previous iterations, but overall retains the core of the series. While faster and less annoying due to lack of certain status effects, it lacks in the variety of builds, and to some degree, depth. Still, with this new system, I've found myself less annoyed with long dungeons and less reliant on turbo mode. If you want to win, just stack Van with CP increase and regeneration gear and just spam S-crafts to win. Music is top tier. What else did you expect?All in All, Trails/10.P.S. Copium for Kai release date late 2025.

_childDocuments_.review: If this was my entry point into the series, I would say its a fantastic game. However, unfortunately, I played the previous series, TCS. Keep this in mind, as Daybreak still blows away most other modern jrpgs, so my criticism here is simply a comparison to other games in the series. Daybreak falls short of Trails of Cold Steel in every single metric; compared to TCS,Combat is clunky and theres very little customization due to having about 1/10th the amount of items, quartz, and other features.The gameplay loop is very repetative, about 70% of the game just feels like fetch quests.The story is, compared to TCS, like comparing twilight to war and peace, it is a simplistic, cliched mess without any of the love and care and detail the TCS story had. It felt like a mobile game or mmorpg quests storylines, zero impact or intrigue.Since this is in a new region of the world, it is perhaps fair to use that as a reason for why the available game world feels small and unintersting.I could go on, but I think you get the picture.Please, keep in mind, I thoroughly enjoyed the game, and it is still better than 99% of other JRPGS on the market, but I cant help the expectation of a continuation of quality from TCS, so its a bit dissapointing in that regard.

_childDocuments_.review: Just as a heads up, this is the 11th entry in the series, if you have not played a Trails game before I would HIGHLY recommend starting with Trails in the Sky, as that is the chronological start for the series. The ongoing story is debatably the biggest draw for the series so while you could start with this entry, keep in mind that you will spoil elements of the other games which are still relevant.With that out of the wayWhile I can't go in-depth on the story due to spoilers I will say the number one thing I loved was the tone.Taking the role of what is basically a private investigator and bounty hunter for people who can't turn to the law, the interactions Van has with clients that would've otherwise been vilified in other arcs leads to some interesting interactions and scenarios. What's also refreshing to see is the series not shunning darker elements of its story, particularly death. It's all too common to see scenarios across media where you're thinking it's convenient that someone lived or villains that should be put to the sword are talked out of being bad, Daybreak typically doesn't have this problem. As a result, this is potentially the highest stakes Trails game thus far, with a real sense of tension at points that really kept me engaged the whole way through.The main cast is also quite enjoyable, with a variety of backgrounds, some familiar in premise, some fresh, but I did enjoy the relations they shared all the same. That being said I do have a some issues, primarily with returning characters/side characters.There's so many characters that feel notable with their introductions, interactions, titles, etc. but their overall relevance to the plot can feel a bit lacking, which is sad to see considering how well prior titles have managed series favourites.My only other real issue with the usage of characters in this story is how some of the main cast have their plots handled, whether it be through a mystery that's built up for so long only for the payoff to feel a bit lacking, or not enough of a story at all, and while I won't go in-depth on this due to spoilers, I will say this doesn't ruin any of the cast for me Daybreak is quite different compared to prior entries due to the introduction of action RPG combat instead of just being turn-based. Despite feeling like a stripped down version of Falcoms other series Ys, this helped speed up basic encounters by A TON! What's great is that if you don't want action combat, the game lets you freely swap between turn-based and action, however turn-based combat is mandatory for all plot relevant encounters. Personally I really liked this system, especially since there's incentive to swap from action combat to turn-based since you get a solid bit of burst damage and a variety of buffs if you enter turn-based with advantage.Daybreak has also reintroduced quartz values, slot quartz with specific values onto a line in your orbment not only for the passive buff a single quartz provides, but also the abilities it can provide when combined with other quartz. While I'm happy they brought this system back from the Sky/Crossbell games, I'm annoyed that a lot of the things you build up towards is just passives for transition from action to turn-based mode, which is useless in boss fights since those start in turn-based, and other buffs which you might not be able to get at all depending on which quartz you can end up inserting on specific characters. While it's not something that should be ignored, the majority of what it provides feels unexciting.Arts (basically spells) unlike prior games actually don't come from quartz this time, instead they come from plug-ins. You have a main plug-in which provides the bulk of your important arts and a few extra slots you can unlock which let you slot in whatever arts you've unlocked on the side, either by purchasing them or as a reward for something else. This is a system I can get behind as you still have a sense of progression with certain arts on your plugins being locked behind the level of your holocore, speaking of...Holocores are basically master quartz from prior entries, something you slot into your orbment that determines your build, the difference here is that while it provides passives that increase in potency as it levels up, there is another resource needed to actually make the Holocore function, S-Boost.S-Boost is a resource that's gained pretty passively through combat that when used, puts you into a powered up state that you can REALLY feel, and it feels great. The most notable thing an S-Boost is used for is S-Breaks, because while you still need 100 CP to use an S-Break like prior titles, you also need atleast two units of S-Boost to use an S-Break. The most notable change this causes is that you can't just enter a boss fight and spam everyone's S-Craft to win instantly The morality system is mostly a miss for me.While I really like how you're given choices that you're not chastised for, what bothers me is how some choices feel better/more conclusive than others, and that the morality system you build up has very little payoff, with only the level 3 ranks having any major payoff.The new achievements system was a pretty alright way of handling rewards that you might go out of your way for, though the biggest complaint I have with this system is how easy it is to grind out some of the best rewards right from the start with little effort.The sidequests were overall pretty enjoyable, I've always enjoyed the sidequests in Trails as they usually help make the world feel more alive and fleshed out, while there were a few duds that I'll forget about, for the most part I feel these were pretty nice.The new recipe/food system also feels very lacking.I strongly dislike how you have to consume every food item you find to build up to the major rewards, as a lot of food items are basically junk and often times I need healing, I have something very specific in mind to help instead of whatever random bits of food I have on hand. Recipes themselves also felt very lacking, as I quickly gained recipes that would become valuable throughout the entire game while ones that came after felt very pointless.I really appreciate the change of artistic style for a lot of the menus and splashart, it feels way more stylish compared to prior entries, great improvement.If you're this invested in the series like I am, you were realistically going to get this anyway, but what we got is what I would classify as one of the better titles in the series, and one I'm more than happy to see where it goes from here.It could drag at points, one of the chapters in particular really bugged me, but there's enough highs and good moments to make it all worthwhile.It's a lovely start to a new chapter for Trails and a good sign of things to come.
