_childDocuments_.review: Trails Through Daybreak is a huge improvement over prior titles in the franchise. Combat has much better pace, balance and direction, exploration feels so much smoother, graphics has improved tremendously, a lot of QOL enhancements have been introduced, and the English voice direction is a huge step up imo. There are still recurring problems like generic dialogue and stilted animations but those feel like franchise staples at this point.In terms of PC performance, the game runs very well and has a lot more options to choose from than most other Japanese developed titles. The amount of graphical options you have for a game of this caliber is genuinely impressive. Full button remapping is available and you can change button prompts whenever you want (displaying PS buttons if you're using a PS controller or Switch buttons if you're using a Switch controller). Heck, all settings can be changed whenever you want. You don't have to exit to the main menu to apply changes like some other games. You can also choose to resume your game when you launch from Steam, skipping the main menu entirely.If you're new to Trails, do know that it is more difficult to get into the franchise from here than it is for other first games in their respective series. The obvious reason being that the gameplay here is so much better that going back to play the older titles will give most people neck-breaking whiplash. The main reason however, is that the Calvard series (the Daybreak games) is so much more involved with the world that they have built up that it might actually be too overwhelming for some people to take in at the start. You're bombarded with terms, organisations, names, events, etc from the get go that's never explained as you're expected to know these things by now. It's certainly not a deal breaker and you can quite easily get up to speed but just know that this game expects more of you than the other titles.All in all, this is a great entry in the Trails series and fans are eating good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game marks the start the unofficial 2nd (potentially) arc of the Trails series. Set in a new region with new main characters as well as improved combat and graphics. For players of the previous games the plot follows similar to Reverie, where modern technology is in tandem with the happenings around Calvard. All in all Falcom have  basically smashed together all the best aspects of their previous titles to create Daybreak. Players new to Trails can start here and experience one of the best offerings in the franchise.*NO Spoilers*As stated in the overview, the plot takes all the best parts of the previous titles and take the player through a most engaging and emotional experience. Van being the centre of this title is different from the other 3 main characters in the best way possible. He allows other characters to express their authentic selves, who in turn push the story along and Van is pulled through the situations he faces. Falcom have been able to get out of their rut with boring 1st chapters in this game by borrowing elements from Zero, it is the main reason why this game is fun to play until the end. The combat system is a new modern version, with a blend of turn based and action based combat. Boost is the central turn based mechanic that allows characters to unleash their full potential. (Octopath Traveler is close reference) I think that this is the best version of the boost mechanic because it requires to the player to focus on different elements to reach each characters potential. Being said Van is set up to be the main damage dealer in this game, this is good and bad but for me it is more bad.Van naturally outshines his companions and is strong against both mobs and bosses, even if you don't give him the best items. This game being as long as it is, as well as being resource poor, the gameplay becomes only about Van ending the fights.  The action part of combat is a step up from the previous way players can engage combat with enemies on the field. The best aspect of this allows fighting to be seamless with no transition screens as well as keeping CP at max points easier. The only problem with this mechanic is that the animations take too long so speeding them up becomes a must. However the enemies also move so fast that it is hard to dodge attacks from them, so i just mostly gave up and went back to the old way of spamming heals in the menu screen. For fans of the Trails games this is the first time you are able to witness what the strength levels of characters from the previous arc are to the new characters. Given that the older characters have fought through defining moments in Zemurian history, it seems logical they would be leagues ahead in usefulness during combat. However Falcom decided that changing from the old combat system to the new one, these older characters also needed changes done to their capabilities. Which left me very confused when a teenager with little combat experience, is much more useful that this older character that has much more renown and experience fighting god like entities. It warps the perception of past events to the point where questions about whether or not these incidents could have been handled by random npc's instead. It it my personal disappointment given i have played most of the Trails games on Nightmare difficulty, Daybreak is by far the easiest game for me. So im left wondering does Falcom not care about each characters mechanical prowess and only their story or "plot power". ANYWAY this game gets a big double thumbs up from me!!

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the best game in the long-running Kiseki series.After putting myself through the hell that is a first playthrough abyss run of Hajimari--KnK was absolutely a breath of fresh air. Utilizing a main character that already has an established history in the canon allows for a much better focus on a core cast rather than the bloated cast of the last 5 games. Clearly the protagonist takes plenty of notes from Sakata Gintoki & I am incredibly glad for it--finally a character that isn't completely one-dimensional & interacts with the world in meaningful ways rather than approaching everything with a bullheaded sense of justice & goodness.Pros- Follows through with a morally gray story & cast (People actually die! Yay!)- Protagonist is established as a developed individual--allows for focused character growth & interactions between generations- Side quests are significantly better than prior games--some are silly, some develop the world or chapter, & of course some are filler (More monster extermination!)- The new engine feels great--seamless transition to combat from the field feels great & intuitive- Music was fantasticCons- Just my take--but I thought the resolution & final chapter was probably the weakest from a narrative perspective. They went from a more fresh take on a JRPG to some real trope-y stuff at the end- Combat was far too easy. First game in a new series so I get it--but for a first playthrough on nightmare just raw stats for your characters are insane. Easily abusable mechanics, but even without them every fight basically goes down by spamming S-Crafts- I understand why it's done... but I'm really over cast members joining through "x event" & now they have some personal vendetta and it forms their motivation to joining the team. And not every cast member is intro'd like this.. but I really would've appreciated a more innovative or interesting way that one of the younger cast members would join the teamOverall, 100% think this game is the best in the series. Crazy to think I'm here 11 games later but excited to play KnK 2 when it comes to the west.

_childDocuments_.review: If, like me, you're a fan of the Trails franchise and you've played all the previous games in the series, you probably already know what to expect from this one regarding tropes, story beats, character archetypes, anime-isms, callbacks, references, and returning characters and plot threads from previous games.. And, of course, the game delivers on all those fronts.And much like the Crossbell duology mixed things up with the game mechanics by changing things while still being recognizable from what you had on the Sky trilogy,  and later the Cold Steel quadrilogy did the same thing, this one makes changes to the missions, combat and orbal arts systems while still making sense based on what you know from the previous games.I like that while the Sky trilogy focused on a couple of teenagers working as this world's version of adventurers in Liberl, the Crossbell duology focused on a group of young people becoming rookie cops in said city, and the Cold Steel arc focused on a group of teenagers studying to be soldiers in Erebonia, this one focuses on a guy in his mid-twenties who runs a sort of P.I.-Bounty Hunter agency in Calvard that is not opposed to taking somewhat shady jobs. So far so good. Thing is, when I installed the game I found it odd that it was roughly 10 GB smaller than Trails Into Reverie since Google said this game's story is longer. But now playing it I see why that is. Seems they opted to cut costs by taking a few steps backwards from previous games because the city of Edith seems kind of empty compared to places like Crossbell and the larger cities we saw in Erebonia and Liberl. And on top of that, most of the NPC's you see have no lines of dialogue so you can't talk to them, unlike the previous games where you could talk to everybody and their dialogue changed several times as the story advanced. You're also much more limited regarding the ability to free roam and, as a result, the game feels more linear and rail-roady, at least at the beginning.As a fan of the series I am enjoying it and I'm sure it will fully win me over as the plot advances like all the previous games have done, but I was a bit disappointed with those changes because I was expecting it to be a clear improvement on Trails Into Reverie in a similar way Cold Steel 1 was improved upon by Cold Steel 2, then by part 3, part 4 and finally Reverie, just lke the Crossbell games improved upon the Sky trilogy. This is the first time I don't feel that is the case since I started playing Cold Steel 1 and I didn't feel it was immediately better than Trails To Azure.Edit: I've finished the game and I really liked it. My complaints are mostly minor and focuus on trival things about game mechancs I liked better in previous games, such as the turn-based combat system or the fact that it felt odd that Van doesn't fish. The only real complaint I have is that the final chapter, titled "Finale," seems a bit disjointed and lke an afterthtought to the story and doesn't seem to flow well with all that happened before, but I can forgive it because the first game in every Trails arc is hindered by the fact that they already know it will have sequels.

_childDocuments_.review: To my great surprise, .Starting at the end of S.C.1208, this game takes place 2 years after Cold Steel 4, and 1 year and an half after Reverie.Which is why it's surprising they managed to make it works for new player. While there are plenty of references and characters from past arcs makes up a huge chunk of the supporting cast, they never outright spoils thing that happened before, and makes the story understandable even without context if you don't mind reference going over your head.Gameplay wise, the game is much more fast-paced, and shakes the usual formula quite a bit.Gone are the 'static' links from Cold Steel, and instead it works on two characters being close to each other while they attack.Movement is no longer a separate actions, but something you can do at willduring your turn.Master Quartz have been separated into Holo-core, which provides the bonuses (only when boosted, which is yet another new machanic), and Art Driver, which contains the arts.And something heavily featured in trailers and the like is that you can now 'fight' in real time, though it is mostly an extension of the old advantage system : instead of just hitting enemies in the field once from behind, you now hit them until they're stunned, at which point you can begin turn-based combat as before, or you can keep hitting them in real time attack (no craft, no arts, no buffs, et caetera makes it unviable against anything but the weakest enemies until NG+ however)All in all, a very good entry in the Trails series, and the best 1st game of an arc since Sky.

_childDocuments_.review: A nice and very much needed breath of fresh air after the previous 10 games in pretty much all aspects - slightly more "raw" tone of the story and characters, protagonist, region, overhauled combat system, engine, UI, vibe of visuals and OST - all of these are new and different from what the series has done up til now in a way that this entry really does feel like the start of a new part of the entire series. But it is definitely still Trails at heart, with all the good and the bad.One of the highlights most people will mention is the tone/atmosphere of the story, which is admittedly a bit more raw/mature than usual, a welcome change in this series for me. It's not like Trails has suddenly turned into some brutal and dark personal story or anything. But during the course of Daybreak, there are things happening on screen that the series has shied away from showing in the past and kept mostly to backstories/lore. Things that you couldn't really imagine any of the other protagonists doing or saying. This tone is carried throughout both the main story and the side quests, as well as the humour.As for the characters, this cast is in the better half of Trails casts for me. I still prefer Reverie's Imperial Picknicking Front and CS3's NC7 though, as I felt that all of the later additions to the main group in this game didn't resonate with me at all and dilluted the dialogue. I wish that Daybreak kept the main cast to a maximum of 5-6 members, like the 2 aforementioned entries, and allowed their dynamics with each other to grow a bit more. In the second half I started feeling that some of the characters are connected only to the protagonist, rather than to each other, which wasn't a problem in the first half when there were only 3 or 4 party members. (I heard Daybreak 2 is a lot more character focused, so looking forward to that part.)Speaking of the protagonist, for a first game of the arc, Van is my favorite by far out of all the previous main characters and he carried the "character side" of the storytelling for me. He is the main example of the different tone of the story.For the setting, I don't love it nearly as much as the cold "blood & iron" vibe of Erebonia. It is still unique and especially the most diverse. But I'm not really into how modern it feels with progress of technology, as a personal preference.The gameplay is... limited. I feel like Falcom has all the great ideas, but I also felt that a lot of the budget/development effort really went into the engine, without leaving room for much else. The combat feels nice and has fun ideas, but lacks a bit of depth so far. Similarly, Daybreak lacks complexity in regards to orbments/quartz, equipment, rewards, exploration and it also has no minigames and very limited side content. All of these aspects always get better with additional entries though, so I'm glad we got the base stuff and new engine established and now the series will just build upon it.

_childDocuments_.review: Great story, amazing characters, fun dialog and story beats (characters interact so well with a lot of moments that cause me to burst out laughing), everything all makes sense with things able to be figured out story wise with a spectacular soundtrack. _childDocuments_.review: New arc, new story, new characters, a new conflict.Also, new combat mechanics and a new country.Everything feels fresh!I also like this new protagonist personality, it's like an anti-hero and it's good for a change of pace and very different from the kindhearted Estelle Bright, the noble Rean Schwarzer and the heroic and analytic Lloyd Bannings, Van Arkride: sharp tongue, foul mouthed, acid speech and a shady reputation. He has his own honor code, not a bad person but he likes the police and the bracers very far from him.The gameplay feels weird at the beginning given the control schemes from previous Legend of Heroes games, but once you get accustomed to them, it's enjoyable.My body is ready to enjoy this game!

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best JRPGs I've ever had the pleasure of playing through, Falcom has really learned to hone their craft of building up, as well as maintaining the rich lore they've constructed over the last 20 years. I normally find it hard to relate or even care about most protagonists in JRPGs due to their simplicity. However, the main character in this iteration, is a morally grey character, that leans closer to the light, but allows for the player to make important choices about his morality that have an impact on your party choices near the end of the game. It's an incredibly refreshing change to a beloved franchise, that rewards players for playing their games. Lastly, the change to combat, where it offers players an option to choose between a simplistic action based combo style system to defeat basic over world enemies, or to rely on the slower more methodical turn based combat system that's needed for stronger opponents, has to be one of my favourite combat systems implemented in any JRPG; it just feels right. While these games come with a rich history of lore behind them that benefit people that have played through their previous titles, I dont believe you need to go back and start with the earlier games in the series to enjoy this game. I would wager playing this game would make a person want to go back to enjoy Falcom's other games in this series to learn more about characters that you liked or were intrigued about in this title, as that was my experience after starting with the Cold Steel games myself.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: Over the years, I've played many games that have tried to combine turn based and action combat. This is the first one to actually do it!At first I didn't like it. But as I played, I grew accustomed to the system. And what a breath of fresh air. Sure, you can still go either turn based or action in any fight, but combining both is the greatest option. And the most fun. I spent 140 hours on my first play through and usually by 60 hours in, I pretty much know the combat system. Tedium ensues. But this game, combat late in story and it's still fun.I've played all the Trails games I that could, starting with Trails in the Sky, on a Dreamcast around the turn of the century. This one is one of the best. At 50 cents an hour its well worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a classic with a breath of fresh air and it makes an amazing gameOn one hand, this is what I expected from a Trails game, you got the chapter story structure, linear dungeons, familiar turn based combat, but on the other hand, a lot of the game feels new and shiny:* darker story with a lot of murder (not just in the past recollections)* revamped skills (quartz) and arts adds a lot more customizability* the hybrid action/turn-based combat feels very well integrated together and makes the game play more fast paced and fun* a brand new set of characters with a few returning casts and the voice cast really out done themselves this time. It's among the best I have heardThere are a few things that I wish the game didn't inherit from its predecessors:* like previous games, only half of the scenes were voice acted. If only Nihon Falcom would stop being so stingy with the voice budget, it would elevate the game to AAA level* too many playable characters already in the first game. I really hope we don't end up with 50+ characters again by the end of the series. 6 ~ 8 max would be my preference unless you are allowed to field more than 4 in combat

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say, this game was an amazing edition to the Trails saga. I honestly think that Van might be my new favorite protag out of the whole series after just one game. They could have put a little more effort into the ARPG aspect attempt, maybe made the enemies have more than one move per enemy, perhaps add a bit more pizazz in the the hack n slash combos. Aside from that the in turn based combat is still above average. I enjoyed the changes to link attacking.With all that said, I am not going to sugar coat it like other reviewers will. If you haven't played all 10 games prior to this one, you probably shouldn't bother. Trails shamelessly references characters and events from the previous games pretty regularly and if you haven't played them it will mean very little to you. Since this game is heavily story focused, like a long running anime with multiple arcs, if you are going to GET into trails, strap in and do it right, I mean from the beginning from trails Sky - Reverie then play Daybreak.As for me, after 136 hours to complete this game, I am eager to see more as always when Daybreak 2 is localized.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. That escalated quickly.So, if you've played Trails games before, you know how it goes - a slow burn start to get the players acclimatised to the world, dealing with small requests in order to world-build, introduce characters, and make you feel nice and comfortable. Then as the game progresses you start to see the underlying tensions in the land your characters live in, before things ratchet up in intensity, you save the day, and a cliffhanger drops before you get landed in the supranational conflict in the sequel.So in that spirit, let me introduce you to Van - a Spriggan. A Spriggan is sort of a cross between a Jaeger (mercenary who sells their combat prowess for cash) and a Bracer (kind of an organisation of good Samaritans that are really good at fighting). He'll take any job, so we are told, regardless of who requests it - be they politician, next door neighbour, or gangster - so long as the pay is good and it doesn't cross his own moral code. We start off with him receiving a request from a student, who can't turn to the bracers or the police for help, and so begins the usual orientation exercise of helping out people who got scammed, leading us onto the usual crime scene of someone being murdered by the mafia and... Wait... what?So, yes... like I said at the top: that escalated quickly. And it escalates a hell of a lot further, I can assure you.It doesn't just escalate quickly in terms of pace of narrative, though - one of my few quibbles is it feels like in comparison to the previous games, technology has progressed a bit too fast, Calvard's military and (in particular) their research centre dwarfs Erebonia's... even when Erebonia was technologically superior, looking at Calvards resources, it shouldn't even have been close - Calvard had way too many savant researchers in comparison to Erebonia. The game would have been improved had everything been scaled back just a tad imho.Gameplay follows the Trails blueprints, in the main. The game is divided into chapters which start off info gathering with a little bit of combat spruced in whilst ticking off quests (or 4SPGs in the game), before the chapters crisis meets its apex and needs to be sorted out by brawn. It's a familiar enough formula, but that doesn't mean it's a bad thing. For my money, the Trails series has amongst the best turn based gameplay this side of full tactical X-Com like battles. Like Cold Steel before it, Daybreak tries to innovate. It's an uphill struggle given just how good its predecessor was, and it probably won't be fair to compare until the conclusion of the series. The combat in Reverie, after all, is actually quite different to Cold Steel I. So, initial impressions - the turn based system itself has undergone a number of changes... many of which I'm yet to be fully sold on (the changes to how ailments work, for example, and the shard boost system are some things that I will have to see whether they grows on me or not). On the whole though, it retains most of what has made Trails combat so great. My initial feeling is that it has probably achieved the best magic vs ability balance the series has had so far, but on the flip side things like information given to the player in general and particularly the UI regarding turn order have taken a sharp nosedive. There is a lot of room for refinement here, but in some ways that's a good thing given this is only the first game of this Arc.The action combat before it, however, is a complete bust for me. It just slows the game down drastically. Whereas in previous games combat against ordinary monsters roaming the map was a simple matter of gaining initiative with a well timed strike, and then getting into the meat of it, or else dispatching weaker monsters with ease if you were revisiting an area, the action combat means that either you have to put up with some fairly straightforward wailing on the enemy before you stun them and start the battle with an advantage, or you skip that completely and just start the battle, but without said advantage. In previous games, you would just one shot these weak enemies and move on, because they aren't meant to be an issue for you at that point in the game when you are revisiting the area. I get that they are trying to draw in people who might usually discount TB games, but I really hope this experiment will be binned after this arc. It's just not satisfying, it drags, and it detracts from one of the series' strong points.What else...? The graphics, now that they have got their new in house engine, are a marked step up from Cold Steel (shame about some of the UI decisions, but...) and the music - well, it's a Falcom game, it goes without saying that the music is top notch - but honestly, I've never considered either of those things to be my wheelhouse as a critic, so I'll leave it to other people. For me, Trails games live and die by their world-building, storytelling, and combat. With the except of the action (pre)combat, it delivers on all of those. I'm a happy customer, and looking forward to Daybreak 2.

_childDocuments_.review: its trials, but a little different, a little new.  especially after the last few games where it felt like every game you started at the end game, this feels pretty refreshing.  its still trials, but its a little new and you're not starting level 50 with piles and piles of backstory you can't possibly keep up with.  my only real complaint is that the performance of the game seems a bit lacking.  like, yes, compared to previous trials games the graphics are improved a bit.  But i mean, compared to other games there's very little detail, the models are simple, there's not that much on the screen at one time - i feel like i should be able to easily get 120fps in 4k on my 4070 super but at 4k ultra i can maybe get 30-40fps.  like, is the performance necessarily bad? eh, not really, but I feel like plenty of other games 'look better' with higher framerates than this game.  not sure what the deal is there but i do hope they work on that a bit.  fwiw i play in 2k and get about 80-90fps (and i expect 120, at ultra, given the complexity of the scenes/characters).  okay and maybe second complaint - the little widget that shows the order of whos attacking next i think is way more confusing than previous entries in the trials series.  this is a step back imho, but maybe its just there to inspire me to learn new things?  idk, but this thing was dead simple in coldsteel/reverie and now its kinda just weird.otherwise, yea, its trials, it will scratch that jrpg itch

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game after not being able to put it down since the english release and it has quickly become one of my top 3 trails game. Van is a compelling protagonist, the main party is generally well-written, and the setting is phenomenal. The game is a nice of change of pace after coldsteel while still being the Trails we know and love. Durante/P3H outdid themselves with this port. However, I did experience a couple of  that didn't affect my enjoyment of the game, but I thought it was worth pointing out in case NISA/Durante are able to fix them. I'll talk about them in the last section.TL,DR: Yes, but it's really not a great starting point.As you may have heard, Trails through Daybreak is the beginning of the most recent arc in the long-running  series, which is generally a decent place to start the series if you don't want to commit to the entire series that is about to span 13 main games or like the look of newer graphics/combat/etc. compared to the older (and somewhat dated) games in the series. I was hoping that this was the case with this game as I have been trying to get my brother into the series, but he values modern graphics somewhat highly - I was considering having him start here because of this so I spent the game being aware of plot-threads or concepts brought back from previous games. Many new characters have important connections to past characters/events that are not re-explained well for new players despite being pretty vital to understanding certain scenes and characters. if you find yourself going back to previous games after playing Daybreak, a lot of the events mentioned will straight up spoil the endings to certain games, plot twists, and character arcs that would ruin a lot of the fun of going through a Trails game. I could forgive this if the game had phenomenal presentation, but the main dialogue is still unfortunately partly-voiced just like the original Falcom release whereas NISA could have pulled an XSEED Coldsteel 1/2 and made the dub feel complete. NISA even went above and beyond for the previous game and added more voicelines, but took a step backwards with this release. I can only hope that they patch in more voicelines in the future while they are still working with this cast. Despite that disclaimer, you can start here if you really really want to as long as you are aware there will be some confusion and it might affect your enjoyment of previous games. Don't let that be a barrier to getting this game or getting into this series, the gameplay is explained well and the main party is a joy to watch. The Trails series is too special to let others talk you out of it.TL,DR: Trails in the Sky, but if not then Coldsteel 1.Obligatory, The best place to play through the series is by release date so Trails in the Sky -> Trails from Zero/to Azure -> Trails of Coldsteel -> Trails into Reverie -> Trails through Daybreak. Other reviews/comments have the reasoning for this so I won't go into detail. However for those of you who want the gameplay/graphics to be a bit more modern, then  is the best place for you. The story of the first game is relatively self-contained and is low on spoilers for previous games. The game is fully 3D for the first time in the series and is nearly fully voiced in English - previous games don't really have english voice acting. IMO, Trails hasn't gotten to the point where I look around the world and find it to be a visual treat so the lower quality character models/scenery isn't very outclassed by newer games. Coldsteel is the most divisive arc of the series, but Coldsteel 1 is very light on the things that people have problems with for that arc. I personally really enjoyed Coldsteel 1 and would rank it somewhat highly compared to other games. Again though, pick whichever start of arc game (Sky 1, Zero, Coldsteel 1, Daybreak) you find the most interesting if previous games are that unappealing and go for it. You don't have to go back to previous games  to enjoy an arc well enough. From the prologue alone, Falcom has set the tone of this arc to be different from Coldsteel in a number of ways. I will spoiler tag some things, but IMO they are very light spoilers that should not affect your experience unless I explicitly say so. Still if you want to be cautious, I would avoid reading my spoilers.  I will say that there is a slight return to the tone of Coldsteel in Chapter 3 but it's not to egregious imo. Definitely my least favorite chapter though unfortunately.The combat system has underwent a number of great changes to address some of the ways the previous system could be broken, but retains the core of Trails gameplay so it is not too big of a shakeup. What is there made the game feel fresh, but it is unfortunately one of the easiest Trails games and I have heard that it can be broken in different ways. I didn't do that and I played on normal - I didn't have to think too hard about my strategy to breeze through most of the game, save for the final bosses (which I still beat in one try each). I would definitely recommend for players to play on Hard at least to keep things interesting. The new field battle system is a welcome improvement and I hope they continue to flesh it out in future games. The text was also hard to read in a couple of menus, but there is a text size option that I didn't use lol.Van is shaping up to be my favorite protagonist. He has a distinct personality and a good character arc.Ranking: Van=C>Estelle>Rean>Kevin=LloydDaybreak is about a 9/10 with no game completely reaching a 10/10 for me. They're amazing games but due to budget constraints or writing issues, I can't call any of them close to perfect.Ranking: Zero>Azure>Daybreak>Sky FC>Coldsteel 3>Reverie>Sky SC>Coldsteel 1>Sky the 3rd>Coldsteel 4>>>>>>Coldsteel 2So despite having this section, I didn't really experience technical issues until the end. Durante/P3H made the PC port phenomenally and pretty - I was able to use by 3090 Ti quite well. There are only two things I noticed during my gameplay and one of those could be chalked up to my computer settings. The first, which could not primarily concerns a guest character during the finale (and probably chapter 5), ACTUAL SPOILER , their field attacks didn't have sound effects and one of their crafts had both English and Japanese text. That was the only instance that I noticed though. The second is that I would have some lag between actions during the later chapters. I would use an S-Break and it would take a little bit too long to activate. Similar things would happen with the transitions between field and command battles or if a cutscene started immediately after a battle and would have issues between loading the battle results and the cutscene. These things were a lot more noticeable but it wasn't constant. I haven't seen anyone else mention this so I thought I might as well. I did set most of the settings to Ultra and tried out the new SSGG(?) feature so maybe my computer couldn't handle it even though it's relatively high end.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoying the game so far. As a newcomer to the series, I don't feel that I'm lacking considerable knowledge from missing out on former titles. The game offers a history of the game world, a synapsis of former events and and a small glossar of the games factions etc.Character visuals are detailed, environments are a bit lackluster as in most JRPGs. As a result, performance faces no problems at any point. Over time, there are plenty of gear option to finetune your party for general purpose or very specific enemy loadouts.The game is story-heavy and even non-relevant NPCs have a few lines to drop if you chat with them. When it comes to voice-acting there have been some heavy budget-cuts as it seems. While the voice actors do a fine job, the use of voiced dialogue is very mixed, even within the same cutscene which makes me wonder why they even bothered at all, at times. This not exclusive to the English voices, but the Japanese ones too. I failed to see a rational pattern behind it yet.The combat system is rather outstanding: you have a mix of basic realtime action and round based combat. In action combat you got base attack, evades and charged attacks. You mostly use it against weaker enemies or to get a combat advantage by charging the enemy and then stunning them by entering round-based combat at will. You can even drop out of round-based to action combat again (not in all fights) and use the mix for highest combat performance. Add synergy attacks with group members, attack boosts and a wide range of combat skills and you get a very entertaining combat system.If you like JRPGs in general and don't mind a bit text-heavy games, Trails through Daybreak is for you.A few pros and cons:+ Good music score+ Good visuals+ Good performance + Excellent & unique hybrid combat system mixing action and turn-based elements perfectly together+ Nice QOL-feature to instantly load the last save game on game start (skipping intros and main menu and loading in a few secs)+ Fast-speed option per button input + Amicable main character working as P.I. in grey zones of the law+ no requirement to have played former titlesCons:Only the very weird use of voice acting without any recognizable logic (both English & Japanese). I can see why they didn't do a full voice over for everything. But at least the cutscenes could have been fully voiced. It's a bit of a mood killer when characters switch between voiced and non-voiced lines in the same scene and sometimes several times.Running the game in 4K (2K native with DLDSR), maxed settings, 80+ FPSFull System:i9 13900k, Gigabyte Aorus Z790 Master, 2x16 GB DDR5 GSkill Trident Z5 (no RGB crap) 6Ghz, MSI RTX3080ti Gaming Trio X, Audeze Maxwell with Dolby Atmos, WD Black SN 850X 4TB M2, Corsair HX850 Platinum PSU (850W)

_childDocuments_.review: As a veteran of the Trails (Kiseki) Series, I have to say this game, after playing around 18 hours, it’s probably one of my new favorites! The combat itself has been overhauled this time around, and while it’s taking a bit getting used to from the previous games, I adore its real time elements. Battles don’t switch to another plane for fights, but happen right before your eyes. I’m also curious about the karma system and where that will lead. Leading into that, I think Van might be my new favorite main character. Funny, cool, and leaning more morally grey than the previous protagonists. I could mention more stuff about the story, but if you’re a Trails fan, it’s more of the same political, slice of life, anime greatness that made the previous games so addicting! If you’re new to the Trails series, while there are more call backs to previous games, it’s a brand new story. Though, personally, I’d recommend playing the previous games to get even more out of it. Maybe when I'm done, which will be, oh, several months from now, I might write a longer review.

_childDocuments_.review: Listen, as someone who staunchly and stubbornly advises all people new to this series to start with Trails in the Sky FC, the very first game in a very long, interconnected story, I have this to say:It's okay if you start here. This game is a perfectly fine jumping on point.HOWEVER, you've gotta promise to go back and play the games that came before it. Even if you have to set the difficulty to easy to just get through the dated gameplay. You can read summaries and synopses all day long, but for this series, there is NO substitute for having that emotional attachment to the characters and the world on a personal level, especially when those characters show up again, multiple times. This game is great, by the way. I think it should leave a strong first impression of what this series has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: A new arc in the Trails series is upon us! Welcome to Calvard!As always starting a new arc in the series is a bitter-sweet feeling, I feel sad to leave Erebonia and Crossbell behind after 100s of hours with it's characters. At the sime time though I am filled with excitement for the new cast and setting that Calvard brings. This game was a joy to play through, the story is quite self-contained and gives you a nice jumping off point for the coming titles, The new party of characters are an amazing group that brings lots of great banter to the table! Calvard is a beautiful place in Zemuria, and I can't wait to get to explore more of it over the span of the next few games. As always the world was filled with interesting people and stories to experience, and I just need to know how some of my favourite NPCs stories pan out. Patrolling Edith and talking to it's inhabitants will be a habit I'll miss until the sequel comes out! The engine change makes a massive difference, everything looks so much more animated and alive, not to mention fast, this was the first Trails game where I didn't feel the need to use the high-speed mode (outside of the occasional wide open dungeon) As with my Trails through Reverie review I feel like I need to high-light the fact that my main playthrough were done on the PS5 and that this is why I write the review despite a low play time (Platinumed the game on PS5 after 151hrs played.)
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak is a refreshing new beginning within the Trails/Kiseki universe. This game starts off in the Calvard region, which is the republic we hear so much about but never see in older arcs. While it's heavily recommended to play all of the other games in the series, starting here is still possible. it's recommended to, at minimum, read the backstory and introductions available in the main menu prior to starting a new game. We see a brand new cast of characters as our primary party in this game, while characters from other regions return as well. This game has numerous references to the Crossbell duology, so if you have not played those yet, prepare for both spoilers and also confusion to come your way.Van Arkride is possibly the best protagonist in this series.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, I'm so happy Katsumi Enami is back for the art. The game looks so good and the optimization done by PH3 is incredible. This PC port should be brought up in conversations when talk of how an amazing port should be. I can run this game in 4K with very minimal drops when all other games I've tried are unplayable. (My pc is not 4K ready, monitor was bought mainly for my consoles) Falcom's new proprietary engine is fantastic and the work put into it shows. The translation is top-notch and the quality is not dropping at all despite how quick they're getting the games translated recently.The evolution of the battle system is fun and engaging. I love the Shard and Field battles, its such a great blend of Action and Turn-Based battles. One last thing I noticed immediately was how the tone is much darker, which I'll gladly take. Zero and Azure's (and 3rd) dark themes made them my favorite of the series up to this point. The world ending calamity looming over the Cold Steel saga never felt that dire since they almost always played it with a light-hearted tone or message. So excited for this new arc in one of the favorite series.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: Must play for JRPG fans, the trails series is an amazing series of jrpg where the world building story expands over its 10+ games. If you love story and deep lore this is a series for you. Daybreak itself is a refreshing redesign on some of its mechanic, I love the combat because it feels more fluid and free now, its own take of turn based rpg
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyable successor to the Trails of Cold Steel quartet, this game shakes up the series combat formula with both on-field and turn-based battles. The story's pretty fun so far too, with an early 20s protagonist, but I can't comment too far on that as I'm only in ch1 so far. Impressive cutscene visuals though.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: I am a long time series fan, and I am in shock how much of a step up these game is. Don’t get me wrong, I have loved pretty much all the games. But you would be hard pressed to not list dozens of flaws. While this game still has some, this really hits way way above the double A budget these games have. This is the kinda JRPGs that we’re peak in the 90’s I would recommend it to any JRPG/RPG fan new to the series or old.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: Very early days but the updates are amazing and it's a ton of fun. The new systems really add a spin and make things interested. I'm fascinated to see how they may change things.As far as the game as a whole it's Trails, so it's the best worldbuilding, storytelling and characters you'll enjoy. Not to mention an amazing soundtrack, as always.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: Trails through Daybreak marks the beginning of a new arc in the Legend of Heroes: Trails series. A lengthy, strong arc starter, with many callbacks to previous games and is just understandable enough for even new players to get used to.If you're looking for an entry point, this game works just fine! Trails through Daybreak is one of my favourite JRPGs of all time thanks to it's fast-paced combat system and well-written narrative, paired with many likeable characters.Yet another strong entry in the Trails series! 9.5/10 (some hiccups in pacing at the end).
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't giving this game's english dub a lot of thought, because usually the dubs for this series doesn't match the quality I expect.I don't think the dub itself is just as good as the Japanese, but it's leaps and bounds better than Cold Steel and Reverie. The game is awesome, and the gameplay is fluid and very good, the port is one of the best Nis have ever done so far, extremely well done. Compared to the Cold Steel III and IV, this one is incredible port-wise. And it's better than Reverie too.Overall, awesome game, and Damien Haas gave Van a pretty good voice, not only that he clearly enjoyed dubbing Van, the guy is full of life and frankly there's a LOT of terms in this series that are hard to say and he nailed them. So far he's carrying the entire game for me dub-wise because at least for the prologue, only him and two other characters have excedingly well-done voices, Agnès is a bit annoying though, but way better than Alisa's voice.Either way eventually I'll make a full review, but gameplaywise this game is perfect I already played it in Japanese before, so all I can say is that this dub is the best direction that NIS did so far.Also, I really love how they didn't tone down the game's dialog, people are complaining about woke, but truth be told, in the original script, they weren't vague about characters mentioning their sexuallity and stuff like that, and I'm glad they kept it instead of censoring it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: With the fans English translation patch, this game is playable for those who can not read Japanese.As you can expect from the newer Trails series, the updated graphics and visuals is a welcome addition for this game. You can also expect the same quality of stories that is prevalent from previous Trails games as well, though I suppose with so many established characters from the previous titles it may be getting out of hand. I think the campiness of the story is what makes Trails what it is, never the less I would love to see a much more mature theme in the future from the series.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: With the new engine, the new entry to the series is a nice breath of fresh air! Story is interesting with some twist here and there, although its repetitive to some extent. if you played reverie where certain scene they showed you how it works, you get to see all of it in this game! Gameplay-wise, kinda have a mixture of turn based and hack/slash (to stun your enemies purpose), engaging in combat appeared to be instantaneous as like action RPG.since this is the first entry to a new trail series, I would recommend people to play this, theres no harm in playing and you would not be losing that much of a story lore, as your first game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: Best first game of a trails arc. The new game engines on full display, combats freaking awesome, NPC dialogue continues to be great, main characters are great, music (in my opinion) is great although some tracks are pretty jarring, story ofcourse being the first trails game of a new arc is pretty slow but still good and expands on the overarching mystery, and love the more mature theme. Feels like a minor refresh to the trails formula and it’s been awesome throughout.Hope Falcon continues to do well and continue with this going forward.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: originally i was going to wait for the english patch. I started this series during covid lockdowns. played the fanpatch and NISA versions of zero/azure. I got to excited on waiting and the moment i had spare cash i got this. Using the fan patch until the release the NISA english patch at which point i'll probably do new game + to see any changes. Absolutely love this series and can't wait for the next game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: Same formula as the other Trails, I appreciate the little changes like the battle, i've always felt there was something missing in the cold steel saga, Daybreak adds just what i felt it was missing, the positioning during the battles. by the way it still feels like an incomplete game, they cut a lot of corners, but it is an enjoyable game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: My personal favorite game of the series. Love the new cast and darker/more mature themes. The new graphics engine is great. The turn-based combat system has been completely revamped and makes for a nice change-of-pace from previous entries. This game also introduces overworld combat, it's really simplistic but is a nice mix-up from exclusively turn-based combat during mob encounters.imho once the English version is released, it's a good entry point into the series for those who haven't played previous Trails games before and are hesitant to start from the earlier arcs. The cast is mostly new, the area is new, and the game was written by the devs to be a good starting entry point. There'll be spoilers certainly, but as someone who started the series with Cold Steel, if you enjoy this game enough to go back and play earlier entries, I think it'll be still rewarding. You'll enter those games with a different perspective on how parts of the story may develop, but watching everything unfold will still be great in its own right.Look forward to English release in 2024, will definitely be replaying then
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: There're only few games that can hooked me for hours and more, get me so invested in it's story and characters, drowned me in its deep lore and world building. Falling in love with Trails series is something that i won't ever regret.No need for further explanation. Calvard Arc has only getting started, the best part will come sooner or later.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: Likely my favourite arc in the series, not because it's new; but the tight knit group and character developments. As well as the MC, Van being way more relatable to a certain degree compared to previous MC's. Story is compelling leading you to look forward to the next chapter as you finish the current. As a long time trails fan I'm very happy with the direction of this game as it dives deeper into the darker aspects and settings of Zemuria, which makes it of course more interesting in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails through Daybreak

_childDocuments_.review: I played this on an ASUS TUF Gaming F15 Intel Core i5 10th Gen laptop with an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650/144 Hz graphics card.And I have to say, it runs like a dream.PH3 continues to deliver with their stellar PC optimisations, with the game running very smoothly at my system's max framerate of 144. While I can't fine-tune the graphics settings due to the game currently being Japanese-only, any concerns I had about performance or compatibility are safely behind me now.As for the game itself, admittedly this isn't exactly a high-fidelity title, but the changes in presentation and artstyle are all for the better. Character models look beautiful across the board, cutscene quality has improved by leaps and bounds since the early Cold Steel games, and I could even see some finer texture work on the clothing of the main characters, and subtle clothing and hair physics effects that added an extra layer of immersion and really show just how far Falcom has come over the years.While I couldn't grasp all the nuances of the gameplay thanks to the language barrier, this game is surprisingly playable in Japanese, with enough visual indicators and quality of life improvements that allowed me to intuit my way around the early chapters. And I had a genuinely fun time doing it.The revamp of the field combat system is the most obvious change, and serves to keep all monster encounters fresh and engaging, as you either bash your enemies into sepith, or try to leverage a few strong attacks to start the turn-based mode with an advantage (which is still where the meat of the combat is, though it can often be activated at your discretion now). The game has done a very good job on building upon the foundations set by Cold Steel and Reverie, as encounters are fast, snappy, and require thinking on your feet.Obviously the story and quest content largely went over my head, but I was still pleasantly surprised at just how I managed to adjust to the gameplay loop nonetheless. I'm incredibly grateful that Falcom's continued to use map markers to signpost main and side quests, and the revamped fast-travel system also shows you exactly where you need to go at any given time. The new Law-Gray-Chaos alignment system is also incredibly intuitive, as the game clearly points out, with visual aids, which choices will impact your alignment, and how. Obviously, I'm barely scratching the surface here, given the language barrier, but it says a lot about the game design quality that even with that barrier in place, I was able to figure out so much.I've had a high opinion of Trails's Japanese voice acting since playing Zero and Azure, and the same holds true here. Van and Agnes deliver excellent performances and Elaine has also left an impression on me. Sadly, it's clear to see that Falcom has cut corners in this department, with several cutscenes not being fully voiced, and alternating between voiced and unvoiced dialogue even within a few seconds. This isn't all that new, as even the Cold Steel games had this issue, but it does make me hope that additional English dialogue gets recorded for the dub a la Cold Steel I and II, regardless of whether NIS America actually goes through with it.All in all, Trails has never looked or played better than it does now, and I'm immensely grateful to NIS America and PH3 for giving us this excellent port to play with while we wait for it to be patched with the official localization one day. In fact, I'm now eagerly awaiting NISA and PH3's port for Kuro II, as playing such an excellent port that I know will be officially patched into English makes the wait a little less painful. Get on it, people.

The sprawling Republic of Calvard is experiencing an unprecedented economic boom brought on by post-war reparations. At the same time, feelings of uncertainty stemming from a massive influx of immigrants and bold political reform by the new president are rife.

Deep within its capital city, a young Spriggan man named Van receives a strange request that threatens to plunge the entire nation into chaos...

name: Sifu
detailed_description: Play now! About the Game Itching for some more good ol' Kung Fu action? The free Arenas expansion adds multiple hours of gameplay that will put your Kung Fu to the test. With 5 new game modes, 15 dynamic locations and 120 challenges, gear up for spectacular combats, brutal opponents, and endless opportunities to refine your moves. Whether you choose to play as a male or a female character, in Sifu, you will ponder that question on your path for revenge, hunting down your family’s assassins. One against all, you have no allies, countless enemies, and a mysterious amulet to bring you back to life every time you die. Yet, be warned! Your secret weapon comes with a hefty price to pay: aging and its consequences. Your enemies don’t wait their turn, and they don’t broadcast their intent. Dodge, parry, strike, use combos and be like water making its way through captivating environments. Learn how to master your art, whether by fighting through the underbelly of a nightclub, scrambling through a refined gallery to avoid getting surrounded, or vertically navigating a towering office building. Careful positioning and clever use of the environment to your advantage are key to your survival. Use everything at your disposal: throwable objects, makeshift weapons, windows, and ledges... The odds are stacked against you, and you will be offered no mercy. Kung Fu is mastery through practice, a path for both the body and the mind. Learn from your mistakes, unlock unique skills, and find the strength to master the devastating techniques of Pak Mei Kung Fu.

_childDocuments_.review: NO DEFAULT MOTION BLUR ON/OFF SETTINGThis might be important to some people who also get motionsickness. After some quick googling however, I found out that you can turn it off by going into the file path and add a settinglocal disc -> users -> (your name) -> app data -> local -> sifu -> saved -> config -> windows client -> open "engine" with notepad and copy paste:[SystemSettings]r.MotionBlurQuality=0Hope this helps and you are now able to enjoy the game

_childDocuments_.review: Sifu is a stylish yet gritty beat-em-up, featuring visceral hand-to-hand combat in a contemporary urban setting. From Sloclap, creators of acclaimed PS4 fighting game Absolver, Sifu follows a young kung fu student on a path of revenge, hunting for the murderers of his family. One against all, he has no allies and countless enemies. He will have to rely on his unique mastery of kung fu to prevail and preserve his family’s legacy.

name: Redemption Reapers
detailed_description: The Story Descending suddenly on the world, the macabre Mort armies destroy nation after nation, leaving humanity decimated in the wake of their overwhelming terror and might. Amid the despair, a small, localized contingent crosses swords with the Mort—the Ashen Hawk Brigade. A cunning band that specializes in surprise attacks, they were once known as the Faithless Reapers and despised by the masses. Little did the public know that this very unit was about to become the only hope in resisting the Mort. Gameplay Redemption Reapers is a dark fantasy simulation game set in a medieval world. Be immersed in the tale of the desperate struggle between the Ashen Hawk Brigade and the terrifying Mort legions. With despair looming as the menacing Mort horde marches ever closer, help your small resistance defeat the enemy masses by bringing together a rich variety of character builds and a meticulous strategy. Experience the exhilaration as you rise up to overcome the odds and achieve victory! Game Features - Conquer fierce battles with tactical expertise. Get to know a small but elite force of five, and figure out how to best utilize each member's unique skills. Carefully manage limited resources, including weapons and recovery items, with an eye on the demands of impending battles. - Forge bonds with the members of the Brigade through both story and strategy. Adapt to every situation by taking advantage of all five members' unique weapons and strengths. Coordinate attacks between members who share the same attack range to join forces and take down powerful opponents! Make full use of each member's special active skills to have each member play their part on the battlefield. However different the Brigade members may seem, all are harboring heartbreak and experiences of loss. Get to know what each member has been through and how they feel to gain insight into the path ahead for the Brigade. - Be transported to a dark medieval fantasy by stunning visuals and effects. Explore a series of strategy maps depicting a doomed and decaying world ravaged by the Mort monstrosities. Be captivated by rich, fully voiced cutscenes and conversations. Resist with all your might against the omnipotent Mort forces as you embark on a journey with no hope in sight! An intense and brutal experience awaits as you put everything on the line to guide the Brigade to the end of their journey.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I want to like this (Huge SRPG fan) I can’t justify the $50 price tag this game demands. It’s really steep for a niche genre and for a game that seems to not have good replayability or a decent narrative hook. I just can’t recommend it, which is a shame as it released after some very strong games of the same genre (Tactics Ogre, Triangle Strategy, Fire Emblem: Engage) At the moment, wait for better reviews when people actually finish to see if you’d like it or it goes on sale (which is highly likely because it seems like the sales for the game aren’t very good so far.)Graphically, the game is stunning. Cutscenes look pretty, the battle animations are varied as well as visually pleasing, and the murky color scheme incorporated into most of the game’s art and maps set the tone for a game looking to present a darker narrative. Sadly, that’s where the positives end for the most part. First off, while the cutscenes are certainly pretty, they lack any direction whatsoever. Very little is done in the cutscenes outside of dialogue and there are moments where characters just stare off into space only to prolong the scene and presumably save on budget, it’s extremely bizarre. On the topic of the characters, I genuinely just do not like any of their designs. Soulless and generic describe them best, and while I praised the dark color scheme, it’s more of a bane rather than a boon here, it just makes everyone look so samey. This hurts on the gameplay end as well because you can barely tell your units apart especially when you’re looking on the top of their small in-game models for the entire map, it’s really tough to tell who you’re controlling half of the time. People ♥♥♥♥ on Fire Emblem Engage’s character designs for being too anime or whatever, (I greatly disagree) but at least they pop out and you can tell them apart… I can’t say the same for Redemption Reapers characters.To add on even more to this, the game’s UI/UX is horrendous. The game just… doesn’t want to give you any information, at ALL. You can’t zoom out of the map or rotate, you can’t show ALL enemy ranges (gotta click on them individually, it’s a modern SRPG damnit), game doesn’t tell you what individual stats do, etc. There’s just too many to list, and, sure, you can argue that this might make the game more difficult, I’d just argue back that the difficulty is artificial and adds to the tedium of a game that’s already filled with so many weird choices for user experience. It’s too early for me to judge on the gameplay and story as a whole, so I’ll update this as I go, but so far story-wise? Really BAD.The world-building is non-existent, bland as heck dialogue, and a cast of characters that fulfill the same generic tactics unit trope. They have no chemistry with one another, really, just there to be there. Games/stories that push onto you a grim setting/narrative but lack the depth or writing to back it up are the absolute worst. There doesn't seem to be any urgency in the characters despite all of the death going around them. We’ll see if this gets any better.Gameplay-wise, the core mechanics are inherently fun (SRPG dopamine hit whenever your unit gets an offensive stat upon level up) and there are some interesting ideas, but the replayability for this game seems to be terrible. The idea of a small squad is neat, can help the writers focus more on a concentrated group of characters (problem with most SRPGs is that there can be too many characters too account/write for) and balance better in combat,  but this kills a LOT of player-choice on consecutive playthroughs whereas in Fire Emblem/Triangle Strategy, playthroughs can be extremely varied because you can choose to train different units / use different builds. So far, the systems for Redemption Reapers don’t allow for that, which is bonkers for an SRPG looking to make a name for itself in the market. Replayability not only allows the consumers to play the game more often, it generates a lot of discussions online like Fire Emblem, where people are still talking about different units in games released TWO decades prior.edit: Also, apparently, new game plus allows you to play on hard mode. While that sounds pretty cool (no idea why the game just doesn’t give you a difficulty option in the first place), the map variety / unit variety so far just doesn’t look encouraging for a 2nd playthrough... And without a strong narrative to back it up, I fear this may be one of the weaker SRPGs to be released in the past decade. Pick this up only if you're really interested in the genre AND it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Redemption Reapers

_childDocuments_.review: Currently a bit over halfway through, but feel compelled to write this because the reception already to this game is… weird. This is a great tactics game. There is great evolution to how you approach each fight. The first quarter feels scrappy and difficult, as you get your bearings and figure out each character’s strengths. The next part is working on building up skills and synergies, learning to beat the enemies in clever ways when the odds seem so stacked against you. The story is a little generic, but it has this extreme dourness that drew me in post FE Engage. It’s also very cinematic, with a ton of cutscenes and discussion. The interplay between the group is interesting - they are a found family, but also there are clear tensions and history between each. Then the gameplay comes along and thematically does something excellent - shows you how important it is to work together.And for some reason people complaining about the graphical settings - ??? It looks fantastic at 1080p! Get your head out of your ass.I’m very keen to see how the rest of the game unfolds, both from a gameplay and story perspective. I’ll be publishing a full review on my site, will update this review when that’s out.
_childDocuments_.name: Redemption Reapers

_childDocuments_.review: I'm stunned by the negative reviews! I have so many turn based strategy games in my library like the XCOM series, Expedition series, Divinity series, Baldurs gate, etc. and this is my favorite TBS game ever! Sure the acting isn't as good as say FFXII or RDR2,  but few games are. But there are things this game does extremely well. The battles are spectacular. They're difficult at times, but fair. My favorite thing is that once you've completed a story mission, you can go back and skirmish it again for extra XP and loot. It's grinding, but it's a fun grind. I also love that you can create your characters with different skills. I started over once after a few hours and it was really neat how different my fights were with different skills. The story is decent and i like the subdued voice acting of Sarah. But the battles are where the fun is. Super cleverly designed zones that get more intricate as the story moves along. I absolutely love the game. I'm not sure why anyone who likes TBS games would rate this mediocre. I guess they never gave it a chance. I got it for 40% off, but would buy it full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Redemption Reapers

_childDocuments_.review: Note: I bought the game on sale for $30 and after they put out a few patches.I don't think I would recommend it at full price, but this game is actually really good once you knock the price down a peg. The cutscenes feel like ps2 cutscenes in a good way, like a little prize you get after clearing a map. They look surprisingly good for an indie title and they are well directed. On the other hand, the still portraits used during dialogue looks really awkward and stilted. Story is basic but good enough to be fun.The normal difficulty feels like modern Fire Emblem hard, that is to say it feels well balanced, difficult enough you can't just rush in, but not so hard that you feel like you don't have enough resources to clear a map. The support attacks from your allies forces you to think a lot about positioning with every move. You have a small party but everyone serves a specific role and I think it's a nice change of pace from the bloated rosters of other games where you bench half of the characters anyway.I feel like the developers put a lot of love and thought into making this game and for that I do think it warrants a purchase. But if you're gonna put a game out at AAA prices, you have to be prepared to be judged at AAA standards(not that AAA games can match those standards half the time). Get it on a sale. Worth a play at some point as it is a very good game with some rough edges.
_childDocuments_.name: Redemption Reapers

_childDocuments_.review: Redemption Reapers has made me mistrust 'mixed' averages on Steam, forever more. The developers of Ender Lilies got done dirty; by the harsh initial reception AND their £40 price point. 'Tis is a strange case given the negativity over technical & difficulty woes made myself and numerous others averse. Has been patched so now runs well, with better balancing in terms of loot/abilities + an easy mode. Thus, I very much recommend going by the most recent reviews. Played on the Deck, after purchasing on sale for £20. Took 25hrs to finish, others likely will in 18-20hrs. Had two crashes; both levelling up skills. Auto-saves on menu before, thankfully.  Only issue in battle had was a temp save not loading. Cutscenes put the fan into overdrive, and given a SRPG opted limit to 40fps. Plays fine at 60. Text a tad hard read.I did not think it was TOO hard, aside from one big difficulty spike at the mines where you're suddenly underlevelled vs new tough enemies that oneshot. If you played Triangle Strategy, that was harder, for me. Positioning and marking enemies - esp suicide shamblers - is key as the AI will punish mistakes. That and grouping up to combo, which is a simple yet immensely satisfying mechanic that the game is built around.Weapon durability is easy to deal with by not doing as I did and selling old weapons, as you can switch weapons in battle. PS: Don't use the legendary weapons till need them.Money is somewhat limited and repairs/upgrades expensive, but as long as you get the loot to sell in missions, you'll be fine. And if not, can replay via skirmishes.Reapers has a straightforward battles -> cutscenes -> menus flow, without fluff. There is however a very nice touch in the form being able to move your units freely before committing to an action (similar to Valkyria Chronicles). I would describe it as the opposite of Fire Emblem Engage, in a good way: no garish colours and running around a 3D homebase pointlessly. Despite being initially rather basic, the more you play and unlock, the more flexibility you get. I was especially impressed with the customisation allowed via accessories. For example, I gave my archer two specific  accessories, one that let her do more dmg if first on a turn, and one if at full health. I had my main tank have an accessory that recovered health killing. And, skill wise, you have to prioritise: do you want to attack first when attacked, or more dmg output? Etc. Some of the skills really change the way you play, such as sentinel stance negating dmg to counter once, but only once. Whilst the Mort are pretty much just unexplained LotR orcs, I did care about the cast by journey's end as they struggled thru a grim (but not grimdark) dark fantasy world, seeking redemption; with a powerful and wonderfully choreographed final cinematic hat caught me offguard. As someone else said, the cutscenes here feel like high budget rewards for progress. Regarding the story, it isn't until the end that the oft mentioned events at Troden 2yrs prior are explored, leaving it with less depth at the start than by the end. Also, in two scenes - the pre-title cinematic with heroine and an early scene with commander/lieutenant - the writing seemed off, ie "it does brighten my day a bit" regarding killing. Rest was fine, and voice acting mostly very good.Going from a metroidvania to a SRPG with lots of cutscenes/dialogue clearly resulted in a few mistakes, such as no way skip or ffward enemy turns (can only make them move faster via a setting I recommend putting on very fast), but it had a lot of love put into it. Maybe there should've been 6 characters, with a spell caster, to let you split your group up more evenly. It also peaked somewhat midway, with the until then varied enemy types growing a bit stale, before picking back up for survival battles at the end. But, overall, 'tis a great game with an addictive loop.Recommended to anyone that likes preset characters in SRPGs, with tactics built around them, as well as people looking for the opposite of FE: Engage.That, or fans of Ender Lilies: some wonderful, if a tad overused battle themes. The soundtrack is one of the best things about the game; so much so that you will stay for the music, if not the game itself, as another reviewer mentioned. Maybe.

_childDocuments_.review: Redemption Reapers is a rather generic interesting take on the tactical turn based genre. The game itself is less tactics and plays more like a SRPG then a TRPG. Instead of the turn system you get Action points that you can store up and that increase as your characters kill enemies in the map gaining you more points. The game does have replayable missions despite reviews saying it does not. And you can swap weapons mid fight. Now on to the general mechanics, redemption reapers has a cast of 5 characters and the idea is that the battle is comprised of you taking these characters and their active/passive abilities to the highest level you can get them and allowing them to work at their best. It's not your typical TRPG in that one or two characters will get super broken and run through every enemy. It's more about taking advantage of each characters strengths, sometimes going backwards to go forward, and letting players compose themselves before jumping into each group of enemies to think of strategies. The biggest challenge and the turn off for people may be that there isn't a skip animation and that you only get one heal with one or two springs on maps to regenerate that healing for one teammate. This can make losing a map more frustrating then when you finally win it but I found it enjoyable. The story I hear stays pretty bland for the first few chapters and for the 4 hours I played I can agree, its not enough to turn me away but its enough to definitely challenge a few others for whether they should stick around. The voice acting is comprised of notables from other fire emblem titles but just done badly and with lacking emotion obviously with the games dreary tone. Soundtrack is nice and adds a level of something to like in the game. Like most TRPG's though nothing game changing as far as the story plot development. And after beating the game the ending was ok but not satisfying that you felt the journey was worth it.Tl:drRedemption reapers isn't a very noob friendly RPG. And its a rather bland take on the genre that can be fleshed out better. The combat stays very simple and generic for the a good few chapters until you get enough skill points to start specializing your units in what they can do best. Whether that be dodge tanking, one shotting enemies from a distance or just soaking damage. The game opens up around the halfway mark with more options then just lining up units to link attacks off of eachother. The story and characters miss the mark and ultimately it ends up feeling very generic and bland. This is a game you could give a 7/10 to or easily give a 4 or 5 out of 10 to.Gameplay 7/10Story 6/10Soundtrack 8/10Replayability 6/10Overall I'd give it a solid 7/10. If it was 40 or 30$ it could probably be a 8 or 9 for what its asking but at 50$ it falls into just a good game with a sadly bad port to PC.

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't recommend for non-SRPG veterans. I'd also recommend e.g. FE Emblems before this; this game is really for people who really like SRPGs and are out of games to play. There isn't really a plot or characterization worth playing for here in what is ultimately a shaggy dog story.That said, the way the support attacks work and how crucial they become in more difficult missions are pretty fun. It makes each round into a mini-puzzle where you have to work out the positioning and the turn order of your units beforehand. While the battles do get same-y, the way supports become literal force multipliers makes it feel good when you find elegant solution to what seems insurmountable. This is, however, pretty much the only real innovation here; everything else is pretty standard FE-clone stuff.The main issue is that the game is quite unforgiving, even at the normal difficulty (the only one available until you beat the game). Non-tanks will generally die after two hits or so, and while there isn't permadeath, losing a unit when the entire point of the game is to chain support attacks with your units is pretty crippling. The game isn't all that difficult if you are familiar with the sort of game, but it doesn't have much tolerance for errors, and the RNG tends to make you (or, well, me) play conservatively in case you get a miss at an inopportune time.Hard mode is kind of silly. It's the unforgiving nature of the game turned up to 11. The very first mission in hard mode essentially has one solution that you have to follow, or you lose (or you restart until you get a lucky dodge). The second mission is arguably even more difficult, though it's also slightly less scripted since you have more options.Still, it was fun enough for me to play through to get into hard mode. Just don't expect anything groundbreaking, or beginner-friendly.
