name: Bud Spencer & Terence Hill - Slaps And Beans 2
detailed_description: MORE GAMES FROM TRINITY TEAM About the Game Bud Spencer and Terence Hill are back again! The new game is a sequel to the first game and just like a movie saga. The story picks up where it left off at the end of the first Slaps and Beans. Our heroes will experience adventures in new places with new events and will also meet many new characters along the way. Slaps and Beans 2 returns as a scrolling fighting game with a retro gaming, co-op or single player look with a platform mechanic that allows the player to control Bud Spencer and Terence Hill in a revised and improved version of the combat system. Brand new environment dynamics that progressively add enemies as the difficulty increases and of course again with lots of funny quotes. New mini-games that can be played repeatedly in a dedicated party play area for up to 4 players. And finally the dubbing in four languages that immerse the player even more in the real Bud Spencer and Terence Hill ambience. The main features of Slaps And Beans 2 are: - 80s pixel art graphics - improved Bud and Terence-style combat system - cooperative mode - minigames in 4-player party game mode - voiceovers in 4 languages - lots of slaps and lots of beans (double at least, of course!)

_childDocuments_.review: Fun.It is fully voiced. Voices well reflect the type of dialogues those 2 and their belligerents can have.There is plethora of interactions between the 2 brawlers themselves and with their environment. The anthological slaps that you probably know from one. And the flying circus from the other. Bud will break a lot of things.It comes with a bit of puzzles.It references the movies quite well.It also comes with mini-games such as eating everything including the meal of the ones sitting next to you at the table. Scenes that you will play like a dance game or a QTE.On the darker side, it lacks of variety of sounds. The audio atmosphere could have definitely been better.The fights are also sometimes lacking of dynamism. Yes, the punches, especially from Bud were slow and heavy, but still. A bit faster in the game could have been appreciated.It is also a bit clunky at times. Pushing a box for example could be a bit hazardous.Anyway, if you like Bud and his pain in the neck of Terence, if you liked the previous opus that I believe a bit better, you should like this one.It won't be the game of the year, neither the best beat'em up, but it is funny enough and may bring some nostalgia.Double hands smash with both thumbs up for me. Followed by one last hammer fist from above.

_childDocuments_.review: This Game took everything that made the first Game GREAT and made it even BETTER!!! Very cool that there is a Voiceover for the Characters, now... _childDocuments_.review: I played it start to finish on Medium difficulty, and it was all I expected as an old fan of the duo (and the first game). Hilarious dialogues, a silly but somehow still kind of threatening villain, great soundtracks, fun minigames and occasional puzzles breaking up the pace of plentiful brawls. The english voices are great, hats off to the actors (say, was Terence's voice misspelled in the credits or "Mattew" is a variant?). Also, nice easter eggs overall (Doc Brown's lab especially made me laugh out loud)!On the criticism side, though... I often mistook Terence for a mook in bigger fights because he didn't really stand out. The hovercraft minigame could use a clearer health indicator, it took me a while to realize that their "bumpers" serve as such. Finally, there was a puzzle (unfortunately I can't remember where) where the two got separated too far from each other and I couldn't really see what I was doing. Since the camera didn't zoom out, I guess it wasn't supposed to happen.Overall, I wholeheartedly recommend it. It's a solid beat 'em up, and a trip down memory lane to fans of the duo. Nice work!
_childDocuments_.name: Bud Spencer & Terence Hill - Slaps And Beans 2

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun! Both story and gameplay wise. Lots of great humor, music, voice acting and great monkey island-like graphics. Some gameplay quirks that might stop you for a minute and you need to check a video walkthrough to make sure you're trying to do it right (you are, the game is just a bit awkward in these few situations), like when you need to jump across ledges with terence, and get catapulted with the see-saw. I didn't mind these hiccups much though, the game is still extremely original and miles more enjoyable than 99% of the boring clones out there today. A must try imo!

_childDocuments_.review: liked the first, loved the second.There's still quite a few bugs to iron out but they aren't anything game breaking as far as I know.I'm sure those will get taken care of.On the other side, this is a great follow up. _childDocuments_.review: I think this is just about recommendable, but only to people who have heard of the two protagonists before and are not looking for the next break-through title in the side-scrolling beat-em-up genre. At its core, this is basically the same game as the first Slaps & Beans - it is still difficult to lose in combat, as Bud and Terence slap their way out of even the most overwhelming situations with their trademark non-chalant approach. However, this entry seems less buggy, the AI-controlled partner does not need to be revived all the time (though he still occasionally gobbles health pick-ups off the floor when he does not really need them), and the game's ridiculous story is fully voiced this time around.The second game also features traversal puzzle sections which require using each character in turn to help the other along: this usually goes along the lines of Terence scaling an obstacle to knock a ladder down for Bud. In terms of combat changes, the charge move can no longer be spammed and is now only occasionally useful, and Terence can now aim his throws at otherwise inaccessible enemies. He can also pick up a stick to bat items thrown towards him to take enemies out. That said, most encounters will likely be spent mashing the heavy attack button, and unfortunately there still does not seem to be much point in mixing light and heavy attacks. In addition to basic enemies, there are lanky, kung furious guys; fat, tanky, charging guys; fit, tanky, blocking guys; hypnotic-telekinetic androids who can only be damaged during windows of opportunity, and even one woman who has to be neutralised in an apropriately non-violent way!The achievement for stealth (in one scripted section) is more difficult to get this time than in the first game due to tighter timings on security cameras, and the introduction of new noisy obstacles like chains on the ceiling and metal trays on the floor. It is not clear they are interactive until you touch them, and the alarm goes off. The achievement for winning the vehicle mini-game while going in reverse only also makes a comeback, and I was actually able to get it after only a few tries - something I was not able to do in the previous title - probably because in the second game the mini-game is not a race, but a boating demolition derby match.Some levels towards the end throw a little too many enemies at the protagonists, which is a bit irritating because the combat is not particularly deep, but the game ends before it gets too old. It took about the same time to play-through as the first - around five hours with plenty of movie references along the way.

name: Ghostrunner 2
detailed_description: Buzz Celebrate one year of Ghostrunner 2 with the final Ghostrunner 2 DLC, the Anniversary Pack! Complete your katana collection with three all-new swords, paired with 3 flashy hand skins, and a sleek new motorcycle skin to slash your way through the cybervoid. EDITIONS COMPARED GHOSTRUNNER 2 BRUTAL EDITION Ghostrunner 2 Brutal Edition Includes: Ghostrunner 2 Game Ahriman's Katana Sword and Hand Skin Modern Energy Sword and Hand Skin Molten Blade Sword and Hand Skin Gothic Blue Sword and Hand Skin Hand Hologram with Username Aqua Animated Sword and Hand Skin Design 24A Motorcycle Skin Ghostrunner 2 Season Pass ($19.99 Value) GHOSTRUNNER 2 DELUXE EDITION Ghostrunner 2 Deluxe Edition Includes: Ghostrunner 2 Game Ahriman's Katana Sword and Hand Skin Modern Energy Sword and Hand Skin Molten Blade Sword and Hand Skin Gothic Blue Sword and Hand Skin Hand Hologram with Username About the Game Blood will run in the highly anticipated hardcore FPP slasher set one year after the events of Ghostrunner. Adventure through a post-apocalyptic cyberpunk future that takes place after the fall of the Keymaster, a tyrant who ruled over Dharma Tower, the last refuge of mankind. Jack is back to take on the violent AI cult that has assembled outside Dharma Tower and shape the future of humanity. Featuring incredible katana combat mechanics, a deeper exploration of the world beyond Dharma Tower, nonlinear levels with complex motorbike sections, exciting new modes, and all the action you loved about Ghostrunner. Plus, boss fights are more interactive, giving players freedom to choose how to survive battles against the toughest opponents. Become The Ultimate Cyber Ninja Ghostrunner 2 introduces new skills, allowing players to be more creative and take on even the most demanding encounters with greater accessibility. However, enemies in Ghostrunner 2 behave uniquely dependent on the skills used against them, providing a fresh challenge with each encounter. The player progression system has been completely redone, providing opportunities to experiment and customize gameplay. Immersive, Mind-Bending Features Master the Cybervoid if you hope to survive. Take on challenging, new enemies as you traverse interactive environments including exploding barrels, destructible walls, helpful neutral entities, and countless improvements that keep combat exciting and fresh. Can’t get enough? Dive even deeper into the lore and plot with the new dialogue system. Sounds of the Cybervoid Save humanity in style as you decimate your opponents while listening to the captivating synthwave soundtrack featuring new music from Daniel Deluxe, We Are Magonia, Gost, Dan Terminus, and Arek Reikowski.

_childDocuments_.review: There are nice base ideas, but overall its an unpolished game.The good:- Nice enemy variety- Somewhat decent story- Nice visuals- Cool customization and somewhat variety in build- Hidden collectible items and nice skinsThe bad:- Controls are not polished enough and platforming can feel very janky, I wished there was more effort here- Random wallrunns on most narrow objects- Never really sure when your character will grab an edge or not- Motorcycle levels: Tracks are very hard to read since everything has sand color- Glider: Clunky and sometimes just buggy, probably the worst glider mechanics I have seen in a game- Simulation missions: Some enemies are just bugged, especcially the ones in wheels that charge youThis game has potential, if you can get over the overall jankyness you will enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh yeah, I love this game. I loved the first one, too, and this scratched all the same itches. It's notably easier than the first one, and the reason why is, I think, because you have a more fleshed out kit as well as a block button. Cons? idk, there's a few glitches, a few invisible walls here and there, and sometimes I just feel like it's a bit too forgiving. But that's just me as a massive fan of the first one. It's not something you'll notice if you're new. It also seems way less focused on completion speed, which I appreciate, since "shaving off a few seconds" sounds more like homework than fun to me. Buy this game unless you were a snob about the ultradifficulty, but in my opinion you'll still find plenty that's hard here and plenty to love. If you played GR1 til you hit that lasertower and gave up, you're gonna love GR2. GR2 doesn't require meth to complete any of its levels.  Start here. You're gonna love this. It's what the first should have been, in my opinion. Can't wait for the ever-based devs to put out content here and there so I have a reason to come back. Hard recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghostrunner 2

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is an amazing sequel to the original game, which I loved. I think the new variety of enemies and the changes to the already existing ones are amazing and make the game more fun and challenging. The game is definitely a step up in difficulty from the original game (or it may just be me not having played it in a while). I personally like the story but think it's just a bit worse than the original. Overall I would not pay full price for the game but if you see it for like 10 quid, I would definitely recommend. Just push through no matter how many times you die.

The new mechanics are fun, but some of them seem too rushed just so there can be "innovative mechanics". 8/10, great fun, I do wish there was more replayability, but the experience was great.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this game could've used another year in the oven. There's a lot of buggy occurrences and most of them have to do with the bike. I'm on a 3080 with no ray tracing and getting a lot of stuttering and freezing both when loading and playing levels. The story being told to you with voice over throughout the game is back and still just as poorly written so i turned subtitles and dialogue off. I think if they either made it just levels without the story or wrote a better story it could really shine. The lack of Daniel Deluxe is very present and the soundtrack suffers from it. There are some good tracks in there but most of them are pretty generic.All I can hope for is that additional content disguised as DLC isn't drip fed for the next year with paid cosmetics, but given the launch edition selection there's little hope.In the game's current state, I can't recommend it despite the less than $60 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: I find the sequel to be outstanding even though others seem to disagree. The plot was great. I enjoyed the aspect of the hub (being able to see my collectibles and see some of the character interactions) and the utilization of the motor bike mechanic and its level designs (though in a few areas it felt a bit unnecessary). The new skill tree and ultimates were interesting. The game had a bit of weird bugs (mostly at the borders or their unapparent lack thereof, others were along the path of the bike levels) but mostly did not interfere with the playing experience (except in the bike levels were pretty frustrating at times). It also felt a bit easier than the first game but make no mistake the hardcore mode is no joke. I'd give it a 4.2/5 (Game should take around 8 hours to complete without focusing on collectibles)

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most underrated action-platform games there exists gets a sequel. The already amazing Ghostrunner (2020) gets obliterated by 2023 franchise expansion. Ghostrunner Number 74, Jack returns to Dharma to defeat the Asura, the original Ghostrunners created by the Architect and Mara. The sequel introduces us to many new mechanics such as the jetpack, a motorcycle, new platforming, ultimate abilities, a full fledged interactive dialogue system and an overhauled motherboard upgrade system. Ghostrunner 2 arguably does everything better and creates an even more difficult challenge than before. Can Jack save Dharma again?Amazing game, please play the first one then buy this. Make it win in Steam Awards 2023

_childDocuments_.review: Overview: We have on our hands here game with a great gameplay loop and a great atmosphere, but not a whole lot else. Ghostrunner 2 is a very cohesive and fun-to-play cyberpunk samurai simulator. it nails the cybperpunk atmosphere and makes you feel super badass by showcasing super smooth and fun gameplay. 	       It is totally worth.a purchase on sale, and if you’re super into the cyberpunk setting and can really crank those graphics, then I would maybe say its’s even worth a purchase not on sale. But this is not worth its full price, at least in my eyes. The experience is relatively short, as I clocked in at around 9 hours. It has great, fun, varied gameplay that doesn’t get old particularly quickly (but it eventually does). It also has a great atmosphere and killer visuals, with minimal bugs. Is that all Ghostrunner 2 has going for it? Yeah, kinda. 	            In the first game, the story was not very prevalent, which I viewed as a good thing. I didn’t need a story in a game like this. However, in Ghostrunner 2, they lean FULLY into the ‘we have a very important story to tell and we will spend a solid chunk of your gameplay making you experience it’ vibe that has created some of the best game experiences of all time. Ghostunner 2 is not one of those games though. It is not ground-breaking in a single facet of its design, MUCH less so the narrative/story. The narrative is incredibly boring, drawn out, predictable, and coming from someone whose 2nd favorite game of all time is RDR2, has some of the worst-written, most cliche, and least likeable characters in almost any game I have ever played. After only 2 hours, I had completely turned off the game audio and was only listening to music, rather than listening to the incredibly cringe, boring, and bafflingly poorly voice-acted banter between the characters. No hate to anyone who enjoyed the story and the characters, but Jesus, not for me.  	           The difficulty and pacing was also very, very weird. Some entire encounters, I would beat without breaking a sweat, while others (specifically 2 of the boss battles) made me want to pull out my hair, having my clock in 30+ attempts. Thank god for mid-boss-fight checkpoints… I also just couldn’t stand the pacing. I think part of this came as a result of me being so incredibly disinterested in the story, but I feel like the balancing between fighting encounters and just those ‘easy platforming while characters talk’ felt super super off. That one open world mission in the middle was also way too long and repetitive… I reckon most of thee issues could’ve been pretty easily mended by a commitment to game testing, so that they could get real feedback and implement it into the game. I’m not sure how much of this they did.  	           Overall, this experience is totally worth your time, though. It is much better than the first game, to begin with. The gameplay amps it up to a whole new level, and the badass potential is a lot hgiher. The game also goes on pretty crazy sales for having released so recently, so you might as well add it to your library during one of those sales. It has some good aspect, and some bad. As any mid game does. Just get a good playlist ready so your don’t have to listen to the god-awful dialogue/Sights and Sounds- The world and atmosphere are incredibly constructed- The set pieces look awesome- Running it on my steam deck limited my graphical capacities, but it still looked so sick- Sound design and music were fine, but a couple hours in, I decided my ears would be better off listening to music- The acting was piss-poor, unfortunately.Gameplay- Really snappy and responsive- Innovates a bunch on the first game, switching things up- Makes you actually feel like a cyberpunk samurai, badass as hell- Consistently introducing new gameplay mechanics like the biker    - Not particularly incredible additions, but really fun nonetheless- The consistently new game mechanics were quick enough that they didn’t really get old- The difficulty was very poorly balanced. I flew through some missions, while I had to bash my head against some enemy encounters because they felt so bullshtNarrative- I’m going to choose not to comment because I don’t want to seem like a hater (I hate it)- Like its so bad and uninteresting even though its trying so hard

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR When one sets out to make a sequel, one immediately loses the grace and simplicity of design that a game like Ghostrunner had. By virtue of being a sequel, this needed to be more and therefore it has more space for things to go wrong. I'm not sure if I like it more or less than the first Ghostrunner, but in isolation I do very much like and recommend Ghostrunner 2.Issues up front for those skimming: - I had more issues with performance than GR1. I put this down to a combination of larger, more cluttered environments, and worse optimisation. I don't think it's entirely attributable to one or the other. - The motorbike is fun, but all the sections with it are very linear and lacking camera control, I found that sometimes I couldn't see where the hell I was going. - The RogueRunner mode is fun a couple of times, but doesn't have a huge amount of variety.The story here is better than in the first game, but it's still not incredible by any means. The tweaks and rebalances made to the gameplay really worked in my opinion, and the choice to slow things down to allow for finer control was I think the right decision to make. The additional "modes" of gameplay, such as the motorcycle and wingsuit are fun and interesting little distractions but don't add huge amounts to the overall experience. The wider environments and more open levels were really fun to explore and spend time with, and I think that barring technical issues (which did happen) the devs did a really good job fleshing out this world from the first game and portraying that. Overall, I had fun with this and I'll probably replay it at some point, though perhaps not right away.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm finding this game to be a bit of a drag. GR1 I remember being a lot more entertaining with the combat encounters actually being a challenge and puzzle-like. You'd have to be agile and quick on your feet to get through encounters, whilst working out a path to success with multiple attempts. In GR2, you don't even need your dash to avoid most bullets. And if you really want to cheese it, you can bust out your easy mode ultimate ability (honestly, the game so far has been such a joke that if I do use the ult, it's because I fat fingered it). The devs also thought it would be a good idea to change the controls for your normal skills so you have to swap your skill on the fly before you can use it and then press another button to activate it, rather than just using dedicated buttons. You cannot have a single button to activate each skill. This decision is mindnumbingly braindead.As cool an idea as the bike missions were, I think they lack polish. Oftentimes, I feel like I'm on a slip'n'slide rather than having any actual control of it. The way the bike behaved generally felt unnatural. There are points where you're riding on walls, but the camera positioning sometimes made it incredibly difficult to see where you're supposed to go next when going fast. Because of the Mad Max colour pallet they chose for the certain areas, they had to do the usual yellow paint thing to point where to go next, rather than just choosing an aesthetic or environmental design that would more easily guide the player without being so in your face. If you got off the bike in any areas you were supposed to go fast in, you would also notice how little effort they put into some of the environments graphically, as they clearly expected you to just speed past it, not taking in the environment at all. They also added a new enemy type for the mad max biome. They're literally the same enemies as the ones you find everywhere else but with a different model. They don't behave or animate any differently. GR2 has also been a pretty buggy experience for me. I don't remember GR1 being as buggy as this. In the last mission I played, I had at least 3 occurrences of jumping on a grind rail and having the game send me the opposite direction of the one I'm facing and moving in. In that same mission, I got an enemy stuck on a fense on which the AI didn't know what to do, even though it was only 1ft higher off the ground than it usually was, and I also managed to get the bike stuck on a rock. The first boss, you encounter quite early on. I think it really set the tone for the quality I was to experience, because the amount of times I'd evade their attack, go for a swing on their blind spot well after their swing was over and die to seemingly no movement other than my sword hitting their back (here come the git guds) was genuinely frustrating. Looking at a list of missions, I think I'm a little over half way through. I've done 10 missions and there's 8 left (18 total). I might stick through it, because as much I've bashed on the game, there is some great stuff here. The platforming is (mostly) fluid and it feels like there's a great balance between combat encounters and platforming. The soundtrack is great.  The 2 bosses I've done have been challenging and interesting so far (outside of the aforementioned bug(?)), one of which was mostly platforming. There was one weird boss encounter which I haven't counted here because it was just a large room of normal enemies with a health bar. The story and characters are okay; they kind feel like window dressing for the gameplay. In some of the missions, they interject so much it's annoying. I've now noticed I'm back to complaining again, so I'm gonna leave it here. I bought the game on a sale. I think I'd recommend the same for anyone who's interested in playing it. It doesn't change much after the first hour though, so don't wait for it to get better, just get a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty good game that is overcharging at 40$ unless you are very much into replaying the same game on a higher difficulty. A step up from the first in so many small ways, but it's pretty tough to recommend unless you wanted more from the first game with a stronger story.++PROS+++ Much better plot than the first game that is consistent in hype and tone throughout.+ Voiceacting is well done, art direction is pretty. Not much to complain about.+ Performance on my system was almost perfect throughout the entire game.+ Lots of small QOL improvements that make the game a lot more fun to play and a tad bit easier.+ ACTUAL upgrade system that gives you strong upgrades throughout with lots of build potential.+ A roguelike mode that is... Fine, it's not great but it's fine.+ Still LOTS of collectibles and they show up in your little HQ to gawk at in person this time.+ ACTUAL BOSSES even if they are a tad bit repetitive, although the bike boss is the best one in the entire series if you ask me, just wild fun.+ A fun open-world level that makes me wish the whole game was designed in that way, where you basically go from level to open section to level.--CONS--- Both Bike and Glidesuit are added too late into the experience to justify being shown off as heavily as they are. The two levels you get with the bike are fun, the glidesuit is wonky but in an arcadey fun way. The Moto-Bike DLC is just not worth it in earnest unless you sincerely want to just blitz through an endless runner scenario.- The wallrunning, wallclimbing and railgrinding can be pretty wonky even after the first game. This has absolutely caused me many deaths for no particular reason other than the game's own design not always working the best.- Some objects have really, really bad collision.- 60~ish gigs of harddrive space is not a typical complaint I'd put down, but here I'll make the exception as it's a pretty big leap up from the first game without necessarily being better. Small nitpick here for sure.Overall a good game, but unless you REALLY LOVED the first game, I only recommend on sale, and I wouldn't recommend the cosmetic DLCs unless you wish to support the dev further. I'd love to play a 3rd game, but if that has the same wonky issue with wallrunning and wallclimbing I'll be a bit annoyed as that'll be the 3rd game in a row to have that same issue. Otherwise the increased budget really shows in these awesome setpieces and some REALLY well done arena levels, but in other places it makes me question why the addition say the bike and wingsuit were needed and why they were done so late into the game, effectively making both feel just slapped in there.

_childDocuments_.review: So...I've played and I believe even beaten the 1st GR game on hardcore, and as annoying as it was. It wasnt usually a fault in the game that made me fail a mission. It was simply myself getting too impatient. Now, GR 2... how is it that the always seem to make the mechanics that made the 1st game good, feel like complete dogwater dooky poopoo stuck on the side of the lid awful. 1. Parrying, a seemingly more and more common mechanic to see in games ( not a real fact, just personal speculation, or from my own experience) which can either be good, or atrocious to play with/ gimmicky or jank. The first game, though I haven't played it in a while, I recall having excellent parry mechanics in that for one, if u click the parry button trying to get perfect timing( which I personally do as most games with parry I play are tap a button or 2 and it instantly parries and will parry an attack within the X amount of frames the game gives u. This game though, though I'm not far in yet, just feels unresponsive and delayed occasionally. I do intend to get further, and ideally beat this game, but so far, just the combat mechanics seem less fleshed out compared to GR1.2. The combat as stated by others, is not really anything new, very few new enemies, etc. having fought the first actual boss...It's not looking to bright imo. Attacks that I know for certain I shoulda blocked or parried via literally seeing my character pull the sword up into the block animation, only to still get hit and killed.Getting killed by an attack you can at least see, and understand, albeit annoying, is what I want from combat in such a game as this and GR1(which mostly succeeded), instead I get killed randomly, even if I appear to be blocking. Now, I will admit that there maybe is just a different play style than in the first game, but judging on the limited reviews I read, consensus seems to be that this game sucks.TLDR: Sequels always remove what was fun in the first game, so just stick to one and done.

_childDocuments_.review: Short answer: (no spoilers until the end, spoiler section marked)Ghost Runner 2 is a proper sequel in my opinion. the gameplay has been expanded upon from GR 1 and Project_Hel. Though I did get quite a few frame drops in large set pieces even after cranking my graphics all the way down, it didn't distract from the greatly expanded combat, new and upgraded utilities, amazing level design, and quite enjoyable story the game has to offer. if performance is what you're worried about I would say maybe wait for a couple of patches before purchasing, but definitely play the demo. But the game is a solid sequel and I cant wait to see what they do next.  8/10Long answer:The combat has seen the greatest improvement. abilities blend together to make fun combos, the new enemies  have very unique attacks that go alongside great with others causing you to not feel overwhelmed by everything going on. the new upgrade system, though lacking the charm of the first games tetris like system, allows you to form Jack to the ghost runner you want him to be, also aiding in exploration due to the upgrade chips being hidden on every level and there being a lot of them. The parkour and movement are good but lacking compared to GR 1. The overall movement speed feels slush in comparison to the first. this is, from what i can tell, done so the combat could be more fluid. Movement in combat feels great (running speed, dash distance, bullet time movement), but the parkour segments outside of combat feel a little slow overall. the removal of multiple dashes is what hurts me the most. the new stamina bar the game bases dashes/blocking/parrying on limits jacks overall movement as now you have to decide between blocking, or dashing towards the enemy, chewing up the same bar. also meaning that if you block bullets you may not have enough stamina for that dash you though you could do, leading to your death. overall if the dash system from the previous game was re-introduced (while the stamina bar was used for only blocking and parrying as i do enjoy the limits on that) i would have no gripes with the how jack feels to control... besides for the games momentummomentum conservation in this game is very strange. certain object give you ridiculous speed/height while dashing or jumping off of them, but as soon as you dash or slide for a second all that momentum is lost. bhopping feels bad in this game due to how slow it feels and that jack cant keep any of his speed doing so unlike GR 1. If the game allowed even just a wee bit more fluidity in jacks momentum it would do wonders.The level design is wonderful. Inside Darma you are treated to bright neon-dystopian visuals like the first game but with so much more flare. Once you reach the outside, the post-apocalypse world took my breath away (as it also did to my frames). The games signature techno-style blended amazingly with the outside environments and the things you run into out there. the game doesn't recycle the same gimmicks too often and comes up with new and interesting ways to do the same thing you've done already. the new sections of the environment you can manipulate add a lot more options in combat and movement.  my biggest issues come with the extreme frame rate drops in some sections, in one section i had to run passed all the enemies as my game was running at about 15 frames and i couldn't do much in the way of fighting. i had many issues with the bike jumps where i would either get too much/ not enough height and crash, or get glitched inside the floor after landing and have to reset. Launch pads are great fun but the hit box could be a little taller for them as i would attempt to jump into one and flight right on over it to my death. the layout of every level was great besides one level where you have to do long drives on your bike from one objective to another without much to do in between.The bike is a great addition when used properly. every bike-only level was the most action packed, edge of my seat gaming experience I've had in a while. each level with the bike is even cooler than the last. shooting with the bike can be a little frustrating as the guns auto holster after a couple of seconds and over heating so fast you have to tap fire to get any real use out of it.SPOILER SECTION:the wing suit has to be the most amount of fun I've had in a long time with a movement based game. the open arenas and parkour segments cause me to almost forget about my issues i have with the game. but you only unlock this ability for the last few levels of the game. making a nice send off to the game but leaving me wishing they added a couple more levels with the wing suit in mind.The story, though not amazing, its great fun to listen to as you're hacking up cyborgs. the main plot was compelling enough for me to be compelled to find hidden tapes to learn more about the lore.  The extra world building put in with the collectibles helps paint a picture of what life is like in this world. the added touch of the descriptions being from jacks POV is a cute touch. the new characters are great fun to listen and chat with though Zoe is a massive step down from her character in the first. Though i didn't care much once Kira and Rahu took main stage as Jack's besties.on top of that, more Rahu. PLEASEOverall the game is a great sequel though the toning down of the movement is a disappointment. the new more open level design is great and is kept very fresh with unique arenas and enemy variety.  the movement could use a couple adjustments but i am very pleased with this game and i cant wait to see what happens next.

The combat is improved and far less frustrating than the first game, parkour feels smooth yet challenging, the level design is more open, there's more secrets to find, and the game overall just feels like an improvement from the already great first game. _childDocuments_.review: Just noticed this review, and I hope someone sees this when I clarify that the smart access memory function for my motherboard had played a role in the stuttering issues. With it enabled, the DirectX11 version of this game suffers from the stuttering more than the DirectX12 version. Once I found someone's post discussing this in the steam forums, I fixed the game to my setup and it has been running relatively smooth ever since.The game itself takes a few steps forward and fewer steps back, as I think the first entry is sharper in delivery. There are more features and sections to look forward to in this game, but most of it feels a bit under-baked. There is a larger story with more characters, but the game slogs through unskippable "hub-sections" that just has you skip through character dialog to move the playthrough along. There are larger missions, including a few open-ended ones, but some of them start feeling like slogs to play through as a result. There are more abilities that you have at your arsenal, but are held back by a few downgrades. For example, you are able to dash as many times as you want without a cooldown in this entry. However, its held back by a stamina bar that is not only tied to the dash but to a new block ability. The block is helpful, but compared to how swiftly you can move through levels in the first Ghostrunner by doing the dash -> slide -> jump -> dash combo as indefinitely as you can keep a rhythm, the sharpness of the movement takes a hit. That sharpness also takes a hit from other areas. For example, there is much more graphical detail involved in this entry, and although beautiful to look at, sometimes plays against the flow of gameplay as you can get caught in the levels' physical geometry. With something as demanding in difficulty as this game, this is a serious detriment. During bike sections, one little rock can kill you're deathless run.This game has things to like, including the flexibility of the arsenal, a good and more varied soundtrack, the bike segment :) For some, the rogue-like minigame this game offers can give a bit more value (although it can seem under-cooked at times, too). I also liked how the story expanded on the games universe a bit and explored areas described in the first entry, like a sequel should.Although I do come back to this game every now and then, I'd see myself coming back to the games previous entry more due to how much better it flows than this one, despite the respective hiccups that this entry fixes. This one doesn't replace the first in the slightest.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say that this is a disappointing sequel. It has some good impovements, but a lot of downgrades too.The first game was a game that knew what it was, a 3d platformer with combat and AAA graphics. Focus was on speed and finesse, which is why every level ended with time and deathcount leaderboards. This game tries to actually be a AAA game, and that's IN NO WAY A COMPLIMENT. A hub where you just talk to people, an open world section, long and tiresome cutscenes, all of that is "Why?!" This supposed to have a focus on speed, why so many levels are well over half an hour long. The pacing is just truly atrocious.There are some good sections, like the action bike levels (not the normal bike levels), the glider platforming, generally the platforming sections felt good, as well as many combat encounters.About combat encounters, they did not learn their lessons from the first game. In the original out of 4 abilities you would ever use just Tempest because it replenished fast and was easy to use, other abilities just were too situational, too risky, too costly, and too unnecessary to ever use. It was a problem.In this game, it's basically the same thing, but now it's the Shuriken, compared to which all other abilities are trash. Not only is it your only ranged ability, and is also the cheapest, it counters every single enemy you might struggle against, to the point there might as well not be the other abilities. The others are not as trash though, and sections where you need to quickly switch them are cool, but to make them usable you have to upgrade them, and you might as well just upgrade the shuriken because it's the one you will use regardless of the situation by just how strong it is.Ultimates are there to be those extra costly things that you will basically use once per level. And you wouldn't exactly want to use them that once per level, they are in a way "skip the encounter", because of the countdown you want to use it basically on the first encounter of the level to have two uses, and most of them don't even sound cool, experimenting with them is especially prohibitive because of their cost. You would think you would be able to experiment in the all new and important hub, but outside of the roguelike minigame you cannot. Great design.That rumble was to illustrate just how the game doesn't feel like an upgrade, a sequel, but is just different. The cool parts are cooler, but the bad parts of the original are transferred directly and expanded upon at most leaving the same issues, at worst amplifying them.Have to mention the open world level, it truly killed the pace of the game and made me see the negatives. In particular want to mention how the motorcycle is great at the action sections, but especially on the open world level it's utter trash, can't look around on it, it gets stuck everywhere and stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, I really do. It's got solid mechanics, an alright soundtrack, and looks gorgeous, so what's wrong? Flow. Compared to it's predecessor, Ghostrunner 2 lacks the same flow that Ghostrunner had. In an effort to flesh out the story and world the developers chose to add a small hub area you return to between missions, chat with NPCs, upgrade, etc. This completely kills the flow that the former game had from level to level. I'm not sure the game really needed this, story is nice to have, but when the original game's story was painfully generic while also being kind of out of the way, it was tolerable. Now when they force you to engage with the story when it didn't really improve all that much and kills the flow of the gameplay, it just doesn't do it for me.I also find myself getting lost more in this game, in the previous one where you were meant to go was very obvious, illuminated yellow was a good indication of where to go, but while they do try to stick to that formula here, it falls flat because of lighting in many areas not drawing enough attention to it. In cyberpunk games like these, you expect to see splotches of dull color off in the distance or in the corner of your eye, when it's illuminated properly, it attracts attention. They don't always follow that formula here. It's particularly bad in areas that are very bright and colorful as a baseline so navigation becomes confusing as the somewhat more dull yellow banners you're meant to be looking for are lost in the sea of bright neon colors.Finally, I don't find the soundtrack to be the same kind of special the previous game had. It doesn't have the same catchiness to make me want to listen to it outside of the game that the original does.Overall, I'm disappointed. I really enjoyed the first game, was hoping they would keep the feeling of flow from one level to the next, and the hub sections just kinda killed it for me. The gameplay is solid as before, so if you can make it past the giant brick walls you slam your face in to after every level, you'll probably like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Purists will say that this game is a significant downgrade from the original. I disagree-- all in all, I'd call it a net improvement that is not without its compromises and missteps.To the uninitiated, Ghostrunner has you play as a parkour cyber ninja that can grapple, wall jump, dash, slow mo, etc. all around the tightly designed maps. You can kill enemies in one slash, but in turn also die to one hit. The primary gameplay loop is a cycle of mildly challenging but extremely fun parkour platforming, and very challenging combat "puzzles". You will probably die a lot, but the quick restarts and satisfying feeling of finally pulling off the crazy sequences necessary make the pursuit more than worth it. MINOR GAMEPLAY SPOILERS AHEAD:First, the good changes: It seems the devs had a bigger vision for this sequel than just more of the same. They added a kick-ass motorcycle, a kick-ass wing suit, and replaced the lame-ass and out-of-place puzzle sections from the last game with some neat mini levels. Music and graphics see an improvement, and there is also an increase in enemy and environmental variety. I also found level design to be better/more deliberate in this entry-- ESPECIALLY the boss fights. The Rogue Runner game mode was also kind of cool. Now for the controversial/bad changes: Ghostrunner 2 adds a block that some perceive as removing a bit of the already perfectly-tuned challenge of the first game. While this is true, I think this is offset by the added complexity that I mentioned earlier. It also encourages people to master the newly-added perfect parry system by reducing the punishment for missing (rather than dying, you just lose a decent amount of stamina). Some also argue that this game feels slower-- this may be true, but as long as you don't have 100+ hours logged into speedrunning the first game, I can't imagine that you will notice or care (I certainly didn't). In my opinion, the biggest mistake that this game made was trying to dabble into open zones. Thankfully, this only happened for a level or two. But GOD did it absolutely slaughter the pacing of the game. Not only was this section slow and uninspired, but it was clearly unnecessary (it was pretty much just 3 levels stapled together Frankenstein style) and performed atrociously on my admittedly outdated machine. As a completionist, searching for the otherwise fun to get collectibles in this area was a slog. I perceived this to be the devs just dipping their toes in experimenting with this genre. If anyone on the team happens to read this, please DO NOT try to go this route if there are plans for a trilogy.I had a lot to say about this game, but the TLDR is that there is nothing quite like it. It perfectly scratches the gamer itch of being a total badass. But rather than just handing that power to you by making you OP, it forces you to earn it through your own improvement. I'd recommend picking up both this one and the first, but I personally found this one to be a tiny bit better on the whole.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: A fast paced 1-hit death cyberpunk slasher/platformer you won't forget!Although it doesn't fit the [1 hr gameplay = 1 dollar spent] criteria, it's  worth the money for the standard edition at least (and an even better deal if you get the brutal edition on sale).Similar to the first game, the fun lay within the wallrunning, jumping, and grappling introduced in the first game, now with added motorcycle! Slashing through enemies while avoiding certain 1-hit deaths is fun beyond compare, an experience tailored for high-skill gamers. This sequel adds new as well as heavily improved mechanics, notably the parry/deflect system, (endgame) flight suit, several motorcycle racing style levels, as well as cleaning up the old game mechanics like the abilities system. High skill, high reward!Short and sweet, half the achievements are challenging and fulfilling, requiring you to put your skill to the test. None of the achievements are particularly tedious if you keep in mind that you must search for collectibles before starting. This time, there's a built in radar for collectibles, so there's no excuse not to get them all! The most challenging achievement is finishing 5 levels without dying. Think it's easy? Think again.Massive improvements over the first game in several areas. First, you can actually see who you're talking with over the radio face-to-face this time! Voice acting has improved leaps and bounds with quality dialogue and meaningful content. While I don't feel particularly attached to any of the characters, there is the groundwork laid for future games. They certainly don't lack in personality, now they just need time to marinate on the player.Very little to hate about this game, but the introduction of new mechanics will always pose issues/fixes that need to be made. As such, only 3 notable problems occurred; 1) The motorcycle feels extremely floaty, and the lerp applied to the camera makes it hard to take sharp turns which are sometimes necessary 2) You can't move the camera while driving, which also makes it difficult to see where you're going at times3) On the motorcycle stage in which you are chased by a large entity, if you die around the beginning of the chase, then you become stuck in a loop in which you can't boost out and the slow speed causes you to repeatedly die. A simple solution might be having the boost accelerate in faster burst initially, or reduce the lag on the boost input.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh yeah baby, we are back. I loved Ghostrunner 1, and enjoyed it quite a bit even with it's flaws. Ghostrunner 2 doubles down on the cool factor, as well as the complexity, and you are left with a game with a lot more going on this time around. It has a few issues here and there, but I feel they are minor when compared to the sheer amount of love that was put into making this game feel as awesome as it does.PROS: - A bunch of new features added: They added blocking, side abilities, and new ultimates, and with a lot more versatility at that. Where Ghostrunner 1 was a lot more simplistic in nature, Ghostrunner 2 gives you a lot of freedom to try your own things. It's pretty rad to be honest. The later half of the game adds a bunch of really neat stuff that I absolutely was not expecting to be as cool as it is.- Less puzzles, more hackin and slashin action: One thing I didn't like in Ghostrunner 1 is that some of the puzzles forced you to be at a standstill and involved standing around instead of harnessing the cool factor. I think Ghostrunner 2 made the non-combative areas feel more meaningful and fun, instead of just solving a simplified mobile game puzzle.- You just feel cool: How do you explain this? Everything in this game makes you feel like an action movie star. Once you get the hang of it, you can do some crazy stuff which is the things of dreams. It's tough, but after getting through a difficult part after a few deaths is so satisfying.NEUTRAL: Where Ghostrunner 1 was more of an arcade style consistent level to level format, Ghostrunner 2 took more of a story based aspect, giving you time to talk to other characters and really flesh them out. They feel a lot more human in this game, whereas in Ghostrunner 1 you just feel like they are just background noise. It's a nice change of pace, but perhaps not for everyone. It's nice that you can choose to talk to characters, but also can just go straight to the next mission.CONS:- PC Optimization. This is the biggest flaw in Ghostrunner 2, the optimization is not the best. There are some times when the game is running at a super crispy 100fps for me, but then there are other times when it drops to 30 frames (especially  (minor spoiler), even when I turn the settings way down. I like to think I have a decent PC that can play most games unhindered, but this made me feel like I need a NASA supercomputer to play it without it dipping past 60fps.- Bugs: Throughout the game I encountered a few annoying bugs, and in all it is not as perfect as it could be. Movement can come to an abrupt stop, hit detection can be a bit wonky, and sometimes it isn't clear if something is supposed to happen, or if it happened by chance. There was one time that I fell through the floor into a random empty space and could do nothing until I restarted from the last checkpoint. I'm not going to knock it too much, seeing as it is the first month of the game, and that it is more of an indie game, and not some massive triple A Rockstar Games title.- Boss Battles: This one is minor, but the bosses really seem to spike the game's difficulty. The game goes from being hard but fair, to being bullet hell territory real quick. The final boss battle is probably the best example of this. It is WAY better than the boss battles in the first game though, which I felt were very much lacking in retrospect, but I still feel is not as fun as the normal combat.IN CONCLUSION: If you liked Neon White, Mirror's Edge, Doom Eternal, or any parkour based games out there, you will love this game no doubt. The flexibility, creativeness, and atmosphere are so awesome in this game, and there is very few games out there that will be able to make you feel the same way. Even with its flaws it still remains my favorite recent playthrough, and I'm excited to see the new game mode coming out later this year.8.5/10, such a badass experience. Just needs some touching up is all.

_childDocuments_.review: running cyborg ascends tower the sequelA pretty great sequel, with some very minor caveats. I'd recommend Ghostrunner 2 for everyone who enjoyed the first.*STORY:*The story is way better in this one. Because of this players will have to spend more time talking and focusing on dialogue than in the first, which may be a downside to some. It definitely slows down the pacing for repeat playthroughs/speedruns, though thankfully, you can skip through all dialogue if you really do not care enough. The characters are better written, especially your machine companions AND antagonists. The character interactions in the newly introduced hub are however a bit less great. It's comparable to Starfield where you just stand there and they stare back while dialogue plays with some VERY awkward silences. Thankfully most of the dialogue is optional.*GAMEPLAY:*The gameplay is improved, but not nearly as much as some people say it is. There are a few more enemy types, some of which are great additions such as a Roller found later in the game, forcing you to think outside of the box sometimes. But most of the new enemy types are very weak and uninteresting, providing either an alternative to already existing enemies or just offering nothing new. There were also a few enemy types from the last game that did not get introduced until the late game, which left me wondering if the developers intended to have more unique enemy types but couldn't do it, or if the overall difficulty for this one was supposed to be lower than the first. Which ever answer it is, it does feel quite anticlimactic seeing the same enemies pop up in the late game, while in the first game they were there quite a bit earlier.That is not to say that the gameplay is worse, because the game flows a lot smoother. There are quite a bit more parkour sections that often take up more time than the combat sections, usually it works quite well. The only problem I found with it is the little platforms you can grapple to your location, I simply do not understand why they appeared so late into the game while they work way worse than a simple grapple point. Some levels are a bit long compared to the first, but when the combat really works, it shines. More abilities, and a currency to buy them with and the motherboard system makes the possibilities in this game way more interesting.*SOUNDTRACK:*The soundtrack to this game was a little less up my alley than the soundtrack to the first. Dan Terminus uses an upbeat, more classic synthwave approach that feels more like enjoying some good times, while having less punchy sound design. Arkadius Rejkowski composed the tracks that play during some of the more desolate segments of the game, and they work quite well, although they are sometimes a little too minimalistic for my taste. The style was bound to change with the fact that Daniel Deluxe only made two tracks in the entire game, but some of the tracks composed by the other composers work very well. A few standouts are "Mind as Universe", "The Temple", "Road Zero", "Already Dead" and "Protocol Overload".*PERFORMANCE:*Sadly (and this is probably just early days issues) some people seem to have quite bad performance, including myself. There is quite a bit of stuttering involved in this game, even when your overall framerate is very high the game sometimes just stops for about half a second to a second, usually resulting in suddenly seeing a "Critical Failure" on your screen. Hopefully the stutters can be worked out for the people who have it.Overall, Ghostrunner 2 builds upon the story of the first quite well, while giving you way more to parkour with. The combat is a step up, when you actually get to fight lots of enemies, use all your abilities, and slowly figure out an encounter using every death, just like the first game. The soundtrack is great for the most part, although the unique style of Daniel Deluxe is pushed to the background in favor of mixed styles.And hopefully this one will be just as fun to pour many hours into, optimizing speedrunning into oblivion just as the first.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner is one of my favorite games, so I really hate to give its sequel a thumbs down, but I was pretty disappointed by this game—not because it was bland or dull, but because it ended up taking many steps backwards from the original. For what it is, Ghostrunner 2 is certainly not terrible, still a pretty exciting platformer with incredible visuals, but it somehow manages to screw up a lot of things the first game did really well. Firstly, however, here are some of the things I think it DOES do a good job of:-As mentioned before, the visuals are absolutely fantastic. This game is even more stunning than GR1, and it features a wider range of environments, all of which look beautiful. I’ve seen people complain about the performance, and while I had a couple small issues, I was consistently getting >100fps on max settings with a fairly mid-tier GPU, so I don’t think that’s a huge problem here.-Naturally, the movement is still decently fun, even if it’s a big step down from its predecessor.-Personally, I really liked the upgrade chip system in this game. The “Tetris block” system in GR1 was fine, but unlocking different chips and arranging them in the motherboard felt a lot more personalizable and interesting to me.-The soundtrack is once again a banger.-The  introduced in the last level is absolutely incredible, it’s without a doubt the best part of the game and I really wish there was more of it.With that being said, there are two massive issues, as well as a few other small ones, that really ruined this game for me.Firstly, the level design is extremely unpolished. To me, GR1 is the pinnacle of great level design. It does such an amazing job of using subtle color patterns and aspects of the environment to lead the player around without them even realizing it. Everything feels super smooth and intentional, and it’s what makes the platforming gameplay so much fun. I’ve even published a video essay on why GR1 is a masterclass in great level design. GR2, on the other hand, very much lacks intentionality. Many of the environments in GR2 are more muted and bleak than the neon-lit parts of Dharma Tower in GR1, which isn’t inherently bad, but when the first game leaned so heavily on using the environment to prevent the player from getting lost, eliminating those patterns with nothing in their stead creates a problem for GR2. I found myself constantly getting lost in this game, finding little visual indication of what I was supposed to do next and frequently running around in circles or aimlessly going to areas I wasn’t supposed to. This was especially a problem with the motorbike levels, which I’ll elaborate on later. But the bottom line is, getting stuck and lost is completely antithetical to fast-paced and fluid gameplay, and it was really frustrating to be constantly losing my momentum because of unclear level design.In addition to its opaqueness, this game’s level design is also poorly implemented and could’ve benefited from significantly more QA/playtesting. I encountered many instances where the gap-jammer (grappling hook) didn’t pull me quite far enough to land where I was supposed to, or it flung me directly at a wall I was supposed to be landing on top of. There are several points where swinging on bars didn’t get me far enough to land where I was supposed to go either. These issues, among many others, indicate a lack of polishing and consistency with the level design. I also quite experienced many geometry/physics bugs where the game would make me start wall-running on something that wasn’t even a wall, or conversely, I would be unable to wall-run on a wall that was supposed to be run on (sometimes there was also a bug where I ended up partly inside of a wall and could only run very slowly on it). The launching air vents sometimes just didn’t do anything when I walked over them. Once again, these issues feel like they could have been prevented or at least recognized before releasing the game, and they drastically decreased my enjoyment of GR2.My other main problem with this game is that it appears to take a design approach of prioritizing quantity over quality of new features. Nearly every single level was throwing some new mechanic at me that would rarely be used again in any level thereafter, and most of these mechanics came out half-baked because there are simply too many of them. It doesn’t seem like the devs took the time to deeply craft any of these features, instead just coming up with something to add for one level and then moving onto the next one. There can be potential for some really interesting combinations when you start to mix mechanics together, but unfortunately, that didn’t really happen here. This leads to GR2 almost feeling like playing with fifty different mods installed that aren’t meant to go together and sometimes actively conflict with one another.As I alluded to earlier in my review, one of the most glaring instances where this flawed design philosophy crops up is with the motorbike. This addition definitely had potential, but it ended up making the middle portion that implements it the worst part of the game by far. This is because, in addition to the motorbike controlling horrendously, having very glitchy physics, and it being extremely difficult to “read” levels while driving it, the motorbike plays into GR2’s identity crisis that so many modern games are having because it wants to be every genre at once. The first level involving the motorbike still feels like a Ghostrunner level, because it’s relatively fluid and fast-paced—it would almost be fun, if not for all the other motorbike issues I already pointed out. But after this, GR2 basically pretends to be an open-world game for the next 3 levels, making you use the motorbike to traverse a world that has almost no visual indications of where to go whatsoever. One level in this open-world section of the game took over an hour for my first completion, because I just kept driving around aimlessly on the motorbike, extremely confused where the game wanted me to go. This is the EXACT opposite of what Ghostrunner gameplay is supposed to feel like! The fact that people complain about the game’s hub world interrupting the flow but then praise the motorbike is absolutely bewildering to me—trying (and failing) to be an open-world game is the single worst thing the devs could have done for the flow of GR2’s gameplay. And I won’t even start on its “roguelike mode” that apparently every game needs to have now… it took about twenty minutes to see everything there was to be seen, and it was even shallower than Ghostwire: Tokyo’s “roguelike mode” which is really saying something.In addition to these two glaring fundamental flaws the game exhibits, many other small issues hampered my enjoyment of GR2 as well. For one, I’m still extremely puzzled who thought that having FEWER control layouts than the first game was a good idea. Having to play GR2 with a different control layout than GR1, like I did, is absurd, and there is absolutely zero reason for this. Also, some of the achievements have very misleading descriptions. For example, the most difficult achievement Godrunner, says that it requires you to “finish any 5 levels without dying,” but as it turns out, boss levels do not count for this. I could maybe understand if the achievement had simply said “finish 5 levels without dying,” but the use of the word ANY is incredibly misleading for an achievement where it cannot actually be any arbitrary five levels. Other achievements have similar problems.Overall, while Ghostrunner 2 delivers some of the same thrill as its predecessor, this sequel ends up shooting itself in the foot as a result of its poorly-intentioned level design and cramming in of far too many shallow new features. It’s a shame to say this, but if you loved the original game, don’t come into this one with high hopes—it butchers a lot of what made the first one so good.

_childDocuments_.review: You can read my other reviews The sequel to Ghostrunner took approximately three years to land on the shelves of fans of this cyberpunk parkour platformer. The narrative follows the end of the previous episode and continues to follow the story of Jack and his group of “friends” in an attempt to discover which side of the barricade they intend to position themselves on. Jack, a unique case of a machine with human qualities, adds a layer of complexity to the story.While the game expands beyond the confines of Dharma, a towering shelter for its residents, the action kicks off within it. Dharma is under attack by an AI cult of metallic ninjas, seeking unimaginable powers. Jack emerges as the sole hope to combat this threat that could upheave everyone’s lives.The journey toward this primary objective unfolds across 18 diverse levels, blending linearity with challenges and side missions marked by roguelike mechanics. Right at this point there’s a difference compared to the first title, the inclusion of these secondary missions allows it to extend its longevity, making it even more interesting. However, one of the main new features will be the inclusion of a motorbike and a semi-open world map, allowing Jack to explore beyond the confines of Dharma, and touch grass. Well… it will actually be more sand.Jack’s special abilities facilitate frenetic movement, enabling swift area clearance. However, receiving damage means revisiting the section, though the checkpoint system mitigates some frustration. Some of the skills and passive abilities are carried over from the previous title, which expands choices in the new skill tree or “motherboard” if you will. These can be acquired using points collected between levels at the new headquarters, where dialogues with different characters become a possibility.The incorporation of a base adds depth, providing a refuge and fostering a team committed to assisting Jack. Despite Jack’s detachment from human affection, the interactions add a layer to the experience. The developers’ commitment to freshness is evident in the introduction of new mechanics, making each level unique. One moment you’re jumping between platforms and the next you have the ability to hover over enemies. Even in confrontations against Bosses, each one presents different mechanics, be it a chase track where it is necessary to jump between platforms or dodge attacks, or a physical confrontation against a giant enemy.I can easily say that the levels that introduce new mechanics were the most fun to complete. Although driving the motorcycle presents some problems, with jumps that make no sense, or ending up with the motorcycle stuck in certain locations on the map, which consequently leads to the loss of level progression. Within my 15 hours spent in the Ghostrunner 2 universe, many of them were spent alongside frustrating moments, especially because I allowed myself to try some challenges after finishing the story.For those with more technic and patience, it is possible to discover attack lines, precise jumping moments, and the use of skills at key points which leads to finishing the level with the best possible time. Although it is not fundamental to the development of the story, I understand that this type of competition is appealing to many people. The premise of this game is very much based on trial and error, in an attempt at personal overcoming with the aim of clearing the place of enemies in order to open a door that allows passage to the next section.Ghostrunner 2 caters to a diverse player base, offering something for both competitive and casual players. The well-developed and intriguing story, combined with frantic gameplay, solidifies its legacy as a remarkable gaming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Meh, Ghostrunner 2 disappointed me. It bored me and was weak on gameplay. I thought about giving this a thumbs down, but it does all the basics of a mainstream casual game right. It's not outstanding in any way but casually enjoyable. The graphics are awesome, the bike ride is a cool new addition (but super basic) and the dark synthwave soundtrack is heating up the action really good. The gameplay though is lacking in my opinion. You've got a melee sword attack only, so you first need to get near the enemies by using your parkour movement. The movement options need to be used in the same patterns repeatedly and don't offer enough to make moving varied. So you avoid getting hit by their projectiles while running towards the enemies and then slice one or several up with a single sword swing. Pretty boring. Most of the times you don't even need to get there, because when you parry an enemy's projectile it flies back to the sender and eliminates your gameplay goal before you started the fun part. Talking about parrying: when standing still the projectiles' distance can badly be seen, because the first person camera is directly in line with the trajectory, no angle between to see a shot coming. There are a lot of projectiles and attacks coming in and sometimes I didn't know what hit me. Sadly there is no kill-cam-like feature to know what happened.Level design doesn't even care to look like a real world, but puts floating wallrun panels and narrow corridors  everywhere and in a way so that you feel like in a devs level and not like in a cyberpunk world.The characters and their talk is so wannabe cool like what kids think is cool how to talk. It was rather awkward for me so I rolled my eyes quite a lot. Also there is unlogical talk like "Uhh I hate all those clans. Why are they pushing everyone down? I just want to survive. We will come through. Even if that means pushing everyone down..." where the character isn't aware that if you are the one pushing others down means you're in the exact same boat of the ones you're complaining about, but it's presented as the right path we're stepping on.Further cons:- Doesn't save key binding. You have to rebind the controls on every startup- Getting stuck in fences, ropes and terrain on foot or with the bike- More bugs like the boss stopped working all of a sudden, doesn't move and is invulnerable and have to restart- A challenge run repeatedly started with the bike turned in the wrong direction- Restarting from checkpoint didn't respawn me near the bike so I had to run a minute to get there- Can't put the Rooting chip upgrade into the motherboard when it's not the same category even though it enables every chip to be put whereever wanted. You first need to remove a column, put the Rooting chip first and then put the others in again which is the same layout as before but it needed to be put in this order.- Some "puzzles" require you as in the first Ghostrunner to go past the visible wanted item, drop down a random chasm and go a secret passage back to the item.- Weird attack hitboxes which hit you after the boss had already swung his sword when you're going in for the whiff punish.Didn't really convince me. Only recommended for casual playstyle. I rather recommend SPRAWL and Armless Samurai!

_childDocuments_.review: For a platform game, it's great. Unfortunately, that's where the good parts end, because for everything the platforming gets right the combat ruins. Where do I even begin with the combat? For starters, no difficulty scaling, so for those who want a more casual experience, forget it, because you have to sweat every second to progress. Then we have the boss fights, what a clunky mess, it would probably be fine if you could use your ultimate abilities but no, apparently your character who is a literal cyborg samurai just forgets how capable he is within a boss battle, how convenient. Then the impossible split-second decisions you have to make are unbearable, it would be fine if I was invulnerable while in mid-blink, but instead, I can still be hit with a stupid stray bullet from an enemy who I can't even see. Don't even get me started on the dumpster garbage abilities that barely even assist you in battle, in the first game, it felt like my character received sizeable buffs for the difficulty scaling throughout the game, but in this "sequel," the only progress you receive is pretty lackluster character boosts. Honestly what a disappointment considering how amazing the first game was. My advice is don't pay more than $10 for this junk if you want to try it, otherwise, I'd recommend just playing the first game which is a lot better.

_childDocuments_.review: Glad the developers got the greenlight for a sequel. Really enjoyed this one. I haven't had to many stutters like many players here, or maybe I'm just used to them. The game runs buttery smooth for the most part, unless there's over 10 enemies on screen, some of the best arenas in the game, slow my game quite a bit and has plenty of stuttering. But that's completely understandable on my computer running a i5 4670k (10 year old cpu) and a gtx 1070 installed on a sata SSD.I kind of enjoyed the ease of using the block button in GR2, with a stamina meter that depletes if you use it too often. You can even upgrade your motherboard to the point where your able to block the mech horizontal lazer rays, and use a shriken to instantly stun and blitz to a tough enemy for an easy kill. Heck you can even use one of many over powered ultimate abilities if you want to completely destroy an entire crowd with ease.With the block button mechanic readily available, it seems like the developers heavily nerfed possibly one of the most highly skilled mechanics in the game. Remember in the first Ghostrunner when an enemy was firing shots at you, if you timed your sword attack at the exact time the lazer shot just about touched you, you could deflect the shot right back at your enemy. Yeah now when you swing, the lazer shot disappears but doesn't bother to deflect anymore. You have to use the block button to deflect the shots. This is especially noticeable in the 2nd to last stage where your using the wingsuit and there's a bunch of enemies firing shots at you all at once. You are unable to block while gliding in the air, but you can attack and use your special abilities. The story is just as laughable or even more so than the first game, which isn't a bad thing at all. The main issue here is Ghostrunner 2 tries to present its horrible story in cutscenes and loads of dialogue in the hub between missions (good thing you can skip most of it if you like). Although some of the dialogue and voice acting gave me a good laugh. I think keeping the story mostly in dialogue channels as you're exploring the world makes the most sense.If you enjoyed the first GR, you'll probably like this one. Even with OP abilities and blocking, I've died quite a bit in all the missions. This game can be quite a challenge for players who aren't used to playing fast paced first person parkour games.

Game didn't get meaningfully better, just more complicated.TLDR More Ghostrunner with extra ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Probably still fun, but worse than the first game.Examples:BLOCK BUTTON. Everything you can do with it could be done in the first game with the sword, no extra button needed. Why add it? It just complicates what should be a simple control scheme.HUB AREA. Completely Unnecessary. The writing isn't good enough for the hub to be enjoyable.UPGRADE SYSTEM. The first game was a simple and unique one-screen upgrade system that worked great. The sequel replaced it with a 4-screen system that is more confusing and less interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: I love ghostrunner. LOVE! one of my favorite games for sure. but this? this isn't it.right off the bat the game felt unpolished, something that would become all the more clear as I continued playing. this is a good example of a game going "release now, fix later". a few example include, but are not limited to: • killing enemies feel choppy compared to previous game. • consistent crashes upon launching the game.• missing audio/sound design.• RTX will come in a later update.maybe make a complete product and THEN release it? it's so sad to see this way of rushing releases are effecting even non-AAA devs. without spoiling anything; the whole bike section was awful and dull, the ending unsatisfactory and storylines just dropped in favor of an "open ended" ending for a third game. the game in general feels too large and long, and you really start to feel that especially when the polish just isn't there.again; I LOVE ghostrunner. I was really excited for a sequel! but I'm left incredibly disappointed and not at all looking forward to the next game that is undoubtedly to come. I don't hate this game, I just don't particularly like it either.
