_childDocuments_.review: wish i could give this a mixed instead of positive or negative, because its both and neither.there's more mechanics, and some are good and equally some are bad. the flying jet is such an obvious new thing, but its so fun to use......and then there's the bike. and everything that came with it sucked.the big levels. waay too big and it's very easy to get lost in the map. the bike is also the most bugged mechanic in the game and i had to restart to checkpoint so many times just because of it.speaking of the levels: the beginning ones were great. and then they turned bad. really bad. i liked the arcade feeling of the first game. this second iteration is definitely more fleshed out: there's a waaay bigger story than in the first game. the scales are way bigger and it shows through the level design. and yet, at some point, it stopped feeling like ghostrunner. and what i loved about this game is that there was nothing like it: a movement-focused first person slash game. that's it, simple! but the big levels, the go from point A to point B to activate a lever in a tower instead of just slash enemies made me miss what the original ghostrunner had: simplicity.and let's not mention the performance issues and the bugs. throughout the first 3-4 levels all i thought was: man so glad for this bug-free experience. and then they kicked in. sometimes, i just wouldn't die: i would fall to eternity, out of the map; sometimes i would just be stuck, you guessed it, the moment i got out of the bike. again, that damn bike: it was a mistake. if there is ever a Ghostrunner 3 (which im asumming there will be, considering the post-credits scene), please never re-introduce the bike. and there were so many times my fps would just drop unexpectedly, and when i would die all the stutter would be gone. then i would die again: and the stutter would re-appear. idk.still, it was fun. the graphics are a beauty, the mechanics are smooth and there's nothing like it out there. but man, this just didn't feel right. unlike the first one, this doesn't have as much replayability.still, appreciate the devs for the game. but even though i gave it a positive review, it's more like a 6/10 than anything.

_childDocuments_.review: A decently competent sequel, all things considered. If you liked the first one you'll get a kick out of this. The new traversal mechanics are pretty cool and add some much needed variety to the level themes/layouts. There's also some really quite incredible set pieces that I won't spoil. Jack's climbing/jumping mechanics also seem a lot less finicky and janky than they were in the first game. They're still far from perfect, but they felt more consistent in this game, leading to less frustration.It's all let down a bit by the story, however. Particularly the ending disappointed me. The way it just kind of... ends after a pretty bog-standard boss fight with Mitra was a real anti climax. It absolutely paled in comparison to the first game's finale and made it feel like the game was rushing to tie up all the loose ends.Not enough of a letdown for me to not recommend the game, but certainly a downer. It could've been a real gem if those aspects had gotten more time to develop. Still a fun game overall. It was nice to see more of this world and its characters.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend Ghostrunner 2, it is a fantastic game with: amazing movement, intuitive game design, a wide range of difficulty in its levels, and fantastic map design. That being said, I have many issues with Ghostrunner 2, and they are the following:Ghostrunner 2 just like Ghostrunner is very short in length (it took me 9hrs to complete the main story).Ghostrunner 2 seems to have taken a leap of faith in many aspects which may be hit or miss to various different players, the developers definitely far exceeded what was needed in order to bring new mechanics to the game, however, this seems to have backfired on them, because as a result the game now feels kind of clunky with many mechanics introduced just to be dropped at later stages in the game, this all makes the game come off as an experiment or a test as opposed to Ghostrunner which felt like a carefully tuned, enjoyable game. Ghostrunner 2 is not by any means bad or not fun, however, there are many aspects to it that just in my opinion don't fit the franchise, for example, the introduction of the motorbike in the game was at first a fun concept that could have played fantastically into one-off chase scenes or obstacle course levels, instead they decided to double down on the importance of the bike by applying an open world aspect to 2 levels in the game. This not only makes the game flow worse with the constant need to get off your bike to defeat enemies and unlock a gate to progress but it also makes the game an incredible pain to try and gather all the collectables. This game is definitely more suited to a linear level design, and the open world aspect should (at least in my opinion) be dropped as Ghostrunner at its core is designed for close-quarters high speed combat as opposed to slow and long distance encounters.Another feature of Ghostrunner 2 that didn't play out as well as expected would be the wing suit introduced towards the end of the game, it really is only present for the last few missions and then isn't even required in the final boss fight, just like the bike after the few levels where it was present the wing suit as just dropped afterwards and not mentioned before, the wing suit once again just like the bike actually slows the gameplay down, does not allow it to flow well, and allows for a lot of annoying and bug-induced deaths.The final boss for Ghostrunner 2 is also majorly disappointing, the final boss doesn't feel like a final boss at all, if anything the second last boss that we encounter in the game is by far a bigger challenge and also more fun to fight, as the final boss seems to be spoon-fed to the player, with constant assists to almost ensure that the player passes within a few attempts.Now, don't get me wrong not all the features added in Ghostrunner 2 are bad, I for one really enjoyed the small breaks between levels where you got to go around the hideout and talk to your team, buy and select your abilities, and the new upgrade menu, however, overall Ghostrunner 2 has definitely bit off more than it could chew, and this is of course not on the developers as they did a fantastic job and managed to implement these features with minimal to no bugs at all, however, unfortunately the game just feels less like Ghostrunner and I fear with the ending of the game, that this may be a recurring theme in future instalments in the game.I hope that this review is helpful to anyone debating buying this game, I would still highly recommend it as Ghostrunner is really an amazing game and experience, it is just important to keep in mind the shortcomings of this instalment when coming directly from the previous one, I hope that any future instalments manage to remove or atleast incorporate these new features in a way that allows for smoother and better gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is sad to play through after GR 1.I'll start with my highlights of the game before getting into why the game is a sad sequel. Beginning with the visuals, same as GR1 they're beautiful, the designer NAILED the look of Dharma (minus bad textures) and the cybercity aesthetic. The first level is a visual treat and so much fun to replay through.The soundtrack too, incredible and also nails the vibe that they were going for. High energy, lots of synths and a tempo that makes you want to play through the game as fast as possible.However, the design feels way off in comparison to its predecessor and the jank is inexcusable, throughout my first playthrough I managed to get out of bounds 3 times and on repeat playthroughs that number just goes up. (Made even worse by the players need to go back for collectables and look around)  Collision is horrible throughout every level and getting inside bits of geometry is so easy it feels like the game wasn't playtested at all. Not to mention the horrible movement system and the way the game tries to take control away from you only to kill you by doing so, making for a frustrating experience. The amount of times I've climbed on a dead body is laughable because how does that happen? You can turn down the assistance in the options menu but there's no off setting, just low assistance. The story is okay, if not a bit hard to follow at first. Little bit forgettable if you ask me. The only really interesting parts were the sections with rahu but I won't spoil them here but they were my highlight of the game, he calls out a lot of stuff regarding morality and the origins of the GR's The mechanics that differ from GR 1 are fine on their own but they don't stop shoving new stuff in your face throughout the game. The last level includes new mechanics and it makes you feel like you've never actually learnt to play the game to begin improving. You're never testing your skills as much as you're just trying to understand what the ♥♥♥♥ the new thing they've given you is The bike was a nice idea, and it can be addicting when you get it right but also feels like it wasn't tested at all. You have 0 camera control while riding it and when moving at high speeds and riding on walls, that makes it impossible to react to obstacles. When you died in GR 1, it felt like you deserved it because you made a wrong move that you COULD see coming. GR 2 breaks this by becoming a throwing ♥♥♥♥ at the wall simulator until you remember whats coming up.The new abilities are okay, the shuriken and its upgrades make for a nice change of pace (when they work and don't switch up the mechanics seemingly at random) but they mostly feel bloated and tend to do the same thing that GR 1 abilities did.The game is also so unoptimised it made me laugh and it has nothing to do with hardware. The game runs at the exact same FPS with max settings to low settings and Im still struggling to figure out how because the game looks almost identical to GR 1 which runs perfectly fine. GR 2's difficulty doesn't really come from new exciting enemies with new ways to kill them, (while there are a few new ones that are fun like the whip dudes)  it comes from the sheer number of projectile enemies they throw at you at once which again forces you into this trial and error gameplay loop instead of improving your skill. You can remember the entire arena your fighting in and still die because the enemy halfway across the arena you ran past at the start is still trying to snipe you. Leading nicely into enemy AI, it's broken a lot of the time. Half the time an enemy will just stop, for no reason and then once you go to kill them the game will suddenly realise that its broken and the enemy will kill youIf you played GR 1, don't ruin your impression of the franchise with this one. The game needed way more time in the oven and it's honestly just upsetting to see this game release in the state that it's in.*side note, the GR1 re-cap is in the extras menu and there's no prompt to have said re-cap play before starting the game so anyone who plays GR 2 first or hasn't played GR 1 for a while will find it even harder to follow the story*

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of ghostrunners 1, I mean HUGE. Recommended it to all my friends had it as my desktop for ages. Then I seen that the 2nd one was coming out and it was great news, I thought to myself, "I mean, all they can do is make it better right? they have the formula down so I wonder what they will do differently?". Well they definitely did do some stuff differently. Parkour elementThe parkour on each story mission I've played so far is so painfully slow for what ghost RUNNERS should be. They have got to capitalise on the golden game mechanic that is dashing then jumping. It would make the parkour much more interactive and fast. I find myself having a slow walk in between some of the parkour elements, and sometimes when I hit a wall run even from a very fast momentum I will end up sort of dragging along the wall like a snail. There is a lack of the dopamine hits that GR 1 provided with its much more unique and planned out environment. They use the grapple as a heavy crutch during most of the sequences and I really don't feel like I have to think about what I'm doing or where I'm going. The parkour in the simulation is much better, way more challenging and thought provoking. It's a shame it's hidden in some weird mini-game. World-buildingThe environments are awesome, perfect mix between urban slum and neon district. The parkour is semi blended in well, as much as you could expect from a game centred around it. The characters introduced in this sequel are incredibly 2D. I never usually skip dialogue, even ones that I feel drag out, but with GR 2. I found myself skipping more that I would listen. Their designs (on direct 11) are painful to the eyes. Very little features and sometimes so incredibly bright and glossy I can only see their eyes. Even the main enemy and their motives aren't really fleshed out.CombatThe combat is alright. It requires you to note your surroundings, look for approaches and utilise mechanics. There is an good variety of enemy types that keep you on your toes, for about the first 3 missions. The shinobi is a great example. After I encountered him once, it became incredibly easy to just parry for an easy window of invincibility and a kill. One of the enemies abilities is just making an electric line on the floor, very boring and all he does. Sometimes they are located over holes so they will just sorta stare at you and perform their move with no success. The game will just spawn gun enemies near a wall run or many melee enemies on a flat plane. Very repetitive.Overall not utterly terrible but lacking in comparison to the first one. I don't mean this review out of spite, genuinely just what I found disappointing about the game and giving my piece on what would make a instant hit for any other games from this dev. I can tell that there is sparks of passion there but I feel as if it has faded from the burning blaze of it present in GR 1, feels a little like a cash grab, and the reason I bought this game for 9 pounds.

_childDocuments_.review: Would you like to practice rapid parkour on a mostly broken system? Now go play this game.This seems like a far cry from the incredible first game. Even down to the pointlessly open regions and NPCs that are always yapping in your ear, it seems like an attempt to imitate high-budget games. This totally destroys the mood that the first game so expertly cultivated, and it's obvious that "more" is more essential than "better."More adversaries, more tricks, more projectiles, but at most slight improvements to the poor hitboxes, poor enemy design, and omniscient enemy AI that makes the game more difficult to play than enjoyable. Additionally, there seems to be less fluidity in the movement. Let's not even forget how they lied about something about the future of gameBut to me, it really comes down to the reality that we won't have anything as basic as steady frame rate and ray tracing. In response to the game's issues, One More Level has gone "Lalalalala" and stuck their fingers in their ears. Their player base is of no importance to them; what matters to them is the money they made at launch. This is further demonstrated by DLC after DLC that barely modifies the game, and the constant barrage of unfavourable reviews for the follow-up to one of my favourite games.To be really honest, I don't give a damn about Ghostrunner or One More Level anymore. Because of the way they handled this game, they have completely lost my respect, and I no longer have faith in them to update or improve their games before release. They stole the money after selling a flawed, incomplete product and passing it off as the final item. They just care about the money they can make off the hype, not the community or the state of their game.Furthermore, to use the words of the Ghostrunner developers "a future optimisation patch would be beating a dead horse," WOW.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: Fun enough you get used to these things. The game offers enough to ignore them. Still, would be nice to not have to deal with them. You get a motorcycle and can ride it vertically down the tower. You get a wingsuit and can skydive enemies. The level design is great and the boss designs are far better than the previous game. Worth.As for the controls, Gap Jammer being mapped to X took getting used to, but it is manageable. L3 to block, however, I'm sure was murdering my stick.Old: Fun but glitchy. I won't not recommend it, but this game needs serious bugfixes from vanishing enemies to incorrect player behaviors from ability interactions.For controllers, the control scheme is WAY too bloated. The previous installment had smooth controls for controller, but this game realistically needs 6 shoulder buttons rather than the 4 that are standard.Block comes with its own button and functionality, which contributes to this problem, and was completely unnecessary as it worked perfectly fine in the previous game mapped to the attack button, you just needed good timing.There's way more use of skills, like shuriken, in this one. This also contributes to the problem. It's not really viable to slap this onto a face button because the precision you need at the speed you need just isn't there if you're not aiming as you fire.This leaves, attack, gap jammer, jump, and dash for your shoulders--which is the GR1 BJ layout. I ended up mapping block to L3 which feels awful and gap jammer to X/square which doesn't feel right.

Where the first game focused on a more linear and close quarters style of combat that allowed you to run across walls more often the second game moves towards a more open battle arena with more grapple hook opportunities and jump fans which made me feel that I was in less control of my character.I did like these mechanics when traversing the map as it felt less like just holding W. The motorbike section of the game was also fun but suffers from QOL with the ability to free look. This is most obvious when riding up / down walls as you can't see what you're riding towards.This review sounds pretty negative, but if you've played the first game you know what to expect as it's more of the same which is is great. _childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner was easily one of the most unique games I’d played in a while. You can find my jumbled thoughts on that one . In summary, it was a really fun, reasonably challenging time, albeit one with a few inconsistencies and odd decisions that prevented it from being a home run. The sky was the limit for the potential of its follow-up though, and I think they nearly fully realized it. Ghostrunner 2 is the prime example of how to do a sequel, expanding on everything great about the first game, fixing what didn’t work, whilst retaining its identity as a challenging one-hit one-kill experience that is unlike anything else.Taking place one year after the original, the Ghostrunner, now fully adopting the name ‘Jack’, is working with the rebel faction dubbed The Climbers to keep order within Dharma Tower. When a group of rogue Ghostrunners named the Asura arise and threaten the power balance against the Climbers’ favour, Jack journeys to eliminate these threats and return some semblance of peace to the remainder of humanity. The writing and plot are much improved from the original; while this post-apocalyptic world was always interesting, the monotone exposition delivered by characters I didn’t care for made me forget much about what was going on. Here though, its presentation is more interesting, largely due to engaging voice performances delivered by the whole cast. You also have more opportunities to learn about its world and characters via between-level hub sections, where you can converse with actual character models of the cast this time around as opposed to their disembodied voices. Nevertheless, the additional worldbuilding is largely optional and can be ignored if you want to get back into the action quicker.Ghostrunner’s unique gameplay is better than ever in this sequel. Levels are split into platforming segments and combat arenas, though your parkour skills will be paramount to finishing all of these without getting hit. The core gameplay loop of dodging enemies and grappling about the environment to close the gap, slice them down and repeat for the whole room is largely unchanged, but it is refined to have greater consistency and offer up more options to outsmart your enemies. While you could only parry bullets in the original, Ghostrunner 2 gives you a short block meter, offering an additional window to slice your attacker down. The abilities system has been reworked to provide you with three options you can consistently use, and one ultimate ability which should result in a few easy kills. The shuriken can insta-kill some enemies, but it can also be used to open up grapple points on the environment and certain foes. Shadow provides you with temporary invisibility, and Tempest acts as a small force push which can dispatch a group of foes if used carefully. As for the ultimate ability options, they all have their uses; Blink and Overlord are back to help you eliminate a few key targets, whilst new additions like Flux give you a beam to disintegrate a bunch of foes instantly, and my favourite, Motoric Overload, temporarily buffs mobility whilst also allowing you to survive a single hit. All of your abilities and movement options can be upgraded by slotting in modules, unlockable with a currency obtained by killing enemies. Easier parrying, longer dodges, more precise shurikens, and bonuses tied to your combo meter are just some of the options on offer here. There are enough viable choices to ensure that many unique builds are possible through this system, it’s just about finding what playstyle you want to lean into.In terms of difficulty, I’d say it’s about as challenging as the original. New enemies such as the Priest, which unleashes a gigantic wave attack, and a killer wheel enemy, which can close the gap on your position really fast, are great additions to the already diverse enemy roster and can easily shut you down. Put these enemies into some of the largest arenas in the series so far, and there are so many areas where you could be caught off guard and need to restart the sequence. For the bosses, while they are certainly more interactive than the ones in the first game, they are low points in the difficulty. Outside of this game’s parkour boss, they are really straightforward, and ultimately feel a bit underwhelming compared to the standard levels. The game’s strongest asset is easily its level design. While most levels in the first game felt similar in structure and visual identity, the levels here are incredibly distinct, consistently offering up new mechanics and locations to keep things fresh throughout the campaign. One standard level locks you into a large environment until you dispatch a certain number of foes, and another adopts a non-linear design to its objectives. Variation is further increased with the motorcycle levels, resulting in new level structures and traversal options, whilst also not overstaying its welcome to overshadow the core gameplay. My absolute favourite level is the second to last one, as it introduces a one-off mechanic which completely changes how you approach that environment. The unprecedented sense of euphoria this mechanic provided me with resulted in the very best sequence I've played this year.A further improvement comes in the form of the reworked Cybervoid sections, which killed the pacing of the original upon level replays. Ghostrunner 2 instead turns these sections into unique traversal puzzles, typically requiring you to hit a series of objects in a limited time window, and these are infinitely more fun to re-experience. My only criticism relates to the coherency of this campaign; some levels begin by teleporting you to the starting point with no animation to speak of, making it feel a bit more disjointed compared to the original. Separately, I’d like to quickly highlight the great soundtrack; each level has a unique theme, and outside of some of the motorbike levels where the soundscape is a lot more subdued, there is plenty of good material to be found here.Once you wrap up the campaign, Ghostrunner 2 also offers a roguelike mode, an addition that feels perfectly suited to this experience. You start with the bare minimum abilities, and work your way through four visually distinct, increasingly difficult stages, selecting between combat and parkour challenges whilst earning upgrades and lives along the way. I hope this mode receives further updates though, as there is not much reason to replay it outside of earning all four rewards, and some level layouts repeated more often than I expected. Overall, it took me 11 hours to roll credits on Ghostrunner 2, earning every collectable along the way. It then took me an additional 5 hours to clear the roguelike mode and unlock every achievement. This makes the sequel a longer game than the original on Day 1, making it easier to recommend even before content updates.I knew Ghostrunner 2 was going to be great, but I was honestly caught off guard by how much of an improvement it ended up being. Almost every issue I had about the original is ironed out, cementing this franchise as one of the pillars of its subgenre. Its gameplay is challenging but always satisfying, its world is more interesting both visually and narratively, and a few of its levels are easily some of the best content I’ve experienced all year. Ghostrunner 2 is an easy GOTY contender, and I cannot wait to see what One More Level has in store for the future.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who endured the first Ghostrunner, I had hoped the sequel would address its predecessor's shortcomings. Unfortunately, Ghostrunner 2 not only retains the original's flaws but manages to surpass them.The game is undeniably longer and introduces a slew of new mechanics. However, nearly every new feature feels imperfect and cumbersome. Checkpoints are frequently unfair and oddly placed, making progression more frustrating than challenging. The platforming is clunky, and the behavior of enemies often seems random, making strategic planning a near impossibility. The motorcycle sequences, meant to add variety, can occasionally be pleasant, but the controls are buggy and junky, leading to frequent frustration.Once again, I’m left with the impression that the game wasn’t properly tested. The sheer number of issues suggests a lack of thorough quality assurance, and I have little faith that the developers will address these problems in future patches.Overall, Ghostrunner 2 is a disappointing follow-up that fails to improve on the original and instead amplifies its flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 feels weird. It's a bigger game in practically every way. Most levels are bigger, almost every level introduces some new enemy or mechanic, with some of them not appearing anywhere else, so gameplay is never stale, almost all old enemies make an appearance (the only one I can't remember coming back is the sniper) with new ones added in as well. Gameplay is as fun as its always been, with the new upgrade system being much easier to use and allowing you make Jack far stronger and faster than his GR1 iteration. And yet, despite all of that, I can't help but feel like the game is worse. I've encountered many more bugs than in the first game, it's shorter than the first one despite having bigger levels, one of which can last for nearly an hour on your first playthrough, game is also less challenging, which being one of the main selling points is certainly a questionable decision. Graphics don't feel like much of an improvement, mainly it's the character models that got the most touches, and yet the game runs worse than the original. I'm running the game on SSD and I often get stutters between combat arenas, though this seems to happen only in specific levels. The last 2 levels (not counting the very last boss one) also had some framerate issues which didn't feel justified at all.Bosses are also a mixed bag. On one hand, they're actual bosses now instead of puzzles. They have proper healthbars you can whittle down with your attacks or special abilities, and overall allow for a much more aggressive style of play. On the other hand, the first and last boss feel very similar to each other, with third boss being forgettable outside of his appearance. The only really interesting boss is the worm you fight on a bike, but that one has issues I'll explain when I get to the bike itself. Overall while bosses overall play like actual boss- now, I can't help but feel like the first game had more memorable fights even though it had less of them and they were glorified puzzles or rhythm game sections.Level design is also questionable. The first game is full of non-stop action, any time you're not fighting you're listening to the story dialogue or doing some light platforming puzzles. The second game did add many more platforming puzzles and platforming overall is a more important part of the game, with the player being forced to use their special abilities a few times instead of simply jumping around, however, there's also a lot of downtime. While levels are bigger on average, nearly half of your playtime on some of the levels will be spent simply traversing the environment or solving simple puzzles with no challenge or threat to you. Bike sections in particular suffer from this. I must say that Cybervoid is an improvement though. It flows much better and is much more varied than the cybervoid in the first game. Speaking of the bike. Its introduction is certainly impressive. You move fast, it handles very well and you can slash and fire on top of it. However, bike sections often don't communicate very well where you're supposed to go, so you might have to go  through a lot of trial and error just to memorize the correct route. Compounding the issue is the absolutely  FOV on the bike when moving upwards. Any time Jack is riding up, be it on a wall or inside the aforementioned worm boss, more than half of the screen is taken up by the bike itself. It can be hard or nearly impossible to see where you're actually going, so situations where the moment camera realigns itself you're suddenly staring at a wall or a moving obstacle are not rare at all. The game's description also boasts about "nonlinear levels with complex motorbike sections", but really, the only truly nonlinear level is the one where you're thrown in a big deserted city environment and have to go to 3 towers to activate them. Almost the entire time you're there the only threat is accidentally hitting a wall from going too fast. On my first run of this level it took me approximately 14 deaths to beat it, and that run took me nearly 40 minutes. Even if we cut out the time I spent looking for hidden collectables, which include upgrade points that you need to get new skills, I'm still confident that I wouldn't be lying if I said that half of that time, if not more, was spent on moving through empty, barren environments. That level is boring, tedious, and feels like it exists to justify the bike's existence and to boast that the game has "nonlinear levels".Platforming also feels strange. A lot of the time it felt like the game wanted me to use various techniques that aren't really taught by the game to progress, such as using the slowdown mid-air to strafe closer to my target or using dash-slide technique before jumping. Otherwise a lot of the time it felt like my character would fail to make it to the other platform or wall and would plummet to his death. Though maybe it's just me.The soundtrack is overall good, but not really much better or worse than the original.The game also introduced the "roguerunner" mode, a semi-roguelike where you go through 4 stages, each of which consists of different routes you can take, including nodes like parkour challenges, arenas, shops to get upgrades, etc. You have a limited number of lives, and if you run out of them, you lose the progress and start again with nothing carrying over. Levels aren't randomly generated, so after some time you will start seeing similar stages, but it's a fine distraction. I do hope they add the survival mode from the first game at some point (though I'd prefer it not to be part of the season pass).The story is alright, I'm not a fan of the new supporting character you spend most of the game with, and there are some weird story points that I'm unsure about , but overall story is fine for pushing the player forward. I did like it more in the first game, but neither of them is really about the story, it's just there to keep the player going.Overall I certainly do like Ghostrunner 2, it's a fun game that I will continue playing for a while trying to get better results in missions, however, it didn't leave as much of an impression on me as the first game did, and I feel like developers tried too hard to make their next game "bigger and better" and didn't quite stick the landing.

_childDocuments_.review: A bit slow and tedious in many areas compared to the first game, with fewer/simpler combat puzzles, and far fewer examples of the game mixing enemies into the linear traversal sections between arenas, from what I can remember. The pacing is especially thrown off in the exterior bike level where you're just riding through barren, post-apocalyptic hellscape for 30 minutes, but almost all the levels reflect this change to greater or lesser degrees. Compare that to the first game where each level is a tightly honed string of set-piece arenas connected with some light platforming, basic puzzles, and parkour combat. Hopefully the devs can release a new mode, as they did with the prior game, that remixes the encounters in each level to provide a more intense experience that aligns closer to what they already achieved.I also don't understand why they felt the need to change the skill and upgrade system. I thought it was perfectly elegant the way it was, where you had to balance your upgrades spatially with the tetris grid and also your upgrade complexity vs. energy regen for your skills. The rows and columns system of this game just seem like an unnecessary over-complication. Why does blink require so many button presses now? I guess the capability to precisely select enemies to target over a wide area is interesting, but it felt more intuitive when you just took out everything in a straight line in front of you in two keystrokes.I will say that there's a ton of variety in the mechanics and enemy units that you encounter, so that will mix things up when there IS something to do. That is, when you're not autopiloting through the long stretches of empty environments listening to VO.Plus, why did they feel the need to add a dialogue system to Ghostrunner? Truly baffling.Some significant performance issues, but what do you expect. Modern gaming, right? The days of getting a working product on launch day are long gone.There's still no other game quite like it, if you like the first, it's still worth checking out. Hopefully in the future it can be made better by adding more enemy encounters and hazards throughout the levels, à la Hardcore mode from 1, because the game has good bones.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Ghostrunner 1, you most likely gonna enjoy this one too. 80% of it is an improvement, another 20 could be done better.As a huge fan of the first game i really enjoyed:- visual design- level variety- increased versatility of combat and movement system - more upgrade options- new enemy types- existence of hardcore and survival mode- new challenges scattered across the levelsSomewhat undercooked, bitter-sweet additions:- open world section (a very welcomed change of scenery, but feels empty and boring at times, not enough content there)- hub area (welcomed addition as well, but too little to do there, not very engaging, feels kinda unnecessary)- bike sections (feels great when it works, but often it doesnt works that well. Problems include awkward camera positioning on sharp turns and no free camera in general, getting stuck in the most insignificant piece of rubble, disability to retrieve the bike from some places so you have to restart from checkpoint)- music is decent, but doesn't slaps as hard this time (there are couple of tracks i really liked and the rest is just okay, while each track form the first game was a banger)What i didnt like:- game pace is significantly slower and everything is easier this time around (first game was faster and harder, but had an option to slow things down for anybody desiring more casual experience. Second game offers just casual experience, with no option to crank things up for the veterans. Hardcore mode is harder, but still as slow)- amount of technical problems, which wasnt the case with Ghostrunner 1 (freezing enemies, occasional crashes, stutters, gamebreaking bug in the end of a level prevented me from finishing it, had to redo the entire level)Overall it's a good game, worths it's money. I just wish it could be even better.

_childDocuments_.review: Immensely rough around the edges, especially for the type of game that it is... but it is fun as long as you play it casually.When I finished Ghostrunner 2 I noticed I was fairly close to 100% the game's achievements, so I figured I may as well go the extra mile. That's where GR2 was at its absolute worst and the lack of polish was even more apparent than my initial playthrough. Sloppy hitboxes, various instances of awkward geometry, questionable level design, erratic enemy response time...And that's without getting into how inconsistent performance is, sometimes working *fine*, sometimes tanking to 50FPS and even below. Especially in the 2nd half of the game, where any sense of optimization is out the window.It's fine if you play the game just to finish it, but going for 100% achievements includes finishing any 5 levels (not back-to-back) without dying. Obviously, player skill plays a part in how painful (or easy) that might be, but it's far from the only factor thanks to the game's everlasting inconsistency.Sometimes you'll dash past a corner and an enemy will take a second to react and shoot, other times they'll be ready to blast you the milisecond you stick your head out. Sometimes you'll manage to connect a jump to a jump-pad just fine, other times you will randomly snap into a wallrun on said jump-pad platform instead. Sometimes you'll counter-attack a Shinobi and all will be well, other times you might randomly clip through the floor once the animation is done and fall to your death.I'm not trying to boil it down to "if you care about achievements, you'll hate this", not at all in fact. I'm just mentioning this in the context of GR2's whole goal. It's meant to be a perfectionist's wet dream, with "trial and error" being the name of the game. But the game has no business attempting to achieve that with this many quirks that constantly thwart your efforts, regardless of your skill level and quick decision making. When you overcome a tough segment in GR2, more often than not, it feels like you got lucky rather than got through it with skill, and that's a shame.That said, I still enjoyed GR2 way more than I have the first game.I thought the first game was an even bigger mess, which offered nothing but frustration. (Slipgate Ironworks's involvement is REALLY felt in that game)I had a bit of hope knowing Slipgate isn't involved in GR2, like maybe it'll have more of a chance to be a more polished game. Sadly it's still broken in a lot of similar ways, but I feel like the gameplay loop is much more refined here.Where GR1 would constantly hit the breaks on your playthrough with boring cybervoid segments, GR2 often makes those a bit more engaging by letting you platform\do combat instead of just walking\jumping basic corridors listening to exposition dump.The bike has been a pretty solid addition in my opinion, but it understandably received a mixed reception. I think the bike in itself is a fun gimmick when used right, but some of the level design really does not flatter it. In fact, the worst level in the entire game involves the bike, so that's another knock against it.A level with a huge open desert where you just meander around between 3 very distant locations in order to get through a bridge. It's butchering the pacing and is not a good time. The more linear segments with the bike are where it shines imo, when you're going full-speed and dispatching threats on the go, while periodically jumping on and off the bike, varying between ground and vehicle combat. Pretty good stuff mostly.I could give two sh**s about the story in these games, but I will say that this game's automatically better for not having the Architect, who was so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoying, a pompous snot constantly babbling god-complex nonsense in your ear as you try to get through GR1's BS levels. GR2 still has an annoying character (Kira's awful) but it's far less overbearing than GR1's dialogue, where it felt like no one would STFU for a second - which can be an issue in a game where your focus is essential.So, TLDR, Ghostrunner 2 is way more fun than the first game imo, but it is yet another game that demands perfection from the player, but rarely extends it the same courtesy. If you're a perfectionist, the game will rarely reward you for it. It has a lot of rough edges to smooth and has plenty of issues that I'm absolutely shocked are still there so long after it launched. It's jank city, but it's fun if you don't try to play into the perfectionist trap.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Don't buy the game unless you want to be heavily dissapointed.Cons:Gameplay Design Choices - The devs decided to NOT fix the bugs/physics inconsistencies from the first game, made deflect into a seperate button from attacking, downgraded tempest to not kill enemies (now its just shoving them away???), made blink into a VERY-rarely-available skill and have a weird three-step activation (instead of point-and-click, you now have to point, click, then press the skill button again), and just decided to slowed down the combat gameplay in general. New Skills Design Choice - Sure its nice to have the shurikens available for combat, but when you never know if the enemy can be killed or is only stunned, or when the enemy outright dodges them, it teaches you to not rely/use them at all due to how much it messes up your tempo when a result u dont expect happens. The other two new skills are useless in combat, and I'm not joking. The game forces you to use those skills for parkour, but are otherwise unused/unusable.Enemies - Instead of making the terrain play in your favor (as is in GR1), it now plays in the enemies favor, where they are given a wide open area to watch you dodge and squirm with amusement. Doesn't help when there are enemies that can target you with long range projectiles from across the map. Doesnt help when you no longer have blink, surge and a lethal tempest at a reliable availability.Motorcycle - The motorcycle part was the worst, if you can't make physics be consistent at a "running" speed, how on earth would a high-speed obstacle-avoiding motorcycle chase be controllable (I'm on MnK), much less enjoyable. Not to mention theres a COUPLE of levels in which you spend 90% of the time driving the motorcycle just to from point A to point B to point C to.............what happened to the game designs principles from GR1 like seriously ?Sound - Its VERY clear they reused sounds from GR1, which is not an issue given that the sound matches the object. Unfortunately thats not the case, as the beeping sound from a falling drone is used for multiple airborne enemies of various designs, which doesn't make sense for them to make that kind of noise.Music - The music used matches the gameplay: dull, tedious, and you get sick of it real quick. GR1 soundtrack is energetic and hypes u up, whereas in GR2, it becomes some sort of background noise that mildy distracts you. Boss Fights - Gone is the very precise and well-timed parrying and attacks to kill a boss (e.g. Hel, funny elevator shaft). Now its just mindless hacking with the occasional dodging. The worst part is you are supposed to be fighting other ghostrunners, which should result in fights similar to Hel's. But nope its just seldom attacks to you while you can slice them up mindlessly.Character design - GR1 made Jack into an aloof badass, Architect an arrogant but brainy and cunning villain, and Mara a compelling i-do-what-i-do-because-i-have-no-other-choice villain. GR2 made Jack into an obnoxious guy who tries too hard to be cool, introduces a quirky scientist who makes fun of Jack for not knowing pop culture references, as well as a random leader who gets killed one-third of the way into the campaign.Conclusion - Just so many design choices that goes against the combat flow made me question if this is made by another dev team. For comparison, ID Software did a terrific job making DOOM Eternal improve upon the combat system and gameplay flow from DOOM 2016, whereas GR2 somehow has a slower, clunkier gameplay than GR1. Pros:New Lore - Aside from continuing the story after GR1, you get to learn a bit of history of the world by interacting with other characters in a RPG-game way (with dialogue options and free roaming).*Update: Finished the game, utterly anti-climatic ending with the most cliche cutscene and cringe monologue.Challenges - Wide variety of challenges. You have timed parkour courses and enemy elimination, target shooting (with tempest skill), arena minigames.Conclusion - Not enough Pros to make GR2 a more fun/enjoyable/better game than GR1, but the lore kept me going.

Graphically, it's the same, the level design is slightly worse, and the soundtrack (for me the highlight of GR1) just doesn't live up to its predecessor. I didn't even mind the open-world level, but the mission hub and dialogue are just painfully boring. The upgrading/modding options are vastly uninteresting, unlike GR1, which had this fun little Tetris-like upgrading system. Jack's new abilities seem cool at first, but cycling through them takes you out of the action. Sometimes less is more.I guess pick it up if on sale or go replay GR1 instead.6/10 on it´s own4/10 considering how good GR1 is

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 has some of the best traversal mechanics I've seen in the past couple of years.  Imagine, wall running, then jumping into a rail grind, dashing to land on top of a drone to ride it down towards a fan, then deploying your wing suit, flying through gaps in walls, dashing towards another wall while freezing time, crashing through a wall, then stunning an enemy grapple hook towards them for an insta-kill all without touching the ground.  Plus there is a mother ♥♥♥♥♥♥ cyber-motorcycle mid game.  This game will have your heart pumping and you'll enter a flow state.  The story is mid, voice acting terrible, upgrade system sub-par, but the moment to moment gameplay, movement, combat all make this game soar above the rest.

A ton of new movement features have been added, and they're not bad, but the original mechanics have all been changed and it just makes it so difficult to move around, coming from 60 hours in the first game. This week has been such a letdown with releases, Cities, ASA, and now Ghostrunner 2.

_childDocuments_.review: If Ghostrunner was Hotline Miami, then Ghostrunner 2 is Hotline Miami 2. The devs did the impossible - they made a sequel that totally surprises you in how much it was able to one-up the previous game. It gives you more badass high adrenaline moments, more cool cyberpunk lore, and more gameplay mechanics, all the while staying true to what makes the franchise so fun and unique. It also continues to run very well even on older rigs and feels just as well optimised as the first game (which is really surprising when you see some of the massive set pieces this game has). It's a masterpiece and I cannot overstate how good it is.  If you loved the first game, get this sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: I really really like Ghostrunner. It has interesting map design, and complex individual bosses with unique abilities and a fairly simple but compelling enough story.Ghostrunner 2 improves upon the story, or at least the bit I played. It also has nicely varied maps.However the combat is completely different. It doesn't feel as free-form as you rely on your stamina so much and the parry mechanic is pretty much mandatory for all enemies instead of just a select few. Projectile deflect just doesn't feel as satisfying and the movement feels clunkier.In addition to this the map design (at least the earlier maps) feels awful in comparison to the first game. There's a lot more really open spaces with only a single path forwards instead of some of the different shortcuts you could do in GR1. I've only played against 2 bosses but they both felt pretty similar even though they look very different with different movesets. It was very much "look for the pattern" rather than feel the pattern/rhythm. It's hard to explain but it just didn't feel as fun to me.I'd still recommend trying it if you enjoyed the first one, but accept that it's not even close to the same game so be ready to refund it. I may come back to it some day but in the mean time I'll keep playing GR1.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is a solid game in many ways, but unfortunately, it fails to live up to its predecessor’s reputation for various reasons. The most important reason is the open world-ish maps that come with the second part of the game. It plays like the original Ghostrunner up until the level called “Licking the Wounds”, then we get a solid, adrenaline-pumping bike level that has been carefully designed around the bike, and then it takes a huge fall by introducing open world-ish levels that force you to use the bike a bit too much to get around. I can understand that they wanted to make use of the new gameplay mechanic they added, but this is not how it should’ve been handled. The huge maps are way too buggy to be enjoyed and appreciated properly; furthermore, they basically don’t work with the Ghostrunner’s gameplay style due to the fact that they completely eliminate the fast-paced gameplay and turn it into a slow, sluggish mess. Add shader completion issues that eventually lead to low performance into the mix, and we got ourselves a mess of a game. The only redeeming quality of those levels is the bike’s handling. It’s quite easy to learn and ride the thing without having to deal with the adaptation process. But wait, it’s not over. Almost after every single level, you get to this hub area where you can interact with other characters that have basically nothing useful to say. I felt like the only purpose of this addition was to completely destroy the pace of the game. If that’s the case, they succeeded. Another thing that bothered me was the constant introduction of new mechanics very late into the game and not making use of the formerly introduced mechanics properly. After the bike levels, we get huge levels that are poorly designed around the new wingsuit mechanic. Just like the bike levels, they are extremely buggy and hard to navigate most of the time; furthermore, it’s quite easy to get lost in those levels if you’re going after the collectibles. Speaking of collectibles, apart from swords, audio logs, and artifacts, we have memory shards to collect to expand the memory of GR-74 so that he can use more skills. The old, unique skill tab is gone, instead, you place them in their designated areas. They also have unique combos that give significant boosts to that specific skill, at least that’s something. There are also Ultimate skills that you can use that are very useful to deal with lots of enemies. However, Blink is part of the Ultimate skills in Ghostrunner 2 and as you can easily guess, it’s not that useful. Overlord is also an Ultimate skill, and I can say that it kind of deserves to be there with the enemy variety in this game, but considering the huge cooldown time, it’s still not worth it, unlike the rest of them. Tempest is a regular one, but it doesn’t kill enemies unless you place that specific skill that causes it to kill enemies on your skill tree. Another useful skill that I used a lot is the Shuriken one. It’s the first one you get and boy, oh boy… isn’t it extremely useful. If there’s one thing I love about Ghostrunner 2, it’s Shuriken. Here's the questionable part of the game: Its story. The first installment gave off the impression that it was going to be a one-shot game. The story basically ended with the first one, but I liked what they have come up with, nonetheless. There are some rogue GRs that formed a cult and trying to create a new race called Scions and make Dharma their new home by eliminating or enslaving the human race in the process. The main antagonist, Mitra starts out as a very interesting character who also happens to be the very first Ghostrunner, but goes into full edgy teenager mode in the end. Rahu is another interesting character that I have a feeling that will have a huge role in the upcoming game and the rest? Not that interesting or worth mentioning in my opinion. Allies are also not interesting since they are all cliché characters with cringe-worthy dialogues. The only slightly interesting ally was Adrian Bakunin. Yes, he’s alive after the incident in Project_Hel. That guy has the biggest plot armor I’ve ever seen in any game. GR-74 or Jack is still the same as we know with a lot more emotion this time around. However, the boss fights are reduced to being regular bosses that you hit until their HP depletes except for Naga which is the only boss that has unique gimmicks. They also added blocking which is an unnecessary addition since deflecting was already better for a game like Ghostrunner. Thankfully, the soundtrack is still a banger. However, they are a lot more atmospheric compared to the first one. Before I forget, Roguerunner.exe and Hardcore Mode are great gameplay modes, but Hardcore Mode makes you think outside the box a bit too much, especially in the last two levels.You may ask why I recommend this game if I mention lots of negative things about it and the reason is quite simple: It’s still a fun game despite its flaws. This is also neither a positive nor a negative review. It’s not what I expected, but it’s still a solid game. I expect Ghostrunner 3 to be closer to the first game with a lot better optimization, though. Trying to blend in RPG and open world elements where they don't belong just doesn’t work. An underwhelming and unoptimized sequel to the original Ghostrunner that fails to live up to its predecessor's reputation most of the time. The bike is a great addition, but the open world and RPG elements are not. It takes one step forward, but ten steps back. It’s still a solid game, nonetheless. Be sure to use DX11 if you want to have a smoother experience since DX12 is literally unplayable.

_childDocuments_.review: More Polish equals less polished (all respect to Polish people, though. Kurwa bober).The game is great, and I enjoyed a lot of it.However, it's way more clunky and way less charming, especially the music, which is still nice, but not as memorable as the absolute bangers from the first game.The character writing and their voice actors are both equally fantastic. Their performances, the humour and the new characters really made the story stand out and really enjoyable.Speaking of... The story is good, but again, not as striking as the story from the first game. The great aspect of this one is the expanded lore and the whole  thing. But the main plot is kinda anti-climactic and doesn't really lead anywhere. While in the first game you were discovering more about the voice in your head, who you really are, and all the stuff that's happening and has happened in the mysterious city of Dharma...Here the main plot is: "ooh, some new bad guys have come up, gotta stop their mischiefs, go go power rangers!" segway...The whole semi-open world wasteland, a.k.a. , is a wonderful addition.It really matches the classic , and now the game can appeal to both BladeRunner and MadMax fans.The motorcycle too, is a very fun addition changing the gameplay a big bit.There are also some other new things, but these two are the most recognisable, and those that really change the ever going stale gameplay, because as fun as it can be, after some time it can get very repetitive.You can clearly see that heart and soul were put into makinf this game.However, as much as I respect that, and am very pleased to see, it doesn't change its quality.The game has very mediocre overall.The most obvious signs being the animations, some models, and other graphical elements.But those don't matter to me. They are not making me rip my ass hair out, out of frustration.What is, is the nerve-cracking, sometimes barely functioning, and unbalanced gameplay and its mechanics.Some upgrades either don't do ♥♥♥♥, or they have such minimal effect it's unrecognisable (like the shield breaker or the guided stars).Some levels are horribly balanced, where the distances between objects you have to access, or the speed at which deadly elements are moving, is way out of proportion.Examples:The challenges being the biggest nuisance and the most broken and unbalanced part of the game. They're just very poorly made and not even fun to play.And most motorcycle levels, which is just constant crashing into stuff, because the map layout isn't correspondent to the motorcycle's capabilities.The frustration from playing can exponentially increase, with a computer "not powerful enough" for the game. Which is exactly my case.For the record, I still surpass the minimum requirements, and being able tu run way more complex games with way fewer struggles kind of indicates the state at which this game is.The voice lines, enemies, and sometimes the whole level itself many times load after you're already experiencing them.Which means that sometimes enemies appear randomly and kill you on the spot.I've got stuck into unloaded objects, fell through the map, and crashed way more times than I am comfortable speaking about.The endless lagging, whenever a new place loads, or some effect happens (like using your abilities or when shooting occurs) is a very detrimental disadvantage to the proclaimed "fast-paced gameplay."I'm saying proclaimed, but there are some levels that if you try to play them "fast", you'll get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the ass.The biggest downgrade has to be the enemy variations.I miss a lot all the different enemies that were in the first game.Here, the enemies are mostly the same throughout the whole game, and they just get a re-skin halfway through.There are some new enemies, of course, but very few. Other than the changing environment, the combat can become easily repetitive.As I've said before, the game is good, and I enjoyed its good parts as much as I could.However, I'll choose the first game any other day ever.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Easy recommendation. It improves on the first game in many ways, but also falls short in others.Longer explanation, I really REALLY like this game, but I don't love it like I loved the first one. It has more interesting abilities, more interesting enemies (although they are easier), and a far more ambitious story and scope. However, this leads to the feeling that it's unpolished in some areas. There's a thousand reviews that mention the "open-world" level, which let me just be clear it is not open world. Instead of just one objective at a time, there's 3 different objectives that you can do in any order but it's very contained in how you actually get there, there's only one way there and back to each objective. Now, I think that it is certainly the weakest section of the game, but I also don't think that it's inherently bad. I see people complaining that it exists at all, but I don't think having an open-world in a parkour style game is a bad idea at all, and I don't think people should write off the idea entirely. It just wasn't implemented very well and ends up being a little...boring. However, I commend the developers for trying new things, and taking the chance on some new ideas. Sometimes ideas work, and sometimes they don't. I just hope they take it as a learning experience, don't get disheartened, and approach the idea again from some new angles.I think the most frustrating part of the game is definitely bugs. Compared to the first, it feels...janky. Like sometimes I wouldn't stick to the wall when wallrunning and just fall off. Or I'd get stuck, or I'd dash in a direction and go hurtling way farther than I should have, or I'll dash in a direction and go straight up in the air for no reason. Or I would parry an enemy's attack, it would travel back and hit them and then I'd drop dead at the same time. It's just a little buggy, but it's not a AAA studio so I expect there to be a few bugs. I didn't have anything game-breaking, just annoying little things.The story is much more ambitious than the first game, and I don't know if I like it more? I like parts of it more, the characters especially are much more fleshed out than the first game, but I also feel like it was a less focused, less tight story. I think this is going to be a personal preference thing, but again, I'm glad they're trying new things.Overall the game is really very good, and if the first game was a 9/10, this one was an easy 8/10. It's a little short, I finished in only 7 hours, and I also was messing around collecting the purple memory slot things, but I would still say it's worth full price, and if you ever see it on sale absolutely buy it. If you've already beaten the first one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the few times you'll see a sequel do pretty much everything better than the original. Ghostrunner is a great game. Ghostrunner 2 is even better. I'll keep it simple: if you liked the first game, you'll love this. The mechanics are there and improved, the level design is terrific (best I've seen since Titanfall 2's campaign), the various game mechanics layer on top of one another beautifully and, by the end, it's a masterpiece. The story is good too if a bit formulaic. I enjoyed the characters, there interactions were good. A little cliche but you care about the characters enough to still be invested. The ONLY issue I had with the story was there were two specific themes they explored but didn't finish. It felt about 75% of the way there and then the story ends which makes it... a little unsatisfying. But don't let that deter you from buying the game. I'd still give it a 9/10. If the story was just a LITTLE more developed, it would have been a slam dunk 10. You'll still enjoy every minute you play this game. No doubt about it.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: I decided to try out hardcore mode, and while I stand by everything in the original review with regards to the first play-through. Hardcore mode is a lot of fun and I kind of wish it was the default. My comments on the difficulty curve and level design don't apply to hardcore mode so far.Original review:I don't love or hate this game, in some ways it is better than the first. It feels smoother for example. However, the level design and encounter design is just worse. The difficulty curve is basically flat and doesn't evolve until much later in the game when you gain a new thing that i won't spoil here.  Like, if you've played the first, you probably remember the laser tower and how fun that was to overcome. Nothing like that in this game so far (and I'm in the last level at time of writing).Yes, the open world level is a boring slog, but it is just one level that could have been split into 3.  So I think other people hark on that one too much as the stand-out example of the blasé level design. The motorcycle itself is fun to drive in the curated sections that it is in.All that said, I think the bosses are better, the writing is better, and the way it feels to play is better. So,  it's a mixed bag. Though the detracting elements mean I'll be more likely to replay the first game rather than a 2nd play of this one. If I could give a thumbs sideways I would. Decided on a thumbs up because I did enjoy most of my time with this one.P.S. if you're concerned about the temp of your GPU, turn the post processing and effects to low. They won't cause stuttering (or didn't for me), but I would watch my GPU temp yoyo in some areas until I turned those down.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner II cranks everything up to 200% and delivers an insane, adrenaline-pumping experience. The action is fast, addicting, and incredibly satisfying, with new enemy types and traversal mechanics keeping things fresh. The movement and environmental navigation are key, rewarding players with fast reflexes and the patience to master the levels. The game’s about 12 hours long—way longer than the original—and absolutely packed with intense set pieces.The story is solid enough to keep you engaged, and the open-world segments offer a nice breather between the action. The dark synthwave soundtrack is pure perfection and makes you feel like a total badass. If you're a fan of the first game or just love cyberpunk madness, this is a must-play. I’m already hyped for a third game!

_childDocuments_.review: What I do like:New enemies, new movement options / more complicated platforming, motorbike levels, new parry animations, more path choices through enemy groups, better boss design and more bosses, the new visual style is shockingly beautiful, soundtrack is as amazing as the first gamesWhat I don't like:Significantly easier than the first game (similar feel to the hel dlc of gr1)New open world concepts and rpg style character dialogue was introduced to have a more story focused approach but it breaks up the missions rather than continuous punishment, I liked the continuous punishment, the home base/ story parts could have been removed entirely and I wouldn't care, but it makes the game more accessible so hopefully more people play because this game and the last deserves more praise and attention.Ultrawide and dualsense controller both fully supported. _childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is an adrenaline-fueled, cyberpunk action game with intense gameplay, stunning visuals, a okay story, and immersive sound design. _childDocuments_.review: i really, really, really love the ghostrunner franchiseand that's exactly why i'm having such a tough time recommending this gamedon't get me wrong, i had a blast playing this game- there was a somewhat interesting story, slightly worse than that of GR1, but enjoyable nonetheless- i particularly enjoyed being able to learn more about the lore of the Ghostrunner worldthe game doesn't fail at providing difficult challenges that go beyond simply completing the levels- the motorcycles, although feeling a bit janky at times, make a great adition to this game of fast and violent traversal/slaughter- the permanent addition of shurikens (among other things) to your skillset was a great ideaif you liked GR1, you will probably enjoy this game as well!HOWEVER- as already mentioned, the motorcycle levels can feel quite janky at times and in addition to that, some of them don't even really feel like ghostrunner levels, and moreso like levels out of an unrelated racing game- a lot of the enemies already move around a lot from the start, which chips away a little at providing a flowstate sometimes- the upgrade system is far worse and far more bland and uninteresting than the upgrade system of GR1, especially because some upgrades are locked behind going the extra mile. if you want the full roster of all upgrades, simply progressing through the game is not enough. in most other games this would not be an issue, but in this instance it takes away some of your versatility which might be required if you're stuck in a section- there are some attempts here and there at open world sections which are simply put terrible- the boss fights measure in no way, shape or form up to the bossfights of GR1all in all, i was very torn right after i completed this gameafter a few days of sitting with the experience i had:if you liked GR1 and want more, then buy this game, you will most likely enjoy itthis is definitely a step-down from the first game, but only because the first game set the bar so incredibly highi'm excited to see what the developers do next

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start this review by asking 2 very important questions:Did Ghostrunner 2 really need to exist? Did it add anything worthwhile to the franchise to justify its existence? Unfortunately, the answer is "No" to both those questions..I'll be honest with you, by the time i started playing GR2 i didn't remember the first game all that well, except that i loved the graphics and aesthetics of it, and although it was hard, it was still fun to experience. I don't ever remember disliking it and wanting it to just end halfway through, something i can't say about this sequel sadly..I don't really want this to balloon into something too big so i'll try to list the things i disliked briefly:- The graphics seem worse somehow, the NPCs look so dated, some of the levels outside the tower don't look that good either (the city still looks good though).- The cutscenes (if you can even call them that) aren't great with 2 exceptions, the GR1 recap & the ending cutscene (i honestly don't remember if there was another animated one at the beginning, so maybe 3?), i would've liked to see a lot more cutscenes of that style even if the story isn't the main focus of this game.- Traversal & parkouring is much worse in this game compared to the first one, it's much jankier, and with some very few but super annoying parts with major difficulty spikes sprinkled between long stretches of easy/meh sections, so even though those super difficult parts are rare, they more than stand out compared to the rest of the game (i feel like more than 80% of my deaths were due to the janky traversal instead of the 1 hit kill enemies which doesn't sound right).- The bike sections add nothing to the game, and don't even feel good to drive, feels more like something that was quickly tacked in to try to justify making a sequel.- The hub is so boring and adds nothing of value to the game, i'm someone who tries to exhaust all dialogue options with all NPCs i encounter in games to try to experience as much of the story & lore as i can, but gosh darn if they didn't bore me out of my mind in this game, they look so bad, there are no decent animations or cutscenes for them to make them remotely interesting, the dialogue itself is super meh and the hub overall grinds the flow to a halt, now that i finished it i wish i just skipped 90% of NPCs dialogue and just went straight back to the action ASAP.- Way buggier than the first game, i got stuck in the floor multiple times, sometimes enemies refuse to spawn so you're stuck unless you restart (thankfully you only have to restart to your last checkpoint instead of restarting the whole level), the game also completely froze for me at least once when i tried to switch skins late in the game, and more annoyingly it refused to save my remapped keys & kept reverting back to default each time i closed it..also the audio for one of the ultimate abilities (Flux) kept randomly glitching & playing non stop driving me insane unless i restarted my checkpoint (btw, restarts count as deaths in the game), i probably encountered even more little bugs & glitches but this is all i can remember off the top of my head.I just want to point out that even though it may seem like i hate this game i really don't, i did enjoy some parts of it, the story was meh but it did pick up a bit by the end, the city still looked beautiful & was cool to experience (i'm a sucker for cyberpunk futuristic aesthetics), and the game still knows how to make you feel like a badass when it wants to.But that doesn't change the fact that it pales in comparison to the first GR in almost every single aspect & even goes as far as making many parts worse instead of building on them & improving them, making you question why did they even bother making it in the first place, and for that i really can't recommend it to anyone except on a deep deep sale.Such a shame..

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner (1) sweat here, 3 hours into GR2. At first the gameplay felt a little off, like I was missing a limb. SDSJ's don't seem to work so well anymore, or maybe the timing has changed and I'm slow to adjust. Otherwise, the movement is just as fun, even better in some aspects. I like the new upgrade system (and the new upgrades) more than the last game and the BOSSES... the devs have massively outdone themselves. GR1's bosses were extremely mediocre but the second GR2 boss is already one of my favourites of all time (not difficult from a gameplay perspective but incredibly visually appealing)The characters have certainly improved over GR1, now with physical presences in between levels rather than being disembodied voices. The dialogue in the Hub is a bit awkward with pauses between sets of lines, but this will likely be polished up in the future and it's still engaging for now. The dialogue in mission is pretty funny, I'm enjoying it so far.I really like the setting and background of Ghostrunner. It's rare for me to be absorbed into lore but GR2's story so far is quite interesting.Also, the soundtrack slaps on GR2. The tracks in the previous game weren't very memorable, but they were good and I did keep them on over playing my own music. However, I can see myself listening to this OST outside of the game.Overall and thus far, GR2 improves on its' predecessor (which was already a favourite of mine) in every single way. I waited for a sale to buy it because I'm broke but if you can afford it, support the devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Ghostrunner 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the only game I have preordered in my life, and I'm glad I did, because it is amazing. Ghostrunner 2 improves on just about every issue that the first game suffered from. The combat flows extremely well and the new ultimate abilities are amazing. New sword inspect animations are incredible, and the boss system is much better.In the previous game, boss fights were just about dodging or parrying the attacks and then slashing them when they're vulnerable. GR2 doesn't do that, and instead opts for a proper damage system, constantly striking your opponent while dodging their attacks. The levels flow very well, and the perfect parry takedowns are a little janky but still pretty cool. There's also a sort of home base that you can explore and interact with in between missions, talking to characters in the game, upgrading your skills, ect.There's a bunch of new skills to experiment with and have fun with. The game looks graphically amazing as well. The cutscenes feel much better compared to GR1, although the facial expressions of some characters in game feel kind of lifeless and they just stare into your soul while talking to you, but other than that they're great.And there's also the bike levels and the levels are kind of more open rather than directed. I won't spoil anything but I will say that the bike is a blast to use and is probably the most fun I've had in a game for a long time.Yes, the game is difficult, just like the first one. There is no denying that. One hit and you restart at the last checkpoint. (there's alot of those thankfully) But if you can get the flow and movement down and learn to use your abilities in unison, Ghostrunner 2 is so much fun, and considering that most AAA games are $80+ these days, this game is definitely worth the price
_childDocuments_.name: Ghostrunner 2

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is a fantastic sequel, it may fall short in some areas but overall this was a fantastic game to play and I loved almost every second of it.Ghostrunner is a hardcore first person, action platformer in which you use your ninja abilities to navigate treacherous obstacles and take down deadly foes all within a cyperpunk setting, you die in one hit but so do your enemies and you respawn right back in the action. Basically take mirrors edge, titanfall hotline miami, cyberpunk and your choice of cyber ninja protagonist, throw them into a blender and you get ghostrunner.I think this is an easy recommendation and would say to definitely play both if you haven't already, whilst this sequel is good it does seem to require knowledge of the previous game and I also found some of the new additions to miss the mark a bit. Let's quickly mention those negatives I find the game to be much slower than the first, it almost feels a little sluggish in comparison but it's ok when you get used to the change.Story is a massive focus this time around, often diverting you into a hub environment, like you can skip these if you wish but I found this change to be a bit confusing. The first game had a decent story but you could ignore it if you wanted and focus on the game, not so much this time.The upgrade system isn't as good, I prefer the original.This is a big one for me, the ost didn't slap as hard as ghostrunner 1, I often revisit that soundtrack but ghostrunner 2 didn't leave as much of an impression on me. Now with that said I want to say that this is still an amazing game, the set pieces are incredible with one of my favourite moments in a game this year coming from this game.The motorbike is an incredible addition and I hope we see this in future games.And the experimental open world areas are decent! I was worried these would be really bad but they managed to pull it off.Overall an amazing game that doesn't quite hit the highs of the first game but still manages to be an incredible experience.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the difficulty of ghostrunner 1 you wont really like this game. Its very easy compared to the first one. The level design feels also weird. Ghostrunner 2 feels like they crafted levels and then randomly slapped enemies in there, there isnt really a flow you get. Also theres a lot more mechanics but the game fails to make them work together nice. Its always now you use the shurrriken, now the push, theres never any combinations or like difficult. The skill overhaul feels also worse compared to the old game. Theres much more what i dislike about the game but mainly its the boring bossfights, lack of difficulty, poor level design, skill system, and the weird open world. It just doesnt feel like this fast paced, diffucult, ninja game.
