_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2: Fast, Fun, Frustrating at Times ⚡️Just sliced my way through Ghostrunner 2, and here's the rundown:Super Speedy Ninja Action: You're a cyber ninja who dies in one hit, just like the first game. Parkour, wall run, slash enemies in half – it's all about lightning-fast reflexes and stylish moves.New Tricks Up Your Sleeve: Motorcycle sections! More gadgets and abilities to play with! The core gameplay is familiar but feels even more exciting this time around.Beautiful Neon World: The world is gorgeous, all neon lights and dark alleys. It's a cool backdrop for all the slicing and dicing.Died a Lot (But Kept Coming Back!): This game is HARD. You will die. A lot. But the restarts are super fast, so you can just jump right back in and try again. (Unless you get super frustrated!)Open World? Not Quite: While there's more exploration than the first game, it's not a wide-open world. Still lots of cool levels to conquer though.Overall:Ghostrunner 2 is a blast for fans of the first game and anyone who loves a fast-paced challenge. Just be prepared to die a bunch (and maybe rage quit a few times). But if you can master the flow of combat, it's a super rewarding experience.   (Thumbs up, thumbs down to represent the love/hate relationship some might have with the difficulty)

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 1 was probably one of my favorite games when I played it. It was a phenomal, difficult, and rewarding game to get skilled at. I have beaten most of the ghostrunner 1 levels with zero deaths, unlocked every collectible, and unlocked every achievement (prior to the release of Project: HEL), and own every cosmetic DLC.My main gripes with Ghostrunner 2 are as follows:The new "block" mechanic is not fun or rewarding. Ghostrunner 1 felt like a puzzle game where you had to find a good route to approach certain enemies or get skilled at parrying. Ghostrunner 2 contrives this by giving players a sort of get-out-of-jail free card in the form of the blocking mechanic.I VERY strongly dislike how the characters in this game interact, most notably their use of modern slang. Zoe and Bakunin are the only characters who seem even remotely serious about anything happening in the plot; Kira, Connor, and even Jack seem detached and have been infected with Marvel level quips and quotations. Slang and 21st century concepts like cosplaying, larping (the characters in the game actually say "larp"), the use of the phrase "bet" and other examples really pull me out of the game; this isn't 2020, it's the far future with cyborgs and a desolate earth. It would be nice if the characters felt like they were actually invested in the life-or-death circumstance they are in and if the dialog didn't feel like it was a fan fiction from a 17 year old set in the Ghostrunner universe.I also feel like the pace at which upgrades are presented to the player is a bit too rapid, and the medium through which they are given isn't satisfying. In GR1, you had to earn them by completing certain parts of the game, and often by completing Cybervoid puzzles (if I recall correctly, I could be wrong). In GR2 most of these abilities are just given to the player, which makes it feel a little less like you earned it and more like someone gave it to you.I'm still playing the game (haven't finished my first run yet) but these are my gripes so far.All of that being said, the combat is fun and the music still bangs. I'd buy it, just expect to cringe at the dialog.

_childDocuments_.review: Blood is dripping down from my energy sword. I see the head of my last enemy still rolling towards a trashheap. I continue to walk forward and don't even turn my head to see the headless torso lying in a pool of blood in the wet street.You are a killing machine. You slice through your enemies and cut them in two pieces. You run along walls, slide, dash through the air and change your direction in mid-air. Hack and slash + parcour running, that's what you were born for. To speed up a bit, you can also ride a bike while using your sword. Absolutely insane.Worked fine with my XBox controller in ultra-wide resolution (21:9). Compiling the shaders took a few seconds. I use the beating soundtrack now while I run in the morning.Is this game a masterpiece? Yes, this is pure adrenaline.Crazy-fast, bloody hack'n'slash orgy in a cyberpunk city.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played the first game, I think there was significant improvement with this sequel despite what some others may think as you can see with other reviews. This review may contain minor spoilers, just depends upon how I type it all up.The most notable thing in my eyes was a greater focus on the game's narrative. Of which I think was an excellent way to go, as it got me much more invested into it.The core gameplay that made the first so great did not feel too changed apart from blocking (that I hardly used) but instead felt more refined and less janky.The SFX team did an excellent job again with satisfying auditory responses to massacring rooms.The soundtrack felt much better to me, leaning further into darker industrial and symphonic tones with some tracks, especially "God Run" and the suite of themes made by We Are Magonia. Despite this each track still feels true to delivering kickass cyberpunk dubstep that you can't not feel.As for graphics, they do have a far higher window compared to the first and feel like they have impressive optimization, much like the first. Even if you are running an older system it will still look incredible and very much stunning on even the lower settings. This allows you to enjoy smooth gameplay and have gorgeous views no matter the kind of system you may have.The focus on bosses that were less platformers and more so actual fights like HEL from the first was an excellent choice. To the point where within these fights both integrate into one with you platforming cinematic attacks and then going in and having an epic sword fight with parries and slashing.The game also felt like it featured a wider variety of atmospheres, of course provided partially by the portion where you exit the tower. Despite that the interior felt different between each level; sometimes more dramatically than others.Overall, just a masterpiece I would have loved to experienced again 10/10 would save Dharma...again.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like a welcomed evolution to the original ghostrunner. Parkour is less speed/twitchy and you are rewarded for taking time to breathe and enjoy the sights. This isn't so much a complaint just as a statement of facts. If you try this game and feel its too easy, play the first one. If the first one got too hard for you, you'll probably do better here. I'm not interested in games that are hard for the sake of it, so the difficulty spikes in these titles tend to feel good and challenging overall.edit: having finished the game I think i can say the parkour is a little tighter in the first game and the extra abilities in this one feel maybe like a little too many.. but man.. the story here is great. _childDocuments_.review: A solid sequel with some flaws.If you have played Ghostrunner and don't want more of that, this isn't for you. This game iterates on the first, but it does not get too adventurous with that iterating.Some of my personal pain points in the first game were addressed in this one:- The Uplink system has been replaced, so you don't have quite so many timing sensitive checkpoints anymore.- The upgrade system is no longer a puzzle. The new system still makes you weigh your options and try out different combinations, but you no longer have the interface hassle of the puzzle system on top of that. Overall a great improvement- The cybervoid sections are now more in line with the real world levels instead of slow puzzles.I would also say that the level design has improved over Ghostrunner 1, with some experimentation on non-linear levels that work quite well. But for me the bike section of the game was a bit too drawn out. The first bike level is awesome, but after that it gets a little stale as driving isn't particularly engaging for the most part. I respect that they tried this to mix up the formula, but 3 levels instead of 5 would have probably been a better choice. Either that or give the bike sections a bit more love playtest cycles.Also like that we get to interact with the NPC cast a lot more. The writing also improved in that regard over the first game.In terms of stability, I had some issues with enemies sometimes spawning inside the ground, which  can make for some tricky situations, but aside from that I had no issues running the game in DX11 mode on Proton.The only thing that really frustrates me as I'm trying to 100% is that some of the checkpoints put you in a spot where you can immediately die again if you reflexively hold forward as you respawn. Oh and also some of the enemy positioning is unfair in my opinion. You open a door and if you forget that an enemy is right there aiming at the door, you will probably die.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to call this "recommended" because I do think it is a decent game and I did enjoy it (hence why I not only finished the campaign but also spent the time to get all the achievements), but that recommendation comes with a lot of caveats. Performance - Playing through the campaign was mostly fine other than a couple of brief single-digit-fps moments out of nowhere. Playing the rogue-lite mini-game was infuriating with so many slideshow moments or just completely freezing for a few seconds (all the more noticeable in a mode where lives matter).Bugs - The enemies would jitter around objects, or just get completely stuck in terrain. The grapple-hook was not reliable, and I would often not go anywhere if I so much as stubbed my toe on a pebble. Towards the later part of my playthrough I frequently found myself sliding forward even when not pressing any keys (a hazard when waiting for a platform to materialise). And when replaying levels for achievements I sometimes found enemies would not spawn, blocking progress.A greater focus on story - I would consider this as a negative, because to me it just feels like the wrong kind of game to be standing around having a chat with your allies. Larger but emptier levels - This was very clear in one of the later levels where you have a motorbike. I imagined the motorbike levels to be high-speed chase kind of sequences with lots of obstacles and needing to pull all sorts of stunts to get by. There were a couple of sequences that lived up to that, but far too much time on the bike was simply following roads with minimal obstacles. The game then gave a massive open area with collectables to find, and yet the location was drab and empty, and there was no fun gameplay in driving around looking for them. But even the levels on foot felt like they were lacking something, even just some background decorations to give the locations more life. Too many interruptions to the flow - What I enjoyed most from the first game was that sense of flow as you chain together abilities to pull off amazing stunts. Somehow I didn't get as much of a sense of that here. The path didn't always seem as clear, or platforming sections wouldn't last as long as I'd expect. Then there would be a minor puzzle to find a switch or push a block. Or I'd have multiple objectives in different directions. All of that would have been fine in small amounts, but ultimately I started to miss the more linear focus of the first game. They even put extra challenges in the levels themselves (races, timed kill challenges, that sort of thing) which not only broke the flow of the level you were on, but also seemed out of place because if you wanted to retry them, you had to replay the entire level up to that point. Easier than the first game - Now this could be a positive or a negative depending on my mood. I certainly didn't die anywhere near as often as I did in the first game. The addition of the block in combat really simplified dealing with many enemies. It is something of a relief to not have a 100+ death count on some levels (I may not be very good at these games!), but at the same time I am left feeling there was a lack of challenge to the game by the end, for both combat and platforming actually. There is hardcore mode of course that I didn't try, but given my other issues with the game, I think I'm good, thanks. I know that is a long list of negatives, but to counter that: you are a cybernetic ninja that can wall-run, dash through the air and insta-kill someone with one swipe of your sword. At that most basic level, this game is still immensely satisfying to play. Also I love the music! TL;DR: If you enjoyed Ghostrunner 1 and want more, and don't mind a less-good version of the game, this is worth a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing through both the Ghostrunner games I'd consider this game as a worthy sequel to the first one. It's a game that sacrifices some of the more hardcore elements of the first game for a more fun experience while still retaining the challenge of the first game. Below I've written what i find is the good, bad and ugly of Ghostrunner 2. The Good:- Just like GR1, the mix of parkour and combat feels really good.- The game adds new mechanics such as blocking (which is a little too forgiving, maybe it should eat up more stamina) and my favorite, the wingsuit.- The story is just as great as the first game, I know some people don't care about the people in the hub but I personally enjoyed it. I felt that the characters gave more depth to the setting and insight to what the world looks like from multiple perspectives. - Just like the first game, the level design is (for the most part) really good. Even the linear bike levels are decent, unlike the open world one...- The sequel also fixes some of the gripes I had with the first game. One of which was the akward timing in order to parry a melee attack in the first game. Here it actually feels responsive and in sync with the enemies attack.- The bossfights are far better than the first game. In GR2 it actually feels like you are fighting a boss instead of dodging their attacks for an eternity until the game says that you win. - One of my favorite aspects of the game is the how alive the game feels when it comes to characters. Everyone has their own personality and you can really see this in what they say and how they talk. The dialog between the characters are coherent and make sence and are even funny sometimes. By far my favorite is the chit-chat between the two guards at the hub area. There's even dialog between Jack and some of the characters when you go around and find secrets. The Bad:- As I said earlier, most of the levels are good. However, when it's bad it's really bad. And yes I am talking about the open world bike level... I've got a lot of gripes for this map. Not only is it the only map that looks weird and really unpolished but the map is littered with random tiny rocks that completely kill your momentum. And if that isn't frustrating enough the map also makes no sense to navigate. There aren't any signs that tell you were to go apart from the 3 dots on your hud, which don't help.- The bike isn't great either since it's handling feels really weird. Whenever you move slow you can turn around but whenever you cross a fixed speed threshold it abruptly lowers your turn speed. This feels really akward and clunky. A better system would've been if the bike could adjust its turn speed relative to your speed instead of whatever the current system is. - Just like the first game, the grapple feels too stiff. Whenever you grapple on to a point you move in a completely straight line height-wise. You don't have a slight arc towards the point which would help it feel more natural. You do atleast have the ability to move perpendicular to the vertical axis. The Ugly:- Your keybinds . I've tried everything and found no solution. _childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is definitely a well deserved sequel. You can tell the development team put a lot of care into designing the feature's. There isn't a big gap between the tools and abilities that you learned from the first game put into this game. Most of the abilities you learned from the first game are unlocked in the first level. This help paved the way to have "Jack" learn more abilities throughout the game. If you are looking for a story driven, SUPER HOT, runner type game this would be a definite buy. It is even a plus that the game isn't priced at 59.99 or even 69.99 as most games are nowadays. There are some negative's that do need to be talked about but they may be ironed out over the games lifetime. At the moment of me writing this review, I have 100%'ed the story and achievements. There were some things that I experienced over the course of the game that weren't joyful. When you unlock the motorcycle parts of the game, I would occasionally hit random bumps on the road where there was nothing at instantly explode. Other times my motorcycle would spawn in weird positions if it had to be respawned. On the later levels, I experienced a lot of frame rate drops to the point that it made the game unplayable unless I somehow made it passed a certain area or restarted the game. My setup currently is running a 4080 so frame rates below 10 aren't expected. Especially that the next feature, RTX, seems to be missing from the game. It seems that Ray Tracing was removed from the release of the game because it was buggy and would cause people to crash. Finally, the Wing suit was a cool addition to the final stages of the game but it seems like the map wasn't properly finished or created for those levels. I was able to go around many corners accidently skipping the main path and skipping ahead in the story in certain areas. Overall, this game is definitely a must buy. The Indie developers have done it extremely well and are always taking feedback from their community to make it better. Ghostrunner 2 also is much easier compared to the first game if anyone stayed away from the games because it was too difficult. The base game takes a little longer than the base game of Ghostrunner 1 + its DLC. I am really looking forward to see what the future holds for Ghostunner 2 and possibly a Ghostunner 3 coming down the line.

_childDocuments_.review: A disappointing sequel to one of the greatest Hotline Miami successors out there.Ghostrunner 2 aimed to go bigger and jump higher, that much is clear. What's missing, however, is the initial sharpness of the formula that made the original click in the first place. It was tight and snappy, calibrated to strike right at the target, one adrenaline shot after the other.Now, with vast levels, complicated enemy patterns, dozens of situational skills, perfunctory puzzles, and story beats that break the momentum, it's as if Ghostrunner no longer wants to be Ghostrunner. It strives to be many things at once, from Turbo Overkill and DOOM Eternal to even Half-Life 2 at times — which are all great comparisons really, just not for this game. A lot of new ideas simply don't go well with the core "live fast, act now, die, repeat" concept, eventually diluting it so much it gets annoying. And when replaying a fight feels like going through motions, you know something is very, very wrong.There are some redeeming qualities, sure. The overall presentation is pretty solid (apart from some wonky-looking NPCs), fundamental combat and traversal mechanics can be fun in the more concise encounters, and the bike is the single best addition to the mix. So good, in fact, that it managed to make the worst level in the game somewhat enjoyable. Yeah, keep the bike, it's cool.Still, I can't remember the last time a short adventure like that was such a chore. Ghostrunner 2 did scratch that very specific cybersamurai itch for a bit, but if I knew what it had in store for me, I would have replayed the first game instead.

GR2 seems to throw all these aspects out of the window and double down on the weakest parts of GR1: the dialogue, story and cutscenes. It also has very buggy enemies and gimmicky levels.I really wanted to make a list right after a session of GR2, so here is the stuff I found disappointing:-Crashes-combat is more dependent on juggling abilities compared to the more streamlined system in GR1.-timed jumps/parkour, not very skill expressive and destroys the flow of movement.-less freedom of movement compared to the earlier title (many walls that you can't wallrun anymore).-way buggier than GR1.-Long cutscenes and cringeworthy dialogue disrupting gameplay.-The hub world being completely useless timewaster. -The music is very bad compared to the earlier title.-Worse layouts on the combat arenas.-Cookiecutter story-Makes me want to play GR1It baffles me how the fanbase literally told them why they love and play the game, and then the devs just ignore it, or worse yet, try to improve it by throwing ♥♥♥♥ at the wall and seeing what sticks. There is a lot of useless fluff in this game, they added fat into an already lean and working system.TLDR: Buy GR1, if you are a fan of GR1, go play GR1 again. This will not be a step up or more of the same. I got it for 7€ and idk if it was worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: The fluidity of the gameplay in Ghost Runner I was one of its standout features. The parkour system, characterized by swift movements and precise controls, The sense of speed is palpable, and the combination of wall-running, dashing, and slicing through enemies creates a rhythm that’s both thrilling and addictive. While Ghost Runner I excels in its narrative depth and fluid game play, Ghost Runner II takes a completely different approach with narrative and gameplay mechanics. the addition of a bike introduces a significant change to the gameplay, adding a new layer of mobility and exploration. While this new mechanic offers fresh opportunities for high-speed traversal and combat, it also highlights the game’s technical shortcomings. Once you step outside the confines of the Dharma Tower, the lack of polish becomes more apparent. The bike mechanics, while promising, sometimes feel clunky, and the open-world areas can reveal inconsistent performance, visual issues and glitches that detract from the overall immersion.Additionally, one significant drawback is the limited key binding options. Despite the game’s release two years ago (23-26-OCT), players are still restricted to rebinding only the WASD keys, although you can rebind all the keys but the game won’t save it….So on each reboot you have to do that again, which can be a major inconvenience for those who prefer or require alternative control schemes. This oversight suggests a lack of attention to player customization and accessibility.The game also suffers from inconsistent frame rates and occasional bugs that disrupt the otherwise smooth experience. There are also moments where the game's design choices such as level layouts or enemy placement can cross the line from challenging to frustrating. The difference between difficulty and annoyance becomes clear when these design elements impede progress rather than enhancing the challenge. Despite these issues, Ghost Runner II remains an exhilarating ride. Its fast-paced action and innovative mechanics have a lot of potential, but the game’s lack of polish and technical flaws are hard to ignore. If you’re willing to overlook these imperfections, there’s a lot of high-speed fun to be had.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghost Runner 2 is the prime example for why it is important to be aware of ‘less is more’. Game Developers creating sequels usually fall for the same trap of quantity over quality. It’s no surprise that once the baseline of the game is created, the developer would then expand vastly different mechanics into the game. This decision design, however, ended becoming more detrimental to the core fundamentals of the game, and instead, alienates what made the original GR1 great.I don’t think I will be finishing the game for this review. In the future I might revisit, and it is a possibility that I would change my mind, but upon other users’ sentiments, the consensus appears to the same. The flow of the game is stalled through more than many cringe cut scenes, lore, chat bubble world hub, item pickups, and mixed level designs.The interesting narrative for GR1 is left soulless in GR2. Many conversations during within the game do not feel engaging in anyway, and also clutters the screen.The level design is hit or miss. There are parts of the game where there was absolutely no music playing. There appears to be more invisible walls and lack of exploration outside bounds. I also absolutely hate the amount of yellow coated paint to indicate where the player should go… I blame Resident Evil 4 Remake for my hatred. Transition from level to level has taken a hit with the world hub.There’s more I could go on about, but with only few hours on this game, it’s whatever. I always have GR1 to fall back to.I can’t wait for GR3 RPG UBISOFT EDITION.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR - An imperfect but solid successor to the first game, 7/10. For context, I'm on an RTX 2080 Super with a Ryzen 7 3700x.If you enjoyed the first game and are looking for more, I'd recommend this one. _childDocuments_.review: I'm straight up not having a good time. I didn't much care for the first one (even though I finished it), but I figured the Humble Choice ought to have me try this one at least for a bit. Who knows, maybe they nailed it?For my money, the only right decision they made was (if I recall correctly) some of the upgrades from the first game come default now. Not many, but a few.What irks me about this game really comes down to the combat design, and a lack of any sort of meaningful freedom in non-combat level traversal. Let's start with that.Just like with the first game, going through the non-combat sections of the level feels less like freedom of parkour, and more like an elaborate QTE where your direction never really changes and failing the right prompt or seeing the right approach on time in mid-air sends you back to the checkpoint. It leads to a situation where you repeatedly die from the more complex traversal course until you've memorized what needs doing.Sadly the game failed to learn from Super Meat Boy, and makes deaths take a second to show the death screen and a button press to retry. On a game where you die in one hit anyway, restarting from death should be quick and snappy and not require any input. You die, one second of splatter against the sawblades, and go, right back into it. Don't give me time to be angry.The combat's another, different problem. When your method of combat exists purely of dash+slowmo, block, and slash, the button layout should embrace simplicity. If I can think of doing it, the game should've already done it. Furthermore, for a parkour-centric combat game, the speed and range of things still feels lacking. Let's elaborate on what I mean by that.First up, speed and range. You're a cyberninjawhatchamacallit, yet your movement speed doesn't even come near that of a satisfying boomshoot. Why? You're meant to be a menace on the battlefield, . The average speed feels like that of a sprint in a CoD game. That won't do, not for this sort of game. Take a look at Sprawl, now that's how you do speed at this kind of stuff, even without that game's guns, AND simplicity.Speaking of which, simplicity. You have Attack, Block, Dash, Grapple Hook, Crouch, Activate Skill and Ultimate. None of these flow into eachother. Other games, like the excellent Revengeance, has you auto-block bullets when you sprint.Let's do some backseat devving and fix this, eh? Why not, I feel like enjoying my review for once.I don't much care how serious these suggestions are being taken, by anyone, really. I just felt like writing them.Also, honestly? 70GB to install? The dialog isn't that good to have this much of it. Why bother having the open-world esque conversations with topic discussions? At least the first one just told you what you needed to know during gameplay and that was it. Now there's a handful of people to talk to at base and what they're talking about just feels like... fluff. Fluff that can't be compressed well so it takes up more installation space.This game doesn't feel good. In fact, Ghostrunner never felt good, but I still bothered to finish the first one. Then I find a challenge that rewards a watchamallit to expand your Motherboard if you achieve Silver on it. The task is to hit all targets with shuriken within a time. This is where a lack of auto-aim on shuriken started to really hurt, and I felt like I was never going to have a good time with it.Maybe it's because I'm using a controller, maybe it'd be a bit better with kbm, but if I'm going to play with kbm I've got better games to sprain my wrist on.The Ghostrunners need to be ran through proper Q&A. Simplify its design to enable the sense of powerfantasy it seems to want you to have. Have its systems interconnect in favor of the player. Right now though, hard no. No surprise it sat on a Humble Choice.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 1 but betterSure, the game is easier but I think the overwhelming difficulty of GR1 was a downside at times, obviously GR2 could use a higher difficulty mode but I think making GR2 more accessible was a good thingThe game I think is a bit platforming heavy and carpal-tunnel inducing on the "oh you just unlocked this new ability lets use it 50 times the rest of this level!" sorta deal, but the combat is still excellent. _childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is the definition of what a sequel should be. It improves upon all the tenants the first game set up and expands the world and gameplay in ways even fans weren't expecting.Visuals in this games are a subtly better than the first intallment but unfortunatelly there is no ray tracing support at the time of writing, with promises of full support in the near future. The game already looks good without it, it can only improve with its addition.Sound and music go harder than the original in almost every level, there are some supreme bangers in this game save for 1 or 2 stages you will be adding almost all of them to your music playlist no doubt.The gameplay includes everything you already knew from rail grinding and wall running to dashes and slowmo but it also adds new trinkets such as a gliding suit, ways to create new jumping points for your gap jammer and much more.There is also the element of story here which is greatly expanded. Characters are given time to breath and show their own personalities but this not being the focus of the game or having enough budget to allow for true engagement, you will find yourself yearning for the next "standard" level pretty quickly. Fortunately these stage are as short as can be so they function more like little add-ons rather than anything else.9/10. Great enough to stand up on its own against behemoths like Zelda and Spider-man at the game awards.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is a great action game but it has very little in common with the first game. It's more open, lacks structure, doesn't care about enemy placement or patterns and most of all prioritizes accessibility above improvement. If that's what you wanted, great, but it was already available in the first game through assist mode. Now it's forced on everyone with projectiles being slower, enemies being less accurate and enemy attacks being smaller and easier to dodge. It takes away from what made the first game fantastic.I have replayed all levels of the first Ghostrunner multiple times on both regular and hardcore to improve my time, have fewer deaths or find all collectibles. While I enjoyed my playthrough of Ghostrunner 2 I find very little reason to go back to any specific level. Partly because there is no feeling of identifying patterns and improving your run, partly because of the size of the levels. While most levels in the first game were 15-20 minutes, many here are much longer with some reaching an hour to play through. It feels bloated. As does the pointless mission hub world and the open bike levels that no one asked for.Lastly I have to question what One More Level did on a technical level. The game looks significantly worse than the first game at a much higher hardware cost. A clean, almost cartoony design replaces the grimy neon cyberpunk from the first game  and many levels suffer from consistent frame drops in the exact same area regardless of settings or resolution. Going back to the first Ghostrunner after playing Ghostrunner 2 feels like going to the future on a technical level.With that said, I still recommend Ghostrunner 2. The story is interesting, the movement is more smooth overall. The abilities bring some variation to the fighting and the Cybervoid levels are actually fun this time around. If I didn't expect a game like the first Ghostrunner I would probably find this an amazing action game and one of the better ones this year, it's just very different from what I loved about the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good continuation of the first game, GR2 picks up where the 1st left off in the story in a seamless way.Pros:The platforming and combat are just as good, with the former outshining the first in creativity and depth.The platforming segments will introduce a mechanic, such as a simple rotating door you can stop from a distance, and then quickly add on to the door with previously learned parkour mechanics, which causes the player to quickly learn how to adjust to the new door mechanic and use it in conjunction with other mechanics. This gives the parkour a nice flow to its increasing challenge and makes the game much more interesting. the blending together of mechanics is done masterfully, to an even better degree than the first. The platforming alone is incredibly enjoyable, and when it is combined with the combat it makes for very enjoyable albeit punishing gameplayCombat is the same as the first game, with some new abilities such as shadow and a time slow ultimate ability, among others. Still one shot for you and the enemies. The combat didn't receive many changes from the first, still very fluid.there are more boss fights, increasing from 1 combat boss and 2 platforming bosses in GR1 to 3 combat bosses and 1 platforming boss in GR2. New mechanics such as the wingsuit and the bike are very fun and enjoyableExcellent graphics and beautiful areas, especially with the more open portions in the 2nd half (no spoilers :3 !!)Characters are somewhat interesting for a game not focused on dialogueI encountered no glitches and only got stuck on terrain once (dashed up a flight of stairs, just crouched and was unstuck)Shares some enemies with GR1, but introduces a few new enemies that are interesting and unique enough to warrant inclusion and can spice up combatStill just as frustrating as the first, but it is easier than what I remember from GR1Cons:Like the first, the focus is not on the story. whether or not that matters is debatable, but if you are looking for a story based game look elsewhere.Is very difficult, so if you want a casual gaming experience look elsewhere.In some levels, the platforming can get a bit stale, but a majority of the levels aren't long enough for this to be a concern.Character models are good but it is obvious that the ghostrunners got more detail than the humansRating: Gameplay: 9/10Graphics: 9.5/10Story: 5/10 (while not bad it is very limited)Worth it at full price

_childDocuments_.review: If you want the quick version this game is better in almost every way compared to the first. From gameplay to story to exploration to progression but its not for everyone that enjoyed the more simple direct linear approach the first game had. Just go play it this game is really good!Before moving on to the review. THIS GAME NEEDS A GLOBAL LEADERBOARD IN GAME. Fastest times, lowest deaths, etc. Would instantly be 10x more re-playable as players would compete for positioning on the leaderboard.Now for the more detailed scrambled thoughts...This game takes huge leaps in a lot of ways exploration story and game play. But takes a step back in a couple ways. One of the games step backs is in terms pacing there's a lot of times where it feels weirdly slow. Where the first game was just go go go this game asks you to stop look around and think and slow down at times not all the time but some of the time. Another direct correlation with this is the music it overall bangs just like in the first but in the open world section which last for about 3-4 hours they are just playing dark slow depressing apocalyptic type music this heavily made it hard for me to power through as slow moody depressing music playing for a few hours is not what you play ghost runner for you want to be adrenaline induced head rocking to fast paced music plowing through everything so that was questionable.Unlike most reviewers i feel most just skipped through the story bit straight to the objective however this games narrative is actually very interesting and if you pay attention and talk to the npcs between missions you'll be rewarded with a pretty interesting story ill admit at first it was generic feeling but once you get the motivations of the characters and back stories of some you start to grow a bond to some of them. So i did enjoy that aspect. Because the first didn't really have much in terms of character and world building.In terms of the progression in the first game it was very gimmicky and in this game they simplified it but added more skills and passives. So that aspect was pretty well done but id like to see more on this end still would be cool to have maybe modifiers or trinkets for the swords or gloves to give even more variety for freedom of play but overall progression was better then the first but not by much to be fair.Another thing i see people hate on is the level design in the first it was so linear it felt pretty good going through them fast but way less rewarding to find collectibles or swords in this one the levels are more open giving you more freedom to explore i felt it was overall way more rewarding finding a sword or a collectible in this game compared to the first just because its a little more open you had to go out of your way to find that sword or collectible which was a good reward and feeling for exploring.Bosses as well are overall better and there's more of them you actually get to fight some of them in the first game i wouldn't really call them boss fights but more just puzzles with a health bar so its cool to see this being improved. In this one there's actual boss "fights" where you actually swing your sword at the boss and it does damage to the boss crazy how that works an actual boss "fight" and not just a glorified puzzle with a health bar. So overall bosses are better.One aspect that kind of lacks in the second game in comparison to the first is puzzles the first game had unique rewarding puzzles to get a skill or get to the next area it was very rewarding and unique figuring them out took some thinking this game it just falls flat it attempts the same puzzle trope in some segments but they aren't really puzzles in most cases its just common sense that takes half a second and 0 effort to figure out so that kind of sucks that they couldn't match the same level of witt and smarts and thinking it took to figure out the solution in terms of puzzles that the first game had.In terms of graphics obviously the second is better then the first although slightly harder to run in terms of performance i had to turn DLSS on after that no more issues with fps and was smooth as butter. In terms of animations this is hit or miss they try to make every animation look smoother then the first but doing so it loses its snappy direct quick feeling the first game had this is most notable in the grapple hook in my opinion in the first it was way more snappy this may just be in animation and on paper it might be the same speed but it doesn't matter if its the same speed if it doesn't feel snappy it doesn't feel good.I saw some people say it doesn't feel as fast which is just not true they might have tuned it back a tad to make space for some of the speed modifiers you can find with some of the upgrades and skills you can get however you definitely go way faster then you ever could in the first game with these skills and upgrades but the fact that they force you to get that speed through the progression system with the skills and upgrades might leave a bad taste on some people its still overall really fast base level though.Also another side note the motorcycle is a pretty fun section but the most fun i had was with the wing suit glider that section is very fun in my opinion flying through the air combining that together with parkour and combat that's when the game felt it was at its best for me and that's towards the end of the game. Also the side mode which is basically a rogue like kind of mode is much improved here the first game had this mode too but it was pretty poorly done in the second game every stage is different and forces you to make tougher decisions the first game tried to do this mode too but wasn't nearly as unique stage to stage or rewarding for making tough choices on what abilities or what path you take. The mode is much more improved for anyone that enjoyed it in the first game.Overall this game is better and i enjoyed it will play through it again on hardcore for sure and grab any DLC that comes out however i can see why its not for every one. Most fans of the first game liked the linear simple less story driven go go go straight forward experience and although you get some of that here in the second game it is very much different and tries to be more open and expansive in every way which some fans of the first game might not care for. Overall better gameplay more progression more story more complexity more open levels more bosses more enemy types along with the same ones from the first this game. Ghost runner 2 is better then the first in almost every way despite a couple draw backs that in reality come down to preference definitely give it a shot. I would highly recommend the game to anyone.Edit: After playing hardcore for a bit i can say its easily worth another play through almost every obstacle is changed and harder now. Enemies feel about the same to kill kind of easy to be honest however boss fights feel harder i think theres extra moves sets added but i cant tell. Another HUGE note some obstacles are physically impossible in hardcore depending on if you have certain skills equipped or not so keep that in mind. I think it was a missed opportunity to not add extra collectibles and swords exclusive to hardcore but regardless it does feel fresh and more challenging.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just.. not good.I really loved the original Ghostrunner, it was one of the best games I've played and it was incredibly fun, and pleasantly challenging (a little bit easier than a soulslike, but the deflect mechanic was really fun to master)It was just the right difficulty and a fun weekend. This game though, I'm less than half an hour in and it's not good. If you're expecting more of Ghostrunner 1, that's not what you're going to get here. The graphics are slightly improved, but the character models took a hit. The swords are not as unique. The leveling system lacks the uniqueness that Ghostrunner's puzzle system had. The story is not as good. Jack lost the dry humor that came with being a robot, and is now too human, and it feels like he's trying WAY too hard. It really feels like this game is just trying to incorporate Cyberpunk 2077 aspects, and it just doesn't work. The level design is worse, the movement is worse, the combat is worse. I don't know why the blocking mechanic was added other than to artificially make the game easier. Ghostrunner 1's timing system was frustrating at first, sure, but it was worth it to learn. And THE BUGS. In less than half an hour, I've fallen through the floor twice and fallen off the wall three times while wallrunning. Oh, and the stamina. It just sucks. _childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 delivers on many fronts, enhancing what made the original great while introducing a few new elements. The graphics have seen a significant upgrade, and the soundtrack is even more immersive, making every moment feel larger than life. The combat has been rebalanced, which may appeal to some, but I found it made the game a bit too easy compared to its predecessor.Combat, which was a highlight in the original, has been overhauled to feel more balanced. However, this balance comes at a cost. The thrill of the fast-paced, unforgiving combat from the first game is somewhat diminished. The battles, while still engaging, lack the intensity and challenge that made them so satisfying. The skills, like Shuriken and Shadow, are well-integrated and add more variety, but the overall experience feels toned down, with enemies that are easier to dispatch and scenarios that are less punishing.The boss battles, unfortunately, still don’t hit the mark for me. They’re too short, forgiving, and predictable—after 10-20 tries, you can easily get the hang of them. The bike and wingsuit sections were interesting additions, though the wingsuit felt gimmicky and repetitive after a while.On the positive side, the skills are more integral to gameplay, offering more strategic depth. However, despite all these improvements, it feels like Jack is only using a fraction of his potential—anything below hardcore mode just feels too easy.The story and characters were another letdown. The narrative felt too linear, lacking the mystique of the original. Most of the characters felt flat and egotistical, except for Bakunin, Saul, and Zoe, who brought some substance but still fell short of leaving a strong impression. Jack seems to carry the team 90% of the time, which makes the group dynamic less believable and engaging.Despite its flaws, Ghostrunner 2 excels in maneuverability and the sheer freedom you feel while playing. The upgraded graphics and level design add to the overall experience, making it a solid but not groundbreaking sequel. If you enjoyed the original and are okay with reflex-heavy gameplay, you’ll likely find this a worthwhile experience.Overall, I’d give it a strong 7 to a weak 8 out of 10, and I definitely recommend playing this with a controller.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the first game, getting this one wasn't even a decision. It's very good, but somewhat different from the first. At its core, it's still a parkour action game, with a cyberpunk visual and musical style.The first one was a very straightforward game, get from point A to point B and try not to die. This one have some "semi" open world sections that might turn some players off. However, it really isn't the focus of the game and it doesn't overstay its welcome.Controls are still very responsive, with some newer commands, like blocking. It feels more robust than the first one in this regard, and i have nothing but praise for this.The visuals are really good, again, just like the first one. Even though most of the game is passing very fast because of your movement, you feel the ambient and the music really helps to make the experience more immersive.There's a great deal of customization for your playstyle as well. There's more options than the first one, with some combinations turning the game into a complete ludicrous experience, where you're running around at lightning speed throwing skills that instakill people, or making your character better at slower, tactical fights.My only real complaint is about the story. It feels weaker than the first one, and the character of the Ghostrunner loses some of its mystery, which is a shame. This time he's much more talkative, in the later stages he even feel like chatting during a crisis that might very well doom them all. Feels strange, but nothing that cripples the game.Voice acting isn't bad by any means; most characters are convincing, especially Kira and Bakunin. What feels strange, for me, is that while you're in the hub area, the characters speak with long pauses, and their models are quite strange, so it breaks the immersion a bit.But, these "problems" are just me nitpicking. It's a great game and it will give you some very good hours doing parkour and slicing people up. If you liked the first one, just go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: : Since this review is trending on top, I want to add that this game is actually great for the people who couldn't beat Ghostrunner 1, or the people who found it to be too hard to enjoy. GR2 is a  for newcommers or casual players. This review is from a perspective of a hardcore-difficulty enjoyer. And while flawed, it is still an good experience overall.Unfortunately they've made a mistake that Doom Eternal as a sequel has avoided. GR2 is too focused on the story instead of gameplay. And as a result pacing and combat become far less interesting compared to the first game.- Combat arenas are too open with large gaps between enemies.It makes all encounters easy and same-y.- Arenas do not involve using parkour and environment to your advantage. Parkour is used only to navigate to the next enemy.- Arenas do not have any advanced level design. GR1 had a lot of great arenas that always challenged their player and required different approach. Like the 5 swordsmen moment. All GR2 arenas have the same approach, kill all enemies and hold block button between the kills.- The Block button makes game too easy, and less fun a result. It acts like a crutch for a bad play-style. I think they should've kept as a part of easy mode and let hardcore players parry with left mouse button just like before.- Enemies were replaced with grey, voiceless zombies that are hard to distinguish from a distance. This goes completely against game's formula, enemies should be easy to read, not memorized.Overall combat is treated poorly with the game doubling down on platforming. Which has also a couple of flaws, but fun and engaging in general. - The new robot platforms are a  decision. They cannibalize the grappling hook point and often I just die because I can't distinguish them. You can also wall-run on a side of them which will result in an unfair death.- A lot of of levels do not have proper death zones at the bottom of arenas. As a result I get stuck on geometry and don't get an insta-death to restart the arena.- All outside sections are lifeless and boring. Replacing colorful charismatic city with green and orange desert was a huge mistake and a blow to the pacing of the game. - The music choice didn't help as well it just adds to the boring feeling of the location.- Bike gets stuck on a geometry all the time.- Replacing charismatic colorful enemies with dull grey zombies that all look the same. It makes combat more punishing because you don't know what type of enemy is in front of you until it shoots.- 3 of 4 levels you spend outside the Dharma Tower do not improve gameplay and only serve the story.While it provides fun soundtrack, good story and amazing environment  design, the game is too short. It's not designed for replayability like the first game and combat design went from advanced to basic. I am looking forward to more additions to this franchise but I feel like developers either do not understand what made the original fun or they've rushed the sequel and didn't experiment enough.If you are a hardcore fan of GR1, replay the game on the hard mode and get the sequel on sale. It's fun but a step back from GR1.

_childDocuments_.review: I normally don't write reviews but the current ratio between negative and positive reviews seem a bit odd to me now that I've finished both the main campaign and hardcore version of it.When I first played the demo roughly 8 months ago (5 weeks before launch) I had some performance issues with the game freezing when performing certain actions like parrying. Because of this I decided to wait a while before buying the game. I bought the full game on sale 7th of May 2024 and have not experienced any form of performance issues in either playthroughs running on DX12 with Proton 8.0-5. From what I can tell, the performance issues other older reviews are mentioning seem to be a thing of the past. (And if not try using proton even if you're on windows, wouldn't be first time proton would be more stable than the native release)Most negative reviews seem to come from the fact that this game is too different in level design & pace. I do agree with some of this, as the other half of the game is vastly different from the first half of the game and GR1. None of it is bad per-se but if you go in with the expectation of this being an upgraded version of the first game then you're likely to be a bit disappointed.I believe the main complaint comes from a level called "The pillars of creation" where the linear gameplay style gets lost and lets the player choose which objective to focus on. Not only is the level slightly longer than most but it becomes very apparent when you're able to see how much of the level is left. Had the developers chosen to make a large abandoned early version of Dharma Tower instead of several "pillars" most people wouldn't have been nearly as annoyed. If you 're aware of this (and willing to spend a few minutes riding a bike to the real objective) you probably won't be too upset with this.I'm a bit torn regarding the ability introduced close to the end of the game as it's both fun but would drastically change the way you choose to approach other levels (if it was available). It is utilized far more in the hardcore version (being added to the level before it's officially introduced) and is a much better experience in terms of pace & difficulty.This might sound strange but I believe one of the biggest faults of the game is difficulty, compared to the first - it's too easy. Not to say that it's a breeze playing through it but since there's no difficulty selector I think the game should be more punishing. Perhaps this is because most players will have the experience from GR1 while the gameplay is designed to accommodate inexperienced players who haven't played the first game. In the hardcore version choosing abilities wasn't a way to be more efficient but essential to even have a chance. Being forced to play at a far more intense pace, being much more careful with how you choose to approach an area filled with enemies made the game feel alive in a way the main campaign isn't even close to. I'm not saying the main campaign should be replaced with hardcore, but it should be far more demanding in essentially every category. The pillars of creation level went from feeling a bit time consuming to "oh wow! ... oh no". The difficulty in hardcore makes up for the larger areas in a way which otherwise makes the gameplay lose its pace.I've had a blast playing GR2 and I will definitely come back to it at some point to play through the story again (and finish the achievements) after some time has passed. I personally found the bosses in this game to be far more fun and challenging than the ones in the first game. If you go into this game with the expectation of this being an upgraded copy of GR1 you will probably be left unsatisfied, but if you buy the game with the intention of this being an extension to the previous game with a new way to experience more of the world of Dharma Tower then you too should have a lot of fun. Also, try hardcore mode, it's daunting at first but once you get used to it (which doesn't take more than a level), you'll be left with a much more intense and fun experience which vastly improves everything in terms of pace & gameplay. (This holds true for GR1 as well)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is such a blast.I think it improves on the first game in almost every way. I particularly love the inclusion of a block button, which often gave me the confidence needed to beat tough encounters in a couple of tries, but is also heavily punished if used as a crutch. Making shurikens a part of the default moveset was also a wonderful addition for both platforming and combat.The motorbike is an incredible addition as well, feeling intuitive to use but also rewarding skill and mastery. I found getting gold in the motorbike challenge to be the second hardest challenge in the whole game, but even through the half hour that took the bike always did exactly what I told it to.Speaking of challenges, I'm surprised getting gold in every challenge is such a rare achievement. Some challenges are certainly harder than others, but the instant resets and fluid movement made them a joy to complete. I also like the pressure added by putting them in the middle of larger levels, so quitting out meant playing the whole level again to retry the challenge.The one-hit-kill gameplay is as fun as ever, and although I'm not a huge fan of the bosses that take a million hits to kill, I still enjoyed them (particularly the one with three bars). The game constantly introduces new enemies and mechanics, so it never really feels stale.The music is once again god-tier, and each level has a distict soundtrack. I've been listening to the soundtrack while I study and I can always picture the accompanying level in my head.This game is such an improvement from the already awesome first game, and I'm very excited to see what these devs do next.

_childDocuments_.review: **Pirated the game, finished it, then bought it.**I will separate this review into story and gameplay:Story: 6/10*No major spoilers for GR 2, but some spoilers for GR 1.*The story in GR 2 falls short compared to its predecessor, GR 1. While GR 1 didn't have a complex narrative, its diverse and well-defined characters brought a lot of interest and contrast to the game.In GR 1, we had the architect—smart, capable, and successful. Zeo was a passionate freedom fighter and revolutionist, while Jack was a cool-headed, efficient military type. This diversity made the story compelling. Even the enemies were distinct, with gangs relying on numbers and tower forces on technology.In contrast, GR 2 lacks this variety. Characters have been homogenized—Zeo is now more cool-headed, Jack more thoughtful, and the other characters similarly blend together. The enemies also feel undifferentiated, diminishing the story's impact.Despite these shortcomings, the story is still adequate, which is why I rated it 6/10. More then fine, but only in a very small way.Gameplay: 9.5/10The game doesn't run smoothly on my system, despite it feeling cool that, even my computer can't handle my speed. It is more annoying then cool...Gameplay in GR 2 closely mirrors GR 1, which is a positive aspect. There are few speed games that can compete with GR 2's mechanics. The game introduces interesting new elements to the already solid core gameplay.However, not all new features are well-integrated. The bike, for instance, feels disconnected from the main gameplay. It's like playing a different game when using the bike, which was disappointing. On the flip side, the game is full of exciting action moments.The game truly shines when you unlock perks that allow you to go full speed. It's an exhilarating experience, making you feel entirely in the zone—this alone makes the game worth playing.*Spoilers for gameplay ahead*: A late-game addition, the gliding ability, integrates beautifully with the core mechanics, offering a fantastic gameplay experience. _childDocuments_.review: Gameplay:Ghostrunner 2 takes everything we loved about the first game and dials it up to eleven. The way you move, the way you fight – it's all a symphony of precision and speed that'll have your heart racing. They've thrown in some fresh abilities and challenges that keep you guessing, making every encounter a white-knuckle thrill ride.Graphics:I can't even begin to describe how jaw-droppingly gorgeous this game is. The cityscapes, all lit up in neon, the futuristic backdrops – it's like stepping into a cyberpunk dream. And the characters, they're so lifelike, it's almost eerie. The art direction here is nothing short of a masterpiece, setting a whole new bar for eye candy in the gaming world.Replayability:Ghostrunner 2 is like that gift that keeps on giving. With different paths, hidden spots, and a boatload of challenges, every playthrough feels like a fresh adventure. It's all about pushing your limits, mastering those moves, and finding new ways to tackle each level. Whether you're chasing speed records or perfecting your combat, this game keeps you coming back for more.Story and Worldbuilding:While Ghostrunner 2 shines brightest in gameplay, the story isn't just an afterthought. The cyberpunk world they've built is a character in itself. The plot unfolds with twists and turns that keep you hooked, and the characters... they're mysterious and layered, adding a whole new dimension to the experience.Soundtrack:The music, oh boy, it's like they plucked it from the future. The beats and synths, they sync up with the action in a way that'll give you chills. It's like they hand-picked each track to amplify the intensity. The sound design is on point, and it's a crucial part of what makes this game so darn immersive.In Conclusion:Ghostrunner 2 isn't just a sequel; it's a leap forward. The gameplay is tighter, the graphics are jaw-dropping, and the replay value is off the charts. Hats off to the devs for crafting something truly special. If you're into high-octane action and diving headfirst into cyberpunk worlds, this game is an absolute must-play. It's a wild ride from start to finish, setting a whole new standard for the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: If it weren't for the fact that the first game's story was integral to most of the circumstances and motivations of everything that goes on here, then I'd say you could just disregard the first game entirely and just play this, because this is better than the original in every way and the writing and worldbuilding are still as token and bland as ever. I do not understand how you have an awesome cyborg ninja character classified as a Ghostrunner and decide to name him "Jack" of all things.But you're not here for the story.  no one is here for the story. If there's one thing I respect about the  games, it's that they did what I wish more games did at the development stage and took a style of play and built an entire game around it.  is *the* cyborg ninja game.  is the game that Genji Shimada looks at and feels inadequate over. Then you have , which took everything that was good about the first game and made it better while still keeping all its flaws, including the crappy boss fights that somehow only get worse after the mediocre first one and the fact that first-person melee combat and parkour just doesn't bloody work because you can't see yourself in relation to the environment.There are a couple other issues, too; as well as the motorcycle controls, it's not fun when you keep bumping into things and coming to a complete stop, necessitating you slowly reversing out and changing direction. Would be nice if the motorcycle reversed on its own. I also encountered a terrible issue where my bike got caught in the environment and there was no way for me to free it so I had to walk to finish the level. Also, devs, I get that you want us to care about the characters, and I admire that; the games could definitely use stronger context. But making us walk slowly around a small hub area and talk to everyone one by one is not how you fix that; you need better writing. And why do we even have a sprint mode in the hub area? We don't even have a sprint in the actual gameplay. I feel like you're trying to replicate something that was successful without understanding why it was successful. Also also... Also also also, what happened to the -style upgrade system? That was so fun. These chips are nothing by comparison. I miss that upgrade system so much.I recommend  for the gameplay; it is very fun and I enjoy it a lot, flaws notwithstanding. The motorcycle levels are amazing; the penultimate level introduces a *really* fun mechanic that, while it's been done for about twelve years now, is still just as good as it was then; and the usual slicing and dicing is better than ever. The roguelike mode has also been expounded on with many more upgrades and cool features. Just be mindful that 's always had some fundamental issues that don't go away with time.

_childDocuments_.review: When i played ghostrunner, i cried tears of joy at a game that did not lack in visual aesthetic, interesting narrative, tight game play and mechanics, AND an all banger soundtrack. it was and is a beautiful and near perfect gem that will stand for an extremely long time. Ghostrunner 2 is the same, plus more. As a game with no scaleable difficulty, this translates for some to simply being harder. In some ways this may be true, but what good sequel hasnt added new mechanics and environments? These new mechanics and environments may present new challenges but they are not shortcomings of the game. That was to address one complaint i have seen that i found rather invalid. That said, there is an area of valid complaint. The NPCs are...pretty lifeless. Granted it is a rather extreme change of pace from the first game, having casual and candid conversations with ambient characters between levels, and it shows. The voice acting is still fine, cutscenes are orchestrated well, but alot of the dialog and smalltalk between jack and the other characters has alot of awkward pauses and lines delivered by swaying manequins. It is worth noting that these lacking points are the smallest and least notable part of the game and are most certainly not meant to be the focus but are simply meant to offer some more spoon fed background lore on the world and its workings. To me the effort and inclusion of an option to get these voiced lines giving me background is a nice inclusion that i can forgive the oblivion npc style of delivery.TLDR parkour cyborg ninja simulator with banger tracks nonstop

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy sequel to GR1 that improved on the game in nearly every way. There are new enemy types, platforming mechanics, and abilities that really freshen up the gameplay. These sections were not only fun, but they also made GR2 feel more like an action/adventure game with a flowing story. By contrast, GR1 - while incredible - was segmented in a room-after-room gameplay loop which made it feel more like an arcade title.The soundtrack slapped as expected and the story had some compelling new characters, despite not necessarily being the focal point of the game. Performance-wise it ran very well with only a few hitches here and there over my 10hr playthrough. This title is just a bit different, but it retains all the fast-paced charm of the original.p.s. The upgrade system is seriously underwhelming and half of the upgrades are almost useless, although the way to piece them together and maximise their effectiveness, similar to the first game, is engaging and provokes some degree of thought. Though in reality it has very little affect.The hub world was probably the worst inclusion that they introduced since the first game. Where Ghostrunner had a continuous flow where the events and plot flowed through conversations had whilst you were playing, 2 now stops you to listen to in a meaningless hub world which only contains (other than characters to talk to) a machine to buy, not even apply as that's done in a menu, upgrades and a machine to play a short mini-game.There was one main inclusion however which I really enjoyed and that was the cyberbike! It provided a break to the core game-play loop of running around and slashing in a positive way which preserved the tempo of the game, unlike the hub world. It was something new to learn and fit the pace of the core game-play which then allowed them to be used together later on in the story.Overall I think if you enjoyed the first game, this is a no brainer as they are almost the same game, although this installment is far less of a challenge. However, it is also for this reason that I cannot recommend enough that you wait for a sale. 100%ing all the achievements took me under 14 hours which for a £35 game, especially one that is a near identical sequel, is atrocious.

_childDocuments_.review: Heartbreaking, but I'm chopping this up as a miss. I loved the first game, but something feels amiss with the second.People have made the claim this is easier - and while that may be true in combat I found  to be the majority of my deaths. These are typically sections of games that you breeze through with the right inputs. Something was chronically wrong with the spacing of travesal objects that I would often fall short, or jump over, things. The swinging poles are a great example; something felt so off (possibly aspect ratio/field of view issues?) where as I jumped towards them I  like I was positioned correctly so that Jack would be able to grab it, but he falls instead. Out of shear paranoia I found myself dashing to each pole, to which felt like if I was viewing the connection in third person, I'd see Jack hit the pole with his shins. Something so very not right with the detection here.Ghostunner implements a 'Hub' between missions (at least in the early stages of the game that I've played). When adding additional features to a sequel the big question is "does this add or remove value". In my experience, it removes. Ghostrunner 1 was a continuous series of back-to-back missions unfolding in a linear fashion. This leaned favourably to the game's pace, as while the combat is fast, so is the feeling of your progression. Being pulled from missions to a safe, at-my-own-pace, Hub area was jarring, and removed the sense of urgency the first game expressed. It's possible that the Hub provided a better opportunity for story expression, but since the story is nonsensical to me, and not the strong point of the series, I think it's ultimately better to abandon thoughts of improving player access to it (if it's ultimately going to hurt other areas). The open area was actually an interesting change of pace, and despite my desire to want the game to feel 'quick', I didn't find it tedious. I would criticise the first section and it's overall game time - significantly more (double?) than the missions prior. There's 3 distinct areas to go to, maybe these could have all been individual timed missions? It's also hard to feel a sense of urgency towards your own game-time (if you're aiming to finish missions quick) when you're driving around an open map where everything looks similar, and efficient pathways are indistinguishable against the wider landscape.Also, and I don't know if this was my aspect ratio and field of view, but the view from the bike was . Half my screen was bike, and that was worsened any time I was going up hill. Some sections require you to go up walls and I was essentially guessing. I was guessing the right path and, if it didn't work, adjusted next life. Absolutely terrible. Naga was probably an amazing sequence for everyone else, but I couldn't help but rack up the deaths (and the frustration) with running trial-and-error blindly. All and all this has the combat that I enjoyed from the first game, but I feel the additional aspects they've added hurt the sequel - and something went terrible wrong with spacing traversal elements considering jump/dash distances.I feel bad to some degree. I liked Ghostrunner 1 so much - but this just isn't feeling fun and it's made worse that I can objectively break-down why.

_childDocuments_.review: Some other reviewers go as far as not recommending the game for a reason that the game focuses more on the story than fighting arenas and other game mechanics. It is very apparent that the devs want more open less linear experience and I feel like they nailed the balance between limited resources for an indie game and big plans and ideas. It is still very linear experience (~which is not a bad thing~), but inclusion of HQ and more open big locations with multiple tasks that can be done in any order makes it feel like a more living actual world. This is something that I missed in the original game, where the game aesthetically was amazing and as someone who loves cyberpunk I missed not being able to interact with the world more. This certainly helps. When I first entered HQ I sat in the office for few minutes just looking out of the windows at the world around.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoying your fast-paced, adrenaline pumping rhythmic game? Time to stop and go back to a hub that could have easily been a menu. The developers added dialogue options, but the only options are to listen to more boring and cringe dialogue — and the order you hear it in; or just leave. I opted to leave. All the dialogue could have been trimmed down and fed to you as radio communications instead.This really leaves me puzzled, they took all the best elements of Ghostrunner, and slapped arbitrary elements on top of it. Open world segments (boring), stamina-based blocking, time trials, a tacked-on rogue-lite game, ultimate abilities... I'm shocked they left out romance options.I'll give the devs props on the atmosphere and the music, but this game leaves me nostalgic for the first game with levels that are tightly designed, adrenaline pumping missions seamlessly leading into another with no downtime at all. Ghostrunner 1 felt like I was dancing a deadly ballet across a chessboard; Ghostrunner 2 feels like dancing the Macarena, fun for a minute, but you wont get 5 hours of enjoyment out of it.I'll be cautiously optimistic for Ghostrunner 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the most enjoyable games I've ever played...and I haven't played much of it yet, because I know it's not an intensely long game, but it's a speedrunner's wet dream, and I love the challenge. It's so fast paced, so when you do complete a level, you'll feel accomplished. Wallriding, sliding, grappling, hacking and slashing, and deflecting projectiles with your giant katana, feeling like an absolute badass by vanquishing everyone who has 1hp...but you also have 1hp. Get hit once, and you die. But...yeah....I feel like I'm going to actually submit results to official speedrun site for this game. Just, once I get better at it. I read reviews of people who died like 255 times during a single level when they first started out. It's not that difficult, especially if you've played the absolute crap out of any fps that has wall riding capabilities, or you played surf in counter-strike, or bhop maps in cs.This is just more  short bursts. I mean, it's very fast paced, so it will just drain your epinephrine from your body until you have to stop. At my age, that happens quickly. But...the game just makes you feel like a god when your movement is perfect. Just...so satisfying. Worth buying and keeping in your library for when you need to vent out some frustration. I mean, you could potentially get frustrated playing the levels, which I did once (one guy killed me with some sort of phaser rifle and then I got the tutorial tip of "press shift whilst in mid air to dodge"), so I got mad that it told me I could dodge after I died. Still though....really good fun. If you liked the latest versions of Doom, you'll like this.

_childDocuments_.review: a wonderful successor to its precedessor, this game is quite an experience. even richer storytelling, wonderful voice acting, a charming set of characters, and new and innovative abilities. it contains quite a number of well-done callbacks (and some notable exceptions; i miss you tempest refund my beloved), and the new mechanics are quite solid. and even among sci-fi games known for their detail, the graphics are breathtaking. (especially in later parts of the game, no spoilers :)  )The controls unfortunately suffer a much worse version of the original Ghostrunner's minor input delay/unresponsiveness issue, with significantly infuriating input fudging to the controls at times. the game also seems shoddy on optimization, as I often encountered lag spikes that would occur at specific sequences and combat locations,  often making combat severely infuriating and the occasional crash (♥♥♥♥ you Madhu). overall a wonderful experience for story and visuals, well-thought out mechanics, but somewhat lacking in map design, lag optimization, and control feel compared to the original. 6.5/10, would recommend to anyone who has played the original

_childDocuments_.review: Literally unplayable. When I say unplayable, I don't mean I ran into performance issues and glitches, I mean the game doesn't work. You'll get past the logos and then stare at your reflection on a black screen until you decide to task manager yourself to reality.Before you have any doubts about my issues maybe being due to a bad system, let me state that I'm running a 12th gen i7 and an RTX 3080, so I'm not short on hardware power. I have 6 hours in this game because I managed to open it 2 or 3 times by closing background processes such as wallpaper engine and trying several times each attempt, but each time I thought about playing the game I would hesitate because I knew I would have so many problems just trying to open it. I decided to try to give it one last go today and make a push to finish the game, and I could not open it for the life of me. I closed wallpaper engine, updated graphics drivers, closed Discord, Riot Vanguard, everything I thought could affect it and the game would always stop on a black screen and not start.
