_childDocuments_.review: I overall enjoy the game more than the first game. The most annoying enemies from the first game are pretty much gone, save for small one-time miniboss encounters. The game is almost fully based on navigating the arena and finding ways to close the distance instead of chasing after RNG teleports or outrunning suicide bombers. This is accentuated by some really fun late game mobility options that really shake up the gameplay enough to avoid the repetitive feeling I got towards the end of the first game. The boss fights are also better, but still easy and simple. I beat most of the boss fights by running in and slashing, parrying whenever the boss made any kind of move, and dashing back in when they knocked me back. It was only ever the segments between the boss phases that gave me issue.There are only a couple of negatives for me to mention. The most major one is the enemy having map hack. There were multiple moments where I rounded a corner to flank an enemy and they immediately opened fire as soon as I came into view, killing me before I could react. I don't know if something changed with the AI between games or if the first game's arena designs simply didn't have that many walls, but this happened enough times in this game to get me heated. I had to start rounding the corner while immediately holding block to survive.Another one is the facial animations being genuinely really bad. There is now a hub level where you can walk around and talk to players. The writing is shallow but alright, and I enjoyed these moments. It lets you interact more with characters that don't make much of an appearance in the story, and highlights Jack's personality more through interactions with more normal people.However, it's really distracting when you talk to the NPCs and their lips are the only thing moving, with their cheeks and eyes being completely static. It's animation from two generations ago and very disappointing.The last negative to mention are the exploration levels with the bike. The linear levels with the bike are fine, if not a little bit unforgiving considering how imprecise the bike feels, but the open exploration levels just don't feel made for the bike at all. There are little bits of geometry dotted all around the map that my bike kept getting snagged on. It happened enough to affect the flow of the map and my enjoyment of them. These maps also had pretty much nothing going on, as once you're forced to properly get off, it just turns into another normal Ghostrunner level, which makes me question how necessary how necessary the massive open areas were.All in all, a pretty good upgrade to the first game in my book.

_childDocuments_.review: The first Ghostrunner game is far better than this one. Ghostrunner 2 is more focused with the maps than the combat. I've spent more time solving map puzzles than actually fighting enemies. That is, when the maps are loading properly. I've gotten stuck and fallen into the sky box multiple times. This is especially true on the desert maps, which are already extremely boring to play on because of the excessive size and dull gray color scheme. It's no surprise so much time was put into the over-designing of maps because the combat itself is lacking. The block feature is by far the worst addition in Ghostrunner 2. Players can lazily press a button and block barrages of bullets. The original Ghostrunner player could only block one projectile at once and it required good timing. This made the gameplay more fast paced and exciting as dodging and dashing were more important. The second game also has a lot of emphasis on the secondary abilities as they charge way too quickly and are necessary to complete the endless map puzzles. This would be less of a problem if ultimate abilities weren't added in. All these extra abilities make the sword play seem less important, which takes away from what made the original combat interesting. There is also too much emphasis on the story of the game. Ghostrunner was able to implement the story into the gameplay through in-game dialog. The story existed to enhance the gameplay, but Ghostrunner 2 feels like the opposite. The story takes priority, even if it negatively affects the gameplay. For example, the game is constantly being interrupted with safe hub scenes so the player can have boring conversations with boring NPCs. The deserts scenes are also proof of this. The writers really wanted Jack to leave the city without thinking about whether or not this would be good for gameplay. As a result, the game is now filled with extremely large, buggy, and dull desert maps which are not nearly as fun to play as the city maps.Then there is the inclusion of the motorcycle. Let's just say driving this motorcycle makes driving in Cyberpunk feel easy in comparison. Overall, Ghostrunner 2 is an alright game, but the original is much better. Overall, Ghostrunner is more exciting, more fast-paced, less buggy, and overall better designed than its sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: In general it was a somewhat fun game for the most part. But compared to the first part and project Hel it just cannot scale up to them and the expectations that came with them.On a basic level this game did deliver a lot of the things i was hoping for - a sequel to a game i really loved with some nice stages and some fun additions to the abilities. The Bike was a good bit glitchy but overall did bring a nice touch and did break through some of the more repetitive feeling. The story was okay, definitly not a masterpiece, but it was somewhat consistent. The graphic was nice, the abilities fun to play around and especially the first few levels really managed to capture the feeling you had throughout the first game. The hub was a sweet addition that a lot of people complained about, but i'm honestly not completely sure why. Most of the dialogue is fully optional and even the needed dialogue can just be skipped through very fast. So it really just provided some easter-eggs and some dialogue for everyone who wanted to see more. But to be honest, that was really where the positives ended, at least in comparision to its predecessor. One of the things i loved most about GR 1 was how smooth and bug-free it is.This game is everything but that. I've encountered more bugs than i could count. From falling through the map, the bike getting stuck, enemies seeing me through invisibility, upgrades/bonuses not working, dialogue and sound cutting out, my gap jammer deciding to quit its job, falling down from walls/not being able to run on them which worked just fine a second ago, or enemies getting stuck and me dying for no reason, it really had it all. The bugs got especially consistent in the later stages and the new "simulation"; which is, as a concept very cool, but nearly rendered impossible due to glitches for me. It just feels like the developers got rushed a lot in the later parts which is such a shame, as the potential is there.The one thing this game really, really did not need though was the one "open-world" - level it got. It was possibly the most bugged, inconsistend, far too long and confusing level it had. Really, the game would probably greatly improve just by removing that level.In total i'd say - it's still a decent game. While it has a good bit of issues it is enjoyable and fun for the most part, especially if you do not aim to get 100%. I struggled a lot on if i would recommend this game not, but i think in general it doesn't really need more hate than it already gets from some people. I would not get it for the full price, nor would i recommend getting it as any of the special editions as of right now at least. If you're looking for a game that feels as polished and great as GR 1 - just stick with GR 1. That game was so insanely good it just set insane expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a miserable shade of the first Ghostrunner. Just play it and skip this one.The first game had parts that weren't fun but it wasn't every waking second of it like this one.Between the inconsistent parkour of wall-running when you want to climb or climbing when you walk to wall run, crouch sliding for half a second before crouch walking and getting killed, not being frame perfect in whatever stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the devs wanted you to do killing you for you to do it perfectly the second or third try, occasionally just having whole new enemy types thrown at you with absolutely no instruction or even a vague hint on how to counter them only to point out how often you died to stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at the end, and the inability to even look around on the motorcycle so I can look up and not IMMEDIATELY smash into a wall on the stupid twisty sections.I really don't understand how a studio can consistently take really cool concepts and consistently make them miserable every step of the way. more fun if it were removed entirely.-Level geometry can be wacky it is doubly so for the bike.-Wing suit was fun, shame it was only for one level.-Ultimates are underwhelming.-The parkour is fun except when it wants you to jump through a small hole in a wall as there is a good chance you will just stand in the hole instead of going straight through.-A lot of the arenas feel samey probably due to the donut design for most of them.-there are a few enemies that are poorly designed in such a way that it makes your default tools for killing enemies insufficient for killing them, namely the _childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is nice. There are aspects to it that I like more than GR1. But that's pretty much where the good stuff ends. On to the bad stuff!The story makes absolutely no sense. Granted, it's been some time since I've played the first game. I also didn't get the DLC for the first game. From what I've experienced so far, though, I guess remembering everything that happened in the first game  the DLC is necessary to get what is going on at all. Nothing makes sense and it just seems you're expected to know things from the first game. Yeah, it's a sequel, okay. But even then, I think giving it its own story that isn't dependent on the first game would've been the correct move. Go find any game with sequels. In almost every single one, you can just start from whichever game you feel, and you can still get the general gist of the story.It's very easy to just run in circles looking for the route the devs want you to take. Indicators for what is the correct route are minimal, and quest markers are used sparingly. It's very easy to get lost in bigger areas.Frankly, the game is a buggy mess. Enemies can get stuck on the skybox, some will just never attack, and hitboxes are terrible. In the first boss fight, after it had gone through an entire attack animation, I dashed up behind it to get some damage in, and just died out of nowhere. That's just naming a few that I've encountered in my first 45 minutes of playing the game, and more have been popping up. It's just an absolutely buggy mess.Just... don't. Unless you are willing to put up with really stupid bugs and you don't care about story at all, then just don't get the game. It's embarrassing how much worse this game is compared to the first in almost every way.

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely preferred the first game. If you haven't played it yet, but that first and then think about purchasing this one. Here's why:Even though it is very fun in the moment, the campaign is way too short for a 40$ game. In addition to this the parkour challenges in the non-story content are often very poorly designed. I also have some issues with the control scheme. For instance, once you get the glider suit it is bound to ctrl, which is the same button as the slide button. You can not rebind this. Imagine being about to touch down on ground with the intention of sliding right after touchdown only to plant face first into the dirt. You may think "that's a skill issue" and to a certain extent I agree. However, the gliding suit gets introduced within the last hour of the 7 to 8 hour long campaign. All of the muscle memory movement techniques containing sliding before touchdown get thrown in the trash and can now kill you.You also seem to not be able to use the gliding suit outside of the last couple of campaign missions which is very disappointing.The bossfights are better than the first game, but they are still very mid for the most part.

Thank you for patching those, but sadly it will not be resulting in my review changing to a positive due to other reasons. I'll break this down into multiple topics;**STORY**I'll admit, I can't speak much on the story because I couldn't stand a lot of what I had to deal with leading up to the big bits - hell, I didn't even get to the point the demo took place during which has made me pretty depressed. But this wasn't a fun kind of infuriating, it was just - irritating.For the story beats I can talk about, they're actually pretty cool. The fact there was ||a series of Ghostrunners that came before Jack|| and it even touches up on the DLC of the previous game is cool, even if I myself didn't get to play it because I was broke when it originally came out. Overall, they seem to be going in an interesting direction as a whole, though a lot of the beats aren't making sense for me yet - but that's probably cause I'm not very far through.Seeing the different characters perspectives on things was also interesting, but that leads me into the next topic of the whole game.**CHARACTERS**||Zoe|| was a character I loved in Ghostrunner 1, so to see them back again in this game was a huge bop and the VA didn't fail at any mark with them I've seen so far. But as for the rest of the characters, they're more irritating then enjoyable to interact with. Having constant blabbering in my ear, especially from the self righteous jackass that is ||Connor||, is outright insufferable more often then not.Especially since we have the stupid hub system that just *expects* me to spend a good 10-15 minutes listening to every characters dialogue between missions. Why couldn't the interesting parts of their dialogue be incorporated into the main story in a fluid way if you plan for the characters to yap my ear off? That'd be better then listening to the self righteous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that thinks he leads everyone go on about ♥♥♥♥ that genuinely does not matter to the story, he's genuinely not interesting compared to the other characters, he feels like some kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ self insert to the story to the point that even other characters tell him to shut up!I shouldn't be agreeing with every single other character that the MAIN PERSON IN CHARGE needs to shut their mouth and stop talking. And if I do agree, you need to make him less vocal throughout the game or at least have him start to change. I'm a quarter in and he hasn't changed once, he's still an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and he still doesn't do anything to add to my enjoyment in the story then just be a 'cool kid'.**NET SPACE**Why? That's the question I wanna ask, because most of the reviews that had anything negative to say in Ghostrunners 1 repeatedly stated - we hated the net space levels. And your guys response is to make over 5-6 in the first quarter of the game that I've counted so far, each having a different gimmick, then having a ||boss fight in another like we did at the end of Ghostrunners 1|| and that was insufferable enough!Genuinely, I don't mind hard mechanics, but the net space levels aren't fun and it's what coaxed me into writing this review. I was genuinely trying so hard to see the game through before updating, but I can't, I couldn't do it. End of the day, I'll probably write more later but the net space levels back to back to back just took so much out of me.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is an incredible sequel that builds on the world and the lore of the first game and really gives it life. The characters are all so much more real, and Jack is full of personality. The levels are huge and yet even without a map I didn’t ever feel lost (the level design is great at pointing you where you need to go). It isn’t just a full game in the tower like the first, too - the late game has two major changes to how you play that keeps the game fresh and exciting. I love the lore and story of this world, and I loved so much getting to dig way deeper into it in this game. I hope we get a third game in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Ghostrunner 2

_childDocuments_.review: More Ghostrunner but with much more refined and improved mechanics. The visuals, game play, and music just screams cyberpunk, a genre I absolutely love. The first section with the bike was pure adrenaline for me as you're zipping through tunnels and down Dharma tower needing to make split second adjustments to avoid slamming into your death.  The sections after it though seem to slow down a bit as it opens up to open ended mission design. It definitely takes away from the previously mentioned as you're just driving down open landscapes to get to certain arena type set pieces where there really isn't much in-between to worry about.Nonetheless, the positives absolutely outweigh the negatives for me. One More Level improved upon the first game while experimenting with a different way of challenging the player with it's fast paced, one hit death style game play with the bike. Definitely looking forward to any potential 3rd installment, they have a great universe here.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from an addict of the first game, the sequel is a massive disappointment. Everything feels like a downgrade from the first game. Combat and abilities: Clunkier. The basic loop is fine, but everything else feels worse. Blink has been completely ruined, now you have to manually mark targets before activating it (which often gets you killed because it does not stop time), shinobi's atttacks land before the attack animation finishes, and the deflect animation stops the flow of combat for the sake of a  mildly cool execution. Movement and parkour: Movement is largely unchanged, which is fine, but for some reason the rails that you slide on pull you in like a black hole whenever you get near them, often leading to death. The wingsuit and motorcycle are neat gimmicks in normal mode, but their terrible controls and handling become obvious in hardcore where pinpoint precision is required. The motorcycle especially has inaccurate hitboxes (you will often barely miss an obstacle, only for it to kill you anyway), a camera angle that makes seeing where you're going an issue sometimes, and a unique affinity for getting stuck absolutely everywhere, forcing a restart. Everything else: They got rid of the unique Tetris-like upgrade system from the first game in favor of a more typical tree in which you place upgrade nodes. The problem is that several upgrades and perks make certain sections of the game literally impossible, leading one to wonder why they were ever added in the first place. The mid-section of the game is an absolute slog, where the game turns into a pseudo-open world that doesn't service the gameplay nearly as well as the indoor sections. The boss fights are fun, except for the Dismantler, who has a move that kills you the second he starts his animation and is also not telegraphed, so if you're right up on him when he uses it (which you probably will be), there is absolutely no way to prevent a death. There are still annoying puzzle sections that kill the pacing, but they are usually paired with some platforming that makes them not quite as obnoxious.Hardcore mode is also really lazy and feels like the devs didn't even play test it with how most encounters are either trivialized by cheese or made almost impossible due to clunky controls and hitboxes.Idk man it's fine but really disappointing after the first game. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is one I'd really like steam to have a maybe option for. Ghostrunner 2 is very good but lacks is certain areas I can see being gamebreaking for some. The motorcycle is very buggy, and you wont encounter it until halfway through the game. The motorcycle can slam into objects and get stuck forcing a restart. The game in general can be lacking of polish at times. I dashed out of the environment 3 or 4 times to my death in the void because of collision detection errors. I noticed 3 or 4 instances of being able to see straight through the ground or walls into the void. For a game that's very hotline miami esc, it can be irritating to have to redo sections because of collision errors with the bike/player. Ghostrunner 2 continues the series' difficulty in a good way. I would say it was slightly easier than the first, but not a noticeable step down. The level design has taken a step down in quality. I mean there is a point where you are breaking colored crystals in line with what the game says to do for basically no reason. It's not hard, it's not fun, and it doesnt break up the gameplay cause it's inherently set to a 25 second timeframe. There are no moments of me admiring the levels for how interconnected and well made they are. Part of this comes down to the increased number of collectible items in missions and general gameplay's less involved nature. There is less than 5 new enemies. There's the wheel zombie thing that involves dashing to avoid and then you kill it. There is the sandworm that spits acid. The zombies are kind of new visually, but are mechanically just reskins of previous enemies. They replaced the warden with the shinobi. That's it. As far as cut enemies... They removed the wreck. They removed the turrets. They removed the sniper. They removed the splitter. So for every enemy they added, they removed one from the original that provided a unique gameplay challenge. This really is so hard to recommend with all of these elements, but I still do. The bosses and gameplay are fantastic. The music is excellent. The story was very mid, as expected. But the good parts of this game are so worth experiencing. So go into this game with hesitance, and just get ghostrunner 1 is you're curious about the series. And, I believe Ghostrunner 1 is longer as well.TL;DR1 is better, and this one lacks new enemies and the amazing level design we saw from the first game. If you dont have 1, get it instead. If you already have 1 and liked it. This one's good, with more problems than the original. But fun nonetheless.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid game to get while it's on sale. I can appreciate that the developers decided to take some risks, but they honestly didn't quite pay off. The first time you get access to the bike is extremely well done, despite the controls for it being a bit jank, it's a fun puzzle to play though. The mission immediately following it is incredibly painful to get through though. The open world level was entirely unnecessary in a game thats core gameplay loop is killing enemies while exploiting movement mechanics. It was a chore to get through and felt like a weird way to artificially extend the time it takes to play the game. The other risk they took was redesigning the movement mechanics from the original Ghostrunner. I don't honestly like the way momentum works in this game at all, and many mechanics felt jank and out of place. Dashing while mid air for some reason cancels all your forward momentum, so rather than getting a boost to the momentum you already have, you might just miss a jump because of dashing. On top of that, many areas feel oddly inconsistent with how momentum works. You can do the same exact thing several times and get a different result each time. Some times you fall short on a jump and then for some reason you make it the next time despite fundamentally changing nothing in what you did. Story is meh just like GR1, not really much to note, it's quick and basically all the characters are forgettable. If you liked GR1, you'll probably like GR2 as well. Despite feeling like it needed more time in development, it's still as fun as the last, just a bit less fluid feeling. If you haven't played GR1 yet, I would play that first before playing this one, since it is the objectively better ghostrunner.

Fans of the first game will most likely find this game fairly enjoyable and probably won't be too put off by some of the differences in this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the video-gamiest video game I could ever have wanted, and it's amazing. The original Ghostrunner was a surprise hit after I discovered it during a Steam Sale, and this could not have been a better follow-up.For one: I appreciate this game's tight focus and lack of padding... with one exception, which we will get to. There are so many games, old and new, where I feel my time is wasted. Ghostrunner 2 is never like that. The levels progress rapidly, alternating between real-world and Cybervoid sections divided into platforming and combat, and the variety is appreciated. One of my few criticisms of the first Ghostrunner was its, while beautiful, repetitive neon Dharma design. This game does a much better job differentiating environments!That pace is matched by the story. There are no threads which drag. Each play session (only around 1 hour) felt like I truly advanced in the game and pushed the plot forward. Compared to the first game, this plot is a massive step up. There is much nuance required in tackling a narrative set after the Big Bad has been defeated, which is where Ghostrunner 2 picks up, but the writers were up to the task. Quality dialogue and a much expanded cast of characters also break up the repetition felt in the first game.The RogueRunner side mode is alright, but it becomes repetitive fast, as it is all set within the Cybervoid. Having to replay all levels to unlock each new reward is discouraging, but roguelites were never my thing anyway. I am glad this is a side mode instead of the major focus of the game.The graphics are beautiful—not cutting-edge, but enough that you will never notice a difference in motion. Ray tracing support is missing, unfortunately. Picking the DX12 launch option brings up the DX11 game, for some reason. Forcing the game to launch in DX12 using command line arguments revealed why: the ray tracing option is laggy and unfinished. I only played with it for a little while before disabling it. For context, the first game ran at a nice 60 FPS with occasional dips on my 3080. Dharma's many puddles will never quite match the beauty from Ghostrunner 1.The gameplay is excellent as always. I found myself stuck on "tough rooms" less often, which could be either down to my skills improving (yay!) or this game being more polished to tone down difficult spikes. Still, I would encounter an extra-challenging room every once in a while that made me appreciate the variety of routes and abilities in the sequel.The boss fights are a massive improvement. The first game's Hel fight was terrible. Parry, parry, parry, parry... the bosses here are much more dynamic. There is still an inescapable jank, especially to the Dismantler fight, but that cannot be avoided.There is one section of the game I would like to discuss here that is a minor spoiler. If you haven't played the game yet, why not? Go buy it right now and get back here once you're finished!Ghostrunner 2 introduces a motorbike with extended bike sections. I found their pace to flow smoothly with the other fast-paced levels of the game. The initial sequence in particular was challenging, but a solid tutorial and a good sell on the new mechanic.Unfortunately, the worst part of this overall excellent sequel is the level "Pillars of Creation." For whatever reason, this level eschews the established linear format for an open area with three objectives to complete in any order. The open design kills the pace and pumps the brakes on what was otherwise a red-hot progression. The dialogue during this section was its saving grace, as the characters and their discussions were genuinely interesting and funny.Ghostrunner 2 is the sequel I wish other games could execute. While the beginning feels like more Ghostrunner 1, the midgame onward expands the world, story, and design in a way I found quite natural. It does not feel like a forced sequel plot; rather, it highlights how unstable the world was at the end of the first game. The gameplay is stellar and playing it in bursts never fails to hit the dopamine receptors. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game. Here are the pros and cons that stood out to me the most in terms of gameplay and story/writing content.Ghostrunner II explored things that its prequel mentioned, but didn't get a chance to delve into. I enjoyed the philosophical questions posed by the story, especially near the end.While the story itself was alright in concept, it's hard to ignore how it just kind of... came out of nowhere. Some of the villains get next to no development, and the ending has no leadup whatsoever. I bought this game for the high-adrenaline action that I got in Ghostrunner I, and for the most part, Ghostrunner II delivered. The game does a great job of challenging you to the point of raging, but still making sure you feel like a badass when you finally pull off the flow you've been practicing for however long. The parkour is also pretty satisfying most of the time, and adds some interesting mechanics by expanding on elements from Ghostrunner I. Especially towards the end, there are some really cool stunts that you can pull off with the gadgets the game provides you with.With all of those pros, the game still feels... unfinished. A lot of walls can be clipped through, and the game just doesn't seem to mesh well with some of the things that were added . The Roguerunner mode is fun to start out, but so many of the modules are just absurdly structured to the point of being needlessly hard to beat without exploits, especially in the later stages. Additionally, Hardcore mode is absolutely unplayable. It's like they went in and slapped a bunch of new obstacles onto the story mode and forgot to test how it actually affected things. The bosses have extremely high amounts of health in Hardcore mode, which wouldn't be a problem if they weren't so repetitive and boring to begin with. WITH ALL OF THAT SAID, I still enjoyed playing through the main story mode, and it was worth the $7 I paid for it while it was on sale, albeit I wouldn't buy it for full price in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: So... Ghostrunner 2. I really liked the first game and I really like this one, too.When you check what's on paper, all the features added to this sequel are reasonable.So why do I still think the first one is the better game?Because I feel that the simplicity of the first one made it more straight to the point. Now we have a base where we can walk around and a lot of story stuff with characters nobody cares about, more puzzles and more open levels. That is all fine by itself, but I feel like Ghostrunner simply did not need a sequel with more features and lore. It does not have to grow into an overblown IP. It is fine as it is. Because of the gameplay.And it's the gameplay that felt a bit more precise in the first one.Still. Ghostrunner 2 is an excellent game. The gameplay still keeps you on your toes. The visual design of every level is peak. The music is even better than in the first game.If you never played any Ghostrunner, I recommend playing the first game first and then playing the second, if you want just more. If not, that's also fine.It's up to you, but I recommend playing both.Would I be happy to see more Ghostrunner in the future, even with more features? As long as it's good and not turning into a completely different game, sure.Because if we gamers demand something, it's quite simple: Just a good game.And Ghostrunner 2 is exactly that.

_childDocuments_.review: I agree with what most others have said about the general game experience. Overall this is a fun game that for the most part improves on the original game. I think overall everyone will have fun with this. However I personally found one massive negative that turned me off to the game and I don't see many reviews discussing it and I think if you played the first one you should know because it changes the game pretty drastically.And that's the hub. I think the inclusion of a hub for this game was a near-sighted decision. I think above and beyond what made the first Ghostrunner game so successful was how well it was paced. You were constantly rushing forward with as much speed as you could muster, and the entire storyline of the game took place while you charged forward. It was so well presented, and so well done the story felt like an actual piece of your character.Now they've added a hub? So when you rushing through a level, jumping obstacles, grappling to a wall and wall running across, jump over that gap, slice that dude's head off and then... STOP. STOP and talk to these NPCs. Listen to all the nothing they have to offer you. Expanding a story is great, making the world feel bigger, more alive and real is great. But a hub for this game was the incorrect decision.It completely breaks that pacing of the first game, you complete a level and you STOP and talk. Stop and talk. Stop and talk. I don't want to stop? I want to keep running and murdering with my sword. It's awesome. That's the fun part of the game, don't make me stop the fun part of the game.Idk how my stats turn out because I was in the testing for this game before it launched, but I do just want to reiterate. I think the game is great and I think most people will enjoy it thuroughly, especially if you loved the first. I just wish the hub wasn't included in this, and I think the game would be 10/10. I do still recommend it though.

_childDocuments_.review: There is like 150% more game to this, and it's all I could've ever hoped for. Despite the occasional jank, the bike sections are quite enjoyable, the setting is slightly more varied, and some of the sections surpass MGR in their ridiculousness. The biggest issue that I have with the game is that some of the new game mechanics are only occasionally useful - so far ultimates and shadow clone seem like very situational abilities that I didn't get a whole lot of use out of. name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster
detailed_description: Supported Text Languages: - Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean - English, French, Italian, German, Spanish, Japanese, Korean, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese - Baten Kaitos Origins - English, Japanese, Korean, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese (Voice overs are in Japanese only.) About the Game Wings of the Heart Take Flight Once More Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean and Baten Kaitos Origins are now on Steam with improved graphics and new features to aid game progression, making them even easier to play! Delve into the world of Baten Kaitos as you strategize with the unique card-based battle system in these two immersive RPG masterpieces. Play as a guardian spirit who guides the colorful cast as they struggle against destiny itself. A long time ago, there was a great conflict between the evil god and the people. After a fierce battle, the people managed to seal off the evil god, but what was left behind was only a desolate land. The people thus chose to abandon the land and live in the sky. Such fairy tales were passed down as legends. At this time, people had wings called Wings of the Heart and lived a peaceful life. It was an era of long-lasting tranquility. ...But the collapse had quietly begun. When a young man calls your name, the name of the spirit, the story begins to unfold. A story set on a floating continent in the sky, where thoughts and prayers intersect. • Unique Magnus Battle System In the world of Baten Kaitos, the true essences of all manner of things, including equipment and items, can be extracted and stored inside cards called magnus. A magnus' contents can be released at any time, returning the magna essence sealed inside to its original form. These magnus form the basis of the Baten Kaitos battle system. Battles run in real time, so you'll need to employ quick thinking to select the right magnus for the situation. Strategize against enemies of various elements using elemental magnus of your own, and experiment with mixing and matching different magnus to discover and unlock powerful combo attacks! • Vivid Graphics Remastered in HD The two titles have been fully remastered in HD, including retouched battle backgrounds, character graphics, and UI. Enjoy Baten Kaitos with even more vibrant visuals. ・ Aspect ratio expanded from 4:3 to 16:9 for play on wider screens! ・ Main character and boss graphics have been completely renewed in vivid detail! ・ All-new menu screens! Enjoy smoother gameplay with refreshed menu layouts, newly added sorting features, and more. Pre-existing graphics have been used for in-game maps as well as some screens and character models. • New Features for Better Gameplay Along with improved graphics, the features below have been added to make game progression much smoother! ・ Auto-save feature ・ Help menu containing terminology and hints for progressing through the game ・ New Game+ mode, unlocked after clearing the game once, which starts a new game while retaining all magnus, levels, and ranks ・ New Game- mode, a mode with level restrictions for an extra thrilling challenge Six new game system options have now been added, including adjustable game speeds and no-encounter mode. Save your settings as a Custom Set and turn them on or off at any time.

_childDocuments_.review: I see a lot of reviews referring to nostalgia of childhood. Well, in 2004, when Baten Kaitos was released in North America, I was in high school; I guess that’s part of childhood. But I didn’t get to play it back then. I didn’t even have a GameCube. My nostalgia of these games comes from them being the first games I played after breaking up with my ex who took all the video games and consoles we collectively had, in 2012. I sat on a folding chair (because he took the couch) and played them on a cheaply bought Wii, on the inferior of the two TVs my ex and I had. It was a depressing time for me and Baten Kaitos/Origins were successfully a great distraction. I remember spending so many days doing nothing but playing these wonderful games with amazing stories that fully captured my attention that I completely forgot about my dreary reality. Upon the floating landmasses of the world, there objects known as End Magnus: powerful magnus once part of the evil god Malpercio. There are those who seek to resurrect Malpercio for their own gain and those who intend to restore the world to its original state, with the forsaken earth and the forgotten ocean.You, the player, are a guardian spirit who speaks to the protagonist Kalas throughout his journey. He occasionally seeks your advice and how you respond affects the bond between you.    • When Kalas speaks to the player, the guardian spirit, he talks directly to the screen, giving the feeling of “breaking the fourth wall.”      • While the game utilizes cards in battle, it is  a “card game.” The main focus is creating combinations, which could be done without use of cards; that’s merely the form they chose. (I feel the need to mention this because so many people are put off by the cards.) (Same for Origins.)    • Taking pictures of enemies during battle and selling them is how money is earned in the game. Bosses are worth the most, of course.    • Collections other than magnus: Star Map fragments, signatures for a  family tree, and animals from all over the world.    • It’s recommended to , as many players have complained about keyboard controls. My PS5 (DualSense) controller worked perfectly. (Same for Origins.)    • HD Remaster Additions: disable random battles option, auto-battle function, 1-hit kill option, simplified post-battle results, and New Game+ options that allow the player to retain items or alter gameplay to make a second playthrough more challenging. For more specific info:  (Same for Origins)    • Amazing story and worldbuilding. (Same for Origins.)    • The plot twist is one of the best I’ve ever seen in storytelling.     • Super fun battle system, because, , it’s  a card game. You put together combos, which is done in several other JRPGs, just not in card form like this one. (Same for Origins.)    • Unique, detailed character design. (Take a look at the artbook images online, if you come across them.) (Same for Origins.)    • For an older game, everything is so pretty and detailed. The HD remaster helped highlight that. (Same for Origins.)    • Enchanting and beautiful Motoi Sakuraba music. (Probably my favorite of his.)    • Non-binary rep. Yes, I mean Mizuti. Minor spoiler:     • No English dub. I genuinely had no issue with the original English dub other than the audio quality could’ve been better. (Same for Origins.)    • Awful romance execution.     • Several achievements require a second playthrough. (More so for Origins.)This is a prequel to , taking place twenty years prior.Once again, you, the player, are a guardian spirit who accompanies the protagonist. The story follows Sagi, who gets framed for assassinating the Emperor of the Alfard Empire, begins a journey to investigate why he was framed, and discovers other sinister plots. Sagi also, quite mysteriously, experiences visions of the past every time creatures known as “umbra” are slain in his presence; such visions predate the landmasses ascending to the sky, over 1,000 years ago.    • Money is acquired through winning battles, like most games. No pictures this time.    • You can pause at anytime during battles.    • Items can be traded to NPCs rather than sold.     • Collections other than magnus: pieces of the magnus town of Sedna, field guide entries (bestiary), letters (as in, correspondence from NPCs), and magnus mix recipes.    • Other side stuff: Coliseum and greythorne quests     • The flow of battle is better and it is much easier to create combos.    • Menu actually keeps track of sidequests (or “subquests”) this time.    • The ridiculous “You win!” after battles is funny. It’s like … thanks for letting me know, mysterious announcer guy.    • Non-binary rep. Guillo is a non-human character with a voice that’s simultaneously masculine and feminine. (They avoid using pronouns though.)    • Overall, the character development is better because there are only three main characters.    • The back-and-forth between past and present keeps the story interesting, as it takes a while before it’s revealed how they’re connected.     • It’s neat to see some side characters from the first game when they were younger.     • No pictures is boring and less lucrative. I had plenty of money in the first game. In Origins, you have to “grind” if you lack enough to get equipment and items.    • While you’re in the “Build Deck” menu, to get rid of things you no longer need, you have to move them to “junk” then sell them at shops, which adds an unnecessary extra step, whereas, you could just sell things directly from your inventory in the first game.    • A few rather notoriously difficult bosses that make players want to pull their hair out.     • Wiseman is kind of a “meh” villain. He’s just this … uh, once a dude? Who is obsessed with heart energy. He’s just not that interesting to me.    • While the romance is slightly better than the first game,  If you care about amazing stories and less about gameplay, you  play the game with “one-hit kill” on if you’re so appalled by the battle system. Though, you could save money and watch a Let’s Play instead. But for real, the battle system is not a card game. It’s just about making combos. It’s not confusing or complicated, and definitely not boring. It just makes me sad that so many people don’t play these games because they see cards and get uninterested, when they’re such good JRPGs.

Whoo boy!Let's see.. the graphics are noticeably worse, the voice acting is in mono, the audio mixing is all over the place and the volume generally too low, the new sound effects are much, much worse, the "QoL features" really don't help you at all (except for the much-beloved auto-save), there's not really any settings to speak of, alt-tabbing and/or using the Steam overlay breaks the game, the UI is a hot mess ripe with input delay, there's some really childish censorship going on (no, I don't mean that inane "yikes!" line that everybody is losing their mind over, I mean them changing every alcohol into juice or water, as well as changing some lines to make deaths less impactful.. as if we were infants in need of coddling instead of boomers who played those games two decades ago) and boy does the game lag for some bizarre reasonIt would seem they just dumped the Switch version on Steam without any sort of optimization, and called it a day! _childDocuments_.review: TL,DR: The Baten Kaitos games are both very interesting and unique 6th gen JRPGs that are well worth your time *if* you're an avid fan of the genre and are willing to overlook some game design quirks (OK, less "quirks" and more just straight-up flaws...) The collection is good and runs fine, but at essentially 50 bucks for two cult classics that are perhaps a bit more "cult" than "classic" it is a touch steep. I absolutely do not regret paying near full-price, but I am a Baten Kaitos 1 diehard, so I am already damaged... If you want to see what TENS of people have been going on about for 20 years, I do recommend both games, but I also suggest waiting for a discount. Baten Kaitos 1 is a strange and wonderful old-school JRPG from the GameCube, which together with Tales of Symphonia is near and dear to the hearts of all aging weebs who didn't have the foresight to ask their parents for a PS2 instead.Taking place in a psychedelic and lushly-realised world of floating continents and ancient secrets, your party of misfits has to foil the plans of an Evil Empire to collect all the Exodia cards and take over the world. The story and characters are both pretty good, although as the game goes on, there's a strong sense that some aspects had to be cut. It does all work out to an effective and memorable narrative in the end, but it definitely feels like some important details were just glossed over.The game is truly a feast for the eyes and ears. Baten Kaitos is both the pinnacle and last hurrah of pre-rendered 2D backgrounds. We never did see anything like it after... It also features hands-down the best soundtrack that Motoi Sakuraba (of Star Ocean and Dark Souls fame) has ever and probably will ever write, with a mix of epic orchestral and operatic songs, rocking prog-tunes and melancholy plin-plin-plonular piano melodies.Combat features an interesting and frankly rather half-baked card-based system that has a decent bit of hidden depth, but which is also badly in need of iteration and polish, on top of being very poorly tutorialized. If you master the combo system (a kind of poker-based damage multiplier), elemental resistances and special card fusions, you can get a lot out of battles. Combat is enjoyable, opportunistic, hectic and potentially quite strategic, but also frustratingly slow.Since basically everything in the game is all done with cards, there are a lot of unique items to find, which makes exploring the world and absorbing all the little bits of world-building scattered throughout towns rewarding and satisfying. There are also a number of large, game-long sidequests to complete as well as a number of smaller optional quests. There's a lot to get out of Baten Kaitos, if you're willing.Aside from the flaws present in the original game, the biggest complaints I have about the remake are some iffy changes to the script, the most egregious of which is that almost all references to alcohol have been scrubbed from the game, seemingly due to changes in Japanese ratings standards. Having barkeepers tell you they're keeping "Fruit Juice" in barrels in their BAR is just primo 4Kids-era cringe.Another unfortunate thing is that they removed the very crap, but very charming English voice acting from the game. I realize that the Japanese voice track is much better in basically every way, but I have such fond memories of Lyude going "THIS WILL CLEANSE THE EVIL OUT OF YOU!" before viciously beating on a tiny frog until it is mulch, that it still feels like a loss... Never releasing in Europe, this was the game I was most curious to play, and I must say that BK2 is a case of two steps forward, two steps back across the board.Taking place about 20 years before the first game, Origins tells the story of Sagi, a friendly young man who is roped into a tale of Imperial intrigue, industrial revolution and giant monsters along with his bickering sidekicks Guillo and Milly. The story is a mixed bag. It pulls a couple of strange and not wholly convincing retcons regarding the lore of the setting, which might upset diehard fans, but it also does some very cool stuff that will pleasantly surprise those same old fans. The party is also much better-characterized than in the first game. With only three playable characters, there is an abundance of charming moments between the three heroes.Gameplay-wise, BKO does a lot to fix and polish the flaws of the original, but in the process adds a number of new ones. Combat is snappier and less clunky, but also extremely confusing and samey. It also makes exploration and sidequesting MUCH less rewarding. You'll have your deck finalized by about halfway through the game and once you dig how the system works, almost every battle will feel identical. Combat is also much more challenging and consequently RNG-based, which can be quite frustrating. They have replaced a unique, but unpolished system with an equally unique, equally unpolished one...Overall, Baten Kaitos Origins is a more polished game in almost every way, but also less charming, psychedelic and memorable. Where BK1 was a strange, mythic tale of gods and secrets, BKO is a fairly normal, medicated JRPG with a quirky battle system. I'm glad I got to play it, but unlike the first game, I really don't see myself ever replaying this prequel.

_childDocuments_.review: I am biased. Baten Kaitos Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean was the first game I remember purchasing for full price with my own money I had earned from mowing yards back in 2004. :D I bought it entirely based off the cover art knowing absolutely nothing about it. So, it was a big gamble, but man did it pay off. I love these games.The backgrounds/settings are beautiful. The music is beautiful. The story is really good too, and has some major plot twists I did not see coming my first time playing, but maybe I was too just young to see them coming. :D I would not consider the combat to be a amazing, but the combat in each game is very unique, and with so many similar games being released nowadays uniqueness goes a long way.This version of the game does not include the English voice acting, and that is a shame. _childDocuments_.review: I loved the first game on the GameCube, but never got to experience the sequel. After well over a decade, I finally get the chance, and I can't be grateful enough.These are some great RPGs with unique card-based battle systems (each game's battle system is different), great stories with some amazing plot twists, and some of the best soundtracks I've ever heard.Now, there is one big problem with this release: the voice-overs are Japanese-only, with no option for an English dub. Sure, the English voices sucked (at least for the first game), but many players have a soft spot for the cheesy dub and miss it. Thankfully, there's a solution: if you look it up, you'll find an easy-to-install mod that restores the English voices. There are a few spots where the wording was changed, so the voice-over may occasionally differ from the text, but it's not a big deal and doesn't happen too often. This mod allows me to forgive this problem.Oh, and do be aware that these games may occasionally be very hard, even frustrating, but that's part of the charm. You have to master the unique mechanics like opposing elements, spirit numbers, and EX combos to succeed. There are options to skip combat by making all your attacks do a guaranteed one-hit kill, if a certain encounter is proving to be too much, and you can also disable normal enemy encounters if you find them annoying. I haven't had to use the one-shot mode yet (though I've been tempted, damn you Holoholobird), but I will turn on the no encounters option when I just want to make it through the dungeon without being interrupted.Oh, and cutscenes are skippable! This makes things way less annoying when you're fighting a difficult boss.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, it's amazing to see these games available on Steam in 2024.At the time of this review, I've only played the first game. My focus will be on the technical presentation since I haven't progressed far into the game yet and didn't play much of the original on GameCube either. Despite its age, the game has aged beautifully, thanks to its stunning background art and unique world design. The only aspect showing its age is the slow-paced combat, but some quality of life options have been added to mitigate this. More on that later.I'm playing it at a stable 90 fps on the Steam Deck OLED, and I haven't encountered the combat stuttering issues reported by some PC players. To completely stabilize the framerate, you can limit it to 60, lower your TDP to 8, and enjoy many hours of smooth gameplay before the battery runs out.Playing it on the Steam Deck is ideal, as the game fully utilizes the 16:10 aspect ratio, and the AI-upscaled backgrounds look fantastic on the OLED screen. While I would have preferred a different method to AI upscaling, it still looks good. Despite all of this, the game does not show up as Steam Deck verified and that is something I expect Bandai Namco to take care of before release, not after.Several quality of life options have been added and are much appreciated. You can speed up gameplay for dungeons and battle scenes (up to 300% for the latter), and you can also disable the battle intermission screens that appear after every turn, which made the original release feel slow. There are also options to remove any challenge from the combat, but I haven't tried those. It's great that they're available for those who just want to experience the story.One minor complaint is that the map screen for the first region doesn't fully utilize the 16:10 aspect ratio. Instead of adding simple black borders to the left and right, they opted for a dropshadow effect displayed on top of the background, which doesn't look great. This is nitpicking, though. I also wish you could switch between the two releases from within the game itself. Unfortunately, you have to use Steam's launcher option, which defaults to your last selection and might confuse some people about how to access the other game. It would have been better to have two separate Steam apps so we could display them in our library individually and only download the one we want to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I own this remaster on the Switch and when I saw it appear on Steam I bought it again instantly.If you're a fan of JRPGs and Card Battlers, you definitely should try these games!True hidden gems from the GameCube created by Monolithsoft and Tri-Crescendo.These two games feature an amazingly fun and unique Turn-based battle system (Baten Kaitos) and ATB-style system (Origins) combined with a card battler, have an amazing soundtrack composed by Motoi Sakuraba (also known for doing soundtracks for the "Tales of" games and "Dark Souls"), and beautiful pre-rendered backgrounds.The PC Port runs amazingly at a 120FPS cap, with no hiccups or crashes experienced so far. It also looks beautiful in 4K.I don't own a SteamDeck but according to others it runs flawlessly on it at 90FPS and supports the 16:10 aspect ratio.It would have been nice to see more graphical settings but these games aren't too graphically intensive, considering all the environments outside of battle and certain scenes being pre-rendered.

_childDocuments_.review: So when I saw this released, I was both shocked and excited... mainly because I had no idea it was in the works lol. But I loved the OG game on gamecube, so I pretty much immediately picked it up. For a remaster, it's pretty freaking good (Except those shopkeepers, stuff of nightmares lmao). Though my first impressions were a bit sour, not being able to display the PC hotkeys on screen when interacting with something or making an action, and perhaps most of all, we are unable to have the English voice-acting in this game. Initially, I felt regret, as I never played the original with the Japanese VA, so on a nostalgia level it really took the wind out of my sails.  The Japanese VA is good, no issues with it, it just wasn't what I expected.  It's my understanding they removed it since they made some changes that made the English VA not line up or something, and I'm sure thats a fine reason... but it's just odd lol.  English VA wasn't even the best, but it was nostalgia. After digesting those couple sour grapes, I still dove in. The original game is obviously a bit dated in general, but the remaster gives it a breath of new life, everything is still fluid (PC controls can be a bit hard to adjust to since you can't click things), we already know it has a great story, and now we can go through it without the grueling process of either finding a crappy port or finding a gamecube and going through the OG graphics in 2024 lol. All in all, I definitely recommend. Just keep in mind that there is no english VA, and if you play with mouse/kb, you won't be able to see the hotkeys on screen in-game; and I definitely recommend re-mapping them to whatever makes most sense to you. I did:-A=M2  -B=M1   -X=R   -Y=F   LB=Q   -RB=E   -LT=T   -RT=G   -Left stick=Z   -Right stick = Cand it feels more natural to me. Great Mizuti is still awesome, Lyude is still my favorite lol.

Anyone should give these games a try, from Balatro player or FF enjoyer anyone can find something amazing in these.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth the price of admission for BK Origins alone - a true GOAT from the GameCube era that still holds up today.  The first game is nothing amazing but it still has enough plot twists and pretty music to keep you engaged.  The removal of the English dub and minor script changes are a little annoying but nothing that detracts from the overall goodness here.  Runs buttery smooth on the steam deck as well.BK 1 - solid 7 / 10+Amazing music and art direction+Interesting (if unrefined) mechanics+/- Story and characters waffle between being engaging and rote+/- Original dub that is missing was frankly not that good, but cut content is not good either.-Babysitting decks for all the characters can get a little tedious.-Battles tend to be incredibly slow; turning up the speed isn't useful because then it becomes difficult to choose cards in the time allotted.-You need a great memory or personal notes to keep up with side quests and possibly story related progression if you take significant breaks.BK Origins - 10 / 10+Even better soundtrack, still solid visuals.+Improvements across the board to deck building, battles, side quests, in-game journal(s), etc.+Significantly less (but also way more useful) cards.+Fantastic story and characters; benefits from a smaller core cast.+Nice balance of difficulty - regular battles are breezy, bosses will test your skills and deck.-Loss of dub sucks for this one.-Takes place in same world as first game, so you see a lot of the same areas again.The additions of NG+ for BK and NG- for both games are welcome surprises.  There is enough content and QOL changes in each game to warrant the price, which is a steal for two niche JRPGs.  Hopefully this means we'll get Xenoblade eventually!
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: These are possibly my favourite games of all time. I don't have much to add that hasn't been said in the reviews already, but as an artist- this game was and continues to be one of my all time biggest inspirations. Everything is lovingly rendered from top to bottom, from the character portraits bursting with color, texture and emotion, to the lovingly hand-painted backgrounds on every new screen. The remaster does an excellent job bringing these elements back to life- I've caught myself staring at little details and brushstrokes in the scenery that I never noticed before- and the character models look a lot better now too. I've been thoroughly enjoying a long overdue replay of these games. Thank you to all the developers, artists, voice actors, musicians and other creatives that put their heart and soul into these games- your efforts have not gone unnoticed. <3
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: Two of my favorite JRPGs, played them back on the Gamecube and finished the first one again on Switch last year. PC port is pretty basic but works perfectly so far. Just like the switch version, the Remaster only has japanese voices, which, at least in case of Origins, is unfortunate. Graphic options only include Resolution, V sync and Anti-aliasing, but just playing this at higher resolutions and frame rates is great. I didn't encounter any bugs or crashes, but of course 6-ish hours is not nearly enough to give a final opinion on this. Controller Icons are for XBOX, mouse and keyboard are supported, but there are no icons unfortunately.The Switch Version of BK 1 had a few broken animations for two of the characters, not sure if they are fixed in this port, but I almost doubt it. BK 2 looks fine in that regard, I played 20 hours on Switch and didn't see any Problems like in the first game, but again, there might be some later. If I encounter some, I will update this review.So far I can recommend the Collection, even if it is a basic one. The combat alone makes these two games pretty unique, and combined with the fantastic music and great story, the collection is a very easy recommendation for Fans of JRPGs (even if the price seems a bit high for the basic nature of the port), especially since these two games are pretty niche.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute treasure of a GameCube title. I skipped out on Switch mostly hoping for a PC port as well as other improvements but I decided to just pull the trigger and get the Steam version once it showed up in my recommendations I had no idea it was released a week ago. The main drawbacks to these HD Remasters is lack of dub and some strange choices when it comes to button prompts (A to cancel, B to confirm). Hoping they patch that or include an a builtin mapping option. Some QoL improvements are nice and this appears be the same game I played back in 2004 with no real added content. The draw of this game is of course the deck building and a unique twist to your usual JRPG mechanics. Not many turn bases games give you the opportunity to react to your opponents attacks - the few that come to mind are the Mario RPGs, the recent Sea of Stars and Baten Kaitos. If you're into deck building games like Slay the Spire, you might end up liking this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like classic JRPGs (ala Final Fantasy I through IX, Chrono Trigger, Legend of Mana, etc.), you'll likely very much enjoy BK1 at least.  I first played BK1 when it came out on the GameCube in the States in late 2004.  I had forgotten much of the story, so it's been great to revisit this world.  I wasn't aware there was a sequel until this remaster came out, so I'm very much looking forward to delving into BK2 soon. Can't go wrong with two games for the price of one! :)Don't let the battle system scare you, either. It's a bit strange at first, and similar to card games like Magic, RNG can totally screw you over occasionally.  However, save points are plentiful, and I find it much more engaging to work with the cards I've been dealt (literally) versus digging through menus to take the "perfect" action.  I appreciate it more now that I'm older and have figured out that "close enough" is often just fine.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the first game, even though it has many flaws, its worth playing it at least once.The card system is actually very easy to learn, just focus on doing pairs or upwards or downwards straight without canceling the elements.I dont understand the hate for the magnus aging mechanic, sure it spoils many healing items, but improves other cards, also you get more than enough cards to ever make this an issue.The added gameplay options save time by skipping much of the grind and occasional backtrack.It feels like a smaller, learning project by Monolith Soft before making 4 straight masterpieces (Xenoblade 1, X, 2, 3).Story 8/10 - another world ending story but with some interesting twistsCharacters 9/10 - i liked the whole party, no one is annoying and all have interesting stories.Music 8/10 - very good music but very few tracks, they get re used a lotGameplay 6/10 - the combat is good, but keeping track of quest, quest items and quest magnus is a mess.Ending 10/10 - very satisfying, no loose ends, very lovely.Bought it on sale and already feel satisfied with the money spent and the first game.Going to play the second game and maybe add more thoughts after finishing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Both games are some of my favorite JRPGs from my middle school days. Deep and fantastical story, awesome battle system and cast of characters, some of Motoi Sakuraba's best tracks, all great stuff. _childDocuments_.review:
A long time ago, there was a great conflict between the evil god and the people. After a fierce battle, the people managed to seal off the evil god, but what was left behind was only a desolate land. The people thus chose to abandon the land and live in the sky.

Such fairy tales were passed down as legends. At this time, people had wings called Wings of the Heart and lived a peaceful life. It was an era of long-lasting tranquility. ...But the collapse had quietly begun.

When a young man calls your name, the name of the spirit, the story begins to unfold. A story set on a floating continent in the sky, where thoughts and prayers intersect.

Two JRPG masterpieces return. Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean and Baten Kaitos Origins are back with improved graphics and new features to aid game progression, making them even easier to play!

name: RKGK / Rakugaki
detailed_description: The city is your canvas. Join the rebellious Valah and her RKGK crew to free the neo-brutalist Cap City from evil B Corp’s control. Collect secret treasures, find hidden paths, and light up the cold and grey concrete with your graffiti. How fast can you go? Chain together jumps, dashes, glides, and grinds. Reach the perfect flow state in Defacer mode – where Valah’s world becomes her animated wonderland. Master routes and speed through levels as you take down Mr. Buff’s cronies with style. Break through enemies, overload your senses, and take back control. Use Valah’s paint abilities for stylish traversal, chaotic mayhem, and leaving your vibrant mark on every corner of Cap City. Channel your power through art and resist Mr. Buff’s mind-controlling technology. Restore freedom to the citizens of Cap City and test your abilities against the B Corp minions. Valah’s creativity and imagination is the spark to guide you through a dark, controlling world. Color is power. Graffiti is resistance. Use art as the ultimate expression to speak for the underdog and light up the world. With plenty of paint and cosmetic customization options, Valah can reclaim her city and look great doing it. RKGK / Rakugaki and Wabisabi are proud to be a part of Riot Games' Underrepresented Founders program, working together to help increase diversity in game development.

short_description: Turn heads. Drop jaws. Be bright. In this single-player 3D platformer, you’re the only one who can take down Mr. Buff and his lackies to restore color and life to the citizens of Cap City. Accompany Valah and the RKGK crew on their journey to take down the oppressive B Corp.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm digging this game so far, and I'll try to explain why in relation to some of the criticism it's been getting (because I think that will be more useful for prospective buyers).It is fairly slow-paced, but I don't mind this because I prefer slower-paced platformers over the ones where you go ultra fast anyway. If you're expecting something like Sonic Adventure then this is not your game, but if you want something closer to Super Mario Galaxy 2 or the Crash Bandicoot games (in terms of speed and momentum) then this is a lot closer to those.There is some momentum loss when you jump, but the faster you're going the less you lose (which I noticed during the boss battle) so it didn't really bother me. I think they did it this way so that you're not constantly overshooting the small platforms and objects (which would have been far worse IMO). They also mitigated this with an Air Dash which helps you maintain your speed if you're trying to go faster, so you have that choice between air dashing for speed or jumping normally for accuracy.I feel like the movement mechanics in this game have a high skill ceiling (if you want to go at top speed) and honestly, isn't that what we've been crying out for for years now? More games with high skill ceilings that don't just hold your hand? If you want to go fast and maintain your speed in this game then that requires a very specific playstyle, which obviously won't gel with everyone but I don't think it's an inherently bad thing either.I personally loved the visual design, music and story. The dialogue is a bit cringe but not enough to be a deal-breaker for me.The game is really polished so far, with no noticeable bugs or frame drops (I set the max frame rate to 60fps).Clearly this game isn't for everyone, and that's fine, but if you like 3D platformers and you want something that's a little bit different from the others then I would recommend this game (especially since it has a low asking price).
_childDocuments_.name: RKGK / Rakugaki

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid, simple albeit slightly conflicted game that unfortunately fell on misunderstanding ears. Not only did RKGK not sell well, it currently also sits at a wholly undeserved "mixed" reviews. It currently goes for 15 EUR, which is a very fair pricepoint for what it offers.RKGK is a very casually oriented movement platformer designed around speedrunning. It is very easy to play and tough to master. Some of the gold medal times this game demands for the levels are absolutely absurd. Unfortunately this was misinterpret by many people as "boring" - which almost certainly means they did not play the game as was intended. The latter is a bit of a consequence in how it presents itself; you can technically make your way through levels by not graffiti-gliding (the core mechanic of the game) and the game even seems to reward this to odd degrees - with many interactable object placed outside the fastest path to the goal. In reality this is not what the game wants you to do - it wants you to be as efficient as possible with your movement. And the game does feel quite good when things click together.The graffiti-gliding mechanic allows the player to generate momentum as if they were on ice. To compensate for the drag the player is also equipped with an immediate dash, allowing you to reset the orientation of your velocity. It's simple and it works. The game feels good when you go fast. Some levels have brilliant mechanics to compliment this movement - I especially enjoyed the level where parts of the geometry glow red before damaging the player - forcing them to skate in a tense weaving pattern.On the other hand the game has this very weird conflicting design, where it wants to reward both mastery of the mechanics as well exploration. The latter should have been pruned to maintain the integrity of the vision, and clearly the game paid the price for this by having these confused negative reviews. RKGK loves to place "collectables" outside the fastest path, contradicting its incentivizing of speed. It also has completely pointless meta-progression in the form of outfits. Just... why? Focus on making a good game instead of this tangential nonsense. If anything reward it for people playing well, as opposed to the opposite.Cool aesthetic, with nice mixed art, animated graffiti works. Soundtrack is very fitting if not a little generic for my taste. Sound design is servicable across the board.Just a solid game that unfortunately didn't quite play its cards perfectly. Absolutely deserves some love. Do not be deterred by the particularly badly uninformed negative reviews on this one.More reviews at .
_childDocuments_.name: RKGK / Rakugaki

_childDocuments_.review: It's decent, but could be better. 5/10.A 3D platformer that has emphasis on going fast with some of the challenges want you to clear the level in under 2 minutes, but the movement is not satisfying to make me want to go fast. You don't keep your momentum when jumping. No new mechanics to make you go fast other than hold L2 for 90% of the time. The platforming sections can be fun, with later areas gets more difficult, although you don't get introduced with new platforming mechanics to give each area some specialty. Your buddies do absolutely nothing other than offering cosmetics and an in-game OST player. Your hideout where your buddies reside is nothing more than a place to get new customization options (character, paint job, graffiti). It feels like the devs had the idea to put the hideout in the game very late in the game's development cycle, which would explain why the hideout is just so underwhelming. And your buddies, they have zero presence in the main story. Literally zero. It's just you versus one crooked bald man in lab coat for the entire story. As such, I feel that the game doesn't want you to care for your buddies at all. There's some light talk, but not enough to give enough character to your buddies.The story is okay I suppose. It's short, and I guess the devs already knew it's not going to be the game's strongest suit. You only get new dialogues when you face the area's boss, and a cutscene after defeating them. That's about it.Maybe get this game if you're a fan of old-school platformers which I guess is what this game is trying to appeal to. There's even a difficulty setting that caps your health to 3 and puts you back to last saved checkpoint if you fall off the ground to emulate the old platformers difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: Came into this expecting fast, momentum based movement, and was disappointed upon sprint-jumping and losing all momentum. Game isn't necessarily bad, but keep this in mind if you want something with a high speed. Feels more like an old-school 3d platformer a la Ratchet + Clank. Again, not exactly a bad thing, just not what I thought I was signing up for.
_childDocuments_.name: RKGK / Rakugaki

_childDocuments_.review: I see a lot of comments about the movement being slow, in a game meant to go fast, which I originally agreed on. But after clocking in 85 hours in the game so far, this is actually an issue of a higher than normal skill floor.RKGK is not a very beginner friendly game. Not in the sense that it's too hard, you can of course get through it if you try. But in the sense that if you actually wish to get gold medals on levels, and/or move fast, you can't just think the game is going to do it for you while holding forward.There are secret movement techniques that are not really explained in the game, but seems to be intentional, which both grants higher jumps, faster movement and ability to keep momentum when jumping (although you move the quickest while grounded).This game is probably not for everyone, but if you like 3D platforming with cool jump mechanics and you have the patience to learn, you will certainly enjoy it.
