_childDocuments_.name: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore the naysayers, this is a great game, and those who haven't played the original should at least play this. If you played the original and don't like the new look, why even buy it again?I discovered the original game a couple of years ago but never played it because a lot of time had passed already since the release and there was always something more recent in my backlog to play.Now I have played the remake twice or maybe even 2.5 times. I first played it in co-op mode with a friend and then played it in single-player mode. Purists might say that it should be played only in single-player, but I think it's better to share the experience. Both modes have different challenges, one is about trying to control two characters simultaneously, and the other is about communicating your intentions with the other player. After 2 playthroughs, I watched the included "making of" video and then hunted down all the remaining achievements.What has changed over the original? It no longer looks like a cartoon, the textures and levels are more detailed, the lighting is more realistic and the cutscenes are more professional movie-like.
_childDocuments_.name: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake

_childDocuments_.review: This version looks gorgeous. Areas and characters look better than ever, new design elements were added to them, and some unvoiced characters have received one. Some scenes were remade, and those are a huge improvement!...but there were some missing voice clips, slight graphical errors and the game even hitches above recommended hardware specs. Music is radically different, some hit a lot less hard during the most important scenes.Would say that the final ~30 minutes of the original are much better, but the first ~2.5 hours are vastly better in the remake. The remake also added a few new cinematic events which I quite liked. These are only a few seconds long at most, and you most likely wouldn't notice unless you played both back-to-back. A lot of them are an improvement to the game.If you have the hardware, play the remake. If not, the original is also arguably just as good. And again, the last two areas are much better there.
_childDocuments_.name: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake

_childDocuments_.review: A bit heavy on the graphics side as it uses unreal 5 especially for game this simple.Its the same as the original and is faithful to it, meaning it contains great memorable story and music, controls are the same which might turn some players off and the co-op mode is a nice addition but it defeats the purpose of playing this game as it was meant to be played with one single player.Overall a solid 8.0

_childDocuments_.name: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake

_childDocuments_.review: What a gorgeous game this is.It's like entering a potpourri of a classic brother Grimm adventure. The visuals here are... Stunning, because it so perfectly fits the setting. Great animations, fun challenges, touching moments... It's one of those small games that stands as a strong reminder of "AAA addicts" like me to also keep a keen eye on the indie scene.This is why we need that scene, really.I played this game in coop with my daughter, and it works totally fine. However I gotta say that the dual controller implementation is a bit lazy. In single player left side of the controller controls one brother while the right controls the other. And in coop, controller A still has the left side working while controller B has the right side. It just feels weird, they could have made both controllers more natural (move with left stick, right trigger for actions etc).But that's really all I have to say of negative sides of this game.It's a must-buy within their genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the original (though I watched it after playing this) I really loved this remake. Other than one slight complaint of 30 fps cutscenes I really loved it. Also, playing coop was so good. I know it was "designed for solo" but I think I liked it better playing with my gf than I would have playing it alone.
_childDocuments_.name: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake

_childDocuments_.review: This game stays mostly faithful to the original and the graphics are gorgeous! Both have their own charms, but really what this game nails is the character design! While the original has incredible character designs already, the remake really steps it up with the  The guard dog and other animal designs are much clearer in the remake. The remake also adds extra little cutscenes that are a nice treat to those who played the 2013 release. The character acting is phenomenal and really makes you feel sympathy for these characters and their experiences.One of my gripes is that the game can be a tiny bit janky with movement, but you kinda have to go out of your way to really break the game. You also have to have a decent graphics card to run this game at a smooth frame-rate or change the graphic settings to a low setting yourself.Overall I give this game an 8.9 out of 10 and I definitely think it is worth checking out if you played the original or just want to try out this experience blind!
_childDocuments_.name: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake

_childDocuments_.review: This Game is awesome! I mean, like if you have played the original; This remake hasn't changed besides the graphics. If you wanted new content; don't buy it. The storyline is an absolute gem—I've lost count of how many times I've immersed myself in it, whether solo or with friends. Sure, it's a bummer that online co-op isn't included, but fear not! With a solid internet connection, you can still share the experience through remote play. Plus, even if you embark on this adventure alone, it's guaranteed to keep you entertained.And let's talk about that soundtrack and storyline—they're simply breathtaking! I absolutely adored the old player models, but let's talk about the landscapes—wow, they're absolutely breathtaking!  And those controls? Sure, they're a tad unconventional at first, but once you get the hang of them, they add a whole new layer of immersion. It's exhilarating to navigate the journey controlling both brothers with such finesse.The controls are unusual because you play the big brother with the right controller side and the little brother with the left. But this isn't quite bad. It's just unusual and sometimes a little bit hard to focus on 2 characters and 2 controller sides. I found myself tearing up nearly every time I played this game.So please, do yourself a favor and give this game the chance it deserves. It might not be the longest experience, but trust me, the beauty of its story will stay with you long after the credits roll. If you crave an adventure that's equal parts thrilling and emotionally resonant, look no further—this game is an absolute must-buy!

_childDocuments_.review: Targeting modern PC’s and current consoles, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake was rebuilt using Unreal 5 to offer striking visual upgrades as well as a newly recorded soundtrack with a live orchestra that elevates the emotions of this game to new heights.  Characters have more complex and emotive faces with moving lips, and environments have been rebuilt with Nanite for increased complex geometry and rendered with stunning new textures.  Animations have been enhanced, specifically character turning, and everything runs silky smooth at 60fps.  At times, the game can easily be confused with a feature animated film when the light and shadows are working just right.  The new Lumen lighting makes the dark forest level even more sinister as you chase off hungry wolves with your torch.  The only critique I have for graphics is that the cutscenes are 30fps and contrast sharply with the gameplay visuals.The developers did a fantastic job of preserving the original material while adding nice flourishes to the overall experience and even a couple of new achievements.  One of the more controversial decisions was to add a true co-op feature which, in my opinion, negates the core design philosophy of the game and totally impacts that “one emotional moment” at the end of the game.  Apparently, a lot of people were playing the original Brothers by both using a single controller, so the devs just added a true co-op mode and thanks to Remote Play Together you can now play this couch co-op game remotely.  I can certainly see the appeal, and playing co-op will definitely shift the focus from manual dexterity to cooperative conversation.Simply put, if you enjoyed the original then you are going to love this masterfully crafted remake that takes all the heart and soul from an already amazing adventure and turns it up to eleven.Read the full review at More Steam reviews on our Curator page -

_childDocuments_.review: Breathtaking Revival of a Classic TaleThe remake of Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons stands not only as a testament to the original's heartfelt storytelling but also as a beautiful homage that builds on its legacy with modernized graphics and gameplay. This re-imagined adventure, deeply rooted in Nordic folklore, unfolds with a fresh coat of visual beauty that breathes new life into the enchanting world. The art direction is nothing short of magical, capturing the essence of a fairy tale that deserves to be retold. I can't help but bring up the delightful encounter with an oddly charming 'punk rocker looking' troll early in the game—an addition that is both whimsical and touching. Connecting with such characters enriches the experience, making it feel like a living storybook that's unfolding right before your eyes.The puzzles within this world are cleverly designed, providing the right balance of challenge and ingenuity without creating a sense of urgency that detracts from the narrative. It's this pacing that allows you to truly absorb every element, from the rustling leaves in the mythical forests, the eerily beautiful ruins of long-forgotten civilizations, to the countless individual and environment encounters you can engage with. One such encounter unlocks an achievement by picking up a sheep and spinning around with it in your arms until it barfs!For sure the harmony of the controls truly sets the game apart; the innovative mechanics have you maneuver two brothers simultaneously, forging a connection between player and characters that is rare and profound. (AND IT'S CO-OP!) It's a game that knows the power of its story and the strength of its silent moments of bonding, grief, and triumph."Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" is a masterfully crafted story experience. Whether you're returning to relive the adventure or stepping into the shoes of the brothers for the first time, this remake is an invitation to an odyssey that will tug at your heartstrings and ignite your imagination.

_childDocuments_.review: Check out my full review on YouTube! Please note I refunded the game on Steam and completed the rest of the game on PS5. Full details explained in the video :)Let me first agree with the litany of steam reviews saying if you have already played the original, there is not much more here for you. But if you are fresh to the game, then you need to work out what kind of experience you are after. If you are prepared to go through boring chore work and traversing for some not new, but touching ideas and concepts, then this might be for you. But it gets complicated when you add in that 2nd player.I believe when you add in the second player, whilst it improves the gameplay, it may impact how you receive the story. I will admit when I was playing this game with my brother, we were cracking jokes, laughing and at some points not really taking it seriously, whereas I feel if I was playing by myself, then I might have been more receptive to some of those tones and themes. But the paradox is if I was playing by myself, then I wouldn’t have bothered finishing the game. Now A Ways Out and It Takes Two found ways to do it, those games you have to play with two people and in both my playthroughs of those games, one being with my brother, we both felt that core impact in the message the game was presenting. Thankfully at the $30 price tag, I think those themes are worth exploring and despite the dated feel, Brothers still will make you stop, question and cherish aspects of your own life and perhaps spark an appreciation for the things or people that matter most to you. Yes there are some gameplay obstacles and a paradox to navigate as both modes to play the game come with their compromises, but if you have a couple hours to spare and a little bit of patience, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons the Remake will reward you for the time you took to listen and understand the values enshrined in this acquired taste of video game art.

_childDocuments_.review: The main draw of this remake compared to the original isn't the visuals, in my opinion. It does look gorgeous, and I think it's a genuine noticeable improvement both in terms of the graphical quality and the emotional impact of certain cutscenes, but what the original lacked in raw technology it made up for with an art style that I think holds up relatively well for what it is. To me, the new appeal of this game is in the addition of the local co-op mode. It does make the game a lot easier when you don't have to coordinate the brothers yourself (it sometimes starts to feel a bit more like a narrative game than a puzzle platformer), but I found myself surprised at how well it worked, and it reminded me more of the games Hazelight would go on to make than I realized back when I first played this. I don't think this game requires co-op in the same way that A Way Out or It Takes Two do, but it's more viable than I thought it would be.In either case, whether you play the remake or the original or singleplayer or co-op, Brothers is a fantastic game that I'm happy to return to, particularly since I think it was kind of overlooked in comparison to their later games. But I should warn that from what I'm seeing from the other reviews, the optimization here is extremely rough. I'm running a 4070 ti so I didn't have any issues, but I also averaged at around 70 fps even with DLSS, and the game in general seems heavily CPU-bound. If you don't have a considerably strong PC, it might be good to wait for updates, if they come; until then, there's no shame in sticking to the original.

_childDocuments_.review: The original  is one of my favorite games. Despite the clunky controls, the rich art and music, vibrant world, beautiful story, and one of the most brilliant marriages of mechanics and narrative I can think of made the experience extremely memorable. Was it a game that particularly needed a remake? Not really. So how does the remake measure up? Overall, fine, though I wouldn't call it a straight upgrade. The environments and the lighting look gorgeous, but in some places they've lost some of the style of the original. The soundtrack, too, sounds wonderful independently, but in some places it sounds a little too grand for the story. The biggest detractor from the remake is the new character models, which don't really suit the game or the story. The best thing the remake did is improve mouse and keyboard controls, which work much better than they did in the original. I enjoyed my time with the remake, but overall I think the original was the superior experience--minus the frustrating mouse and keyboard controls of the original.

name: Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior
detailed_description: After half a millennium of peace, a new danger hangs over Antala. Its fate depends on you, Imë, Lysfanga of the New Kingdom, protector of the realm. The ancient cities, previously locked in time, are now free again, and an old evil has escaped, threatening the peace. But you won’t be alone. Gifted with temporal powers from the Goddess of Time herself, something no other Lysfanga has had before, you have the ability to rewind time in combat to summon clones of your past-selves to help you. Master your power to become legion, and crush hordes of the escaped demons, known as the Raxes . With your army of past-selves , progress through the ancient cities to extend your arsenal of weapons and learn new spells, preparing for the much greater threat ahead... Use Imë’s godlike powers to rewind time a few seconds in the past and summon clones of yourself – remnants – to create an army and overpower your enemies. Challenge your skills and your wits to outdo yourself. Master and replay each arena to beat your high scores, and challenge yourself by changing the difficulty settings and adding combat modifiers to unlock new rewards. Each arena can be approached in countless ways. Adapt your strategy and use all the tools at your disposal to emerge victorious. Success will only depend on your combination of remnants, spells and weapons. The old time-locks are gone. The Raxes are now free to create chaos again. Explore the abandoned cities of the old continent previously locked in time and uncover the truth behind the resurgence of the Raxes.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hyped for this after seeing the reveal at last year's Gamescom but after finishing the main story I'm fairly disappointed. The game does some things well: the world-building and lore are fantastic and add a lot of life to the game, and the resulting plot of ancient rival kingdoms and the conclusion to centuries-old grudges is also quite engaging. The gameplay concept of hack and slash meets strategy with time-shifting mechanics to solve puzzles is also great on paper. Where I feel the game lacks overall is in its execution. The aforementioned plot is brought down by lifeless characters and stilted, oftentimes 'gamey', dialogue, and the gameplay falls into this awkward middle ground between its two genre inspirations, not leaning enough into either to feel particularly rewarding. Other than being able to survey the battlefield arenas before a fight there are no features to allow you to deeply strategise (things like being able to pause and zoom out to see where and what your remnants are doing as a potential example of something that would help), and because arenas are time gated and set up as puzzles the hack and slash elements are restricted. Another fault lies in how utterly repetitive the game gets. Exploring feels unrewarding due to generic collectables and linear-level design, so all that's left is arenas and combat that play out similarly each time. It's a shame too as the art style and levels look gorgeous, and when the combat deviates from its basic premise, like in the boss fights, it can be incredibly fun. Overall a lot of cool ideas, just lacking the execution for me, but worth a buy if you know you enjoy the combat as there is a good bit of depth in the game with varying levels of goals and challenges to aim for.

_childDocuments_.review: Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior is an . But it’s also a game that , since that’s firmly where the core of its gameplay lies.So first things first: I’m seeing lots of people compare this game to other games which I think have very little in common with Lysfanga. Some expect it to be an isometric action RPG like  or . This is not the case, as  instead of being randomised or procedurally generated. Other people compare Lysfanga to , which is perhaps even more confusing, since   (from the same developers as ). Much like , Lysfanga is all about following mostly linear paths from one combat arena to the next, and all fights are essentially handcrafted combat puzzles that task you with dispatching your enemies in the most efficient way possible. Both games are also :Fights in Lysfanga are  featuring a bunch of enemies with unique gameplay mechanics – some of them carry heavy shields which make them invulnerable from the front, others are magically connected in pairs of two so both enemies have to be killed at roughly the same time or else they’ll revive, and so on. . You can repeat this multiple times, creating more and more ‘remnants’ of yourself, until you’ve reached the maximum number (which can be further increased with collectibles). So now you can spend one loop getting the attention of the large shield-bearing enemies, and use your second incarnation to backstab that same enemy while they’re distracted by your previous self. The gameplay loop repeats for every combat encounter: .Now, normally I’m the kind of player who quickly gets tired of constant combat in games, and I usually prefer my combat to be more organic, with enemies roaming the world instead of being corralled into self-contained arenas. But Lysfanga does enough to keep me entertained and motivated throughout, by giving me lots of  to flesh out the story and setting, as well as some collectibles to hunt. Sure, , but the storytelling and easy-to-find collectibles create just about enough variety to tide me over. As should have become clear by now, however, this is very much a ‘your mileage may vary’ situation and I can absolutely see how the formulaic arena-hallway-arena-hallway structure of the game may become tedious to other players. Worst-case, you don’t even like the idea of the time loop mechanic that’s so central to the game, at which point I’d say Lysfanga is a definite ‘pass’ for you, because that’s pretty much the entire gameplay right there.But if time loop puzzle fights sound interesting to you and you don’t need much more than some collectibles and story dialogue for variety, . Having played the original Itch.io build from when the game was a humble student project (called “Lysfangha” instead of “Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior” – I can see the SEO and PR teams hard at work there), I’m doubly impressed by how they managed to take their already gorgeous visuals and their interesting gameplay idea, and turn them into a full-fledged game with a constant drip of story segments as well as new abilities, weapons, and enemies to keep you entertained. That alone may be enough reason to support a fledgling development studio, and let’s be honest: Many other small studios have also started by focusing on perfecting a very limited set of gameplay systems instead of going for massively complex games for their first outing ( comes to mind, since I’ve already name-dropped  and  here). Who knows where Sand Door Studios may be headed if Lysfanga sells well enough...

_childDocuments_.review: Under a hundred steam reviews on a game of this quality is really quite saddening to see. This is a good little combat puzzler with an interesting world with lots of lore to read, a pleasant, adventurous atmosphere and some solid time loop gameplay as you and your copies run around defeating enemies as fast as possible.If it suffers from anything (other than being completely overlooked), it's how it feels like a game of two halves, and they don't always complement each other in the best ways. There's the story, cutscenes and exploring the environments for upgrade spheres, bits of lore and new outfit colours. It's all pleasant and interesting enough, if maybe not the most gripping and sharply written stuff. It's got an air of a saturday morning cartoon, a kind of "we can do this, together!" tone that can be both endearing and a little on the nose in equal measures. I appreciate it avoids going for too much melodrama, and a hopeful, positive tone is definitely welcome.The other half, the thing that really makes the game special, is the combat puzzles, but if you are following the first half, the narrative, you will just bash your head against each encounter, mashing away at enemies, taking hits, dying, looping again, until you either run out of copies and have to restart the encounter, or you eventually clear it.But in order to really make the mechanics of the game sing, you need to play, and replay each encounter until you reach the presented par times. These really bring forth how carefully planned each encounter actually is, and how much depth all of your abilities and skills have. Each encounter adds a new skill or a new enemy type or some new twist to shake things up. Playing for the par times really pushes you to plan your routes carefully, requiring clever use of timing, placement and the kind of 5-dimensional chess stuff you'd only expect in the weirdest, most demanding indie puzzlers. Destroy this thing here, so that it opens a gate for your next copy to dash past to get to the exploding enemy sooner, so you can launch it against another group of enemies you will be fighting with your third copy, which will free up the crystal your fourth and fifth copy can destroy together before the fifth one can join the second one and distract the shielded enemy for the fourth copy can smash through the other crystal and-" and it's really compelling stuff. It's just that it gets really tough, and it can be exhausting after several of them back to back. And so you kind of end up with a choice: do you proceed with the story, intending to maybe replay previous fights later for the par times? Ignoring the par times and just going for normal completion means the combat encounters can start feeling repetitive and more than a little annoying interruptions when you're trying to just get on with the plot. Ignoring the par times, there is no challenge really, you just run against the wall until you clear it. OR do you grind story progress to a complete halt, embrace the robust play mechanics and really learn and route every encounter to get the most out of the gameplay and reach those par times? You risk exhausting yourself, but it's a more rewarding game to PLAY. It's just that there is a LOT of encounters.So it's hard. I don't know how to solve that problem, and neither did the team. They chose, probably very wisely, to let you take everything at your own pace, and hope you will have a good enough time to want to engage with the deeper mechanics when going for the par times later. By request the team updated the game and added online leaderboards for comparing and competing for the best times in each encounter. They even added even more optional challenges for replaying past fights, with additional modifiers, enemies and tricks. If you don't exhaust yourself, there is a wealth of stuff to play, but if you're just trying to "get on with it" a lot of that feels like it's just in the way.So it's not perfect, but it has a lot of love put into it, and I have to stress how rewarding reaching those par times is. I hope the team gets to make another game, I'd love to see what they do next.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost the bulk of the content should be taken more as a puzzle combat game, and less as a sheer mechanical skill check. I thoroughly enjoyed routing each encounter and pushing the times below the challenge benchmarks, and hope to continue my time perfecting every encounter to reach 100% completion.There is mechanical skill, but it honestly is much of a side factor compared to the strategy and planning each encounter demands you do. The move set of each weapon is individually simple, but combined with the large quantity of different active and passive abilities to choose from it leads to many interesting approaches for each combat encounter. --  in particular is worth calling out, as once unlocked it opens up huge depth to how you can interact with the time-loop mechanic. It was my go-to active for the majority of the game.Other elements of the game are serviceable for what they are; the story gets fairly predictable, the characters are tolerable enough, and the environments look good, albeit slightly irritating to navigate at times.The largest disappointment with the game I had was the "Motes of Magic" system, which are collectible items you can pick up throughout your whole journey. They are entirely useless until around half way through the game, when you recruit a smith. -- I expected these to be another form of character upgrade to reward diligentexploring, but ultimately they ended up just being purely cosmetic. The game already had completely separate cosmetic collectibles. Why bother making two entirely separate and conflicting systems for cosmetics?Overall, I highly recommend Lysfanga.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of reviewing I'm not too far in, but I think I'm ready to give my thoughts! Once I finish the game I might put an edit at the end if my opinion changes further in. Honestly? Pretty solid game! There's definitely some parts that are more rough around the edges, but I'd say the good absolutely outweighs the bad! I'd give about an 8 out of 10 on the whole.Incredible. A good gameplay loop is a top priority for me in games, and Lysfanga does not disappoint. I'll admit that I picked up this game primarily because its combat kinda looked like Hades and I wanted to play something Hades-like that... wasn't Hades (I play too much Hades lol—also go play Hades it's good). There's definitely some superficial similarities to Hades in Lysfanga's action elements (two different attacks, a cast, dashes, and a call) but in practice it plays completely differently—in a very good way.This is obviously due in part to the headlining time-shift mechanic. It lets you replay the same battle scenario over and over as your Remnants perfectly replicate your prior movements, allowing you to tackle other new areas while they handle the work you've already completed, which by itself would be an interesting gimmick.However, it's the hard work that the developers put into the   that elevate the time-shift mechanic out of gimmick territory into something...  I can identify 2 things in particular that contributed to this: handcrafted encounters and the timed challenges.Each and every encounter in the game is entirely built by the developers. This means that instead of enemies being placed haphazardly or procedurally,  is placed with a purpose. This, combined with the fact that each encounter has an optional time challenge (which I consider required for optimal enjoyment), means that you really have to strategize about where you go, who you hit, how you hit them, and when you do all of this. You can't really afford to just mindlessly go to the nearest enemy: you have to think about it.   is what makes the game so good. There's a kind of cerebral satisfaction that I get when I'm on the last loop of a really hard room and you see all of your Remnants go and expertly take down an entire army of monsters at once  within the time limit that I haven't gotten from another game before. This game struggles with crashing the most out of any game I've played. To be fair, the games I play are usually polished very, very well so I might not be the right person to ask, but it is enough to be bothersome. My issues usually happen while menuing—if I switch too fast between the menu and gameplay or in a specific spot, the game crashes. My rig is no slouch either, so I doubt it's a hardware issue. There are also a couple of occasional framerate issues; for example, there's an area early on where there's a wall with a few waterfalls coming out, and I went from a smooth 60 fps to chugging at 25. The environments are actually quite pretty, for the most part! I'd say that my big issue with them is the fact that they feel WAY more constrictive than I think they should. Sometimes I think "oh I want to go look over there", but then there's this convenient pile of rubble and tables blocking the stairs. It kind of breaks immersion for me because it reminds me that it's not a real game world: it's just a path from point A to point B. This isn't always the case though—occasionally the game rewards you for going off the beaten path, but then it just feels like that's the only reason you were supposed to go off the path at all. Idk, I feel weird about this, take it however you will.This is an opinion from early gameplay, but I get the feeling that the rest of the game is like this.Hit and miss here. Sometimes it's done well, sometimes not. I have gotten a couple of laughs out of the intentionally funny bits though! To be honest I'm not terribly invested in the story yet, but who knows, maybe it'll get better? This is a bit of a downer, because gameplay and story are both really big elements for me. Here's hoping hahaDefinitely recommend this from what I've seen so far! Not a perfect game, but creative and ingenuitive in ALL the right ways. With a bit of bug-fixing and optimization, I could recommend it a little more strongly.

_childDocuments_.review: This thumbs up comes with a word of warning - AMD video card users need to be wary, as there is currently an issue that can cause the game to crash in menus from time to time on 6000/7000 cards (had it crash my video card drivers over 10 times over the course of completing the game, necessitating a system reset each time) - wager this will be fixed with patches eventually (hopefully), so be sure to check any upcoming patch notes.As for the actual game, outside of that issue, and why I give it a thumbs up - it is actually a decent game, with an okay story, if you're looking for what amounts to essentially an action puzzler (aRPG combat, with more 'puzzle-like' combat arenas) - I also hope that some of the weird gremlin bugs (ie bugs that are hard to reproduce) are fixed in the future too - namely a bug with a unit called "boombats" that makes them malfunction on death (getting stuck in dying animation, rather than doing their death explosion effects - and can sometimes result in them flying weird directions), as well as the game sometimes forgetting an enemy got killed, even if you avoid interacting with it in future loops.Neither were super consistent, and I was unable to find a specific, repeatable, trigger for them, but they were there.Game will take 7-12 hours to reach the credits on a casual playthrough, but some people will sink a lot more in it to get all the achievements and extra bits and bobs for 100%. Completing the game is relatively easy, targeting the optional time goals on the maps can sometimes be moderately difficult, and there are higher difficulty challenge maps to try too, but they're mostly optional.If you want to see the full video review, you can check it out here:

_childDocuments_.review: For the love of god let us skip Cut scenes, and stop wrestling control from me every 5 steps, also while i appreciate that you want us to look around a arena before the fight starts dont do it, it completely takes you out of the moment if we fail the time limit because we cant preview the arena thats fine, you actually did a really good thing by putting the fragments to try again either in the arena or close by so they are supper easy to get to, and we are not punished for failing the time limit so lean into the fact that those 2 parts of your design are good and just let the game flow naturally until THE player decides to slow it down and do extra stuff. _childDocuments_.review: A really nice game. The gameplay is easy to pick up and very effective. You immediately understand what to do and how to make the powers interact with each other, which is very intuitive and enjoyable. Combat can be a little repetitive at times, but the new enemy types, new stipulations and new scenery make it quite varied in the end, so you don't get bored. As for the game's technical and artistic aspects, I find it graphically beautiful. The universe is a real success, and it's a pleasure to get caught up in the game and discover the story. The story is fairly simple and basic, but that's not a flaw. It's a fairly classic story, but one that's fun to follow and discover. It's all served up by an original soundtrack, beautiful graphics and beautiful music. I totally recommend the game. Give a chance to independent developers who try to make small, original, complete works with more than reasonable monetization for the content offered by the game. Bonus point for Sitiss.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm having a lot of fun with this game so far, having finished Act One. Combat is puzzle-based with encounters centered around defeating enemies using time-shifted clones, each having an optional time goal that effectively translates to defeating all enemies using as few clones as possible. The earliest zone is somewhat repetitive, but combat variety increases substantially as the player progresses - via new enemies, spells, weapons, and other mechanics. The world itself is charming and polished, supported by solid graphics and strong sound design. Lysfanga is conceptually unique and I recommend giving it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: A quite successful game, the first time I saw it at "Gamescom" it caught my attention. The game is presented in a good and captivating way. The way the game is built is a good one and it blends very well with the story. ( the world-building and lore are fantastic and add a lot of life to the game ) The idea of ​​the game is an interesting one, being represented by the war between two ancient kingdoms and the desire for revenge, at the same time combining in a good way with the rediscovery of the family and the discovery of a new warrior to end the war that lasted for centuries. The gameplay is quite simple:--> action--> hack and slash ( which combines in a very good way with the unique mechanics of going back in time )--> puzzle / challenging ( only if you want to experience more and you are not here just for the story ) Overall, a pretty successful game, with a captivating story and some great ideas in gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior

_childDocuments_.review: The world, characters, lore etc. is all very dull and unimpressive. The combat is definitely fun for a while, but wears dull about 2-3 hours in. If there was anything here worth it for me to keep going, I would've been able to recommend it. But the combat gimmick isn't strong enough and the rest left me feeling underwhelmed and not wanting to continue playing. Refunded it.
_childDocuments_.name: Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Well worth your time - smart, fun, detailed, gorgeous, and makes you focus on your timing and combat execution as much as your movement and routing across multiple runs through a single encounter.I came into this from a quick brush with the trailers thinking it was Super Time Force x Hades, but left my first (short) session with it suitably impressed with what it is instead: an action puzzler where the goal is to work through each independent, hand-crafted combat puzzle in as little real-world time as possible. No randomization or rogue-lite/light elements (so far), no stacking up well-placed "remnants" to nuke a boss in record time (again, I'm barely clear of the tutorial here), but instead it has you focus on movement, combo execution, and manual rewinds to keep your total real-world time under each encounter's par. It feels almost closer to a more level-based speedrun game like Neon White in general structure and goals. The leaderboards for this will be crazy once people really get their hands on this.
_childDocuments_.name: Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior

_childDocuments_.review: The premise for this game is so simple, yet so brilliant, that it hooked me right from the first trailer, then the demo, and the game itself. This is a game to hone your skills, like Ghostrunner, Hollow Knight, Katana Zero, Commandos, etc.The game is very tactical. Some kind of 1-character DotA with a Commandos-like pre-game analysis phase and Katana Zero post-game analysis. It is not just one gimmick, though. New game mechanics will keep coming up, adding more and more depth till the end, so it doesn't get repetitive. If you like to repeat a boss or a challenge, you can, you can even play an 'enhanced' version of the fight if you want to practice.As the story goes, Imë, an iron-abs Eastern-looking woman who would give Krishna a run for his money, but with a very British accent, goes on an adventure. In which she can spawn multiple images of herself to do her job in parallel, perhaps a not so different dynamic compared to the modern iron-abs British lady life. She has an even more British-accented brother, who she will try to save from some dark web things, and between fights and sips of Earl Grey, they will meet ferocious magical (but very Britishly polite) beasts. She will also eat nuts which she will crack with her abs.The discoverability of this game has been very bad. My favourite game of the year so far, and hard to imagine a game along these lines coming up anytime soon. Yet I haven't seen it in any trending or top 10 of any kind, buried below the mountains of anime nonsense. I just wish this game gets the recognition it deserves.

_childDocuments_.review: Lysfanga is a rundimentary top down Action-Hack'Slay, with the typical what I would call "blink combat" fighting system. Your natural dodge is a short teleport, besides this, there is not that much going for it. You unlock 3 weapons over the course of the game with basic combo potential and one secondary attack as well unique properties. The sword & shield is the only weapon that can stun enemies for a split second, the Chakrams can be thrown and do great AoE-dmg if the the normal attack is pressed right when the charkam was catched again and the trident has a storable ranged AoE attack, that need to be charged first by quick normal attacks.Overall the weapons are well balanced and there is an justification for all of them I thought the trident you unlock last might be very strong with it's piercing attacks, but it's biggest downside is it's aim, as all attacks have auto-attraction to the closest enemy, while the spear has the lowest wide range of all weapons.This is a solid foundation albeit still quite simplistic, but that basically suffices, there is a customizable component as well, you have one additional magic attack with an cooldown that can be swapped between battles, one ultimate attack (where you have to fill up an bar) and an passive perk, that gives you one advantage like making more damage from behind and such shenanigans.I think the game pretty much nailed the right amount of simplicity, so it doesn't overload you cognitively if you try to accomplish the tasks which the premise of the game provides.You have only about 20 seconds to kill all enemies on the field. Since that doesn't suffice, you're able to go back in time. Yet your past self will remain as an clone unhindered by the present, yet able to damage the enemies, your player performance was recorded and is executed again, now it's on you to kill the remaining enemies called "Raxes".Basically this results in two interesting tasks, for one you have be wary not to distract the beaten enemies, so the past can play out unhindered and second: you have to fully utilize this abilitiy to kill the Raxes as optimized as possible, reducing the downtime to an minimum, basically at best letting all cycles end at the same time with no buffers between.With that in mind a more complex combat system would highly detract from the more puzzle/tactical orientated approach. Enemies are simple and serve to create an interesting level layout to untangle. So if you expect an combat heavy game isometrical game you will be probably disappointed, you are so under time pressure, that you're rather relieved if you kill the enemies as fast as possibe.Unfortunelately that also means you can never really adore your elegantly planned out route, since the game has no replay function or at least an end result where you can watch your temporal clones working together.The first levels are quite simple and like it should be in all games, each of the 3 worlds slowly ramps up the difficulty, new enemy types will be introduced, some of them are more sturdy and dangerous (you can still die, which just ends the current cycle and starts the next one) but most of them serve an purpose that forces you to consider the order how you kill the enemies. Like there are "Twins" who need be killed relatively close within an 3 seconds timespan or Raxes with huge shields who can be only killed efficiently if they are are distracted by a past clone or if you use up an ultimate attack. This will always force the player to carefully lay out their path and incrementally new elements will be introduced even near the end of the game.While I really like complex game mechanics it also comes with a detriment as I thought that the later levels became quite straining, there was so much to consider, that each level took me some time, it's not a game where you can just turn your brain off as well one where you most likely won't succeed the first time... well at least if you try to accomplish the "par times".Actually the game is quite easy, almost trivial if you merely play for the storyline, since you can only truly die if all your "remnants" are used up. These are the amount of clones you can create when rewinding the time, and the numbers increases steadily at the end of the game you have 15 clones, So you have to become hit 30 times at minimum until you die and then the whole screen is already crowded with clones doing 14 times the damage. I think the par times are there to make the game more interesting with actual time requirements, otherwise you can play as sloppy as you want. Though asides from achievements there are no further stipulations for the time requirments and most of the time they still felt rather benelovent. Just low enough to require you to fully utilize the level layout, but high enough that you didn't really have to optimize the right approach. This makes the early levels really underwhelmingly easy with par times beat about under 20 seconds and more, the later levels yet will be a bit harder, since they are just more complex and like I said complex to a straining level.At some point there are enemies, you have to kill twice, respawning at another place, shields you have to deactivate first, switching polarities each cycle, enemies that can be only killed if you killed other enemies, enemies only vulnerable to specific weapons, closed gates, alternating gates, yada yada yada, and each of it eventually becomes topped on another, at some point there are even vertical stages where you can't see the whole layout at once. It's quite rewarding when you figure it out, but sometimes it also feels quite exhausting considering the game doesn't have much else besides it's combat.Yes the game consists basically of almost 100 combat encounters scattered across 3 worlds, you progress linear going from one arena to another, between them there are basically just some forked paths with pretty useless collectibles strewn across (that are sometimes really hard to see depending on the color palette)No puzzles, no plattforming, only sometimes dialouges. So it's basically just one arena combat after another, with walking sequences and some story in between. (which I won't comment on I liked it for what it was, bu the character limit of reviews is pretty dense you know?)Considering this, winning one fight with a really complex layout will just lead you 1 minute later to another even more complex fight with even more intricate layout, as such I could only play the game in small bursts. People nowadays ♥♥♥♥ on "variety" in combat focused games like god of war and so on, but basically this game proves why it's important to keep some downtime between tense moments. Halfway throughout the game you will unlock the "Figments of Battle" these are basically the best part of the game. Yet part of me wished I could've done them from the get go, the game has a lot of levels, yet to fully master it, you have to redo them now on more tight specifications, measuring not just your time but also the amounts of remnants you required and the effiency. It's great because each levels comes with modifiers that make these old stages quite interesting so I understand why you have to unlock this mode first. It's only that it's just too much considering how long the base game took. I S-Ranked 30 of them for story reasons (great idea to have one last stipulation at the end to clear them) but now I feel I really need a break, considering how much I still have before me, with almost no tangible rewards.Reaching the end of the review character limit 2 remaining remarks:- The bosses were awesome, I wish there were more of them, really great design!- Some abilities still seem a little unbalanced and slightly overpowered (Goddess Blades giving you invulerability, 50% speed perk)Overall splendid Core-Gameplay, just could need more variety. Yet I love the high skill ceiling the FoB's provide. At some point I will probably return to this.

_childDocuments_.review: The game knows what it wants to do, and does it really well. First few arenas are just to help the player wrap the head around fighting within consecutive timeloops, and then the things begin to get complicated. Every 2-3 arenas a new mechanic is being introduced, making the fights more like puzzles than just hack and slash. Still you need to hack and slash and dodge fast, if you want to make it to the end of each loop and milk every second of each run on the arena count.The graphics are nice, the story is nothing very special, but it's not what the game's about. It makes you feel very, very smart at the beginning, and then incredibly stupid by the end, when you cannot figure out how to master your moves on arenas so complicated, you need to spend some serious time assessing, how you want to approach the monster / environment / variable powers scenario.Last few fights got me terribly frustrated but just because I was to tired to understand, how various mechanics introduced earlier lock with each other. The game was always fair, and the difficulty level is being increased steadily, to reach unfathomable heights by the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior

_childDocuments_.review: Original gameplay, very fine design on every plan. Despite a narration/writing that I find a bit clumsy, this game is worthy of your time and offers a satisfying gameplay that is convenient for both casual and experienced players by making the combat system easy to handle, and, at the same time, proposing optionnal challenges with a timer to beat for every combat, having you planning and timing your actions with great care.
_childDocuments_.name: Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun and frenetic and even if the difficulty curve is really slow i had my fair share of fun playing it. I Would recommend it only if you like the genre since the story is a contrivance that exists only for the gameplay to take place. The only thing that really bugs me is the inability to toggle off the subtitles. I wanted to screenshot the amazing artworks that appear during the narration and i would like to have them without an ugly text at the bottom. If the feature is available and i missed it is either well hidden or i'm really stupid.
_childDocuments_.name: Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I recommend the game, the time shift mechanic is pretty unique and fun. Took me a little over 7 hours to beat the story so I personally don't recommend getting it at full price, wait for a sale. Game is a little to easy, as long as you explore and upgrade how many clones you have its near impossible to fail levels. Biggest con is that the mouse cursor color is very similar to the environments so there will be moments where you lose track of where your mouse isThe combat puzzles don't get that complicated until the last few levels but by then you already have a lot of clones so its hard to fail.Replay ability is pretty much replaying levels to beat your old time or trying harder versions of existing levels. There isn't an upgrade system to work towards.Story is passable, I don't recommend getting this just for story.
_childDocuments_.name: Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome. It is not a hack'n'Slash. It is a puzzle fighting strategy game. That'ts it. The story is OK.  Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior can be repetitive, but they never sell it to be a fighting game only. I can't understand why some reviews are pointing this out when it clearly shows (everywhere) that this is a PUZZLE game with combat. The only thing I think they should've added was a way to us PLAYERS to compete with our steam friends (or a dev time)  to see who did the best time. it could have been PLUS for those who wants to compare their times.Also, the game reminds me so much of LARA CROFT : guardian of light. It has a little of exploration. This game could easily be a totally different game. YET for what it is. Its a good game. But It definitely could be more. Is it fun? YES. Does it worth its price? I guess, but a discount is welcome.ART is beautiful (but nothing WOW)Environment is AMAZINGGameplay is fluid and easy ( the more you go in, the "harder" it goes)Sound effects are OKStory is below average but nothing horrible

detailed_description: Digital Deluxe Edition *Please note that tracks can only be played on the app and cannot be downloaded in any audio format, such as MP3. Digital Premium Edition *Please note that tracks can only be played on the app and cannot be downloaded in any audio format, such as MP3. About the Game Step into the shoes of a transfer student thrust into an unexpected fate when entering the hour 'hidden' between one day and the next. Awaken an incredible power and chase the mysteries of the Dark Hour, fight for your friends, and leave a mark on their memories forever. Persona 3 Reload is a captivating reimagining of the genre-defining RPG, reborn for the modern era. Key Features: - Experience the pivotal game of the Persona series faithfully remade with cutting-edge graphics, modernized quality-of-life features, and signature stylish UI. -Fully immerse yourself in an emotional, gripping journey with new scenes, character interactions, and additional voiceover. - Choose how to meaningfully spend each day through various activities, from exploring the Port Island to forging genuine bonds with beloved characters. - Build and command your optimal team to take down otherworldly Shadows and climb closer to the truth. --- Persona 3 Reload Digital Deluxe Edition includes: Base Game Digital Artbook: Filled with 64 pages of character art, concept art, backgrounds and other illustrations from the game! Digital Soundtrack: Listen to newly arranged tracks from the original Persona 3 plus all-new tracks from Persona 3 Reload, presented by the Atlus sound team for a total of 60 new songs. --- Persona 3 Reload Digital Premium Edition includes: Base Game Digital Artbook Digital Soundtrack Persona 3 Reload DLC Pack: P5R Phantom Thieves Costume Set, P5R Shujin Academy Costume Set, P5R Persona Set 1, P5R Persona Set 2 , P5R BGM Set, P4G Yasogami High Costume Set, P4G Persona Set

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10Persona 3 Reload is a magnificent remake of the original PS2 classic JRPG that only is hindered by Atlus forcing microtransactions.Positives:- The story is incredible with characters that become your friends over the course of the 100+ hour adventure that really makes the emotional moments hit. You cry with them and you cheer with them throughout the story.- The combat is peak turn-based combat, while you can become overpowered quite quickly the combat still requires strategic planning around weaknesses and resistances like the SMT combat we have come to expect. - The music is peak. Easily ranking in the top video game soundtracks.Negatives:- Microtransactions on day one. Cosmetic, personas, and bgm packs as paid content in a $69.99 single player rpg is scummy, but at this point with Atlus it is not surprising.- Missing story content present in previous iterations of the title in what is supposed to be the definitive edition of the game. The Answer and the femc storylines are not present which may come later in DLC but it still sucks.- Certain textures and visuals do not match the overall visual fidelity of the game. Overall, Persona 3 Reload is my favorite in the franchise and is highly recommended!

If you came from P5 better play P3R first, if P4 then P3P first.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever since enjoying P5 Royal and Strikers, I was ecstatic about the rumored P3 remake. I did not, though, appreciate the shady release of P3 Portable months before the announcement of the remake. P3 has many versions out there, and normally, remakes are complete editions of said game, yet, this lacks the female main character route, and the DLC/epilogue of the game at lunch. This is an expensive game all things considered, especially in its Deluxe Edition; but I still went for it thinking this was a one-time purchase as they openly said they had  for the game. Although I am happy and will look forward to The Answer aka Episode Aigis coming to Reload as well, considering it's almost the same price, had I known, I would have spent that money on the literal epilogue of the game over a few costumes and DLC Personas...I know these choices are not up to the developers, but I still think Sega and Atlus should have aimed at delivering a full experience, instead of squeezing every penny from their exhausted community to the point of specifying there won't be a "Royal" like version of this game.That said, each penny was worth it and this game left an impression on me.P3R follows the adventures of the, canonically, Makoto Yuki, and his friends. In this world when midnight strikes, some people can exist within what's known as "Dark Hour", a time in between days when normal people transmogrify into a coffin and don't perceive it unless they have the potential. The potential is not only to exist in the dark hour but to wield a Persona; a reflection of their own self, that gives power to the wielder, similarly to a stand in Jojo. Whereas in P5 they'd awaken their persona by accepting themselves, in P3R, persona-users normally use a fake gun called an "evoker", and symbolically shoot themselves. I like to think it's because of an understanding of life, acceptance of death, and sacrifice - as these are themes recurrent in the game - but the fan-base consensus seems to be that this is just a way to summon their power without too much explanation or depth into it, unlike the mask in P5.The main character, as a staple in Persona, can wield multiple of them at the same time, making them the chosen of our story. During the Dark Hour a giant structure known as Tartarus appears, with our objective being to understand its connection to the Dark Hour.In short: what an amazing story!As in P5, the appeal of the game to me is the dailiness, allowing you to really live in these character's shoes for months at end. It's not possible to rush through the story, as each day must be experienced besides some story-related time skips, even if only by going home early after school and going to sleep early. Because of this, going out with friends - social links - or doing activities, while it does make the experience longer, is the best choice. I had the impression confidants were not as memorable as in P5, but the game is simply a late bloomer, with many of the most interesting social links available in the second half of the game. In P5 for each main boss, there is a unique dungeon with unique mechanics. As a side yet required activity, Mementos is a procedural extensive dungeon that is unlocked as you progress through the story. P3 obviously being older, in simple terms features only Mementos. Tartarus is a finite procedural dungeon that gets unlocked as you defeat the main bosses. Tartarus as well is mandatory, but in this case, is also the only dungeon of the game, with main bosses happening in other locations on their given day. I decided, knowing the format of the game, to use a non-spoiler calendar guide, only to make it easier to keep track of everything and go for 100% on my first playthrough. When it came to Tartarus, I thought the guide was just trying to optimize my days as much as possible, but that's not the case. Tartarus' design invites the player for longer sessions, with bonuses given when exploring that will stack during the same session, and when maxed out, will raise the quality of rewards. This leads to binging to the next block, with a strong change of pace, and especially difficult early with fewer characters.When it comes to the dungeon itself, I must give my kudos to the developers for doing as much as they could to zhuzh-it up, making each block of Tartarus different in its aesthetic and tileset. Still, this does not change the exploration is quite limited to running around, attacking enemies, and opening chests. Compared to Mementos, there are also a lot of important dialogues within the exploration of Tartarus, demanding your attention during a repetitive task.I overall enjoyed it still, but dreaded the long session change of pace sometimes.The combat flows amazingly, and boss fights are interesting from the get-go. Each boss is unique, without falling too much into crutches of artificial difficulty. I'm sure they have rebalanced a few of the fights as P3 was well-known for some unfairly broken fights.Although a newcomer to P3, I informed myself on some, but not all, of the additions of the remake after completing it.New is the ability to pass the turn to allies when matching weaknesses or doing a crit, and new are also special abilities - like ultimates - for each character. Much more of the game has been dubbed, and more activities have been added to pass the time.Should you forget to save, a great new addition is the "Rewind" mechanic, similar to autosaves, that keeps a few savegames made before an activity was chosen; say you enter Tartarus and forget to buy new equipment, you could just rewind to the start of the evening should you have not saved in a while. I hope this will come back in future games!Many additions were made for Tartarus too, adding a "Shuffle Time" when fighting well, allowing you to choose for some bonuses like ability cards, more XP, money, etc. New are also destructible statues around the map that when destroyed can award items of any type, from gems that can be sold for money to HP/SP restoration items.Taking from P5, the UI has been completely redesigned and while it does not reach the same heights, it does fit the game well and is stunning.All soundtracks are either new or have been rerecorded to fit the new package better. I can guarantee you many will make their way into my personal playlists as it happened for P5.Last, but not least, I just want to make a note for the game's optimization and polish. While graphic options may not be many, the options are there, with unexpected ones like ray-tracing on all glass/wet surfaces. When playing at 1080p I had the game's internal resolution at 125-150% to avoid aliasing with the many straight lines the game has, but when I moved to 1440p, the game looked fine at 100% internal resolution. Still, it would have not hurt to have DLAA, or any of the image reconstruction techniques like DLSS, FSR, and XeSS, as an option. Regardless, the game runs great with no issues that I could notice.The idea that for Metaphor: Re Fantazio I need to go back to the same in-house engine as P5 makes me cry. I have never seen Persona look so good, lit so good, and run so well even in busy environments.In conclusion, Persona 3 Reload is a wonderful remake of the roots that led to masterpieces like Persona 5 Royal, with the potential to be called nothing less than that. It is sadly not the complete package, lacking an entirely different path for the main character and epilogue that I think should have been there from the beginning.As the first of its genre, it's rough around the edges on many things, that the remake has tried to smooth out.I'm happy I had the chance to play this, and I'll be begrudgingly waiting for The Answer in September!

_childDocuments_.review: My first time trying Persona and I enjoyed this a lot. I don't usually like the high school setting very much but it's hard not to fall in love with some of the characters here and I can see why this game has so many fans prior to the remake. I did really enjoy the story and character development throughout.Presentation is incredible, Atlus sets the standard for the anime style and turn based RPGs generally. It's so good that it's hard to get tired of seeing it despite getting some of the game battle animations hundreds of times.The combat is pretty good, when you get a hard fight there's plenty of strategy and builds to the Personas that makes it interesting to overcome each battle. Tartarus is a little monotonous but I was definitely grinding too much fighting every shadow at first, it paid off to be more careful about when to take fights and most of the boss fights were fun.Playing on hard is a good idea too, a few points later in the game I think were undermined by playing on normal.A couple things I really didn't like, why are there fan service outfits for high school girls? Some of the worst aspects of this game were changed in this remake but this one stood out to me and it just feels like a weird choice given the tone and presentation of the rest of the game. I'd also have really loved to get Kotone as an option for the protagonist, it sounds like her story is a little different and it keeps this from being the definitive version of the game.Perfect on the Steam Deck if you disable ray-traced reflections.

_childDocuments_.review: This game never has a moment or in-game day or time to waste or that's a dull moment. Atlus once again delivers stellar presentation and while the core elements and story is the same there are some added features and gameplay to make it just different enough to not seem like a faithful remake. I do recommend playing this game on Normal or even Harder modes if you're a returning Persona Veteran because this game, once you've learned the ins and outs, can be quite cheesy and even trivialize battles. But at the same time, it does take some work and hard effort to reach that point. I was indifferent about the the new VA but after getting through the stories and hearing them more, i've grown to like them, honestly even more than the originals. (Not saying either is flawed or bad) It's also worth noting that every single social link event-from level 1 to level MAX 10 in the game has fully voiced lines, making them a lot more engaging to hear them express themselves and become inherently more attached. I personally don't think there was a moment where I thought the voice acting was considered "bad". Please don't let the new cast put you off from enjoying the game amazing content; they're all great.Persona 3 Reload is also a really friendly game for newcomers wanting to try the Persona series.Music overall is needless to say is exceptionally good. I enjoy faithful remixes of the original soundtrack and the added tracks while not that many are still absolute BANGERS. The sound mixing is also done just right where sound effect played during gameplay are just subtle enough to overtake the music and vice versa, especially in battle.Story...I won't give anything away. Take your time and enjoy it. There's a lot and never a dull moment with it.  Even coming from the original, expecting what I am supposed to see, it was amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: I am truly baffled by this game.  I assume this is more a money grab then anything.  Sure as a remake I guess it’s pretty decent.  However, I don’t know why anyone would buy this game.  This has an extreme feeling of being a rough draft of Persona 5.  It’s very hard to recommend a game that is just a worse version of Persona 5.  I don’t doubt when it came out originally it was amazing…but now…I don’t see why you would play it unless you are so desperate for more Persona games that you are willing to play objectively inferior games.When I say this game is a rough draft…I mean like literally.  Character story arcs are literally identical, but worse versions, of story arcs in Persona 5.  It’s kind of crazy…Mitsuru (P3)/Haru (P5), Kazushi (P3)/Ryuji (P5), ♥♥♥♥♥(P3)/Futaba (P5).  You are also collecting all the same Persona’s as in Persona 5.  The twists in the story are basically identical to the twists in Persona 5.  Even the character designs are basically identical.  It’s just painfully obvious when they made the masterpiece that is Persona 5 they were directly modeling off of this game.  It’s not like the difference between different Final Fantasy games that might have similar themes and ideas…it’s just lifting entire characters and story beats.The game also just doesn’t go far enough in fixing some just real stupid things.  For one, you spend all your time in Tartarus…which is this extremely boring tower that doesn’t really change.  You are just climbing this grinding levels in the most boring environment imaginable.  Mementos in Persona 5 is a masterpiece in comparison.  The enemy design is also some of the worst in any game…it’s just the same enemy design over and over and over again with just the color pallet changing.  You are spending dozens of hours in this place and I think in total there are no more then maybe 10 enemy character models.  It’s baffling…this game has like a hundred + persaons…but instead of having you fight models of those personas as enemies…they just refuse the same bland 10 enemy models.While Persona 5 has the character dungeons which are all amazingly well designed, Persona 3 doesn’t.  You only really level up in Tartarus.  It’s like having to be stuck in Mementos for dozen of hours but it’s a worse version.  The main game of Persona of walking around hanging out at school is at least fun and enjoyable…but unlike Persona 5 you really can’t hang out with everyone.  Which I guess is ok, but I would say I ran out of time to complete probably half of all the character stories.  In Persona 5 I think I missed 1.  I just felt like the game was balanced pretty heavily against being able to level up character stories which is foolish as that is the only good part of this game.I also felt the overall story had real problems, Look, I had fun with this game…but I don’t think it’s a good game, and I certainly wouldn’t recommend it.  The best parts of the game are hanging out with your friends…but the game puts up too many roadblocks to doing this and the rest of the game outside of hanging out with your friends is just extremely poorly handled.  I find it absurd that this is a $75 game…it is absolutely not worth that, maybe $30…but you shouldn’t buy it you should just buy Persona 5 and if you already played that…well go play Baldur’s Gate 3 it’s far more worth your time than this.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're going to ask for full game price for a remake, I expect quality and effort. So far, I've been disappointed. I'm fine with some things not being animated cutscenes that were in the original, but in key moments, like Orpheus awakening, not having the hand drawn animated cutscene feels awful. Sure, they had a rendered cutscene, but it just isn't the same. The remixed songs have mostly been not great, which is a shame because I really enjoyed the original's soundtrack. I'm mostly fine with the art direction, however, not drawing the protagonist's clothes feels lazy. There's just a shadow over the clothes. Also, there still isn't a definitive way to play this game, which a remake should have fixed. There's no female protagonist option, no The Answer, and no Desert of Doors. Junpei doesn't sound as good or as young as he did in the original game. I'm going to continue to play the game because the frustrating thing about FES and the original was not being able to control your party members and this game gives you that, but so does Portable. Maybe they'll add the content in DLC, but considering what feels like a lack of effort and an insane asking price for the base game, even if they did, I might not buy it

_childDocuments_.review: For whatever reason, though I've tried on several occasions, I was never able to finish P3 FES or Portable. They were fantastic experiences, but for whatever reason - perhaps just burnout from dungeoning through Tartarus so much-  I always stopped before the game's conclusion. I loved Persona 4 Golden and Persona 5 Royal, so it bothered me that I'd never fully experienced its predecessor. Consequently, I'm thrilled to say that I've finally finished P3 thanks to Reload. ^_^ The quality of life changes made to the game helped make both time management and Tartarus progression a smoother experience for me. The updated graphical presentation is gorgeous and the updated soundtrack is phenomenally put together. I love the added opportunities for the MC to connect with the male party members that was missing in the original. So for me, this has become the definitive Persona 3 experience. I greatly look forward both to the Answer DLC and replaying the main game in future :)

_childDocuments_.review: I played the portable version a couple years ago and the social links are still this game's strongest point for me, especially now that all of them are voiced. The way they are presented, the problems they are going through, and how you help them live with their struggles is very down-to-earth and believable. I also really like the fact that you don't just magically fix their lives, instead you simply give them someone to be with them during their hardest times.The voice acting overall is superb and really helps you to immerse yourself in the game.Even though I knew the story, during the most critical moments it still gave me teary eyes, because the VAs did such a good job.I would recommend it to every fan of JRPG's, in particular if you want to play a game that isn't all happy-go-lucky and is more on the darker/realistic side.

_childDocuments_.review: i had tried to play FES on my ps2 two separate times, and never got farther than September. FES was just rough and hard to play, and required so much micromanaging due to mechanics like party member sickness. you couldnt spent alot of time in tartarus because your party would get sick and literally leave on their own. or someone (including the protagonist) would randomly get sick and you couldnt go to tartarus for a few days and really hinder your plans. you also couldnt control any of your squad members, and theyd constantly waste their turn. you also had to constantly wait to attack a shadow from behind just so you didnt get the disadvantage literally every time.most of the problems i had when trying to play FES were addressed in in reloaded, as well as a handful of new stuff that they added to keep things fresh and interesting. even with a total of around 120hrs played on FES between 2 saves, it still took me 130hrs to complete 1 playthru of reloaded.. mostly because i didnt remember alot of stuff and was basically re-experiencing the game again and getting into it, as well as spending plenty of time in tartarus.it is a bummer they replaced some of the original soundtracks, as i feel the original soundtracks fit the vibe of the game better.. and while the updated and modernized graphics are absolutely fantastic, it isnt the same dark and dreary vibe that was in the original game. however, they really made each block of tartarus stand out and distinct, so exploring each block was interesting and visually pleasing.as for the main plot, its slow and takes awhile for you to get answers.. the first month or so of gameplay set you up with loads of questions and gets you interested in the story, then youll go several months with barely any answers and probably more questions raised. although during this time, youll be focused on sub plots such as the social links. there are some big emotional points throughout main plot, and also a few good twists.. but the ending is sure to leave your heart broken once you understand it. overall, a must play for any persona fan, but also a great into to the series for those that havent played a persona game before. its easy to pick up and theres plenty of QoL features that were added in this to make it playable and made exploring tartarus far easier than in the original.

_childDocuments_.review: ATLUS really made a masterpiece with this one... I can not put to words how incredible the soundtrack is for this game. Every original track has been beautifully remastered to fit this game perfectly, with some actually managing to surpass their original forms. All the new songs are out of this world yet still fit in with the rest. ATLUS has gotten so much better at 3D modeling to the point where I'm actually glad they opted to start doing cutscenes with them as opposed to what would have been a 2D animation, (don't get me wrong the 2D animations are probably still objectively better and look stunning even in previous entries), following the pattern of other games in the series. As for the arguably controversial new voice cast, I'll admit I was definitely not a fan of some of the new voices when they were announced. However, with a good amount of time sunk into the game, I've gotten used to them and actually enjoy them. In particular I think ♥♥♥♥♥ and Ken got much needed and fantastic improvements from their original voices (need I explain?). Shinjiro, Yukari, and Junpei all got slight upgrades in my opinion, however I think the tone of Yukari's new voice isn't quite as good as it was. Mitsuru and Aigis are about as close as you can get to being on par with their original voices although Aigis doesn't sound quite as robotic when you first meet her in comparison to the original. As for Akihiko, I'll admit he was by far my least favorite during the announcement, which disappointed me as he's my favorite character, but he's certainly grown on me as I've played on. My main issue is that he's missing his raspy voice that just seemed to fit the character so well, along with getting an even deeper one. Not to say his new voice is unrealistic as I think it's still a really good voice for him, it's just the only one that seems really far from the original. Strega all got massive improvements. Makoto/Minato/MC/Whatever got a deeper voice which fits him better, but you never hear it much anyway so this really didn't matter.As for gameplay? I don't really need to say much besides "Oh my God I don't despise Tartarus grinding anymore". They made it fun and interesting. The actual battles are all majorly improved obviously, as it's pretty much just Persona 3 with a bunch of Persona 5 QoL improvements. (It's a Persona game do you really need an essay on the battles?)Story is the same as the original obviously, just add in a bunch of much needed development for all the characters that got little screen time, or done dirty in the original (especially Strega).Graphically? This game is a true masterpiece. Even on a basic Steam Deck this game looks INCREDIBLE.Easily my favorite Persona Game (heck even just my favorite game in general) of all time. Episode Aigis managed to make this game even better.
