_childDocuments_.review: Strayed Lights' issues are difficult to describe; it's not a bad game per se, and although I enjoyed the combat, so many of its features feel hollow and lack substance, so much so that I often felt I was playing for the sake of completing it rather than because I wanted to. Whether it be the boss finishers relegated to QTE-riddled cutscenes, the unimaginative, linear level design, or the story that provides little to no direction or context for my actions, I never felt drawn in or engaged by the world, instead mindlessly trudging through skin-deep environments, not entirely understanding why.Combat is, to its credit, entertaining and unique; enemies attack wreathed in different colours, and for the strongest parry, dealing damage and restoring health, you must receive the attack matching the colour, swapping between blue and orange with the press of a button. Unblockable purple attacks force a dodge instead, keeping you on your toes throughout an encounter. However, Strayed Lights is a cripplingly easy game: enemy damage is non-existent, and the amount of health restored on a successful parry is absurd, failing to follow through on the intensity this combat model should invoke.Nevertheless, combat is varied: alongside the parry, you have access to a basic dodge and attack, with a few unlockable abilities down the road, all providing substantial depth to an encounter. It plays great too; with each action, particularly the dodge, providing a tactile and responsive feel. However, the parry is both your primary defence  offence so, in practice, much of the expanded moveset doesn't offer enough to be worth using; for example, bosses tend to end a flurry of attacks some distance away, and by the time you've closed the gap to get some basic attacks in, they're ready to go again with another combo.Bosses are the highlight of the entire experience: despite their movesets lacking much variation, each attack chain can be surprisingly complex, mixing up all colours of attacks into a tight string of blows. Learning the patterns and perfectly dealing with the assault, parrying each strike with the right colour and dodging when necessary, gives rise to a riposte, offering immense satisfaction when executed. Unfortunately, these encounters are sullied in their conclusion: upon ending a fight, you're presented with an awkward cutscene in which you watch your character deal a climactic finishing blow with accompanying, equally awkward QTEs. The key word here is "watch"; although I'm the one pressing the buttons, the disconnect created by using a cutscene completely takes me out of the moment, leaving my opponent defeated, but a sour taste in my mouth.The quality of combat encounters is far from consistent: basic enemies litter the landscape, and with their 2 or 3 attacks that never change or evolve, there is almost nothing worthwhile about them. Furthermore,  enemy shares the same visual motif, including the bosses, and you wind up feeling like no enemy feels particularly unique to fight because they don't  unique. New variants of enemies show up now and then, but a groan always escaped my lips as I saw another skirmish come into view. As far as the story goes, Strayed Lights gives absolutely nothing: I couldn't give you a synopsis even if I wanted to. Stuff , and things play out on screen, but with no dialogue to contextualise anything, I couldn't make heads or tails of what's actually going on; "stuff" and "things" become the only words I can use to describe it. Yet that doesn't mean an attempt at a story isn't made; the first hour or so is just  with 30-second cutscenes literally every few minutes, though they don't say or show anything worth seeing.Now I imagine you think this doesn't matter; it's an action game, right? But it needs  and it bleeds into every aspect of the game; why am I fighting this thing? What am I looking at? What is my character's goal? If I'm asking myself these questions, I can't become invested in the epic boss battle. I don't bother looking at the scenery, however beautiful it may be. If I know these questions won't be answered, why bother asking them at all? And therein lies the problem: if I don't care about the world and characters around me, the whole experience becomes soulless, it becomes monotonous and it becomes forgettable.I wish I could tell you that there's environmental storytelling, but there's almost nothing to speak of. Each distinct area is visually very appealing: the composition is pleasing, the colours are superb, and the positions of the moon or a mountain behind an eye-catching centrepiece are all executed well, but again, without context of any form, there's no deeper meaning between the brushstrokes. Suddenly all the beautiful art lacks intent. I don't look at the space and wonder how it came to be; it's  a forest, it's  a tower in the distance, and I never found myself compelled to care.The playable space consists of two small hub areas leading to five moderately sized areas, each housing its own boss and making up the majority of the playtime. These locations are almost entirely linear, however, with very little room for any exploration; the most you get are occasional, slightly hidden side paths that lead to nothing more than an optional enemy or a collectible. Brimming with empty corridors, slow crawls along ledges, and far too many repeated enemies, these spaces feel like their only purpose is to slow you down. It's easy to tell that the intent during these long walking sequences is to give the player a moment to take in the views, although they only present as mindless slogs due to the narrative reasons outlined earlier.With only two types to find, the collectible economy is scarce and essentially not worth bothering to engage with: the primary of the two improves the speed of "energy" buildup, the bar that fills up with successful parries and attacks, ending the fight once full. This buff, frankly, isn't felt at all; not once did I feel I was dispatching enemies faster, to the point that I'm not entirely sure I've correctly understood what it does. The other collectible is somehow less interesting: found in the hub areas, you can take them to a large shrine to unlock what is essentially concept art and more of the first main collectible. Added to the fact that both of them are easily missable, due to multiple unexpected points-of-no-return locking you out of finding them all, the whole system feels more like a checkbox than a properly implemented feature.To reiterate, this is not a bad video game, but it's far from exceptional either, and in an indie scene awash with life, individuality, and personality, I feel that Strayed Lights failed to leave much of an impression on me. There are glimmers of an excellent game buried in this, and I think that Embers should be proud of what they accomplished in their debut title, but as it stands now, completely ignoring the £20 price tag for a four-hour game, this is not an experience that I can recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to like this but I can't shake the feeling that it's wasting my time.  All the core elements are really solid, great art direction backed by a wonderful colour palette, interesting core gimmick, largely well-designed bosses and enemies, I want to emphasise that I like what this game is doing!The problem is that it feels like the map was scaled up to twice its original size at some point in development, and I don't mean the breadth of its scope, I mean in the scale of its literal geometry.  The bulk of my time in the game so far has been consumed by holding B to slowly traverse ridiculously enormous stretches of empty space, an emptiness so enormous it makes the player character feel bizarrely tiny, with no fresh scenery to take in, extremely sparse collectables to find, and no enemies to fight.  It feels padded, and considering I've heard it's quite short, it's possible that is actually what happened.  I might return to it at some point but right now I've got a lot of stuff to play and I really don't want to spend this much time running in a straight line toward a rock that might or might not have something behind it.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, very pretty....And that's it.Parrying and matching parry colors is the game's general combat premise, but it feels... so painfully flat. No, I didn't get lost at the start. I'm not unfamiliar with the vagueness of the soulslike genre, and parrying is one of my favorite playstyles, with Sekiro shooting up to one of my all-time favorites. So I went into this feeling hopeful, and I found my way to progress pretty quickly, and... there's just no impact or excitement to anything going on. For one thing, I don't mind the choice to eschew vocals in favor of visuals and interpretation, but, that doesn't mean you forget about sound design altogether. Traversal felt uninteresting, like I'm playing a walking simulator, supposedly swept up in the environment to notice that I've been just holding B for fifteen seconds to get to the next mini-encounter. Each encounter is, itself, like a checkpoint where you throw yourself at what amounts to a puzzle sequence of parrying, dodging, and hitting until you use your fancy execute button on the whole pack a-la-Sekiro or die and restart that specific encounter. And this feels like I'm being railroaded, and the options and tools that I'm given to work with are not diverse enough to make up for this linearity. Yes, I just started. The skill tree showed me an entire two other (beyond the first freebie) unlockable powers to look forward to, yippee. Making a heavy attack is also a skill tree unlock, taking up one of the four or five slots on the "lower" tree. The same half of the tree that has health upgrades as one of the slots, yes. It's not promising. And, for all the emphasis I've left to give to the visuals... the game starts you out in some pretty bland, one-color environments. The screenshots show promise, sure, but if you were hoping to hook people on sightseeing, you won't get there early enough before it's time for a refund.This game feels like it's REALLY banking on its color-parry gimmick to grab you, and it's just insufficient. I made it to the first boss on Hard, gave it a fair try, and after chasing it around as it leapt across the arena like I was fighting Elden Beast again, it flattened me mid-parry combo with an unblockable purple poomf of near-silence, my character playing their same exact "fall over slowly and die" animation they do against everything else, and I realized that I just felt utterly bored with the experience. Want to see a really cool and exciting, parry-focused, soulslike AA game? Try Nine Sols.

_childDocuments_.review: A short, straightforward, and visually-pleasing experience. Strayed Lights is an wordless, atmospheric action game about growing up and confronting your inner demons.The key combat mechanic involves color matching your opponent while parrying blue or orange attacks, which heals you and fills your energy bar. Purple attacks cannot be parried and must be dodged. Combat is at its best during boss fights (which all feature a single opponent), but falls short on the two-mob trash packs between bosses. I found myself playing much more aggressively on the trash packs than the bosses just to take one of the opponents out of the picture quickly. The boss designs were all unique and flashy.The environments are beautiful, and poking around in corners rewards the player with an energy boost. I found that it ran fairly well at high settings, with only occasional framerate drops.  (Ryzen 9 5900x - NVIDIA RTX 3080)Not a perfect game, but an enjoyably contained 7-hour experience on the Standard difficulty for me (there are also Story and Challenge difficulties). There are Trials available after completing the game for those who want to revisit specific bosses.

_childDocuments_.review: Is it worth 20 bux?  I'd say so.I mean, a lot of work was put into the game, obviously.  The music and visuals fits into a coherent theme.  Every camera angle  during scenes could be captured in an artful screenshot, and the level design is very well thought-out.  Like the cut scenes, the every piece of monument and architecture -- what little there may be in the lost civilization apparent in the game -- is placed with visual purpose.The gameplay is the right amount of challenge.  If you're familiar with action games, it's a bit of a slower-paced combat; so it's a lot of waiting and timing, but it is fun.  For me, I'd say it's basically a game if you find From Soft games to be total bull, this one's a good alternative.  Not a long game at all, but I think $20 suffices the visual work put into this game. The developers deserve a commendation for the beautifully crafted natural world in the game.Players equating the pricetag to game time really need to kinda shut up, and realize despite the play time, the game had a LOT of thought put into it.

_childDocuments_.review: A small and enjoyable experience, exactly as long as it should be. The color-swapping is an interesting addition to the usual dodge/parry mechanics, and while they it was a bit of a struggle for me to get used to juggling both, once it clicked it came very naturally. The controls also were very tight, which is something a lot of Soulslikes fall prey to, especially from indie developers.Combine that with fun bosses with neat mechanics, gorgeous character animation and environmental setpieces, and Austin Wintory's compositions, and this was a great way to spend an evening.Some small critiques include some frame drops in certain foliage-heavy environments which suggests it could use more optimization, and that while the quicktime events didn't bother me (as setups for fun and flashy finishers), the icons indicating button presses having the BLACK space be the button to push was strange and not very intuitive. I would recommend inverting or changing the icons so the button to press is highlighted in white and not black.To end on a positive, I very much appreciate how the devs added in a colorblind mode to make sure the mechanics are accessible to colorblind gamers. While I didn't personally need it, it's vital and all too often left out of games where color is such a focus. Well done, Embers, for keeping your game accessible.

_childDocuments_.review: I would say this is a solid showing if it were a solo dev or a student project or whatever. But I just couldn't have fun with this. The tutorial is extremely slow, taking 20 minutes to show you how to walk, walk walk, crouch, walk, jump, walk, run, run, run, parry, parry, parry, parry, parry and parry. The opening was bizarre - Your negative/upside down guy split your ember brain into shards and sent minions into the multiverse? What?Levels are quite linear once you start down a path, only broken up by combat rooms, which are okay (oh and by the way "souls-like" here really means parry mode). But most of the time is spent walking. What finally broke me and made me return the game is that your camera gets hijacked constantly to pan out vistas that are...fine. Or to look at a monkey, which walks near you. Really riveting stuff that requires a 15 second disconnect of the controls to fully appreciate, I guess.Also, it feels like the game was done, then someone just said, "lets' increase the size of the world by 400% so that it takes longer to get everywhere and increases game completion time". Even the big baddies don't fit in the world right. The massive world scheme works in games like Shadow of the Colossus and Praey for the Gods, because you actually fight behemoth baddies.The world looks decent, movement feels good, enemies seem varied. But the whole product just didn't come together in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Strayed lights has a very unique and abstract story, simple but very beautiful visuals and an interesting Sekiro-light and fun combat system. The enemies have exciting combos that have quite a steep learning curve and the main character is pretty and adorable. The game has some similarities to the Ori series which are very pleasant and the environment reminds me of a surreal, beautiful place that you see, when you meditate.  However, I can't help myself but have the unbearable urge to scream so loud that the developers can hear me. It seems to be a trend to not finish a game before releasing it nowadays. Strayed Lights doesn't feel polished at all.I get random fps drops from 60 to 20 or sometimes even 2 frames per second. You can imagine how terrible that feels in a fast paced combat design. The game randomly freezes in the middle of an attack and the next frame I get hit without being able to do anything about it. That is becoming very frustrating to a point, where I just want to pause the game and take a break. Changing graphics settings doesn't have any noticable influence to the framedrops. As I am playing on challenging mode, I die pretty often due to enemies changing their pattern rather quickly. However, that is very fun to learn and I enjoy such hard challenges. The problem is that it seems like everytime the game reloads a save, it gets more and more broken. The stutters increase in frequency and become more persistent, letting the happening freeze for a couple of seconds in the middle of a battle. It goes up to that point, where I'm even unable to restart the game and close its window. I once had to force reset my computer to even use it again. What it also does is crashing my Steam app, when it tries to close the game. Really, something like this just must not happen with any game.Strayed Lights unfortunately, is very poorly optimized. I just can appeal to the developers to finish their game. Just give it another year, if that's necessary. But please, stop ruining player's experience in releasing a game too early, completely unpolished. I can only imagine how it runs on the Nintendo Switch. I hate to give the game a thumbs down, but in its current state it's a laggy impertinence.Please finish your game.

_childDocuments_.review: Steam Deck experience here.The game crashed a couple of times and killed my Deck once, so I had to shut down and reboot.I also couldn't launch it on a day, after switching Proton version it worked again.Overall it runs pretty bad with major drops in framerate and stuttering with really no recognisable reason. I tried different settings, proton version and tinkered around quite a bit.Considering the deck runs games like RDR2 or Elden Ring just fine I guess it's because of bad optimization.The game overall has a nice art design and grafics aren't bad at all.The combat system is a nice idea but unfortunately very unpolished, unbalanced and at least on normal difficulty not challenging at all.The boss fights and designs are pretty good but unfortunately with the combat system not challenging and repetitive. _childDocuments_.review: It was a joy to play this game. The music atmosphere was lovely, thought a tad quiet at some points. Very much a guided story-line on where to go while still having the freedom to choose the order etc. Ori of the blind forest aesthetic, with a souls like style of combat and bosses, though much more lenient & not as punishing. Different difficulties allow for the player to decide how aggravating or easygoing the game is. The last 3 bosses' fights were *chef's kiss* and it was super satisfying to beat these especially after figuring out the boss patterns and mechanics.The story was a bit confusing, the cut scenes helped piece together, though I wish there was a proper explanation at the end. It was well enough to understand the gist of what was going on though, especially with no dialogue. I believe part of the concept was to try to piece it all together. For their first game, they did great, and I would love to play again one day. Side note: I recommend using controller if you have smaller hands as the changing color aspect of combat was difficult without doing so for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Strayed Lights

_childDocuments_.review: Im going to start off by saying that I think the dev team has a lot of talent and I cant wait to see how they take their experience with this game and use it to make something in the future. The art team especially went crazy in this game, and it is beautiful as a result.However,This is not a game that I can in good faith recommend to anyone else. Let me explainThis game suffers from a number of serious issues that i will go into belowThis Should Have Been A Boss RushIn my opinion, this game should have been a boss rush. The most enjoyable parts of the game was seeing the environments and fighting the bosses. If you have played games like Eldest Souls, both are pretty achievable, and this game would have benefited from it, because the worst parts were finding the collectibles(of which I couldn't find all of them) and fighting the small enemies, whom of which not a single one were enjoyable to fight. The Sound Design Is All Over The PlaceWhy the F does a regular non perfect parry have nearly the same sound as getting hit? How do I learn what moves are giving me trouble when I have to stare at the screen and not the health bar and cant hear what the game is trying to tell me? This would have been such an easy fix too. This is especially bad in the final bossMissable AchievementsThis game came out in 2023, its not really excusable for half the achievements to be entirely missable.Inconsistent Telegraphing, Parrying And trackingWhy are some moves unreactable for no reason? Why cant the final boss track me like at all? Why do some of my parries still work when I missclick by a million years, but others feel like accuracy to a couple frames is necessary? The boss fights are the highlight of this game, and they should have had longer to cook. Standout fights were butterfly phase 1, forest monkey phase 2, and final phase 1. Most of the others had a serious downside that made them less fun to fight.This is a short game for the price. Tying back to the boss rush comment, this game could have had twice the bosses that took twice as long to fight and were more polished, and it would have been way better. the bosses are always either getting utterly steamrolled or winning, there is no middle ground, because once you half learn like 2 attack patterns you can always heal the mistakes easily. Also, the achievement to no hit a boss not being available in the section where you can just fight the bosses makes little sense. Why be able to attack when most of the bosses take little damage and just run away when they aren't attacking? Why the quick time events that take away from what could have been incredible cutscenes? Why is there no way to track the meet again achievement? Why does playing on a lower difficulty make it so you cannot get the unlock all skill achievement because it reduces the amount of NON RESPAWNING enemies which have a vital resource tied to them? These are questions I kept finding myself asking and not finding answers. This game is just a really really beautiful series of major game design and playtesting issues, but has the foundations to be awesome. I hope the developers take this feedback into account when designing the next game they make, because I fully believe they can make something awesome. If anyone would like to talk with me further about possibly improving the game or more in depth discussions about these issues, you have my email, I reached out to support 5 days ago.TLDR this game has serious game design issues and I would not recommend playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Strayed Lights

_childDocuments_.review: Strongly recommend this game. Strayed Lights enjoys a wild color palette, strong soundtrack (shoutout Austin Wintory), tight combat mechanics, and a surprisingly zen atmosphere. The two-color parry system is both unique and intuitive, lending itself to some blistering combat encounters. Story is pretty minimal here; come for the action and not the plot on this one.Strayed Lights is primarily a boss rush (a few brief levels serve as interludes, with minor enemies to practice against). Each boss is memorable and has a strongly differentiated vibe and moveset. I played on Challenge Mode for my first playthrough, which was only recently added to the game, and I'm given to understand that it is significantly more difficult than the normal mode, where combat is more relaxed and meditative.True to its name, I found Challenge Mode to be extremely tough: boss combos come at a relentless pace, they flip between colors rapidly and dish out punishing amounts of damage, and the telegraph windows for each combo are pretty severe. The payoff here is that once you've figured out a boss's moveset, countering each combo with a perfect set of parries is massively satisfying, and I felt like an absolute champ dancing around each of these encounters, similar to mastering a boss fight in Sekiro. Having perfect parries restore a bit of health was also a great design choice, adding a bit of a tug-of-war element to each fight.Strayed Lights and a fairly rudimentary upgrade system, but my only real complaint here is that some of the upgrades feel way less helpful than others. For example, the "hold the parry button and release for a stronger parry" upgrade actually worked against me. Enemy combos come quickly enough that you'll never really use this move, and I would regularly prep the "charged parry" without meaning to, throwing off my timing and leaving me defenseless. With no way to respec or undo upgrades, I came pretty close to restarting my playthrough just to get rid of this disadvantage (in the end, I worked around it by training myself to only ever very lightly tap the parry button).I thought Strayed Lights was great, and I'm excited to see what Embers puts out next. For anyone else plowing through Challenge Mode, I strongly recommend picking the upgrade that lets you do a powerful riposte after perfect-parrying an enemy's full combo; it's probably the most satisfying maneuver to pull off in the entire game.

_childDocuments_.review: Not for me. I loved Sifu and I mostly liked Sekiro so I'd say I enjoy difficult combat games. Just seems like an unnecessary and not particularly fun mechanic to me. I also found dodging to be very unintuitive in that some things I thought I could easily dodge I would end up getting hit by while other times I'd be surprised I didn't take damage. There is also the issue I hate with games where the pause before a heavier attack from the enemy is super exaggerated and then the animation plays at almost the normal speed of a normal attack. Another more minor complaint is that I'm not sure why they felt the need to have a sprint mechanic when that should just be the default run speed. The sprint button should be a "move slower" button for the parts that require you to walk carefully areas so you don't fall.Also, there should be a level of difficulty between the mid and hard difficulty. Mid was easy and Hard I was a little ridiculous with the time given to switch colors properly and parry.I'd say try it out if you like fast combat games because you might like it, but I just think there are much better options out there and I don't the this brings anything new to the table.

New attacks would be amazing, but even just those simple options would create replayability).There are some... Issues with the release, the biggest being that the devs compiled with the SteamVR enabled at runtime which is a hallmark of bad developers, but I am proud to say that the game itself isn't in the terrible list of other games that do this. The game also does not offer proper Playstation controller support. However, both of these things are fixable; for the PS controllers just run DSX or DS4 as an Xbox controller, and to disable SteamVR booting on launch just right-click the game in your library, choose properties, and type "-nohmd" in the launch options box under the first general tab.The game is very short; any veterans and people familiar with parrying in games will be done in around 3 hours, 3.5-4 hours if fully exploring the limited areas but... I still absolutely recommend it as a purchase. It was worth the money for me at full price for the journey alone.

_childDocuments_.review: This was such a treat to play and also an absolute “how to” guide when it comes to making video games. I picked it up a while ago in a humble bundle, but only just now got around to actually playing it. Lemme tell you folks, this is absolutely my favourite game from that bundle.I always find myself b*tching in these reviews about excruciating cutscenes and long sections of reading in what should be a game. Ya know… not a book? Well to my absolute delight, every bit of storytelling done in Strayed Lights is done exclusively through visuals and gameplay. There’s a boss fight early on where you can see that the monster is just trying to play with you and all it’s attacks feel bouncy and playful.That brings me around to the combat which feels pretty well tuned. For funsies, I tried to see how far I could get without upgrades and the answer was surprisingly far. I was playing on normal difficulty and found it maybe a tad easy? That being said I’m so over the trend of soulslikes adding difficulty in place of making fights fun an interesting. Even when the combat wasn’t difficult, it was still engaging and entertaining to figure out. If you’re looking for a balanced challenge, I would suggest avoiding specifically the health upgrades as your starting health pool is pretty generous and there are no attacks even late game that will knock off the whole thing. Having the slightly smaller amount just gives a sense of jeopardy and forces you to think harder about risky plays.I’ve been told that the combat is inspired by Sekiro, although I have no experience of Sekiro, and nothing meaningful to add to that. For what it’s worth it’s functionally a rhythm/parry game where you need to match the colour of your parry to the colour of enemy attacks. This flows really well and makes for a delightfully tactile combat system. Oddly enough, it kinda reminded me of the action command system form Paper Mario TTYD, but maybe I’ve just still got that disappointing remake on the brain.The story is also beautiful and spoke to me in some surprising ways. There’s so much love and effort gone into this game. It feels like something someone cared about and put a lot of thought into. The world feels intuitive to explore and I rarely felt lost. Travel times between locations can be a bit of a drag, but the game doesn’t outstay its welcome.I finished it in about 6 hours, but I reckon you could probably do it in 3 if you weren’t stubbornly avoiding upgrades. That sounds short, but it’s exactly as long as it needs to be.Overall, if you’re curious about soulslikes but feel a bit daunted by the idea, I strongly urge you to give this a go.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives: It took about 3 hours to beat this game on its Normal/Intended difficulty. (I'm sure it may be completed much faster)The parry mechanic was quite interesting and I enjoyed learning/mastering it throughout the play-through.I think for what it is, the game is quite enjoyable. The art is definitely the selling point of this game for me. HUGE props to the artist. I took many screenshots on my journey. I hope to see more of this world in the future. Perhaps with co-op to explore it with your troubled siblings. Negatives:Playing the game on the highest available settings, and native 4k resolution I encountered many "lag" spikes when the world was rendering in or loading the mobs. That said, I didn't find it too distracting. And I was able to complete my play-through without any crashes. There is also some "jank" in a couple of the animations (namely the jump recovery and crouch recovery). This didn't affect me but may impact others. As many other reviewers have stated, 3 hours is quite short. While she story concludes quite nicely, it does leave the player wanting more. I believe that is what the second game mode you unlock after your play-through is intended for. While this will add a little more play time, the mainline story content (though enjoyable) still leaves the player wanting more. Verdict: Should you by this game? $25 retail is quite steep for 3 hours of mainline story content. Yes the world is beautiful (subjective) and the game play quite enjoyable (also subjective) this only leaves the player wanting more from it. Hopefully a DLC will follow, or a sequel/prequel to add to this world. I believe many will enjoy the game for the right price.

_childDocuments_.review: Strayed Lights is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played. The scenery is 10/10, it's immersive, it's colorful, it's grandiose, it's peaceful... granted it doesn't have AAA graphics, but it really doesn't matter. The game also never holds your hand. No minimap, no "GO HERE" texts, nothing. Just you and a beautiful linear world to explore. But don't worry, you won't get lost. The game still does a great job making the way clear.Story wise, it's a fully voiceless game that lets you interpret it's background without telling you anything about the world via text or voice. It's all visual. I must admit I'm not good at figuring out these kinda stories, but I still have some idea of what the game wants to say, and it's pretty cool. Gameplay wise, it is very simple but very challenging. The gameplay loop is very very engaging and it's one of the few games I can confidently say I never got bored with. I played in max difficulty, which tests your reflexes and your patience, as this game is heavily based on parrying. You have basic attacks, but you can very well not use them ever if you don't want to. I guess you could say this game is kind of a souls lite, though it didn't feel like a souls game to me. In souls games, I can get very frustrated in those times when you die over and over again to the same enemies. In this game, I genuinely never wanted to close the game because an enemy was beating me up. And they DID beat me up plenty.Overall, if you love magical and atmospheric visuals, this game has some of the best in the market. Really, it's surreal how beautiful this 10 hours journey was. If you like engaging and challenging gameplay, with very satisfying mechanics and colorful fights, this game has it. And if you like to interpret vague and deep stories and figure out what's going on in a mysterious world, then you will be pleased.Loved this game, definitely worth it's price! If you don't mind spending what it's worth, I'd encourage to go to their website and buy it there to support them. I unfortunately didn't do this, which I regret.

_childDocuments_.review: Strayed lights is a very pleasant experience. Being someone who comes from the souls-like genre, this game quite scratched the itch. _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, but if you're looking for a challenge this probably isn't it. It says souls-like but it's mostly parrying and you're not really punished for dying. That said, I love artsy, aesthetic experiences and in that aspect, it really delivers. It felt magical walking through the environments and I loved all the little...people? Well, the inhabitants of the world.The story leaves a lot to interpretation, but you play as a little creature looking to retrieve something stolen from them, meeting and helping other little guys on the way. It just gives off a super wholesome vibe.It's a great game for a chill night, for people who enjoys beautiful visuals, casual combat and/or adorable fantasy beings.

_childDocuments_.review: Strayed lights is an unbelievably underrated game that deserves so much more recognition than it gets! It has super unique and creative core mechanics which lead to some of the best bosses i've ever had the pleasure of fighting whilst looking and sounding absolutely wonderfull. Even better is that, thanks to the 3 difficulty options, strayed lights can be played by absolutely anybody. Those less profficient at action games can enjoy the easy difficulty while the average joe (that's me) can try normal. For the most hardcore soulslike fans there's even a challenge difficulty which i will certainly try my hands on later down the line. I enjoyed this game so much that i'm willing to try it at it's absolute hardest, something which i only did for ori and blasphemous before this. I hope this is enough to convince you but if it isn't i'll go in some more detail below to try and get you in on this amazing game!The combat in strayed lights has a certain rythm to it. The core mechanic is that your avatar can switch between blue & red flames to try and parry attacks in the right colour. Parrying in the wrong colour isn't punished as you still block damage but blocking in the right colour heals you and damages your enemy. This simple mechanic is a stroke of genious because not only are you trying to get the timing right on the parry itself, you also have to constantly adapt on the fly to maximize your output. For the enemies & bosses start of simple with the colours but by the end they mix and match constantly pushing you to respect the game's mechanics and engage with them! The fact that parrying in the wrong colour does not punish you is also brilliant. This game really does want you to succeed and such positive reinforcement is really refreshing within the souls genre. I can only hope more developers adopt this method of positive feedback.If that was all the combat had to offer than it would already be tons of fun, but the addition of purple unblockable attacks is that finishing touch. Purple attacks require a dodge roll at the right time, which is harder than it seems. Later bosses can throw in a purple attack into the middle of their combo, and timing this right after a few perfect parries feels incredibly satisfying. You really do get into the rythm of parrying and dodging the bosses attacks after a few attempts, making it almost feel like a dance. There's also light attacks, heavy attacks and special attacks you can throw inbetween enemy attacks to really push the game to it's limits. For regular enemies, of which there's only a few, this is already pretty fun, but when you face one of the game's several bosses the combat shines. You fight most bosses several times throughout their level, each time with new or alterred moves. This natural progression really does make you improve rather quickly to face their final form. Each boss and their phases are unique in their own ways, so rarely do they feel similar. None of them felt unfair and none of them were boring. Even the least fun fight in the game was miles better than 90% of the games i've played or seen. I'm not exagerating when i say that these are some of the best bosses i've ever faced. One of them would even make my top 10 bosses of all time list. Needless to say the bosses are the highlight of the game for me, and already reason enough to play the game. But that's not all the game has to offer.There's also a gorgeous world waiting to be explored, and while the path with each level is mostly linear you get to chose which order you tackle the levels in. These environments are varied and jawdroppingly beautiful. From lush forests to dark caves and towering ravines. From ancient ruins to spiraling crystals and waterfalls. I just got lost wandering around in this world, entranced by serene vistas and a mesmerizing soundtrack. Austin wintory delivered another brilliant OST for strayed lights, and while the music wasn't as exhilirating for the bosses as some other games, it fit the exploration before said bosses perfectly. All in all the game is a treat for the senses as much as it is for the brain and reflexes.Lastly then narrative and performance. Strayed lights' story is pretty vague, but the imagery is beautiful and the symbolism is elegant. It's up to interpretation but not so obtuse as to not make any sense. Every individual can give meaning to it in their own way, which is nice as it makes the game more personal. Strayed lights is also incredibly well polished. The game runs silky smooth at maximum settings and i didn't have a single bug in my full playthrough. The only unintended thing that happened was an enemy dodging into a cliff once or twice, which was hilarious and a true halmark of a proper souls game. As far as i'm concerned there's no real negatives to this game. Sure i'd have liked some more variety for regular enemies, or a deeper upgrade system but the game doesn't overreach its scope. It knows what it wants to do and does it incredibly well. I'd have liked more of this goodness as well but the game doesn't overstay its welcome. For some the lenght might not be enough but the quality is high enough imo to warrant a purchase. If not at full price than certainly at a discount. Please give it a shot, it's really REALLY good :)

_childDocuments_.review: I would absolutely recommend anyone to play this game. I'm not sure whether it was just my audio balance, or the choice of music being used but it did not get me immersed the way the rest of the game did.The art style is what drew me to purchase/play this game and I'm glad to see it's as beautiful as I had hoped. I only encountered some small issues/glitchy behaviour with the jumping, but otherwise this seems like a very well polished game with a lot of passion.The combat is maybe slightly limited in scope, but I enjoy the almost rhythmic flow of combat and found the parrying system very satisfying. _childDocuments_.review: I'm not a fan of souls-like games, but it was really enjoyable experience. It just get's tiring and boring playing against bosses that take a long time to beat. Luckily for me, the hardest boss for me only took about 30min. (And that was mainly because the color-blind issue I mention below.) I was a bit anxious to play it since it was outside my comfort zone, and the screenshots made the game feel pretty same-y. (I was happily wrong)Maps are linear, but there are hidden collectibles around the corners to power yourself up. (Encouraging some kind of exploration, but not mandatory.) Music was quite appropriate for the levels and fights. I played the game with a controller like it recommended, and it was great. Some enemies have some questionable timings, but overall everything is fairly memorable. There wasn't much to the story other than you physically growing up and getting stronger by beating all the bad guys. Graphics were decent without being demanding, but sometimes lacked some textures to really give some definition.My only gripe with the game is having to turn on Color-blind mode to see a couple bosses switch elements easier. The light blue they used is quite similar to the purple they use, especially when the enemy is switching back and forth. (Blue and orange you can parry and swap, purple you cannot do either as it is an enemy corruption element.) The boss that gave me the most trouble had a predetermined string of attacks that kept switching between blue and purple and then an orange to keep you on your toes. Now that is fine and all, but the boss was super aggressive and changed element per action, AND the background was all blues and purples that matched the color of elements. I just had to put the time in to learn his attack strings, and better my skill level a bit. Which I really didn't have to do against any other boss. (There was an elite type enemy that attacked similar to this boss, and by the end level of the game it was VERY common) Final boss was actually fairly easy compared to the 2 bosses before it, which includes the one I mentioned before I had trouble with.Game has plenty of scenes where the build-up is nice and refreshing when it comes off. And also a built in camera mode for all the pretty and great scenery you'll be going through. I give it an easy 8.5/10. If you can get it on sale like I did, then I would push it upto a 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art style, immediately engrossing.Intuitive, tight and exciting combat and emotion that invokes Kena/Journey vibes all the way through. Tons of heart and a good variety of enemy types to keep the combat evolving beyond just parry, parry, kill. Multiple Enemies at once was a bit problematic when the A.I. was clipping through eachother or being out of line of sight and still acting as if they're the main focus, but not enough to deter the quality.Austin Wintory killed it, as usual, on the score. Beautiful music that is always undertone until it takes forefront and it shines then fades happily back to the emotion behind the visuals.Genuinely an awesome experience that didn't muddle its own systems too much just for the sake, but did what it does well and kept the experience the size it needed to be.

_childDocuments_.review: While there is a lot I like in this game, there is also a lot that I don´t enjoy. I applaud the creators for trying to make a game with no dialogue and no written words. It is very rare and they did a decent job in trying to capture many of the emotions of the "light creatures" that you meet throught the game. Especially the boss that acts like a giant gorilla. You can see his character and also understand, why his actions are wrong, even though in a basic matter, they are completely normal and understandable.The issue I have with the game though is the combat system. There is beauty in simplicity, but the game has no way of making the fightings of the general enemies in any way entertaining. I hate that they are forcing you mainly to try to parry all the attacks (since that is also the way your character heals), because it gets incredibly stale very quickly. Dodging is much harder than it looks (most of the time I got hit anyway), the timing of the parrying sometimes feels broken and when you face 2 enemies... it gets incredibly hard (if you don´t pick the right skills). The attack button here feels mostly more like a formality, because you don´t actually get much stronger in your attacks (or at least you don´t feel stronger), there are no interessting combo attacks, and you get hit much more often. Boss fights are better, as they are much more dynamic and less frustrating, but even those can not save the combat system in its own. I just don´t like it. And sadly that is a big part of the entire game.

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend Strayed Lights to any fan of action-adventure game :- the art direction is simple but beautiful, and the animation work is outstanding : the world and all the characters feel alive even if there's no talking involved. On top of that, the lack of hand-holding really helps with the immersion in the world, and it's a joy to explore it.- the combat gameplay is parry-based but the colour switching adds a nice twist to it. Mastering it feels really good and it never feels unforgiving.- you can see the influence of many classic adventure games such as Soul Reaver and Shadow of the Colossus but Strayed Lights manages to have his own identity.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing visuals + soundtrack! I liked the combat as well :D It really shines during boss fights and the QTE sequences were neat 👌 I do have some notes I want to share 🙇‍♂️- The regular enemies got frustrating over time. They felt like scaled-down bosses with how crazy some of the attacks are and how often they change colors during chains. At some point I just skipped all the small guys just so I can get to the boss.- Fighting two enemies at a time was difficult (admittedly some skill issues on my end). It relates to how often they change colors + having to parry w/the right color. Maybe a difficulty option can be given so that pairs of enemies will only take one color each.- Having the Ability Points (AP) replenish based on 'enemies defeated' doesn't work with boss battles . Once I use up all my AP, I have no choice but to fight it w/the regular combat mechanics. The abilities are great and it's a shame I can't use them much during bosses. Replenishing them through (a couple of) parries would be a nice balance I think :DOverall, I still really enjoyed the game. Learning the attacks of the bosses and finally beating them felt very rewarding! _childDocuments_.review: Strayed Lights is a stunningly vibrant action platformer with environments and a world that feel as soothing as Journey's, but with challenging and rewarding Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice-style combat. Developer Embers asks players to control a small creature of light who must find their lost siblings across otherworldly regions corrupted by shadows. Players will grow stronger, more beautiful and gain new abilities as they explore Strayed Light's vivid environments and battle dark creatures with a simple and fair parrying system.The story of Strayed Lights is told with no dialogue, and Embers manages to craft a compelling tale entirely through environmental storytelling and character actions. After waking up and emerging from a strange pod, players start as a small creature of light who eventually grows into a pseudo-mystical entity that can control firey red and bright blue powers. Fellow siblings of light are waiting to be found, and a mysterious shadowy energy has even corrupted some. Defeating enemies and bosses unlocks new abilities that add depth to Strayed Lights' combat, and it's the game's parrying and color-coded combat that sets it apart from other action titles.Exploring the lands of Strayed Lights can be a relaxing experience, but corrupted enemies lie in wait throughout the adventure, which should take between seven and nine hours to complete. While players and enemies have standard health bars and attacks, both can use color-coded red/blue attacks. If players can time a parry with the corresponding color of an enemy's attack, damage is negated, and some health is restored. Any well-timed block still blocks damage, but the many epic bosses will challenge players and switch modes rapidly. With the right timing and color coordination, winning can feel as rewarding as beating FromSoftware's best Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice bosses, a game that's combat feels like an inspiration for Strayed Light's mechanics.Besides the game's stellar visuals, Strayed Lights' music accentuates each of the game's areas with a soundtrack that reflects the mood each area's creatures are feeling. The atmospheric music can feel tranquil and pleasing or hauntingly mysterious in the game's shadowy regions illuminated by few rich light sources. Austin Wintory, the Grammy award-winner composer behind one of the PS4's must-play games, Journey, has worked on the game's composition, and it meshes well with the already impressive visual cohesion of Strayed Lights. Each area feels more unique with its moody soundtracks while pumping up the excitement during boss battles.Strayed Lights is perfect for players who do not have much time to invest in a game that demands dozens of hours to complete. However, that is also to its detriment. There are a small number of collectibles to discover and a minimal amount of lore that feels like a tease for a world that is so interesting to look at and explore. While each boss is unique and requires different tactics to defeat, generic enemies throughout the map can start to feel repetitive with a lack of varying enemy types.Still, for Embers' first game, this is an especially impressive showing. Strayed Lights is a visually pleasing game with epic bosses and intense combat that any fan of action-adventure platforming games should check out, even if it's over before it really manages to create something unmissable.

_childDocuments_.review: I found Strayed Lights to be a really enjoyable game that strikes the right balance between fun and challenge. The game's visuals are incredibly vibrant and colorful, reminding me of Ori and the Blind Forest. The combat mechanics are reminiscent of Sekiro in that they rely heavily on parrying and timing, which adds a rhythmic element to the battles.One of the things I loved about Strayed Lights was its beautiful and moving soundtrack, composed by Austin Wintory. The music fits perfectly with the game's visuals and adds an extra layer of emotion and depth to the overall experience.Overall, I would definitely recommend Strayed Lights to anyone looking for a visually stunning game with engaging combat mechanics and a great soundtrack. Whether you're a fan of Ori and the Blind Forest or Sekiro, you're sure to enjoy this game.

Strayed Lights is an atmospheric action-adventure with fluid combat and an intricate world imbued with mystery. You are a tiny, growing light seeking transcendence. Explore a land of otherworldly ruins and glowing trees, where entities of flickering lights and luminescent shadows reside.

Challenge rogue shadow creatures in fast-paced, rewarding combat. Use a fluid mix of parries and dodges to absorb their energy levels until you can unleash an ultra energy attack. Shift your light from blue to orange in sync with enemies using timed parries, then push energy back at them in vivid finishers.

name: Howl
detailed_description: Reviews About the Game Howl is a turn-based tactical folktale set in medieval times. A sinister 'howling plague' has ravaged the land, turning all who hear it into feral beasts. You play a deaf heroine plunging into danger in search of a cure. Plan up to six steps in advance to outmaneuver your opponents: wolfish creatures filled with hunger and rage. Various types of fiends are lurking in the shadows, each of them possessing different abilities and their own levels of vitality. So, you need to consider carefully the strategy that will bring them to their knees. Not only do you have your wits to rely on while plotting your attack, you also have an array of abilities at your disposal. As you slay more wolves, you acquire skills like Vault, Smoke Bomb, and Piercing Shot. Venture forth on your journey to upgrade your skills and unlock more Action Slots and Undo Round Points. As you plan your moves, you will also shape your own prophecy, composing a dynamic work of scripture as you fight. Howl's visuals are created through 'living ink', a flowing art style that paints the story as you play. Carve your way through a dark, fairy-tale world made up of obscure yet magical places where you fight and write to rid the lands of the plague. Foretell the actions of your enemies in tactical, turn-based combat Beautifully illustrated in a unique, living ink artstyle Outsmart the different wolf species, from fast predators to enormous pack leaders. Unlock and upgrade new skills like Shadow Step, Exploding Shot, and more Save villagers from the claws – and howls – of the wolves. Play through 60 levels in 4 chapters Plot your route on the world map to uncover new skills and secret paths

_childDocuments_.review: Positive review, but with grounded expectations about what you're getting.This is more a puzzle game than strategy. The AI is completely algorithm-based and will have the same output for a given input. The sole exception is the final level where there is (very annoying) RNG that will determine how many times you're clicking Restart. While each puzzle is entertaining to figure out, there's not much replay value.I've got pretty sizable experience in this type of game (Incredible Machine, Into the Breach, etc.), so I was able to easily reach the end in about 3.5 hours without trouble. Going back and wrapping up all the Steam achievements took an additional 3 hours. Your mileage may vary if puzzle/strategy is difficult for you.The graphics have a very pleasant and unique "hand-drawn" art direction, like you're looking at mobile ink on paper. It's not high-fidelity, but the artists knew what they wanted to do, and I respect that.I was not impressed by the story. On each level, the narrator says a couple sentences about what's going on. The problem is, almost all of it can be summarized as "The Prophet is going to this place now," or "People are scared of the Howl," or "Civilized areas are in disrepair." Without spoiling specifics, the ending had one sentence and then a brief art sequence depicting one of the most "esoteric happy endings" I've seen in a long time. It's the kind of ending that makes you react: "Really?"For the low price tag, it was still a fun bit of puzzle solving. But absent any surprise content updates, I'm probably not ever going to pick it up again.
_childDocuments_.name: Howl

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Into the Breach and the XCOM series, I feel right at home here.The puzzle aspect to the tactics are fun and engaging. All with wonderful narration and stellar art that compliment one another perfectly to create a super charming storybook atmosphere. The voice of the narrator is calm and soothing, while the art is alive and gives everything so much character, especially the wolves, who have so many little dynamic expressions that constantly shift to telegram exactly what action they're about to make. The music perfectly suits the vibes of the game, the faint strums of guitar strings are exactly the kind of music I want for a puzzle/tactics game like this.Having the hero be a deaf woman in a world overrun by werewolves whose very howl's turn you into a beast is a story set up I absolutely adore. Representation by itself is important and needed, but representation as a key element of the plot - a crucial part of the story which cannot be removed or else the story falls apart - is masterclass.I've only just made it to Chapter 2, but as you can see i'm really into it so far!

_childDocuments_.review: I fired up  for the first time after a hard day’s work. The main theme on acoustic guitar and cello soothed my mind. The folk tale atmosphere drew me in as the player character’s letter-writing voice-over narration set the tone for a dark adventure. It took me back to reading the original fairy tales as they used to be, before they were censored and infantilized by modern books. is a relaxing game with a minimalistic turn-based combat gameplay that rewards elegant solutions. The aesthetic and the setting work well together to carry the gameplay, and the soundtrack and narration keep you interested. This not an elaborate strategy game, but it is challenging in terms of finding the correct, intended solutions. If you go in with that in mind,  is fairly compelling.
_childDocuments_.name: Howl

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended for fans of tactical xcom-like games. The fight/hide mechanics are rather limited, but there are multiple ways to use them in a particular level and with ever-increasing number of enemies on each level it's not easy to get through the game, especially if you're in for all achievements and don't use assist mode. I have little experience with strategy/tactics games, and I was lured in by pretty visuals and music (both are great and add a lot to the atmosphere). For experienced players the game is easy enough as is.
_childDocuments_.name: Howl

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the whole demo of this game and LOVED IT, and I'm slowly playing through the full game! The art style and ambiance in this game are soothing and somber, like a well-loved fairy tale, and the music/narration add so much as well. The levels are well-crafted and I'm having a great time puzzling out the optimal paths through each one. Love it! Perfect relaxing vibe for a gray and rainy day.
_childDocuments_.name: Howl

_childDocuments_.review: I adore this game! The art style and music had me hooked immediately, as did the story, even if it is immediately a bit cliche. I like the challenge of completing each level within the shortest route possible and that there are options to replay a level for side objectives you missed, such as skulls and strangers.Definitely recommend if you want a relaxing puzzle game!
_childDocuments_.name: Howl

_childDocuments_.review: A nice little puzzle game. All of the enemies movements are 100% predictable, so the goal is to plan your movements in response and kill all the enemies / get to the goal in a certain number of turns without getting killed by the monsters. You unlock a few potential powers to give you additional options. The levels are all hand-designed.There's not huge amounts of depth here, but there's enough to spend an enjoyable few hours. Similarly, the story isn't super deep but it's sufficient to add some narrative bones for a few hours. Ultimately, I enjoyed the time I spent with Howl, and I think it accomplished what it was trying to do without overstaying its welcome.
_childDocuments_.name: Howl

_childDocuments_.review: I really love the idea behind the gameplay. It makes for an interesting story. The music is good as well and I'd have so many things to say about the graphisms. I must admit that sometimes I have difficulties reading the layout of some parts of the maps, but the game isn't punishing and I just try it out to see if you can step on the tile or not.

_childDocuments_.review: Neat little game with turn-based puzzle combat (a bit reminiscent of Into the Breach). Probably on the simpler side and not too long (it took me 5.5h to complete, doing all missions, but not trying to achieve 100% everywhere). The story is relatively straight-forward, but nicely narrated as if it was as bed-time story. The visual style is great and fits this decision. Overall, I would recommend it and I think the regular price of ~10€ is fair.
_childDocuments_.name: Howl

_childDocuments_.review: Howl is a short and sweet little game with a very interesting story premise: a plague that turns people into beasts if they hear another beast's howl. So the hero is deaf making her immune to the plague. The game has a great art style, music, and narration. Each level presents a map where you move across a grid trying to reach an endpoint. This is complicated by obstacles, beasts, and people you need to rescue. Each level has 2 (possibly 3) goals: get to the end under a certain number of turns, kill all beasts, and rescue all the people if there are any on the map. The pace of the game is great; Howl does exactly what it sets out to do and doesn't overcomplicate things just for the sake of checking boxes.
_childDocuments_.name: Howl

_childDocuments_.review: I immediately liked the game's storybook visuals and was intrigued by the promise of challenging tactical gameplay. As far as promises and trailers go, they can be hit and miss, so I appreciate there being a relatively comprehensive demo. It lets you play about 70% of the first chapter and made a good case for the game. The early levels seem a bit more restricted and puzzle-y, especially considering that enemies are acting deterministically, i.e. they follow a known set of rules, no randomness involved.However, after unlocking the first couple of skills, the player's options really open up and levels generally feature a number of enemies that will make it feel properly tactical and less puzzle-like.I have yet to complete the full game, but the number of side-paths on chapter maps and the challenge of 100%-ing each level seems pretty substantial to me. Speaking of acing levels: I found myself flush in "Confidence & Skulls" (the currency for unlocking and levelling skills) pretty early on - Whatever skill I want, I can usually get right away, without having to actually work towards it. I'm guessing this is hard to balance without frustrating more casual players, but I thought I'd mention it.Super-minor, but I enjoyed the game properly recognizing the Switch Pro Gamepad I use on PC and showing me the correct button-prompts, even adopting a sort of Switch-style assignment of confirm/cancel buttons. It's not mentioned on the store page and might not matter to most, but I thought it was a neat touch worth mentioning.Presentation-wise, it's best not to expect anything crazy. Story presentation is pretty simplistic, but I think it fits the style of the game and all the ingredients (visuals, writing, audio, voice work) blend nicely. Reminds me of SNES-era games, before everything had to be a twenty minute animated cut scene. If you dig that, definitely check this out! The game is pretty to look at, offers a solid challenge without feeling tedious or stressful.
_childDocuments_.name: Howl

_childDocuments_.review:
A turn-based tactical folktale in living ink

Howl is a turn-based tactical folktale set in medieval times. A sinister "howling plague" has ravaged the land, turning all who hear it into feral beasts. You play a deaf heroine plunging into danger in search of a cure.

Plan up to six steps in advance to outmaneuver your opponents: wolfish creatures filled with hunger and rage. Various types of fiends are lurking in the shadows, each of them possessing different abilities and their own levels of vitality. So, you need to consider carefully the strategy that will bring them to their knees.

Not only do you have your wits to rely on while plotting your attack, you also have an array of abilities at your disposal. As you slay more wolves, you acquire skills like Vault, Smoke Bomb, and Piercing Shot. Venture forth on your journey to upgrade your skills and unlock more Action Slots and Undo Round Points. As you plan your moves, you will also shape your own prophecy, composing a dynamic work of scripture as you fight.

Howl's visuals are created through "living ink", a flowing art style that paints the story as you play. Carve your way through a dark, fairy-tale world made up of obscure yet magical places where you fight and write to rid the lands of the plague.

name: DRAGON QUEST MONSTERS: The Dark Prince
detailed_description: Overview DRAGON QUEST MONSTERS: The Dark Prince comes to Steam®! Compose your very own team of monsters from across the DRAGON QUEST series and engage in thrilling battles against your foes. Recruit monsters from the wild world around you and combine them to synthesize new creatures as you see fit. With over 500 monsters to choose from and a revamped synthesis system to explore, you can mix and match to you heart's content to create your favorite cute critters and dastardly supervillains, as well as brand-new additions to the monstrous roll call. Your quest to become the greatest monster wrangler of all time starts here! Story Psaro is cursed and is unable to harm anything with monster blood. Now, he must become a Monster Wrangler to create an army for battle. The hunt for high-ranked monsters takes Psaro through the ever-changing seasons of Nadiria and its unique environments, with rivers of bubbling lava, mysterious ancient ruins, and soaring towers of cake. Along the way, Psaro meets the kind-hearted elf, Rose, who joins his adventure to seek out ever-stronger monsters. The key to Psaro's success lies with synthesis: the ability to combine two monsters and create a stronger offspring. Each new creation brings Psaro one step closer to his goal of becoming the Master of Monsterkind. (The network mode Online Battles from the console version, where players battle one another in real time, is not included.) Game Features - A Wondrous World Awaits As time passes in Nadiria, so too do the seasons change, with different weather conditions tempting new monsters out of hiding and revealing paths to undiscovered areas. The Circles of Nadiria are sure to provide a fresh experience every time you visit. - Over 500 Unique Monsters With such varied environments to explore, you can expect them to be inhabited by a plethora of monsters. While many can be recruited in battle, occasionally a defeated monster will ask to join your team of its own accord. Befriend as many monsters as you can, then combine them to synthesize new creatures and build a unique party to your exact liking. - Enjoy All the DLC from the Console Version The Steam® version includes the DLC packs from the console version: the Mole Hole, Coach Joe's Dungeon Gym and Treasure Trunks. Make the most of their unique features to enhance your adventure. - Test Your Might in Quickfire Contests Register your team for the network mode Quickfire Contests to participate in automated battles against the party data of 30 other players. Once a day you can earn stat-boosting items as a prize, and the monsters from any team you defeat will be added to your roster (up to rank B monsters only).

name: Trinity Trigger
detailed_description: Trinity Trigger Deluxe Edition This Deluxe Edition includes the Trinity Trigger game, the Extra Episode Set DLC, and the Weapon Set DLC. Will the power of three defy destiny? About the Game Step into the world of Trinity Trigger, an all-new action role-playing game combining the look and feel of iconic RPGs of the ‘90s with a modern emphasis on fast-paced, customizable combat. As Cyan, a young man burdened by the gods with the mantle of Warrior of Chaos and an inevitable clash against the Warrior of Order, players will set out on a grand adventure to defy fate and save Trinitia. Cyan and his companions Elise and Zantis are accompanied by strange creatures known as Triggers that can transform into eight types of weapons, and players can switch freely between the three characters to implement a solo combat strategy, or team up with up to two friends for local co-op. Together, they will write a new destiny. Master the Weapons of the Gods Solve puzzles and defeat enemies alone or with friends in local co-op as you traverse the dungeons of each Arma, towers made from the fallen weapons of the gods. Seek Out Trinitia’s Mysteries Reveal hidden passages by exploring every last bit of Trinitia’s diverse biomes. Chat with townsfolk for clues to uncover the heavily guarded secrets held in these forests, deserts, snowfields, and more. Change the Tide of Battle Make expert use of the Weapon Wheel in battle to change between eight weapon types on the fly. Every enemy has a weakness—finding and exploiting it is the key to victory. A Generational Role-Playing Epic Trinity Trigger was inspired by the iconic RPGs of yesteryear, but its accessible and rewarding gameplay incorporates modern flourishes to make it an exciting new adventure for players of all ages.

short_description: Caught in the middle of a divine clash of epic proportions that has left gigantic weapons towering over the landscape, Cyan and newfound allies Elise and Zantis set out on a quest to save the world…and defy the gods. Claim your fate in this fantastical adventure inspired by classic JRPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: The premise is that divine weapons crashed to earth after a war between the God of Chaos and Order, drastically changing the realms around them. These swords represent a multi-story building/dungeon, countless floors high. The main dungeons of each area are also sections of fallen armories of former divine grace, and they are now filled with monsters that guard the sacred altars within. So-called Bringers will summon spirit beasts known as Triggers to serve as both mates and weapons, and then seek out these altars to expand their Triggers weapon-forming abilities. So one of the goals of the narrative is therefore the exploration of dungeons, helping townfolk by doing quests, and the acquisition of new Trigger forms.The other goal is the continuing clash between the God of Order and Chaos, fought in the mortal world by two champions who are destined to meet in an epic showdown that will decide the issue once and for all. In previous iterations, the issue was settled by an outside group's assassination of one of the champions before things even got that far. This does not seem to please the protagonist Cyan, who happens to be the reluctant Champion of Chaos. The flow of the storyline is a steady line from dungeon to dungeon, with only a few distractions left and right. There could have been more variety in the area layouts or more areas not directly related to the weaponry and alteration.In terms of gameplay, Trinity Trigger is still very much an homage to Secret of Mana, with better attack chaining, action gauges, and special moves. All party members can eventually gain access to every weapon type by exploring dungeons, but they all have their own expertise. Cyan excels with the sword, Elise with the bow, and Zantis with his axe. There are a few puzzles here and there, but they're never really demanding. The game is presented in an isometric view with real-time action combat and is ultimately very straightforward and beginner-friendly. Attacking consumes stamina, which refills itself by waiting a few seconds. All of the healing and status effects—like being poisoned—are done via menu, so I found myself navigating through the menus a lot during battle. The only downside is that the AI is pretty useless in group fights and will blindly follow you into enemy traps on the ground, causing you to use far too many healing items for your AI partners.One gimmick of the boss fights is that the large monsters will always have some sort of shield that has to be worn down before they can be stunned and become vulnerable. In most cases, this shield has one or two specific vulnerabilities to certain types of weapons. While this is a good idea in concept, it doesn't come together very well. Certain bosses escalate into a "Rock, Paper, Scissors" kind of combat with enough shield to take multiple times their total hit points in damage before they are defeated, and that can definitely be annoying.A lot of flavor is actually added by the voices of the characters. The music is appropriate for the respective area, even if it isn't a big highlight, and the anime-like cutscenes fit perfectly into the story.The game definitely has its interesting and, especially gameplay-wise, nice moments, but unfortunately, they are somewhat overshadowed by the simple JRPG cliché of an amnesia story that only gets better halfway through. It's definitely a serviceable JRPG. It takes about 16-20 hours to finish the game, and this includes >50% of the side quests. It really needed more from everything: more optional stuff, more types of enemies (especially among the bosses), and a generally better handling of the plot points. I still had a lot of fun with it, and I hope that FuRyu will continue to make this kind of videogame in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Tldr; you miss absolutely nothing by side stepping this one, or to say you gain nothing by playing it. I played it so you don't have to.I've finished the game in 15 hours with all the side quests available before the post game.  Final boss is a tedious cancer after which you unlock some post game content, which is infinitely more tedious.It is as mediocre as it gets, with all the dungeons being reskins, companion AI being brain dead to the point where I believe they would die less if they stood in place, lest they run into every possible hazard. They'll register the red indicators for enemy attacks, run to the edge of it and still get hit. Story is, I don't know, there, your usual "teens save the world", toppling literal gods and stuff. I digress, but there is this one section where you get to a town where everyone is driven mad by the nearby relic and there is no cure (doctors who attempted to find it were equally driven mad), and then the very first side quest in the said town is a woman asking for some herbs that are keeping her from going mad(?).Combat is casual attack/dodge/get stunlocked or hope the enemy is weak to the axe in which case you facetank everything since you don't flinch while being hit. 8 different weapons in total with two sets of selectable combos and a unique attack. There is a nice touch where the weapons visibly change form as you level them up.All in all if you REALLY need to scratch that Mana itch, Oninaki is currently on PS Plus Extra, an equally mediocre experience. Wait for a sale :D
_childDocuments_.name: Trinity Trigger

_childDocuments_.review: Also yes, it runs very well on Steam Deck but some minor aspect ratio issues.For what it is, Trinity Trigger is a great JRPG for those who love 90's RPG like Secret of Mana or Illusion of Gaia. While the story is short and somewhat generic, it does a great job at delivering simple but classical feel of an Action RPG with PS2-like graphics.However, it's quite expensive for what it is. If you want an action RPG where you can turn your brain off, wait for a sale on this one.
