_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: the game has been given to me via Daredrop for streaming purposes.that being said, these opinions are entirely my own.1st of all let me mention that the game does have good parts too it. it's creative and has some cute looking characters and good looking art.the character designs are quite nice and the story is ok.i must sadly say tho. that after streaming this game for 3 days, i don't actually like the game.i had to think long and hard about it and as much as i'd love to see it succeed. has some glaring issues to the game.the game will unlikely get any updates, if it did. i might recommend it.but like i mentioned. it has some glaring issues. like a whole laundry list of issues.so let me get started on it shall we,1, repeated voice lines. over and over and over and over and over and over again. like endlessly repeating voice lines.i noticed this problem early on when you unlock the 2nd character. as she constantly repeats the same 3 attack voice lineslike a broken record. at some point you go numb too the voices to then suddenly hear it all again.it's so mind bogglingly annoying that it's obvious that the sound department didn't co-ordinate with the development department, why? because it's not just the characters. the menu's the creatures EVEN the g darn merchants repeat the voice lines over and over and over and over and over and over again. you buy 1 item (mainly blueprints) and with every single purchase they repeat their 1 of 2 voice lines. you open a menu or quick menu. and you're spammed with voice lines.you upgrade a skill and another voice line repeats. it's so stupidly annoying that i hate it. i would mute all the voices if i wasn't streaming the game. and honestly. i think it impacted the viewer experience as well.2, the ai is absolutely terrible. your allies won't attack enemies unless you attack them 1st. they will often run out of an enemy aoe only to run back into it, they will often times stop attacking altogether. eat hits or not even avoid the attacks.your best bet is to place them all on range and keep your main unit as melee. just to hopefully prevent needless damage.allies can't use status recovery items. only healing items to heal themselves. not even helping allies. 3, the spam of ailments and terrible healing items.i don't know who's idea it was to give 90% of the enemies the ability to poison you. it's a good thing u can carry 20 antidotes as you will go through them constantly. at the point it's permanently fixed to your quick menu. this combined with point 1 is terrible. as every time you open the menu you hear the same voice lines again.then whats with the potions? seriously they should have been % based potions. you can only carry 10 of each type and honestly it's stupid how often you have to recover health. due to the bad ai on point 2 you're constantly spamming potions to heal your allies. recovery with "manatides" is ok but only situational and often times doesn't help your other party members.4, mimics mimics everywhere!o m f g dark souls could take a page out of this book over here. mimics absolutely every friggin where. seriously you can't turn your butt without being attacked by them. and you need to beat them for their gems (that be a point to mention later)gods these things are everywhere! not only are they stupidly strong, they poison you and just soak up a needless amount of damage. 5, too many weapons, too little innovation. so you obtain a excessive amount of weapons which would be the selling point of this game. unfortunately you only have space for 4 weapons on your quick bar, no way to quickly change weapons on your party members, and constantly have to switch out for weapons that are "effective". ontop of the fact that each weapon has their own loadout. (which we will also mention later) there is simply a needless amount of fluff. honestly the amount of weapons would be fine if you go with the damage type style of blunt/piece/slash/magic kinda gameplay. instead everything has upto 8 different weaknesses or strengths related to a weapon. which is stupid. not to mention that your characters have an "element" yet there is absolutely nothing in the game related too it. o he's fire, she's water? woopti do! does it give any benefits? non at all!5b combat becomes a messdue to point 5 having a needless amount of weapons and a lack of switching around properly. the combat becomes a complete mess. bosses are needlessly tanky due to their "shield" bar which drains faster if you have their weapon weakness equipped i guess. but due to the fact that each weapon has it's own loadout, you're reluctant to switch out weapons.while also some bosses constantly change their weaknesses. making it a complete mess to fight. suddenly the boss isn't weak against swords. but against your fists! great. but i never leveled up these weapons! (o welp another point to mention i guess, guess i'll mention it now)5c weapon upgrading/skillswith as many weapons there are. they sure as hell lack allot of depth too them. each weapon has a 3hit combo, a special and another special. gods if i know what they are called.the 3hit combo can be reconfigured each combo stage has 2 skills to chose from (unless you bought the dlc for whatever fluffin reason) so effectively each weapon has 6 attacks. some objectively better than others.you then have a skill you can use when your weapon glows and another when your charge bar is full. that's the full extend of combat honestly.yet they also added skill upgrades. where u can upgrade your weapons to make the attacks stronger. but the TP required for it is shared between ALL the character's weapons. meaning you have to either spread out your points. or do like me and focus your points into the skills you like to use on your favorite weapons.you can see how 5b conflicts with 5c as you end up having to switch weapons too often to focus on anything.5d weapon loadoutswhat? you thought we were done ranting about weapons? gods no.each and every single weapon of a character has 3 attack and 3 armor slots. each used for gems.attack slot gems can only equipped once while defense slot gems can be equipped 3 times.if you want to slot every single weapon with better or the best stuff, you would need roughly 150 gems!while you can only carry 300 gems. mind boggeling to me honestly. this is not helped by the fact that there are ALLOT of different tiers of gems, as well as different rarities.effectively i ended up slotting only 2 or 3 weapons per character as i could not be bothered with it anymore.the whole of point 5+ ends up being. you switch out weapons too often, have to slot too many gems and have to farm too much TP level up the skills. after 3 days of streaming the game, i only maxed out 1 maybe 2 weapons per character.6, needless amount of gems.so i mentioned earlier that gems are used to slot into your weapons.each and every single gem has at least 5 different types. each can have 3 different rarities. this in itself would not be as big of a problem, but as you need so many of them for your equipment you end up juggling gems from weapon to weapon until you have enough to slot everything.and let me tell you, there are allot of gems that are not even worth looking at. the best thing they could have done is to give each weapon the same kind of armor slots are they did with attack slots.the attack slots can only have 1 of each type equipped. so only 1 gem that increases attack ect ect.as the armor slot you end up just slotting in mass amount of exp bonus (in my case) honestly i didn't see a reason until late game not to equip exp as obviously having a higher level is more important than +5 flippin defense.---did i cover everything? think i did. i think.anyway.what they should have done is to give every character x amount of weapons, limit the repeated voice lines and tweak the allies so they don't just stand around doing nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that was build on inspiration from 90s era rpgs and it does pay homage to the childhood memories of that time to some extent. However, it does fall short in the sense that it cannot rival classics from that time. This is a game that most jrpg lovers will not play because there was hardly any marketing for it and the overall reviews for it will not have it standout from the sea of games released this year.As you progress throughout the story, you be moved to different areas quickly but the story progresses very slowly. Add to it the fact the story did not draw much my attention. You control a character named Cyan born with the mantle of Warrior of Chaos meaning he is destined to fight the Warrior of Order, his sister. He along with characters to some extent just join you traverse throughout the land of Trinitia in an attempt to defy the fated duel. These three "Bringers" in the story will summon spirits known as Triggers that will serve as their destined teammates and their weapons in combat.The battle system is rather simple. Each Trigger serves as a multitude of weapons that will unlock as the story progresses,  enemies have weakness to certain weapons being used against them. There is even a feature that allows you to equip your weapon with certain things that makes them stronger. There is also charged up single attacks for each character and a group attack. You can change weapons and companion to control at any moment during battle. The battles are real time and fast paced; however, the companion AI is stupid. They literally run straight to danger while you move along with the other character which makes some battles harder than it should be. The music does blend in with the environment and it does complement the artstyle with each character along with the voice acting. To me along with almost if not every reviewer agrees with is the direction on the artistry the developers embarked on. For a game that came out in 2023, there are little adjustments available in the menu.  Very few graphical settings, no difficulty adjustments, and texts move slow.Having said all that, I do not recommend this game. Whether there is a good reason for the price tag along with the dlcs, that is debatable. This is a game in which its developers should have dedicated more time in adding more features to make the game more enjoyable and flesh out even better what was already presented.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's a 15-hour minimum (basic story) game with evocative to old-school handheld gameplay. In which you spend a few hours leveling up your heroes and unlocking progression. A time sink. Sure, visually. Most people are turned off by it because they want the greatest, most realistic 8k quality graphics and eye candy from studios like Ufotable. That will not be found here. It's a Japanese role-playing game. It is more concerned with grind and story/character development. Because it is usually the dialogue that is to be focused on, visuals are usually given less priority and that is perfectly fine with a lot of fans of the genre. My negative view of this game isn't that the game itself is bad, but I don't warrant the purchase of this game as it is. You have roughly 20 maybe 25 dollars worth of gameplay here. It's a lot of fun and might help you pass the time if you don't have anything else to do. However, it is not on par with other games in its price range. The only thing I can say is that if you like xSeed and their other published games, yes, purchasing the game will more likely result in more games being published to Steam, but this is generally bad practice because it will continue to raise the prices of games that are not worth anywhere near $60-100.It's not worth the price tag. Buy it on sale and you've got yourself a pretty decent game.The AI is complete garbage. You're better off killing them all and controlling one player or getting friends to control them, because they will absolutely eat damage for no reason.

_childDocuments_.review: Wanted to point out some glaring issues with this game is that looking at the controls layout with a keyboard and controller will softlock you in that part of the menu. You have you kill the program on task manager to get out of this to restart. buttons can't be remapped to a mouse and keyboard buttons cannot be rebound. For a game at 50 CAD MSRP i expect basic keyboard and mouse support, but this game does not provide it. While the game is not terrible he story thus far is pretty generic and uninteresting with passable gameplay. So a mediocre game with a mediorce price point won't sell. On steep discount (> 60% off) the price point is okay if you just wanted a mindless action-JRPG meant for young kids, but be aware of the issues i pointed above with keyboard support.Another dumb thing is that the game resolution does not support beyond 1080p. And for those of you who have an 21:9 Monitor the game does not have utilrawide support.PS: The post game after makes me regret my purchase and i wish i never bothered to play this game. The ai companions are so badly programmed that they will opt to suicide into the post-game final bosses attacks. Not only was this infuriating, but the final 3 bosses are essentially copy and paste of one another with a different colour and the attacks become a bullet hell game with very little visual screen clarity making this a very unpleasant experience. For a game that had very little grind for the in-story gameplay the end game is a grinding nightmare for materials for slot in bonus stats gem crafting.

_childDocuments_.review: Continuing the fine (?) tradition of FuRyu games that offer similar experiences to popular JRPG titles of yesteryear, Trinity Trigger doesn't attempt to innovate or stand out (and in fact is rather ugly for a game whose lead platform is the Switch...graphics are on par with Alliance Alive, a 3DS game-very odd considering the star power behind the game's creation) but it plays well enough and the characters aren't repulsive. Music, provided by veteran composer Hiroki Kikuta, is pleasant, but not the most memorable of his discography. One mark in the game's favor is that multiplayer is an option here, for those that were disappointed that the Trials of Mana remake lacked it. Another positive is the inclusion of customization of your normal attacks to an extent, something that should be focused on if a sequel is in the cards.

_childDocuments_.review: Reviewing this as a full price title I can only give a thumbs down. If this were a 2-man indie passion project, it would be a different story. The soundtrack is good, everything else just feels cheap and lackluster. To give 1 example: All dungeons are just reskins of each other. They look the same, they feel the same and it's the same plain corridors over and over again. If you are looking for an action RPG as good as the Trials of Mana Remake, this is not it. Buy it for 20 bucks but not full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Trinity Trigger feels like they wanted to make a game similar to Secret of Mana or Trials of Mana, but didn't put nearly enough love into it.I recommend picking up Trials of Mana instead if you haven't already played it. It is a much better game. However, if you have already played Trials and Secret of Mana and are looking for something else that is similar to fill that gap, then this game may be for you.I don't feel like the $49.99 or $59.99 price tags are warranted however. The quality just isnt there. This should have been a $39.99 or even a $29.99 game.--------------------------------------------PROS+ Combat feels like a modernized Secret of Mana.+ The weapon system. There are 8 weapon types to unlock. Customize your attack combo with each weapon on each character. Lots of weapon options to taylor to your playstyle.+ The crafting system is nice once you get used to it.+ Japanese voice acting is decent (can't vouch for English, haven't tried it)+ The music is pretty nice. Most of the sound track is written by Mana composer Hiroki Kikuta, so the music really does give that Secret of Mana vibe. There are a few standout tracks that are especially good. The final boss theme was great and really reminded me of the Flammie fight theme from Secret of Mana.+ The Manatite system, which is similar to Materia if you've played FF7. In this game it replaces armor entirely. You can customize a your traits with different combos of Manatite+ There is A TON of post game content. Extra sidequests, dungeons, bosses, and weapon upgrades galore open up after you beat the game. --------------------------------------------CONS- DAY ONE PAID DLC!!! I got the Deluxe edition because I wanted to try the extra side quest DLCs. On the plus side, they were short sidequests that fit well into the midgame. They had good rewards and added just a little bit more character to each of the characters involved.. But they SHOULD HAVE BEEN INCLUDED IN THE BASE GAME. They were like 10-15 minutes of content each! There was no reason these short sidequests should cost an extra $10 for the 4, much less $20 (4 x $5 each) to those who didn't buy the deluxe edition. This was a ridiculous cash grab trying to take advantage of 'the fear of missing out'.- World building was done poorly. Zones are thrown together haphazzardly and they make up flimsy excuses in game as to why things are that way.- The lore seems thrown together and feels half-assed.- Character development is minimal- There are some clashing art styles. NPC models for example look comically lower quality compared to the models of story characters.- There are no magic or abilities. All you have is weapons and items. All attacks come from your weapons. All healing and buffing comes from items, with some minor exceptions. It feels somewhat shallow.- Level design. Sometimes the maps feel very VERY cheaply put together. Not every map/level is bad, there are definitely good ones in there. But the ones that are bad are really immersion breaking. The Aldo Desert maps are some of the worst examples, made of clusters of blocky square sections. Heres a screenshot: - Multiplayer is locked until a few hours into the story.- Starts slow. I had a hard time getting into the game until a few hours in. --------------------------------------------KNITPICKING* There is no option to display HP as a number instead of a bar in the HUD. I liked seeing my character's growth in Mana games by seeing the numbers go up over time. No such luck here.* The number of different kinds of fodder drops you can find everywhere can be overwhelming at first. * Not enough monster variety

_childDocuments_.review: This game is better than I expected, but it may only appeal to people who look back fondly on .  is an upgrade in gameplay compared to the SoM remake, but it's not a totally modern game.Dungeons and areas tend to be pretty small, but significantly larger than SoM.Combat is still stamina-based, but you can attack around 6 times before being out of stamina. That's compared to attacking once in SoM.The difficulty is also similar to SoM. Getting stun-locked for several hits is the most dangerous part. However, enemies can't be as easily stun-locked in , so it's better in that regard.The progression is similar: explore an open area, get to the next town, get through the next dungeon, get some new weapon or power, and repeat. Especially in the early game, this can feel repetitive, but the game throws some twists into this formula by the middle.The story is pretty simple, but not as simple as SoM.The music is by Hiroki Kikuta, who did SoM and other Mana games, including the recent . I felt the soundtrack was pretty weak early in the game, but it gets much better; there are some great tracks.Stamina-based combat, a dodge roll (with iframes, I think), somewhat limited healing, dungeon crawling, bosses, moderately-paced combat.Is  a proto-Soulslike? By modernizing the combat slightly,  comes so close to being a Soulslike that I can barely tell if it is or isn't one.It's not as difficult as most Soulslikes, and it's a lot more colorful. But there are some optional bosses that are very difficult, and you have to be constantly upgrading your weapons and Manatite to keep up with the enemies.Is this game much different from  or ? I really don't know.I hesitate to say this game is "great," but it's a real step up from . It's very good for what it is, but it might not offer the complexity that modern gamers expect.But I really like it. On sale for $20 for the Deluxe Edition, I felt it was worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay but I'd wait for it to go on sale. Can't recommend it at full price.Plot progression seems kind of slow despite moving through different areas quickly but overall the characters are likable and party banter is decently written. Combat is simple but interesting enough. AI is a little dumb so this is probably better to play with friends than solo but you have to unlock it after a couple of hours of playing solo. As it is, the AI gets damaged 5x as much as me and I'm not necessarily good at the game. Generous amount of potions and other recovery items/abilities sort of compensates for it. My only real complaint is that there's no vsync setting in game and without it, there's a ton of screen tearing. Can enable v-sync in graphics driver settings to fix it though.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels aweful... There is little to no feedback when hitting enemy. Feels like hitting air. Lack of sound design. Bosses are just bullet sponge slug fests. Your companions will make no effort to avoid attacks and will consistently die, so you'll end up alone fighting a battle meant for 3 people.The music is pretty fine. It feels like generic JRPG music and it does the job it's supposed to do.While I like the design of the character sprites. What I'm getting tired of however is the Visual Novel esthetics, that every conversation takes place as a visual novel mini show. I am just tired of this. It takes me out of the game world that the devs crafted.Standard JRPG fair: find crystals, and then kill god (I assume, haven't finished the game yet, not even sure I will).No option to rebind my keys/buttons?It's obvious this games tries to be like Secret of Mana, even replicating the multiplayer that unlocks 3 hours in, which was dumb then, and even more dumb today. But even then, Secret of mana wth all it's flaws, was a pretty good game IMO. Trinity Trigger is not. And that is mainly because the combat feels so bad. And combat is everything in these types of games. You could have no story at all, but if the combat is fun, you have a game. But have an excellent story with aweful combat, and people will just go watch masochistic playthrough on youtube. I really regret paying 90$ CAD for this very mediocre experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is mostly fine. There are few points I don't really like in general, though. _childDocuments_.review: Rating:7/10I would only recommend this game when it is on sale!You play as a party of 3, 2 are controlled by AI and let me tell you. _childDocuments_.review: If you like Secret of Mana, this game is inspired by it.The combat is very similar where you can only attack so often. Attacking costs meter so when your meter is empty, you do minimal damage. The meter refills over time. You can attack up to a three hit/chain in a combo. Like Secret of Mana, you can unlock and have access upwards of 8 different weapons. Each of the weapons also have upwards to 3 different moveset for each string so you can customize your weapon's attack style. Unlike Secret of Mana, each of your party members can equip the same weapon at the same time. You also have a buff you can activate when you have full aura meter and a super/charge attack along with a big team attack. Instead of armor, this game has a gem system that you can slot into your weapons to increase stats, resistance or gain extra passives.There is no magic spells like Secret of Mana in this game.The music has a very similar tune/feeling to Secret of Mana.The difficulty can vary depending on how you play the game. You can get by with fairly well if you keep your items relatively full each time you venture out.Some cons/nitpicks-your attack animation is kind of slow which makes you prone to getting hit very often-the enemies, especially the smaller general mobs, have fast attack animation and will interrupt your attack strings-enemies don't flinch therefore you can't interrupt them-you have no invincible frames so getting stun locked to death isn't a rare thing-the bosses have a guard break mechanic (you have to delete their guard meter before you can do damage)-multiplayer doesn't unlock until you get all three party member-your ai party members are fairly dumb, they will only stand in a single place and spam attack, very very rarely will they dodge-every single weapon type for every single character has it's own set of slots for the gem system, meaning by the end game you have to probably mess with 144 different slots which is a hassle if you just want to play the game, Luckily you can get by with few gem slots.It's a fun game but you can't play the game recklessly or aggressively due to how harsh the combat is towards the player. Like most multiplayer able games, you'll have more fun playing with others.EDIT: Now that I've beaten the game and the post game finale, this game is a very difficult to recommend. The enemy designs does not complement the game play design, you are ALWAYS at a disadvantage. There is a particular build that helps mitigate some of the problem but being required to play a specific way doesn't help much with the overall impression. I still stand that if you're playing multiplayer, you'll have a fun time, single player however might be less enjoyable until you have that build.

_childDocuments_.review: Although the game was ok, the dungeons were very generic looking and was a copy and paste throughout. What really made me not pursue the game further was the inability to play coop during remote play sessions. I thought it was my connection at first, but when I tested other games in coop using remote play (Ex. secret of mana and Portal 2) they worked fine. Every time i attempted to play in coop mode (Trinity Trigger) using remote play the game slowed down significantly as if the game switched to a slow motion mode. It didn't seem like any lag I experienced from network connectivity. After a couple of attempts and some changes to the settings in both the game and remote play, the game just didn't run smoothly in remote play coop.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is alright so far. Multiplayer with friend would probably up my enjoyment of the game. The music to me is just mediocre, the story is meh, combat feels great. I guess that is how i feel, the game is just average so far. The boss fights and even the harder optional ones are not really hard, they usually do 2 or 3 patterns that are easy to dodge around and it is just hitting a sponge for a while. _childDocuments_.review: Not recommending purely because its way to expensive for the experience. So far so good. The game not bad. The price is WAY too much (I got if half price).I will say my main distaste for this game is the npcs you have following you. They die....a lot. They are not very good at dodging boss mechanics. I wish instead you could have them not follow you but still swap to them in combat. (I hope that made sense.) It would be easier to keep them alive if the bosses aggro stayed on the person you are controlling but instead it kind of randomly picks someone to focus on and then swaps people every now and then. Also having the npcs auto use their big skills would be nice instead of having to swap back and forth to use it which can be a little disorientating.Over all not a bad game.WAY TOO FREAKING EXPENSIVE! Totally not worth 50 bucks no matter how you look at it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's definitely not the best game or JRPG you can get here, but it's a cool little one. Yeah it's not amazing in any ways, it can even be frustrating as the other 2 characters played by the AI are so dumb they can't jump out of an attack, but it's still a fun little ride.Story is OK, but messy. _childDocuments_.name: Trinity Trigger

_childDocuments_.review: Trinity Trigger has some bad and good things. The story is certainly interesting. Even if the dialogues are sometimes generic. I found that the 2d conversation animations, lack expression. The fighting is fun but having to pause to switch weapons is just a core, in the long run. I dislike a lot, the fact that all the characters can have all the same weapons and powers. In that sens, your party is all the same. You decide which one can have that power or that weapon, but if it's not into the game, it makes every upgrades an after though. Some bosses have a difficulty spike. The color system that block a weapon on a boss is especially aggravating. Since switching weapons or characters in fight is tedious, you can imagine how those fights become frustrating and story blocking. Yes there is some good production value, and you might get 20 to 30 hours before hanging the game. But that won't be because you complete it, you might get bored or angry before that. I give it 65%. Mainly because the base is there, but the structural decision around the game seems weak to me.

_childDocuments_.review: DO NOT BUY AT FULL PRICEIt's a fun enough game, it has a typical JRPG storyline, though feels a bit rushed in the story telling.  The side quests are fun in helping out learn more about your character and teammates.  The art look great and the voice acting is enjoyable.  The areas look nice, and are fun to explore.  There is some crafting in the game, but only to make potions and supplies, which I don't mind.The combat is rough, but doable.  While I enjoy the free movement, the AI for your teammates isn't the brightest and seems to have a mission takes themselves out on enemy attacks or environmental hazards (watched one ping itself off spikes all over a room until it keeled over).  There is no magic in the game, just different weapon types to chose between and upgrade, and abilities you can attach to them.  The dungeons are relatively simple, and so far, have easy enough puzzles.  The bosses are meant to have you choose your weapons once you've learned which on they are weak to, but honestly I didn't notice much of a damage difference between a normal and buffed attack.One of the biggest draws that I looked forward to was the coop feature to play with friends, but it is only for local coop and using Steam's online local coop feature ended up causing too much lag for us to actual get anywhere.  It was a big letdown after spending almost 3 hours to unlock it.Overall, I do enjoy the game itself, even with some of its quirks.  I am glad I bought it on sale though, and highly recommend anyone looking to get it to wait for a similar sale.  While it is fun, I can't say it is $50-$60 fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend this game if you're looking for a very casual action RPG. I beat the main story and all non-post-game side quests in 20 hours. The story is fairly simple, and falls apart a little at the very end, but I didn't really mind.If you're looking for a masterpiece, this isn't it. But if you go in with modest expectations for something casual to scratch a particular genre itch, you'll have a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed playing this game. All throughout my time playing, I got mad 90's RPG vibes à la Trials of Mana and the like. It's a really cosy, albeit a little short game that's perfect for chillin'. I haven't had the chance to use to use the co-op, only ever played single payer. I've played the game for roughly 30-ish hours by this point and I'm very close to completing the achievements, with only 5-6 left. A lot of the achievements are basic grinding or story element related, nothing particularly difficult.  That being said, it isn't perfect game by any means; the game for some reason will stutter a fair bit, which is annoying at best, but still annoying. A far more frustrating grievance is how bad the AI companions can be at times, especially during boss fights -- repeatedly walking into lava, or spikes for example. Sometimes the true boss fight is keeping your AI companions alive rather than the boss itself. Overall, good game. I would play it again and encourage others to try it. 8/10. TLDR; Pros: + Decent story. Nothing amazing, but certainly something to chill to. + The character art was really well designed IMO. Big fan of all character's designs. + Amazing voice acting. I played with the English audio and it felt the voices really matched the designs. + Music complemented the individual areas quite well. Cons:- The frame stuttering. I eventually got used to it and ignored it, so it's not unbearable, just annoying. - The AI can be really, really frustrating at times. Biggest problem with the AI is during some fights your companions will voluntarily walk into hazardous elements and kill themselves. When you have a limited supply of healing, this becomes a problem.

name: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader
detailed_description: Explore the Koronus Expanse. Begin your adventure aboard your personal, giant voidship, traveling between the multitude of systems within the Koronus Expanse, a barely charted and incredibly perilous region of space. Despite being considered a backwater of the Imperium, this region encompasses an enormous stretch of the void, filled with dangerous creatures and prodigious opportunities for profit and exploration. Gather your crew. Rogue Traders never travel alone. Gather your retinue of righteous heroes, twisted psykers, and perfidious xenos. All of them are ready to follow you into the darkness between the stars. They will offer you counsel, aid you in battle, and allow you to amass ever more power. In return, you can guide them through their own personal journeys, changing their destinies forever. Your decisions matter, Lord-Captain. During quests show your subjects mercy or disdain, stay faithful to the God-Emperor, or consort with enemies of Mankind - your every decision and every act, even in character creation, is changing the in-game open world and those who inhabit it. Plan your actions carefully. Slaughter the enemies of Mankind in a fully-fledged isometric turn-based tactical combat. Take advantage of cover, the environment, and careful positioning to overpower your enemies. When that is not enough - use your companion`s powerful abilities to turn the tide of battle and achieve victory even in the direst of situations. Our video game adaption of the classic Rogue Trader ruleset allows an enormous number of possibilities for you to explore.

_childDocuments_.review: The Positives:1. Orchestral Grandeur: The game’s soundtrack is a symphony of celestial battles. From the haunting choirs that accompany desperate last stands to the triumphant brass fanfares during epic space battles, the music elevates the experience.2. Narrative Warp Jumps: The story line weaves a cosmic tapestry of intrigue, betrayal, and ancient secrets. As a rogue trader, you’ll navigate treacherous warp currents, negotiate with xenos species, and uncover lost relics. Each decision ripples across the stars, shaping your destiny.3. Visions of the Emperor: The graphics and animations are a testament to the Emperor’s grace. Whether you’re aboard a creaking voidship or exploring a desolate planet, the attention to detail immerses you in the 41st millennium. 4. Vox Transmissions: The voice acting is stellar (pun intended). From grizzled space marines to enigmatic Eldar seers, the characters breathe life into the dark expanse. The Negatives:1. Warp Rift Rush: Alas, after Act 3, the game seems to hurtle through the warp like a desperate escape pod. Pacing stumbles, leaving some plot threads unresolved or hastily tied up. The Emperor’s patience wears thin.2. Silent Sectors: While the major characters receive voice acting worthy of the God-Emperor, minor NPCs communicate via text. Prepare to decipher more runes than a Tech-Priest in a data crypt. It’s a missed opportunity for immersion.3. Codex Overload: The game’s lore is as dense as a neutron star. Be prepared to read extensive codex entries, mission briefings, and dialogue logs. If you’re not a loremaster, you might feel like a novice scribe deciphering ancient scrolls.4. Close-Combat Warp Spasms: The combat system favours tactical depth over accessibility. Casual gamers may find themselves lost in the warp during levelling-up and hostile engagements. The learning curve is steeper than a Space Marine’s pauldron.Overall: I would recommend this game for hardcore RPG fans and zealots of the Warhammer 40K universe. While Warhammer 40K Rouge Trader is a little rough around the edges; it provides a celestial voyage for those who crave intricate lore, strategic challenges, and the thrill of exploring the unknown.

_childDocuments_.review: I am writing this review during Chapter 2 of Rogue Trader and I have to say it is an absolute blast. And I want to start by addressing the elephant in the room, which I will circle back to at the end: Baldur's Gate 3. If you want one of the most inclusive, wonderful, and what is essentially the pinnacle of CRPGs in our generation, absolutely buy that game. It is one of a kind, with its own unique play style and atmosphere. It sets the bar impossibly high.However, If you're here because you're looking for a dark, bloody, Gothic atmosphere, where the God Emperor reigns supreme, and also want a CRPG, then look no further because you've found it. The game plays incredible tribute to the source material, to the point it almost feels like you need to read several books to understand the terms they throw around (don't worry, they have their own encyclopedia in-game). It perfectly captures the wartorn 40th millennium, where conflict and despair seem impossibly high, but so too does the worship and praise of the immortal God Emperor.Like many CRPG's, this game is turn-based. And while it is so, it is also fast-paced and visceral, with *ample* opportunities to manipulate the turn order. I am currently playing as a Commisar, which exists to buff and give bonus turns to allies, allowing them to act outside the turn order and eliminate foes to shorten the length of time before they can act again. Other classes, such as the psyker, apply a myriad of debuffs against targets and can, at times, apply buffs to teammates that will debuff enemies in the zone. The support classes certainly live up to their name.Warrior and Soldier classes provide their own way to tackle combat scenarios, and that is through as much violence as possible, while extending their turn as far as they can. Argenta, a Sister of Battle, has access to area abilities that have the possibility of hitting more than one enemy (and if you're unlucky, hitting no one at all), and a Run and Gun action that reduces the cost of her next attack by one Action Point, and gaining more Movement Points so she can maneuver herself around the battlefield, lining up the perfect shot.There is also ship-to-ship combat, where you must maneuver your ship around the vastness of grid-based space, firing torpedoes, which also have movement turns so, should the original target be destroyed, it can move around space targeting another craft. You can also assign your teammates to different parts of the ship, giving your voidship more benefits.Suffice it to say, this game, for me, hits all the right notes. It is not as polished as Baldur's Gate 3, nor did it have the budget BG3 did, however, while they are both CRPGs, they are apples to oranges. Rogue Trader captures the spirit and atmosphere, conflict and turmoil the 40K series is well-known for. If you are here because you are looking for a deep, mechanical, and complex 40K experience, you have found it. Owlcat are masters of their craft, proving that through the successes of the Pathfinder Series that they know how these games work and should function. I am seriously impressed, and you will be too.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Trader is a joy. For the most part. I'm on my fourth playthrough with others abandoned. You can seriously gimp yourself, the systems are deep and complex and I find it less forgiving than OwlCat's other games. Combat is a slog and utterly brutal if you've wronged your build somehow. I personally find Werglia's video is be enough to have competent team and the thought of using a guide isn't heresy for me because the complexity. You can easily gimp your reputations by spreading yourself thin, as well.I feel there are some insane difficulty spikes but they DO feel manageable. It just seems rough for someone not using a guide. Space combat is pretty fun though admittedly sometimes you'll find yourself in an eternal dance around the enemy where nobody is firing.Storytelling is amazing. Choices seem impactful. Planetary management is pretty fun with the projects having neat outcomes. I've enjoyed Iconoclast, I adored Dogmatic, and I'm REALLY enjoying the heretical story branches.This is a CRPG through and through. If you want that in a warhammer setting this is a must play for me and if you want that but are intimidates you'll have to do some reading. And you better like reading because LORE LORE STORY STORY galore but it is in text. Let the flow of your imagination take you to amazing Warhammer heights.I'll admit the bugs can be frustrating. Especially when they cost you navigator insight +15, if you know you know.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re looking for some screenshots  to view all the ones I took for this game.Your position as a Rogue Trader, one of the Emperor’s most important Chosen, will allow you to traverse the Koronus Expanse; no text is spared in outlining its lore, characters, factions and events in detail. Hundreds of well-written and sometimes voiced pages of dialogue will be the joy of avid readers. The characters part of your retinue or surrounding most major events are competently-written, while the variety of reactions and changes based on your action is impressive, although half of them feel out of place or pure nonsense, like an Astartes saying nothing after seeing you commit heresy.Visually, RT doesn’t impress; aside from the beautifully drawn comic panels and portraits, the graphics are modest for 2024 standards. Even with that, it still manages to have FPS issues in several locations. The world is built with solid care and attention to detail: even side locations have their own atmosphere and identity, although the keener eye will spot a large number of half-assed or borked elements, since the devs clearly preferred quantity over quality. The grimdark feel of 40K is there, but you’ll never feel fully immersed in such a setting. Exploration is divided between planetside and space. On the ground, you’ll lead your retinue of up to six members through a variety of locations, from Imperial cities to forgotten bunkers and even dimensional anomalies. There’s always a huge amount of secrets to find, with the help of your Awareness stat, which house unique items or secret level sections. Traps might be hidden anywhere; you can disarm them, or run through without a care since you’ll always have healing items far in excess.In space, your ship can jump between systems through the Warp, which may trigger enemy encounters or debuffs unless you make the routes safe using your Navigator’s limited Psyker powers; you’ll have to choose which paths to use the most in advance. Planets can be scanned, vessels hailed, pirates battled, which leads to a number of dialogues and text-based roleplaying panels that will put your party’s stats to the test.Fights play out in a turn-based fashion, with separate points for actions and movement, a high/low cover system, attacks of opportunity, but no overwatch mechanic. The system is vast and factors calculations to determine the outcome of every single shot, dodge or action—everything, from equipment to stats to perks, will be factored in at all times to the finest degree. Enemies are varied and have an enormous amount of unique abilities, weapons, perks and AI diversity based on the faction you’ll be facing, while bosses, at least early on, feel like decisive challenges. Having a synergistic party composition is paramount for victory, as usual you’ll be put against overwhelming numbers; the consequences of your fights, such as wounds, will weigh you down for the level, unless you heal them. The “Momentum” mechanic, based on enemy kills, rewards aggression and allows you to unleash a character’s “Ultimate” skill once charged, different for each class, raining destruction on your foes or buffing your team tremendously.This is all good and exciting, except from about halfway through, your party will become so OP that none of it will matter anymore. You’ll steamroll everything once you figure out what perks and items to stack together and create absurd combinations of statistics. Bosses and enemies that in the 40K lore could slay entire Astartes companies are demolished in a few turns.Space combat works in the same way, but in a simpler fashion, having your ship usually put against many foes, with a shield then health separating you from the void. A number of skills and maneuvers, depending on which character is assigned to what station on the vessel, will prove critical to succeed against foes. The balance is, again, screwed majorly except for late-game enemy ships, which are OP, forcing you to resort to kiting strategies to emerge victorious, even with the best gear money can buy.All your characters can choose various specializations that will define their role on the field, with the possibility to respec and even create custom mercenaries from scratch to build the ultimate party that suits your strategy best. Leveling up will have you access the next tier of your current class, which may unlock stat bonuses, new abilities and more. They can also acquire proficiencies to use new types of weapons or armor, and their moral inclination will allow them to use specific items that are restricted, such as some only being usable by a Heretic character. You’ll also be able to upgrade and customize your ship with better guns, engines and so forth, other than upgrading the vessel to have more armor and HP, if you have enough resources.As a Rogue Trader, a number of colonies are under your command, and not only you’ll have to order them to execute research projects that consume the resources gained from planetary scans and space battles, but also react to the events happening on them and decide wisely on your next move. Such random events can majorly alter how a colony functions, and often lead to situations you’ll have to personally deal with, and result in unique skills or items should you manage them in the right way.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE AND EDIT:I am very happy to be able to flip this from a No to a Yes after today's patch.The game is not exactly bug-free, but after today's patch, the most egregious are fixed; the progress blockers and save-brickers especially. Devs claim that remaining major annoyances, such as the myriad broken or malfunctioning abilities, will be addressed within the week, and so far they have kept to their word on patch releases.At this point, if you don't mind a few (or a lot of) eye-rollers, the game is worth buying without wasting your time - it's playable to nearly the end in its current state without major issues hampering (or completely rolling back!) your progress.And with that breakage out of the way - I can tell you this is one of the most enjoyable games I've ever played in any genre, but should be especially good for RPG players who enjoy player path choices and build-making, as well as a good story so far in the WH40K universe.

_childDocuments_.review: Heavy Bolter go BRRRThis game is excellent - good writing that pulls you into the 40k universe, interesting characters, tense decisions, and a good balance between combat & dialogue/exploration. The combat itself is also a lot of fun, giving you lots of opportunity to figure out how to use your characters abilities most effectively & adapt to the situation- this is supported by character progression and gear choices which give you a lot of different ways to optimize you characters and combine their strengths.There are, apparently, still a fair number of bugs at time of writing- I have not encountered any that had any serious impact on the story (softlocking quests etc) that some players have reported, only minor ones of specific gear/talents etc not working exactly like they're supposed to. I haven't found it intrusive, but the devs also seem to be releasing bug fix patches pretty rapidly, so hopefully the more critical ones will be dealt with shortly anyway. I am 56 hours in and just about to finish Act 2, so if there are bugs later on in the story they will probably be fixed by the time you get there :)Edit: I have now completed the game, nearly 100 hours in- I think it is extremely good, but the highlight definitely becomes the writing. I played on normal/default difficulty, and for the later acts found that combining solider/arch militant with few officers meant that I could pump out truly absurd damage, and many fights were effectively or literally over before the enemy could do anything to me. I still found it fun to execute the combo & figure out the most efficient ways to do things, but combat was not particularly tense at any point after acts 2-3.However, the writing is very engaging, and they stick the landing with some really excellent conclusions to companion questlines.  and  are personal favorites, the former for being a really cool way to build on existing 40k lore & some fun metatextual symbolism/jokes, and the latter for just being extremely fun execution of a straightforward concept. The central plot also has some really high notes and ends with a flourish, with (at least for me) a great balance of foreshadowing and sudden reveal of how things interconnect. I think the core stories & the overall tone and attention to detail in the writing make this game very fun for both 40k lore buffs and newcomers alike.I ran into exactly one "important" bug, which did lock me out of completing one of my companions quests, though I didn't mind too much (I had been increasingly apprehensive regarding the character & where I thought there story was going, so I decided my rogue trader simply decided not to help them out), but I didn't encounter this until I was ~ 80 hours in, so given how fast they are putting out patches it will probably be addressed before new players can encounter it. The other bugs I ran into were random abilities or items not working as intended, and I never found it particularly impacted my experience, but be aware there are still plenty of those if that will bother you.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure this game will be a fine CRPG one day; the writing is fantastic, the space exploration is fun, the combat is passable (except the space battles, which are dreadful).  Unfortunately, though Act 1 is largely playable, Act 2 will almost certainly see players encounter quests that are hard-locked from completion due to bugs, and everything is only downhill from there, with the game reportedly becoming impossible to continue without extensive use of the Toybox application around the start of Act 4, if not earlier.  That's not even getting into the matter of numerous abilities and talents either having inaccurate descriptions or being entirely nonfunctional.  Unfortunately, as it currently stands, Rogue Trader is an embarrassment, which was obviously released in an unfinished state and indicates either an almost complete lack of playtesting or care by the developers for selling a working product.  I cannot recommend the game in its current state.  Perhaps I'll update this review after Owlcat finishes patching their game.

That's what I have been doing as of recent. -The animated cut-scenes are really bad, so bad in fact i think it would have been better not to put them in the game. _childDocuments_.review: Just beat this game after approximately 90 hours with most content completed. WOW! Owlcat absolutely nailed the atmosphere of 40k! In terms of immersion Rogue Trader is EASILY the best 40k game to date. Genuinely surprised this game is sitting at Mostly Positive (70%). Reading the reviews it seems some players encountered numerous bugs which I never came across with an Iconoclast/Heretic 50/50 play through. The handful of bugs I did happen to came across were solved via patch one so no complaints here! Pros: - Intriguing and excellently written story with a deep choice/consequence system. - Fun combat system with plenty of offensive/defensive/support roles.- AMAZING atmosphere and world-building. Just about every facet of the setting receives some love in one form or another. Most of our favorite factions and races are represented!-Many complex gameplay systems which interact well, making you actually feel like a Rogue Trader in the setting (space combat, colony management, economic system, exploration etc).- Interesting and varied companions with their own quests.Cons:- Several bugs that were fortunately ironed out for me in patch one!- Bloated/too many talent choices where some are absolutely useless and can lead to feeling overwhelmed.- Combat is wayyyy too easy on anything under the normal difficulty.- Rushed final act in terms of concluding the main story.Rogue Trader is a MUST BUY in my opinion, particularly for fans of 40k and CRPG's. Really, really looking forward to starting a second playthrough when the DLC's come out, this time as a loyal, dogmatic servant of the Imperium... THE EMPEROR PROTECTS!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is mostly good, and if you love numbers and complexity you'll love it. The problem is, like a lot of games recently, it suffers from 'more'. Someone will create a great mechanic that plays really well, and rather than refine it - they add more. And more. And yet more.In most RPGs you look forward to levelling up. In this game, I dreaded it. Every level up means randomly getting <thing> and then stepping through a huge list reading arcane descriptions. Things like 'Adds (2 x TGH + 1/2 REL) CG per stack, removes (0.25 x WP) stacks'. Is it good? Is it bad? No idea!In essence the core mechanic to 'win' a battle is to get as many 'free' turns in as possible. Turn it into an art form and you'll win in practically a single round. Fail with your levelling up, and enjoy failing your battles. It's not so much a tactical battle system, as a specific formula / checklist you need to follow every single battle. Every turn it's the same buffs, the same extra turns... every... single... turn.So why all the extra super-complex fluff? I can only assume the second anyone in the team thought 'this would make a good ability/skill' they just added it straight in on top of the core stuff. It's all fluff, just there to make anyone who isn't super attentive and actually chooses it, lose their battles.And this is the problem. The story and characters are interesting. The graphics are great. The bugs, well they're annoying. But the real issue is the combat. It's monotonous and entirely down to optimisation rather than per-scenario tactics.For me, I just had enough. If you love a game that's basically a spreadsheet, you'll love this. Go min/max crazy! Otherwise, honestly, just don't bother. This is a job, not entertainment.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like 40k even a little you should play this game. Getting to walk around in 40k like this is a dream come true for me. Hopefully these will be addressed in future patches, many other bugs already have been.2) The game kinda railroads you a bit for the first 5-10 hours. If you are feeling bored in the beginning just stick it out, once you are done on Footfall it gets so much more fun3) There are sooooooo many skills and talents. Making builds is fun, and it feels amazing when you discover something that's so strong it's practically game breaking, but a lot of the time when you are leveling up 6 characters at once it feels like you've been taken out of the action. If I were going to play again (which I definitely will at some point) I'd just keep a note of all of the talents I liked on all of the characters so that I wouldn't have to keep rereading everything every time I leveled up. But yeah, all of those complaints are nothing when held up to how awesome the whole experience of playing the game is. I can't wait to buy every last bit of DLC they release and have another go at it.

Selling stuff for reputation but something else entirely defines if you can buy something, and wares don't even replenish??The Warp Mechanic is just a cluster ♥♥♥♥, you need Insight from the Navigator to get to some systems, but you only get a random chance to gain this insight, so worst case scenario: You are completely stuck with your quests until you get some Insight by Chance.On top of all that you can make colonies, and can gather ressources other than what you trade, and you can upgrade your ship and you can do space battles and and and and and.It seems to me that this game wanted to be something that does everything but the saying:Jack of all trades - Master of none seems very fitting here.On top of that some quests/mechanics require time to pass. _childDocuments_.review: At review time, I think I'm close to 70 hours of playtime.I don't know if the very obtuse and overly complicated RPG background is how the WH 40K RPG was designed, but I suspect that is the case. I don't think a modern video game design team would opt for this convoluted structure. Though it took, many, many hours of play to get comfortable with that RPG ruleset, the game is excellent. Writing, voice-acting, pacing, combat (both ship-to-ship and team), graphics... all are all on par with Owlcat's previous releases. I mentioned my ~70 hours playtime as I am just breaking into the ship to ship combat and solar system exploration. It is opening new options and I love it. Now, at level 20, my team has a huge array of tactical options and skills, and the strategic options for combat are huge. There are too many good things about this game to list because I have a short attention span, but it is worth mentioning that overcoming the clunky RPG framework behind everything was worth the effort. 40K is a neat setting to boot. This is an easy recommendation for any RPG gamer and possibly any turn-based strategy/tactics gamer that can stomach a story. I expect to get another 30 or 40 hours out of this. My interest is strong if the content holds out.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an awesome RPG! It is probably the best thing to play after BG3, in my opinion. It has all of the good features of an Owlcat game, but unlike their Pathfinder games, the systems feel properly adapted to the video game medium. Also, you can finally quicksave during combat.: - The Warhammer 40k setting provides decades of deep lore for Owlcat's team to draw from, which helps the game feel very fleshed out. You don't need to know anything about Warhammer in advance to appreciate this.- The "grim-dark" setting of Warhammer 40k encourages and enables a playthrough that diverges from the typical "good-boy" RPG protagonist who is the champion of the downtrodden, unfailingly nice to everyone, etc, etc. You get to choose between being "Dogmatic," "Iconoclastic," or "Heretical" at numerous points throughout the story, and while I don't always appreciate being railroaded down a certain path by specifically tagged choices, I actually think this system does a great job of pushing you to experience the story in a way which is characterologically internally consistent and which integrates well with the logic of the larger Warhammer universe. It also encourages at least three playthroughs of the game to see the outcome of all of the paths.- The build options for characters have a ton of depth, and numerous classes are very fun to play and combine together. This is typical Owlcat.- Combat is purely turn-based, not the hybrid approach of the Pathfinder games, and to this I say "thank god." Making it turn-based allows for the encounter designs to be properly calibrated and not drag on the way they do sometimes in WOTR. Also, as I mentioned, you can finally quicksave in the middle of combat, which is ideal if you're in a long fight and you need to get up and do something that isn't a video game for a while.- I have enjoyed the story so far, including the Void Shadows DLC, which I bought along with the base game and have not played without.- The "Profit Factor" system which replaces currency is an innovative and excellent way of enabling the fantasy that you, the player, are the Rogue Trader. I haven't seen anything like it before, but I love it.- (So far) I have not experienced any real bugs or progress-blocking events, just at most some misleading tooltips.:- The balance/fun factor of the various classes--and therefore of your companions, since you can't change their starting classes--is extremely uneven, and the "recommended" progression isn't particularly helpful as you're leveling. Some of your companions have strong and interesting subclasses that you will never even realize they have if you just follow the recommended progressions for their characters. I appreciate the complex leveling options of Owlcat games, but they do require a lot of thought and are overwhelming on a first playthrough.- There are a ton of loading screens everywhere, and they last just a bit too long even on my powerful computer. This isn't a dealbreaker, and it's probably completely unavoidable, but it has been wearing on my nerves.: Play the game; it's good.

_childDocuments_.review: +++ Warhammer: Rogue Trader - A Love-Hate Odyssey in the Koronus Expanse+++After 100+ hours and a rollercoaster of emotions, I've finally beaten the story of "Warhammer: Rogue Trader," and I'm left with conflicting thoughts that could spiral me in the clutches of the changer of ways with ease. Only faith in the emperor of the most dogmatic approach can let me recommend this game. But recommend it, I shall.This game is a paradox, offering a deep dive into the life of a Rogue Trader, ready to chart your own way. this review is a tale of both adoration and frustration.+++ The Highs ++++ Narrative Brilliance +The campaign and its conclusion are nothing short of perfection. The story captivates from start to finish, with a richness that beckons for another playthrough. Despite broken quests and clunky UI, there is a gem of a narrative to play through.+  Grandiose Systems +The game nails the feeling of being a true Rogue Trader, where wealth is more about influence and power than coin. It's a fresh take that I greatly appreciated and the sprawling scale of it is something to compliment. You go from bashing the heads of lowly rebels to negotiating and making diplomatic deals to commanding your starship into space battles and managing your colonies all in the same game, and they are all meaningful experiences that add to the aforementioned grandiose feeling. Well done.+ Stunning Visuals and Environments +Each of the hundreds of unique locations is a visual treat, brimming with detail and atmosphere. I wish I could go down to eye level on this game, the fixed camera doesn’t do it justice.+ Engaging Combat and Strategy + Once you crack the combat system, it's incredibly satisfying to dominate battles through tactical genius.+ Meaningful Connections + The relationships you build with your crew and the systems you interact with add a compelling depth to the game.+ Varied Quests and Playthroughs + The quests are thematic and engaging, offering distinct experiences based on your choices. Whether you're playing it safe or going full heretical, the game feels different each time.+++ The Lows ++++ Difficulty Spikes From Hell + The game's difficulty can be as unpredictable as the Warp, forcing me to adjust settings just to keep my sanity intact.(My rule of thumb was 3 unfair reloads = “story” difficulty for the first round of combat)+ Overwhelming Complexity + Between leveling, gear selection, and inventory management, the game sometimes felt more like a chore than an adventure. The cheap non-existent icons and confusing (or just lacking) skill descriptions don’t help.+ Clunky User Experience + Navigating the game's interfaces often felt like battling an ancient tech-priest's worst design, detracting from the overall experience.+ Loot Logic That Breaks Immersion + For a game that excellently captures the essence of being above mere monetary concerns, having to sift through trash for loot felt disappointingly out of place.+ Lack of Seamless Transitions + The jarring shifts between scenes, like going from planet to ship, unnecessarily broke the immersion.+ Broken everything + The quest bugs are the worst because you never truly know if it is a legitimate quest state and you just lack context or if it's truly broken. It didn’t stop me from enjoying my 100+ hours with it, but I just had to get into a “war is hell” mentality and let go of my desire to have my beautiful quest log clean and finished.+++ Final Verdict +++"Warhammer: Rogue Trader" is a game of contrasts and grandiose ambition. It masterfully captures the essence of the Warhammer 40k universe, offering an immersive experience of life as a Rogue Trader with a narrative depth that's rare in the gaming world. However, it's a journey marred by frustrating gameplay mechanics and design choices that can test your patience.For fans of the 40k lore who dream of navigating the complex life of a Rogue Trader, this game offers a rich, thematic experience that's hard to find elsewhere. Be warned, though: for every moment of awe and victory, there's a potential frustration waiting around the corner. Despite its flaws, I recommend "Warhammer: Rogue Trader" to those willing to embrace its chaotic blend of brilliance and bafflement. It's a love-hate relationship, but for a 40k enthusiast, it's an odyssey worth undertaking and echoes the complex bureaucracy of the verse, it feels like this would be a game made by the administratum itself!

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Wait a year or play now with Toolbox. A for effort, needs work.My feelings on this are uh, pretty complicated. A lot of the issues with the game seem to stem from the setting of 40k just kinda sucking. Games Workshop also apparently has put their hand on the scale at least once, almost certainly more than that, which probably lead to a few of the more questionable story decisions.I am leaving this positive despite my takeaway being largely negative because I know in about a year or two this game will be pretty dang good. Everyone already knows about the bugs, Toolbox is mandatory to progress in the game at times. I couldn't start Chapter 5 without manually inputting the next cutscene that was supposed to trigger but didn't. The game is also really easy to break combat wise. After chapter 2 I found myself breezing through combat due to some pretty messy design choices being incredibly exploitable. It's very common for enemies to never get a turn against me, including several bosses.Large issues with the narrative are due to, well, bugs. I imagine a lot of scenes that were meant to trigger for me simply did not, which left me with two endings that are nearly identical and lacked closure for what had actually happened. I could go on, but the long and short of it is: Rogue Trader lacks an emotional core that makes the ending feel very hollow. 40k's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ fascist nature makes an unwelcome appearance more than a few times, overall making the game a bit of a downer.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was great, however it was not as polished or as epic as Owlcat's other Pathfinder-Themed Games. I had a great time finishing missions, exploring planets, and getting into the hard decision trees that these games are known for. However, in the final segments of the game, I kept feeling like my decisions did not have the same type of impact that Kingmaker and Wrath of the Righteous had. Additionally, the map felt massive when it was first revealed, but so much of it ended up being unused/empty. Critique aside, the mechanics and built choices were a lot of fun, but hard to master.  The fights were varied and interesting (Until the end when my builds broke the mold). The Companions were [mostly] well rounded and had interesting stories to boot. Loot hunting was good fun as well!I wanted a game that brought the world of Warhammer 40K to life and I was not  disappointed in that regard. I really got a good feel for how it is to be a human in the Imperium as well as a deep look into the relationships humans have with some of the other races in the universe.Kingmaker and Wrath of the Righteous both compelled me to play the game immediately after finishing it to experience the choices over (and I have subsequently played both of those a third time). Rogue Trader will get another run from me, but it will be a few months before I feel compelled.Thanks again, Owlcat. I look forward to the rest of this map being filled by expansions!

_childDocuments_.review: Combat is a mess. It's buggy, it's confusing, there are too many little feats you must take that don't really do anything useful. The Defiler fight is absolutely ridiculous. Make combat more of a chess game rather than "hey we're gonna kick you in the balls with steel-toed boots, see if you can handle this, k?"  The good parts of this game is everything they took from the Rogue Trader TTRPG that Fantasy Flight Games did all the hard work for. It's like they took the book from that game and said "let's take this but have the combat make X-COM look like a reasonable cake-walk"

_childDocuments_.review: Baldurs Gate 3 is the best RPG of all time, no question there. I loved that game.But if an Inquisitor would put a boltgun to my head and ask me which game really enslaved me as my ruinous master, it's Rogue Trader.I mean, the basic system is ridiculously complicated. Most of the time I really had no idea what skills I should chose, or even what class as good at what. And then come the synergies. It is a maelstrom of chaotic madness in itself. And unbalanced like a fistfight against a Terminator.But boy oh boy did I love playing that game. It made me mad. It made me rage quit. It tarnished my soul and drove me into hatred of khornish dimensions.But nevertheless. It is the best Warhammer game I ever player. The best RPG I ever played.Thank you for this fantastic, weird, ungrateful, horrifiingly glorious masterpiece!

_childDocuments_.review: I havent played for that long yet but the game is really good. You can pick to be a full on baddie/strict person in the game too as far as I've seen, or you can be good, or neutral. Game gives you a lot of choices that you can make and they all seem to have drastically different consequences. It also hits you with a lot of walls of text and lore dump, and it has a built-in encyclopedia for literally everything, which I enjoy a lot, if you are a sci-fi lore nerd you will love it. Kinda hard but simple and cool turn-based combat. The world building, dialogues and the choices you can make are amazing, and your character stats seem to have a huge effect on some dialogue choices, that you can pick with success/failure rating like in Disco Elysium/BG3. My only wish is that this game had full voice over for every dialogue, it only has for some but it's still cool. Overall it's great so far, love it, especially the choices you can make. If you love CRPGs, give this game a try, but beware that it is indeed buggy and the optimization isnt that great. I have experienced a few bugs, soft locked in a combat for example, my characters couldnt do anything in battle so I had to reload a save. Ild suggest saving a lot in this game in case something like that happens, but I believe the game has an auto-save feature as well.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the few games that gave me the Warhammer grime-dark vibe; some seemingly innocent decisions might cause huge issues, like letting mutant refugees onto your ship. Thumbs up to the narrating and visual designs; you can tell it's from someone who has an in-depth view of the Warhammer 40k universe. Dialog is interesting and immersive, visual design is definitely top-notch. However the pace of the game needs some rework. I love the turn-based strategy part, but assigning perks and abilities after leveling up is a huge pain. I think at least 20% of my playtime was spent on leveling up, and the UI is rather unfriendly; some abilities avatars are repetitive, you can't identify which buff is what at first glance, and some perks don't even have any avatar. Also, the worst part is it has an insane amount of bugs. Not to mention the UI and graphical glitches.  I have encountered a bug where I can't assign any character to my ship post, making naval battles in late-game extremely hard. Overall, it is a good Warhammer game, but it isn't worth the full price at the current state; I may change my mind after a few patches.

My old review is left in it's entirety below so people can see why I updated to this current one!OLD REVIEW - 3 separate gamelocking bugs in 3 separate playthroughs, and many, many non gamebreaking bugs affecting everything from dialogue to combat. As it stands currently, the game is not worth it, but given time and polish it will be an excellent game and I will update my review once that standard has been reached.

_childDocuments_.review: So I got this game thinking it will be a better experience than the other Owlcat games because unlike pathfinder, I actually like the warhammer lore. I can safely say that they didn't change anything about their game design since Kingmaker.Act 1 starts off strong and then the Owlcatness occurs so allow me to place everything in bullet point form so I can show my dissapointment of this game and Owlcat in generalPros - it's warhammer- the actual system that was taken from the TTRPG is presented well- that's itCons!!!- constant combat for every scene. I can count on one hand how many times I could influence combat through my stats - the ship combat is utter slow garbage. Ships move at a snail's pace and even when you clear the board of ships you still have to wait 1 more round until enemy torpedoes explode!- exploration post Act1 is a chore. If you get an event on the other side of the map and you don't have navigator points, you have to click on each individual system until you get there and God forbid you run out of navigator points and have to go through Dangerous warp paths because you will have to do combat on each individual jump- everything moves slow. Ships, companions, text, all of these move ungodly slow even with the anymation speeds cranked up to max.- SO MUCH TEXT! Owlcat is known for it's purple prose and this is no different. Mind numbing pointless text on 80% of events.- Most quests don't go anywhere. If you go to random events on planets for some extra xp and exploration, you would be shocked to see that the lore behind them is basically non-existent. Why is this here ? what happened ? ♥♥♥♥ if I know! and i read the 2 little entries and wall scratching in those places - companions are not detailed. Apart from the default introductory text that you get, they have almost no interaction with the outside world, no input on pretty much all of the quests and generally a lack of point. The party banter is relegated 100% to this format: "statement" -> "Response". That's it, all of them are relegated to 1 line of dialogue each and done.In short, I'm done with these guys. They're mediocre developers that are stuck 20 years in the past, have mediocre writers that ♥♥♥♥ the bed usually after Act 2 in every game and have no idea that while you can make a 100 hour game, if you fill it with pointless fighting and opening 1000 chests of junk this doesn't equate to good game design. I wanted to slog it and finish it like I did WoTR (another dissapointment) but I can't. It's too much of a mind-numbing chore!
