_childDocuments_.review: A very immersive CRPG experience in the 40k Universe, the atmosphere and narratives are phenomenally done. You have quite the variety when it comes to building your character(The lord Captain) as well as customizing the builds of the companions. Combat is very fun and well thought out, though a few of the combat archetypes are less enjoyable to use (Looking at you Grand Strategist and Bounty hunter). I will say though, you can pretty easily get 'overpowered', but I fixed that by bumping up the difficulty to daring. There are two gripes I have with the game however, One, In act 3, its very easy to get permanent debuffs on your characters, and not entirely know how to go about fixing them. Some of the debuffs are pretty easy to figure out how to remove them, the others are less so; They arent like MAJOR debuffs either, but it is still annoying. The other gripe is the complete and utterlack of greenskins, how are you gonna do us orktheuists dirty like that? I hope we see an addon in the future with some Greenskin combat encounters, and maybe if were really lucky, a Freebootah / Mekboy secret companion to replace those degenerate elves -- Hell, they could even butt heads with Pascal for some extra narrative fun.Overall, a really fun RPG with lots of customization, a gripping narrative, flawless atmosphere and enjoyable combat and I strongly recommend this game to any CRPG or 40k Fans.9/10 needs more WAAAGH.

_childDocuments_.review: This has potential, it's biggest drawback is that its unfinished/unpolished/buggy.If you liked WOTR or Kingmaker then you might enjoy this.  I say might because its not based on the Pathfinder system, its a weird hybrid of a few 40K RPGs and its not bad, just different.Be ready for XCOM levels of percentage missing while the AI scrubs nail every shot.The game has a feeling of being rushed out the door.  Sometimes there is voice acting, most of the time its text reading with no voice, and its very noticeable how it bounces back and forth.  Bugs are all over the place.  Sometimes combat freezes during the AIs turn and you have to hard quit and restart.  Sometimes LOAD files are corrupted and you can't load your save, very annoying.  T poses all over the place.  Grenades disappearing from your inventory.  Clicking to move results in nothing happening.  I could go on but you get the idea.This is a very good game marred by virtually no polish.  My suggestion wait a bit for a few patches then pick it up on sale.I'll revisit this review later once they iron some things out.New Patch today:  Still broken and unpolished, worse some of the "fixes" have actually broken things that were working.  Not minor things either, like STR not adding to damage for melee.  Some of the states "fixes" aren't working either.  They obviously don't have a Q/A team at Owlcat.Still recommending skip this game for now.  The biggest issue of Saves being corrupted still hasn't been fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: Great Warhammer RPG, provided you are ready for a lot of systems and a bit of jank.Fun writing and interesting characters, with a pretty broad range of 40k factions and concepts making an appearance. The dialogue is competent and well voiced, haven't found a "Metal boxes" style line that really threw me yet.This game has so many systems and you will be getting tutorial pop ups well into your time with the game. It gets a bit wearying after a while to have to learn yet another menu, but most systems are fun in their own right. In terms of jank,  there are a number of QoL issues and bugs that will crop up. In our multiplayer game we found that having someone other than the host activate a shooting ability after a movement ability would sometimes revert the movement ability or even place us somewhere entirely new, not where we started or where the movement ability took us. Also party grouping can be a huge pain, because unless there is a dialogue or cutscene, characters remain where they were when combat starts and then have to move to the arena using their turns. This led to many frustrating early moments, but is an issue you won't encounter solo.Speaking of cutscenes the cutscenes in this game vary wildly. There are some well done story book scenes to transition between acts, and a particular favorite of mine a nice introduction to my favorite faction as an enemy, but a lot of the dialogue scenes were really bare bones. Its a puzzling part of the game because the combat animations and effects feel fine, but when someone interrupts a chat to execute someone or when two characters hold hands the animations are ponderously slow and feel very low effort. In combat the game flows really well, the way the abilities stack and the system of momentum and heroic/desperate actions is really satisfying to use. In particular I want to shout out the officer class as a support that isn't consigned to only healing and whose abilities are so powerful and fun to use that I rarely leave the flagship without 2 in tow.  Overall I find Rogue Trader to be a great game that falls just a bit short of being excellent.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader

_childDocuments_.review: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader could be described as a love letter to 40k but at the same time it could also be described as a colossal buggy mess that should have never launched in the state it is in, while I am confident that Owlcat will fix things much like they did with both of their previous Pathfinder games and it will be a great game one day - it also speaks volumes how little the studio has learned from the awful launches of Kingmaker and WotR.My completionist style playthrough on the daring difficulty took roughly 106 hours out of which at least ~5 hours is lost progress due to bugs/issues and ultimately I had to resort to using toybox to actually finish the game as nearly every combat encounter in final chapter crashed my game - sometimes when casting a pyromancer ability but mostly when an enemy did something.That being said lets start with what the game gets right: Writing for the most part is good even if it lacks reactivity especially on the heretic path, music and sounds nail that 40k feeling, combat delivers a surprisingly visceral feeling experience for a turn based game and there is a good amount of enemy variety. Entire experience is quite front loaded on the good stuff and I thoroughly enjoyed my experience from the prologue to the start of chapter 3.Unfortunately that is where things start to get messy and the entirety of the latter half of the game feels quite a bit weaker than the first half which is a shame. Combine that with the myriad problems the game has: Bad design decisions, blatantly unfinished systems, poorly distributed loot/rewards, balancing that is all over the place, combat loop that never really evolves beyond stacking more HP on stuff and an incredibly huge amount of bugs.While there are plenty of bad design decisions I could write on and on about I want to highlight one regarding "Foulstone" planet which players encounter fairly early on in the game if you explore a little. You can choose to plunder a shrine on the planet which nets you a pretty generic thunder hammer but it also prevents you from colonizing the entire planet which in turn: Blocks one quest from being finished, blocks player from all the colony events related to said planet and also blocks players from finishing some colony projects on other two planets - while someone might say something about consequences I would say that sabotaging one of your core systems to such a huge degree is not a meaningful consequence it is poor game design at best.Many of the core systems feel half baked such as the faction reputation system: Maxing out a faction takes obscene amount of reputation, rewards are all over the place and some of the higher rewards even include generic loot. Not to mention one of the factions even has trophies that cannot be returned to them as you only obtain them when you no longer have access to said faction.So what about the bugs then? Talents that don't work, talents that work a little too well, quests that are bugged, dialogue with incorrect flags, dead npcs appearing in dialogue right after you have killed them, disappearing character models, dialogue that can brick quests if you pick wrong choices, game ignoring some of your choices etc.While this is a game I will eventually recommend as it is a solid take on 40k universe for now I would simply recommend waiting for several patches and perhaps in 4 to 6 months from now the game will be in a solid state. This is one of those cases where I think it is worth waiting for the polished up experience as it is a rather lengthy game and right now you will simply get a subpar experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Prefacing this by saying I'm not much of a fan of 40k, but I saw some gameplay and saw that it has a "co-op" mode and thought that'd be a good idea. This is primarily my view of the co-op gameplay from a non player one point of view. If you want to know about game balance, story, progression, etc. Read another review :D---Co-op. There is only one Rogue Trader, this is obvious, you can't have multiple of the main character. Instead the other player(s) gain control of the party members. This sounds okay in theory but in reality the co-op is very much a thrown together pile of ♥♥♥♥. You never have any control over ANY dialogue or decision making. You can click the options to show what you support, but it's all at the whim of player 1. At least while the main player is doing dialogue you can do other things like browse the inventory, or look at your stats, perform level ups- Oh no wait sorry i've lied to you, while dialogue or any other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ menu is open, you HAVE to look at it too. Enjoy constantly telling your player 1 to stop so you can equip that item that you didn't buy, because you can't buy it, only they can.Hope you enjoy waiting for player 1 as well. When on the ground you can split up and explore, but if you want to perform an athletics check to jump a gap, EVERYONE is moved there. At least you as a co-op player can perform this action, but I cannot imagine how annoying it must be with 3-6 players to constantly be teleported around because people keep interacting with things.While split on the ground, if one player group encounters a fight, if it's a dialogue before fight situation then grab some popcorn as you wait for all the characters to auto-path over to the dialogue. If it goes straight to a fight, hope you enjoy 6 turns of slowly walking over to the fighting area, because unlike some other CRPGs, every player is in combat regardless of how far away they are.Let's say you can stomach all these issues, you don't mind not having agency over anything but combat encounters. Hah good luck, cause desync issues are here to ruin your game. Sometimes you'll perform an action and the game will present you with two options: "Reload the save to resync your games, OR, cancel and hope it still works." This can happen anywhere from once in 6 hours or 3 times a minute depending on where you are in the game and what abilities you use. We started off resync-ing, but as the game goes on the save file gets larger, and to resync the game you have to fully download the entire save file, and then reload the map. Even on a modern high speed PC this takes 20-40 seconds. Ridiculous. We also tried clicking cancel and hoping, which resulted in lots of "It's your turn" "No it's not I'm dead".Further, let's assume you can put up with all that like I managed to. WELCOME TO ACT 3 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Your character of choice might not be playable for up to 2-4 hours. No more game for you, embrace fully watching the game here, because unless player 1 just spam skips through dialogue then you might as well not be there for the day.Okay but you powered through all that as well, and you're presumably getting towards the end of the game, surely you'll make it to the end, right? _childDocuments_.review: Introduction:Embark on a journey through the grimdark galaxy with Rogue Trader, a game that manages to capture the essence of the 40k universe. I’m 60 hours of gameplay in, having just completed Act 3, so I feel I’m ready to share my thoughts in case it helps others.Learning Curve and Lore:Prepare yourself for an immersion overload as Rogue Trader catapults you into the complex world of 40k. If you’re like me, for the first Act, you'll be often scratching your head, wondering if you missed the memo on the meaning of literally half of what people are on about. The tooltips try to help, but unless you’re coming in fully up to date on 40k lore, expect a bit of ‘so what was that thing again?’. It took me hours to get a grip, and I practically grew up with the tabletop 40k!Morality System:The moral compass in Rogue Trader is a bit like choosing between a cannon and a chainsword. It's all about extremes, making it tough to strike a balance. Either you kill everything, because For the Emperor. You kill everything because Blood for the Blood God, or you save all the puppies from the mean, nasty men. Personally, I help but fence-sit to avoid missing out on content, but hey, the lore is the lore, and chanting "For the Emperor" does have its charm, even if it's a tad one-dimensional.World Building System:The concept works, but the UI feels like it could use a little something. Maybe a simple colour coding of what buildings go with what. Just some quality-of-life adjustments to make navigating the system bit less clunky. A minor detail, but hey, even a Rogue Trader appreciates a smooth ride.Character Leveling and Skills:If you like to min/max, then Rogue Trader's character leveling system is your playground. However, sifting through a gazillion skills can be overwhelming. I would have liked to have seen some UX improvements such as 'this thing does x damage (then tell me what ability is providing that number in brackets), as it stands most of them are the other way around, they will be listed as 'does x damage based on skill x'. Just tell me the number! When I have to scroll through 50 skills every level, for every character, sometimes I want the stats to pop out to me so I can make a good decision, without having to re-read all the skills each and every time. I love depth, but I don't want to feel like a theoretical physicist every level-up.Act 3:Inventory:(probably spoilers) Now, Act 3 brings a mixed bag. Inventory stripping? Sure, why not, it’s been done. But how about an option to "put it back how it was" when I recover the gear? Spending an hour reorganizing gear when I get it back isn't my idea of a good time. Don’t forget you gave us a system of no limits and no weight. That means some of us (like me) will hoard literally everything, if I get it all back in one go…Space Marine Fiasco:It’s insanely EASY it is to MISS OUT on the space marine character. I won't get into it, and I don't know if it was just my choices or a bug, but that’s it, chance gone. 60 hours in, I’m not going back 5-10 hours just to get him. He's a Space Marine. People like Space Marines. A secondary method to get him or clearer guidelines would've been appreciated. Give the people their Space Marine fix! A big disappointment for me.Boss Battle:The boss battle at the end of Act 3 is a rollercoaster of difficulty. From no problems to "blink and my party got wiped in a single turn" in a heartbeat. The only way I could get past it after like 15 tries was to lower the difficulty! Did you read this? Lower the difficulty! I felt dirtier than a Nurgle Deamon on his worst day. One level down, the play reversed, and I utterly steamrolled the fight. Googling around a bit, seems like this is a common theme (difficulty level of the fight). Was it playtested enough, or did they expect us to be 40k savants at this point? Mysteries of the warp, indeed.Combat and Ship Warfare:Combat is a blast (sometimes literally). Limbs flying, skills popping—just the way we like it. Ship combat is functional, if not as fleshed out. It's the side dish, not the main course, but still tasty.Final Verdict:Despite my laundry list of nitpicks, Rogue Trader is undeniably fun. Owlcat nailed the 40k vibe, bringing the universe to life with commendable effort. I’ll be playing on till the end, and I eagerly await what Owlcat has in store for their next cosmic escapade. For the Emperor!

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend to all fans of the 40K setting and/or all Enterprise Management simulator enthusiasts.And yes, there's also a very decent RPG in there.********************************************************************************************After a full run, some update: while the game is good and represents the genre, as well as the source material quite well, it's far from perfect. Bugs are definitely an issue: I found myself googling around for solutions more than once just to be able to progress. Saving often helps there. Some talents are evidently also bugged, as showcased by my character who ended up having infinite heroic acts per turn at his disposal (and yes, happened to be of the attack type).The way the game and the writing both sort of just melt away into a meaningless dungeon crawl towards the end was also a bit disappointing. Getting a rundown of events supposedly happening after the big finale helped a bit in getting back some of the illusion that choices mattered - even if some of the bits were contradictory to what my choices actually were. Overall, still, I spent plenty of hours on this with no regrets and am planning on spending more. The depiction of the setting in general is refreshing in all of its grimdark ridiculousness and I'm looking forward to seeing how a different approach will affect things. And patches. Definitely looking forward to patches as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Patchy but compelling.Pros:- Interesting combat system with a lot of depth.- Engaging characters with involved back-stories.- High-stakes, difficult choices to make in the story.- Excellent job of evoking the look and feel of 40k.Cons- Buggy as all hell. Especially in the late game.- Presently many important quest-lines can't be completed.- Continuity is too often a bit weak.- Menu system is extremely inefficient.- Minimal voice acting- A couple of weird little canon conflicts.- Exciting set pieces too often replaced by story-book sections.Conclusion: Feels like this could have done with another year in development. Feels like the devs knew that too because this is the first game with a £40 price tag that I've seen with a bug report button placed prominently in the main UI.The freedom and replay-ability common in other CRPGs feels like it may be limited by the current state of the game.However, would broadly recommend. Fun to play. Best suggestion would be to wait a few months for some big patches to drop. Maybe even the first major DLC if you want a really pure experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll update my review later if I can play a finished game. For now, Roguetrader is not in a release state at all. And that only by the end of Act 1 ! There are 4 more, and anyone who has ever played a game made by Owlcat knows very well that it always goes worse from beginning to the end.I'm not glad writing this, because I liked the previous Pathfinder games (though Kingmaker was rather unplayable by the release too), and also because despite the very unfinished product, Roguetrader seems to have quite an enormous potential. Its combat mechanics are nice (when everything works, that is not true  half the time, even in the first act), the Warhammer 40K setting is interesting enough, the companions look properly written, and the cooperation is actually a good idea, almost more refined that the game itself.As long as Roguetrader will not be heavily patched, and even if I would like to love it, I can't accept how unfinished it is.If you want to give it a try, suit yourself, but know that you're paying for a medium/low quality early access of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but as someone who's brand new to the series, doesn't know the lore very well, and only has BG3 under my belt CRPG wise, it just was not enjoyable for me.It doesn't help you with anything, and no matter how much you read you just are not provided with enough information or help to lead you in the right direction. I often felt like I had no idea where I was going, the map is just not good enough at leading you to your objectives without clear quest markers. There's also so little indication of big story moments, I remember moving on from Act 1 and completely missing out on a whole questline because I didn't know it had to be done first and the game just isn't clear enough about these things. By the time I was somewhat into Act 2 I just sat down and realized I barely understood anything about what's going on, and I had dedicated most of my weekend to playing it and reading everything. Combat wise I felt the same. Unless you really study up excessively and follows guides for your builds, you will struggle immensely. This is also just a gripe with controller but movement with controller is downright aggravating, I can't count how many times I walked close to a steam vent and my entire party just walked ahead of me, standing in it and injuring themselves beyond anything medkits could take care of. It was infuriating. Combat isn't too bad with a controller though, it actually feels very managable.A lot of the companions felt very one note or one dimensional, at least in the first two acts. I only really found Henrix to be interes Your dialogue options also fall victim that. You're either a God Warrior, Mother Teresa, or Satan Incarnate to the point of absurdity even in the most mundane of situations. I often felt like there was no decent dialogue option for what I wanted to say. I wanted to like it, but I just found it frustrating and clunky. I do think it's a good game and CRPG fans who can dedicate themselves to it will enjoy themselves, I just unfortunately never got there.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit:Many people are reporting game breaking bugs in chapter 3 and beyond. I was only in chapter 1 when I wrote this review. While I still believe this game is awesome, it feels like a Beta and not a full release. Really disappointed. I wish there was a middle thumb - as I want to recommend the game, but the developers releasing the game in this state is a business practice I do not want to encourage. You may want to wait for patches.  Leaving review as positive in hopes that patches will come.Original Review:Shaping to be one of my favorite CRPGs of all time. The setting does so much to make it interesting, and the story so far has been a lot more captivating than Pathfinder: Kingmaker (haven't played much of Wrath of the Righteous, so can't compare this with that game. I loved Kingmaker, but got burnt out after 80 hours). Your choices seem to really matter. I also like the companions a lot more in this one. I had my clear favorites in Kingmaker, but here I struggle to decide who to take on a quest. Combat is awesome and designed to be turn based from the ground up (unlike Owlcat's previous games). There are a lot less trash mobs and combat encounters are fewer but feel more engaging and interesting than Owlcat's previous titles. I feel I've barely scratched the surface of the story, this game is huge! Hopefully I don't get burnt out with it, as I definitely want to see how this one ends. I have encountered bugs, but trust me, this game is worth getting now -- especially if you like Warhammer 40K.

_childDocuments_.review: So far it's been a solid meh, a huge step back from Pathfinder WOTR in almost every regard.Will continue playing hoping it gets better, but so far it's been little to no fun. Pros:- Writing seems solid if a bit humdrum and trite. Mind that there's a lot of it, even for a cRPG. - The Momentum combat mechanic is an awesome experience the first twenty fights. - eeer, that's about it I guess.Cons:- Environments are bland, repetitive and boring. It's all enclosed spaces and tight corridors, not a great fit for an isometric party-based RPG. Exploration is cumbersome and unrewarding.- Levelling up and skills in general are boring. +(x + 1/2y)*z % to some skill or a talent, woah so exciting. And you level up basically every other fight.- No option to auto-level up your companions or pick a set archetype.- Not enough classes for a party of six. Roles and kits overlap quite often.- Itemization is boring. 95% items is a vendor spam. - Combat encounters are overdrawn, repetitive and - yet again - boring. With the game being turn-based-only they should have focused on good encounter design. Less is more etc. Instead it's just trash fight after trash fight, all in slow-mo, all painfully samey. No memorable encounters so far. It's also surprisngly easy (for an Owlcat game). - The novel Momentum mechanic (along with all its combos and synergies) gets super samey super fast. Survive the first two rounds and kill as many weaklings as possible, thus building up momentum. Then obliterate the battlefield in a single turn. - Game mechanics in general do not seem to be working as intended. Enemy AI just keeps killing its own units. Line of sight is confusing. Some skills are clearly OP. - The plot does not seem interesting, maybe it will pick up later on but so far it's rather run-of-the-mill meh evil cult doing evil things kind of story (~40h into the game).- Companions are bland, nothing like WOTR. They do not seem nearly as reactive as they were in WOTR too. - Voice acting ranges from average (Heinrix, Abelard, Idira) to laughably bad (Cassia, Jae, Pasqual). Another step down from WOTR.- Animations are embarrassingly bad, a third of your actions do not have any animations of FX at all. Enemies sometimes float in a locked pose, with no animations at all.- Same goes for in-engine "cinematics" - boy does it look like 1999. Hilariously bad. I know it's a cRPG so graphics are not that important, but why create these shoddy cutscenes at all? The book parapgraph thingie with some hand drawn illustration works better for narrating set pieces in these type of games if you're on a budget (WOTR did it as did Pillars of Eternity). - Even the OST - something they nailed in both their PF games - is just... there. Nothing spectacular, nothing as memorable or as powerful as 'Mythic Power' from WOTR. - Jank & bugs. Some skills are bugged and do not work as written. Some texts disappear. Some in-game settings reset on their own or do not work at all. Some animations are bugged. Loading times and optimization are both abysmal.Basically, it's a mediocre averageburger. The only good thing about it are the dialogues (not all mind you, some are just plain exposition dumps or some generic drama - and it's pages upon pages on end), but then it's supposed to be a game and not an interactive novel. Right?All in all the game lands way below Kingmaker, miles below WOTR. A big disappointement, especially with WOTR being imo one of the best cRPG ever created. This just feels like a bootleg Owlcat, I dunno, Team B effort or something.It's a decently written WH40K novel attached to a painfully average cRPG. Not a bad game mind you, just... average.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Trader (RT) is better than Baldur's Gate 3 (BG3) in many aspects. If you liked one, play the other too. In this review I will mainly be comparing these two excellent games, and in the process presenting the merits of RT. I'm honestly amazed that Owlcat has made a 10/10 game on a much smaller budget than Larian.LORE. RT >> BG3. I love both the DnD and the 40K universes, but the more focused and extensive world-building in 40K outshines the broader 'template' that DnD provides. Sword & Sorcery has a charm, it is cozy, it has that timeless LOTR vibe, but for me, a grimdark setting will always feel more complex, nuanced and well-developed. Owlcat has done an amazing job of building on the tremendous mountain of lore and world-building that has developed the 40K universe since the 1980s. It is riveting to experience. Furthermore, since Larian went with full VA (huge production and time cost) BG3 has less alternative quest branching, paths, and overall lore text in general. RT has partial VA, which is more than enough, and the resources freed up by this has clearly allowed Owlcat to explore a staggering number dialogue trees and branching outcomes. The hauntingly beautiful soundtrack will leave you not even wanting VA anyway.MORALITY. RT >> BG3. First of all, the three-way alignment chart in RT is far superior to the binary good-evil axis (highly unrealistic, LOTR-esque duality) forced on the player in BG3. RT has three alignments: Dogmatic, Iconoclast and Heretical. You gradually descend into one as you make choices throughout the game, and it changes everything around you. These are very well fleshed out and they make sense. There is no good one; sometimes Dogmatic feels morally right, sometimes Iconoclast. But in a grimdark setting you can not always go for the 'fairy-tale good' choice, as you will see, there are severe repercussions for naivety. This is one of my biggest gripes with BG3. Even within its subpar good-evil binary, the 'evil' path is severely underdeveloped and unrewarding. You can 'feel' the developers wanted the 'default' path to be the good one. By going 'evil' you miss out on so much content, and so many side quests and companions quests. It just does not make for a satisfying alternative to the 'default' good play-through, which is my complaint since RT manages to show how this can be done with the Heretical path. The only really well done thing in BG3 is the Dark Urge path, which honestly should've been the default game mode.IMMERSION. RT = BG3. RT gets a head start here for the immersion provided by the richness of its lore and world-building. But BG3 has full VA and more fluid character animations and scenes - think romance scenes for example. And particularly the narrator VA is amazing in BG3. Both games have a number of romance arcs, both are well developed and nuanced, but BG3 has better cinematic 'scenes'. So that's an immersion plus. Both games have excellent music, but as I said, I love the grimdark orchestral gloom exuded by the 40K soundtrack. On the other hand, I am not sure if any game can ever replicate the goosebumps I felt the first time I heard Hope singing during Raphael's Final Act in BG3. There are several close contenders in RT (and its DLC, which is also excellent), but nothing quite like that scene (a bit of a bigger budget, bigger studio win for Larian here).COMBAT. BG3 >= RT. This one is close. BG3's main advantage here is environmental interactivity. It has many creative ways to use or manipulate objects and use the terrain. RT does not have these to anywhere near the same extent. BG3 has a tried and tested class and combat system using DnD-5e, which is robust and well implemented. That being said, I thoroughly enjoyed the novelties to the CRPG combat style that RT brought. The sheer complexity of the different archetypes and ways to build characters, and ways to then use abilities/skills and synergize them is astounding. The replayability is nigh endless - but that can be said for BG3 too. In any case, while a navigator's Lidless Stare in RT is indeed conteptually and gameplay-wise very fun, nothing can beat the Hunger of Hadar spell in BG3: my favorite combat ability in any CRPG I've ever played.COMPANIONS. RT = BG3. Both games have companions with their own complex quest chains that develop through the acts of the game. Both games provide diverging branching and many fateful choices in these, and both have a 'camp' area to talk to companions whenever (the voidship bridge in RT). It's honestly hard to say whether Shadowheart or Cassia, Abelard or Gale, etc. will stay more in my memory as times goes on. Both games truly get you invested in the characters. All these are roughly on par in both games. I think RT has more companions numerically (10 by default plus a further few secretly), but anyway.VILLAINS. RT > BG3. I loved Orin the Red, Raphael and a few of the lesser story characters in BG3. It's a DnD world after all, it contains the classic trope of monsters and beings that many of us gamers have grown accustomed to; we expect to see them. But the villains and story characters in RT far outshine all that. Again, this is not a point to Owlcat's genius or anything, it's just that 40K has such a rich repository to pull from. The whole warpspace, webway, realspace stuff, the Chaos gods and their infiltration of realspace, the concept of navigators, the concept of the astropathic choir, the idea of Tyranid hive fleets consuming galaxies, the very existence of Necrons, the fall of the Aeldari to the temptation of Slaneesh, Commorragh and the Drukhari psychic channeling of agony, the inquisition, the undead emperor etc. etc. etc. - the list is endless. The world is dark and fascinating. It's mesmerizing. The politics in RT is also more interesting and nuanced. Do you aid the inquisition, do you help this noble house or that, do you help the Xenos, etc. Compared to this, BG3 has way less in-game politics and world-sculpting, aside from maybe a bit of stuff in Act3.PROSE. RT > BG3. Being more text-based and having more dialogue and text in general, RT has such beautiful prose in many places. For example, the way Cassia the Navigator sees everything in colors and the way she continuously chimes in is so beautiful. Descriptions of chaos, warp-matter, blood and gore, the might of the imperium, and various Drukhari practices, to give a small selection, are often screenshot worthy in themselves. Owlcat has some good writers, kudos to them. The banter between characters as you walk around is also so well done and sometimes very funny (this was also quite good in BG3 too).CONCLUSION: IN THE GRIM DARKNESS OF THE FAR FUTURE, THERE IS ONLY WAR!

_childDocuments_.review: So i finished the game after 140 hours.This is a great CRPG, the game overall is great. It lacks in some departments. Can it hold up to the graphic fidelity of Baldurs Gate 3 ? no it cant. Same with the voice acting, which in itself ist good but only very few core scenes are voiceated, mostly with your NPC companions. most other stuff is not. So there will be a lot of reading. however what you read is well done. Quests, Story, just normal lore Stuff all great and fitting in the 40k Universe. Overall this is a great 40K game in terms of Lore "accuracy" and also a good introduction into the W40k universe.The D100 System and general leveling system takes some getting used to. There are an almost overwhelming amount of option when leveling, you can respec as well. However once you get a grip on the system you can make some truly game breaking builds.As for the game itself Act 1 is a good tutorial, introducing basic game systems and the whole of 40k pretty well.Act 2 Introduces the rest of game systems, and expands the story.From there on out your have 3 more Acts of varying length.After Act 1 you can fly around small part of the universe the game is set in. kind of like Mass effect explore systems scan planets for resources and point of interests. besides main quests you have, companion quests, can follow up on rumors you collect throughout the game, dialog etc. some might be fruitful and lead to more quests or loot, some might be duds. while running around the planets you might encounter some puzzle which can be fun.Bugs: Rumor has it that after ACT3 the game becomes noticeably more buggy that the first 3 acts. Not in terms of the random T-Posing character but broken quests etc. Personally i havent encountered any of that, or at least i didnt notice, but that doesnt mean you wont too. The game has loads of branching quests and permutations in the story depending on your decisions. However the devs are patching the game constantly and fixing stuff, might take a while to get it iron clad though. I think its known that the game was a bit rushed and stuff got cut, but that might be reintroduced later. In that process some stuff got broken. like the "moral" System has 3 "flavors" with 5 ranks each but i think on some of the flavors you cant reach max level.Balancing: in the beginning you are fairly weak and with a lack of understanding for the level and skill system you might struggle a little. However the higher level you climb the more gear you aqquire the stronger you get. There are some game breaking builds and combinations of gear/skills/classes etc that make loads of fights trivial even on the hardest difficuty. might get patched, might not. If not i recommend have some fun with it and when you get bored with it respec your character(s).For PC users there is a mod called "Toybox" that allows for some tweaking if you run into some bugs.TLDR:Overall the game is very good, sound and music is good, voiceacting too but sadly only few scenes get that treatment. Graphics are OK the style and art is good but it lacks a bit in fidelity. However you will only notice when zooming in. The Story is great and has room for several different playstyle and repeated playthroughts. It has some rough edges but is good enough that i put 140 hours in to finish the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I truly enjoyed my time with this game. It's really solidly written, though I'd imagine for someone not as interested or experienced with 40k it'd probably be a bit harder to get in to, but even then they provide enough information that I don't think that should be a major problem. I'd say it's probably about a 7 or 8 out of ten.However,The technical quality of this game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ abysmal. It is infested with bugs in a way that was never truly game ruining for me (though I did have to manually complete the occasional quest step utilizing mods as it would sometimes just not progress and you'd be stuck), but rather it just truly made the moment to moment experience of playing it really frustrating. I really enjoyed the game's story and character, they weren't perfectly written at all times but it was clear the writers had a lot of respect and care for the setting they were working in, and they did a really good job. Despite that I can't recommend it as this game feels like it needs so much more extra work on the technical side of things that I highly doubt it'll ever getIf you like 40k, AND are willing to put up with a game so rough around the edges that it should never have been released like this, get it on sale. Otherwise, stay away and do not bother. It's a real shame that is the case though, because this really could have been something really really great. All the pieces are there, good story, solid characters, an interesting combat system that is stupidly easy to break in half (turns out extra turns are really good), but the technical side is just so so so bad that it ruins it. What a waste of potential.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing this shortly after completing Act 1 and will update it once there's further progress made.The game, while fun, is heavily buggy with oversights that make it feel like I'm playing an early access game. I have had numerous visual and audio bugs that are glaringly painful (especially the constant 'Vine booms' on the ship's bridge). The in game cutscenes can look especially jank with effects and movement.Owlcat also didn't carry over the reverse of the lesson they learned from Kingmaker's Enhanced Edition, with only one gameplay style available, turn-based. Real-time with pause is just gone and the easiest of fights can drag on for nearly half an hour as cultists soak up bolter rounds. This isn't helped when enemies often bug out and don't end their turn, sitting around for a minute until they are auto skipped.I will give the game credit for being heavily customisable *at first*, but if you wish to respec any characters, you must pay an increasingly demanding amount of Profit Factor which is a heavily limited resource. Furthermore, you can't edit a character's name, portrait, appearance, origin, first archetype, and so on. Not even for your own character. If you want to change into a DPS, buffer, psyker, etc., you're ♥♥♥♥ out of luck.This is worse for companions as they are presets and can have their initial level choices gated off. Even mercenaries are subject to this along with the issue of there being no way to dismiss them.Also, there should be the option for people joining in on multiplayer to make their own characters. As of now, you either play as pre-existing ones or backseat the host to make a mercenary for you to later take control of, or vice-versa. An import and export feature would be appreciated.uhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh the story is good at least, so far.TL;DR Wait it out for a couple of bugfixes, QoL changes, and a sale. Play Owlcat's Pathfinder games for a gaming fix.

_childDocuments_.review: Owlcat has made another good game in an interesting system but it has some teething issues.The good. So far after getting through most of the game it seems that the characters are really well done the prologue introduces a good start but chapter one will introduce the majority of the cast and they are all really well done, their voice actors are amazing and the characters are built with intrigue and charm. The player character has many options but three main 'morality' choices Dogmatic, Iconoclast, and Hereticmaking the thought of three replays instant in the game. The warhammer 40k title is really well represented in this as we get to look through the lens of the grey area that is the rouge trader, taking any cuts in order to make order or chaos in the expanse.The Bad. So far the character creator is by far the limited compared to the current modern standard, their main focus is portraits which all are done very well but are stuck to a limited quantity, Mostly each portrait covers generally the background options like Noble, commissar, psyker, ect. and a male and female variant. generally combat feels real hit or miss early on but much better later on, but I feel that is due to the archetype classes which can feel weak until hitting a sweet spot later into the game the easiest I can think of is the operator and solider archetype which feel weaker early but hit their stride around level 16 when you get another archetype to further specialize making both much more powerful. However operator combos still feel weak unless you go hyper single target focus like a certain companion you get on Janus early into the game. but the two companions you get at the start, Pascal and Idira never feel that strong more like skill jockies to pass certain kinds of skill checks in the game.The Ugly. The game doesn't have much of this until the later sections where I started to notice straight up bugs that would prevent me from progressing though most of the time a simple restart of the game would fix it up it certainly was annoying and as of the time writing this I cannot progress to chapter 5 due to a bug that loads a space combat early and stops loading the game. so until some bugs are smoothed out it might be worth it to wait to buy if you intend on doing a long sit through the game.There was a part in the game that had a check for 'morality' later on in chapter 4 that required a point that was far above what I had even though I felt I had made every single Iconoclast option I could pick, the only thing I can think about is missing one companion and ending another companion which both could have contained Iconoclast decisions to boost the 'morality' to a high enough score I imagine that this would not come up often with players as most people will probably collect the companions and not try to kill them, but there are plenty of times where the option to kill a companion does come up in dialog. overall a small tweak increase the 'morality' gain might be nice to allow for those end game dialog to be easier to obtain.tl;drGood game over all, needs some polishing but a really good warhammer 40k entry. worth buying now or when a few patches roll out for it.

name: Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney Trilogy
detailed_description: Apollo Justice's Legal Journey Begins Anew! Join rookie attorney Apollo Justice and his mentor, the legendary Phoenix Wright, in this collection of 3 games! This title features the 14 episodes of 'Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney', 'Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney - Dual Destinies', and 'Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney - Spirit of Justice', and the 2 previously DLC-only Special Episodes for a total of 16 episodes! Also included is a mountain of extra goodies that's sure to satisfy any Ace Attorney fan! Orchestra Hall - Listen to the in-game background music and select orchestral arrangements! Art Library - View illustrations, design specs, commissioned pieces, and even the special Spirit of Justice Prologue anime! Animation Studio - Play around with character animations and recreate your favorite scenes! This collection supports Japanese, English, French, German, Korean, and Traditional and Simplified Chinese. Mix and match to play in whichever languages you'd like! Immerse yourself in this beautiful collection as you shout 'Objection!' in these newly renovated halls of justice! Some of the contents of the games in this collection are presented as initially released to preserve the games as originally created.

_childDocuments_.review: The Ace Attorney franchise quickly became one of my personal favourites the moment I wrapped up the first few cases of that initial game. Its iconic presentation, smart scripts and nuanced characters made binging the re-issued franchise utterly effortless from start to finish. Needless to say, my expectations for this third collection were very high, and I hoped I would find plenty to love in spite of the fanbase’s more mixed reception of these titles. Thankfully, I found much of this trilogy to be a great continuation for the series; while this is the most inconsistent collection, it offers plenty of intriguing cases and characters to make these games worth experiencing. As this collection consists of the 4th to 6th mainline entries, I’m going to assume you know the gist of what to expect from an Ace Attorney game, as there’s nothing here that significantly deviates from its established formula. Let’s start by looking at the trilogy as a whole. While the other two collections deliver a more singular overarching narrative, this trilogy largely opts for standalone narratives with three major plotlines that carry through each game: the development and backstory of the eponymous Apollo Justice, the disbarment and resurgence of Phoenix Wright, and this idea of “The dark age of the law”, which paints the picture of a murky legal world where the finding the truth is secondary to conviction. I think these latter two plotlines are handled well; Phoenix has compelling reasons to be present past his initial development, and the dark age of the law is used to derive distinctly fresh character motives and plot elements, even to a satirical degree. With Apollo Justice, I unfortunately think that this loud yet unwaveringly passionate character is largely mishandled. He never steps out of the spotlight of Phoenix at any point during the game named after him, he mostly takes a backseat in Dual Destinies to focus more on Phoenix’s return and the character of Athena, and it’s because of these two games that his development in Spirit of Justice is quite rushed, even though I love where he ends up.The underdeveloped nature of Apollo’s character is a large part of why I feel his eponymous game, the last mainline entry released for the Nintendo DS, is the weakest in the franchise by a good margin. Despite it being angled as a soft reboot to the series, Apollo and his new partner Trucy are largely overshadowed during crucial plot moments. Which is a shame, as this new pairing has great chemistry that only improves as the story progresses, but they don’t get much of a chance to prove their abilities unassisted in the courtroom. I also find the four cases on offer to be rather average; their writing largely lacks the punch and tension that the other collections consistently delivered so well, and I was ultimately left underwhelmed for most of their runtime. However, this writing style does not apply to Klavier Gavin, who is a breath of fresh air amongst the prosecutors for being surprisingly likeable, to the point where his presence carried much of the trial segments for me. Separately, I also really enjoyed the expanded gameplay offerings; most evidence can be thoroughly examined in three dimensions, the forensic minigames offer a nice change of pace during the investigation segments, and Apollo’s perceive mechanic, which allows you to zoom in and identify nervous habits of the witnesses, leads to some varied progression in the trial segments. Ultimately, there’s a good amount to enjoy here, but it’s the only game in the series I cannot see myself coming back to.Then we have Dual Destinies, the first 3D entry in the franchise, that thankfully survives the transition from 2D graphics quite well. While some of the models of the returning characters take a bit to get used to, all of the new ones look fantastic, and their animations ooze even more personality than ever before. Of the six cases on offer, I’d say all but the second one are consistently intriguing, ranging from a murder surrounding a detonated bomb, to a stabbing amidst the launch of a rocket, to…defending an Orca? It’s all as over the top as you’d expect, yet somehow feels more grounded than the original trilogy, steering around spirit channelling as a plot device to explain the killings in more ‘realistic’ terms. Athena Cykes makes her debut in this game in style. She’s the rookiest of the lawyer trio yet sets herself apart with a bubbling personality, a shockingly dark backstory, and is the source of the new gameplay mechanic of Mood Matrices, where a witnesses’ emotions are questioned to help draw out further testimony. While I think there is untapped potential with having more segments that require you to decide between assessing emotions or testimony, the presentation and theming of this mechanic easily makes it my favourite addition to the formula. Separately, Blackquill and Fulbright, the new prosecutor and detective respectively, are brilliant additions, in part due to their personalities being polar opposites, and the returning characters are handled excellently. Overall, it’s a really solid entry from the get-go, allowing me to get over that disappointing first game rather quickly.That leads us to Spirit of Justice, the most recent mainline entry to date. Taking place primarily in the fictional kingdom of Khura’in, this title seems Phoenix take on quite literally his most vulnerable cases yet, as the Defence Culpability Act threatens to make him face the same fate as the accused, should his arguments fall through. Matters are further complicated with the addition of Divination Seances, which allows the courtroom to have a glimpse at the victim’s final moments, ultimately damning the accused very easily if this evidence is not questioned further. It’s the most complicated mechanic in the series, but once you understand how the contradictions are usually found, it leads to some very satisfying revelations.Part of the game also takes place back home, largely serving to give Apollo and Athena more time in the spotlight. While Apollo gets one of the best standalone cases in the series, Athena is given arguably the most boring case in the whole collection, killing the great pacing up to that point. Thankfully, all of the cases in Khura’in are excellent, alongside the epilogue case which is a nice throwback to the original trilogy. However, this game undoubtedly stars the worst prosecutor in the series, who very quickly becomes an irritating catchphrase machine that is not deviated from until the end of his final appearance. Despite this gripe, Spirit of Justice is my favourite entry in the trilogy because of how well it executes its intriguing premise and develops most of its characters.I really enjoyed this trilogy overall. While it never reaches the consistent heights of the other collections, it nonetheless has plenty of great stories to tell, nuanced characters to meet, and satisfying objections to obtain. Clocking in at a beefy 80 hours, with a few nice art and music bonuses in the extras menu to boot, it’s hard to argue against the value for money on display, even if some cases fall flat for you. I can see myself fondly revisiting a large portion of the 3D entries, and I hope that the next mainline entry doubles down on everything these games do well, whilst also not forgetting why the original trilogy is still highly revered. But while we wait for that, an Investigations 1+2 collection needs to happen, and I hope to not be lying coldly on that for too long.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a no brainer purchase for any ace attorney fan that's out there. For everyone else I would suggest to start with the original trilogy first prior to playing this game. The music is the best in this trilogy IMHO. Dual Destinies starts really slow with 2nd case being garbage and then slowly getting better towards the end of the game. It's worth playing for getting to know Athena and Blackquill and absolute banger of a last case. This game also has the best bonus case.Spirit of Justice is a hit or miss for most of the people. I did enjoy it even though it felt pretty long and some cases felt like being out of place completely. Overall great games, hopefully more ace attorney will come in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDW: the games are good but the series discards too much of Apollo Justice (Ace Attorney 4) to ignore completely.The good part of this trilogy is that it's got all of the engaging mysteries, fun character interactions and excellent music of the previous games, and if you like those aspects these games are absolutely worth playing.However, as much as I'd love to say it's as good as the PW trilogy I can't, mostly because of the more disjointed feeling between the games. Apollo Justice was a game which thoroughly changed the status quo of the series and the problems with the trilogy mostly stem from Dual Destinies trying desperately to ignore those changes. A good example is Phoenix Wright's character whiplash (don't worry, I'm not going to spoil anything).In short, in AA4 he is slightly too different from his T&T self, while in AA5 and 6 he is too similar.In long:In Apollo Justice, Phoenix is presented to be much more confident and clever, thinking things through much more thoroughly than in his previous games, however other aspects of his character are unfitting even for a more jaded and bitter version of the Phoenix we knew.While his character change is drastic, it is justified decently well, the problem is that Dual Destinies undoes all of this development, he loses any bitterness or distrust, as well as losing a lot of his cool confidence; the best (non spoiler) example I have is that Phoenix doesn't overreact to being surprised in Apollo Justice at all, however in Dual Destinies he overreacts to pretty much any setback using his surprised sprite.

_childDocuments_.review: I have waited years for these games to finally be ported to something that isn't an iPhone or Android device.This collection of games were such a vital part of my teenage years, I am so happy to be able to relive these absolute classics on an HD screen! Dual Destinies may not be the best Ace Attorney game in the franchise, but I have so many great memories anticipating the 3DS release of the game. From the web based Japanese demo that I would play over and over to the trailers that were so good at making the wait for that game almost unbearable! Dual Destinies is what helped get my foot into making YouTube videos with my old Music Compilation videos. I owe a lot to Dual Destinies, and it's about time that it leaves the 3DS and Mobile Phone landscape of gaming! I still cannot believe that Dual Destinies came out 11 years ago!!! I have a lot less memories with Apollo Justice Ace Attorney, I've only played that game once on my DS, and Haven't returned to it since then. That's not to say it's a bad game! I still love every single AA game that's been made! I WILL, however, say that whoever was responsible for Spark Brushel's armpit tell... you know what you did.Spirit of Justice is the best game out of the whole collection, without a doubt. From the long awaited return of Maya Fey (side note, genuinely where is our boy Gumshoe!?), to the infamous clown girl...... to the gut wrenching final case that finally let Apollo shine in his own trilogy. I truly believe that Spirit of Justice will go down as a highlight for this franchise.I really want to say thank you to Capcom for not letting this franchise die with AA6. Thank you for giving us more updated versions of the Original Phoenix Wright trilogy, thank you for translating the Great Ace Attorney games and letting us finally play those amazing titles in English. Thank you for giving us Apollo Justice Ace Attorney, Ace Attorney Dual Destinies, and Ace Attorney Spirit of Justice on modern platforms. This series has meant a lot to me, and I cannot wait for what is next for Ace Attorney. Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: Great games, IMO the original trilogy is still better but these are still excellent titles.By the way, if playing on Steam Deck, go into the game's Steam Properties and set the Game Resolution to 1920x1200, and turn on "Set resolution for internal and external display" (if this doesn't show, exit and re-enter the menu). After this, go to the PC Config section in the game, and set the resolution to 1920x1080. This removes jagged edges from Apollo Justice. _childDocuments_.review: As of this writing, I've finished Apollo Justice and am on Chapter 3 of Dual Destinies. I've played Apollo Justice before, but that was over 10 years ago on my DS. I've never played Dual Destinies or Spirit of Justice since I didn’t have a 3DS. I appreciate that all the Ace Attorney games can now be (legally) played on PC instead of requiring old retro consoles.Objection! That said, I can’t say I love this trilogy more than the original Phoenix Wright Trilogy. There was a certain charm to the first three games.Maybe it’s the sprites? There was something endearing about the hand-drawn art of the Phoenix Wright trilogy. I don’t love the 3D sprites they started using in the newer titles—they didn’t age well, in my opinion.Maybe it’s the pacing? The text scroll in the Apollo Justice trilogy is slow, and you can’t adjust it. I read faster than the text appears, but you can’t just press "A" to skip because you risk also skipping sprite animations, which I want to see. When the game dictates your pace, it can get a bit frustrating.Maybe it’s the wacky gimmicks? The Ace Attorney series isn’t known for its realism, but the crimes became more outlandish and harder to follow—they completely lose me at times.Hold it! It’s still a fantastic experience for anyone who loves the Ace Attorney series, and is a series worth recommending. If you're itching for more after the original trilogy, this has the Ace Attorney formula that you can come to expect.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the second installment for the Ace Attorney Trilogy that Capcom brings to the steam store. While the first one revolves around Phoenix Wright, this Trilogy (as the name already suggests) follows Apollo Justice to some extent.Since 2 out of 3 games are ports from the Nintendo 3DS this collection is a tiny bit more hardware hungry/needs better graphic cards as the first one. Now lets come to the meat of it: The game itself. As typical for Ace Attorney games you have a WIDE range of characters and many are fleshed out to be deeper than "I am bad guy doing bad stuff". The background music always completment the situation and accentuate sudden shifts in tone, let it be funny or dramatic. The graphic is much more polished for the first game and nicely scaled for the 3DS ones.The controls are well ported over, but since many of the forensic minigames were just DS/3DS gimmicks it obviously is not as engaging as they used to be. But they are still fun to do, dont get me wrong.Apart from the normal stuff we got on the handheld there are also PC only additions like art books and music/sound sampling. As things that we take for granted but takes a bit of optimisation: The loading times.I tested it and from hitting "start" on steam to my loaded game save it took only 7 seconds. SECONDS! I know, its not the hardware intense game there is, but some other games dont even have their start loading screen up after 7s.I did not talk about the story? Come on, its a no brainer. The Ace Attorney games are always riddled with plot twists and nice character arcs.But I also have some not so nice things to say (so I dont look like a total fanboy):By god, I forgot how annoying most people are in the first game (Apollo Justice). Maya was already sometimes hard to get around but Trucy takes the cherry with lacking all common sense and sometimes being downright criminal (ofcourse without any repercussions). In addtion this "Phoenix Wright being transformed into a hobo" never was my favorite plotline as it does my boy really dirty. Gladly its not permanent, but we will never forget. Also it does not help that everything is VERY constructed. Some problems or even murder could be prevented with some normal human interaction.Since I dont want to end on a bad note I sandwich my negative points with something nice at the end:I absolutly love the variaty of new abilities. In the first Trilogy we had the magatama that helps us with the investigations.In this one we have SO MANY MORE. From body language perception, over our old friend magatama to emotion analysis and others (I dont want to spoil too much), this game is packed with "minigames" like that.As a final line I only hope we also get the Miles Edgeworth Investigation series to steam soon, but after that running low on Ace Attorney games to scratch our OBJECTION itch.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the original trilogy for the Ace Attorney series back during my senior year of college during the pandemic. With an excess of time, I sorted through the highest rated games on steam and made the plunge into the series. The original trilogy had many positive traits going for it. The cast of characters were memorable & the plot lines that played out had many of us on the edge of our seats. It was a fantastic set of games that left a deep impression on the way I think about how information is presented in stories. A truly timeless series.Now, if you think that this is a review that will admonish the Apollo Justice trilogy in favor of the Phoenix wright trilogy, you'd be wrong. The original games, due to the time & budget constraints, recycled assets & characters in order to stretch their budget. However, the strength of writing is undeniable. The Apollo Justice trilogy finds itself in a different position entirely. For various reasons, each game in the AJ trilogy had a different director involved. Each game in the AJ trilogy feels distinctly different. The fact that this series is even called the Apollo Justice Trilogy is a hell of a red herring when the focus is split on three different defense attorneys in the series.  This lead to some confusion when you enter the name game & find that there's very little connecting everything except for the characters who even then tend to change. If you are willing to overlook what is undeniably a growing pain for the series, what you'll find is trilogy packed with a lot of charm, fresh ideas, and a stream of new characters to fall in love with. While not perfect,  I do appreciate the amount of effort & the willingness to make mistakes to take the series forward. I'm unbelievably excited to see what the future of this series holds.TL:DR Keep Cooking, 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney Trilogy? Balancing Justice and Nostalgia! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)"It masterfully blends nostalgia with modern enhancements, offering an uneven yet richly rewarding legal adventure."The "Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney Trilogy" emerges as a delightful treat for fans of courtroom drama and video game storytelling. This compilation, featuring rookie attorney Apollo Justice and his iconic mentor, Phoenix Wright, bundles together "Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney", "Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney - Dual Destinies", and "Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney - Spirit of Justice". With a whopping 16 episodes, including two that were previously only available as DLC, this collection offers a comprehensive journey into the world of legal battles and intricate storylines. Language support spanning English, French, German, and several Asian languages ensures a broader appeal, inviting a global audience to partake in the thrill of courtroom action.Diving into the specifics, the trilogy shines in its presentation and extra content. The remastered graphics and soundtracks enhance the experience, with the Orchestra Hall and Art Library serving as delightful bonuses for fans. The Animation Studio adds a fun, interactive element, allowing players to recreate their favorite scenes. These extras are a testament to the developer's dedication to the series and its fans. However, the collection isn't without its shortcomings. While "Spirit of Justice" is often hailed as the standout game, offering depth and a chance for Apollo to truly shine, "Dual Destinies" receives mixed feelings. Some fans find it lacking compared to other entries, feeling it doesn't quite reach the heights of its predecessors. This disparity in quality between the games can lead to an uneven experience for players journeying through the trilogy.In terms of user engagement, the trilogy has been warmly received for its nostalgic value and replayability, even as a linear visual novel. Long-time fans appreciate the opportunity to relive these classic games on modern platforms, with HD graphics enhancing their experience. The extra content, including art and music, adds a layer of depth and appreciation for the series. However, there are critiques regarding the pacing and strength of some of the storylines in "Dual Destinies" and "Spirit of Justice". Some purists argue that these titles don't quite live up to the charm of the original trilogy. Nonetheless, even the less favored games in the collection are acknowledged as worthy of play, underscoring the enduring appeal of the Ace Attorney series.In conclusion, the "Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney Trilogy" is a commendable effort in bringing classic games to a new generation of gamers and satisfying long-time fans. While not every game in the collection is equally celebrated, the overall package offers a rich, engaging experience that both honors its roots and embraces its evolution. _childDocuments_.review: This trilogy is the weakest AA releases on Steam, but it’s still worth your play, nonetheless. AJ is a fun game, Apollo & Trucy’s chemistry makes the investigations fun, and I loved the return of Ema as a detective this time around, while Klavier Gavin fills in the prosecutor position here (really like him, especially compared to the other two in the trilogy).  The OST is easily among the best the mainline has to offer (along with the AA1’s). All cases are good, Turnabout Trump and Turnabout Succession obviously outshine the other two, but Turnabout Corner and Turnabout Serenade are definitely some of the better middle cases. Dual Destinies is hot garbage as far as AA goes imo. It almost feels like another team made it, without grasping the essence of the previous games and make it feel like a celebratory comeback, while discarding the entirety of Apollo Justice (ahem). The 3D looks horrific. I don’t know how DGS and the Layton crossover (which released before DD) can look this much better than Dual Destinies, all of them being released on the 3DS. The cases feel immature in a sense, not the crimes (and their depictions) themselves, but with the character designs and general dialogue. It’s even weirder that Turnabout for Tomorrow depicts the by far goriest and most disturbing murder that’s ever happened in Ace Attorney. All of that said most parts of cases 3-6 are still enjoyable, even if they don’t reach the heights the previous games did.I do like Spirit of Justice more than Dual Destinies, the change of setting and splitting of the cast for most of the game works in its favour as Phoenix being more like in the trilogy works better without Apollo and Athena next to him. The second case is really good and personally I loved the Khura’in cases. The 4th case is utterly misplaced and underdeveloped, the final is a bit of a mixed bag. I really enjoyed the first investigation (that felt more like Layton than like AA) and I liked the second trial, but the middle part is a bit rough, especially the foundation the first trial was built on was abysmal to say the least. The DLC was decent, even with Edgeworth returning to his AA1 character for whatever reason.I really hope they won’t let Ace Attorney die and release AA7 some time in the future, whatever that may bring.

_childDocuments_.review: While this trilogy doesn't quite match the quality of the original, I still believe that the Apollo Justice trilogy contains a fine set of titles.Apollo Justice was a bold new direction for the franchise, which is unfortunately still contentious to this day. With a time skip and a new protagonist, the game tried a lot of new things that a lot of fans didn't like, hence why a lot of it was undone in future titles. That said, I think that it's a strong set of characters and a good plot that's let down by weak cases. Overall, I think it's a good game and I would have liked to have seen more of what the creator had in mind when writing this game.Dual Destinies is unfortunately, not a title that lives up the rest of the trilogy. The playable character space is crowded by not only the return of Phoenix Wright but also a new protagonist, Athena Cykes. The cast struggle for screentime, reducing Athena to only having a single case in her debut game! The filler cases are weak and the overall plot is a tad predictable. It's also a lot easier than earlier titles, mostly due to the fact that the characters have a habit of hinting towards solutions to puzzles before you've even gotten a chance to answer.Spirit of Justice is definitely the best in the trilogy, with an engaging (if absurd at times) plot set in the foreign Kingdom of Khura'in. It introduces what I feel to be the best cross-examination mechanic in the series, the Divination Seance, where the last moments of the victim are analysed. My biggest criticism of this game is that the prosecutor, Nahyuta, lacks personality and only receives character development until near the end of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: These games play like homework. It's agonizing.AA4 gets a pass. It feels a little lost rather than outright bad, and it has some good ideas like the Mason system- It could have used a stronger thesis and more time to marinate on its ideas because of how... let's say "narratively dissatisfying" the motives of Zak Gramarye and Kristoph Gavin are, but I can see what it wanted to be. Valant and Klavier are great characters, and so is Hobo Wright.I genuinely don't understand what AA5 and 6 are going for other than "it's more ace attorney so we should raise the stakes without raising the stakes". They feel more kid friendly, and also are trying to have an overarching plot, but they're also not going into that plot... at all, sometimes. There would be substantial nuance if I were to go into individual cases of course, since there's plenty of below average quality cases in the first series as well, but those problems didn't feel systemic as a rule. To say as little as possible, 5's biggest issue is that it's definitely written for kids and gives its own game away literal hours before it lets Phoenix/Athena know what the player knows, and 6's biggest problem (of which it has many) is that the threat level is so comically unbelievable that you know that the heroes are going to win anyways. The Avengers Issue. I know we expect to win in all of the games, but it's absolutely catastrophic how nonsensical the situations presented are in this game- mostly due to the DC act and what an actual dictator would do in a situation where they have PW held at gunpoint. How did they think something like the DC act was a good thing to put in Ace Attorney? It's a good thing they made him forget about Matt Engarde. Nahyuta directly compounds practically every issue in the game somehow.There's a huge number of minor issues that I've frankly lost count of, but I can only say for sure that they're for a different audience.Oh, and they better kill off Apollo because these backstories all surely contradict each other.

_childDocuments_.review: Full transparency: I've bought these games on many different pieces of hardware before - DS, 3DS and Android specifically- so this isn't my first rodeo with any of these games. I'd say of the 3 games, Spirit of Justice probably is my favorite: the overarching story, for me, remains a treat even on revisits and has some of the most emotional high points of the series. But the other two games are still phenomenal in their own right with some incredible cases: the most noteworthy for me being Turnabout Trump, Turnabout Succession and Turnabout for Tomorrow. If you're new to the series... while I'd say the Phoenix Wright Trilogy or the Great Ace Attorney Chronicles are overall better starting points, you could do worse than start here! But if you're already an Ace Attorney fan who's at least played the trilogy... well chances are, you were probably going to buy this anyways and are just reading the Steam reviews for fun. Either way, you're in for a fun set of mysteries that have been nicely updated for the modern day and make for great nighttime reading before bed! Especially if you own a Steam Deck.

_childDocuments_.review: Apollo Justice - Great start to an awesome trilogy. Apollo is a nice character - even if he's surprisingly not the focal point of the game - and the story has some deliciously dark undertones.Dual Destinies - A sequel that tells its own story from Apollo Justice, but it really works. The writing is top-notch and brilliantly witty, the pacing is excellent and playing as 3 different lawyers helps to make the story feel so fleshed out. Plus Athena & Blackquill are just the best characters. In the whole series.Spirit of Justice - Big in scope and probably the longest game in the series yet the brilliant pacing never makes it feel dull. Khura'in is a very expansive, well-detailed environment and the artistry is breathtaking. The music may even be some of Noriyuki Iwadare's best work. It's also nice to see Maya again, even if what you expect might happen to her... happens to her.All in all, a brilliant trilogy that I'm so grateful I'm FINALLY able to play on other than my 3DS. And it has only made me more excited for what Ace Attorney 7 (Athena Cykes game plz!!) may bring.

Apollo has never really been one of my favorite characters, and it might be due to how overshadowed he si in the fourth game, seemingly childish in the fifth game, and a sudden messiah in the sixth one. _childDocuments_.name: Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney Trilogy

_childDocuments_.review: The Ace Attorney series is my boo. I've played every single game on the first collection and this collection twice over. So is this trilogy just as good as the original? I'd say yeah. I know a lot of fans didn't like these games as much as the original three, but they felt to me like a new, more modern era of Ace Attorney that I enjoyed quite a lot. With the march of technology came new ways for these stories to create mystery and suspense, such as forensic analysis, psychological analysis, seeing through the eyes of the dead and stuff. The patented funny, witty but also suspenseful Ace Attorney writing is back in full force, and hey, that's what this is all about. Apollo Justice:This is the best game of the trilogy for me. It had the best music, fresh characters, and the most mind-blowing last case out of the trilogy that also ties nicely into the original Phoenix Wright trilogy.  Dual Destinies:Dual Destinies suffers from the "second game of a trilogy" problem of being relatively mid - like Justice For All was. Emphasis on relatively because it's still an Ace Attorney game - meaning it still blows most other mystery games on the market out of the water. It still has its fair share of trademark Ace Attorney moments and mind-bending plot twists. It just wasn't as memorable as Apollo Justice or Spirit of Justice for me. Spirit of Justice: Spirit of Justice is the climactic third game that caps off a trilogy. While its highs weren't as orgasmic as Trials and Tribulations, it was still really good. The new trial gimmick this game added was quite haunting, and I liked it a lot. TLDR: If you're a fan of the first trilogy, definitely get this one too. Everything you love about this series is still here plus a bunch of new stuff too. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney Trilogy

Nothing beats the original Ace Attorney series but this one has great moments and lots of interesting characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney Trilogy

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of this review, I've just finished Apollo Justice. I know it's kind of controversial in the Ace Attorney fanbase, as it puts Phoenix aside. But I genuinely think it's one of Shu Takumi's best works, along with the Great Ace Attorney. It was fresh and interesting, even when playing the third case, the infamous Turnabout Serenade. Which is memed to death, but I still think it's one of the best third cases in the series.The only "fault" I see within the collection is that neither Dual Destinies nor Spirits of Justice really feel like Apollo's games. In fact, when opening the game you see Athena representing Dual Destinies and Phoenix representing Spirits of Justice. Even worse, Dual Destinies in particular feels like it misses the point of the original Apollo Justice, bringing back on the table the theme of a corrupt law system. Also, it's kind of not great as a game for Athena either, I think.But putting that aside, I think it's a good collection. The quality of life improvements are huge compared to the original games, and all the extra bells and whistles (like the whole museum) are great too. Even if Dual Destinies and Spirits of Justice aren't really my favourite, it was so worth it to finally see Apollo Justice in HD. So yeah if you enjoyed the first Ace Attorney trilogy you should give it a try
