_childDocuments_.review: I can’t recommend this game, as it falls short when compared to playing the originals on emulators. I paid around R$50 ($9), and it didn’t feel worth it. A more reasonable price would be R$28 ($5).The game suffers in terms of performance, and key features, especially for Top Gear 2 and Top Gear 3000, are missing. For example, in Top Gear 3000, you could use passwords to start with a fully upgraded car or unlock an "alien car," which is both overpowered and colorful. These options are unavailable because passwords aren’t supported. Worse still, it seems like the developers didn’t even play Top Gear 3000 themselves. When you finish the game, cheats are unlocked, but you can’t actually start with a fully upgraded car due to how the upgrades are handled. Cheats also don’t provide unlimited gadgets, which is the core mechanic of the game.Other minor issues:* Online play is dead and irrelevant.* The UI is clunky, requiring too many clicks to start a race.* Only one save slot per game (single and multiplayer), making the save system more of a limitation than a helpful feature.* Top Gear Crossroads is just Top Gear 1 with reskinned, overpowered cars. One of them is even a Brazilian joke car. People talk about “balance,” but there’s clearly an overpowered car that beats the rest.* The music in the UI is terrible; they should have just used the main game themes.Instead of keeping the original game menus, they wrapped everything in a worse UI. Features like save states, custom cups, and online multiplayer could have been added without altering the main game menu.* The achievements are uninspiring and generic. They missed the opportunity to add interesting challenges through Steam achievements.This purchase is only worth considering for people who want to play these classic games online without setting up emulators and LAN parties, which isn’t difficult but can be a hassle. Another potential reason to buy it is for Steam achievements. For most players, it's better to stick to emulators. It’s not even a good platform for speedrunning.
_childDocuments_.name: Top Racer Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Some might say, "Don't buy this game, just play it on an emulator," but let’s be real—the legality of that route is murky at best, especially since there don’t seem to be any official options to purchase the ROMs in this collection as of now.So, what does this collection bring to the table beyond the classic SNES Top Gear games? Quite a bit, actually. It includes modern enhancements like leaderboards for competitive bragging rights, network multiplayer for racing friends online, and a solo race mode with selectable tracks—perfect for practice sessions or casual play. There’s even a mirror mode for each track, which adds a fun twist, though it’s worth noting that the mirrored UI might feel a bit disorienting at first.Overall, this collection does justice to the golden age of ‘90s arcade-style racers, giving both veterans and newcomers a chance to relive (or discover) the magic of Top Gear. It’s a well-crafted package, and I’d wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone with a love for retro racing games.

_childDocuments_.review: As a Kid, Top Racer was one of my favorite games, and it was something that helped me in my upbriging.it teached me 4 passions i have up to this day: Math, Geography, Astronomy and Videogames.yes, you heard that right. it was Top Racer 1 and 2 that made me a Nerd on Geography, wanting to know more about the cities and places depicted in the game, its climates, when it rains there and everything.it was also Top Racer 1 in particular that did teach me about Math: calculating time and fuel strategy is essential, to win, since the CPU is always breathing on your neck. and to this day i know that if you're using the Sidewinder in the original game, San Francisco, Chichen Itza and Hiroshima are tracks you don't need to stop to fuel up if you're fast enough (Black forest and Bordeaux are another ones but you gotta be extremely fast and lucky not to hit anything on the road). also, it teached me a lot of efficient strategies on how and where to pit, usually piting early to open a good gap and undercuting the CPU taking advantage of the fact there isn't many backmarkers on the first laps of the race, and that the computer named CPU tends to slow down to follow your pace. with the passage of time, the strategy became second nature to me, calculating fuel times to the second to maximize each strip of juice and be stoped as little and as early as strategically viable.and 3000 teached me all about Astronomy... many people may not know this, but the system stars all do exist in real life as white-blue stars in the milky way, altough some are miswritten by one or two letters like Toygeta (in real life Taygeta) or Vega 5 (wich is only Vega, but there is a planet called Vega too on the game so i think on this one they did that to differentiate). it made me look to the sky, even if i couldn't see the stars themselves anymore due to the light pollution the city of recife, where i live, got over the years. and made my imagination run wild with what alien civilizations might be there or what kind of Sci-fi buildings and societies we might find when we get there....and then this collection launches... i could not believe in my eyes that those games, maybe lost to history were being revived and re-sold, by some compatriots of mine that got the license from Kemco and Gremlin Graphics. i thought they were just found memories i got to relieve here and there in an emulator... that i never could own 3000 again, even if only digitally... so i had to get them for myself, even if they would end up only as a collector's piece on my steam library... for old times sake...so i thought that i would just touch them once... little did i know that after 18 hours of pure gameplay later i would be writing a review praising these games and a lot more...the graphics are all there, the nuances, the little glitches, even the old pit strategies were all there... it hadn't changed one iota from what i remembered. and it offered me more... i... couldn't be more happier... to be that 7 year old kid with that top racer 3000 cartridge on my hands again gifted to me by my now late mother...and there was even crossroads, that made me LOVE the Twilight car and learn new strategies all over again since its fuel consuption is different. it accelerates fast, runs fast, and is a pure bliss to drive... to experience all the circuits i know again from a total new perspective...i simply couldn't be more happier... so i played... and played and played untill platinum it. and for me... there is little if anything i can say to criticize it other than super minor nitpicks: of course the dificulty on the last cup and especially the last track on 3000 could be toned down a bit. that track felt like a Kaizo hack... but it made me sweat, breath heavily, to say: "you are not beating me, not after 25 years of experience. the true champion is ME, and i'm here to claim my trophy again, EVERY TROPHY on EVERY TRACK IS MINE!!!". i spent some hours there praticing, geting every corner right, every nuance, every curved ball that planet called Mechan could trow at me, to triumph (albeit using modern tools) in the end on the champion dificulty. it's... a frustrating but ultimately unforgetable experience.other thing was the upgrades on 3000 unlocking earlier than i remember... i thought my eyes were playing tricks on me, but later i did discover that yes, there was this boost by the new devs to prioritize more urgent tech you need on earlier races. and on the Champion dificulty, it made everything much better and smoother.another small nitpick is the minimaps on TR3000, their road bifurcations not always are there for you to read out, and it is something they could've touched up. but hey, it wasn't in the original either, so can't blame them for it.\and one last nitpick on Top Racer 2, the last dry tire, it isn't slick, but "bald", if you know what i mean. zero grip. maybe that's again my instincts playing tricks on me... but this one i have more concrete doubts if it isn't a true bug.you see, little gremlins and bugs like this, since no one is perfect. but that didn't subtract one iota from my experience. maybe i have an overpowered PC (I7 8th Gen, 48GB ram, 2070 RTX), but this ran so flawlessly and in 60 FPS on all 3 games, it even bugged my brain on how smooth it was on the first top racer. but it just took one or two races in pratice mode to get me on the groove again.I just... cannot give anything other than my highest praise, QuBite. you brought back part of that 7 year old kid that was sleeping again. and even if just for a moment, you transported me back to the past. back to that old apartment, where i could hear her voice, the old small 15 inch tube Tv, my toy die cast cars, and the feelings that i was there once again, and more with the new content.i cannot thank you enough for this, for making me relive something i thought i would never be able to again.Kudos, and thank you very much for everything.

_childDocuments_.review: If like me you're old enough to remember these 1990s Super NES games (American & European gamers might know them better as Top Gear, Top Gear 2 and Top Gear 3000), these are those games with a few modern day tweaks and a new compilation game added. The games are simple but fun and challenging, in particular the first Top Gear because it added dialogue bubbles where players would randomly taunt others or make relevant comments, and they had good multiplayer too. I in particular liked Top Gear 3000 for it's space theme and extensive car building. These games also inspired the excellent PC/mobile game "Horizon Chase". They also added 4 new cars for the "Crossroads" game, one which looks exactly like it came from "OutRun".Yes they are simple, but also challenging (Top Racer 2 in particular) and they are also fun and now you can play multiplayer with up to 4 people too. If you liked the original games on SNES this is a must-buy, but it's also worth picking up if you want simple yet deep racing with some good multiplayer.

name: Europa
detailed_description: Features An emotive story-driven adventure, with around 3-4 hours of playtime. A breathtaking world of lakes, meadows and mountains to explore, scattered within the remains of a fallen civilisation. Free-flowing movement that empowers you to glide serenely from boost to boost, building power and momentum over time. Uncover secrets, solve puzzles, and navigate hidden dangers in the ruins. An intimate story about growing up and humanity’s relationship with nature. About the game On the moon Europa, a lush terraformed paradise in Jupiter’s shadow, an android named Zee sets out in search of answers. Run, glide and fly across the landscape, solve mysteries in the ruins of a fallen utopia, and discover the story of the last human alive. Europa is a peaceful game of adventure, exploration and meditation. As you travel you’ll gradually upgrade the capabilities of your Zephyr jetpack, boosting yourself further through the air until you can flow freely into the sky. “Come to the Island if you ever get lonely. Come here, and think of me.”

_childDocuments_.review: I should preface this by saying that I would prefer to give a neutral review, neither recommending or not. I really wanted to like this game. There's so much to recommend here, but the end result is not as great as it should be. And I don't mean in a "I got hyped by Peter Molyneux before release and nothing can live up to my expectations" kind of way, I mean that the dev's vision is so simple and clear, but the delivery falls flat. What could go wrong with a stunningly beautiful Ghibli-esque setting with movement and puzzling like Journey, and a lovely story behind it all? Well, a lot I'm afraid.Firstly I never thought that I'd complain about a game that's all about floating for being too floaty, but here we are. I don't mean the levitation though. It's just that there's no sense of weight to your movements. To make matter worse, the controls are clunky too, and the world pushes back on you both literally and figuratively all the time. That's not even mentioning how you're given a vast beautiful landscape to explore, then gated off from almost all of it.As an example, very early on you're walking through a gorgeous canyon when a series of wide flat ledges come into view that set off your spidey senses--there must be something up there! A nice view at least, surely?--but you really shouldn't bother trying to reach it. Not only can I guarantee you there is nothing there, but you might spend a minute devising a way up only to hit an invisible wall in midair, or have the wind at the edge of the map blow you back off the cliff, or worse, blow you into a crevice that you could escape from if only the wind would stop blowing, but it won't stop until it has blown you far enough away from the edge of the map, which it can't because of the crevice, so have fun reloading. It's like this absolutely everywhere--every hill, every mysterious stone machine/creature, every sunken building--you can get stuck, or bounce off of things, or slide uncontrollably past your landing zone, or stop to "climb" a ledge the character should have stepped up without stopping, or stop and not climb at all when you reach a ledge that looks the same size as all those other things you climbed automatically, and you lose your flow. And that's the crux of my complaint--there's no flow to Europa.Again and again the game will stop you to pan the camera around when you should be moving, put a levitation recharge point awkwardly low to the ground or out of your path, or put a "boost pad" in your path when you have just arrived in a new area and want to stop and explore. There's no way to keep your flow going when you just want to zip around. Similarly, the buildings that you can enter mostly look identical to the buildings that you can't, and the same goes for landscape features--a lot of the time a promising hill is just a bump on the map with no reason to go there. All of your instincts from years of playing games will be frustrated.So what about the beautiful vistas? In a game this pretty, can't I accept that sometimes a cliffside ledge is just a ledge, and enjoy the view from up there without any other reward? I would love to, believe me I've spent hours enjoying the view in less pretty games than this, but sadly the camera in Europa doesn't cooperate. It won't spin around to let you, the player, actually see the view. The camera has a strangely large "personal bubble" and won't go near any solid object, so you're stuck looking at Zephyr's disturbing little face as he takes in the view that you are denied.All told, this is a game that should be about the fun and beauty of exploring that actively punishes your efforts to explore, and that's just sad.

_childDocuments_.review: If you value gameplay over aesthetics, you best steer away. But if you enjoy relaxed exploratory gameplay set in stunning environments, head to Europa.First, the soft spots.The controls, as others have noted, are a bit dodgy. The jumping control operates more or less exactly backwards from every game since Mario. Normally when you hit a jump button you instantly jump, with the height of the jump determined by how long you then hold the button down.In Europa you don't jump until you  the jump button, so you can 'charge' a longer jump. If you push and hold the jump button again while in midair you will 'glide'. Over time I coped with this mechanic, but it never felt natural, it doesn't flow well, and occasionally when leaping to a floating crate I would instead bunny-hop into the abyss.Combine this odd jump behavior with the competing floating mechanic of the 'Zephyr' (the cylindrical device you wear on your back) and hilarity ensues. The Zephyr lets you fly and float--but only if it is charged. If you intend to 'jump and glide' but instead 'jump and float' with a depleted Zephyr, well, enjoy your plummet to the ground.In any case, the eccentric controls are acceptable because the game doesn't require tight, precise maneuvering. Even my fumbling fingers got the job done. The margins for error are generous, and failure is rarely punished. Europa's heart is closer to 'walking simulator' than '3D action platformer.' Do I wish the controls were better? Yes. Is it a fatal flaw? No, far from it.Likewise, the story is a mixed bag. Early promise that this might be an interesting tale, with faint allusions to Genesis and Milton and Shelley (probably only in my mind), sadly gives way to banality. And as often happens when developers attempt to have a narrator wax profound, the results are sophomoric. For roughly half of the game, the story falters to ensure the player gets 'the message,' forgetting the cardinal rule of storytelling: 'show, don't tell.'I also found the protagonist almost a non-entity. Except for the wilted little grunt he emits every time he jumps, he doesn't speak or emote or reflect. His character development is a huge missed opportunity: there is none.But enough criticism. While the story is lacking, the journey itself is compelling. The environments are grand and glorious. The music is excellent. The in-game cutscenes are fabulous. As a game of exploration and discovery it delivers the goods. I goggled at the sights and sounds, which changed from scene to scene and stayed fresh and interesting from beginning to end. The world is alive with intriguing creatures, both friendly and hostile. The hostile creatures add some needed conflict to the gameplay without overwhelming it; dodging their ranged attacks is simple fun (there are no melee attacks).The visual navigation cues are well done. I found where I needed to go easily enough without getting lost, and I can get lost in the time it takes me to put on my socks. Puzzles are intuitive and add a pleasant change to the pacing. You won't be stumped.As a game world, Europa is well realized and a delight to explore, making its strengths far outweigh its defects.
_childDocuments_.name: Europa

_childDocuments_.review: This is a lovely experience... I just wish I felt satisfied with it.I feel like this is trying to be like Journey, but missed on what made Journey such a great title and is instead bogged down by controls that want to feel fluid, but instead feel clunky at times.Pros: Gorgeous atmospheric scenery, with moments of flying around and through it.Cons: -Invisible walls/ceilings: I wish these were telegraphed better than just wasting your flight energy running into them, getting blown back, and turned around. I found it tedious to the point that I didn't want to explore too much to avoid running into them and stalling me for a few seconds each time. I probably missed a few collectibles partially due to just going to the obvious telegraphed way forward and trying to just avoid running into the boundaries. -Getting your joy of momentum stolen by unavoidable swarms that only exist to do just that. I feel like these things only exist to clip your wings, rather than lend themselves to any particular challenge or "fun", vs the land mines or turrets  This title sets much of itself up to be this wonderful free-flying exploration adventure, and there's so much that just robs you of that experience.-Controls: I think with a little tweaking, things could "move" better. The platforming feels stiff, and when you're not able to fly, you're forced to slowly move through the terrain. Even the flying could be better, but it's still a smoother experience that makes the walking feel horribly bogged down and torturous by comparison.-Story: It's serviceable, but nothing that grabs me or makes me endeared to the characters. I feel like it's more background to the game than anything.Overall it's not an awful or bad game by any measure, and maybe this is best as an 'entry to gaming' title for kids. I wish I could give it a middle rating, but when I found myself near the end, trudging to get through for the sake of completion and not desiring to replay it any time soon (if ever), I think that was the turning point from a thumbs up to a thumbs down for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Europa is a relaxed 3rd-person 3D adventure with beautiful environments, a bittersweet story of humans and their exploitation of the environment, and very easy puzzles.  You play as Zee, who appears to be a young boy exploring the Jupiter moon Europa. Europa has been terraformed by humans into a lush and vibrant world, but the humans are long gone, only overgrown ruins remain. As you explore, you keep finding diary entries from your father, which gradually reveal the story of Europa and its human settlement.I like the story's general message, but it certainly didn't knock my socks off. It remains very superficial and descriptive and is all told through the voice of an old, jaded man. There are only three characters (the father, the son, and an unnamed starship captain), most of the time there's just talk about what "the humans" or "the gardeners" do. The story never provided any hooks to draw me in emotionally, it has very little relevance to the gameplay, and it's also extremely predictable. It does enhance the game, but remains a little stale.The game has 15 chapters. Most of these consist of a linear sequence of areas, separated by doors, and you have to solve a small puzzle or action task to open the door. The puzzles and tasks are usually very easy, but can still be annoying due to slow movement or clunky controls. You usually always know what to do. While there is no map (which can make orientation difficult at times), points of interest are clearly marked by light pillars.The game tries to keep things fresh by gradually adding new puzzle mechanics, but since I never saw a need to actually switch my brain on, they eventually felt like chores rather than an engaging experience. From about halfway through in my playthrough, I started to feel a bit bored and mainly wanted to get it over with - though I did eventually run into interesting environments that renewed my interest. But for the most part, I would have enjoyed the game more if the chapters had been shorter and/or if the puzzles had been more challenging. Also, given that the movement was very clunky already (see below), going through sequences where wind gushes kept throwing me off my path felt extra annoying.I should clarify, though, that I regard very little of the above as a "problem" of the game. The dev is very clear that he was aiming for a "zen-like" experience. The repetitive and easy puzzles are perfectly in line with this goal. It just also creates a playstyle that feels a bit too passive for my personal tastes as a player.While progress through the game world is entirely linear, many areas leave a bit of room for exploration. Veering off the beaten path may get rewarded with a collectible. However, apart from those, there unfortunately isn't much to find. All buildings are empty, there are no additional notes or other lore elements, and there are no resources to collect. On top of that, the world is full of invisible walls and areas that you can never enter because storms keep pushing you back.What discouraged me most from exploring, though, is that the game kept taking the camera controls away from me in order to show me scenes that it found interesting, and then blocked me from moving the cameras to the scenes I actually wanted to explore. As a result, I never truly felt like an explorer who was discovering interesting vistas and sights. Instead, I felt more like a visitor who was taking a guided tour that someone else had prepared for me. A more passive player might enjoy this type of presentation, but I would have liked the game more with an option to turn the guided camera off.A third gameplay element are obstacles such as mines, turrets, or projectile-shooting enemies. They cannot hurt you (you do not even have a health meter), all they do is hurl you a few meters back and stun you for a moment. Since there is never any actual danger and movement is clunky already, this is more annoying than challenging. It can be turned off in the options.The game does offer a few collectibles as an incentive for further exploration.Europa uses low-poly graphics to create beautiful, imaginative, diverse environments. For reasons I find difficult to pinpoint, they did not really "click" with me. In some areas, I would have liked a higher resolution, sharper lines, and/or more detail. But I think that something in the art direction just feels a bit off to me. I played many other games with low-poly graphics and didn't have the same reaction to those. I'm quite sure that this is a "me" problem, though, I doubt that many other players will feel that way,Sound and music are functional and stay mostly in the background. Voice acting is provided by a single actor who reads the diary entries that you find. He has a memorable, gravelly voice and his acting is competent, but a bit more variety wouldn't have hurt.The game provides standard display options (screen mode, resolution, FPS lock, Vsync), a brightness slider, 4 presets each for texture quality, AA, effects, shadows, foliage, and post-processing, and 4 volume sliders to finetune your acoustic experience. Subtitles can be toggled on or off and changed in size. Keys can be fully rebound, and both mouse axes have their own sensitivity slider and can be inverted separately. It's nice to see a game implement those features so competently in a world where many triple-A offerings struggle with standard features such as key rebinding.Unfortunately though, the game provides no accessibility features whatsoever. This is a missed opportunity since the game targets an audience of "passive" players, doesn't usually require quick reactions, and lends itself fairly well to be enjoyed by players who may need more time to grasp a scene or make an input. Perhaps some features like visual audio cues or color blind filters can be added in a patch.The game's biggest problem (imho) are the controls. They are intentionally floaty since the game's movement is a mix of walking, sliding, flying, and gliding. But that created many situations where I missed a platform I intended to land on, or fell off a ledge that I intended to stay on. Together with the fact that I often couldn't move the camera the way I wanted to, this made traversal feel uncomfortable in a game that is mostly about traversal. It's the reason why I won't go for the collectibles after having finished the game - I just never got comfortable with the movement.The game provides a "chapter select" function that helps hunting for details and achievements you may have missed, which is nice. Many games forget that.Personally I'm a bit lukewarm about this game - I did enjoy it enough to finish it, but I felt a bit bored at times. I think it's mostly geared at "passive" players who like a relaxed and relatively guided experience. The more active and challenged you want to be, the less you'll probably enjoy this game. But if you're in the target audience, I think it has the potential to be a great experience, hence it gets my recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really is something special. You play as Zee in a gorgeous terra-formed world on Jupiter’s moon. The landscapes are absolutely breathtaking—lush meadows, sparkling lakes, and the ruins of a once-thriving civilisation all come together in a way that feels both magical and a little melancholic. The movement feels really smooth. Upgrading Zephyr jetpack to fly and glide effortlessly through the air is a total joy. It's like building momentum as you explore, and it really makes you feel in a trance.The story is super touching, too. It’s about a today's current topic of humanity's relationship with nature. I loved piecing together the narrative while solving puzzles and uncovering secrets hidden around the world.The game length is around 3-4 hours, and during this time I was completely immersed in this peaceful journey. If you’re into exploration and heartfelt stories, I can’t recommend Europa enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Neutral / Mildly positive.Europa is a love letter to Journey, nothing more, nothing less. Journey is one of my favorite games, so I'll review Europa with my knowledge about it. I recommend getting and playing Journey before this game, and possibly to stop reading this review and playing Journey first.Imagine Journey but in a lush green world instead of a desert. I truly cannot complain about this idea, especially because Europa's art style is so beautiful and a pleasure to watch throughout the game. The puzzles are very easy, they serve only to give you something to do - not that Journey had anything revolutional here either.But after a while you realize, there are literal carbon copies of Journey and you feel a bit iffy about this seemingly lackluster approach, when there was a lot more potential for Europa.Let me give you a few examples of these similarities:- You can levitate for a set amount of time with an incremental upgrade system- There are relics of giant stone-based serpents ("guardians") laying between giant ruins of a lost civilation, but later you see them flying through the air - this goes as far as cinematics with these floating guardians being exactly the same- The regions cycle through first bright wide open areas, to underground, to snow, to mountaintop, to finale, with the final goal always in sight in the background (mountain / floating island)- both games have literally the same puzzle where you restore a giant bridge by exploring in a large open area and reactivating the 4 broken bridge pieces- automatic sidescrolling section for nostalgic effect- underwater-looking area with kelp and jellyfish- hide behind structures from wind gusts in a snow area.There's more but I'll stop now. Besides that, the story of Europa is alright, nothing that will make your jaw drop. The same goes for the music. The sound is alright, with some weird effects that should return to Bejeweled.Why am I still giving this a positive review? Because you can see that a lot of love went into this game. They tried to build a convincing world and that they did succeed at. Also I feel a lot of polish went in. I enjoyed my time in this world, I want to live in it, and even if after a while I realized that the inspiration from Journey maybe went a bit too far, I still liked to go on.But it was also fine when the game was over.

_childDocuments_.review: Europa is like a mashup of Journey, Gris, Super Mario Sunshine, Pokemon Snap, BOTW and somehow even Halo (chapter 14).It's mechanically simple and utilizes a pretty straightforward gameplay loop.The art direction and music composition are stellar. While it doesn't push the genre forward, it borrows from what came before & provides a extremely fun experience and delivers a beautiful message.Great job Helder Pinto & Co. !

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this after playing the demo. The game looks nice and it's fun to explore the different places. The platforming isn't too hard, and while there is some timed stuff, you don't need to be that fast, just don't stop for too long and time the jumps right. I didn't like the enemies during the first playthrough as I wanted to explore, not dodge bombs. After finishing the game, I started a new game in the Zen mode that got added in the update, and that's more fun as the enemies are passive and you don't need to worry about them. I also like that the collected emeralds carry over to a new game, not just when you use the Chapters option after finishing. If you like Journey, you'll probably like this one too.
_childDocuments_.name: Europa

_childDocuments_.review: Europa is a beautiful game with an intriguing story and a wonderful narrator. All of the achievements are missable, gladly the game only takes around 4 hours to beat. So a second playthrough with a guide to mop up what you missed is very doable.  Around 8 hours or so, counting on 2 playthroughs 5/10 Can be done in 1 but most likely you'll need at least 2 Not yet No Yes, all achievements are missable No No No No No I think that you can play on any difficulty and still unlock all the achievements, but not totally sure NoWhoah, Europa is such a beautiful intriguing game. I fell in love with the artwork in the first few seconds of the trailer. It looks stunning! And the narrator they choose is amazing. He does such a good job of telling the story. His voice felt so fitting for this role. When I started playing I thought the movement felt a bit floaty, but after a few minutes, I got used to it. I'm also so impressed that I always felt like I knew where to go while the game didn't tell you directly. The level design is built in a way that it is where you'll be going without having way markers to tell you where you need to go.  Another great thing is the world-building is amazing! The narrator will tell a lot about the world, but the state of the world also shows you a lot of the story.As an achievement hunter, this game will be a challenge. All the achievements are missable. There are achievements for finding everything, while there are no counters to know how many in each area there are (this would be awesome for new game+, but sadly isn't there), and you can't go back to previous areas. There are also achievements for not getting hit by boom Beetles and turrets and don't trigger any bombs. If you go for this in a separate playthrough of finding all the collectibles, you can easily get Alt+F4 out of the game when you get hit. I'm not 100% sure this works as when I played the game, those achievements were bugged but they are fixed by now. (The developer did an awesome job in how quickly they fixed them!). There are also achievements for finding the emerald behind the waterfall (this one is in an area with many waterfalls) and riding a sky whale.I hope there will be a YouTube guide to show where to find all the collectibles, as the areas don't have clear names, so a written guide would be even more challenging. I'm not looking forward to playing Europa while watching a guide simultaneously, but I think that will be the way to mop up the missing achievements. And that I'm not looking forward to that is not because I dislike the game, it is just my least favorite thing to do. Written guides, or reading/watching something before playing and then doing it myself is more fun but I don't think that will work with Europa.I give Europa 3.5 out of 5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a simple yet cozy game that has very few mechanics and relies heavily on the main characters ability to fly to encourage exploration and puzzle solving.Problem is, the Devs decide to frequently take away the ability to fly in large chunks of the game, forcing you to slowly walk everywhere and lose all interest in exploring anything on foot. Flying is indeed fun, but it uses up fuel that depleats way too quickly and refuel sources are usually too far away from each other.The puzzles are also too simple to the point where they are more of an inconvenience than fun.I was able to beat this game in 3 hours and even that felt too long. That's how shallow it's mechanics are. Visually it's fantastic, but looks and vibes alone don't make an enjoyable game.

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful story game. I felt like I just played through a Ghibli movie. The animation style is beautiful in an anime inspired way. The game took me just over 2 hours to get through. I'm not a completionist, but I did get all of the story collectibles and I did do some extra exploration. The game is fun to fly around. The puzzles are easy. Exploration is limited. There are height and distance boundaries that the game pushes you back into the main path if you go too far out. The game isn't open world. Some maps are large, some are pretty small. The creature and design elements are somewhat limited, but it's acceptable for the limited length of the game.If I compare this to the price of a movie, it's worth the experience. Though I probably would have waited until it was a little cheaper just because I don't know that I'll ever play it again and there are many for games out there with a better time investment cost value.

_childDocuments_.review: I only played for 30 minutes, that's not long at all, but for a short game like this, I usually make up my mind pretty quickly if this is a game I want to continue. In 30 minutes all I've done is just walked and glide around (in a mostly straight path, because the game drags you back to the main path if you stray too far). None of those feel good, because of the way it feels to control the character. It felt way too floaty, like the charater has no weight at all, ecspecially when gliding. I liked the way gliding felt in breath of the wild, in this game it just felt too fluid, like the character weighs nothing at all. I get that this is supposed to take place in another planet than Earth, maybe the gravity is supposed to be different, but still, it felt too floaty for my liking. Jumping feels weird, sometimes when I pressed the jump button it decides to do a charge jump. Walking feels weird, partly because the camera just taking control of itself. The game "pulls" the camera in a direction because it wants me to look that way, I hate that and I want to control the camera the way I want too. Also, when walking around, the character just glides across the ground even with the slightest (downwards) elevation change. It even glides across the floor of stone. That doesn't feel realistic at all, and it got annoying very fast. What also was annoying was the constant "huhhh" sound the character makes by doing the slightest bit of jump/climbing up a small rock. It was the same sound every time, no change in the voice or the sound he makes. I couldn't stand it.On the gameplay side of things it felt a bit stale. Not a single puzzle, not a single platforming piece in those 30 minutes I played. It felt like a bad walking sim. And I  don't count doing a little jumping from stone to stone as platforming. That's as barebones as it gets. I came across one collectable, and some upgrade to my gliding ability. None of those felt rewarding at all, ecspecially the gliding part because it just don't feel nice to glide at all. It doesn't even make a satisfying sound when you collect it, you just walk past it and some particles go to your character. Music was somewhat lovely though, and I really liked the narrators voice acting. The artstyle didn't click with me. It felt "flat", like it lacked depth. It also felt a bit generic to me. I feel like I've seen this kind of artstyle in many games, but it lacks the bit that makes it unique. It's pretty, yeah, but it has no depth. It's like when you meet a pretty person, but he/she is so boring and generic that it doesn't really matter how pretty they are.Sadly, this is a return for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I think overall its a glorified walking sim with not much to offer in 3D platforming. I'll be fair and start with the positives. The Music and Graphics are fantastic. I do find it pretty interesting you are on one of Jupiter's moons if it was terraformed. The atmosphere is great and there was a lot of cool spectacle moments. The movement is decent. Being able to fly around with a reasonable fuel system feels pretty decent and there isnt much limitation with where you can go with it. Now for the bad. The game lacks content for a $20 experience. The game is pretty short and there is only 1 collectible that really matter gameplay wise which is the upgrades for Zeyphr. Theres really nothing to do after one playthrough unless if you want to achievement hunt. The story feels incohesive. I'll do you a solid and not get into the generic environmentalism message this game is trying to push because we all know what it is. Human bad. Creatures on planet good. Except they are more like robots rather than creatures. The old man goes on how the Captain is a meanie weanie for taking down a threat that almost cost them their lives. But at the same time, a robot is what killed Zee in the first place. So I can't really feel sympathetic for creatures that are not only robotic, but are dangerous to humans and even Zee himself when he is a cyborg. The old man said the hell with humans and sympathized with creature that killed his kid. And he had to live with it. Also the giant dragon at the end was sh*tting out mines that are in Zees way when he wants to get in the island. This is despite the fact having connection with said dragon. It just doesnt make any sense. Another thing I have an issue of is the lack of 3D platforming. There is barely any in this game and that was extremely disappointing to me, especially with how decent the movement is in this game. Its really just a glorifed walking sim with sprinkles of 3D platforming, some 3D platforming mechanics, and a hint of exploration. The exploration is piss-poor as many buildings are closed off.I feel like this is one of many games that would work way better as a movie than a video game. The saddest part about this, is that this might be game of the year for me. Thats how bad this year was. I wish there was a "mixed" review for steam instead of yes or no recommendations. I think this game is a mixed bag, but I cant not recommend it for the price and lack of content.

This game is unique and deserves recognition for what it offers both to players and the game development market. 10/10, well done HP!

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game, much shorter than I expected but the art style was absolutely gorgeous and the movement mechanics were a lot of fun and really simple to pick up. The puzzles were quite easy for me to complete however it's a good thing if you like games that aren't too confusing with how to progress. The journal/art book was a really cute addition, seeing the raw artwork of all the animals/machines was a lovely touch. I love the art style inspiration that has been taken from Studio Ghibli. It was mesmerizing. The music and atmospheric sounds were a 10/10 for me. I also loved the environmental sounds of walking/gliding through water, snow and grass. _childDocuments_.review: Europa is a beautiful game that is often at odds with itself.It wants you to enter a flow state of flying and gliding through the gorgeous terrain and lose yourself in the serene music. But it actively prevents you from doing this at every turn with turrets, bombs and finicky puzzles.The game has several types of hidden collectables, but I honestly wish it didn't. Interrupting your flow state to search every nook and cranny just isn't fun. Not to mention the maps have firm boundaries that aren't marked - you'll randomly run into them.I'm not a fan of the very patronizing way the story is written and delivered. "Generic British" was a strange choice for the voice acting. But the story did eventually hook me and take an interesting turn. Although I was left confused by the ending, which felt weirdly ambiguous - unsure if that was on purpose.So, yeah. There's a lot gone wrong here, despite the gorgeous visuals and music. It's a delight when it gets out of its own way, and it doens't overstay its welcome. Maybe wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Europa is an emotionally intense game that explores themes of loss, isolation, and the fragility of human connection in a beautifully haunting narrative. Set against a backdrop of hauntingly atmospheric visuals and a melancholic soundtrack, the story follows a protagonist grappling with profound grief and existential despair. While the game-play is immersive and thought-provoking, the heavy emotional content can be overwhelmingly sad at times, with moments that could be triggering for some players. Given the depth of the emotional themes, a trigger warning might be necessary, especially for those sensitive to topics like loss, depression, and trauma. The game's raw portrayal of these difficult emotions leaves a lasting impact, but it may not be for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was beautiful and relaxing. I am a huge fan of this kind of piano style, so I immediately fell in love with it upon first hearing it. I agree with other reviews that said this felt like a studio ghibli film but a video game. Originally I thought it was going to be open world but instead learned it was split into levels. I've really missed this style of game design where instead of throwing a ridiculous amount of things to do in an open world, instead you get levels that are each uniquely designed.I've seen some varying reviews on the gameplay so I wanted briefly say my two cents on it. I think people are missing the point of this game. The focus is on the music, visuals, and ultimately a relaxing atmosphere. There are some problems here and there (boom beetle pre-firing at you before you get through door in next area), but overall I wasn't judging the game based on how tight the controls were, or how complex the platforming bits needed to be. What I was looking for was a game that removed all stress and really allowed me to chill out. This game did just that.I do recommend that if you use a controller for this game like I did (xbox for me), map the jump/glide button to the left trigger or one of the bumpers instead of using the "a" button so you can reliably use the camera while flying around.

_childDocuments_.review: Europa follows the footsteps of games like Journey while adding a flavour of its own by focusing on the movement more technically and the art style being often compared to Studio Ghibli works. You get a unique experience that will most likely be unforgettable, but you need to come with the right set of expectations and concessions. You get around 14-16 chapters that take anywhere from 3 to 6 hours total depending on your play style, 4-5 hours will be the most common time. The gameplay is mostly comprised of going from point A to B, exploration, minor puzzles for a change of pace, collectibles and story enjoyed through notes in audio form since all the notes are fully voice acted. The puzzles are mostly turn switches on in particular ways or find them all in order to advance, so it’s fairly basic stuff. The actual thinking comes from how to get from point A to B in a graceful manner with the different movement options and limited energy that allows you to fly temporarily. Moving optimally is something that you need to master because Zee can climb automatically on certain objects while you still have 2 forms of jumping, glide and actual flying. It might feel weird at first but it can turn into second nature when you know which best option to use at a given time. The game’s movement IS one of the main reasons the game is fun and it’s a great feeling when you can fly around. This is also precisely the part where you have to set your expectations correctly. If you’ve tried the demo or looked at a gameplay video, you might have expected to fly around more freely and you might have expected a vast world to explore with no limitations, which is not what the game provides despite how things might look. Your flying powers will be taken away from you on occasions, limiting your freedom. And even though you can explore the levels, the game has many invisible walls or winds that gently push you in the only correct path you’re supposed to take.This disappointed me at first but I managed to look past that and I managed to enjoy what the game DOES provide. The graphics look dreamy and they’re wonderfully colourful. This game puts me in a positively weird state of relaxation that makes me forget about the world’s worries for a moment. The audio side is sublime, the music is really good. It has a nice balance between making its presence known while not being excessively overbearing. And the voice actor of an old man comes with lots of emotions and passion. The gameplay can be easily picked up and enjoyed by many, especially with the newly added zen mode that removes all threat. You can tell the game is translated professionally in English or they at least did a good job of giving that impression. You won’t see any typos or sentences looking off. I’ve seen a couple of translators in the credits, so I’m expecting this to hold true with the other languages that are supported. The collectibles are fun to collect, they’re in some cases meaningful and creative. I especially enjoyed finding all the animals/gardeners to fill up Zee’s sketchbook. The achievements are fun and some offer enough challenge to make you sweat a bit. Some of the achievements can be a problem with how strict they are though. Three require you to not get hit by threats the entire time. And the Zephyr upgrades MUST BE gotten the first time. Chapter select won’t help you, so you’ll have to start new game if you fail, same with the achievements where you’re not allowed to get hit. The game also misses basic quality of life options for the collectibles. The game doesn’t tell you how many collectibles there are in each level like with Gris and Rime. You’re left in the dark even with chapter select. This is just unpleasant if you’re releasing a game with such an emphasis on collectibles (crystals, upgrades, sketches and journal pages). An update did allow one of the final chapters to show you the crystals you’re missing in a physical form. This is an improvement and better than nothing but it’s still not where it should be.I had a great time playing Europa, it was unforgettable to me. I enjoyed completing the game three times, every run appreciating the game more. I would say the price is worth it based on what I experienced but this is a bit more subjective than usual if you expected something more than what the game offers.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is beautiful. The music fits the landscape and the colours do not irritate eyes that are more sensitive to bright sensitivities. _childDocuments_.review: It really is just beautiful. That is the best way to describe this game in a single word that encapsulates the entire experience.The visuals are stunning. From the way the colour palette works together to the subtlety of the shaders developed for each material combine the gentle lighting give it the overall aesthetic of playing a cartoon. This aesthetic then ties in with the theme of the story as you explore the world with childlike wonder.The game is very much an artistic and emotive experience influenced by games like Journey but does its own thing and offers up some gentle collection and puzzling sections with very light platforming. Nothing is too challenging and yet its enough to provide a little tickle to your grey matter while you let your mind get absorbed in this gorgeously realised world and its rather touching story.The price point is absolutely spot on for what is on offer here.My only criticism isn't really a criticism - its just a desire for more because i love the world and aesthetic created. I wish there was a reason to spend more time in this world once you have finished. While you can go back and collect things you missed ultimately its a single experience that feels complete once finished.I'd love to see a larger game created in this aesthetic and art style.

_childDocuments_.review: Europa offers gameplay and beautiful visuals for fans of games like Journey, ABZU, Sky, AER, or numerous other art-forward experiences (with a pinch of 3D platforming collectathon, reminiscent of Mario or Spyro). If you enjoyed those games or others like them, you will probably find something to like in Europa. However, its over-reliance on nostalgic familiarity with these obvious influences is both its strongest asset and largest fault. Players of Journey and ABZU in particular may recognize many direct homages, and combined with the overall charming aesthetic of Europa, with its bright color palette and striking environments, these moments certainly deliver positive vibes. Unfortunately, there are far too many familiar set-pieces and ideas throughout, which by the end can leave you feeling like you just finished a subpar clone of previous games, rather than a uniquely new take on the sub-genre.While such derivative presentation could be a major turn-off to some, I still enjoyed my time overall with Europa. It's not too long and has some genuinely fun segments to play through and explore once you get a firmer grip on the somewhat unintuitive controls (especially the jump button). It's not too challenging for players looking for an easy, casual experience either.As briefly mentioned at the beginning of the review, there are collectibles to gather along the way, so there is a bit of replayability in finding all of the hidden secrets of each area. You can access the chapter select after finishing the game and collectibles are persistent, so completionists have an easy path to minimize their time spent.The story is simple, borrowing some heavy influences both visually and thematically from the Studio Ghibli film Castle in the Sky. The audiovisual presentation tells a clear enough narrative that the numerous notes found throughout the game with explicitly spoken explanations feel, more often than not, unnecessary. This isn't too pervasive though, as you have the option of skipping these or exiting the book after playing each page to listen while continuing to make progress.Pros:+ Beautiful environments and art direction+ Great soundtrack+ Doesn't overstay its welcomeCons:- Somewhat confusing controls- Derivative gameplay and story elementsScore:6/10 - Only recommended to superfans of Journey-likes and simple 3D platformers.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, beautiful, relaxing game. It's all about collecting items in a world reminiscent of something our of a Studio Ghibli film.You play a sort-of Pinocchio-styled little android, "Zee", that is all that remains of a failed colonization attempt of Jupiter's moon, Europa. It's up to you to uncover the story of what happened via journal entries (narrated by the fatherly inventor, "Adam"). It's a short game (clocking in at just over 4 hours) and it doesn't contain any combat. It's strictly a platformer with some simple puzzles tossed in.  It's not very challenging but that isn't much of an issue as this game is more of a "cozy" experience than any sort of game that will frustrate younger players.I enjoyed it and I look forward to see what else this studio releases in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: A Beautiful, Thought-Provoking JourneyEuropa is a simple yet deeply engaging game. At its core, the mechanics are straightforward: jump, fly, and collect. But beneath that simplicity lies a touching narrative that raises profound questions—what defines a person? How might humans and machines coexist? And how should we care for our planet in the future?The art style is absolutely stunning, reminiscent of a watercolor palette, creating a visually soothing and immersive experience. While the game could benefit from some technical polish, it’s hard to overlook the heart and creativity poured into it.For a game that takes about 3 hours to complete, Europa offers a wonderful, reflective journey. It’s a perfect choice for those looking for a meaningful experience, especially when picked up on sale. Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys beautiful visuals, thought-provoking stories, and relaxed exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: Europa.   When I first started the game it gave me similar feelings as playing The Legend of Zelda Breath of the Wild. In the art, sounds, music, even the way your character doesn't remember who they are. I wouldn't say it's a puzzle game, Yes there are puzzles. They are not hard and don't offer much of a challenge if you're looking for that.   However, something about the game is magical. Maybe the ancient creatures, the beautiful story line, the environment. Whatever it may be, this game has me hooked on finding out who the character is. At the same time it doesn't feel like just a story game. There is so much adventure and exploration. If you have a couple hours to spend, this game is worth it. The story telling is beautiful, the art is magical, the voice acting is top notch. I highly recommend this simply unique story game.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the setting of Europa and the atmosphere is on point. The puzzles are not difficult to figure out, and I did not mind that the story is told through journal pages. I also like that the pages were narrated. However, there are a few things I did not like. The first is the forced camera perspective when you get to certain areas and the camera automatically adjusts to a specific angle. Also, every time you find all the items for a puzzle, the camera focuses on where you need to go or to the door opening. Some of the creatures are annoying, especially the ones that zap you out of the sky and I do not know how many times I have run into those round exploding ones. Lastly, when solving the puzzles, you often have to jump to certain areas and I found that Zee would glide off the edge and I would have to start over, which was frustrating. Besides that, I did enjoy the game, and there is replayability with finding all the emeralds and completing the Steam achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid concept for a first game and really impressive what was accomplished. The story is cosy and the style is super pleasing, although the ending felt super abrupt! The controls need to be tighter and the sound effects are very stock, especially with the energy source sounding like a child's fairy wand toy. Zee feels too heavy for being able to glide basically everywhere(which we should have had more opportunities to glide and fly, as well as have jumping be more responsive), if he was given dash or boost to get your momentum up it would have made movement a little more fun. The jumping boxes, having the camera stolen from you for doors, and most enemies were frustrating rather than challenging. The cinematic parts where you were in the wind tunnels felt flat since I had little control on where you could actually go. Otherwise its a cute experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Full gameplay(about 3 hours) with commentary: Europa is a touching story told with the visualization style of Studio Ghibli.  It's a pretty chill platformer/exploration game with only a handful of puzzles for you to solve.  None of them are particularly difficult, and the game does an excellent job of giving you a linear adventure that at times feels more open than it really is.The graphics are easily the part of the game that stand out more than anything, but the gameplay is just as solid.  You'll explore some really beautiful locations, upgrade your jetpack thing, and really just do a lot of very cool stuff.  The levels are cut into "Chapters," and as you play you'll start to unlock new challenges and story bits that give you more information as to what went on here at Europa.In the end it's a charming adventure that really captures your attention.  Once you start it is difficult to put down.

_childDocuments_.review: Europa is my game of the year 2024:Europa is a must play for anyone who admire well written narrative/adventure games. _childDocuments_.review: As a fan of many cozy games and Studio Ghilbi films especially, this game is a delight. It's a beautiful game that caused me to pause at moments to breath it in. _childDocuments_.review: This is a barely recommend for me. The only reason it's a recommend is because I loved the movement and art style of the game. Indies are also always worth playing. That being said, this was overall pretty disappointing. The game introduces "flying" mechanic pretty early on and it's by far it's most fun and engaging thing you can do. I expected them to introduce new abilities and mechanics over time, such as higher jumps, fly boosts, timed challenges, sky puzzles, etc. This never happens. You go around a small level, interact with 3 or 4 things, and then it transitions you into another small level. This never changes. Another thing they like to do is not let you fly, (remember, this is the most fun thing you can do). Towards the middle, they introduce "purple crystals" which deplete your flying meter instantly. This starts showing up a lot. It doesn't do anything interesting with it either, it's basic platforming, such as the platforms randomly disappear or disappear with your jump input. Was this made for kids? If so, my bad.There are also some weird design decisions that are sprinkled throughout this game. What is the point of the random walking towards the light sequences where your "dad" repeats what he says in the diary entries? What is the point of the mines, turrets, and mortar creatures if they don't kill you / make you restart the level? What is the point of the extremely extended flying sequence to the island? Couldn't you have just allowed us to fly there ourselves by providing the refill collectibles in the air? I would love to see a sequel or DLC to this game that expands upon all the mechanics introduced here. I finished it in about 2.5 hours. I have no problem with that. With nothing new being introduced, this game was overstaying its welcome and a longer campaign would've only frustrated me. TL:DR Game is a barely recommend. Play the demo and decide if you can tolerate the exact same things for 2.5-3 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Europa

_childDocuments_.review: Europa is visually beautiful, however I found this to be the only positive feature of the game.Control is loose and unpredictable, and the character's hover-backpack is over-constrained. The 'levitate' function is bound to the same control as the 'glide' function, making it hard to predict which one you'll get.The open-world looking graphics belie the fact that this game runs on a VERY narrow rail, and the mechanic for keeping the player on that rail (sudden wind and clouds that blow you back on the beaten track) comes out of nowhere to spank you for being curious.The story has the makings of engagement, but the character won't stop grunting so it's hard to care about him.Finally, the game has a habit of freezing camera control at unpredictable points, which totally destroys immersion. I deleted it.

_childDocuments_.review: I will give this a positive review, but I would prefer it to be a neutral one if I could.Europa is, from an artistic standpoint, a beautiful game with clear Ghibli inspiration and a peaceful vibe that is helped by the soundtrack. There is, however, a clash in style when it comes to the playable character, Zee, who in my opinion looks sort of out of place, perhaps due to the puzzling lack of shading on his model.The real problem with Europa is, unfortunately, the gameplay, and when you advertise your product as being aimed to a more passive audience this becomes a problem.The movement does not feel good, it is slow (you can't even run) and extremely buttery to the point of becoming unwieldy, especially in one of the sections where the ground itself is slippery, resulting in a very,  unpleasant experience.The movement mechanics are thankfully better and since this is a short game they don't need a ton of variety, same with the platforming, which is fairly run of the mill, but again that's ok for the scope of this project.I think 20 bucks is a bit too costly for this game, I would recommend getting it on sale for like half that price.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: First I want to preface my reviewing by saying that I think many people will love and adore this game, and if they don't suffer from motion sickness they likely will have a great time playing it as well. However I can't personally recommend the game with the current state of the camera. I was able to play around three hours during a stream (got to the start of chapter six, playing leisurely) and won't be able to return to the game unless more camera settings are added to the options to mitigate motion sickness. Specifically how the camera movement has a bit of ease-in and ease-out after being moved manually, and how many parts of the game force camera control away from the player to attempt to show them the next path (and often don't give control back to the player for quite a long time). If we could toggle those off it would greatly improve my experience of the game. I would be thrilled if the developer was interested in adding these adjustments as options in a future update and would gladly return to finish the game on stream and change my review.

_childDocuments_.review: A nice modern platformer game?Now, I know this game has been made mostly by a one man, Helder Pinto. However, it has been in development since 2017 and has been in early access for a while.I read that this game had some new, fresh ideas. Now, I'm a big fan of 3D platformer games and decided to give this modern one a chance, especially considering the generous pricing and the 10% sale. Notable platformers I love:- Crash Bandicoot Trilogy- Jak and Daxter- Ratchet & ClankCompared to these, Europa is not a platformer at all. It feels more like a tame, sanitised walking simulator with very little narrative or challenge. And while those games have been developed by AAA studios back in the day, I have seen Crash Bandicoot fan games that had more narrative, a better atmosphere, and gameplay depth.My issues with the game:- Boring and sleepy piano/synth music, the same music I listen to fall asleep.- Predictable level design and fairytale-style sound effects.- Uninspired gameplay loops: Running around collecting glowing insects to advance instead of any meaningful gameplay, or pressing buttons to shut down laser-emitting robots.- Platforming is far too easy. It's easy to levitate and glide all over the place.- Enemies are too easy to beat. There is no reward in finishing a level.- Story is mostly told by reading text and listening to audio logs. While the theme of a terraformation to rectify humanity's mistakes is very interesting, the delivery is lackluster due to the remaining issues with the game.- Falling down from a great height causes an unskippable stumbling animation, which can be very annoying.Sadly, I cannot continue playing. I had to give up early on.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game is a good experience if you like games like Abzu and Journey, with great visuals and music. However after the first hour, some mechanics begin to frustrate.The developer presents a video at the end of the game about their intent to induce a state of flow and provide a meditative zen-like experience. The game is really at its best when you are in that state of flow, however many things hamper this flow, these being:-Turrets-Mines-Disruptive fields-A recovery animation about 3 seconds long after falling-Jumping puzzles which require walking back to the start upon failure (the ones which assist you are slightly better)-Lack of blue orbs to provide boost in some areas, resulting in excessive walking (other areas have this in abundance)Highly recommend playing with the update where the disruptive effects are turned off, and you will have a more relaxing time and be more in that state of flow.

_childDocuments_.review: This is simply an absolute masterpiece of a game, it's a short one, but Impactful. The music is simply amazing, the art makes me feel like I'm walking through a Studio Ghibli dream right out of Miyazaki's mind, and the story is sweet, bitter, and hopeful - which in short is what you'd need from a story to connect with it.The flow and pacing of the game is natural yet, swift enough to keep you ever moving on, the puzzles add a nice little challenge yet nothing so bad as to have you stumped for hours, and you can speed through the game (if that's your thing) or take in the breathtaking scenery, vista's and flora and fauna at your own pace.It remains me of a mixture of Ni No Kuni, at a fraction of the total playtime; mixed with the swiftness of Journey (2012) or Flower (2009.) The developers certainly placed their hearts into the design, the pacing, and the feel of the game, to make it more than a game, - to make it an experience in of itself. It has a very reasonable price tag too, for it's length, and - for what you, and certainly what I got out of the game enjoyment wise x time x feels it is more than worth it's pricing.The charm of it's replay-ability is in it's styling, it's collectables and it's modest achievement list. All in all, from my experience, I would rate it a full 10/10 and, for the brief reviews I leave on games here and there, given the amount of games I own vs the reviews I've left, I rarely if ever will rate something this highly; due to fare counters against the game where needed, but 10/10 would and WILL play again.

_childDocuments_.review: Dev needs to play some games with real puzzles and better platforming for inspiration. Supraland, Crash DLC and Six Inches Under and even a weird little game named Omno come to mind. I actually downloaded Europa after completing Omno hoping for a similar experience. Like Europa, it has a strong "peaceful" and non-violent aesthetic but at least the puzzles and platforming were challenging. Europa, on the other hand, focuses way too much on that peaceful aesthetic, to the great detriment of actual gameplay. The "puzzles" (find wisps, move balls, rotate blocks, etc) are like toddler-level easy. Platforming skills aren't really even needed, another defect that makes one lose interest quickly. Moving from area to area is no real challenge. Even with Zen Mode OFF Zee has no health meter and cannot die. So when you get blown up by gardeners or mines, or shot with lasers the only thing you "lose" is a couple seconds while Zee recovers back to normal speed. No challenge = no risk = no fun. I completed the game and found myself thinking, "ok, just finish it" after only around half-way through. There are no player level-ups aside from zephyr capacity which I don't even think is necessary to get through the game. There are no coins or money to find and use for upgrades, no hidden chests or other things to find and no enemies to fight. The most "engagement" you have with enemies is to defensively disable them. Really? I can't even shoot back when things are shooting at me? Booooring. For a game with a backstory about war and death, Europa is much too pacifist. The lack of combat and any real challenge in completing areas just makes the game boring. Here's another "too easy" overdose: There are far too many "efields" for recharging the zephyr. They also instantly regenerate which means they are limitless and there's no risk that a player might run out of energy and be unable to reach some objective in an area. Again, when things are too easy, it makes a game un-enjoyable.  Also, I experienced an infuriating technical issue: The game IGNORES "inverted Y" settings during the "flying" sections when you have to avoid mines and floating rocks. For anyone familiar with aviation, "inverted Y" is the NORMAL Y-axis setting (push forward = DOWN, pull back = UP, try moving your head around and understand how it works!) but the game ignores inverted Y-axis setting and makes those sections frustrating for those of us using it. Not that it matters really... since you can't actually die, you don't even have to touch the controls during those sections to be carried through them on autopilot. Again, no challenge = too easy = boring. Nice looking game. Controls and zephyr flying mechanics are fun and I enjoyed following the backstory narrated by Adam, but that's where the fun ends... Dev needs to go back to the drawing board on gameplay development and make this game an actual challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: Europa is a simple cinematic flying/walking simulator story game with some simple puzzles strewn throughout it. With a world heavily inspired by Studio Ghibli's castle in the sky it delivers a nostalgic experience and leaves me with a yearning for a more complete game set in such a world. The gameplay is spent exploring each location while looking for pages that tell the story, collectables to give more achievements, and upgrades to allow more flying. Each location has some beautiful vistas to see, delivers some unique creatures to sketch, and often leaves you wanting a bit more of it. There are some simple puzzles which usually involves finding some hidden buttons to press, rotating cubes around, or sometimes evading enemies. The controls are fairly good, the biggest complaint I have with them is sometimes the camera locks to show you how beautiful a place is and then it can get a bit weird to control anything. My biggest issue with the game design is how often it forces you to walk instead of fly. The flying is definitely one of the most compelling and fun parts of the game, but for some reason we are forced constantly to do very simple jumping puzzles that usually just takes me out of the world. Some parts definitely feel a bit like filler puzzles and such to force the game-time to be a bit longer.The game is still a nice and short experience, I am not sure if I feel it was worth the full price, but on a discount this game is worth picking up if you like story driven walking simulator games.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had my eye on Europa since the day it was revealed and I'm pleased to say that the game met my expectations.It's clear to see that they were going for a relaxing, cozy type of experience. The main character of this game is just as much the world as it is Zee. As you explore and find journal entries left by his father you see the budding of a utopia, and then the seeds of its demise. I found myself as eager to find the next journal entry as I was to explore the world.Speaking of exploration, there is some, here, but it is not as vast and open as the landscape my lead you to believe, but I would hope no one was expecting such. This is an india game by a small studio and in my opinion, they delivered on the experience they set out to provide. The lands are lush and vibrant, animals run and scamper about as well as the remnants of the previous age that humans contributed to destroying. The game leaves you with a moral question of what decision you might make, given all that transpired. I thought this was well done.Action: This is a cozy game about learning of the past and discovering the world around you. It is a tight experience with a small amount of exploration that I found to be fun and a worthy addition to my library. Will definitely revisit this again one day. There is no combat, but there are threats posed by the roving machines or stationary sentry guns. Taking damage merely leaves you dazed and seeing stars, so there is no death or real threat. This isn't meant to be that type of experience, and you can even turn the danger off if you just want to kick back and enjoy exploring without having to take cover at times and avoid the dangerous machines.On the technical side, the jumping mechanics are a tad floaty and feel imprecise, but it is a minor thing that you get used to. The hovering and gliding are fun and make traversal easier and quicker at times. I encountered one minor glitch toward the end of the game when I came out of a wind tunnel to an elevated structure and Zee wouldn't move forward. After a moment or two it worked itself out and I continued on. I give a happy thumbs up for Europa. It was a quick 3.5-4 hour experience that I hope you'll enjoy as much as I did.Thank you for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Europa! The movement was satisfying and fun, and the environments that you glide around in are absolutely gorgeous. I loved seeing the game's different influences peek through in different sections, all while maintaining its own distinct identity. Without spoilers, the story handles its subject matter well and with the appropriate weight, much of which is very close to my heart and it ultimately left me with a lot to think about. I typically prefer to play games with a controller (and that is an option here) but I decided to use mouse+keyboard and found it intuitive and easy to pick up! The main downside for some might be the game's length, as it is on the shorter side, but personally I enjoyed this about it. I really love when I'm able to play through the entire experience in one afternoon, and then come back to it later for any missed collectables or just to revisit some favorite moments (or the whole thing!) I am very glad that I got to spend time with this game, and I am happy to see it released! Genuinely beautiful, in both content and visuals!

_childDocuments_.review: Europa is a gorgeous studio Ghibli art-style adventure set well into the future after humans have colonized Jupiter's moon Europa. But a war between man and machine has changed the course of humanity's future. You play as Zee, a young child who might be humanity's last hope. I very much enjoyed the adventure, it took me about 3 hours to complete since I took time to poke around. I thank the team for the Steam review key! Here are my top takeaways:1. Relaxing vibe with no fall damage. And gliding from place to place feels so freeing!!!! Stamina can run out easily but there are lot of crystals to replenish yourself. 2. The story is told through journal writings. Zee has been left behind and his father is guiding him along the way through the writings. The journals are pretty easy to find, I didn’t have to go out of my way too much to find them so you’re sure to catch on to the story.3. The little creatures are really adorable and it's nice to have other leaving beings along there with Zee as he travels through this empty world. Although some get a bit aggressive near the end but if you show them a little love, they’ll show you some love right back.4. Puzzles are pretty simple, perhaps a bit too simple... I know cozy and chill is the vibe but it doesn’t really ramp up much in difficulty. This does, however, make it a good game for younger gamers and non-gamers. Something that's not too overwhelming but also really fun. 5. For a game that appears so open, not a whole lot to explore, which was a bit disappointing, but climbing to the top of ruins and cliffsides gives you a lot of time to take in the beautiful views!
_childDocuments_.name: Europa

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully stunning, stunningly beautiful.  Either way this game looks amazing!  I'd been following Helder on twitter for a while, eagerly waiting for Europa's release.  Purchased on release day, I was not let down!  Initially taken in by the "Zelda" look, I held off trying the demo as I prefer not to spoil anything form the full release.  While the game is relatively short, I couldn't stop playing and completed it on 2nd day of play.  "We're here for a good time, not a long time" comes to mind.While the initial reaction on seeing Europa is surly "looks amazing", there is a lot more to this game.  Game mechanics and controls are probably different than what you'd expect but are quickly learnt and have some refreshing ideas behind them.  Puzzles are relatively easy but fun and I think that fits in with the over all style of the game.  Chilled music, beautiful world and a chilled gaming experience.Then there is the story, narrated by Zee's father Adam through a series of diary pages which you collect in each section of the world.  It's been a long time since a game has provoked any emotion like this in me and during this short but excellent adventure, I really did get to feel for Zee and Adam.Helder has done a fantastic job here and you can really see the passion the team have put into Europa.  Titles like this just show that indie games can give you just as good (if not better) experience than any AAA game.
