_childDocuments_.review: I've got all the achievements as of now(12th July 2023) and I think I can write my review now.First of all - great game. Fun to create builds, fun to run around, fun to dodge stuff, just fun altogether.That said game needs some QoL's and rebalancing. - straight up sucks. Roll build is terrible and dps build is hindered by golem being late to the party all the time, even when he's not he doesn't do what he is supposedly capable of. I had 36 Attacks per second 100% crit 500% crit damage 174 base golem which is supposedly 32k dps (on single target, not even counting his cone) do 3 attacks and stand around in a boss. The roll really hinders dps build by resetting his position and taking him out of combat.Remove roll entirely, I don't even feel like it fits the ability. If not, make the DPS evolution remove roll entirely and rework AI/make it faster/make it teleport to the target.Really lackluster, even with both evos it does decently but it's overshadowed by other abilities and doesn't really do anything better than the others, maybe clearing offscreen, but the Ring Blades do it better.Make it physical? At least some synergy with the splash ring.Also pretty lackluster, it does fine but lacks in other departments. I tried full orb extravaganza build(14 orbs with a lot of movespeed) and it didn't really do anything. I do understand that I severely cut on its damage but what's the point of increasing orbs then.Buff roughness and base movespeed? Maybe add movespeed scale with a fraction(like .2) of attack speed? I also don't really feel like they need the crit build path in general.I feel like this is the only truly balanced ability which is not too op but is just good and has a great diversity in build paths all of which work nicely.Jack of all trades master of none. Speccing into anything will probably do worse than any other ability. Lightning strike is just plain better option. Base damage is laughably low, only decent build is stacking electrify with it I guess, but even at that it's not really reliable.Remove the damage branch or rework it and pivot into something else, maybe like thunder crown. In general also a bad thing to have crit build path on.Decent abilities, can work in a lot of situations, but really hindered by being unreliable. Dragon's breath needs some other evolution instead of the push one and its constant evolution really suffers from the burn limit.Can benefit from buffs in anything really, AS/Area/Base damage.The best abilities in my opinion. While Phantom needles and Ring blades are S-tier, Transfixion is SSS-tier. Does it all and does it great. Stacking fragile for single target DPS, screen clearing, great AS for stragglers or killing banshees, great range, great area, scales with anything you throw at it.I feel like they are really neatly balanced and fun, maybe except the Warlock, for me personally he really lacks single target damage. Also summon rings are kind of worthless, doing full summon build isn't that fun and your main weapon will oudamage all your summons combined by like 3x. Summoned units suffer same fate as golem as in coming too late, that's why main weapon is that good for clears. I feel like characters that can't crit can get some alternative scaling from crit and crit damage i.e. 5% crit = 0.05 Attacks and 20% crit damage = 10% cone/area or whatever.There is some decent variety and room for creating builds but some of them are just straight BIS. Like in most situations you can't really go wrong with AS head, projectile gloves and XP necklace. The real fun build-changing things drop too late for you to care as you are way too overpowered by that point, like the standing still armor/def increase armor and the AS/MS ring. The unlock point same as the 66% ability gloves would benefit them. Some items like the 1%hp boots, and the 100x damage necklace are just plain bad. Honestly a lot of boots are just plain bad. The elemental rings are also kind of useless as I only found myself using them when I wanted to increase burn/elec on characters already using fire/electricity already. For physical users the splash ring is too good to pass and cleric/warlock do fine regardless.The 100k recovery quest is really tedious, I suggest it be cut to a lower number, as for others they pose a nice amount of challenge.Fun in general but really tedious to recover through well. I suggest well have two slots, one for potions only and second for items or potions. I am done with the game and still need like 6 potions and 5-10 items. Maybe make some crafting bench to make an oblivion potion from 2 reroll potions and vice-versa and so on. The ingredients part I feel like was really minor and didn't really constitute the amulet and search minigame but I guess its fine.Please let us see what alternatives are available for that trait level in-game. It's really annoying to consult wiki when making a specific build to check if, say, lvl 5 orbs have AS increase trait available at this level. This is my main gripe.First boss is way too hard without quest, I can see why there is quest but considering this is first area you are basically playing until you unlock cleric to kill him if not using quest. Also, since there are no quests on following maps might as well just nerf first boss and remove quest from it since it kinda creates expectation of quests being a thing per area. All in all first area is well designed.Decent up in challenge but harbors just plain annoying mobs and a lot of visual clutter. The breathing worms are annoying, absolute abundance of green zone slimes and a lot of exploding imps/slimes just make it marginally less strategical, you basically must stand in one place and hope you have enough range to kill the worms from where you are standing. Second boss is the hardest of three both because of the spinny blades and the orbs he spawns ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ up your abilities' targeting/splitting damage. Also very tanky. Can't say I'm a big fan, I probably played area 2 the least.Good area, does everything last(at least for now) area is supposed to do, mobs be tanky, mobs be strong. The start is really slow and it only picks up in the last 5 minutes. I don't really like gargoyles since they take forever to close in on you. Banshees are the only annoying mob in area 3 so its fine and honestly I feel like hydra+banshees is more of the last boss than the actual last boss. The last boss could use some buffs as I honestly found him the easiest of three, telegraphed abilities, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, no nuke and plenty of room to dodge. Also could probably make some more destructible boxes to farm hands but it's also fine as is if you have decent pickup range.

_childDocuments_.review: Starts out great then the game ramps the mobs up to the point you can't move, you doesn't give the player any tools to deal with it like in VS. They leave no space to walk, no hole to aim for. You are not given anywhere near the power to deal with the insane difficulty spike. The scroll powers are garbage. Dragon Wave is good, the rest are trash and not worth taking. 0.15 health per second? WTF? Early impression was 10/10. After several games and a few unlocks, every single run is the same. 15-20 minutes in the screen is filled with enemies all the sudden and you can't move. The enemies in a game like this are not all supposed to be freaking tanks. Need serious balance patches. I've gone all dps, all tank and combinations of defense, block or the specials and it's the same run every time. Starts great then BAM! Overwhelmed by tank mobs. Thumbs down for now from me. VS is better because the devs give the player the tools with powers and mob placement/patterns. You are under powered in this game, in VS YOU are the bullet hell, which is way more fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Vampire Survivors by way of Diablo 1, by way of Smash TV. The circling and kiting gameplay is still at its core, but the different character classes have their own quirks that require a more in-depth approach to leveling and making builds. Also BUILDS are very much more at the forefront, as meta-progression involves acquiring gear and equipping your class before a run. Also, different mobs have different pathing behaviors and abilities that change how you deal with them. I also like that as you unlock more stuff, the game actually becomes harder because abilities you acquire come from a much larger pool, and so your goto build becomes harder to guarantee and you're forced into rolling with what you get and figuring out how to make it work. It very much becomes more of a roguelike the deeper you get into it. Overall, a great progression of the formula.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible evolution on the survivor concept introduced by Vampire Survivors, while mixing in the great progression system of the Diablo games, as the inventory and item retrieval mechanic show, being the one of the greatest additions to the survivor genre the game brings.The items create diverse build possibilities, not only are they fun to mess around with, but they also give a great sense of permanent progress that other survivor games lack. While the retrieval mechanic adds some risk-reward decision making to the mix, do you take the first good item you come across to make sure you don't lose it? Or do you hold out in the case of an even greater item appearing, risking death? It's neat.Something that elevates the game beyond others, is the ARPG gameplay, Halls is not the first survivor game with active gameplay, sure,  but when combined with the item and character progression it makes the system truly special.Another thing I like is how diverse each character is from one another, sure, they differ in a lot of their stats, but they also each have their own quest tree, and an unique weapon that is unobtainable with the other characters. Unlike VS, where most characters have abilities that can be found by any other, with 1 or 2 advantages to set them apart.There's a great deal of enemy variety, there are many types of enemies with different attack patterns each. The skeletons charge straight at you. The hell hounds enter the screen at a circular formation trying to box you in. The imps charge at you fast, but will back down if you push back. The slimes do a small dash at your immediate location in bursts, and explode into smaller slimes when you kill them. This results in a more engaging experience where you're always noting which enemy you're fighting and what their pattern is, creating greater gameplay depth. The bosses are also very good, serving as difficulty spikes with big, hard to dodge attacks, where you need to control your fight with them and the enemy horde at the same time, creating tense gameplay moments where you're dodging his attacks while trying to stay away from the enemies that are closing in, while at the same time, aiming your attacks at the boss to maximise your dps. It's exhilarating, and gives me something I didn't even know was missing from Vampire Survivors.The game also has a great visual identity that makes it stand out over most other survivor games, whereas most other games of the genre are viewed top-down, and are generally light-hearted in tone and minimal on detail, Halls is isometric, with a dark fantasy setting, and detailed aesthetic, wearing its Diablo inspiration on its sleeve. However, even though the visuals are pleasing they also present one of the only flaws the game has compared to others of the genre: poor readability.The reason why most other survivor games have simple colourful visuals is because they basically have to, one of the core gameplay loops is finding breaches in the enemy formation and finessing through them, the simple visuals are there to clearly indicate the boundary of the enemy's hurtbox, allowing the player to properly and quickly measure where they can walk without taking any damage. The colourful aesthetic is there for similar reasons, the screen is almost always filled with enemies in games like these, so it is important for the player to know at a first glance where every single enemy is, even ones out of the player's focus. However, Halls ignores most of these, while it is still possible (and very fun) to waive between enemies, the isometric perspective means there are way more instances of taking damage when nothing seemingly touched you, or the opposite, not taking damage when it looks to you like you should have. Similarly, distant or out of focus enemies often tend to blend in with the background because of their subdued colour-scheme, as a result, there will be times where you'll only notice an enemy is right next to you when you've already taken damage. However after a while you become more and more used to the weird perspective, so it becomes a much smaller problem later on.Overall Halls of Torment is an incredibly fun game with only 1 kind of big flaw, IMO it would be completely worth 20-30 bucks with this much content available, which is why it's such a steal that it only costs 5 dollars, game is completely worth it.tl;dr: Vampire Survivors + Diablo = Lots of fun, game looks pretty but that sometimes makes it hard to play, recommend. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Simple game loop but very fun and addictive.The ability and trait system is interesting and evolves with the new classes to bring new elements. Quests - which are more challenges than traditional quests - give new traits and upgrades, or unlock other features. You start with one class, but each run is rather short (~30 minutes) and you'll quickly get new classes to try. Once you defeat the final boss of each level, another one becomes available, but you can still revisit previous levels with increased difficulty.The currency is gold and XP, earned mostly by killing enemies, which allow you to buy permanent buffs and items at the end of each run, and make you level up.The game isn't too difficult, but the amount of enemies, items, missiles, etc. at once on the screen can be a little overwhelming, which also makes it thrilling and fun. Great for taking one's mind off a hard day's work.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: It always amazes me when small games like this completely outshine the game play of AAA competitors. This game has ten times more thought put into progression, itemization, and its game play loop than Diablo 4 which released around the same time. I am embarrassed to say that I payed $70 for Diablo and $4 for this. If I could reverse those price points I would say that both games were worth the money I payed.

In Vampire Survivors, there is skilled play only in the movement. In this game you aim where you want the attacks and move skillfully. It is Challenging and rewarding, with interesting boss mechanics and a great game feel. Trust me spend your lunch money on this and get a great game!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Bizarre balance changes in the Frozen Depths update made this game an arduous chore to play.It's a real shame considering this game felt really well balanced for one of these bullet hell, Vampire Survivors type games; you could become very powerful at higher levels and satisfyingly mow down thousands of enemies in a single run but the game didn't become boring because you could never leave the game to just play itself since you had to look out for mini-bosses which could tank tons of damage and shred your health if you weren't paying attention to their movements and attack patterns.Now, you destroy mini-bosses in a few seconds but get overwhelmed by tanky regular enemies which you should be killing in droves at higher player levels because you can no longer dish out enough damage due to the latest update's severe and unnecessary nerfs.Until the game is in a better balance state I can't recommend buying Halls of Torment anymore.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: One of the better Survivor/bullet heaven games. The feel is the closest to Vampire Survivors in terms of having stuff to unlock for a bunch of characters and levels with secret objectives.Combat's solid, pacing is good and unlocks are fun. It's great for people who wants more of that Vampires itch.The combat feels better than a lot of Survivor games as it's one of the better balanced ones. Modifiers can be hard but are optional and add benefit to the risks beyond just straight currency reward. More mobs means more experience on top of the xp bonus scaling faster/harder into the late game.A lot of modernized quality of life stuff like toggling on and off auto attack and auto aiming seperately, twin sticks. It's missing manual level up (which needs to be a standard in this genre) so a level pop up screen will inevitably show up at the wrong time and disorient.The unique schtick of HoT is the itemizations which adds a layer of meta progression with builds playing with loadouts before a run. That layer adds so much to the enjoyment of a bullet heaven game. Getting more variety for wacky builds adds a lot to replayability and carrot on stickiness.I enjoyed it a lot and would definitely pop back in for a run from time to time.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Very good take on the Bullet Heaven/Vampire Survivors formula, without a doubt one of the best I've played. Unlike others in the genre, aiming isn't always optional, which does a very good job of making the experience more engaging, while also enhancing the perception of being on a power trip when you're dishing out enough damage that standing still and waiting for enemies to die on you becomes a viable strategy — at least briefly, I haven't reached a point where the last two minutes and end game boss didn't require me to move again, and I'm happy with this. Compared to VS, where you're often only really moving to increase your own DPS, rather than avoid enemy projectiles, the gameplay here feels more dynamic, the AI more like a conscious threat you're able to avoid through careful routing.The variance between characters is also much more significant. You have to rethink your strategies to play a mage vs a swordsman, the limitations and strengths of each character's main weapon must be observed in how you build your deck throughout a run, rather than being simply the first "spell" they have available. This is further enhanced by the ability to grind for and equip items that provide stat bonuses, besides the abilities you acquire during a run, which can further alter how a given character plays, some very significantly.Currently some concerns about balance of some damage types over others, and the interface not necessarily making it clear the odds of each effect to proc/what each stack of an effect does, but I'm sure that will be expanded on with time.Also, bonus points for native Linux build. Great to see more games on Godot <3
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★★ - Amazing 7 hours (At time of EA review)	- Game is Survivors-like (Action Roguelike Reverse-Bullet Hell), of similar kin to 'Vampire Survivors' with the flavour of 'Diablo 2'.	- Combat is simple and autonomous yet satisfyingly addictive, focusing on balancing a variety of upgrade abilities and strategies to employ against a massive horde enemies.	- The puzzle of making it through to 30 minutes in each level without dying is challenging without being overly frustrating, providing a good balance between difficulty and enjoyment.	- The upgrades strewn across the map encourages exploration and rewards players.	- Multiple characters with their own quests and expansive traits for additional replayability.	- Finding a items and taking it back to a well for one-time purchase and permanent use in future runs adds depth to the gameplay experience, offering additional content beyond the main storyline.	- The graphics in Halls of Torment are faithfully themed to the Pixel Art of 'Diablo 2'.	- The upward trend of enemies and your ability upgrades fill the screen with effects, causing the feeling of both pressure and power.	- Make sure to balance XP to upgrade with retrieving scrolls to add additional abilities.	- Focus on using gear and upgrading abilities that complement the character that you've picked.Perfect game for when you want to mindlessly waste 30 minutes+ and not have to think too much.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: [/h2] TLDR: Did not regret buying, had quite a bit of fun, but only positive because of very fair price point [/h2]Sorely in need of a balance far as I can tell. Some of characters feel like choice of build barely matters because you won't make it past 15 minutes regardless, and the rest feel like choice of build doesn't matter because you could run borderline anything and still win with some minimal effort. There is very clear power level disparity between classes and so I feel like this game has more or less run its course for me simply because I can't play the classes I think I'd enjoy due to the balancing issues. Complete enough that it's worth the purchase even in early access at the price, but a tad disappointing at the moment considering it has lots of unrealized potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Very Good game, best in it's genre even overall for an early access but I do have to critique heavily, currently having done every single level, attempted multiple times on agony with most characters (Beaten all maxed agony at least once), this game desperately needs a rebalancing on a lot of the items, characters and abilities. About half the characters aren't really viable of Agony Chambers, and about 80% of the items aren't really reasonably usable because they are too weak, and most abilities are just worthless to a degree, even in their intended builds.About half the cast can't get past Agony Chambers due to poor balancing, while some characters very easily can clear it. Items are moreso the big issue, no matter if you are an HP or Crit or Elemental Build, etc. you must run the same Ring*, Chestplate, and Amulet basically to clear (Unless you are a very strong character, who could really bring no items and probably do fine). Healing is too hard to come by naturally in a run, yet some items provide things like near-infinite late stage healing, +3.0 or higher Regeneration with additional burst healing, and lifesteal. Basically invalidating items that are even 100% damage boosts, let alone the other 80% of items weaker than that. This causes builds to feel samey, and it doesn't help that some abilities (Primarily morning star) can just be thrown into any build and completely fodderize a lot of runs, similarly there are abilities that just are completely useless even in their own build (Primarily because they lack targeting, or otherwise don't deal enough to deal with enemies, things like Golem or Kugelblitz just don't provide any utility early, yet they are 1 of basically 2 options even with other abilities unlocked for their builds), you notice this most on Sage, if a character has no real bonus to any stats, downsides to all defenses, yet can run any build by choice, it becomes very easy to notice you can run a crit build and basically fodderize any content with it, yet with summons, lightning, ice, and defensive builds sage just is almost unrunnable in later agony stages.The primary issue is movement speed, you regularly have an enemy in chambers who moves faster than the PC if you are playing a slower character, and generic enemies that move faster than the slowest characters, singlehandedly invalidating all but a few builds that very quickly melt enemies or have a slow effect base on them. Really, all characters have to be above 8.0m to survive those stages if they don't melt, and really only 3-4 or characters get to that point beforehand or can baseline melt those enemies, causing basically the rest of the cast to be unable to be used there unless you run 2-3 extremely specific builds on them.Overall, at 26 hours, even despite wanting to grind more it just feels like there isn't any content past this point worth pursuing, even if one would want to try every build and character in the hardest difficulty. Worth 5$ for me personally, but i could see anyone capping out at 26hrs in any roguelike and finding that unsatisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: 50-70% reduced power overall. If The game was very enjoyable and fantastic until the recent update. It's still ok... But for a game that was awesome it's just sad. Base stats for character and weapons have zero buffs but average power reduced by 20-40% across the board. Permanent upgrades with gold reduced by around 30% on average no buffs to anything. Items reworked and things phrased differently. In some cases some junk items you will never use are unaltered any usable item nerfed by 20-80%. Upgrades while leveling generally nerfed in small ways. Specific weapons and there upgrades massive nerfs when you consider base power reductions with additional nerfs to nearly all 10 levels or upgrades while playing. New weapons are rather pathetic and weaker than old weapons even though all the old weapons were nerfed HARD. I really liked this game and was excited for the update. But the devs went full Diablo 4. You're having fun with the game enjoying builds well we'll channel our inner Blizzard and NERF BAT OF DOOM. I'll never understand how a dev can expect the player base to find it enjoyable to have the power they had reduced by 50-70% overall. I played 4-5 stages and tried the new character once but I'm done it's too disappointing. Uninstall time I have many games to play and even better games like this to play. Vampire survivors or nordic ashes for example.

_childDocuments_.review: It would be a yet another vampire survivors clone, but this one I like. It has nostalgic old school diablo 1-esque graphics.  There are several forms of metaprogression: you can spend money on perks, unlock and purchase equipment, unlock and purchase level up manipulation tools (rerolls, banishes and buffs). There are milestones/feats. which the game calls quests, and they unlock additional content and/or move metaprogression forward. There's a substantial variety between different characters. Bosses telegraph their ranged attacks. There's a substantial variety among mobs and bosses, their movement and attack patterns. Definitely and improvement on VS formula.

_childDocuments_.review: Similar depth to the great Vampire Survivors yet still unique and stands out from the rest. I had high hopes for this game and it still exceeded my expectations. Just a great Roguelike with an incredible art style that is reminiscent of the late 90s to early 2000s RPG style which I absolutely adore. The characters are unique and fun and there is simply a metric ton of content available already (over 300 unique quests !). If you enjoy roguelikes and had enjoyed Vampire Survivors, give it a try ! _childDocuments_.review: EDIT: This game is better than I originally thought. You can get "abilities" which are similar to Vampire Survivor's weapons, which give more build variety. It's still not as good as it could be, but I'm switching to a recommendation. I'm leaving the old review below in case anyone runs into the same thing.OLD REVIEW:I wanted to like this game, because the aesthetic is great and I love the old-school Diablo vibe. But the pacing is way off, and it feels boring as a result. Each run doesn't have much variety per class, it's just selecting the same old "Strength I/II/III", "Attack Speed I/II/III", "Crit Chance I/II/III", etc. And the power fantasy of Vampire Survivors is not there. _childDocuments_.review: It's a good game. Especially on sale.But compared to something like Vampire Survivors it's very much lacking in content in its current state. Which is fair considering it's early access.Aesthetic is good. Music is good. Just like Vampire Survivors, the gameplay loop is addictive and fun.I did 13.4 hours into it as of writing this so I definitely got my money's worth.But after playing this long and unlocking everything in the game currently available, there are some glaring issues.1. There's not much to do after you unlock all 5 classes and 3 available stages. Nothing changes after that. You're just trying to get bigger numbers. Since each run takes so long, at 30 minutes, with no way to speed it up... that means it will probably take about 6 - 9 hours to do the same thing as I did.2. There's some very obvious power differences between classes and skills. For example, lightning bolt with max attack speed can singlehandedly beat the entire game. On the other hand, golem is beyond useless and it's almost impossible to get the damage achievements for it without gaming the system. Same with classes. Shieldmaiden is crazy strong due to her insane talents she can get but Warlock is really pathetic.3. There's a real lack of enemy variety. Even though each round lasts 1/2 hour, the entire back half is just killing the same mooks over and over again. Even in the first level, after you kill the Lich it's basically just the entire map repeating itself with no bosses until the final one at the end. And that can be up to 10 minutes away depending on how fast you kill the Lich. It's pretty boring at that point.I think it's not bad in its current state, but there's no harm in waiting a couple months for it to get more content.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd seen this game called many things before I bought it: "Bullet Heaven" "Walking Simulator" "Diablo Survivors." Hell, I'd even seen someone call the well for saving items (a dangling pail that descends from Earth into the underworld) the "lotion bucket." After four hours, which I find is a relative wealth of time with games like these, I've come up with my own way to describe Halls of Torment: Podcast Companion. It's the perfect thing to do while listening to Sanderson wax poetic about speculative fiction, or Rich Roll sit down with Arnie for a discussion about coddling kids a little less, or--if you're really in the mood for torment--Rogan or Peterson going on with their inane drivel of the week. Whatever you're into, HoT is a great way to feel like you're doing something while you're doing another something. It's fun on its own, too. Even if you prefer, for some reason, just listening to the sounds of the game (at least put on some music, you serial killer) it stands on its own two feet so that you can sit there on your own one butt and enjoy killing skeletons, and blobs (one of the more anemic enemy types, but hey, it makes me hate them and want to kill them even more, so mission accomplished, right?).TL;DR Its fun, but it ain't no ear porn. Learn to utilize the lotion bucket.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Halls of Torment is a horde survival game that is clearly inspired by Vampire Survivor but adds a some unique mechanics. (As context, this is only my second Vampire Survivor-like game, so can't compare to the other competitors in the genre.)One big difference is the art style. HoT takes on mid-90s PC games as the low complexity art style home base. I'm guessing the team took a lot of inspiration from Diablo 1 specifically as many characters and monsters look like they would be right at home in that game, and the UI, voice overs and story delivery strike similar nostalgic notes. I don't think I like it quite as much as the Castlevania-inspired 16-bit art of VS but it's a matter of taste and certainly gives HoT it's own distinct flair.Mechanically, there are two major differences. First, HoT uses a more familiar dual stick shooter format rather than VS's move-only and auto-fire gameplay. Secondly, HoT has a gearing system with a way to unlock gear, so you are sending characters into the levels with a gear loadout, and there is a gameplay loop in which you are unlocking gear, finding the gear drops in the levels, and then sending them one at a time to a pool that opens them up for gearing.As of July 2023 in Early Access there are only three stages and seven classes but similar to VS way more than enough game here already to make it worth your while. I'm excited to see the game develop as the dev team takes it up through release.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes yes, everyone says it already- Vampire Survivors meets Diablo.But here's the real meat and potatoes - this game has Gear. Certain stage Bosses you defeat drop chests that (unlike in VS, where chests give random ability upgrades) give you one piece of gear from a choice of 3 items. The loot pool in the beginning is pretty basic, limited items - not much to show for. Doing "Quests" can unlock more items for you to find in this loot pool. (Basically, achievements with a different name- things as unimportant as Do X amount of Physical/Magical/Fire Damage to enemies as CHARACTER, or Main Story events like freeing characters, beating bosses, etc) Quest completion also nets you more XP for total game completion, so the more quests you do the more XP you get per XP pickup, so the game gets progressively quicker and easier with more and more achievos.Now where the game's meta-progression comes in and shines, aside from spending collected Gold to purchase permanent ability upgrades (Blessings) - you can also, once you follow the story a few quests in, send 1 item per run OUT of a level to be purchased separately and then used PERMANENTLY* in any subsequent dungeon run.* You have a standard RPG Paperdoll, allowing for equipping 7 different items of 6 different item types (1 Chest Garment, 1 Footwear, 1 Glove, 1 Necklace, 1 Headpiece, and 2 Rings)You also, in-dungeon, have a Bag inventory that can store 4 additional items, where you can store multiple gear of the same slot type. This allows for some, if you plan well, situational gear swapping - like say, if you're low on health and you have some gear that can regenerate health, you can pause the game, swap the gear, and do whatever the gear requires to get health back.It's a different layer of strategy and planning than VS, which I appreciate. Each class you unlock has their own loadout so you don't have to worry about changing your Warrior gear just because you're swapping to the Archer for a run. ------Aside from that, I'd argue that the game is much harder to start off than VS. Stuff like doing quests to get more XP, unlocking better gear, and unlocking cooler characters, better ability upgrades, and permanently upgrading stats all make the game easier, but you don't ever get to the completely idle bad@$$ery that VS offers - you have to be much more attentive of what you're doing and where you're going to avoid the different enemy types. Although, with my experience from VS, I was able to complete the first stage (Kill the 30 minute Level Boss) in just 5 hours of total game-run time. It was actually in my 4th or 5th run. Pretty happy with that!------Anyways, that's something I hadn't seen mentioned in any reviews yet so I thought I'd highlight that. It's a lovely game, and if you like VS (and to a minor extent Diablo 1 and 2) then you already know this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Halls of Torment: A Worthy Successor with its Own TwistHalls of Torment has undeniably taken inspiration from Vampire Survivors, but it carves its own path with unique mechanics and a distinct flavor. While the core loop of mowing down hordes of enemies remains, Halls of Torment introduces elements that set it apart and provide a refreshing experience.What Sets it Apart:Character Building: Halls of Torment offers a deeper character-building experience. You can choose from a diverse roster of heroes, each with unique starting weapons and abilities. This allows for varied playstyles and encourages experimentation.Meaningful Choices: The game introduces a "Trait System" which presents you with randomized choices throughout your run. These traits can significantly impact your build, adding an element of strategy and customization.Gothic Atmosphere: Halls of Torment embraces a darker, gothic aesthetic that distinguishes it from Vampire Survivors. This creates a distinct mood and contributes to a more intense atmosphere.Similarities:Core Gameplay Loop: Both games share the satisfying core loop of surviving waves of enemies while collecting power-ups and upgrading your abilities.Addictive Nature: Halls of Torment captures the same "just one more run" addictiveness that made Vampire Survivors so popular.Roguelite Elements: Both games feature roguelite elements with persistent upgrades and unlocks that carry over between runs.Areas for Improvement:Visual Clarity: While the gothic aesthetic is appreciated, the visual presentation can sometimes feel cluttered, making it difficult to track your character amidst the chaos.Enemy Variety: While there's a decent range of enemies, some players might find the variety lacking compared to Vampire Survivors' extensive bestiary.Overall:Halls of Torment is a worthy successor to the throne established by Vampire Survivors. It successfully builds upon the foundation laid by its predecessor while introducing its own unique mechanics and flavor. If you're a fan of the genre, Halls of Torment is definitely worth checking out. It's a thrilling, addictive, and surprisingly deep experience that will keep you hooked for hours.

_childDocuments_.review: is a dark fantasy Rogue-lite horde survival game that faithfully re-creates the retro look of the popular 1990s isometric RPGs such as Diablo, Planescape, Baldur's Gate, etc, has a solid progression system and difficulty curve, and implements a few unique things that make it stand out from other games in the genre.Overall, I recommend it because, despite not adding many new innovative things to the genre, it's a solid game which is simply addictive and fun to play. Although the gameplay is typical for the genre, its unique sub-systems make the journey enjoyable and I always found myself wanting to complete the next quest, get another piece of gear, and become stronger via the meta upgrades and equipment to the point where I became unstoppable.Note: this review is current as of the 1.0 patch released on 10 October 2024.- The gameplay is standard among the genre, though it does add a few unique and thematically-appropriate sub-systems (quests and equippable gear) which make progress more tangible;- The replay value is quite high as there are a huge number of classes to unlock, equipment to collect, and meta upgrades to purchase;- The bosses and mini-bosses are varied, well-designed, and engaging (although they can have an excessive number of hit points on the "Agony" setting and take eons to kill);- The graphics look quite nostalgic due to their intentionally low-res and polygonal nature;- The soundtrack is composed of generic atmospheric dark fantasy songs which gets lost among the sound effects;- The voice acting is surprisingly good in quality and adds some charm to the game; and- The story is non-existent and there isn't even anything listed on the store page.The game has 500 achievements which provide good milestones to strive for and help keep you engaged in the game. None of them require any extra grinding and they will all be acquired as you play through the game casually which will take anywhere from 60-80 hours depending on your proficiency in, and experience with, the genre. That being said, around one achievement per class and stage of the 190 new ones that were added in the 1.0 release are asinine and simply not fun as they force you to play the classes in a way that is antithetical to their natural playstyle or play the stages in a way that just isn't enjoyable such as not being able to attack or move for x minutes.The gameplay is typical for the horde survival genre: you die during a run due to being too weak, return to the hub to purchase gear and meta upgrades, and repeat this process numerous times until you are powerful enough to complete a stage. You eventually unlock an optional "Shrine of Torment" mode for which, when enabled, spawns extra mini-bosses every few minutes and has a variable difficulty level that scales based on your performance during the current run.There are 11 different classes that offer very distinct playstyles from one another since they each specialize in a certain set of stats, have a unique starting ability, and have access to upgrades which are exclusive to them. There are also 18 abilities to choose from, of which you can have up to six per run, and each one has three upgrades which considerably increases the build diversity and replayability in general.The bosses are easily one of the highlights of the game because of the way they telegraph their attacks: they mark locations on the ground that will be affected by their attack a second later which gives you ample time to react to and dodge them while also keeping the combat relatively engaging. Unfortunately, one downside is that the bosses tend to have an excessive amount of hit points when playing in the Shrine of Torment mode which unnecessarily extends the length of the boss fights unless you have most of the meta upgrades, have gear which synergizes well with your class, and optimize your build during the run.The bosses also sometimes drop equippable gear which can come in the form of a torso piece, helmet, necklace, ring, boots, or gloves, and is very similar to Diablo-style games. Furthermore, many pieces of equipment offer special passive abilities that you can't get via the meta upgrades or level-up choices which is a fantastic design choice that expands the gear beyond just increasing various stats. Some examples include the ability to summon minions, create hazards on the battlefield, and unusual stat increases which typically have a specific trigger but also a downside to counteract it to make you consider how good it is for your character and build and the overall risk versus reward of using said piece of gear.Like most games in the genre, grinding ends up being ubiquitous but is at least handled in a unique way that gives you palpable milestones to pursue: each stage and class has its own set of quests for you to complete which give you a large variety of rewards and a minor experience bonus for each one that you complete. You also acquire gold throughout a stage, for completing a stage, and through the completion of certain quests, which allows you to purchase meta upgrades and equippable gear.The graphics accurately re-create the retro look of the 1990s isometric RPGs that were popular at the time, to the point where the game looks a little low-res and you can make out the polygonal shapes. In fact, some of the finer details seem like they were ripped straight from the Diablo series such as the red orb which represents health and some of the pieces of equipment. The three character portraits in the game look especially polygonal which actually adds a certain level of charm to the game.The soundtrack is made up of atmospheric dark fantasy songs that suit the area they are played in but are otherwise forgettable and often get lost among the sonorous sound effects; however, there is only one final boss theme in the entire game for five of the six stages and it becomes extremely repetitive when you are playing on the Shrine of Torment mode and the final bosses have a copious amount of hit points. Additionally, there is voice acting for the three characters that you can interact with which is surprisingly good.The story is completely non-existent and there isn't anything in-game or even on the Steam store page which is odd because developers usually put at least some sort of backstory in the description on the store page.The developers have been doing an outstanding job with the game so far by releasing frequent updates to the game in order to balance the game and add new classes, quests, gear, abilities, quality of life features, and many other things since its Early Access release. In fact, most of the qualms that I had with  have been assuaged as they added most of the missing quality of life features that I listed in my review of it (which you can find  if you're interested). Additionally, the developers added a feature which checks if you have a save file from  and carry over its data if you do which is very convenient and generous.Overall, I highly recommend this game if you're a fan of the horde survival genre as it's one of the best ones on the market: it's well-executed, polished, fun, engaging, and it even manages to deliver a hint of nostalgia. If you're not sure whether the game is for you then you can always try out the free Prelude which I linked above to see if you like the core concept of the game but be aware that it's missing a lot of content compared to the main game.

_childDocuments_.review: Hear me out, I love this game so I will still give it a positive rating no mater what but in my opinion the developers are committing a BIG mistake. This game can be quite confusing (especially to new players) because of all the stats. You really have to understand what you are upgrading and check your stats screen to see what you are doing. After playing for a while you will figure out what you are doing (kind of). Over time the developers introduced new characters and abilities during EA, some of which are overpowered (only if you specifically know what you are doing and upgrade the right stuff). Which in my opinion shouldn’t be a problem because the player still has to put in effort and manually figure out which abilities or characters combinations are OP. It takes time to figure this out.I play this game casually once a month or so (a run here and there) and so I vaguely remember what build worked last time, however the developers GO OUT OF THEIR WAY to nerf every single overpowered character or ability making the game not only much harder but also more boring because nothing stands out anymore. The fact you could figure out an OP build was part of the fun for me. The developer goes out of their way to nerf base values/ characters/ abilities meaning every time you come back to the game (especially when you only play once in a while) nothing you remember will work out the same as it did before causing disappointment because most items which used to be good before are straight up mid now. And these aren’t small changes either, often the item or character is nerfed significantly. And they do this all the time, like every time I come back to this game something has been fundamentally changed, and it’s all in the stats only so you don’t really know what changed unless you read all the patch notes (I guess). This entire process of going back and overhauling base values randomly just ruins the game, there is no way to come back to this game or learn the game if they keep changing everything (usually for the worse). It should be possible to play this game in a casual way and still have fun but in my opinion this isn’t possible because they just change stats way too often making the game a confusing mess always causing you to be under-powered (because your previous strategy randomly doesn't work anymore). Often times when a new character is introduced the character is significantly buffed or nerfed weeks after they are introduced and sometimes they even completely nerf an ability that’s been in the game for months until they randomly nerf it after months lol.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been playing this genre of 2D horde survival shooters most of my life, with games like Crimsonland and Alien Shooter. I have experimented with roguelike hybrids like Swarm Grinder and Brotato but I never really found one I could fall in love with until I played Halls of Torment. The Diablo or Age of Empires-esque pixelated graphics are phenomenal, and the gameplay is incredibly intense and chaotic. Choose your hero (you unlock more by playing), survive the horde, defeat minibosses, and upgrade your character by collected xp dropped by enemies. My favorite thing about the game is the fact that there is a time limit. Once 30 minutes have elapsed, the horde clears and a final boss fight begins. This gives you a clear goal to work towards rather than just endlessly slaughtering hordes until you die. Also, this is a very good game for stat ♥♥♥♥♥♥ like myself. Lots of numbers and percentages to look at. Furthermore, there are 254 achievements and I got 28 of them in 1.4 hours play. Very good choice for anyone that enjoys Risk of Rain or any of the other games I mentioned in this review. Absolutely incredible bargain at $4.99 (I got it on sale for $3.99), I would gladly pay $20 for this.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll compare this to vampire survivors as that's where most people will come from.- Vampire survivors is a bit more addictive and fun, but that's because this game is not even done yet while VS even has DLCs now. Halls of Torment will catch up, I'm quite confident of that.- The focus is a little less on epileptic exploding screens with hordes of enemies at all times, and more on steady progression after runs and boss fights.- I'm missing the regular loot box drops from VS, this game relies more on upgrades after leveling up. That is fine, but a bit less interesting.- The equipment system is a nice addition and something VS lacks.- The tone of the game is less humorous and quirky, and more "Diablo 1 and 2". Some NPCs having voice lines and some (hidden) story elements are also very reminiscent of Diablo.- Final level bosses turn a round from an undead genocide simulator to a bullet hell. I like it, but might not be for everyone. Those bosses serve as a "test" for you if you leveled your character correctly.Huge potential, already a really great game. Correctly priced. Get it!

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best VSlike roguelites. The game just has that satisfying snap and oomph to the combat and fluff, and the gameplay/game design are a masterclass in the genre. Not overly easy either although these games are never really hardcore in any way.The early PC game graphics/voice acting have their own charm. But it's all about the combat, each ability and class feels good to use, and the upgrades all feel good and quite expansive. There's a little bit of grinding though. Solid boss design aswell, and arguably the most interesting enemy walking patterns out of every VSlike.Could use some more stages/items/abilities... few more enemies and classes too perhaps. Upgrades are a bit generic at times, it would be nice to see some unusual passives or ability modifiers (talisman), but this game manages to make stat boosts feel rewarding to pick.Some negative reviews do bring up valid weaknesses of the game, though you should ignore anyone who praises Soulstone Survivor, the most grindy, content bloated VSlike with 90% of the abilities and effects copy pasted and reskinned to give the player the fakest kind of "variety", all that in a messy screenwide fest where your abilities are devoid of impact and identity as they are just your entire screen doing damage to enemies with random colors after a single aoe increase. A game where you just run around in circles spamming dash while looking at enemy disappears with zero effort to earn it. Halls of Torment outclasses it in every aspect, if you actually care about good design.HoT could use bigger variance between OP runs and unlucky, bad runs, but you can pop off nonetheless.

_childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY: A Vampire-Survivor inspired game with bits of Diablo and Dark Souls?  Not quite!  Halls of Torment fits into VS-like games but with it's own twists, using VS mechanics in service of something (somewhat) different.  A good buy even in Early Access.Another Vampire Survivor type game?  Well, somewhat, but Halls of Torment is more than that.  Let's take a look . . .You start the game on a bleak mountaintop outside of the Halls of Torment.  You pick a character class and venture inside for your doomed(?) venture into the halls.  Selecting a level you sally forth, kill monsters, find treasures, and seek growth and hope . . .Like games of its kind, you wander across a more or less open map destroying enemies, grabbing experience gems and stuff, and leveling up.  So what's it like?First, the game has hordes of monsters, but the pace is more leisurely, which is good because many enemies have distinct movement patterns and abilities you'll need to pay attention to.  There are colored "tells" of where attacks may go, enemies that split apart or shoot at you, and more.  Bosses have various attacks you'll need to pay attention to - or end up dead and outside the halls.Don't exepct to be able to charge through enemies easily.  Movement, positioning, and constant checking is required.  Not paying attention will get you killed.  It's not rapid-twitch gaming, but it requires thought.Leveling up gives you a choice of abilities to level up, altering gameplay, sometimes considerably.  Initially you may just attack faster or get more health.  Later you're gaining elemental advantages or piercing attacks.  Customizing characters per run can take on some complex and fun combinations. - like a flamethrower whos bolts pierce enemies.Exploring levels and defeating bosses also gives you abilities and equipment that boost attributes or provide special abilities.  Managing and chosing these further alters you run - and as we'll see, may have repercussions beyond the run.At the main hub, you can check on quests, boost your "blessings" at an altar with gold, and more - as you complete quests and unlock more.  In fact, unlocking is a major mechanic of the game.Fighting enemies for gold and equipment is part of each run and has advantages, but the core of the game is quests, conveniently displayed at one of the mysterious monuments at the hub.  Quests require you to do things like kill so many enemies, use a kind of attack, etc.  When you complete them, you get a bonus of some kind, such as new skills, equipment you can find, or even new "blessings" that give you ways to invest gold in permanent boosts.  As you play the game *changes* what you find and even what you can do - from hoping for good drops every run to permanently unlocking equipment - for a price.Halls of Torment seems to use VS-like mechanics to deliver an experience more akin to a mix of Dark Souls and Diablo.  Grinding, combos, finding ways to meet challenges is a huge part of the game.  This is Halls of Torment's major contribution to the VS-alike genre - it leans heavily into achievement-like unlocks as a way to advance, and that even evolve the usual pay-to-boost mechanics in the grenre.  It's slow, regular, thoughtful progression.The game itself is done in a kind of dark, retro aesthetic that recalls the early Diablo.  It's a different choice from the oft-colorful Vampire Survivor-alikes.  It's not exactly anything that's exciting, but it is different.So is it worth it?  That depends on your tastes.  It's pace is different from most VS-inspired games, and you have to really enjoy unlocking, challenging, and grind-like advancement, and it's not one that is really adrenaline-twitch gaming.  However the challenge is compelling, and working out just the right unlocks is fun - if that's for you. But at the low price?  It may be worth your time - at least give the demo a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing video games for close to 25 years now, so I've been around the block and enjoyed games from many different genres. Like a lot of people, I got introduced to the Survivor Roguelike genre with Vampire Survivors and I'm a big fan of that game. I think Halls of Torment blows it out of the water and I consider it one of my favorite games of all time, enjoying it enough to be one of the 0.6% of players to get all the achievements. Deep customization options, cheap price for the amount of content (200 hours to 100%), addictive and fun gameplay loop, solid incremental progression, and a strong endgame that keeps me coming back for more. _childDocuments_.review: I rarely see an Early Access title come out as sturdy as this one, don't let the tag scare you away, because you'll be walking into a ton of content!Halls of Torment is an enjoyable, pleasantly addictive game in a retro jacket reminiscent of classics like Fallout and Diablo that'll always have you pushing forward with a healthy 'alright, just one more run' mentality.This game knows it doesn't have to reinvent the wheel, with its incredibly solid base systems, like its combat, movement and impressive, unique character variety with their own play styles, but it is not afraid to add bells and whistles. Unique, meaningful upgrades and a great variety of enemies and skill paths will keep every trip through the Halls fun and memorable, yet also satisfyingly challenging, which I personally feel these type of games oftentimes lack.Every new character you unlock will have you experimenting and getting used to new ways to play, with a new, shiny weapon to use and fresh skills to spice up their respective tools.I highly recommend Halls of Torment and I can't wait to see where it'll go!

_childDocuments_.review: Think Vampire Survivors, or really just about any of the "Bullet Heaven" genre, mixed with the vibes of Diablo 1. The combat is generally slower paced than many of its peers, requiring tactical choices to survive while also multitasking to solve puzzles. Run-based trait development often has multiple variants of a trait-line, designated within the (parentheses), leading to weighing if you can wait for the perfect upgrade or just need to take what you can get now. The inventory system also forces you to make tough decisions: if you find an awesome item during a run that you want to keep for the future, you'll have to sacrifice it for the rest of the current run, losing access to it temporarily. You can also only do this once per run, so there are times you find yourself making some tough decisions.The game has awesome potential, and it's certainly carving out its own niche within the genre with a formula that others are already trying to imitate and build upon.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you love rogue-lites?  Then you are in for a treat.  This game is fantastic.  There are 7 classes to play/unlock with varied play styles. For the price, you are getting incredible value for your dollars spent.  Highly recommend this game.  After toiling away in Diablo 4's awful grinds for the last month, Halls of Torment is a welcome reprieve.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Slash and hack, auto or on precise aim, as you desire. Epic boss fights, critical rewards, 30 minute sessions, which you most likely won't survive for the first 5-10 hours,Instant recommendation if you enjoyed previous Hack and Slash games, and want more out of vampire survivors. The ability to automate attacks, and auto-lock on to enemies is but a click away, during the game, OR you can aim, and attack, on command, when you want.The cooldowns are real. The  level ups are intense, and will require many times to figure out a good strategy.You start off with the Barbarian, with more heroes to unlock as you keep playing. Next comes Archer, Exterminator the fire-casting hero, next a cleric, and their abilities have everlasting level ups on the eternal upgrades for all heroes that enter the halls of Torment.It's a small purchase for many hours of fun,If you know you enjoyed 20 minutes till Dawn, Vampire Survivors, The Boneraisers, Rogue Genesia, you will enjoy this without a doubt :) What makes Halls of Torment Unique: No Dashing unless with a specific hero, it's an ability, not a commodity. Your evasion of enemies comes from zig zagging, while attacking The attacking itself, is customizable, and not fixed, like VS, [auto attacking :on/off auto-aim :on/off]  Up to you. [] First two heroes have their work cut out for them,Melee- Great difficulty, after you play with Archer™,  but once you find the balance of level ups, and your intended build, you will have better control of your fights.You can add Crit chance to attacks, you modify crit amount, you get applied force,By level 14 already, you're being swarmed so hard, that if you proceed, you need both damage, and area-of-effect for your weapon to get you where you need to be.The levels seem to be more difficult than the other, so for example, Level 1 is fighting on earth, but level 2, you're in the depths of hell, the enemies feel stronger, the swarms look and feel bigger, when these enemies shield up on their first wave it's like 3 hits to wear down the shield,The way you level up your character needs to be focused, - You need to think about it every time because you do not get re-rolls :) like in other games. You get  4 options every level up, which is more than fair, so it's something to work with,Enemy-Boss-Kills - Are intense, especially because they can summon more creeps into the spawns, they're super boss-fights actually, melee can't even reach the boss if you don't build for swarm-protection first.Archer breezes the first 1 or 2 bosses in a level,The reward from a boss fight, is sometimes a choice of 1 of 3 equipment items, a super rare spell that triggers and now has a chance to feature in your level up abilities. Negatives, Avoidable, with extra skill, and visionLand-blending, enemies don't really get stuck into the terrain's objects like we do, [Fixable but at the same time, it makes sense that it camouflages because it's part of the terrain] -= Can't wait to see what the new engine does for the game! <3Much love to this great success, and it's a game that lasts for a long time,There are also 243 achievements :) in-game quests help attain them,After 3 hours, I have just kept enjoying it, and upon reaching the 30th minute with barbarian, I was actually beaten by the first level's end boss, - I kept trying to get health from barrels, which can either contain, vegetables, or potions +70 HP, or a level up helps give HP when you need it most, I had 14 minutes left on the barbarian run earlier, and went as low as 8HP from 952-max - and recovered all the way to the end of the level getting to 30 minutes, and 200+HP for the boss fight. This was not enough,Learning to dodge - as if you're tapping movement keys, is a skill, If you use a controller, then it's even easier, because you can use the analog's pressure, of how fast/slow you move, it's not just a 100% on, or off movement, which is like some of these games in this genre.The Auto-attack actually shows you how far your upgrades have come , toggling it, off, accidentally, can have some level-ending consequences... but it's part of the learning curve ;)The next really epic thing about this is statistics, from always scrolling./moving across a level, the 5000 meters in one run is achieved, small things like this shows deep love for the underlying structure of this game.It's a real gem! :)

_childDocuments_.review: I can easily recommend this game as one of the better entries in the current canon of survivor/bullet-heaven games. The devs here have nailed that aesthetic, btw, and it plays a large part in making HoT a blast to play. Other factors include tight gameplay, player-controlled directional aim (with the option to set things to auto if the player likes), a fun roster of characters to unlock and choose from, loot and custom gear loadouts, and a whole bevy of achievements which are also tied to in-game unlocks. The game is still in Early Access but is receiving regular updates and I'm sure will have a lot more content to keep players busy by the time it's in finished, and it already has a good amount to do in it's current state.So yeah, hats off to this game and the devs. Lots of fun and an extremely great value at just five dollars.

_childDocuments_.review: Halls of Torment captures the dark, immersive essence of classic ARPGs like Diablo, with modern twists that make it a blast to play. If you’re looking for a rogulite bullet-hell game that combines intense combat, a brooding atmosphere, and challenging gameplay, this game won’t disappoint.The retro-inspired graphics are a huge part of its charm, blending pixel art with a gritty color palette that brings its dangerous, enemy-filled halls to life. Every level has a distinct, creepy vibe, setting the stage for relentless waves of enemies that will test your survival skills. The game has a rewarding progression system, allowing you to strengthen your character, unlock new abilities, and customize your playstyle as you grind through increasingly difficult foes. The bosses are truly formidable, and they demand both strategy and fast reflexes, keeping you on the edge of your seat.One of Halls of Torment’s best features is its roguelike structure. Each run is unpredictable, offering fresh challenges and different layouts that make each descent into the halls feel unique. But unlike some roguelikes, it strikes a perfect balance between difficulty and reward, so you never feel like your efforts were wasted after a tough run. Instead, you come back stronger and better equipped for the next attempt.With its addictive gameplay loop, engaging retro aesthetics, and well-paced difficulty, Halls of Torment is an easy recommendation for fans of action RPGs and roguelikes. Whether you’re an old-school gamer or just looking for a thrilling, atmospheric dungeon crawl, this game will keep you coming back for more. For its price, it offers tremendous value and hours of challenging, rewarding gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Having followed the game since the very first public announcement, it is very nice to see Halls of Torment reaching its Early Access release.Halls of Torment is the answer to "what would happen if Vampire Survivors and old-school Diabolo had a baby?"While many might look at this and sigh "yet another VS clone", HoT is much more interactive and poses much more of a challenge compared to VS.It sports a unique set of levels, characters, enemies and bosses.Each enemy has a unique visual style, attack pattern and damage type.As you play through the 30-minute runs in the levels, you earn coins to unlock permanent upgrades, which help you to kill enemies more quickly and which in turn adds to the satisfaction factor.There's also a ton of challenges/missions you can complete which unlock abilities and collectables, each of which increases your attack power.A small heads-up I'd like to give to new players is that it can be a bit grindy at times, as the levels' final bosses pose an interesting challenge to anyone surviving for that long.TLDR: Chasing Carrots hits the mark yet again with a very good game. Despite the "Early Access" label, Halls of Torment is surprisingly polished and definitely worth a try.edit: it also runs well on deck! :)

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specifically geared at providing feedback to the developers as per their request.After 13 hours and defeating the last boss of the Frozen Depths, I have completed all of the basic content for the game, unlocked and tried each character once, and seen all abilities. Keeping in mind that this is early access and that the devs still have plans to implement a deeper progression and end-game content cycle, I have high praises for the game. In simplest terms, this game brings the satisfying wave-slaying gameplay of Vampire Survivors and expands on it by introducing more interactive gameplay and RPG elements. Aesthetically, the game captures the gritty retro look of the CRPG golden age. It looks fantastic and has crisp sound design. The primary attack being controllable with manual aiming and attack buttons is great. It allows you to seamlessly swap between auto-attacking the nearest enemy and focusing groups or boss enemies, especially with how the weapons scale. This approach makes each class play very differently from one another. Chain-lightning, longsword, bow, frost spear, etc. all function radically different making the characters feel distinct. The enemy behavior variety is a great improvement over the Vampire Survivors formula as well. It keeps the player engaged and provides a new layer of challenge and interaction to a genre that can tend toward AFK xp farm simulators. This game avoids that by providing reasonable ways for you to deal with enemies while also making it impossible to afk until you get a very very good build going. This does not seem possible with just basic equipment and levels, so, there is definitely more to explore here after the point I am at. The different damage types and status effects are very cool. Building not only "damage" but physical, magical, fire/burn, electric, and frost as well as a kind of "holy" build is very satisfying. The different colored damage numbers may seem like a small detail but it provides visual feedback that what you are doing is working and is a pretty genius dopamine booster. Lastly, the variety of builds is great. You can tank out, aiming for defense or block strength to deflect damage. You can go for physical damage and crit, various magical damage types and statuses like burn, frost, electrifty, etc. In short, there is a great foundation here for an in-depth RPG type experience.First, all characters are not created equally. For example, the Shield Maiden is intended to be a character with the ability to avoid most damage while also having knockback and damage that scales with block strength. However, at least without late-game item options, she feels terrible to use out of the gate. She is tanky, but, she cannot get to the point where she can fully tank the wave of enemies. She still dies. Since she has terrible damage and attack speed, I see no use case for her character. On the other end of things, the Exterminator is just busted. His base weapon eviscerates everything with fire and flame. Once he acquires a few fire-based abilities and a basic burn-amplification item, the game is practically won. He melts bosses and destroys waves of enemies. Basically, while the character niche system is great, it needs to be tuned to allow non-DPS classes to function better. You should not be afraid of allowing the Maiden to fulfill the fantasy of being an unstoppable tank. There need to be more defensive ability options similar to the laurel from VS because, as it stands, you essentially want a class that can stack a damage type/debuff type and just clear everything. There are not good options for the Shield Maiden or the Necromancer who require significant investment to merely function at a subpar level. By the way, the necromancer is horribly glitched graphically. Please fix that ASAP.I have played a full 13 hours without unlocking a single additional potion. I beat the game without every utilizing that aspect of the game. It could be luck, but, I think having a few more basic potion options would entice players to explore that aspect of the game more. There is essentially a dearth of content here. More stages, enemies, abilities, and items are all necessary to really push this out of early access in a meaningful way. There is only one frost ability, for example, but there are three or four fire ones. Because of the available abilities it feels much better to play Exterminator, Sorceress, or Cleric thematically than any other class. Many players such as myself, I imagine, like this game for the RPG element primarily. I have tended toward these classes that can build thematically yet powerfully for this very reason. Getting ringblades and phantom needs on the warrior just felt wrong to watch. I would really like there to be more physical, tank, holy, and frost-themed abilities to round-out the roster. The Huntress, Maiden, Norseman, Cleric, and basic classes would feel much better with more options to let them shine and fulfill their fantasy. So, it seems that you are already partially aware of what you need to do since you mentioned more meaningful progression and options for replayability. I really think this boils down to just MOAR stuff, but, I would definitely suggest that the MOAR you prioritize revolve around the basic essence of how you build characters. We need more abilities and more interesting item/build paths to allow every character to shine. You have a winning formula with how Exterminator and Sorceress (and, with a little help, the Huntress) function. Make tanks, burst damage-dealers, and niche classes able to fill that same space with abilities that work for them. No sense in having a slew of stats if some of them don't have clear build options to the same level of satisfaction of chain-lightning or burning everything to death. So, in short, I would suggest more variety, but very focused around revitalizing the lacklustre classes and promoting the RPG element of the game much further. You have a great thing going here, and leaning into the RPG side of things will push HoT to the next level.

_childDocuments_.review: I get why this game has high reviews; it's a clean, well-implemented survivors game, has a wonderful, nostalgic art style, and a pretty satisfying meta-progression that is one of the aspects better than vampire survivors with gear that you can acquire in a run and then send to the camp for future runs.But the design is flawed in a lot of ways that make me disinclined toward this one.While the art is quite fun to look at, the game is almost completely unreadable.  More often than not, you take hits because enemies are the same greyish/brownish/reddish color as the background and everything else.  Enemies bullets are, fortunately, bright purple, but their ground effects are red again, and you can have summons that are just brighter versions of regular enemies.  Telling what is going on is painful.  Sometmies, enemies even used the same sprite but behaved differently (lava slimes in the second zone were just tough slimes, except in some other waves they also dropped poison ground on death like the green poison slimes in zone 1?), making it that much harder to tell how to play.The pacing is.. ok.  It definitely does not have the excellent pacing that makes VS the king of the genre; at least some waves are not harder than the last one, but the leveling curve is standard D&D style longer for every level.  Sometimes you are the hunter and sometimes you are the hunted, at least, so there's a little variety after the first hour or two (you're only being hunted until you get some meta upgrades).The level design is not usually a very important focus for games in this genre, so it isn't surprising that there is no level design here, just big open area with props that block movement every so often.  It's definitely boring, especially if you've played the VS DLC levels that actually have interesting designs.The bosses are.. very very bad.  The all have projectiles and/or ground effects that are very difficult to read, but they also have incredibly stupid designs.  The first zone's boss puts a 40 second timer on you.  It's a pure DPS check.  If RNG didn't give you enough offensive options when leveling, or you are using one of the starting classes with weak main weapons, you can't really beat it until you have a huge amount of meta upgrades.  The second boss has a health pool that is so large that after 10 minutes he was still over half health so I suicided out of boredom and came to write this review.I will say that the hitboxes seem fair, the meta progression seems generous - I was always unlocking stuff after each run, even when I failed, and the general balance except the final bosses progresses acceptably, but honestly why play an inferior product when you could just play vampire survivors instead?  Halls is just the same game with the ability to equip custom gear and nostalgic but bad-for-gameplay art direction.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: DEFINITELY worth the price. Almost played for 4 hours straight first time. If you loved the OG Diablo II then you will like this game. It really feels like that had a lot of influence on this game. The replayability of this is awesome. You have multiple characters to play as, all have different skills and you will never choose the same build twice. It takes a little bit to figure out exactly where you are supposed to go and what does what but you will figure it out quickly. My main advice is do not waste any skill points into "Long Fingers" that increases the range that you can grab fallen objects. The reason is because throughout the level there will be these hands that drop on the ground, and it shows you where they are to run to. If you pick up the hand it will grab EVERY SINGLE DROP on the map and give it to you no matter how much you killed and how far away it is. So killing a bunch and running for one of those hands or trying to find one in a barrel or something is key to getting massive levels quickly. The boss fights are intense as hell. I've only beaten the first 2 areas but Jesus that first boss. For 4 bucks this game is a steal. I've purchased games for 20-40 dollars that I didn't enjoy as much as this. Thanks Game Developers!

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - If you like survivor games, but this game now.Cons:Music - Same tunes over and over again.  I wish each dungeon had its own soundtrackAchievements - Some of the Achievements are just a grind fest.  I wish there were more Achievements that focused on exploring combinations of characters, builds, skills, abilities, gears and artifacts.  I hope new content will center more around build exploration.End game content - The last dungeon, The Vault, isn't all too compelling to want to play.  I basically played The Vault to complete out my Achievements and never went back inside.  QOL - I wish there was more clarity in how information is displayed when picking certain traits and stats.  I would like to know how picking something will impact my character build.  For example, it's not always clear how picking "Force" will impact my build.Pros:Gameplay - the game is responsive, intuitive and addictive.  The character classes actually feel different and are not just cookie cutter versions of one another.  Every class is viable in end game (although, lets be real...Shield Maiden is OP AF).Setting - The developers nailed the setting...many people say it reminds them of Diablo 2....and as a fan of Diablo, I will say that they're partially right.  The art style is definitely reminiscent of Diablo 2, but I think they've taken that art and made it their own thing.  The music and sound is also well-done (I just wish there was more).Gearing/progression- The gearing system is much better now than it was in Early access.  It's too bad the game doesn't encourages players to explore more builds. I like the potion system, it opens options to really make an OP build.  I think the artifacts has a lot of potential in future expansion/dlc content.  I don't think artifacts has reached its true potential, but I can definitely see room for growth.Overall:I sunk in soooooo many hours into this game.  I think I got more than my money's worth.  I decided to write this review after getting all 500 achievements.  If you just want a game you can get sunk into and lose hours and hours of your time, just buy Halls of Torment already.  I can't wait to see what the developers have lined up next for this title.
