_childDocuments_.review: Another entry into the seemingly endless list of roguelites. And while it sticks to the formulae, it does a lot to distinguish itself at the same time.As you play more and start to level up and complete the long list of challenges provided by this game (some requiring you to not move at the start of a run or requiring you to critical hit 50,000 enemies in a single run!), you'll start to unlock more characters to play as, more equipment to equip them with and, as I just discovered, the ability to craft potions which offer different abilities, with this most basic letting you re-roll your choice of traits when you level up.This game is very rewarding, allowing you to spend coins to upgrade your base perks (you can refund and swap these at any time) and the wellkeeper, who lets you buy gear from him that you may find when doing runs. This is the best feature, as once you buy gear, that's it - it's yours! This gear cannot be lost, even on death during a run.I very much look forward to sinking a few hundred hours into this, easily one of the strongest entries into this constantly expanding category of games. If price is a problem for you, don't worry, this developer is awesome - go check out "Halls of Torment: Prelude" - it's free and a great way to test if this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is based on a 201/201 100% completion on build version 2023/06/28 (Not sure why the game uses the date for game version instead of a build number but that's all I could find.)  Yes I do recommend the game, stating that now because some people don't care for the details about what I do and don't like and just want to know that.  It may look like I am critiquing the game more than praising it but that's only because it's easier to find faults in something than praise it. Despite the things I say below I did enjoy the game.What I liked: The games artistic direction and setting is very reminiscent of Diablo which I'm pretty sure everyone pointed out, Even the music has a similar feel to it along with the little camp you can wander around in to set stuff up before runs. The classes while not overly unique do encourage different skill builds, The game has achievement based progression so to unlock features, characters, upgrade types, potions and so on requires you to complete specific achievements in game, then you usually have to find them and purchases them with gold as well. As of this build the game currently has 3 maps and while that doesn't sound like a lot if nothing else is added to the game after this (which more has already been announced) The amount of game-play you get for the price is more than enough.  What I didn't like:    The rough truth is many of the systems in game I liked the idea of more than the actual execution. For example.- Having to find the gear in game and send it back to town so you can use it in future runs. Great, but I didn't like only being able to send one piece back per run, you lose the use of it during the run you are on, and then you have to pay with gold to unlock it even though you sent it back. It requires more runs to send everything back (over 40 items and 10 potion bottles) than it does to get all achievements.- Having a variety of skill choices that appear at random during a run to make each run different. Great, but the skills themselves aren't balanced at the start let alone after various upgrades so a few skill choices will always distantly outshine the rest making the runs more similar than intended, unless you are trying to unlock a specific achievement for skill or damage type.- Having various equipment choices to design a build around once you've unlocked them. Great, but the majority of the items are uninspired and really add nothing and are out shined by the few that do like a helmet that increases attack speed by 1% per kill for several seconds up to 50% vs a helmet that adds 3 defense, or the amulet that increases EXP gain by 50% which is practically required if you want to get to level 100.  - Leveling up to become more powerful. Good, but the experience points aren't balanced properly. Currently the only map you can get to level 100 and above (around 110) is map 3 and doing so requires you to have around 90% achievement completion to boost exp gain, wear the necklace that gives 50% exp boost, and as high of a kill speed as possible. But balance is the bigger issue with this. With those things killing 17k - 18k enemies will get you to level 100 and possibly over on map 3, but killing 30k enemies on map 1 with the same set up wont even get you to level 85. With full completion of 201 achievements which gives 100.5% exp boost, and the 50% exp boost amulet, and EXP boosts you can buy with gold from the upgrade shop. 30k kills still wont get you to level 85 on map 1 but 17k will now get you to 110 on map 3. Making map 3 the only map many achievements can be completed on.- Using gold earned in run to unlock upgrades. Great, but the gold you earn isn't enough to unlock everything by a long shot by the time you've completed the game, If you don't want to grind an extra 40 or so runs you can refund all of your upgrades and just buy potion bottles to finish up the purchases 40 items achievement but doing so leaves a lot of items still locked (not that you would use them usually anyways) and a few of the upgrades wont be fully unlocked anymore (Not that you should ever need the 25k upgrade to give you a second revive.) Grinding money is one of the least pleasant aspects of this game. -Potions to change choices being required to alter level up choices for attributes and skills. Great, but having to find 3 ingredients for each potion and send up the potion bottle then buy the bottle isn't worth the time investment I had less than 10 achievements left to unlock before I even got everything together to use potions and that's with only a few flasks. Overall I think many things need to be re balanced in the long run so there isn't such a heavy dependency on the 3rd map, and specific skills over others. Summoning in its entirety is just mostly bad over all, It sounds great but in its current state it's not. In the end I enjoyed my time with the game and will probably come back to it with future updates if only because I want to keep it at 100% completion but honestly the grind for the last 15 or so achievements just  burned me out and that's without moving on to the gold grind, and while i hope at least some systems are re-balanced in the future for the price the game is more than worth it already and most people probably wouldn't burn out as easily as I do. This is one of the top games in this genre right now and I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Halls of Torment is a pretty interesting (and affordable) bullet heaven - with a nice mix of character distinction and fun universal skills. The changes between the Prelude (which you can download for free) and the Early Access one are pretty solid improvements to a formula I already liked.While it does have the usual cons of any other bullet heaven (can get a bit chaotic and hard to see towards the end, but this is true of the genre period) - but it brings positives like:- a proper equipment system- character unique skills while not getting rid of the global skills that are so fun in other bullet heavens- a nice variety of meta progression (quests, equipment, and blessings between runs)- The in-run upgrades are still "good enough" (with a few transformative ones after you've leveled a given skill up a bit)- much better enemy patterning than other bullet heavens (enemies don't always run straight at you, there's actual variety)I would say try the prelude before you buy, but I think if you enjoy bullet heavens, this is a solid pickup.Things that are in the Early Acess version, that aren't in the prelude:More Classes, More Maps, more items, Capstone boosts/changes to skills that make them even more interesting, and there are also buffs that can be picked up on the maps (which isn't a feature I ran into in the prelude)Gameplay is pretty similar to the Prelude - which you can see here:  And I look forward to seeing how the game progresses throughout early access.

_childDocuments_.review: It is addicting and the gameplay is fun. Characters are unique, and the item system is fantastic. The early game was much more fun than any other survivor I played. I got 25 hours of fun from it so I cant not recommend it, but it has some issues that really show in the late game:- There are very few ability upgrades and options per run:Abilities are obtained with scrolls, and each scroll offers you three random abilities or upgrades for abilities you already have. If you want to focus on a specific build, you need abilities plus two to three upgrades for them to be powerful for the late game. The issue is that you get like ~8 scrolls per game, and most scrolls are useless. Even if you grind for the reroll potions, which are stupid rare, the lack of scrolls make focusing on specific builds VERY RNG dependant.This is not really an issue for completing runs, since you become quite overpowered with meta progression. But it does feel like making builds is a huge gamble. Ending up with 6 abilities that do not synergyze at all is lame.- Most abilities are useless:Some skills are almost necessary in the early game for harder difficulties, whereas the other skills do pretty much no damage until you put some heavy upgrades. Combined with the fact each run has very few scrolls, the huge pool of abilities gets reduced to like 5 useful ones.Overall both issues just increases RNG to annoying levels, especially at harder difficulties. If the devs fix the rng and make some abilities more useful, this game can be the best survivor like game on steam frfr

_childDocuments_.review: This is what gaming has become.Every so often a new 'indie' game comes out that is an instant classic, while every single game released by a larger studio comes out like a steaming turd. I'm assuming it's because hardly anyone puts any effort into basic communication skills. Their team is just a bunch of developers and artists on payroll who don't care at all personally about the product. In reality the 'art' of game design should be that you could "enjoy" your own end product. If all you're doing is working to sell this product, the game, it's empty and it has no soul. That's why games like this shine, you can tell it was a small team. The goal of this game is to be "fun", it's not groundbreaking in any one particular way. _childDocuments_.review: There's essentially two phases to the game, before and after Agony. Agony took me around 8 hours to unlock while diligently collecting the collectibles from each stage.Before Agony, it's fine. It starts off slow, gets more fun as you actually unlock some options, then gets less fun as you outscale the game due to the stat-increasing meta progression that's so common in this genre. You collect all the equipment you care about and things start to feel pointless.After Agony feels like how the game is meant to be played. Enemies scale up based on your performance, you can find upgraded gear that only lasts for that run, and you can add additional modifiers. Once you unlock it, the game goes back to being fun and you can enjoy having more reasons to go back to the different maps. Though, according to the steam achievements, only 10% of people have finished a run here, so chances are you won't experience it.There's a lot of quality of life missing, and confusing text. One upgrade says "Additional damage bonus depends on the distance between you and an orb." So, does it do more damage when close, or when far away? Does the damage bonus apply per orb or to all orbs (which is how it reads but wouldn't change at all due to how the orbit works)? I do not know. You also can't look at the stats of the unpicked skills during a run as far as I can tell, so if you want to know the crit rate of that skill before picking it, you'll have to look it up. Sending potions up doesn't consume your return chance, but you can't send them up if you've already returned an item, so if you get a potion and an equipment, send them up, and later get another potion drop, too bad you can't send it up. Hope you find a bucket drop. The enemy attacks also have no consistent colouring, and sometimes are identical in colour to your own projectiles, for example frost champions spawn ice spikes that are the exact same colour as the frost avalanche skill and become very hard to distinguish or recognize as a threat. Those are also layered under the enemies so when there's a lot of enemies you can't see them in the first place.But, overall it's a good time for the price, if you've already played games in the genre and want to try something new. If you haven't played other games in the genre, start with HoloCure and come back to this if that leaves you wanting more.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE:So I've changed my review from positive to negative. Why? Ironically, my biggest fears (which I commend on my original review which I'll leave untouched bellow) about devs taking too long to bring updates AND making some questionable changes became real. To make matters worse, this game has developed a strong fanbase where any criticism will be attacked and makes the devs even more closed and narrow minded for eventual changes. Early Access is all about trying out new stuff to see if it works or not. But when the hardcore community simply accepts anything that the devs bring and the devs can't take criticism... The point of EA is thrown away. I remember the development of Rogue Legacy 2 for example. Devs weren't afraid of trying new stuff nor were stubborn enough to abandon/rethink that idea if the community wasn't pleased with it. It was a pleasure to take part of that EA. In this game it's just pain. It's still good and promising. But I would suggest you to wait for it to develop further to see if the devs finally give us a clear idea of where this game is heading to. ------ORIGINAL REVIEW:Sure, yes. I've played nearly 40h and had fun with it. This game has a lot of potential and blah blah blah. Although I have to state that I'm always concerned with EA games because most start off really solid and promising and then... Usually the development goes into a slow painful process, devs start taking questionable decisions and so on.(I've seen that many times on this "swarm survival genre")Other than that, it's a nice mixture of swarm survival and Diablo.It's easy to pick up and play, as it should, mechanics are easy to learn and understand, there's actually an option for auto shooting AND auto aiming that's easily toggleable by a press of a button, without needing to go through a menu (that should be mandatory for any swarm survival game) and, best of all, this game doesn't go bat***to crazy on flashy effects and hundreds of thousands enemies on screen which means NO SLOWDOWN (which is a plague on pretty much any game. Maybe VS, Soulstone Survivors and Rogue Genesia being the worst).Most improvements I would like to see are QoL related (I've made a post on the forum about it), but my biggest gripe so far is... This game desperately needs a way to speed up the runs.This game has 30' runs, like VS.However, in practical terms, each run will last about 40-45' because there'll be small pauses leveling up and choosing which upgrades to take and then the end boss for each stage that can take *really long* depending on your build.So a "hurry mode" of sorts would greatly be appreciated.Yes, this review is a bit critical and skeptical for a Positive review, but I would be a hypocrite if I couldn't recommend a $5 game that awarded me 40h of good fun.This review may change as development goes on. Stay tuned :p

_childDocuments_.review: Just the Facts :Good : It looks and sounds like Diablo IThe Rest : Starts feel woefully weak and slow if you are not ready to walk 5000 Kilometers and collect a Skill and kill your Run right then and there, you are ill equipped to kill Elites that drop the same horribly uninspired and weak Feeling Skills, the Item Retrieval System is a Chore and feels arbitrary (but that One is probably on me), Level Ups add veeeery little to your Damage or Survivability (If you can get at the Mana Vials, Pickup Range doesn't matter too much when the Hordes simply eat up your Shots and push you away from the Xp... the List goes onI am not ready to die the first few dozen Runs so i can feel marginally more powerful somewhere in the far Future, Dev Streams and a Couple "OP" Runs i watched didn't look all that interesting either...Hate to dump on an Indie Game, and i am more than ready to apologise and eat my Words down the Line,but why this is sitting at an O P Rating atm is beyond meI'll refund for now

_childDocuments_.review: Updated review, updates below dashes, all prior review still applies.Bought this instead of Diablo IV and don't regret my purchase.Only played about five runs, and I think this is a pretty good game in the Vampire Survivors subgenre. Bosses have actual patterns, there appears to be more nuances in play such as resistances, and progression feels really satisfying, which is the most important thing for a game like this. The weapons don't feel like one to one clones, unlocks are interesting, stats are fairly clearly defined in what they do (I'm gonna be honest I don't understand block but I just don't spec into it so that may be why), and everything has a cohesive visual design.The only downsides I can say so far is the damage sound sounds like you're collecting money, and I would like to see the character visually change when they equip armor, but I know that last one is probably a pretty big undertaking and probably won't happen. I don't know where this game plans on going, I didn't bother to even read the early access stuff, but as it is now, definitely worth the five dollars.--------------They've pretty steadily been adding content and improving the game since I've owned it, with somewhere around four patches a month to add items, fix bugs, add characters and add a new biome. They also made some of the more insane challenges more reasonable (I have never, ever hit level 100 and I think that would be difficult to do with any character, much less all of them) It doesn't feel early access for the amount of game that's playable, and the game you can play is still very quality.I found out blocking works like a reverse- crit where depending on damage taken you have a chance to nullify all the damage. The higher level of this skill increases the odds and damage threshold this applies to. I find speccing into defense more worthwhile, but I take it if I have a roll that isn't helpful.the one nitpick I do have is I can't find a way to pin quests. Unlike Vampire Survivors which has very linear, straightforward goals, there are hundreds of little branching achievements you can get in this game which make them more complicated to track. I have a goldfish brain and it's hard for me to actively remember which quests I want to work on and having a simple feature to pin 1-3 quests to reference while I was in an arena (or maybe all possible quests with the specific character and level you're instanced into) would be helpful. If it's there already feel free to correct me.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good entry into the increasingly crowded Vampire Survivor like game market. I will say that VS is still the better game overall, and if you don't have that, then get it now!While this has a lot in common with VS, it manages to be its own thing, and it feels like it has a lot of Diablo DNA in it. The runs aren't as varied or fun as VS as it is more about character improvement and you will play the same class a lot and you don't get many new weapons during a run. A key difference over VS is the ability to manually aim at targets, which is crucial sometimes. You can toggle autoaim/autofire while playing.The controls are very tight and allows you to thread the needle between mobs of enemies with precision. The game feels a lot more skillful to play than VS where the weapons are doing the hard work rather than the player.This is an easy recommendation for fans of VS who are looking for a different take on the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: After diving in to the Halls of Torment, I can say it is an absolute blast! The art style is beautiful with its 2.5 D styling. _childDocuments_.review: Overall: 8/10Halls of Torment is a very fun survivors game that gets a lot of things right. The enemies are varied and interesting, the gameplay is smooth as butter, hitboxes feel fair, the weapons are interesting with cool evolutions to em. The game offers a deep progression system that allows for many, many builds. You can really cook some cool stuff up in this game and as somebody that recently 100%'d the game's achievements, I really enjoyed being able to theorycraft and come up with solutions for some of the more involved achievements. It was almost like solving a puzzle. The game does get some things wrong though. The balancing is all over the place, some of the characters are much stronger than others. The same can be said about the powers, one in particular is about 4x stronger than the next best power. Items are also in the same boat, once I got a specific item the game became piss easy even on Torment 15. Progression is also pretty slow, it can take a long time to collect all the items you want. The game also has some bugs, none of which are overly impactful but they're definitely noticeable. The ice map is pretty terrible and the boss there is deceptive, his attacks go much further than their animations. Not something that matters when you're comically strong but definitely noticeable when you aren't. Another very specific gripe I have is that 100%ing the game is a pain in the ass. 500 achievements is pretty hefty but that isn't even my real issue. My issue is that artifacts aren't guaranteed drops, once you have collected around 24 it becomes an RNGfest to collect the ones you are missing with no way for you to influence it. You have to finish an entire run for a chance at getting one of the remaining artifacts you need which is super tedious. Definitely didn't appreciate that my last 12 achieves took hours longer than necessary because of this. Was gonna knock the score down a point for this but decided against it because of how specific of a problem this is. Super lame and frustrating though, devs should fix this arbitrary and unnecessary wall. TLDR: Game is very fun and does a lot right. _childDocuments_.review: Not to trash on Vampire Survivors in any way, but Halls of Torment is what I wish Vampire Survivor was. And I mean it in the sense of pushing the roguelike sub-genre of "horde survivor" or "bullet heaven" games to the maximum. I am referring to Vampire Survivors as the pioneer and leader of this category. HoT goes very in-depth when upgrading items, abilities, and character traits inside a run and really pushes the "vanilla" experience you expect from a horde survivor game. It really makes building up a run meaningful. Every character has their own traits and really adds flavor to the game itself, since progressing on a single character unlocks their stuff onto the new one, making character building before a run very versatile. Vampire Survivors ends up being "how fast" you can break a run, where as Halls of Torment really makes you push those enemies and levels to get the upgrades you want and need. 100% Achievements is totally doable and guides you through the "full" game experience.Can't wait for full release

_childDocuments_.review: Halls of Torment is in an upper echelon of Survivor-like games, not only because its cost is so great, but also the amount of things to do for a completionist is also significant.Not all things smell like roses, but for the most part this game feels complete from start to finish.It has good meta-progression. Lots of things to unlock. This game is made around its 500 quests/achievements (at least that's the amount in version 1.0) that you want/need to do. Many can't be done at first, or even unlocked at first. So you have to put a good amount of time even to be able to tackle some of them. Which is good. That's where the hook of this game actually resides. The gameplay itself is great for the first ~30ish hours or so. You unlock character after character, every single one has unique abilities attached to them. And later on you can mix and match those with other characters. Which is really cool. After that everything kinda blends in into choosing the same skills every single run just to complete an objective asap.The balance of spells is not so bad too. Of course, some abilities are very good for every single character and situation, but I had successful runs with every single one of them as my main damage dealer.There are 5 different levels and one extra (The Vault) for the endless run enjoyers. Sadly, that one is a bit of a miss. It's just extremely boring. Enemy variety is lackluster, you can't get skill upgrades fast enough and after 1h or so you just either stand and kill things, or run around big packs of monsters while slowly poking them with ever-decreasing damage. The level is very small. And I only did it for quests/unlocks/achievements. I think The Vault needs quite a bit more time in the oven to make it enjoyable to waste your time.I really like the item saving option for later runs via the well. Later on you can save up to 3 items every single run and even collect better versions of same items. A bit tedious, but it's a mechanic that makes you choose wisely, at least at first, when you don't have the best all-around items for every single character or strategy.I think the best thing this game has for customization of runs are the potions. They are well made, they are awesome and you can make some REAAAALLY crazy strategies to min-max your survivability or damage output with your main attack/abilities. The options are endless here. Another thing that's a bit of a miss is artifacts and the way you unlock them. They are cool as a one-time thing for the achievement(s) or if you want to make your runs handicapped in one way or another. But that's not that bad. The bad thing is that once you get a good amount of them - they stop dropping after every boss kill.Once I still needed like 4 of them, I had to replay so many levels just to have a chance to get a new one. I even cycled from one to five and still, sometimes you get on level 2, sometimes you don't, sometimes you get once again. I think that the devs should have made another artifact which would guarantee an artifact drop (or even two). It's a win-win, since every artifact you select during a run - increases that run's difficulty. Or at least put an indicator on level selection where artifacts can still drop...Something like that. There is no need to have rng behind artifact acquisition. It's just gives more frustration than "Oh I need to do another run for a chance to get the last one!" kind of fun.Lastly, It is not a friendly game for your eyes. Many projectiles can make a discotheque on your screen if you choose the "right" abilities and their upgrades during your run and your fps can dip below 20 easily too.

_childDocuments_.review: Welp... I said I would change my review if they fixed the issues I had, and they have. In that example the variations likely don't really matter, but when it become crit dmg vs attack speed, then it gets a bit different.Overall... fun game. 8/10. _childDocuments_.review: A Captivating Descent into DarknessRating: ★★★★☆Review:Halls of Torment delivers a dark and atmospheric dungeon-crawling experience that will enthrall fans of the genre with its immersive world and challenging gameplay.From the moment you step foot into the foreboding halls of this twisted realm, you're enveloped in an atmosphere of dread and despair. The game's grim aesthetic and haunting soundtrack set the stage for a journey into the depths of darkness, where every corner holds new horrors to confront.One of the game's standout features is its procedurally generated dungeons, which offer endless replayability and a fresh challenge with each playthrough. The layout of each dungeon is dynamically generated, ensuring that no two runs are ever quite the same. This adds a layer of unpredictability to the gameplay, keeping players on their toes as they navigate the treacherous corridors and confront the malevolent denizens that lurk within.Combat in Halls of Torment is fast-paced and satisfying, with a variety of weapons and abilities at your disposal to dispatch your foes. The game's intuitive control scheme makes it easy to execute precise attacks and dodge incoming threats, adding a layer of depth to the gameplay that rewards skillful play.While the game's graphics may not rival those of AAA titles, they effectively convey the dark and oppressive atmosphere of the game world. The eerie lighting and detailed environments help to immerse players in the haunting setting of the Halls of Torment, heightening the sense of tension and foreboding as they explore its depths.That said, there are some areas where the game could be improved. The difficulty curve can be steep at times, particularly for newcomers to the genre, and some players may find themselves frustrated by the relentless onslaught of enemies. Additionally, while the procedurally generated dungeons offer replay value, they can also feel somewhat repetitive after extended play.In conclusion, Halls of Torment is a captivating dungeon-crawling experience that delivers thrills and chills in equal measure. With its atmospheric world, challenging gameplay, and endless replayability, it's sure to delight fans of the genre looking for their next dark adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Step into the Halls of Torment, and brace yourself for an exhilarating and terrifying experience as you explore the vast and perilous halls of a fallen realm. This captivating game delivers a gratifying gameplay loop, combining intense monster slaying and challenging boss battles with the thrill of collecting gold and discovering rare equipment in every run.Survival is no easy feat, as you must endure the treacherous journey for a full 30 minutes before facing the formidable end-of-level boss in each hall. Triumph in this battle, and you'll secure your hard-earned gold to invest in stat upgrades and gear purchases through the enigmatic well-keeper, who (once you find him!) will pull up your treasures from the depths below.. for a fee of course!For fans of Diablo II, Halls of Torment will feel familiar as it boasts retro graphics, an eerie demonic soundtrack, and a relentless difficulty level that promises to put your gaming skills to the test.Halls of Torment promises countless hours of entertainment and will undoubtedly leave you craving more. Its seemingly straightforward appearance belies the fact that it is destined to become a classic. Prepare to be enchanted by the dark allure of Halls of Torment and embark on an unforgettable adventure.This game is a tribute to a time when games were simple and fun, with surprisingly more depth than the surface would have you believe. Give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic, rogue-lite, horde-slayer similar in the vein of Vampire Survivors, with it's own genre; "Survivor-like"For those unfamiliar with the genre, the basic concept is to kill Mongolian hordes of monsters and demons, level up to get upgrades to your stats, weapons and abilities, and then survive as long as possible until you die or beat the final boss. Once your character dies, the run ends and get gold based on how much you picked up and your performance. Said gold can then be used to upgrade your stats for the next run and purchase items/potions you've acquired in the halls. Slowly, but steadily, you'll get stronger, unlock new classes and abilities, and make runs more chaotic and fun.Now onto the review:Absolute banger of a video game; has a great dark fantasy aesthetic with a simple yet pleasing set of visuals. Streamlined progression system based on acquiring items, potions and gold in your runs, which you can then use for future runs. Each class has it's own weapon and set of traits that let you personalize your play-style each time you enter the battlefield. Combat is very simple but also very satisfying when you take out 30 enemies in a single swing when you started out taking out one enemy in five hits. It's also incredibly intense the further you make it in the run, ESPECIALLY near the end. A good variety of classes, play-styles and items is fantastic for an early access game; especially one that's released not so long ago. Beyond the content, the game feels rigid without many, if any technical issues. Haven't had any game breaking issues nor crashes so far in the 12 hours of play. The only complaint I've had is that the game can take a hit on performance once you dealing damage to 100's of enemies at once, but that only happens for me near the end. Overall, fantastic game for a fantastic price that'll easily leave you hooked and satisfied. If you're at all a fan of Vampire Survivors, Diablo or PoE, I'm sure you'll fit right it. If not, this is a good entry to start your delve into the genre. I have good faith that they'll do right by this game and give us a grand experience once they've finished the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely phenomenal game iterating meaningfully on this emerging genre of "horde survivor".I really can't praise this game highly enough for really examining and understanding what makes the genre fun and where it can be improved. The systems are all crafted with the utmost care and work flawlessly together. The progression is smooth and fun - every run feels meaningful and different because pushing through focusing on different skills or stats is the way to progress fastest.There are subtle signs that show that immense thought and care have gone into crafting the player experience: there's no intro and minimal help but it's easy to get started and play. It's very easy to understand every decision that you need to make (no need for a wiki here) and it's easy to understand what you need to do next in order to hasten progression or unlock new content. Little details (like how the well only works once per run means that you may agonise over sacrificing your first piece of gear but you know for sure that you can keep your second piece without even thinking about it) may seem like limitations but they smooth out the progression and keep the runs enjoyable, even when they're being done largely for the grind.Even the way that some systems work in the background and add to the experience without even being noticed or understood (e.g., I didn't discover until several runs in that each unlocked achievement boosts XP gain by 0.5% but I was feeling the effects of it through longer, more powerful runs).This game knocks it out of the park as both a rougelite and a horde survivor. I would happily have paid $30 for this game and I really hope the devs get all the success that they deserve.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: The 1.0 release might have gone under a lot of people's radars due to factors such as timing and other "bigger" games releasing this month, but Halls of Torment is a testament to how well the ARPG/roguelite genre can actually shine if it reaches the apex of its form. From the top: mechanics and details of the game, depth of each class and map, replayability through heaps of achievements and build possibilities, all the way to the importance and utility of each skill/tree/unlock; Halls of Torment understands all the great qualities of games from the golden age of gaming (90s to early 2000s), resulting in a torrent of nostalgia reminding us of the peak form of games we all loved like Diablo, Torchlight, and Titan Quest.There's not much to be said other than the fact that I wholeheartedly wish games like these were introduced more to the younger generations, so that they know quality content can be included in a game without the use of a credit card being swiped every week.Halls of Torment has proven that "graphics isn't everything" and games can be enjoyed today equally as much as they were 20-30 years ago. With the right ingredients, this game is a reminder of what the gaming industry has become, and what it should return to being if it wants to survive.Buy this game. It's inexpensive, it's worth every penny, and it will remind you of what it means to "just kick back after a long day of work and have a good time enjoying video games."
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: It's not my favorite game in the genre. It's not bad, I suppose. And I like the nostalgic aesthetic.The gameplay is good. However, the runs take too long compared to other games in the genre and you begin thinking about your time management irl during the runs. HoT receiving a rework where the average duration of each normal run becomes about 15-22 mins would make it a far far far better game. 30 minutes for a run just feels unnecessarily long when you could be having way more fun in the same amount of time in another game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game play is simple at its face, but underneath it can be pretty complex. Don't let the simple graphics fool you. As you progress you unlock more passives to level up as well as characters (9 so far and the devs plan to release more). Progress unlocks passive bonuses that affects everything. Unlocks future equipment and traits you can see when leveling up. Each character feels unique and entirely different. One negative thing about the game and it is minor, is the lack of explanation with certain interactions and abilities/traits so you have to go to steam community for the answer. Sound is generic, but gets the job done. Or how to unlock certain quests. _childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from Vampire Survivors, this game feels like the next step in the right direction. This game has enough of a different feel, different mechanics, different leveling system, and different character functions to feel very distinct while offering a familiar gimmick and gameplay experience. This game also may be genuinely more difficult than Vampire Survivors, which isn't necessarily a huge feat, but the game makes you work for the power spikes you'd normally feel in Vampire Survivors, definitely requiring more technical skill to strafe enemies and more game sense to know which upgrades will best suit your character for the run. The game's progression is easy to pickup, as unlocks and objectives can be found before starting each new run, as well as permanent upgrades and equippable gear that modifies stats and abilities. I do have a small gripe with this game; the game does not hold your hand or help you understand much outside of the fundamental controls. I could see this being a rather frustrating learning curve, since the game expects you to learn a lot through trial and error or through repetition. This works for some and won't work for others; it is a bit hard to get into, but once the ball starts rolling and you start engaging with the content, understanding how the game works, the game becomes a lot more enjoyable. Only time will tell, but I think this game has the potential for me to like it even more than its other contemporaries. Another bonus are the plethora of achievements to collect, giving any player something to strive for and major satisfaction when obtaining many at a time. I would recommend this game to anyone, especially since the price is generous for the potential fun to be had. However, do some research to see if this game will be a good fit, it definitely will not be for everyone and the difficult learning curve could turn people away.

_childDocuments_.review: New York styled Pizza:Pizza dough:14 g instant yeast617g water - 95F950g all-purpose flour19g fine sea salt25g granulated sugarAmerican Pizza Sauce and Toppings:1 tablespoon (14g) butter1 tablespoon (9g) extra virgin olive oil6 cloves garlic, rough chopped2 teaspoons (4g) red pepper flakes28 oz (794g) can of crushed tomato2 teaspoons (2g) dried oregano1.5 tablespoons (21g) granulated sugarsalt and pepper to tasteSplash of olive oil2 cups (227g) low moisture mozzarella, fresh grated2 cups (200g) Monterey jack cheese, fresh grated1/2 cup (26g) parmigiano reggiano, fresh gratedAmerican Pizza Dough:Preheat the oven and a baking steel or pizza stone at 500F for 45 minutes before utilizing it.Whisk yeast and sugar into your water, and allow it to sit for 5 minutes. In a separate bowl, add flour and salt and mix by hand to combine. Pour your water mixture into your flour and mix by hand until you get a rough dough, then transfer to a work surface and knead until it starts to pull away from the work surface and is relatively smooth.Place your dough in a greased bowl, then cover with plastic wrap and let rise for 1 - 2 hours at room temperature or until double in size.Punch down your dough and dive into 300g pieces. Form those pieces into balls and place them in a floured proofing pizza box, cover with a lid, and proof at room temperature for 3 - 4 hours. (If you do not have a proofing pizza box, you can use a floured baking sheet, cover it with an inverted baking sheet and wrap it in plastic wrap.)American Pizza Sauce and Toppings:In a medium sauce pot, add butter and olive oil. Set that over medium-high heat; once the butter melts add garlic, cook until fragrant, add pepper flakes, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the garlic begins to brown on the edges.Add crushed tomatoes, oregano, salt, and a splotch of olive oil, boil over medium-high, reduce heat to low, and simmer for 12 minutes, stirring occasionally or until thickened and viscous—season with salt to taste and let it cool down.Assembly.- Place one of your pizza doughs onto a floured pizza peel, and flour your dough generously.Punch your dough down in the center, working your way out to create a ¼” wide. Pick up your dough, place it over your closed fists, and rotate it around, gently stretching to 13” to 14”.Place a couple of spoons of your sauce, starting in the center, spreading in little circles, and working your way to the edge until it gets evenly spread out.In a medium-size mixing bowl, place mozzarella cheese, Monterey Jack, and Parmigiano; mix until combined. Sprinkle your cheese mixture to your desire and place in the oven onto your baking steel and bake for 5 - 7 minutes or until the edge gets golden brown and the cheese melts.Enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Started with Vampire Survivors, I think I'll end up sticking with this game in the long run because of the incredible dark fantasy style and much better mechanics and design overall (not to mention frequent updates). Seems like a lot of passion has gone into this, with more to come. Honestly can say I'd buy this for $30+, but I'll say what everyone has already; "try it yourself, it's only 5 bucks anyways."
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: While I enjoy this game for what it is, I can't help but feel disappointed at the missed potential. The game is a Vampire Survivors clone with Diablo-esque itemization thrown in. But in what I can only assume to be an attempt to avoid over complicating the game, it ends up feeling very watered down in both aspects. Leveling traits are straight stat number increases that are filled with obvious oblivion targets (basically banishing) like defense and HP regen speed. Even in full release, there are skills that are just objectively better than others, and the difference is not small either. Transfixion is among the strongest in the game while Frost Avalanche is among the weakest, and the difference between having them is night and day.Items are just stat sticks for the most part with very few of them offering interesting game play changes. The ones that do offer interesting game play changes are typically weaker even on hero's with builds tailored to abuse them. The highest rarity of item you can farm for is also only uncommon, as you are not allowed to keep rare items that you find during runs (you're also not allowed to keep uncommon items until you reach the endgame).The result is that your runs end up feeling very repetitive. They're also 30 minutes long unless you obtain and enable an artifact that makes them 20 minutes long. There's no real turbo mode, and you'll spend those 20 minute agony runs doing the same thing you've been doing the entire time. Picking the same traits, the same abilities, the same ability upgrades, and rerolling chests for the same rare items that you don't even get to keep.I still enjoy the game for what it is, but its important to point out how repetitive it gets. If that doesn't bother you, try it.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Seems simple but the more you play and unlock the more insane each run can become on its own. from the warrior who can barely hit 2-3 enemies at first but by endgame with gear and unlocks can aoe circle over screen with just basic attacks. A ton of stuff to experiment with that isnt so cookie cutter like in other iterations of these games.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun with a lot of interesting build choices to be made. A lot of in-depth synergies between perks and general stats. About every single ability is viable, save for like 2-3 that require a lot more stat allocation just around them. As of the time of this review, I've managed to 100% it and I consider it a very fun experience; the price is more than justified. Game crashed on me like 3 times, likely due to the absolute chaotic SFX nature of some builds at max level on certain characters, but up until the point where I afforded to have such ludicrously stacked builds, it didn't occour once.I cannot really find a fault with this game, other than maybe some balance around certain characters being baseline underwhelming when compared to others ( Norseman, and Beast Huntress to a lesser degree).
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: A great Survivors-like game that even surpasses its inspiration in some areas. The aspects where Vampire Survivor falls short, in my opinion, are presentation and atmosphere—it's functional, but not much more. Halls of Torment, on the other hand, truly shines in this regard: the environments, settings, presentation, UI, sounds, and characters have a very convincing style reminiscent of the early Diablo games. It's not perfect, though—I personally wish the game leaned even more into this direction, shortened the gameplay time, and instead created a denser atmosphere with more NPC interactions and lore or a different style of gameplay beyond the classic VS horde mode.The gameplay itself is also very fun however, though the different abilities aren’t as distinct as those in Vampire Survivors. The various classes do have notable differences, but some are still a bit too similar or don’t offer enough uniqueness.All in all, Halls of Torment is well worth it if you enjoy Survivors-like games, especially since it offers amazing value, even at full price. 4/5
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, it's an okay game. Played it for a bit, was fun for a little while, but the upgrades for leveling are really boring, the spells you can acquire aren't really creative at all, and the gameplay loop gets really repetitive.It does bring a Diablo-like "gear/equipment" system, but they are just a bunch of stats without much thought put into them. For the same price tag, I'd recommend Death Must Die.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, but i realized the only "fun" runs are the ones, where you get a "Hand of Greed" pickup at the end of the run (pulls in all XP gems).Some runs they just don't wanna drop and it feels like i have wasted 30 minutes...Not picking it up and waiting till the very end is a valid strategy, yes.But it just feels annoying to hover around an area and missing out on other potential vases/crates/barrels for buffs, food or health pots.Idk i don't like this playstyle, it doesn't feel strategic, rather laborious...But for the low price and the time i have spent on it, i would still recommend it.7.5/10Edit: No matter what Build/Gear/Ability/Trait combo you try, Warlock is F-Tier compare to all other classes.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Can recommend this game. It's a genuinely cool twist on the genre Vampire Survivors pioneered, adding unique weapons for each Character alongside Equipment loadouts for even greater customisation before you even step into the Halls. Once you do, you have myriad abilities to choose from as you progress, each with their own upgrade paths which you unlock and choose from as you progress through the game and it's challenges. Challenges which test your ability to get the most out of every character and every ability.My only snag with this game, as is likely something somewhat personal, is I had sound issues the entire time I played Halls of Torment. Apparently, having done a bit of research, this has something to with users of Focusrite external audio devices. It results in the audio lagging behind and becoming distorted, either gradually as you play or pretty much immediately. I'm hopeful this is something that can be fixed, considering this is still an Early Access title, but something to be aware of potentially.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: One of the better Survivors-likes I've played. And I've played so many of them, I'm embarrassed to admit which ones. In that subgenre it does many things right and I'm thoroughly absorbed by this game already.That being said, if you're expecting a Diablo-ish ARPG experience, you will probably be disappointed. It has Diablo graphics, a Diablo theme and a bunch of progression systems that look like Diablo, but really aren't (Items that are just unlockable upgrades, quests that are just achievements, etc.). Other than that, it's just a very good Vampire Survivors imitator.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying this game. Fun characters and weapons allow for unique builds. I would love to see more dungeons and enemy types added in the future, but I've already got way more out of this game than I expected. I think it's subjective but I also really love the aesthetics of the game. Really fun to pick up and play.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: A horde survival game with lots of characters and unlockables to customize them with.Presentation is similar to the early Diablo, Fallout and Legacy of Kain games. More of a Twin Stick shooter compared to Vampire Survivors.The variety of monsters, bosses and power-ups feels good in this game!Devs have been active in updating the game too!Def worth the low price! A real stand-out horde blast!I also like how achievements are handled, giving you even more equipment and power ups to unlock in future runs. Makes trying out the different characters and builds more rewarding!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only about 5 runs in BUT, I like big buts, I cannot lie, games like this i haven't ever liked and I really likie this one. A lot. _childDocuments_.review: the best survivors-like game i've played of the 20+ full games and demos in this genre. it's fully thought out and designed, many characters and weapons, tons of abilities, hard achievements that are meaningful for progression, etc. etc. it takes the best parts from some of the titans of the survivors genre and packs it in this wonderful 90's graphic style. extremely satisfying to play, easily addicting, and lots of room for progression.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Man this game is pure genius game design. The wau you level up traits, the fact that you can equip items but you have to retrieve them first from a well and then byt them, the abilities that add more flavor, the potion system just exellent. Took the survivors genre and made it their own. This game is just so good designed. Kudos to the devs and highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: This game is simply amazing. The diabloish design paired with Vampire Survivor's gameplay is a really good match, it's fun, it's nervous, it's hard.One of the must fun meta progression I ever seen on this kind of game, not rellying on farming ressources but rather by achieving some quests (and some of them are really hard to do). And as the final quests are complex, the game remains a challenge even after 65h+ of play. The number of possible combinations (spells/equipment/potions/characters, etc.) makes every game different.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first run, and I'm really impressed!Vampire Survivors + manual aiming. Diablo aesthetic with graphics and music.Intensity starts out higher than VS and keeps escalating. Manual aiming adds engagement and challenge. There is an option for auto-aim but I didn't have it enabled.Sound and music are good. Mowing down hordes of skeletons and hearing their clinking bones crumble to the ground is very satisfying.Enemy variety is good and new enemy types keep coming at you throughout the run. There are boss characters to focus down while managing enemy hordes coming at you. Very engaging.Native Linux client. Full controller support.Looking forward to playing more and seeing where this game goes!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine Diablo, but all the enemies come to you and swarm you. You need to evade a bit and kill dozens of thousands of them.You fail, but you can get now some upgrades and...you die again, but you can kill them more. As you progress, you unlock new characters, new gear, new features, new quests and achievements.Game is fun, so far no feeling of getting stuck, but also not getting stuff for free.Also, this game has the dark sinister feeling of Diablo 1, which I totally love.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, fun to just pick up and play, keep in mind assuming you don't die each game is 35 Minutes (30 Min plus select gear and traits) so don't start a game if you have 10 minutes or you will not want to stop! Easy to learn but has a lot of depth if you are trying to get all the achievements. Only gripe I have is I have unlocked everything possible and hate it in runs when it drops gold and not a scroll or gear for improvement as gold is now useless, and I have had runs where 80% of the drops are gold, I know its all random but its annoying. Don't let that detract you this game for its price point and fun is 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Spent 3 hours in this game and really do not get all these overwhelmingly positive reviews. It's the same as Vampire Survivors, with better graphics, but worse gameplay and super boring skills. Enemies suck big time. Skeletons. Skeletons with shields (fun as f***), slimes of different colors, poop-like beasts - that is all. Also, what is the point of collectin all these healing items if they restore less hp than one basic enemy attack takes?A big thumbs down.P.S. Music is great tho.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I love the graphics, and I love the character customization. My biggest gripe of this game is that it punishes the player with unneeded drawn out fluff. I get that there isn't a lot of content, but drawing things out is not entertaining, and in fact mind numbing and boring. After about 5 minutes of fighting the end boss, I was sitting there saying to myself, "Unless I just let them kill me, I am going to be here for an hour doing nothing but wasting my time with no sense of accomplishment."
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I played this first, and then Vampire Survivors afterwards. Had to refund the vampire game, since I was used to the high standards of the Halls of Torment. It's a fantastic game with a coherent artstyle, nice music, and a certain flow in gameplay that is great. Haven't managed all ingame "quests" (= achievements) yet but I'm not far from it either, it's def some of the best times I had. Big plus for each playthrough being a pre-determined ~ 30 minutes which makes it great for an in-between session. Big recommendation!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I wholeheartedly recommend this game.Pro tip:Do the quests for the $, get blessings, focus on traits that suit you and your items.Also, rescue the dang wellkeeper already!I came over from the prelude, I've already beaten lord on first stage. It's very doable, difficulty is not a thing here. The more quests you do, the more xp bonus you get, so you put in the time and you get worth out of your dime. Don't think you'll beat it in your first run, unless chuck norris was your dad.I'm in love with this game. It's well put together.Audio is good, music is fine and fits the atmosphere. The art is amazing.The gameplay however, feels really good, it feels responsive, when i want to do something it does it. When i take damage, it was my own fault for having fat fingers.All in all, I give this game an 8. It's well worth your lunch money.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: A fun take on something that looks like it was ripped out of old Diablo mixed with Vampire Survivors gameplay.  Instead of amassing a whole set of weapons in a run of Halls of Torment, you tend to have a character, their main weapon, 1-2 additional power up shots, and various equipment stuff in between.  By default there is a need to manually fire and manually aim which adds a different element to the game since this is opposite of VS where everything is done automatically.For the price it is worth a shot anytime while it is still in Early Access.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Love the CRONCH. Such a satisfying game to play, this is also the only bullet hells I've played were your positioning makes a noticeable difference, letting you corral enemies to mitigate the damage your taking and deal huge AOE attacks in return. The achievements are challenging, but not impossible, making it a great title for people looking to 100% clear as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: A very good entry into the Survivors genre (vampiresurvivorlike? Who knows). The crunchy graphics remind me a lot of diablo 1, the gameplay is basic, as is expected from games of this genre, but still different enough from VS to feel fresh, the upgrade system is nice and has a lot of strategy to it rather than just "make number go bigger", there is some actual build variety. The meta-progression is also quite helpful and makes you feel a lot stronger with enough time and upgrades. I wish some stats (like Force) were a bit better explained, but overall it's a solid experience with very good replayability for early access.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Yup.It's the best of the survivors games.It never slows down.It feels like old school Diablo, or Gauntlet.Gameplay feel is solid and weighty, unlike other survivors games which usually feel floaty to me.Different enemy types employ different tactics to attack you, only sometimes swarming in a bullet-hell style pattern, which is hella satisfying to navigate. You can push enemies back, it matters where you aim the cursor, and you can step through tiny gaps between enemies sometimes, which is also hella satisfying.The smaller pickups that most enemies drop will level up to improve stuff like walking speed, blocking strength (yeah blocking is a thing in this) as well as to power up your weapons, but they don't actually give you any new weapons, such as in other survivors games.Larger enemies (the ones with health bars) drop lots of gold, plus either a new weapon to add to your arsenal, or a treasure chest, which give wearable rpg-style items, like armour.If you have access to "The Well" you can give wearable items to the wellkeeper, which loses them for the rest of that run, but enables you to buy those items back from the wellkeeper in the hub area and give them to your characters permanently.When you first buy the game, you don't have access to many spells/weapons, stages, or characters (just one at first) but all of that grows quickly. I have about 11 characters after 20 hours, all levels and tons of items.Most importantly, you can summon golums and imps and skeletons.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: The epitome of 'bang for your buck'.This game could easily have been four times as expensive and it would still be worth it. Took me over 100 hours to 100% the game but I do think people could do it faster. This 'survivors' genre is getting crowded and hard to see true value when they often play and feel the same with similar ideas. However the variety is there to have it's own impact. The aesthetic of a mid-late 90's dungeon crawler/RTS works very well with the gameplay too and sets itself apart from other games that play similarly.Each quest being it's own achievement kept me playing and wanting to return by showing the end goal(s) and makes progression feel more rewarding. Once you reach a certain point you can beat almost any run with a specific build, but there's still enough variety in the characters, equipment, abilities, artifacts and spec building etc that there's likely combos and builds you would never think to try but would be super fun. The quests do force you to try other ideas which was welcoming too.The difficulty is spot on for me, but I do feel more skilled players would want a bit more of a challenge in places even with the artifacts adding debuffs, nerfs and negative modifiers.Well worth the price-tag and I hope to play others like it!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Good auto-slasher for the weekends. It has well-working game loop - equip the loot you have collected previously, kill them all, find new piece and try to get it out of the map in order to collect itImplementing some in-session/in-game skill\spell customization alike talent trees will definitely help the game get its depth and offer some real build crafting.

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely can't play this game without falling asleep. I have to do some Nightmare on Elm Street to try and make it all the way to the end of a 30 minute level. If you want a game that makes you take a nap, this is very much a recommendation. If not, probably skip.To begin with, I was interested in trying this one out because of two things:1. Classic Diablo aesthetic, which the game wears on its sleeve2. Vampire Survivors format but with more control over your attacksI like twin-stick shooters and grew up with some schlocky ones, like Aline Shooter and Zombie Shooter, so I was kinda hoping that it could scratch that sort of itch. Huge mistake, massive.While yes, you do get more control here and have to make more decisions, it puts HoT in this awkward space where it's not hands-off enough to stand AFK and let the numbers squirt out onto the screen, yet it's also not engaging enough to really get into the game. If you can, please refer to the flow state chart right now. As you can see, the flow state happens when the challenge and skill almost perfectly allign. If the challenge too high for the skill it gets stressful, and if it's too low it gets boring. HoT is the latter. You have to move around and aim but you don't have to think, you don't have to actually aim, so I think the brain just shuts off during this time to spare itself from acknowledging that its user is pretty much just pouring water from one cup to another in perpetuity (30 minutes).It feels bad to say this because the game is otherwise pretty well made. They fleshed out the visuals, the music is a perfect fit, sound effects are on point, and for those who want an infinite grind game, it sure seems like there's a lot to grind. There's milestones you need to reach for certain unlocks, multiple stages to clear, permanent upgrades to every stat in the world, a whole equipment system that is designed in a way that makes permanent unlocks excruciatingly slow. People who work in coal mines will come home thankful that they don't have to grind as hard as you do. That said, I legit just can't play it because I end up nodding off and taking damage.If you do want yourself a roguelite twin stick shooter though, shout out to Crimsonland. They were doing this over two decades ago and it's still fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Halls of Torment is a great addition to the Survivor-Like genre. It brings with it a Diablo-style set of graphics, and is isometric as a result. People have said that the game is more straightforward than Vampire Survivors. I think that mainly applies to the abilities. Every upgrade to health, damage, defense, etc. has a detailed description on how it will effect you in-game. For abilities that branch based on what character and weapons you have, you are able to see what you will lose as a result of picking one of the branches over the other. Characters are fewer than in VS, meaning that you don't get the girth of combinations. However, each character has a special weapon. Apart from the scrolls you pick up after mini-bosses, these are hardlocked to the character and are not changeable. But, some armor/charm unlocks not too late into the game do have modifiers that could, lets say, change the damage type. For instance, an amulet of the fire element might change your sword from a physical damage type to fire damage. Without spoiling the story, I'll leave you with this... It's a cool game for early access. I only encountered one glitch and luckily, it happened after my run was over so I could just exit the game and not have to worry! So overall, just try it! You won't be disappointed!

_childDocuments_.review: I asked an AI  what it thinks of HoT."Halls of Torment emerges as a beacon of excellence in the shadow of Diablo IV's lackluster attempt at dark fantasy. Unlike its competitor, Halls of Torment doesn't just invite players into the underworld; it immerses them in an enthralling blend of survival and strategy. The relentless onslaught of terrifying monsters keeps players on their toes, delivering a true challenge that Diablo IV fails to muster. With each descent into the Halls of Torment, the game unveils a dynamic and ever-expanding array of treasures, coupled with a diverse cast of heroes that elevates the gameplay to new heights.Diablo IV, on the other hand, seems trapped in a cycle of uninspired demons and predictable encounters, lacking the freshness and excitement that defines Halls of Torment. The latter not only triumphs in creating a gripping atmosphere but also excels in providing a roguelite experience where every triumph feels hard-earned and every defeat sparks a burning desire for redemption. _childDocuments_.review: There's a... problem with Vampire Survivors - it's made so good that any game that tries to replicate it is at a huge disadvantage. There are many, and I believe while 20MTD was the closest, it's still far apart from the original.Halls of Torment understands it well. It doesn't try to replicate VS, but it tries to expand on the core idea, and puts a clever twist to it. An equipment system, which is deceptively simple, but satisfying. Change from single to twin-stick gameplay. Challenges have simple missions woven in-between to give an impression of steady progress. Characters actually differ in playstyle instead of just only weapon.A lot of people bring similarities to Diablo, because of setting and equipment. Fair point. But I'd also bring a difference between VS and HoT which is especially visible in late of the run. Whereas in VS at the end of the run you're god of destruction and can basically AFK the entire waves, Halls of Torment is then more similar to... Touhou. Your player character has very small hitbox, intentionally so, so you can, with a little bit of skill, dodge whole waves of enemies. There's not a lot of "golden hammers", because every character differs so much in playstyle - while Crit and Damage would be great on Archer, they are useless on Exterminator (attack speed is good everywhere though).In short - most fun I had in the game since several months. It is much harder than VS, but at least as much as satisfying. It's tough, but it's (mostly) fair. $5, native Linux build and runs beautifully on Deck - it's a no-brainer.

_childDocuments_.review: Unquestionably the best game for the price point. Couldn't have asked for a better experience nor updates for the game with the current price tag as it stands. GOTY material right here.If you guys want to take something to improve on; continue optimizing the game until you get so much head-room with the frame-times so you can gradually keep on increasing the amount of concurrent enemies on the screen (assuming you're hitting 300+ enemies 5 times/s in a cone-area, while dealing DOT and AOE, doing all those calculations while moving).This would definitely allow you guys (the best Devs<3) to expand and flesh out your own visions (also the players', when required) for the future capabilities and game modes. I'm kind of hoping that this game will keep its' perfect and simplicit design, but make it possible for the player to keep engaged for a longer period of time, resulting in replayability.If you're asking for something concretely analogous to my previous point; I'd throw out something along the lines of Diablo III:s `Torment` -difficulties.I'm not saying you "SHOULD" implement that exact system, but something along the general idea of what that system is designed to achieve -- it's not intrusive, nor game breaking. Nor is it trying to sell you something which takes away from the player or from the overall game experience. That system achieves at giving more headroom for increased play-time and thus more opportunities to get even more hooked to explore and try out new things, like builds.The next idea which would totally make the game "endless" and exciting would be procedurally-generated maps from the assets. Going beyond that, maybe having some mip-mapping so that you could have "biomes" that interpolate smoothly from one map style to the other, which would then trigger biome-specific mob spawning in the early game. Maybe even put a rare cartography table as an item somewhere hidden inside the "starting" chunk-zone so that you can open an overlayed map to show the outlines where you've been, but I'd say -don't- display locations of any crates, items, etc.After this, I would argue to incorporate endless waves/hordes/survival -mechanic where the timer goes reversed (how long can you survive). Also probably a good idea to disable the revive blessing and the ring from this game-mode (or make it an option to disable it, by which you could for example, give the player +x% XP gain while revive is turned off, or post-increment the torment score by a factor of some percentage that seems fair and balanced [thinking of leaderboards]). A substitute for this could be having a generic "Hardcore" mode which would achieve just the same, which might better suit the perfect simplicit game-logic design.Thank you so much for this game<3

_childDocuments_.review: Aggressively bland and unimaginative.There are very few skills and the choices you make during a run are extremely boring and limited. Just static 10-20% bonuses to move speed/attack speed/crit chance/crit damage. No synergy at all, which is the point of these games. Every run feels the same because you're never going to get that "perfect" combo of skills because there are no skills and they have no interplay and synergy. The bonuses you DO choose won't make you overpowered, either, they'll increase your power at about the same rate as the enemies, so everything just feels samey throughout. Presumable once you've bought enough permanent upgrades for gold, this will change, but the meta progression system is ABSURDLY grindy and unrewarding. Build variation is virtually non-existent and you have a good idea of exactly when you're going to die on any given run based on how many of the meta-upgrades you have been able (or more likely unable) to afford between runs.Many deaths feel cheap in a way that other survivors games don't. I often feel like my deaths in this game are a result of the game throwing unfair obstacles such as massive waves of enemies that cannot be avoided and serve only as a defense/health check in order to kill you until you've upgraded you stats enough to weather the storm. Other (good) survivors games give you more control over that via interesting and powerful choices while this game just... Doesn't. When I die in Death Must Die or Vampire Survivors, for instance, I can usually pinpoint the mistake I made, whether it be my choice of skills or immediate actions before my death. That isn't the case in Halls of Torment. Much of the time I've had a pack of enemies spawn right on top of me (or close to it) and it was obvious that I was at the point that I was SUPPOSED to die because I have to grind for several more hours to afford a 40% health upgrade. It's very bad design and feels extremely demoralizing. The opposite of what these games are supposed to feel like.The bosses all have attacks that telegraph as circles on the ground but you have no mobility skills that I am aware of to avoid them, so you just walk away from them. Feels extremely low energy and not exciting at all. Bosses in general are just massively spongy and aren't really a threat as much as an annoyance. It's the waves of enemies that spawn with them that are challenging, but as mentioned earlier, often just an unfair defense/health check.The loot you receive is just as uninspired at the stat upgrades you choose during waves. Flat % bonuses to the exact same pool of stats you choose from when you level up. From what I have seen, they have no other unique or interesting effects. Many of the stats are also not explained properly via tool tips, such as "Impact" which tells the player to refer to some other part of the game for more info which of course you can't do during a run.Looking at the forums, it seems like many of the updates are not well received and that the game has some sever balance issues with regards to some of the classes.I don't say this lightly, because it's an extremely overused critique of games and it's often undeserved and it sounds pretty harsh, but this game really feels kind of lazy to me. It's just an extremely flavorless and obviously padded-out game with an extremely grindy meta-progression system that only further emphasizes its lack of creativity and direction.Maybe it gets way better once you invest hours into it, but it's given me no reason to waste that time when much better survivors games exist and the refund window is two hours. If it does have a lot more to offer, then it should really showcase more of it earlier on.Play Death Must Die or Vampire Survivors instead. Both are leagues better than this and are extremely fun to play from the very first minute.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an iteration on Vampire Survivors (addictive roguelike action RPG with autocast) that mixes in a heavy dose of Diablo I worship.Aside from touches like an actual equipment system, the game is much more mobility-based than VS... It's harder to set up static killboxes, and you'll have to keep moving around for more than bosses in most scenarios. The bosses are also much more interesting and have actual attacks and AOEs.This has more bullet hell DNA than VS, but is still fairly forgiving as long as you're making any effort to move around/play to your current character's strengths. You might consider it a problem that you have to be more actively involved in playing than you typically do in VS. It's harder to level and gear.The look, music, and sound is essentially 100% Diablo I, for good or ill.My biggest hope at this point is for a game speed slider.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great game before the latest patch, but the changes made really feel like they have been made for the sake of frustrating players. Enemies have been made harder.Items have been made weaker.Achievements have been made more difficult to acquire. (and not in a good way)This is all especially apparent in the newly added area and the new hard mode called Agony, where a lot of characters and builds don't even function properly. And that's not including the plethora of bugs introduced, missing icons & enemy behavior being aberrant. The entire patch feels rushed.All in all it's kind of a miss as of right now, hopefully they will make the game more viable to play free-form without having to look up rigid build paths like it was before this patch. I implore the devs to stop trying to balance this game as if it's an esport, and instead focus on the great pick-up-and-play feeling the game had before.

_childDocuments_.review: Has potential. I get it’s trying to be vampire survivors but with more skill. You can aim weapons, can’t get too overpowered, bosses have attacks that require skill to dodge, enemy attacks like lasers and such require more situational awareness. These are good things to add to the genre. Unfortunately, the game design just doesn’t hit well enough to really offer  such potential and ultimately culminates in a sloggish grind, slow and tedious gameplay, and a lack of replayability. Meta currency takes too long and the upgrades feel so incremental.  The game itself has so much dead time, with only few minutes per run offering much of any tangible gameplay.  Bosses in early parts of the run are absolutely insanely spongy, requiring sometimes 5+ minutes of shooting a pea shooter to take down, base movement speed is too slow and leads to unavoidable deaths, level up upgrades are extremely boring and extremely incremental stat upgrades that feel meaningless, the characters themselves don’t differ enough in movement speed or overall stats to be interesting. There’s not really much “secrets”, features or modes to unlock like in vampire survivors.  No turbo/hurry mode, for example. Overall, the game had potential to be a better Vampire Survivors with more active and skillful gameplay. unfortunately, its gameplay design is just overall too timid and incremental, and the combat is too spongy, tedious, and limited to take advantage of the potential. In the end, its ironic that such an inactive gameplay design like Vampire Survivors without even weapon aiming can offer more skillful gameplay due to its more bold and flexible level up stats, character differences, leveling systems, and additional modifiers/modes.  I do not recommend Vampire Survivors either (check my review), but I can’t say this game is an improvement on the formula, as VS does succeed in many ways.  Still waiting on a game in this genre that truly requires an engaging amount skill and strategy.
