_childDocuments_.review: When I first bought the game a few months back, it was a blast and had tons of fun. Each character plays differently enough to keep the game fresh. I loved working through the blessings and quests. The music and characters are top notch, especially coming from a $5 title.The last 2 updates (including the one from today) have taken a lot of the fun away. I'm not 100% sure on details for what was changed. Experience seems to be nerfed into the ground which leveling up was a lot of the fun. I use to get to around level ~105 on the 3rd stage. After the last 2 updates, I can't even complete the stage now using similar 'tried and true' builds. On the first stage, I end up at around level ~60, previously was ~90. I know the jade xp amulet was nerfed (warranted but give the xp elsewhere?).I thought the game was about a power fantasy and slowly getting to the point where you can make any build/skill work and be fun. From other comments and posts, it seems this game is no longer for me and is meant to be a bit more on the hardcore side instead of just blasting through enemies.I guess I've gotten my money's worth at 52 hours so I can't complain too much. I would not recommend this game anymore to people like me who are looking for a bit more casual power fantasy experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game should be illegal like other dopamine-flooding, addictive substances.I was initially lured in by its gateway drug, "The Halls of Torment: Prelude" and eventually found myself where I am now.The more you play, the more It becomes so infuriatingly addictive.  I am finally contemplating deleting this game from my library as a step towards detox and rehab,,STAY AWAY, especially if you love watching those vacuum cleaner ads, industrial rubbish shredding demonstrations, carpet cleaning videos, or anything that involves similar themes.  I cannot emphasise this enough. For those who choose to play, it may be useful to know the following prior to venturing into The Halls of Torment.You may;1) Experience arousal as you watch your powerful All-in-One vacuum-shredder chew through batch after batch of filthy debris, processing them into shiny blue, yellow and purple remnants.  2) Achieve wave after wave of increasingly agonising climaxes as your powerful machine sucks up the scattered remnants and offers you options to make it even more effective at its job.  3) Feel your eyes glaze over and drool escape from the corner of your quivering mouth as your brain becomes overloaded with pleasurable, real-time monitoring about how your uber-machine is performing via overlapping, flashing, red and white numerical feedback.  They will ultimately become illegible but by that stage in the game, you may find their legibility irrelevant.4) Experience post-nut clarity and regret as you realise how many hours of your finite life you had cumulatively spent upgrading and testing your virtual vacuum-shredder.5) Eventually realise the name of the game is a fitting metaphor for your own life.You have been warned.----------------------------References: trust me bro

_childDocuments_.review: Diablo I meets Vampire SurvivorsAs in Vampire Survivors, you control your character's movement with WASD. But not like in Vampire Survivors there is the possibility to aim with the main weapon itself and hit with the mouse. The option with automatic aiming and hitting can be toggled one at a time by pressing a button.The game already gives a lot of options for builds. When leveling up in a run, you can select traits that boost stats like critical hit rate, movement speed, attack speed and much more.Bosses can drop items for a character to equip, for example a ring that switches the damage of the main weapon to fire and thus unlocks more build options that centrally buff the fire damage. These items can later be permanently unlocked, then you start a run with these items, which you can previously equip to a character.Furthermore, there are ability scrolls that unlock abilities for a character in a run (e.g. Dragon's Breath, an ability that throws a wall of fire in the direction of the cursor).At the time of writing, there are only 3 halls but each hall has a different setting, different enemies, different bosses and unique end bosses that correspond to the setting of the hall.All in all a pretty good early access game with even more content planned. Best 5 euro I spent on a game in the last few days.

_childDocuments_.review: Short answer: Playing the Exterminator with the right gear and abilities turns this into a pyro simulator and is extremely fun to play. Just look at this screenshot I took and tell me that the fire doesn't look glorious. Come for the Diablo looking Survivors game and stay for the fire. Crank up hits such as "Born of Fire" by Slayer and "Burn it Up" by Offspring and you will have a great time.If that didn't get your interest here is a more detailed review.The two things that brought me into the door for this game was it was survivors like game and I find those fun, and it had the aesthetics that reminded me of watching my parents play the original Diablo when I was a kid. Needless to say since I am recommending this game, I have a lot of fun with it. To start with I want to talk about the two NPCs that standout for me: the wellkeeper and the cupbearer.Once you save the wellkeeper you can find items in the halls that you can send to him. This is important as once you send an item you then have access to it buy from him and once bought you can never lose the item and you can equip it as part of your kit before you move out into the halls. That's right! You risk your life to not find the item but also save the guy and you still have to buy it from him.Once you save the cupbearer you have access to potions that will allow you to do various things such as reroll, banish and other good things. All you have to do is save the guy, risk your life to find the ingredients, risk your life to find a bottle for him to fill and then buy the bottle from the wellkeeper guy. (The wellkeeper guy must be related to Tom Nook somehow or learned from him or something.)The next thing this game provides to help boost your power is the ability to buy blessings which give you a permanent boost such as doing more damage, raising defense, revive and all that good stuff. Getting achievements actually provides an in game benefit in the form of boosting your earned XP. So while the Exterminator class maybe the most fun, it is still worth playing the other classes to get the achievements associated with their class to help raise the boost of XP you get. This will be really helpful for when you decide to tackle the Agony versions of stages as it makes them more challenging. This game to me seems to be more challenging than other games of this type I have played but I think that just adds to the fun factor of it and is most assuredly worth your time to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Initially it seems like a rather shallow, slower-paced Survivors game, but the deeper you get, the more the complexity comes out. "Winning" isn't particularly difficult, but there's a lot (200+ as of now, still in EA) of in-game challenges (which are also achievements) that have rewards and unlocks associated with them - those are the real game. Some of them are fairly easy, but others require some real effort to 'solve'.The unlockable potions are also surprisingly deep. They let you affect the upgrades you're offered in various ways - rerolling them, saving one for later, doubling the effects of one, or removing one from the pool entirely; this is a much more important system than it initially looks like, too. The 'save an upgrade for later' one actually lets you take two normally mutually exclusive upgrades, and choosing what to double is a very important decision for some builds.There's a lot of characters (who all have unique achievements and who all play differently), and at the current time 5 maps, and a 'hard mode' on each map, as well. Really, there's a lot of content here, and it's well worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game for the price, plenty of stuff to do and I bet the developer will bring more stuff with time. Its and easy buy, you won't regret it!Abilites are fun, traits are very good and well balanced for the most part (will talk more about that later) and you have A LOT of unique characters to choose from, each one completely changing the way you play the game.Visuals are nice, animations are good and sound is well developed. Boss fights are unique and challenging and throughout the maps you learn a few of the attacks the final boss will use, very nice touch of game design there.Improvements needed:-Some traits seems useless, incrementing 0.05 of any base stats its a waste 99% of the time even with all the percentages upgrades applied on top of it.-The "course" traits are also useless (like the one that gives you fragility and something else), it would be nice to gain some buff at the cost of getting the debuff, maybe after each course, all traits multipliers could be increased by X% or something like that.-We should be able to open the inventory from the trait selection menu, some times I can't remember if I need 10% critical rate or if I already reached my desired %, or I can't remember if an ability is affected by a certain trait.-Some items should display what buff they are giving when you hover over it on the main interface in the right side, for example the Mask of Madness, I need pause the game and hover over crit rate, crit dmg, attack speed, multistrike... to see the % stats provided by the mask.-Boss items collected on each stage by completing a small quest should give a description of what that item do when you hover over it. That is a REALLY cool design that gives you a purpose and a little help on each map but after you get the item you don't really know what that item does.-Its easy to get bosses stuck behind walls (specially on chamber of dissonance) allowing you to cheese some of the fights.-After you finish the final boss fight you should immediately be teleport out of the map, you can cheese some quests like the Golem total rolling time and archer walking distance.-Maybe a little buff to Dragon Breath (or maybe I wan't able to use it properly) but it seems like the ability does not follow the same progression as the others. Maybe a speed buff to the wave is enough because a lot of the time the enemy is killed before the wave get to it.

_childDocuments_.review: A very solid Survive-Rogue. Ironically by being one of the most "return to form" variants out there, it's also one of the more unique as it handles in a much different way than your usual Survival-like. This is a plus for me but some people may just want the stack abilities on abilities until everything is dead approach compared to Halls' more traditional hack and slash build.Upgrades are meaningful and there are a lot of achievements and unlock for you completionists like me who crave the dopamine hit of seeing that little rectangle box at the bottom of the screen. Each character is vastly different functionally due to the weapon they have equipped so in my short play each run has been a little different. It's a little harder than some other Survival-likes I feel but that's a bit of a plus. Highly recommend it for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly just play Vampire Survivors. This game is fine but has a lot of issues (Both technical and gameplay wise) that Vampire Survivors simply does not, and the game is so close to the same formula that it kind of comes off as a blatant copy. There's so many effects/ideas that are 100% rips from Vampire Survivors.It's basically the exact same thing but this game has less visual clarity, more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and worse spawns. The amount of times I'd be running away from enemies and I'd have enemies spawn directly on top of me was insane given how much time I've been playing.I have to play this game permanently muted because of a crackling audio issue that I've tried numerous things to fix including:1) Setting all the audio settings across my entire PC to run on 44100 sample rate.2) Restarting my PC.3) Running the game in admin mode.4) Verifying the game files.5) There is supposedly an Audiofix Beta version that is no longer available. If it was ever available in the first place, why take it away? I tried getting it but it's just not there anymore.In 72 hours of Vampire Survivors, I never had anywhere near as many visual clarity issues as I did with this game in a short span of time. I've been having projectiles look like they clearly went underneath me kill me, and lots of the enemies are the exact same colour and shade as the ground underneath them. This really doesn't mix well with the fact that this game is extremely punishing in terms of how fast you can die from touching enemies.This game is fine but it could be so much better, and the fact that it does so many things worse than a game it blatantly copies that came out like 18 months before it is extremely disappointing. I actually prefer the vibe and atmosphere of this game over Vampire Survivors but yeah. It is what it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Thoughts about  after playing Early Access for about 25h:I've enjoyed this survivorslike a lot so far.  It follows the 'standards' of the genre fairly faithfully, if you've played any other survivorslike you'll be instantly familiar here, but there's a few things here that make this game stand out from the rest.First is the 'feel' of the game, it's retro, but its very authentic about it as well.  The visual and audio style really brings me back to loved classics like Diablo and Baldur's Gate.Second, the game feels tight.  There's so far around 7 different classes you can play, and their all have distinct play styles, and at least for the content currently in the game, they're all equally viable.  You can just pick which you like the most and have reasonable success with it, whether its a melee warrior, archer, cleric or spellcaster.That said, after the hours I've put in I'm pretty much finished with what the game currently has.  I didn't buy all the upgrades yet and there's still a few achievements I can hunt, but the game only has three maps and no difficulty or challenge settings, so at this point every run is pretty much the same.  This game has a great foundation but for its 1.0 release I think it needs a little more flesh in the form of more maps and challenges for the more dedicated player.I'm hopeful for more and eager to see how this game develops in the future, but if you're eager for a new Survivors like game and don't mind the gamble of Early Access, you can do far worse than this.  I certainly feel like I've got my $5 worth already from this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played many of the other Survivor-like games, this one is the best, hands down.The art style is impeccable. _childDocuments_.review: Good game, as you'll read from any other review. 3 maps, 7 different characters to progress with and many combinations and upgrades. It's biggest pro's are the diablo inspired looks and the first 2-3 runs you'll play on any class. Also, it's generally pretty fun and you can play without breaking your wrists since there's a key to turn on aiming at the closest enemy and continuous fire. More of this type of game could benefit from these options.It's biggest cons are the achievements and how unnecessarily grindy it is. One of the achievements requires you to purchase 40 items from the well keeper. Meaning you'll have to run at least 40 runs and send items through the well to the well keeper. Then, you also better have the gold to buy all those items. You are also in a run for a limited amount of time, so if you finally got the right rng for whatever spell and you're going for the 3 mil damage and you run out of time, too bad, go for another run.Where it can improve? Well it's already early access, so chances are things will be added, but it lacks content. It lacks a lot of content. There should be more maps than playable characters, progressing speeding up, less pointless grind, and revamp of the achievements to not artificially increase playtime. There's also a bug with the ui, at least when I launch it, it seems to go into windowed mode and the cursor is all over the place, so I have to find my way to the options menu and find the spot on the screen where the mouse is on top of the fullscreen option and press it twice to fix it. Every time.Overall not bad, hoping some more "game" will be added to this.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Its like Vampire Survivors but looks like DiabloHas some small differences compared to Vampire Survivors.- Everyone has an unique Attack (that can be clicked and aimed). You can put the settings on "auto" and it will attack automatiicaly for you, however, there are passives that icrease the damage of your main attack if you dont permanently auto-spam it.- Every other boss drops equipment that is comparable to typcial RPG equipment (Either pure statboost, an additional passive effect for your build or an unique ability).- After 30 Minutes, the run doesn't just end. A Boss pops up that has to be killed (Comparable to MMORPG bosses (run out of the damage zone and kill it).All in all, the game is great and feels different enough to give it a try if you like Vampire Survivors (or the genre in general). Furthermore as of this Review, the game is still in early access. There might be more to come making it standing out even more.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently, this is the best game in the "Bullet Heaven" genre. Everything from the art style, to the sound design, to the itemization and gameplay is cohesive. This is what we imagined Diablo 1 was actually like, back when it came out in 1997. Each class you pick has their own unique weapon that tends to be the primary focus, rather than selecting spells or weapons that are accessible to every class in Bullet Heaven games. Non-unique spells do play an important role in complementing your offense, but they tend to be the dressing or sides. Upgrades, whether from leveling up or finding gear somewhere in the level, feel meaningful. You will notice distinct builds and playstyles for each class, greatly differentiating how even the early portion of runs start. This developer needs all of the support they can get. It would be an injustice for this game to not get more thoroughly crafted and considered content.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best survivors type games I've played. I'd rank it 2nd place right under the OG vampire survivors. The pacing is fantastic and it always feels like I'm gaining *something* with every run. The characters are varied and the equipment effects are interesting. There are a lot of options and builds you can make!Only gripes I have currently is that there's no way to know what my other potential options are for the tiered upgrades so unless I memorize everything or wait until all of them cycle through, I'm just guessing. And that the levels are kind of big and empty and there's no map to tell me how far away stuff is. And lastly that the abilities don't show up when you look at your stats in the pause menu so you have no idea if certain stats are affecting them at all or how (force?). All in all, highly recommend and can't wait for more updates!

_childDocuments_.review: 16 hours in and I can barely scavenge enough gold to get the basic meta stats. yet you need the basic meta stats to complete the ridiculous quest lines that half of which don't even make any sense. Quest says to deal 33,333 damage in one hit. I dealt up to 100,000 and it still didn't count.Progression is far too slow and most the abilities either suck or are completely unfun to play with. Where vampire survivors rewards you for playing, this game punishes you. Upgrading ability quest lines just adds more clutter to that ability upgrade path. You're far too weak until you upgrade all the meta stats and you get so few gold from actually playing vs completing quests. Most quests require the meta stats to be upgraded to achieve. There is some good to this game. The blue potion is an amazing new addition to this style of game that gives players the choice of dramatically improving one of their abilities. The equipment system is also a nice addition, although it is also a drag to collect the gear. On top of that it costs gold to obtain. Something which the meta stats also need. _childDocuments_.review: This is a very good horde survivor/bullet heaven. It wears its inspiration on it's sleeve, and in my opinion, that's a good thing. There's a wide spread of interesting characters to pick from and the equipment system lets you adjust how they play to your liking.If I had to pick one thing that I don't like about the game, it's that your equipment unlocks are limited to one per run (you can only put one equipment item in the bucket per run), which seems to really only serve to artificially increase your playtime. In fact, I'd probably have more time in this game if it didn't have that restrictive mechanic.Still a very high recommend though, especially for the price. There's so much to do with various builds if you like to experiment, and a literal bucket full of achievements to hunt if that's your jam.

_childDocuments_.review: Just beat the current endgame boss—although there's tons of quests to finish and achievements still to unlock, and I'm definitely not done playing. I've got to say this is my favorite Vampire Survivors-like of all time.I love the art style—it's retro, but in a tasty nostalgic way that doesn't sacrifice variety and has some pretty cool animations thrown in. Very old-school dungeon crawl monster manual kind of aesthetic. There are a lot of very different and cool characters, lots of weapons and abilities, and there's a lot of room to craft unusual builds that work.But the best part is the pacing and balancing. You know that feeling of definitely being screwed this time, and you're absolutely not going to make it, but you might as well keep struggling? And then the tide imperceptibly turns and you wriggle out of your doom yet again? To me that's the perfect balance of difficulty, and at least for me, this game has served it up consistently. It's something you can very much tweak to your preferences. Whenever I feel like I'm winning just a bit too easily, it's simple to add a couple more modifiers (with quests and rewards attached) and right back to barely mostly squeaking by.At the price, if you like bullet heaven games with lots of meta progression and a consistent aesthetic (which I think this game does WAY better than Vampire and most of its descendants), it's super easy to recommend. The demo is generous with its content and free, give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Halls of Torment is a Vampire Survivors clone... but it feels like it doesn't understand the elements that make Vampire Survivors shine. There are design decisions that undermine what makes the genre work (covered below), elements desperately in need of polish that get in the way of what could be fun... and a few elements that feel really great but are currently impossible to enjoy (stat clarity, strong character identities). A boss fight should challenge you or test your abilities in some way. While bosses in Halls of Torment have unique attack sets and decreasing cooldowns with increased movespeed as the fight progresses, they're mostly an exercise in monk-like patience. Attacks are predictable, and you either have the move speed or sustain and defenses to ignore them or you don't. Meaning that fights are decided after about a minute (during which you'll have memorized the entire attack set), but you'll be fighting the same boss for 10-30 minutes depending on your particular build's DPS. This is exacerbated by the passive recovery speed of about 1 health per second, and the removal of consumables... meaning that the best option can often be to spend 5 minutes running away while you heal.  This has the unfortunate side effect that there is no predictable discrete unit of play. When you boot up a run of Vampire Survivors, you can predict how long a successful run will take down to the minute depending on your individual settings. That's no longer an option here, and the 30 minute run timer becomes deceptive if you have only a short window to get a game in. Short of failing a run there's no particular way to save your progress, and it's not obvious that a successful run will often take about an hour.The game would be improved by removing boss fights altogether, at least temporarily. Halls of Torment opts for Diablo 2-esque graphics, with reds and grays and browns taking up most of the color palette. This works fine for Diablo, where individual attacks aren't all that important, where the field of view is much narrower, and only part of your screen matters at any given time, but works considerably less well in Halls of Torment. A single stray mob can put you on half-health for the rest of a run, a mob that falls off of your screen can respawn in a lethal position, and many enemies have color palettes that blend into the background (see the burrowed worms in stage 2 for an example). I don't envy any visually impaired players who give the game a try.Bosses have unique outlines of blue or orange or magenta... which are also applied to most or all of their attacks. Meaning that, in extreme cases, your screen can be filled with magenta particles making it very hard to see attacks with softer edges and glow effects, while being very visually jarring. Gold standards in this genre (Vampire Survivors, HoloCure) have discrete decision points that really matter, and then the UI gets out of your way. Halls of Torment takes these discrete decisions and spreads them out over the course of a dozen or more level-ups. Each attack has several types of upgrade available at each rank, titled ambiguously in parentheses. This means that each level requires reading the specific effects of each option, even if you're familiar with them already. This breaks up game flow, especially since a single misclick can seriously compromise your build, and consumes mental bandwidth since you can't see the other options side-by-side for comparison.Finally, the game's NPC dialogues have text in long, slow crawls with no ability to move forward more quickly. These dialogues often happen mid-run, and abruptly change the tempo of gameplay unless you decide to skip them altogether. Which is very easy to do, and you may never have the opportunity to read them again.Once more, this feels like an element that the game would be better without, until it can be polished more fully.

_childDocuments_.review: I have really Mixed feelings about Halls of Torment... This is another one of those games that isn't terrible, but I don't want to recommend. I expected this to be a Vampire Survivors reskin but this is more of a twin-stick shooter with Diablo aesthetics. You might like this if you really want to feed that old Diablo nostalgia, but you could also just buy the original Diablo DRM-free on GOG for $9.99. The gameplay overall is decent but it didn't scratch the same itch provided by the Dopamine drip feed that was Vampire Survivors.VS was addictive for the constant slot machine effects going on, new forms of randomization, and tons of unlocks and upgrades to find. Even compared to vanilla VS, there just isn't enough content variety, and the content that is here feels spread too thin. There's only five maps plus an additional endless Vault that can be unlocked after a massive gear grind. VS had a similar map count on launch but there was a story throughout them, secrets to find along the way, plus the aforementioned unlocks. This game doesn't even have a level map to help with navigation... You can feel the grind in each area because the level design is repetitive and boring with visible, intentional waves of enemies.I didn't even know VS had static waves of enemies until I started looking up guides and "spoilers" while trying to 100% the achievements for it. Halls of Torment fails on that point because you can literally see when enemy waves start and stop; enemies will despawn if you move too far away from them, only to be replaced by the next wave's enemy type after a delay in another part of the screen. This is less noticeable once you get into Agony (hard) mode, but for the first dozen or so hours you might be literally waiting around for enemies to spawn. Even when the combat flows well, it can be difficult to tell what you need to unlock or upgrade next mid-mission because of a lack of guidance and too many options.Every time you level up you get access to four randomized options for stats to upgrade. The problem here is that once you start picking up ability scrolls (passive offensive spells), the upgrades for those will bloat your level up pool too. Picking up more scrolls will give you access to more abilities but will also have separate mutually exclusive ability upgrades too. You can also dual class in the pre-mission gearing menu which adds even more bloat to the pool, in addition to sometimes even blocking you from picking skills from your own class. Each character has multiple unique trait trees that can be unlocked that are unfortunately all tagged the same, including cross-character traits. For example, Exterminator's Proficient Stance has Conflagration (+6% multistrike and area) and Hellfire (+10% burn chance and burn damage) mutually exclusive options, but a cross-class trait like Sorceress's Weapon Proficiency trait (Strength [+30% damage] or Strikes [+10% force, +6% attack speed and multistrike) will occupy the same level up slot. You can fight this a bit eventually by unlocking reroll potions but the amount of bloat in the pool makes this feel like picking the lesser of two evils. There's other options with potions to help with leveling up, but one of them really breaks the game balance: a potion that lets you *double* the effects of a trait, up to three times per run. Certain options like Shield Maiden's Weapon Proficiency Mace trait for +30% crit damage are completely broken with this. Everything else about this feels uninspired at best and unfinished at worst. This is yet another Early Access game that needs more work, in addition to a full pass to clean up some of the older systems. Parts of this game feel just arbitrarily slapped on to pad the little content that is here, like having to buy back your own gear you send up the well. This needs better enemy and ability variety, more levels, more character archetypes... basically more of everything except grind. Vampire Survivors at launch was a $3 game that felt like a $30 game but this is a $5 (now $6.66 ecks dee) game that feels like a $5 game; this is shelf filler that you'd find in a jewel case on a rotating metal cage rack at a supermarket in the 90s. This might improve in the future but for now there's better VS-likes and better Diablo-likes out there.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is okay. 5/10. Right at average. The graphics are nastolgia bait for me. I love that oldschool pc style CRPG look. Obviously, it's inspired by the Diablo I art style, but it also reminds me of my old favorite - Baldur's Gate (the actual first version not the EE version). The gameplay is a bit ... meh. It's your typical survivor game where you have nothing but movement to control. Though, they do let you toggle your auto-aim and your auto-fire - which DID become useful.They actually have the best dodge (Block) mechanic I've seen. In short - it actually complements your armor stat (Defense). In most games of this nature, a dodge mechanic would just be consisting of adding number to some sort of logarithmic equation, which they do a bit here; the logarithmic equations to determine their stats. (e.g.) 20 Defense actually equals an 18% damage reduction and there's a point of diminishing returns. Like 40 defense would only be 28% resistance not 36%. However, their dodge mechanic is structure with the equation like normal but it break it down like this: "Damage from 0-X has a 100% damage block chance; Damage from X-Y; Has a 50% chance; And Y-Z has a 10% chance." This is actually BRILLIANT! They work WITH armor instead of 'despite' armor, which is how most games (even the greats) use the dodge mechanic. I cannot give this game enough praise for this mechanic. Everything else however, is ... just meh. The way you get your skills/abilities/equipment is just underwhelming. Almost all bonuses are either super weak, or come with a pretty big penalty to use it. ...Just meh. You are FORCED to replay maps to unlock the ability to buy your equipment. Because, the mechanic they have is if you pick up a piece of equipment you don't own, you need to put that item in a 'well' that sends it to 'the base camp camp' where you can buy it from an NPC to have as a permanent equipment.  It sounds cool, but in-effect it becomes a slog because you can only send ONE PIECE back during a run.... which is the other issue that makes this g ame feel incredibly meh. A Run...by default... is 30 minutes. These games bennefit from not being tied to the timer. I believe they're best when you're given a goal that isn't related to time such as: Defeat 5 bosses and those bosses are triggered by killing X amount  of Mini-Bosses, which are triggered by y amount of normal enemies. So, these games are designed to lost 30 minutes and to be fair on the game - the game is entertaining enough that you can accidentally spend way more time on the game than intended. It's just by having the time limit, you're not really encouraged to do many-many runs to collect all the items. The information given in the game is awful. They do have tool tips ... for SOME THINGS... to let you know what it does, but it's not consistent. There's many abilities I don't know if they effect a skill or not - even though some of the skills label their stats with the 'normal' stat name if it's being used for something weird. (e.g.) Force would be next to the word "Chaining" to signify how many hops a chain will get, or it'll be next to "Piercing" for how many enemies a projectile pierces through.  But, it's not consistent with that, it also appears there's a heavy amount of skills that don't work with many abilities and only benefit from 3-4 of the abilities you can put points into. The character all play different.... but holy crap are some over tuned than the others. Archer - best class in the game I have unlocked. BAR NONE. Nothing can compete with its' dps, range and speed. The summoner class is almost unusable because its' dps is just so insanely low and it has no other utility. Hell, the summoner class barely is a summoner class - it just has projectiles shaped like birds (ghosts actually, but they look like birds if you aren't paying attention). And a weird thing, this is the first survivor game where they try and NOT let you get your full equipment load out - unless you're doing the 'Agony" mode which is their challenge mode. (e.g.) You have 6 skill slots and a main weapon. You start with the main weapon, and only get skills from defeating bosses, which seems to have a similar timer to Vampire Survivors, being; at 5 minutes in a mini boss shows up, 10-12 minutes another one, 18-20 another, and 25 another. BUT these bosses will drop 2 items, instead of skills, so out of the 4 mini-bosses you get 2 skills and 2 items. SO, you can go on a map and find scrolls which will give you another skill per scroll (the most i've seen on a map is 2). So... this is also the way you give your skils their 'fully leveled special traits'.... so you either have 3 at max or 1-2 with one being beefed. <-This is TERIBLE - this is actually what makes the game not all that fun to play. Normally, I would put 40+ hours into these games, but 12 hours in... I'm bored, tired, and annoyed. I don't feel like the game WANTS ME to play it. It always punishes you and says "play again, nerd!" Without making the game better the next time through. Oh.... I do like how you have to complete quests to unlock some of you permanent skill buffs, but .... the quests aren't really prominent enough to make that a great way of doing it. _childDocuments_.review: I never really understood the craze behind Vampire Survivors and the dozens of cheap chyneze clones of it that were created later. Untilone day  I saw a bald incel play Halls of Torment on YouTube. I got immediately intrigued by the unique art style, making me nostalgic for the bygone era of the end of the last century, when 3D graphics became advanced enough to create assets, but not efficient enough to always render them in real time. HoT looks like many of the games released back then - a collage of 2D sprites pre-baked from 3D models rotated in a variety of angles and animation states. It is pure art in how it imitates old jank while remaining functional in a modern way. The animations and effects are fluid and everything looks and feels exactly as it should. It has some Diablo in it's DNA, including awesome sound design, but it also reminds me a lot of the very early DOS & Windows 95 action / arcade and indie games, the ones that you'd try to break to see how much entities you can spawn into the game until your processor starts to give up. The game screen often looks like nuts.WAD or that silly RTS custom map you made in the editor just to reach the absolute unit capacity.I haven't played many Survivors games since then, but nothing seems as good as HoT on the surface - there are tons of content to discover and unlock, dozens of mechanics to play around, endless variety in the combination of upgrades that you select during a run. It has an extremely engaging roguelite meta-progression, where each Quest, of which there are literally hundreds, requires you to perform a specific feat in exchange for a reward. Sometimes it's just gold to buy items and boost stats with and a reveal of the requirements of further Quests, but it might be a new ability, a new upgrade path, a new character or something else. Whether you fail a run or succeed, this makes you immediately think of the next one - planning on what you might want to try to achieve and what strategy you'll assume.The moment to moment gameplay mainly consists of movement - keeping the right distance between you and the enemies, picking up the experience that they drop, going after faraway ability scrolls and other pickups, avoiding attacks. I play it with auto-aim on a Steam Deck (docked to a TV), which means that, unless I am pausing the game or making an upgrade selection or something, I literally play it with one finger most of the time. There's rarely a need to manually aim at a specific enemy (depending on your builds) and even then 99% of the time you can get away without it. This makes HoT a very accessible game for people with manual disabilities. At any rate, playing with a controller seems to be much better than being limited to 8 directions.I think everyone should just buy it and try it, it costs next to nothing and provides dozens of hours of fun. It is brutally difficult at times, keeping you on your toes, and at the beginning it might not be very obvious how to progress or even if you're playing it right. But be warned - once it clicks for you, this game is extremely addicting and hard to put down. I bought it months ago in Early Access, but it didn't seem like it at all, I think even back then most developers wouldn't mind releasing it as a feature complete game in the state that it was in. And now there's even more content and QoL improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: Halls of Torment is a game I feel may be propped up a bit harder than appropriate, by rabid Diablo fans and contrarian Vampire Survivors detractors. Overall, it's alright and competently made, though it's easily the least fun game in its genre. I went in expecting to love it, but here we are.I usually have a fair tolerance for boredom and grind, but Halls of Torment is kind of devoid of any amazing discoveries or engaging unlockable content. Just about every single achievement is an uninteresting grind milestone. Nearly all upgrades and progression are slight percentage increments on the stats of a basic attack. Passive damage, passive regeneration, passive health, passive range, passive crits, passive blocks, and such. If you want an interesting rogue-like, you need to give the players a more creative assortment of stats, attacks, effects, modifications, and amplifications, to make playthroughs far more varied.The really simple abilities you can pick up are... Mostly not at all interactive or fun. Many merely provide some passive damage around you. You'll find a few choices for each item slot, but end up with a best-in-slot for most, anyway. There's only a few progression mechanics, only a few stock Diablo characters, and only three maps. Unlike its inspiration games, the randomisation will never provide you with a broken run, but will occasionally give you a weaker than usual run, and that's just less fun. Many achievements only offer gold, so you don't have that many new features to keep you playing. This all adds up to make a rather stale experience.It's a moderately challenging experience, sure, but you always end up strong enough to clear screens anyway. The first final boss has a poorly implemented charge attack, and the other two final bosses didn't hit me once on my first encounters of each. And even with a high damage build you will find they've got way, waaay too much health, so be wary of the mechanical complexity of dying of old age. Checking their health every so often feels like watching the clock too closely while you're at work. So ultimately the game never gets that brutally hard, you just need to figure out what stats don't apply to your character, then concentrate to conserve your health for half an hour, and finally slap some meat for a handful of minutes at the end.I've always found Diablo 1 & 2 to be utterly, headache-inducingly hideous, but Halls of Torment's cloning of its art style actually works pretty well for this style of game. The main drawback is that enemy projectiles can be very easily lost underneath the spell effects for your own attacks. Placing enemy projectiles on a higher layer would greatly aid clarity. Despite what I think of the graphics of Diablo, I do actually love ARPGs and horde survival games, and was really trying to like this one. I'm not even totally done playing it yet, though I'm finding it very easy to quit out to go do some of my more tedious household errands instead. At a point where I've seen most of the content, I must concede it's a let downSound design and music are wonderful and authentic, too. Other than that, and the baseline addiction of "Smacking more skeletons with an incrementally stronger character", there's little reason to recommend Halls of Torment over contemporaries like Vampire Survivors, Brotato, and 20 Minutes Till Dawn.

_childDocuments_.review: Slow, boring and repetitive.Pros:- lots of classes with unique basic attack and it's unique upgrades- choose starting equipment that suits your play-style for specific classCons:- terrible level-up upgrades: on each level you choose a trait like +5% damage (or attack speed or range etc) or +10% with with specific ability. So you get like x3 base dps and x2 survival by the end of a run.- You get ~5 abilities during run (like orbs flying around you or lightning strikes at random enemies), ability upgrade counts as an ability and is almost useless (orbs deal additional minor electricity damage with low chance of micro-stun etc). Most abilities don't benefit from most stats (or just general traits are too weak to see difference), there are no synergies (some have low chance to slightly increase vulnerability to physical/magical damage or status effects like burn but that's all)- slow meta progression - per run you can resurface only one gear piece to add it to starting gear pool for a huge price, there are some permanent stat boosts with increasing gold costs and you don't earn much per run. To unlock new gear, abilities and traits you need to complete quests like deal gazillion damage with specific ability requiring  you to get and max it asap ignoring other upgrades and using that ability as a primary source of damage = boring an extremely annoying run. And there are so damn many of them- low number of maps with tremendous "difficulty" spikes - complete 20 runs to get enough gold to get +10% to all stats to be able to pass dps check on next map, there are ~5 maps so you will be mostly playing 1-2 maps to gather gold and complete quests- enemies have long death animation and you will want to have high movement speed and you will be wondering whether you step over dead enemies or are they still alive and will damage you- music is ambient and most sounds are indistinctive - it is slightly atmospheric but mostly makes gameplay quite boring- no map - there are icons to sow direction to pick-ups but it's hard to tell far they are, and they are mostly in different directions from starting point so no way to calculate optimal path, this gets even worse on diagonal maps- very limited statistics in character menu - no way to check burn chance of flamethrower, can't understand whether it's worth upgrading without knowing base value.You will be mostly playing same map each time with another calss or maxing specific abilty to grind unlocks/upgrades. Each time there will be a lack or ability synergies, your stats at the end of the run will be just slightly higher than at the start of the run - no interesting builds or characters that devastate everything using fun strategy. Just circle around monsters  while auto-attacking for half an hour to unlock some minor garbage. Repeat x200 times.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played more than ten bullet heaven games at this point - I like the genre, and I tend to be forgiving in my reviews. Bullet heaven games are cheap, simple, and you know what you're getting - a few hours of fun for a few bucks, perhaps double digits if it's really good.This is my first negative review of a bullet heaven game. I disliked pretty much everything about Halls of Torment.The graphics are bad. The quality is bad (pixelated), the style is bad (fugly), the color palette is a monotonous litany of grays and browns, the skill animations are underwhelming and in some cases (the needles) barely visible, the character models are tiny and unimpressive, the menu buttons, the items, everything is just profoundly uncool. It's one big old pile of meh.There is no skill variety - over the course of three hours, I only saw the same four unimpressive secondary skills. Don't worry, they are all equally bland and underpowered.The upgrades are generic and repetitive as well. There is nothing even remotely interesting or creative - it's all just incremental changes of basic stats. I didn't see a single cool thing in the entire game. The only thing that impresses in Halls of Torment is its commitment to blandness. Save your five bucks. If you buy this game, you are encouraging unapologetic mediocrity.

_childDocuments_.review: is another one in the line of " clones", but I feel it's even better than the game it was inspired by. By combining the classic bullet-heaven formula with loot mechanics inspired by old-school  games, it makes a tired format feel new and refreshing.First off, movement is king, and you can actually die in this game. Instead of becoming an agent of chaos in the first couple minutes and laying waste to anyone crossing your path, here, you have to mind your step all the way until the clock strikes zero.Second, your build can make or break a character, leading to a lot of unsuccessful runs in the beginning until you pick up and save some crucial gear pieces.Third, the bosses are not just bullet sponges; they are strong, quick, ruthless, and standing still spells out a certain death.My only criticism is that the rounds just felt too long, but the developers have actually mentioned that they are working on a shorter 20-minute mode. Once that is implemented, I'll have nothing to complain about. Definitely worth its asking price!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very realistic Beta Testing Simulator. The game realistically simulates the job of a beta tester dealing with an unstable and unfinished software. Basically the mechanic of the game consists of tweaking settings and other things I won't say not to spoiler the game, in order not to crash the software. Sometimes the game is also interrupted by some kind of a mini-game about greek mythology, but these are short intermissions that don't distract by the main purpose of the game. I particularly liked the meta-game of having to access actual forums and rollback actual drivers (oops, I spoiled part of the game, but this was during the prologue so you'll pardon me). Like "Outer Wilds" the main mechanic is a repeating cycle (start game, tweak, play, crash, repeat). Sometimes all this could feel frustrating, but fortunately at the start of each "cycle" there is half a minute meditation exercise showing a nice picture of a temple with nice waterfalls, inviting you to "check additional contents" which I guess means that there is more to life than all this, and you should check inside yourself... at least this is my interpretation.All in all, whatever price you paid, it's too much for this Beta Software Simulation game.I liked the mini-games, though, and I would like that some publisher - other than Ubisoft - would take the idea and extrapolate it into a standalone game, which I would call Zelda Creed.

_childDocuments_.review: Immortals Fenyx Rising is on sale right now for $8 and for that price it's a no-brainer.  Imagine a recent Zelda game done in the Ubisoft way and this is what you're imagining.  The voice acting and writing here are just fantastic.  I don't want to oversell it and have you be disappointed, but honestly it's the most entertained I've been by the dialogue and narration in a game... maybe ever?  I certainly can't think of anything else that made me chuckle so often.  The constant banter between Zeus and Prometheus is worth the price of admission all by itself.  Combat in the game is quick and responsive, and just feels good.  The difficulty options make it easy to decide if you're just playing for fun or if you want a challenge.  Puzzles are about like you'd expect from a Zelda-style game, not too challenging but fun enough.  The open world is very pretty and exploration is constantly rewarded.  Honestly, there's nothing here to dislike.  I bought it at full price and I have no regrets, so when it's on sale you should not pass it up.

_childDocuments_.review: Other games: "Sorry, you can't go there right now. You could run into sequence breaking content, or unbeatable enemies, or puzzles that are impossible with your current abilities."Immortals Fenyx Rising: "Do what you want, I ain't your dad."The game's an absolute blast. It offers a level of freedom and power you just don't see in other modern games. It offers cleverly designed puzzles, but gives you options to blow through them using your divine powers. It offers challenging combat, but lets you become so powerful you'll be able to take down most enemies in a couple hits. It makes you earn your upgrades, but is generous with materials and currency. It deals with some weighty themes and surprisingly detailed Greek mythology, but does so in a way that's consistently good-natured and hilarious throughout. Basically, it prioritizes fun over everything else, and it absolutely succeeds.I wholeheartedly recommend giving this one a play.

_childDocuments_.review: Actually a pretty good game - mythology, puzzle solving, nice music, a lush world to explore. I think the impressive part is that it manages to be good  being an Ubisoft game, and you can see where the Ubisoft middle managers have had their hand in the pie, with the currencies and 'map vomit' of activities. But somehow the developers have, thankfully, contrived to push those to the side as much as possible so that you can actually forget it's there. The 'map vomit' is more of a 'sneeze' and is actually more spread out and manageable, and the currencies are just something you can easily forget about or ignore and doesn't make itself known too much. As for the game itself, it's a decent story, about as much as you can expect from an open world one. The best part for me is that it doesn't take itself seriously, there's a good dose of seriousness and humour everywhere.  The mechanics are fun and build up slowly so that you get that sense of empowerment as you progress. There are plenty of activities on the side that help you build up your power, the vaults were especially fun for me. I didn't face any of the technical issues mentioned so it always pays to be a patient gamer. I'd recommend it if you're a fan of open world and puzzles and something that isn't trying too hard to please.Get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: NB: This is a review of only the base game, I have not played the DLCs yet.The prevailing opinion I've heard about this game is that it's a Ubisoft's answer to Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, which I cannot comment on, having never played it, however as someone who has played a lo of Ubisoft's open-world games — for better and for worse — I can say that this one will also feel familiar, so if you also can't get the comparison above, think of it as "Assassin's Creed for a younger audience, with much more puzzles, and much less stealth". It's not an entirely adequate summary, but I'll elaborate below.First of, this is an open-world game. The map is separated into several regions, which, after you're finished with the tutorial one, you can tackle in any order (with the exception of the last one). The world feels rather large, probably larger than it really is, and while the level design is not very inspired, you can clearly see that the level designers did seem to have a lot of fun with what they had.The main focus of the game is three-fold: combat, puzzles, and traversal, with the latter two often intertwined. Let's talk about combat first.Combat is, overall, pretty simple in concept: you get light attack, heavy attack, dodge and parry. Later on you could learn new moves and powers to actually pretty significantly expand these options, though I didn't see the need to use most of them in the end playing on Normal difficulty. In practice, however, the combat might feel difficult, though maybe not for the usual reasons: it just feels... off. The timing windows for parrying and dodging can vary vastly between different enemies and even different attacks, and since you will be facing a mix of enemies most of the time, having reflexes to successfully avoid their attacks can be very tricky. The enemies can and will attack from anywhere, including if they aren't on screen, and don't seem to have the gentlemanly agreement to not chain their attacks between one another. Lastly, the indication for the attacks can be weird. The unparryable attacks have the enemies glow in red, which is already a bit of a problem for enemies that glow red all the time (less of a problem later in the game, actually, since they switch to blue and purple glow), but the normal attacks usually just have no indication whatsoever other than the animation itself. Sure, it makes sense for other games, but, again, here you will be fighting many enemies at once and it could be hard to keep track of all of them in the midst of it.The second issue with the combat comes at about the mid-point of the game where you start noticing that the enemies now look different, glowing blue instead of their previously usual red. Well, that's the thing: there are three tiers of enemies in this game, red, blue and purple, and they switch to the next tier automatically as you progress through the game (though some areas have tougher enemies from the start). That means that, depending on how you've been investing your various "currencies" and how well you've been exploring for them, the combat can get a lot tougher (enemies of a higher tier have more damage and health, as well as new attacks), and this happens twice. Luckily, by end-game, if you've been thorough with exploring, you do outclass even the highest tier of enemies so that the combats aren't really challenging on Normal difficulty, but the middle of the game can become quite a chore because of that.The second and third prongs of this game are, as I've said, the puzzles and traversal. The game uses a stamina system, which, while integral for a lot of mechanics, might be the biggest frustration with it: your stamina is still used out of combat, and every kind of traversal other than just jogging and jumping uses it: sprinting, swimming, climbing, double-jumping, gliding, etc., and since you're going to spend a lot of time doing that, you'll have to spend a lot of time just waiting for your stamina to replenish or keep chugging potions/eating mushrooms to replenish it that way. When even Soulsborne games, such as Elden Ring, have dropped stamina use outside of combat, this decision is baffling here, and the only reason I can think of for it is that *some* puzzles use stamina as the factor you have to puzzle around, so to say. However, they are few and far between, which is why I think leaving this system as is was a pretty major misstep/The rest of the puzzles range from very simple sliding puzzles (just 4 pieces) to a lot of physics-based ones, to first-person arrow courses, to "parkour" courses, etc, etc. Most of them are pretty easy and have very lenient timers, but there are some that were frustrating, mostly when it came to a slightly wonky physics puzzle or a traversal puzzle hampered by the game's very sensitive movement controls and odd issues such as the gliding mode not being queued properly after any action. The real "meat" of the puzzles comes in Hades Vaults, separate "maps" from the main one, each using a completely different layout with its own gimmick (other than the combat arenas which all use the same one, but with different traps and enemy combinations), and I have to give the devs props for just how many things they could think to do with them.The story is pretty simplistic, though kind of confusing, since you spend most of the time restoring the gods to being the terrible people that they were, but it kind of makes sense thematically in the end, I suppose? There are a lot of jokes, a lot of truly terrible accents, so you probably shouldn't even try to take the game seriously: it certainly doesn't (bar the Daedalus's "log entries" which are pretty dang sad for something that doesn't have any real pay-off).I haven't 100% the game (there is no free-roam mode after the ending), but even with that I got more than 50 hours out of it.All in all, I'd say that it's an alright game with some deep, but not entirely ruinous, flaws, and no real ambition to become anything much more than that.

_childDocuments_.review: Never played BOTW so I can't compare it.The music is FANTASTIC. Same guy who did the Ori games. If you're going to play this game, don't do side quests first. Follow the main story for a bit, get your wings, the ability where you do spears upward (also handy for a triple jump), upgrade your stamina and health and go from there. Yes, the game is puzzle heavy, but you can actually adjust them to make it easier by some toggles in the options as well as switching the difficulty down to easy or story if you wish. I started on normal, but after a few hours it felt kinda difficult so i switched to easy for the rest of the game with all puzzle assistants on. Yes, there are some puzzles that are really dumb and/or annoying. But there's also a lot I liked too.Story was good, some funny humor here and there. I'd love to see some sequels but do it like Prince of Persia Warrior Within and make it more angry, add some blood and gore, etc. However that's one bad thing about the game- the puzzles and combat are tied to the same adjustment. You cant make the puzzles easy and the combat difficult for example. I did all the main quests, side quests and about 23 vaults. I also upgraded my character to about 80-85% abilities. There's also new game plus.You can switch difficulty at any time. Got about 35 hours total. I just played the base game, no dlc.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like a light-hearted cartoony take on Assassin’s Creed Odyssey and much like that game I loved this. It is one of those games with a big map full of things to systematically tick off that are like crack to me. It looks great, there is a great range of character customisation and weapons. The upgrade system is not too complex and you unlock some fun mechanics as you progress.  The story is fun, the slightly silly take on Greek mythology is excellent, I like the commentary by Zeus and Prometheus; almost like Statler and Waldorf. The gameplay is a nice mix of exploration, puzzles and combat. The combat is nice and easy. The puzzles are mostly satisfying however a few of the puzzles are annoyingly difficult. They put in a few puzzles to sell the DLC that are clearly meant to be played near the end of the game once you have got used to the mechanics, but some of them are in the starting areas. So don’t get disheartened if you think you are just doing an easy early game side mission and find yourself stumbling into a seemingly unfair really difficult puzzle. The other annoyance is how you find things on the map. Instead of the nice viewpoints in Assassin’s Creed you have to stop every once in a while and tediously scan all round you to find things to get them marked on the map. It breaks the fun fast flow of the game with its tedium, I really don’t know how they thought it was a good idea. But these are just a few ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in an otherwise excellent game.

Overall, a solid addition.

_childDocuments_.review: I wonder how many times Ubisoft higher ups intervened during development and said "Now how can we make this part waste people's time more".This game does not respect your time at all. It has a good foundation (obviously since it's just ripping off breath of the wild) but then they sprinkle on the good ol' Ubisoft secret recipe of making the game worse. Not everything is worse, I will say I enjoy the sword, axe, stamina, skill combat system (sometimes). Flying bosses are the worst, even when I spec my equipment into airborne. You can't grab the treasure chest you missed in a dungeon and then warp out, you have to complete the entire dungeon AGAIN. You can't even go to the entrance of the dungeon to leave or you'll lose progress, Ubisoft purposefully implemented you needing to redo the entire dungeon to waste people's time. Gliding parkour is the worst since it's incredibly sluggish. Collecting health ingredients which is probably the most important is the most tedious and time consuming to grab, needing to get off your horse, hit the tree with the axe, then back onto your horse instead of just running past ingredients with auto-grab on horse. Amber in tree trunks require you to wait for the trunk to topple over for no reason so you just stand around waiting. They copy the Breath of the Wild scouting mechanic more or less but there's so much busy work and the environment is done so terribly that you're just going to be manually panning the entire screen to get any hits. There's puzzles in the dungeons that aren't even puzzles and are a lot of busy work. There's a puzzle in the open world where you need to find lettuce in a village type area so you'd think maybe you go the market for the lettuce. Nope, it's just locked inside building the size of a large cage whose sole purpose is to have the lettuce locked up inside. So many puzzles are exploration puzzles where it's usually wander around and hope you find the thing you need to find rather than actually thinking. I don't know, there's far more things that make this game, in my opinion, more egregious than the other Ubisoft sandbox games or maybe it's the only one I've bothered playing a good amount of recently. Also the main antagonist is some stupid overbite looking fool that Ubi actually tries to push as menacing even though the rest of the game is lighthearted.Edit: Oh and also it's appalling how aggressive they are pushing the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ live service paid cosmetic daily quest model. It's also incredibly disgusting that it is okay nowadays for a game to heavily advertise their new game or DLC in the game you already bought. It's awful for DLC since 99% of games always make it REALLY obvious you're missing out on the actual intended experience of the game because you're too stingy to give them more money. Ubisoft does the same with advertising their DLC everywhere and also as a "quest" on the map. It is incredibly disengengous as they advertise what you'll get in the DLC but maxing your stats out completely. This will make endorphins rush as power fantasies usually do, especially when contrasted versus when you weren't, but that's because they are trying to trick you to thinking the DLC is better than it actually is. As example, a normal enemy without special heapth probably takes 2 hits + 5 hit combo on Nightmare difficulty. The gold bordered enemies in the trial took 1. Despicable.

_childDocuments_.review: It is fun for the first few hours. After that, puzzles and vaults get boring. Even the most difficult vaults aren't difficult. It's more like trying to find the object or entry you need, after that it's basically solved.If you play like me on difficult settings and do everything on the first and second region, you are overpowered. When you complete the gods regions you are already completely equipped with max health, amour, weapon and stamina. So I would suggest playing on nightmare but in the description it says reduced timers which in most cases is fine but in some vaults I find some timers to be too short as in difficult it was barely manageable. You can change difficulty in the settings, but I never did.Some vaults make the impression that they only exist to extend your playtime. Also climbing is a frustrating mechanic in this game it just takes a lot of play-time for no reason.Stupid animations when opening chest, upgrading or collecting some items are just annoying. I skipped them all the time after watching them once.For me, the controls are just clunky. If you fly and press forward you fly in the direction of your perspective what caused me some issue. The turning radius in flying mode is just too high. The choice to set special abilities on the same button as potions is just bad. You have to press the middle mouse button to change function between them. It's pretty often that you waste potions.I would have preferred a selection wheel for one of them. The story is not interesting, at first I listened to everything, but after a while I was just skipping almost everything because of how it was narrated.  Most of the interactions aren't relevant for the story but they give you some information about Greek mythology. Because I ignored the narration most of the time, I don't know if the information about Greek mythology is accurate. Nevertheless, it's not a lot of information you would learn more by reading an article, book or watching a documentation. How it was narrated seemed like it was made for children. Enemy variation is almost non-existing. You have some bosses distributed on the island, but they are just bigger and stronger versions of already existing enemy's.One big issue is that Ubisoft Connect isn't unlocking achievements I did. I got achievements who you couldn't get without others which didn't unlock.After completing everything except just a few chests, I cannot recommend the game. The only reason to play the game as much as I did is for the sake of progress in unlocking everything. But most things are just skins you can collect. If you want to play the Story, you can play it in less than 20 hours. But like I said, the story is not particularly good, at least in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Seems like this is the game ubisoft wanted to make all the time, but they werent confident enough to create a new IP instead they created assassins creed origins, assassins creed odyssey and assassins creed valhalla. But now they build up enough confidence and dared to create a new IP: Immortals Fenyx RisingI was surprised that the game was made by ubisof, because it was such a fun game.This truly feels like a work of passion.There are only a few flaws: being "forced" to manually spot the treasure chests and the enemy variety.The idea to spot everything manually is alright if you do it once in the tutorial, after that it is just annoying, but you dont have to collect every treasure chest etc if you dont want to, so you are not forced to use the mechanic.Regarding the enemy variety, there arent too many types, so you encounter nearly always the same enemies just different colors, indicating how strong that enemy is.But this is just nitpicking.It runs very smooth, the story is enjoyable, I can only recommend the game.And for the future, hopefully ubisoft will keep their newfound confidence to create new IPs for their various new ideas instead of forcing them into already existing IPs (e.g. Assassins Creed) just because they fear it won't sell well enough.That being said:Congratz Ubisoft, you created a really nice game

_childDocuments_.review: Fenyx Rising is a clone of the Zelda. With own bad and good sides. First of all, is an Ubisoft game. With all the consequences that entails. For almost 20 years, they still didn't change the template of game making. Grind times grind. Endless chests, items to collect and ctrl+c\ctrl-v activities. If you're a collector, get ready for a nearly endless gameplay. And this is a positive and the same time a negative moment. I mean, many side-activities are interesting to explore, but a lot (A LOT) aren't. Sometimes riddles are unclear to understand. That's why it is difficult to solve them. Sometimes you can meet similar riddles which you already solved many times before. For example, murals on the floor where you have to make a picture from its pieces.I liked graphics and art here. It's wonderful in my opinion. The game looks flamboyant and bright. The world is big and alive. Everything moves - trees, grass, birds in the sky, particles in the air. A mesmerizing sight. Enemies are different with their own abilities. Monsters from an antic mythology, and you easily can recognize them.But the battle system for me wasn't so interesting. Because once I found two-three overkill patterns to attack and didn't use others. And this is not about attacks only. I didn't use a bow and a sword at all. Only an axe with a regeneration health ability. A bow was a tool for riddle solving. Like in the Zelda you can climb, craft, fly, ride mounts and many classical things. Probably, the biggest problem for me here was a storytelling. Characters are faceless, annoying and boring. Specially narrators -Zeus and Hephaestus. I hate when powerful entities, like gods, in games turn into clowns in a circus. And yes, antic gods here are pathetic clowns. They make references to a modern culture. Characters all the time desperately try to joke, but this completely unfunny. The cringe parade in the flesh.  This may be funny only for kids. And it should be Greek kids, 'cause from time to time narrators remember a myth and discuss it without the context. I mean, all of us know the most famous myths about the twelve feats of Hercules or The Trojan Horse, but there are a lot of not so famous myths, which we don't know (or only me). My point is when narrators discuss something, they often don't give a context. Not only they. Even the game doesn't give a historical note. Nobody cares if you're understanding or not what they're talking about. And all the story comes that way. The plot here, as simple and dull as it can be. Came Typhoon and took the Olympus from gods. So help those helpless hipsters gods and take their place back. But I believe they don't deserve it.A very uneven game. You can enjoy some elements of it and hate others. Is it a good game or bad? I don't know. Buy on sale and if you REALLY want it. I played IFR for 40 hours half on a year ago and dropped it. After such a big pause, I had come back to it. And finally did it. The game completed. And the final part was the best. P.s. You can find all my short reviews .

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not good. I tried to give it a chance, but the uncanny valley graphics that were meant for Xbox 360 Civilization advisors kills all I can even attempt to put into this game. Everything looks like it was made with free assets off of the unity store. Most enemies are obnoxiously boring sponges that you chip damage off of until you fall asleep. The dialogue is peak millenial writing, with every single character being a quirky little fellow that has something very funny to say! Hey Zeus, Typhon gave me some epic odyssian zaza! Etc, just garbage dialogue meant to get likes on Twitter. None of the characters feel like they give a ♥♥♥♥, instead everyone is in on this "hilarious" meta view of this world. Like I'm going to fall over laughing at the truly gutbusting lines of Zeus and Prometheus exchanging witty quips about what they're smoking and how they need to get back into shape. Instead, I'm going to cringe in disgust as I turn off the game and uninstall permanently.It's really like the creators of AC Odyssey were like "Hey Ubisoft, we'd like to make the last game but with more fantasy elements." And the Ubisoft corporate guys gave them a budget of $500,000 instead of the 500 million for the last game. Everything feels cheap, the UI feels like an embarrassing mobile game, and the dialogue/story is so mind numbing I just turned it off during the middle of a cutscene. Ultimately, this is a game devoid of passion and creativity. To me, this game perfectly represents everything that is horrid about the game industry in it's current stage. Please, devs, ubisoft, whoever was truly responsible for this waste of time and space, look to games like God of War or even your last game Odyssey for inspiration. Stop making this bloatware trash just to fit in with the rest of the industry. You can do better.
