_childDocuments_.review: It started really good, but that did not last for me, unfortunately.First of all, a bit of context: I have not played "Breath of The Wild", which inspired this game, but I did play "Genshin Impact", which is supposed to be (and is) quite similar gameplay wise. This means, that some of my complaints may be intrinsic to this type of games in general, not this game specifically. I also finished "Assassin's Creed Odyssey", which is somewhat similar both in terms of open-world and general Greek mythology theme.The prologue of the game felt quite nice. There was a lot of humor, but it was well-paced and [usually] well-placed. The way you were introduced to mechanics through the story was good, even though the "mystery" of the first quest chain ended up to be a bit contrived. The quest chain also did not feel as if it was forcing you to just follow it, providing you enough time to wander about, if you wanted. The combat was simple, but fun, although I do not understand why most of the monsters were flying away from me at high speeds almost on every kill: that felt out of place. It was quite a good experience overall. But then I reached the point, when the game truly became open-world, and everything collapsed.The humor in dialogues started feeling stale and even annoying. There was too much of it, even though there were moments of silences during free-roaming. I honestly became tired of it pretty soon, because almost every line of dialogue tried to be a joke of some kind. Furthermore the gods did not differ that much from each other, essentially just voices and some theme for jokes, that carried over from dialogue to dialogue. They were annoying and utterly pointless in their existence. To me this also ruined the story, which obviously did not try to invent anything to begin with.The combat became stale pretty fast, too. It was quite repetitive, and I honestly did not see much point in skills, that you can buy with coins here. There was not that much depth to it. Perhaps, if I played on higher difficulty, that would have been different, but I think it would have just made me use dodge more often. Although, it did bring a little bit of satisfaction when I tried to keep the combo meter high and succeeded, which did not seem to do anything in terms of rewards. I also did not like the fact that 3 or 4 of the skills (godly powers) were unlocked through coins without any story behind them, as the rest of them. I find this a wasted opportunity, because they are god powers, not regular physical skills as in latest Assassin's Creed trilogy, so some short story would have been nice. It could have benefited from elemental effects, too, because they can make fighting a bit more diverse.What's worse, the open world felt pointless, or rather it was here to stretch out the experience. A very good example is a quest, where you need to move a large pearl into the sea. First you need to walk quite a distance towards the pearl, and then you need to push it towards the sea for like 10 minutes, if not more. It felt like a chore, and not because of monsters forced on you along the path: it was slow and uninteresting. Before this I completed a vault where you needed to push balls to solve a puzzle and even that was much more interesting.But even if that was not the case, I did not feel inspired to walk around this world. Yes, it looks quite beautiful, no argument from me there, and there is stuff to do there, which is mostly puzzles and vaults (which are kind of puzzles, too), but that's not enough. When I played Genshin, I was progressing slowly through the story, because I was constantly noticing something interesting a bit off the path I had to follow and I went there to investigate, even if there was nothing interesting, in the end. Things were placed on the map in right places to specifically trigger your curiosity. There were not things like this in Fenyx Rising, most of the things I noticed when looking around were generic or just mountainy landscapes.Even if there were more things picking my curiosity, I do not think I would have went for them, because traversal of the world was boring, too. Or maybe just because I did not like quite a few things about it:1. To jump higher you can hold jump button, but there is not that much difference in height. And it's mostly pointless, since you unlock double-jump pretty earlier in the game, too (as part of main story).2. To glide you need to press jump button and then press glide button, which is a separate one. For me it often resulted in losing just a little bit of height, because I needed to switch to a different button. I would prefer to start gliding by holding jump button, and I believe this is how it worked in Genshin.3. There is not that much difference between running horse and running you. There is a small difference in speed, but it's like 10 vs 11 meters/second. Maybe 10 vs 12. The only real benefit from a horse is that it's a secondary stamina meter, meaning that you can move at this speed longer, but this gets ruined by the fact that you need to summon the horse and then to drop off of it.4. There is a lot of  mountains that you just have to climb, and climbing is slow. Of course, I would not expect the speed of AC Odyssey here, but... No, scratch that, here it would have made much more sense, because this is a fairy tail, while AC Odyssey is, technically, not. Increasing speed even at the cost of stamina would have been a godsend here. Or at least a way to speed it up through upgrades.I remember playing AC Odyssey and just loving to go around checking those question marks on map. It did not have the design filled with curious things "along the way" as Genshin had, but the feeling that traversal of the world had was really good. Not as good as web-swinging in Spider-Man games or even in AC Unity, but good enough for me to get satisfaction just from running around.Overall, I think this game suffered from its ambitions. If this was a more linear experience with somewhat smaller world, which is open more in a sense of Bioshock type of games, rather than true open-world, with traversal having feeling closer to Assassin's Creed games, with elemental effects in combat, a bit less humor, but more detailed characters - it could have been a really good game. _childDocuments_.review: What baffles me is that there are people who played Zelda BotW, Genshin Impact and this game. They immediately compare the games to Zelda, fair enough as it was the original concept before the other two, but somehow... just somehow... I don't comprehend how... they tend to rate this game as the worst of the three.In terms of characterization, open-world, moment to moment game play of exploration and combat, and overall quality of the three games, I'll have to say: BotW > IFR >>>>>>>>> your cat putting a dead rat too close to your foot >>>>> Genshin Impact. Anyone who talks down at IFR and, in the same breath, praises Genshin cannot be trusted. That or they just didn't play the game for more than an hour. The free demo alone has more game play and depth than all of Genshin.I have like 400 hours in BotW (600 if you count TotK too), 160 hours in Genshin and about 80 in IFR (I started the DLCs so I'll easily get to over 100).Turns out, I like open world games. I bought this game to experiment if I like them and it seems to have been fairly successful. My first attempt to play this game resulted in my computer overheating and shutting down, hence my deleted old review and I refunded the game; but after figuring out that it's not IFR but it's actually my computer, I fixed my computer I tried again. It works no problem.If you don't have a Ubisoft account thing, make one -> link it to Steam (there is an option for that) and no more problems. Steam launches the ubisoft app thing without any additional inputs (after I hit play) and I face no problems.The game never crashed on me once and I was playing with high settings. As for controls: M&K is fine, but I didn't like it. I played the game with my PS5 controller; and to do that, I went into the Steam Options and turned OFF this game's steam controller thing (there's a guide for this) AND I used DS4 to emulate a PS4 controller. That worked perfectly.The biggest things that I want to complain about at this moment are:1) climbing in this game can use some polish. It has a realistic approach to it, better than all other BotW-ripoffs, but it comes at the cost of making it less fun. Case in point: the moment I hit circle to drop, the moment the character needs to let go (unless she is mid-climbing-jump). 2) Basic Shield enemies starting tier 2 (so, blue and beyond) are the most annoying enemies in the game. I don't like the "you can't parry this" mechanic, but that's a skill issue (though, I swear perfect dodging in this game is really weird. I can perfect parry for days but perfect dodge just doesn't work as well), but they run up to you and start charging up a shield bash that you can't knock down with an axe swing. Sure, I can use a power to remove this problem entirely, but I'm trying to combo man. Getting my combo into triple digits and having blue flashy lights is what I'm going for. On top of that stupid thing that should be just deleted, seriously, just delete it, if I do Axe -> Sword -> Sword, the second sword hit here is Fenyx's extra long start-up finisher which the Shield enemy just blocks. This is also incredibly stupid. Frankly, just delete this enemy and bring in a different enemy.So... overall, not so bad. It took me a while to get used to Fenyx's voice and Greek Mythology is... well, if you're unaware of how the Greek deities are humongous jerks, especially Zeus, then prepare yourself because oh boy this game kinda holds back, it isn't rated M, but you'll learn quite a bit. If you wanna smack any of them, then you're not alone.I, for one, appreciated the commentary during game play, especially since it isn't intrusive, and I found it funny. Zeus's voice actor specifically did a fantastic job. As far as in-app purchases, it's all cosmetic. All proper gear is only obtainable in-game and, importantly, upgraded together. For example: If you upgrade your armor to level 3 -> all new armor you find afterwards is already level 3. Sure there is grinding but it isn't more than BotW. I say this as someone who maxed out all armor in BotW (thrice) and TotK: this game's grind isn't bad at all; it is just less varied as in BotW where you have to collect specific loot for each upgrade of each armor piece; while in IFR, you need blue things + red or purple things. Also yellow things for potion pouch and arrow pouch upgrades.Puzzles are fine. With a big ol' open world, you gotta have stuff for players to do as an empty open world is a failure. BotW fills this with Korok Seeds for puzzles and they are quite the copy-paste going around and TotK is in this same boat. IFR's least fun puzzle is the sliding block puzzle but it has an upside that they're almost always locked and there is a puzzle to solve to unlock them. The game does this to add some variety and I appreciate it. There is one unique puzzle that's only used once where you cover a statue's eyes with rocks nearby that I had to look up, so there was someone on the team trying to add more variety but it didn't seem to work out that well.I've seen a lot of people complain about the mechanic of going to a high place, entering first person mode and marking nearby stuff, like chests, puzzles, challenges, etc, but I wanna comment that this mechanic is kinda IFR's equivalent to Zelda's sensor mechanic. If you don't like it, then don't do it. If you're like me and enjoy wandering, then you'll just trip over chests, enemy groups, puzzles, challenges, etc all on your own. They're not invisible unless you mark them so I don't get why people complain about this mechanic. Furthermore, and this is important: you don't need to go to a high place to mark stuff with this mechanic. You can enter first person mode at any time and mark stuff through walls, so if you see a chest in the distance and you don't wanna lose track of it, you can just mark it right there. It's like dropping pins in BotW but upgraded significantly. One last thing I want to mention is how IFR respects your time more than BotW (and TotK). When it comes to finishing a shrine in Zelda, skipping as fast as possible will still waste like 10 seconds. Meanwhile in IFR, if I mash circle to skip, I'm out in less than a second. That's one example and there are a whole bunch more but this is long enough and no one is going to read all this anyway. If you did, well, trust me, there are other ways IFR respects your time by not wasting it on unskippable bits like Zelda loves to. Not to mention my computer >>> the nintendo switch, so the load times of entering and exiting shrines is super fast that I don't get to read the snarky Zeus comments on the tips that show up during the loading screens. I'm not going to say IFR is better than BotW but IFR is 100% much much better than Genshin. If you finished TotK recently and you're looking to scratch that itch some more until TotK gets some DLC or something, then this game is very much worth the $20 on sale to get it + the DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: Game that was started developing by game designer and finished by effective manager. Good ideas wrapped into "oh look how many activities do we have" Ubisoft open-world. I'd recommend to buy it only when it is on sale (without Season Pass).I've spent 100+ hours in a game and 90 hours of them I was thinking "why am I continue playing?" and I can't find an answer. It's not a bad game, but Ubisoft really tried to make it bad. It starts good, you have a desire to explore this world, but after 2-3 hours you understand the core concepts and realize that you'll need to do the same thing over and over for 20-40 hours depends on difficulty and how many activities you're focusing on. You can check other reviews for more information about "good parts", but I wanted to focus on "controversial" design decisions.Personally, the story is the weakest part of the game. Have you ever heard a story about "the only one who can save us all"? This is it with exact same twists. You're the mortal who should fight Typhon and his servants, because other gods lost the battle . The game is about Greek mythology? Yes, but from mythology you'll get "legendary beasts" as a common enemies and short myths retailing in a humorous manner. Game just points out "Hey, here is Daedalus Wings. Here is Odyssey. And this is Cyclops. Want to know more? Go to wiki".There are a lot of them in this game:As I said, the game isn't bad, visual style is good, combat feels dynamic (but don't expect to much from it), movement is not restricted, so you can get pretty much everywhere in measurable amount of time, some puzzles are interesting to solve, builds (via combination of armor and weapons) may provide a small variety of gameplay (Ubisoft was trying to provide a balance for all builds, but as usual the choice between "45% damage if you have full health", "45% damage for 6 seconds after you perfectly avoid *and make exact two attacks with a hammer after double-jump and left-right strafe" and "30% to sword damage passively" is pretty much obvious).Mostly, doesn't worth it:So for me it looks like someone wanted to make a good relaxing game for 8-12 hours, but effective manager said "I need an involvement for 40 hours" so we just copy-paste \ scale all those ideas 4 times. I'd recommend to get this game on sale, set a normal difficulty (it doesn't really change anything except the time you spent fighting and solving time puzzles), play a bit, choose activities you like, get through the story and don't really focus on grinding everything (as I do). In this case, you'll enjoy the game (most likely)

_childDocuments_.review: Immortals Fenix Rising is a game that unfortunately was a bit overshadowed by Assassin's Creed Valhalla, a game in Ubisoft's cash cow franchise. In my opinion, it should’ve been the other way around because this is one of my favorite Ubisoft titles. AC Valhalla uses that typical Ubisoft open-world formula, which is getting more and more stale. Immortals was developed by the AC Odyssey team, but it’s a completely new IP, and more importantly, a breath of fresh air.The best way to describe this game is what would happen if AC Odyssey and Zelda: Breath of the Wild had a child since it combines the best parts from both titles.It uses Greek mythology as its setting, but has a more light-hearted tone and lots of humor, reminding me of some PS2 platformers. The graphics are stylized and colorful, and work really well for this style. The story is alright: it's simple and to the point. Enjoyable, but nothing special.Gameplay is simple but fun. It's mostly an action-platformer RPG, with a lot of simplified features. Combat is enjoyable, although nothing special in the end. It's simple but fluid, with some build customization.Exploration is also a big part of the game. It's open-world, but it's quite small, and this size felt perfect to me. Content is more packed, so there’s always something new to find if you look around. It's much better than having a big, empty map.The closest this gets to the Ubisoft formula is scouting around for nearby locations, marking places on the map for you to clean. You can explore naturally, but even if you want to find everything, it doesn’t feel like a chore.And the main reason for that is that this title, like Zelda, has a lot of puzzles. There're other locations like guarded chests, but the vast majority is environmental puzzles. And while there aren’t a lot of mechanics, each puzzle is unique. I really enjoyed the puzzles, although since they are physics-based, sometimes they are annoying because they don't feel consistent.Now, if you don’t like puzzles, then maybe this game isn’t for you. There’re also a lot of small dungeons to find, with a lot more puzzles to solve! Even if you just want to play the main story, puzzling is still a big part of the game.Some things are limited by stamina, like special-moves, sprinting and climbing. Some special moves can even aid in moving around, although those are more advanced techniques and aren’t required, unless you aim for 100%.Loot is mostly gear with different cosmetics and stats, without levels. You can level up gear, but it’s streamlined in the sense that when you upgrade a type of gear everything levels up at the same time. And I prefer it this way. Besides chests, there’re also other items to find that allow you to upgrade stats like health and stamina. It’s not hard to upgrade everything, and there’s even a mastery system to level up further, especially if you’re going for a new game plus.The soundtrack is enjoyable, and I really enjoyed the transitions when combat ended. A small touch, but I like these details. Like the random chest opening animations, those were a nice touch as well. You can see this game has more passion, since the devs had more freedom and weren't shackled to the Ubisoft formula. The result is a fun and enjoyable title.There’re also 3 DLCs available, and they’re all played independently, although it’s recommended you finish the main game first.The first DLC is basically a post-game epilogue, with a heavy focus on dungeon puzzles. They are harder, and will require some of the advanced techniques, but they are taught to you. You even level up further, but it’s contained here. And it should, otherwise it would break the main game. It’s more of the same, so I’m not complaining.The second DLC tells a new story in an eastern setting, and gameplay-wise it’s basically the entire main game condensed into just a few hours. The map is much smaller, but it has the same design and upgrades, just on a smaller scale. Once again, more of the same, and after the first DLC, I preferred starting progression from the beginning.The third DLC is the weirdest one. For the most part, gameplay is similar, but there’s one crucial difference: the game is played with an isometric perspective, severity limiting your visibility. The game is designed around that, but I wasn’t a fan of that. You also need to gather resources, and the combat has way more enemies but with a lot of customization. I think these two elements alone would make this DLC feel unique, without the restrictive camera. It wasn’t terrible to play, just meh.So, I really enjoyed the game and can easily recommend it on sale if you enjoy the genre. However, I have some criticisms, all related with Ubisoft and their stupid launcher.For a single player game, the game has a lot of unnecessary microtransactions, even if they’re all cosmetic. The game already has a lot of options, but most of the cool skins are unfortunately locked behind the in-game store, which sucks and it’s only an attempt for Ubisoft to get more money.There’re daily challenges that reward you with premium currency that can be used to buy those exclusive items, but only a selection of items is available per week. It’s a live service model that has no place in here.The Ubisoft launcher has a LOT of bugs. You can’t check your stats in-game, only on the launcher. When I started playing, they were available in the overlay, but disappeared a few weeks later. I can check them of the desktop launcher, but it’s extra steps for something that should be in-game.It’s the same for the achievements. They’re available only in the desktop launcher and at least unlock correctly, but there’s no way to check them in-game, and worst of all, there’s no notification when you unlock one. It wasn’t like this some years ago, so definitely a stupid regression.The new unit system is dumb. Before, at least you could get all exclusive rewards by doing all the in-game challenges, since you would get enough units, with a few exceptions. Now, even if you complete all challenges, including the DLCs, you’ll only get around half the units you need to unlock everything. I could even get more stuff if my previous units hadn’t expired…The only way to get everything now is to get points from another game (and giving up rewards there), or grinding weekly challenges for years… And even worse, the community challenges are bugged during the time I played this. Just unnecessary and annoying BS Ubisoft decided to put in all their newer titles.And those are my main criticisms, none related to the game itself. These doesn’t ruin the experience, but this game would be better without all this BS.And to top it all off, Ubisoft cancelled a sequel, moving the developing team for yet another Assassin’s Creed title, something I was extremely disappointed with.

_childDocuments_.review: 1) I think I could never take this game seriously (when it first came out) due the name 2) It's under Ubisoft which means I generally stay away from their games due to their extra drm crudI picked this game up during a recent sale due to a friend's recommendation. So far I'm about 37 hours in, maybe halfway through the main story and it's been a blast. Yes, it's open world, has combat and small dungeons - and there's a lot of puzzles - I get the Breath of the Wild (BOTW) similarities and can only say: BOTW feels both large and sometimes empty. This game is both big AND there's generally SOMETHING around a corner, some sort of activity or fighting area or something else going on. While I It has fighting: A few different combo variations with reactive combat - more of a watch for 15 seconds on new enemies to "see what they'll do" than just run up and pound everythingIt is Metroidy: It takes a variety of abilities to access all the content in the game. Even some treasure chests may require a specific ability (or set of) to unlock.It has puzzle dungeons: some logic, some manuvering (yourself / objects), time based, etc. Powering up some abilities can be VERY useful in either solving these areas, most puzzles are open enough to allow some taking advantage of the abilities / area to perhaps not solve them in the intended fashion - I have actually bugged out a couple of dungeons due to unforseen results occasionally to "alternate" solutions to solving the puzzleIt has equipment upgrading - and many "types" of equipment which can give perks that reward a variety of playstylesIt has decent respawn allowances: You don't feel like you just wasted 30 minutes because you walked off an edge instead of jumpingIt has big boss fights - where paying attention to mechanics can greatly shorten the encounter (hit: learn how to parry - it's way too useful not to abuse as much as possible)It has backstory being told primarily via some rather good Voice acting which has some pretty funny riffs against Greek Mythology. It flows behind you as you play rather than interrupting playI can't say that I've had any issues with Ubisoft Connect. I did see that the in (cash?) store where you can spend electrum was completely non-functional for me. Wasn't too surprised but it didn't keep the game from being functional

_childDocuments_.review: Actually not bad. It's very clearly inspired by BOTW, both in shading (very bright colors and cell shaded cartoony shaders for bodies of water) as well the way combat pans out. Unfortunately it's nowhere near as "free" as the aforementioned due to the lack of meaningful interactions with the terrain. It basically copied weaponized rigidbodies and stopped there.First and foremost I want to mention very clearly that this game is Ubisoft. It RADIATES Ubisoft. Progression is tied to, and I kid you not, 8 different currencies of gems. It has in-game real money cosmetic purchases, including horse armor (again, this is not a joke). It has a season pass for its DLC. It tries to tie the story into having you buy aforementioned microtransactions in a completely offline single player game. Whoever came up with the design here made the marketing lead at Ubitrash jizz their pants. Over half the available space is in the main menu is dedicated to advertisements for in-game purchases. It's so unbelievably greedy it's almost like satire.Fortunately these can be fairly easily ignored, and the remainder of the game is quite nice. Aside from your starting gear new equipment that you find are actual sidegrades; which is exactly how I like it. On the flipside there is still linear power progression, only it is tied to currencies. The overworld is actually beautiful, but also feels very devoid of life and more like ambient set-pieces. Enemies live somewhere in the realm of "decently dynamic"; some of them actively react to the environment by picking up rigid bodies. Other simply spawn rigidbodies to throw. Enemies seem to have different attack patterns based on the proximity to the player. It's too little to be impressive, but it's much more than most modern games can be given credit for.The gameplay loop is decent. There is a very strong state economy going on due to neither health nor stamina regenerating during combat (technically it does, but VERY slowly). Hitting stunned targets regenerates stamina. Parrying regenerates stamina - more so the closer you are to the active frames. Enemies have a stun-bar, which once filled, causes them to be, well... stunned. The game effectively rewards you for alternating in your strategy, which is of course great. The flipside is once again that it implements parrying without trying to reduce it; implying that you just have to learn the animations for each enemy to be effective. Outside the rigidbodies projectiles can be hard to read. You have heavy attacks, light attacks and a bow - all of which can be transitioned between seamlessly. You also have aerial attacks for each (which seem to be extremely overpowered). They're just simple three or four hit combos, which is a true and tested implementation and completely fine as is.One of my primary gripes is actually with the traversal; stamina regenerates faster outside combat, but you still spend it way too fast in my opinion. This means that you can't just run anywhere. You randomly have to halt and wait for it to regenerate. This makes sense for vertical traversal (which is great in this game by the way; you can climb ANY piece of geometry, only limited by your stamina), but not for running around.The story is annoying. The game has this whole "you guys know, like, greek mythology???? Here is a funni reference to it1!" theme going that's amusing for maybe 1 minute and then starts to overstay its welcome. It makes very obvious references to the Odysseus and paints the pantheon through the most obvious "comical" caricatures. Especially Zeus they reduce to a pompous numbskull (they really go to town on Zeus, it's almost like a vendetta).Overall it's all quite good, and a pretty surprising game to have developed by Ubitrash. I presume this was greenlit to try and cash in on that BOTW hype - which clearly failed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game would be so so so much better if it WAS a clone of Breath of the Wild. I honestly wish they had ripped Nintendo off completely, what they’ve scraped together here pales in comparison and fails in so many ways the newer Zelda games never could. It isn’t a carbon copy, it’s more like the scribbled notes of someone seeing Breath of the Wild played on a CRT through a crack in the door. They ripped the constant narration and bad "humor" from other annoying games, threw in some RPG-lite upgrading, stuffed the rest with a confused replication of the newest Zeldas’ mechanics, and set that all over an overdone, uninspired setting. Following the trend of most AAA games, it feels like nobody playtested this game at all, or someone would have mentioned that it does NOT feel good to play. The game is exceedingly clunky, every action has a full animation that has to play out every single time before any other action can even be attempted. There is a big delay from when you press a button in combat and when your character actually carries it out, and that also extends to gliding, climbing, platforming, puzzle solving, etc. There is no fluidity between actions like the newest Zelda games, if you press a button on your controller when your character is in one of the MANY animations for any little thing in the game, nothing will happen. This makes every action you take seem like you’re fighting the game to make happen, especially: climbing upwards, dropping from ledges, vaulting up ledges, opening/closing your glider, diving while gliding, sprinting at all, jumping combined with anything else, the list goes on. In another page out of Nintendo’s book: every chest, collectible, and puzzle has an unskippable animation, wasting hours of your life over the course of the game. Player upgrades in the hub also incur a lengthy, detestable cutscene each time, which incentivizes redeeming upgrades in batches to avoid watching it.You have no idea what a button in the world is going to do before pressing it, and a lot of the time even after pressing it you don’t know what it did. No blue lines connecting the switch to what it affects, no camera change to show what’s being powered or moved, and you definitely can’t see or hear the results of your actions in way too many cases. Any given door could have a puzzle to unlock it AND a button to unlock the puzzle, and both could be in completely different zip codes, with no way to tell what goes with what. Most of the puzzle solutions are trivially intuitive, the rest are oblique purely because you literally can’t see what you are supposed to do. It should go without saying that all of this is antithetic to good puzzle design.Luckily they give you two or three dozen ways to speed up traversal across the exceedingly large map. Unfortunate for us that they needed to. It would have been more than enough to make a smaller world packed with the same amount of filler (or less), but instead we have featureless landscapes to completely bypass in the sky, or by a mount that can’t jump, or fast traveling instead of seeing the world on the way to the actual playable content. A small, tightly designed world doesn’t align with “bigger number better”, so to our detriment we are stuck with this AAA status quo of an ever increasing map size. Not a surprise given the devs also worked on AC Odyssey, a poster child for map bloat. Combat is fairly simple, some strategies are better than others I guess but the system is so restrained you don’t have a choice but to fight enemies exactly how the devs decided you would. Generous windows for the dodge (and parry) and small enemy hurtboxes makes defense trivial, but not getting hit doesn’t shorten the high time-to-kill on these large health pools of some enemies. I’m not positive that combat actually gives you anything worth the time taken, maybe a few resources you are going to get from the mandatory combat or open world anyway. Which means that you are best off avoiding combat entirely when you can help it, and you certainly can. There’s also a suspicious amount of input reading, enemies will stand passively with you and attack only after you do. Doesn’t make the game difficult, just annoying.And that wraps up all of the traditional gameplay pillars, with not a single one done half as well as this game’s obvious sources of inspiration. I saw a post somewhere saying that the best way to play the game would be to NOT tag all the points of interest from the synchronize points, and to instead discover everything naturally while on your way to the next quest marker. That honestly makes sense, it’s less like a list of tasks to work down and more like you’re actually exploring the world, and that’s how BOTW worked. Unfortunately, nothing you come across is actually fun enough for that to be worth doing, so I can’t recommend playing this game like that or at all. Also, they added this cool mechanic that causes a “local” (mapwide) debuff after you do some very low number of objectives (sometimes none at all). As if you needed another reason to NOT play the game, they’ve included a deterrent built right in.

_childDocuments_.review: It's another open-world  game. Oh yeah, and you have mounts for some reason... and they suck lol. I thought with the game emphasizing having wings it was going to develop deeper into it, but its just a double jump and a glide, not even like a super jump on Cooldwon to gain height, nothing, just 2 options...I went into this game not for the gameplay but for the comedy aspect of it and being set in the Greek mythology, but I regret buying this game even with a discount; it's so f*cking boring, the player has almost no facial expressions, the player's conversations are really boring, and their tone really doesn't match most of the situations. _childDocuments_.review: Unironically the best Souls-lite Assassin's Creed game. It uses all the same gameplay mechanics as Odyssey but cuts out the pretenses and is just a good fantasy action game. The only thing it lacks is social gameplay, but the Souls-lite AC games sucked at that until Valhalla anyways.It has the same climbing and combat mechanics of the Souls-lite AC games, but a much better gear system that's more constrained where all gear is upgraded by type, such as upgrading all light weapons, all heavy weapons, or all bows with a single click. You don't have to manage too many resources or collect hundreds of items to unlock every cosmetic.And all the gear and cosmetic unlocks are tied to Vaults and heroic chests specifically, so you always know you're going to find a totally unique and new piece of gear in every vault, and that every heroic chest you find will give you a new cosmetic for your gear.The crafting/upgrade system is straightforwards and incentivises exploration, with all upgrade materials for skills, gear, and consumables being stuff you find in the open world. And you loot everything in a wide radius when you find it, so no need to pick up individual nectars or pomegranates, you can loot an entire patch in a single button press.

_childDocuments_.review: Inevitably this game will get compared to The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, and fair enough because it's clearly heavily inspired by it, but this game does not have the weapon durability system. In my opinion this game is probably the definitive "Breath of the Wild experience" for PC gamers. For me personally, this game really does knocked it out of the park in almost every way. Immortals Fenyx Rising is an open-world adventure/action/hack and slash/puzzle game that really does make you feel like a hero in a Greek myth. The characters are endearing and well-performed. The humor is full of amazingly awful dad jokes and self-awareness about how messed up a lot of Greek mythology really is. The humor, gameplay, and art style reminds me a lot of older PlayStation 2 games like Jak & Daxter and Sly Cooper. The banter between Zeus and Prometheus that you overhear while running around fighting minotaurs and gorgons is really something special. (Jokingly) my only issues with the game is that there isn't more of it. I'd love to see sequels made by the same team take on Norse and Egyptian mythologies and more. Realistically though I'd say this game has a few small flaws that you can avoid if you know what you're doing, which most new players won't. First and foremost, don't try to 100% the game on your first playthrough. I tried to do that and ended up being way too strong and I had accidentally optimized myself into boredom. The stun system is way too easy to exploit once you get a handful of items and if you have enough stamina you can basically stunlock every single enemy and boss without even trying. My second issue is that the whole "play any way you want" as advertised with the incredibly diverse gear system gets left behind once you realize there are like two or three dominant strategies and 90% of the gear is pretty irrelevant. There are three main weapons which are the sword, axe, and bow. A lot of items buff different weapons differently. However the bow will never be as good as the sword (especially since you can jump and sort of hover in the air while you attack), and you never need to use the axe for stun damage when it's so much slower than the sword, and your special powers like Athena's Dash will deal way more stun damage than the axe can ever dream of. Sure, you can build a character who focuses on aerial combat and stunlocks enemies out of the sky but that's probably not as effective as just equipping the right armor and spamming Ares's Wrath while chugging stamina potions. My third issue is the Difficulty scales both the puzzle and combat difficulty at the same time. Combat difficulty is self-explantory, and just changes numbers like your health regen speed and enemy damage output. This game has a lot of puzzles that are based on timers, like you flip a switch, a door opens, and you have to run across a complicated room to get through that door before the timer expires. So increasing difficulty lowers the length of the timers, requiring much higher skill to complete. Now if you're like me and you're really good at combat but really bad at puzzles, you're out of luck because you either get bored from the combat or you lock yourself out of doing any puzzles. It's not a big deal but it basically requires you to be a big fish in a small pond by intentionally avoiding making yourself overpowered for combat. Like I explained above it's very easy to accidentally "over-level" and cheese the game to hell. These are issues that are pretty easily remedied and avoided but only after you've sunken a few dozen hours into the game. My advice would be to play on Normal, focus on the actual quests, and don't try to 100% the game the first time around. There's New Game+ and a "Nightmare Difficulty" which will give you a nice victory lap to 100% the game on and I definitely think you should because there are so many clever puzzles and Zeus and Prometheus have little conversations based on the smallest things you do in the game. I think this game really deserves a lot of attention for how great it is.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend this game, but I don't *not* recommend it. If there was an "Eh" option, this would be a low Eh. If you like Greek mythology, pick this up while it's on sale, but let me spin you a story first:So it's winter 2020 or something. I had a laptop, bought this game, and it ran like ♥♥♥♥ because the game insists on having, like, literally an entire solar system worth of stars fully rendered on every character. (I'm not kidding, look up the opening cutscene, Zeus just inexplicably has the entire milky way galaxy on him for no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason)Fast forward to autumn 2023. I buy the game *again* and now I can run it because new laptop. And it's... Fine? Something about me. When it comes to mythology games, I will always play them, but I have a VERY high standard. You need to make something really special if you're stepping into my territory of mythology. And this game is not special. The game has zero identity, the world is incredibly bland. You know how in Zelda BOTW there are like 10 different biomes spread across the world, and each one also has tons of interesting stuff to find in it? Well this game has five biomes. Tutorial, grassy plain, grassy plain (but there is brick and ♥♥♥♥ everywhere and the grass is orange), snow, and lava. 100% this game and tell me if you remember a single pixel of the world. If you've got a PC that can run this game and want an ancient Greek game, just get Assassin's Creed Odyssey. The dialogue is fine. I like the occasional interactions between Zeus and Prometheus. The twist at the end, no spoilers, was really dumb and didn't really add anything to the experience.Speaking of endings, let's talk about the final boss. And speaking about the final boss, let's talk about bosses. And speaking of bosses, let's talk about the combat. It's meh. Your abilities don't work because the controls are very unresponsive most of the time, so you'd quickly press the buttons for an ability and have Fenyx just stand there while like four minotaurs beat her like she owes them money. The game loves to arbitrarily crank up difficulty and completely ruin the flow of the game. Like, 11 or so hours in I was ready to face the final boss. Beat the boss, got the twist, beat the final dungeon, fought the *real* final boss, and got my ass kicked because all of his attacks are screen-clearing instakills that cannot be anticipated or avoided in any way because the game locks your camera to some random direction for no reason whenever it feels like. So the only way to beat him is to tank him with like 20 billion potions. So fast forward to like *20* hours into the game, I finally had enough potions to tank him. Why is that a feature? Why do I need to ruin the game for myself just to finish it? Why can't completing the main storyline for the game adequately prepare me for the ending? Why do I need to slop 10 hours of grinding on top of that? It's a 5 hour game that gets stretched to 20 hours because it randomly throws roadblocks that require hours of tedious grinding in your way. Other than that, upgrades don't feel meaningful (Upgrading your weapons increases damage, but whenever you upgrade them, the enemies in the world become stronger so you're just dealing the exact same percentage of damage to them, the numbers are just slightly bigger). There's a lot of "Now go do this thing!" questing instead of "You did this, which caused this, so therefore you need to do this!". It feels less like a story, and more like a laundry list of pointless chores. If you react to seeing mythological characters the same way Marvel fans react whenever some dude named PeepeePoopoo Man shows up in the post-credits scene of Avengers, then you'll get a kick out of the constant "Now go slay this random mythological monster that was completely unrelated to the questline until now!" You'll definitely struggle to find motivation to play this game. But if you push through it, you have a middling and slightly charming open world game waiting for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool AAA open-world game with lots of flaws and no Steam integration.- No Steam achievements.- DLC are standalone games: you are either playing good open-world base game or either of 3 DLCs.- No end-game and rudimentary new game+ with 0 fun.- Balance issues: game is super easy even on Nightmare difficulty, but then vault with lasers or timers and you MUST reduce difficulty temporarily.- Annoying "checking for additional content" message every time you go into main menu, takes 1+ minute EACH time game is started.- Poor controls which often do not work, hard coded keys which makes certain popular keybindings (ESDF) dysfunctional.- Annoying repeatable animations: almost every action you do, opening chest, upgrading, crafting, picking up will be followed by useless animation, each of which you will see 100+ times if you made to the end.- Unexplored things are added to a map with poorly implemented exploration mini-game, where you need to spam one key, while trying to find something unexplored by looking at every shiny thing in the distance.+ Big world to explore, 5 biomes, diferent enemies, lots of hidden treasures, various puzzles.+ Nice story, good cut-scenes with remarkable main characters.+ Music, sounds, effects, surroundings, art-style of a solid AAA game.+ Enjoyable combat.+ Gliding (who do not like to fly?)I bought this game with 90% discount, which is well worth the time it takes to complete base game. Some fraction of this time was spoiled by poorly designed puzzles, not working controls, bugs with physics or targeting issues. But otherwise it's a solid game.I wish there were no DLCs, but more base game content, more weapons/armors, various enemies and some sort of end-game. I wish there were Steam achievements so I'd spend some extra time trying to complete them.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the story of Hades and the gameplay of Breath of the Wild, this is probably for you. Your actions are narrated by Prometheus to an audience of Zeus, and it's frequently hilarious. Very few games have made me laugh as much as this.Biggest differences from BotW:- no weapon durability- stamina is very forgiving once you have a few upgrades (to either stamina or potions)The gameplay quality bar is probably not as high as BotW. The writing is fantastic, but if you are a completionist, by the time you get to the end of the game (thanks to all your upgrades), you'll be so overpowered even on the max difficulty that you can stunlock mini-bosses. I increased the difficulty multiple times to try and counter this, but that's a band-aid that doesn't quite fix the issue.Even so, I am now approaching 80 hours of play, have nearly 100%ed everything on the map, and haven't done the DLCs yet. Well worth the $15 sale price I got it for. $60 for a 2 year old game might be a bit much, but you'll probably get your money's worth.Side note: if Greek Mythology is of much interest to you, there are references to pretty much every story I've ever heard, and quite a few I had not heard of. The writing is definitely done by mythology nerds.Disclaimer: I haven't actually played Breath of the Wild, but I've talked to a number of folks about it.

_childDocuments_.review: Immortals: Fenyx Rising is a near-perfect game in my eyes. As Fenyx, you are the protagonist in the tale of Prometheus, exploring the lands of the gods to free and unite them against Typhon. As a fan of anything mythology-related, the greek mythology is represented very well in this game. You are constantly being told new small tales from greek mythology, even when just exploring and happening upon some ruins, or fighting a legendary foe. The story is told very tongue-in-cheek; the game does not take itself too seriously and remembers that it is, first and foremost, a game. Not all of the humor lands, but most of it got a good chuckle out of me and helps keep the game light and fun while teaching you lots of cool mythology. I don't get some of the negative reviews; I had no problem with crashes, the Ubisoft Client works fine (surprisingly) and it DOES work on the Steam Deck without any setup necessary or any problems; I played it on there for a while.The gameplay consists of exploring the lands of the gods; 5 main areas and 2 small side areas. The combat system is active, with light and heavy attacks you can mix and match. The more you explore, the more you can upgrade your stats, learn the powers of the gods and obtain their blessings, which power you up further. The game's power curve is excellently done - while fighting against a simple bear at the beginning can prove fatal, you will feel like a god by the end of the game yourself, effortlessly cutting swaths throughout the enemy hordes. The game also has a fantastic artstyle and looks downright gorgeous, though the optimization could be slightly better.Exploring the areas is typically Ubisoft, though this time, there aren't really any collectibles - anything you find serves you in some way. Chests give new equipment and cosmetic variations as well as upgrade ingredients while splinters and ambrosia upgrade your weapons and health. The landscape is also dotted with tons of vaults - small puzzle side areas which, I thought, were surprisingly well done. There are a lot of puzzle ideas in this game, from moving boxes around to playing pinball with heavy balls and using controllable arrows to light fires. 50 hours and I never, ever got bored and the game never got repetitive, which is honestly a feat in my eyes. I heard the game being compared to Zelda: BotW at times, and while I have never played that, after reading up on it, the gameplay loop does seem to be very similar. It's high quality stuff, never too hard but can make you think at times.The only two downsides I can find is that, first, you have to "mark" things on the map yourself by entering far sight mode and hovering over the treasures, like in Mad Max for example. Far Sight has a limited range though, so you have to sometimes stop and scan your surroundings. It takes only a minute though and its cool to populate and check off your map. The other thing is that there is an ingame store - it's all cosmetics, though, and the game has daily / weekly quests that give you a currency for cosmetics you can't find by playing the game normally. That currency is very easy to obtain and by the end of the game, you will have unlocked several of those extra cosmetics, on top of every cosmetic equipment variation you can find just by playing. A single player game having an in game store can be argued about, but it's all cosmetic stuff and I never bought anything. Since the game does use the Ubisoft launcher, you will also get experience in their Ubisoft Connect system, which also allows you to unlock some cosmetics. You can ignore all of that, though, if you want, but it should be mentioned; game is awesome, though.Finishing the main game, with exploring everything and finding all the things, took me about 50 hours. The DLCs are very solid as well - I reviewed those separately. Either way, this game has an insane bang for your buck if you are at all interested in epic open world adventures with a tongue-in-cheek story, addictive gameplay and lots of things to do and find, including a ton of secrets. This is a true gem and one of the best games I ever played, simply because it knows that it's a game and is pure fun. A definite recommendation!( As mentioned, the game works fine on Steam Deck; if you logged into it on a PC before, you don't even need to enter your UPlay credentials. It doesn't use Steam Cloud Save though; your saves are automatically backed up through the Ubisoft launcher after closing the game, so they are there when switching to / from the Deck.)

_childDocuments_.review: Not gonna lie, it felt a bit weird helping these gods instead of slaughtering them. Heard the name “Hermes” and I immediately clenched my fists in anger.It looks like Zelda and Assassins’s Creed finally had a baby. The game is flawless, and creative in every way. This game is definitely one of the best sleeper hits of 2020. The story is a blast and hiding the pretty factual lore behind two bantering narrators was genius. Honestly, I absolutely loved this game. Even though I joked about it, I feel those that call it a "clone" of AC or Breath of the Wild were giving it an incomplete assessment. It's WAY different than both of those games, despite being clearly inspired by them.My biggest gripe with BOTW is that there was very little story and no structure as far as where to go and what to do. This game remedies both of those and makes for a more engaging experience.BOTW is about exploring a vast world with stuff to do spread out over a largely empty map. Fenyx is about exploring a smaller, denser world with a lot more (and better) stuff to do condensced into a very full map.I had a blast playing it and actually spent the time to almost 100% it because it was that fun to me. It’s not a deep game, and the comedy falls flat 90% of the time, but I have no regrets in buying it.I love when a game doesn’t take itself too seriously just like this one, all those jokes and “deliberately” corny narration is just nice laughing material, it’s like playing Monty Python’s Greek version.I will admit my dumb monkey brain did struggle with a few puzzles which felt a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to me, but most of them felt super rewarding after completing them.Combat was pretty neat. I liked all the special abilities you could get as well as the combination of aerial combat to combo into different things. Ubisoft games in general tend to have kinda repetitive combat to me so this was a nice change of pace.I also loved how bright and vibrant everything is. I know the cartoony art style is hit or miss for a lot of people but I found it charming. The enemy designs were also super cool too.The only real gripe that I had with it (besides the occasional frustrating puzzle) is that towards the end it got a bit easy. It may be down to me just getting better naturally but in the last 1/3 of the game, enemies felt super easy and I could do entire rooms of fights without getting hit at all.Overall, it's great and definitely worth picking up on a sale. A shame that everything went against it, including being launched a week before Cybercrap 2077.This game would have been way more popular with a better name and not stuck on Ubisoft's launcher.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Immortals Fenyx Rising is a perfectly cromulent open world icon hoovering sim. What makes it different from the million and one other icon hoovering titles is that it's cartoonish and light-hearted. You never have to kill any real people because all the baddies are ghostly monsters conjured up by the big bad. The story does not take itself seriously at all. The jokes are bad, barely even dad joke quality, but they're not offensive. They're just kinda... there.In fact the whole game is just kinda... there. The movement and combat is a bit janky, but not unplayably so. There are some tedious parkour and platforming sections, but most of them are optional. The puzzles are polished versions of lever and trapdoor, Sokoban, that sort of thing. They're actually pretty decent if you like casual puzzling, and really push this game from "meh" up to "solid way to spend a bunch of hours".You're a hero. You explore Greece. You help the gods. You save mankind. Do not expect a compelling story or an unforgettable multimedia experience. It's just cheerful, harmless fun. Sometimes that's all you need.

_childDocuments_.review: I never fully embraced Ubisoft’s open world games until I played Immortals: Fenyx Rising. Don’t sleep on this game! It’s different, and in a good way.Immortals: Fenyx Rising has a similar look to Zelda: Breath of the Wild, but the colors in Immortals: Fenyx Rising are more vibrant; and the textures are more consistent. Zelda: Breath of the Wild includes some more realistic textures along with its cartoony look; Immortals: Fenyx Rising does not.A word about the comparison with Zelda: Breath of the Wild. I never understood why gaming journalists criticized the similarities. Obviously Immortals: Fenyx Rising was inspired by Zelda, but why should this be a bad thing? Nobody would say that a Souls-like game is “too similar” to Dark Souls either.The gameplay in Immortals: Fenyx Rising encompasses three major areas: exploring, puzzle solving, and combat. Minor gameplay features include role-playing mechanics, i.e. leveling up, gathering materials, and crafting potions. Exploration is fun, as the open world is reasonably sized and offers an unusual but welcome amount of verticality. Fenyx, our protagonist, is equipped with the wings of Daidalos – and gliding through the air is just so much fun in this game. Solving puzzles may sound boring at first; aren’t minigames and puzzles in most games? Yes, I think so, but Immortals: Fenyx Rising is different because the puzzles never exhaust you. While playing through the game, I never once felt the need to look up any solutions online. Even after more than 40 hours into the game, the puzzles will still introduce new mechanics. Don’t expect Portal or The Talos Principle, but I’m sure that some of the puzzles in Immortals: Fenyx Rising will surprise you. In short, the puzzles will demand your wits, but they will rarely, if ever, frustrate you.The combat is pleasantly over the top as your abilities are more than just human. You have superhuman abilities, such as Hephastios’ hammer, my favorite: a giant hammer appears in your hand and you simply smash your foes. It never gets boring. The only bad thing I can say about combat in Immortals: Fenyx Rising is the lack of variety in your enemies. Then again, you spend more time exploring and solving puzzles anyway; so every fight feels like a welcome change of pace. Also, dodging or blocking enemy attacks is an effective and fun way to make sure you get the upper hand in every fight.The soundtrack is another big plus. Previous works by Gareth Coker, who composed the soundtrack for Immortals: Fenyx Rising, include the soundtracks of Ori and the Blind Forest and Ori and the Will of the Wisps. If you want to get an idea of how well done the soundtrack is, just listen to the main track “Heart of the Hero”.Fenyx’ story is told by two narrators: the always smug, boastful Zeus and the more thoughtful, idealistic Prometheus. They comment on many of the events in the background and I personally find their dialog hilarious. You will understand many of the jokes and even more if you are somewhat familiar with Ancient Greek mythology. For example, at one point Zeus comments: “The sincerest form of flattery is kidnapping someone so you can get some alone time, just ask Ganymede.” I laughed my head off. The other gods are fun, too. Ares, for example, [minor spoiler:]  He is helplessly in love with Aphrodite, but doubts his chances: “Oh, so a gorgeous goddess in love with a ? I’m sure that’s illegal.” Zeus only comments in the background: “Definitely not illegal!” There are also wholesome moments, like Prometheus saying: “Fenyx couldn’t help but reflect on what the god of war had taught her. That true courage isn’t the absence of despair. But triumph over it.” So, yeah, I enjoyed the dialogue quite a bit in this game.You won’t pass a test on Ancient Greek mythology by playing Immortals: Fenyx Rising, but Ubisoft Québec has done a really good job integrating Ancient Greek mythology into their game. If you’re unfamiliar with it, you will learn many stories on your adventure; and if you already know them, your knowledge will be refreshed and you’ll understand the insiders.You can grab the Gold Edition of Immortals: Fenyx Rising for like $15 during a big sale and it’s definitely worth it. Another reviewer here called this game “criminally underrated”; I agree.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it overall, but it is a bloated with collectibles and puzzles. I'd also like to extend my "screw you ubisoft" for including microtransactions and daily/weekly challenges in this singleplayer game. They have  in singleplayer games. So, I'd only recommend buying this on a sale.The game itself is not bad, but it did take me a while to get used to the rather dated graphics and animation quality. I usually don't pay that huge attention, but it was quite jarring at first in this game.The gameplay is fast paced. The movement takes some time to get used to as well. The progression (upgrades, skills, some exploration stuff) is directly copied from the RPG Assassin's Creeds, unsurprising since the game runs on the same engine. The map is fairly large and is filled with collectibles and  puzzles to complete.Music was surprisingly good.Narratively, the game doesn't take itself too seriously, constantly trying to make jokes.I didn't quite like the voice acting of the protagonist. I don't why, it just didn't feel right.Some of the controls are also frustrating, most notably the way you activate your "godly powers" has the same key bindings as using potions, but with holding middle mouse button. This results in quite a lot accidental potion usages.I also didn't like the fact that there's no "post-game" as such. You get a "point of no return" warning + a save and that's it, so you can never complete all quests and collect everything. The final quest will always be on your map. There's also no checklist for game completion of any kind, so you will never know if you missed some boss, puzzle or collectible.I also had a bizarre bug 2 times after playing this game all day long, where my entire Windows would get bricked - being unable to do anything, open start menu, open task manager, open files, could not even shutdown my PC without a hard reset. I don't know if it is something with the game or not, but this has never happened before or since.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a real treasure. A huge amount of content awaits you in a really big open world, which you can freely explore.The story is set in Greek mythology and right at the beginning I have to say that as an classical archaeologist I was very pleasantly surprised by the accuracy, details and references that the game offers. The whole thing has a more light-hearted tone and lots of humor, which is really perfect. Especially the chemistry between Zeus and Prometheus is very good. A huge advantage for me is that the game doesn't seem repetitive to me at all. Puzzles, vaults and also enemies are original and except for a few basic units, they are not repeated at all. The combat system is enjoyable, the game offers multiple fighting styles that you can use at the same time. Quick short sword, a long heavy axe or a long  distance bow. A stealth option is also present and the whole thing is further enriched by a large number of special attacks. Finally, I would like to mention flying, which is really amazing. Yes, the ubisoft launcher isn't perfect, it would be great to have achievements on steam and there is also an in-game store with microtransactions, but I personally didn't notice it at all while playing. Definitely give this game a try, it´s worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: A bit like BOTW but not restricted to poor hardware. Overall a very chill, relaxing and fun experience aside for the second dlc. Beautiful world,  lots of humor, nice puzzles, and a fun enough fighting system, and it doesn't feel too big or long. Seems to be the exception for an Ubisoft game lately.  Lots of small drops of greek mythology by the narrators here and there is also nice ! Difficulty is clearly not the goal here.Though the humor is not for all ages, the game itself is very accessible for everyone.I really liked the artstyle, very pleasing to the eye. Some animations too are really funny, especially the cyclops.  Sounds design is good, and both the ambient and combat music are good enough too.  Oh and the story, is quite good. One of the main point here is how its told through the two narrators that you hear talk and banter during the whole game.  I wish there was more of it, and that there was more gods in the based game, that would have been even better, more greek gods drama ! Once stats are maxed, you can keep grinding to go over the max which gives very smalls % benefits that aren't worth it except if you're a completionist. So skipping normal chest becomes usual once you have done 2 zones.Hermes taskboard also takes a bit to complete but to my surprise, completing all tasks doesn't give anything special. Some vaults or even locked chests have puzzles that are time based with very precise timings, which brings a bit of frustration.The last area, the mountain, is annoying to move around.About the DLCS : _A new god :  more and almost only puzzles, a bit more challenging than the base game but fun enough and worth it._Lost Gods :  the problematic one , isometric view that doesn't translate well for some things, far less story content, combat is far more difficult , too difficult at times because of other changes, which made it extremely frustrating. _childDocuments_.review: Oh, Ubisoft, can you just make a good game a good game and not ruin it for a while?.. Immortals Fenyx Rising is a Greek mythology based action adventure in an open world that attempts to marry The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild to the Assassin’s Creed formula from Origins to today. And the concept is genuinely solid as are the basics, but… Well. It’s Ubisoft, so despite liking the game a lot, I’m writing this exhausted and after deciding not to play the DLCs.To get it out of the way first – I have not played Breath of the Wild yet myself. I’ve not found Switch comfortable enough to own or even borrow, so I’ve avoided that title and, if I’m going to be honest to myself – I doubt that I will like it that much. The promise of a completely free open map with no little handholding, systemic approach to design sounds both impressive and also super boring to me. I just tend to prefer more guided titles, even if they leave a lot of freedom to what I can do, I just don’t particularly care about games that want me to wander around and find entertainment for myself.That’s one of the reasons why I thought Immortals Fenyx Rising might click with me – it’s a far more guided experience. To the point where it’s a more traditionally story-driven game. It has a lot of similar basics as BotW, but most of the systems are simplified and you get a lot of what you expect to find in a modern AC instead. So, unlike BotW, it’s not a question of – you can fight the final boss from the start, it’s just going to be stupid hard unless you get better gear and upgrades by doing the rest of the game. It’s more of a – you can do most of the game in any order, but you cannot get to the ending without going through all linear story arcs.And I’m mostly fine with that. The story is… I’m sure a lot of people will roll their eyes at the approach to writing in this game, as it basically takes the Ancient Greek mythology and tells it as a fourth-wall breaking somewhat anachronistic “modern” story, with social media lingo and memes included. But it manages to do it well enough to not sound like “how do you do, fellow kids”, and on top of that the underlying story is good and the voice acting performances are fun.Plus it doesn’t usually get in the way of gameplay, which (unlike AC games) is more central here. As mentioned, it’s far closer to modern AC, so while you do get limited stamina, just like in BotW, the climbing itself is basically lifted from Odyssey as is. And you don’t get any additional systemic elements on top of that – there are no rains to make things slippery or lightning to strike metallic things or anything like that. But still, just adding stamina, making the world full of small and bigger puzzles that are fun to solve and which are very varied, makes the game feel entirely unlike modern AC titles and, gameplay-wise, much more interesting.But then they Ubisofted all over the map with Stuff To Do. As mentioned – I’ve not played BotW myself and neither did I watch anyone ever 100% it. But finding treasures and solving optional puzzles in Immortals feels very un-Zelda and extremely Ubisoft. There’s just way too much crap, most of it is useless (no really, most of the rewards are just skins for equipment), simple upgrade materials are measured in thousands just so you must get more of them… The quality of a lot of puzzles and puzzle dungeons suffers greatly from it too. Like – for example, there’s a fun little one-off puzzle dungeon which suddenly turns the game into pinball. Fun and unexpected, but it’s so unrefined and random that instead of having fun, you’ll be wasting several dozens of minutes trying to achieve the goal the game set because everything is slow and random. That, or do it very quickly because again – totally random. And it’s just one example among dozens of icons on the map screen you’ll get if you mark them (you can decide not to mark them, though).And if the game had about half of it simply cut while the rest better refined, I’d be singing praises for the game right now. Well, no, first I’d be playing DLCs that I, otherwise, just had no patience for right now, then singing praises. Instead, I consciously understand that I’ve enjoyed the game and I love what they were doing here. But also I don’t want to play it anymore.Then again, it’s not the only thing cooling my excitement. Despite clearly being a lower budget (not as low budget as poor Prince of Persia: The Forgotten Sands got, mind you), Ubisoft wanted to double dip hard into this release, so the store and microtransactions are pushed hard down your throat from the start… Even though all of them are purely decorative. The Steam release is also clearly a throwaway thing for the company as they didn’t even bother to make a proper compatibility check for Steam Controller system, so without additional (if simple) tweaks, the game won’t properly work for you. It also loads super slowly, because it “checks for additional content” every time you have to get into main menu for about half a minute. And after you close the game, Ubisoft Connect (ex-Uplay) throws a million errors at you. Just – no care for the title whatsoever.It’s a real shame, because I did like this game. And I would’ve liked it much much more, and maybe the DLCs too, if it knew when to stop and not Ubisoft its pants. But no, sadly it does the exact same mistakes all recent Ubisoft titles do. I’d say – it’s still worth checking out. It’s fun, funny, with some good puzzles, descent combat… And it feels more fresh than what you usually expect from the developers. Plus, this feels like a passion project, reminding me of how exciting Origins felt. Like all of the nerdy fun things the team learned from Ancient Greece research finally could be shared with the world, because it sure as hell wasn’t in Odyssey which was just sterile and boring in comparison. But do expect it to get stale and you stopping playing it not because you finished it, but because you got bored.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fine game. There is a good atmosphere, a decent moveset, good progression, interesting armor/weapon builds, loads of playtime, and exploring is fun. About 40 hours to 100% the game, and another 30 in the DLCs.But there are too many things that irk me to leave a good review. -I bought the upgraded version with all the DLC, and the menu screen is 80% covered with ads for the DLC and store. -The ubisoft app integration is super bad, about half of the time I launch the game, it cannot verify my ownership and won't let me play. -Anytime you enter a cutscene, it will hardlock all your inputs at that time. So if you are opening the map when it starts, you will continually open the map afterwards. As soon as you close the map it re-opens. You can't access the menus because the map opens in 0.5 seconds. You have to alt+f4 the game to fix it. Completely unreasonable for a game that's been out this long.-Many of the bonus rewards in the puzzle vaults just require you to spend 10 extra minutes ferrying around heavy objects and don't do anything interesting. Just a super tedious chore.-The enemy AI is really simple, even bosses seem to only have 3 moves. And they have a very long projection to the point there is no danger. Combat is made too easy with high stun god-moves that you can spam. And I'm not even abusing the completely broken potions that basically negate combat (100% protection, reflect all projectiles, return 2k damage in a single defense potion that lasts the entire fight).-Scripting and voice acting is super cringy. The characters are supposed to have Greek accents, but Zeus sounds more like a jewish grandmother. The dialogue is sometimes straight Greek mythology and okay, but other times it's over the top youth-speak, trying to be relevant to Gen Z or something. The two contrast so much and just doesn't make sense.-They decided to put online player screenshots all over the map, so when you try to fast travel or select a quest on the map, you often have to navigate your way around player screenshots to select the actual thing.-Cutscenes are in 30 fps, but don't appear to be pre-rendered because they use player cosmetics, so why are they so low? Same with menus, opening menu sections can sporadically drop your fps if there is a video preview of an ability in action.DLC Review:A New God was just a castle with vaults of tartaros-style puzzle rooms. There were something like 25 puzzle/platforming rooms that took a bit of time to work through. Some were okay, some were really tedious, none really added anything beyond the main game. Definitely not worth a purchase, even if you liked the vaults of tartaros.Eastern Realms seems like it was the initial development of a sequel game, but is super unpolished. Voice acting is super bad, some of the character recordings are echoey and poorly done. Puzzle rooms are very poorly crafted, many can be easily cheated by flying under the level to the final lift. Would have been a much better setting for the game than the original Greek mythology. Really seems like they were working on a sequel and then just dumped it as a DLC for a quick payout before layoffs.Lost Gods is a top-down version of the game that removes all of the best features of the original game, like stamina based climbing, gliding, and being able to see more than 20 feet away from you.

_childDocuments_.review: Is it really a bad game? No. Is it a long and tedious game that would have been better as a linear PS2-era action platformer instead of an open-world one? Absolutely.The game is like Zelda: BOTW made by minimum-wage employees. There are puzzles, but they aren't fun and repeat themselves all the time. There is dynamic combat, but target switching is the worst, enemies are damage sponges, and most of the skills are useless. There is an open world, yet there is no exploration - you just mark objectives on your map and navigate to them afterward. There are several layers of leveling systems, yet nothing excites you about leveling up - you just kill damage sponges faster.The story is not bad, and the humor is... Well, it's there, but basically, the story of the game is a big Manzai of Zeus (who plays "funny" (a.k.a. cringe) man) and Prometheus (who plays the straight man). It can be really funny sometimes, but most of the time, it's just mediocre stand-up. There are also other guys, but in their cases, it's even worse...Overall, I would give the game 6/10. It could have been around 7.5/10 if the game were shorter and more focused, but I just felt really, really tired at the end. Maybe worth checking out, but that's it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's your typical Ubisoft game. Massive open world full of pointless busy work only now it's combined with the annoyance of the stupid puzzles from the last couple of Zelda games.Stamina is a big deal as you need it for attacks, swimming, jumping, gliding etc. How do you level your stamina? You have to do these 'rifts' (think Zelda temples only more annoying) full of jumping, gliding, moving blocks and shooting puzzles. Then you get a 'lightning bolt of Zeus' at the end. The fun part is each stamina bar requires multiple bolts to upgrade on an ever increasing scale.The jumping puzzles would only rate as annoying if the keyboard controls weren't utter dog sh*te. Want to double jump? Yeah, good luck with the game responding to you on a very random basis. This makes the jumping crap utterly frustrating at times. The same can be said for the dodging controls....one option is a double tap of the direction button but the game just fails to respond to this on a regular basis making those 'flashing red attacks' unavoidable. (It is NOT my KB as both by corsair and razor KB get the same results).Want to upgrade your weapons to d a bit more damage? Yeah, you need red and blue crystals. Blue are fairly easy to get by killing mobs or opening chests. The red come from specific types of chests and the very rare outcropping in the overworld. But you need LOADS of the damn things and the upgrades just feel so MEH....it might turn a 30 shot enemy into a 25 shot one......Want to open the map up? Climb a statue and gave from the top with a 'vision' setting that allows you to scan the map pixel by pixel to highlight points of interest. It's just another innovation free Ubisoft radio tower..WARNING FOR HIGH END CPU USERS:: The game starts with an unlocked frame rate. Your CPU WILL say "hold my beer!" and boost itself to maximum frequency to see how many FPS it can achieve. mY I7 13700kf PEAKED AT 260FPS before I realised and limited the fps to that of my monitor in the game settings. _childDocuments_.review: A college recommended this game to me, and just the day after, it was available on Steam for a good price so I bought it. Sweet coincidence.The game itself is really great, it is an open world game with a number of different riddles and enemies everywhere. You have a couple different fighting styles which you can switch between, but you should probably pick one to upgrade first. Speaking of upgrades, there are a bunch of them, and it feels very rewarding to collect all the loot in the world and use it for upgrades and potions afterwards, probably my favorite aspect of the game. Story wise it has a humorous spin on Greek mythology which I enjoy, gave me a chuckle more than once.^^ Now to some points others are critical about:- No achievements on steam is a small downside for achievement hunters like myself, but in the big picture it is not a big deal. I still enjoy grinding for the achievements and challenges.- Ubisoft Store: You can buy a bunch of different Skins with micro transactions. But since you get a tons of skin by just playing the game itself, I was never tempted to spend any money there. So no downside for me either but good for the people who enjoy the skins. :) You can also slowly grind some currency by doing daily challenges and hope to get the skin you want in the weekly rotation but while the challenges are fun by themselves it won't probably be enough to get the skin you want before you are finished with the game. But again, no downside for me since that's not important to me. And if you are really annoyed by all of that, just start the game in offline mode on ubisoft connect to remove all store related things.All in all this is a great game and you should give it a real chance.
